Field-to-Test Loop: how the whole system works, how errors are found, and the methods it uses

A computer talks to its storage drive (the SSD) over a wire. A capture tool sits on that wire and records every packet. It saves a table file (CSV) with 113 columns. Stage 1 reads that file. It finds each error and pins down where it starts and which side caused it. Stage 2 takes that error and makes it happen again on purpose. It then turns it into a test file that a computer can run, once the admin approves it. Stage 2 looks up the knowledge base first and gives what it finds to the AI (RAG). The admin's decisions are the learning signal. No AI model is trained.

0. What the project asked for, and how this work does it

Why this part is here: The project statement lists what must be built. This table shows where each item is in this document and whether it is done.

A few words used everywhere below. PCIe is the set of rules for sending packets on the wire (the PCIe rules). NVMe is the set of rules the SSD uses for its commands (the NVMe rules). The official rule books for both are called specifications.

The project statement is in docs/project_statement.html. It asks for steps, driven by an AI, that do five things. They find a defect from a recording of the PCIe wire. They start a learning-by-trying search from the AI's suggested steps. They reward the search when the same error fingerprint appears again. They turn the most stressful conditions into tests a computer can run. They keep a knowledge base that makes the next repeat faster. docs/REQUIREMENTS_TRACEABILITY.md maps the statement sentence by sentence, with proof. This table is the summary.

1. The whole system as one picture

Why this part is here: It shows every step from the recording to the test file in one view.

The user gives the path of a recording. Stage 1 reads it once, from start to end. It finds every error it can prove. Stage 2 takes each found error and looks it up in the knowledge base. It suggests, or recalls, the order and timing of commands that make the error happen again. The admin decides. Then the lab searches and checks that the error really happens again. Then a test is filed. Every admin decision is saved as an event in the knowledge base. It changes what is looked up, and in which order, the next time.

485known errors in the error list
437 / 485found from the packets alone
483 / 485with the computer's logs added
0false alarms in normal traffic
0AI models trained or changed

What can go in. The Run step takes two kinds of input. The first is the table file from a PCIe capture tool. That is the Teledyne-LeCroy file with 113 columns, or a VIAVI file once its column names are matched. The second is a saved result file from a work run (workload-result artifact). One such file is the stage1.json made by the boot_etl ADK steps (Fast-Startup). Any JSON file in the general shape described in app/workload_import.py also works (PCMark 10 and other runners). The unusual results in such a file become the run's errors. Each gets an error fingerprint. It holds what was measured, what was seen against the normal value (baseline), the phase and the part. Stage 2 looks them up and writes the starting scenario. It files that as a proposed test for the hardware test machine. The reason is that a Windows start-up cannot run on the practice test machine made of software.

2. The packet: what one line (row) of the table file (CSV) holds

Why this part is here: Every check in this document reads these lines. So you need to know what one line holds, and why only some columns are read.

The capture tool (Teledyne LeCroy) sits on the wire (link) between the computer and the SSD. A packet is one small message sent across the wire. The tool records every packet. It saves a table file (CSV) with one line per packet. The file has 113 columns. A column is one kind of detail about each packet. Most columns are empty on most lines. This is because each kind of packet fills in only its own columns. The checker program (the app screens call it "the analyser") reads 57 of the 113 columns.

2.1 Why only 57 of the 113 columns are read

Why this part is here: A reader will ask why 56 columns are left out. This table answers that for every group of columns.

The other 56 columns are not used, for the reasons in the last column below. The facts come from three places. The first is 10_defect_isolation_engine/PRODUCTION_READINESS.md section 2. The second is the list of 57 column names in stage1/pcie_isolate/schema.py. The third is the column list in the error list (section XII.2).

GroupColumns readColumns not readWhy the unread ones are not needed
Every lineMarker, Packet, Link Dir, Time Stamp (4)Time Delta (1)Time Delta is only the gap between two neighbouring lines. In this test recording it is the gap to the next line. The error list says some capture tools write the gap from the line above instead. It also changes when the capture tool hides lines. The checker works out every gap from Time Stamp, which means the same thing in every export.
Kind of lineOrd.Set Type, DLLP Type, TLP Type, Link Event, Jammer Phase, Action, CXL Pkt Type (7)Jammer Target Packet, Jammer Result Packet (2)The checker only needs to know that the capture tool broke a packet on purpose. Which packet it aimed at is not needed to judge the SSD.
Wire-training signalsTS Link, TS Lane, Training Control, TS Data Rate, TS Gen3 Eq Control, TS Gen3 Pre-Cursor, TS Gen3 Cursor, TS Gen3 Post-Cursor (8)N_FTS (1)N_FTS is about a fast wake-up from a power-saving state. None of the 167 checks uses it.
Small receipt packetsPSN, AckNak Seq Num, HdrFC, DataFC, Feature Support, CRC 16 (6)VC ID, HdrScale, DataScale, Feature Ack (4)An NVMe SSD uses only one channel on the wire. So the channel number (VC ID) is always the same. The two "Scale" columns only matter for very large credit amounts. Feature Ack repeats what Feature Support already shows.
Head of a request or data packetTC, TH, TD, EP, Attributes, AT, Length, RequesterID, Tag, CompleterID, Address, DeviceID, Register, st BE, Last BE (15)LN, NW (2)These two belong to features an NVMe SSD does not use.
Answers and messagesCpl Status, Byte Cnt, BCM, Lwr Addr, Msg Routing, Message Code (6)noneAll are read.
Power and timing messagesScale (Snoop), Value (Snoop), Scale (No-Snoop), Value (No-Snoop), PTM Propagation Delay (5)Snoop, Requirement (Snoop), No-Snoop, Requirement (No-Snoop), PTM Master Time[63:32], PTM Master Time[31:0], PMUX Channel ID, PMUX Metadata (8)The checker reads the delay numbers it needs. The flag columns repeat what the numbers already say. Clock-sharing times (PTM master time) and the PMUX columns belong to other features. An NVMe SSD does not use them for its work.
Bytes and check numbersLCRC, ECRC, DATA (3)noneAll are read. DATA holds the NVMe commands themselves.
Side management wire (SMBus)ARP Command, Slave Address, PEC (3)20 columns (Target Address, Vendor ID, UDID Version, …)These describe a second, slow management wire, not the main wire. The checker only needs to know that this traffic happened.
CXLnone18 columns (OpCode, MESI, Poison, …)CXL is a different kind of device (memory and accelerators) that can share the same wire. An NVMe SSD does not use it.
Total5756

Four columns must be present: Packet, Time Stamp, Link Dir and TLP Type. If one is missing, the checker stops with a clear message. If any other column is missing, the checker treats it as empty and carries on.

There are no NVMe columns at all. The NVMe commands and their done notes are hidden inside the DATA column, as bytes. The checker reads those bytes to find them.

2.2 The kinds of line, and the order the checker sorts them in

Why this part is here: Each line must be read as the right kind. Otherwise a check would judge it wrongly. This part says how the kind is chosen and why in this order.

Every line is one of these kinds, checked in this fixed order:

  1. a packet the capture tool broke on purpose (Jammer)
  2. CXL traffic
  3. side-wire traffic (SMBus)
  4. a request or data packet (TLP)
  5. a small receipt packet (DLLP)
  6. a wire-training signal (ordered set)
  7. a wire event (link event)
  8. a note the capture tool added (marker)

The checker looks at the columns in that order. It stops at the first one that is filled in. Why this order: one line can have more than one of these columns filled in. A packet the capture tool broke on purpose also has a TLP Type. So the "broken on purpose", CXL and side-wire checks come first. Then such lines are never mistaken for normal SSD traffic. The order comes from the error list, section XII.1.1 ("a minimal row classifier").

The table below shows which columns mark each kind, and what each kind tells the checker's notes.

Kind of lineColumns that mark itWhat it tells the checker's notes
Wire-training signal (ordered set)Ord.Set Type (TS1, TS2, EIEOS, SKP, EIOS, SDS…)the start-up steps of the wire (link training, LTSSM). The speed and the number of lanes the two sides agree on. When the wire goes quiet to save power (electrical idle).
Small receipt packet (DLLP)DLLP Type (Ack, Nak, InitFC, UpdateFC, PM_…), AckNak Seq Num, CRC 16"arrived fine" receipts (Ack) and "arrived broken, send again" receipts (Nak). Sending the same packet again (replay). How much room each side has (flow-control credits). The power-saving hand-shake.
Request or data packet (TLP)TLP Type (MRd, MWr, CfgRd0/Wr0, Cpl, CplD, Msg…), Link Dir, PSN, RequesterID, Tag, Address, Length, Byte Cnt, Cpl Status, LCRC, ECRC, EP, TC, Attr, DATA…every request and its answer (completion). Every doorbell. Every command the SSD fetches (SQE). Every data move. Every done note (CQE). Every "work is done" signal (interrupt). Every read or write of the SSD's settings area (configuration space).
Wire event (link event)Link Event (Link Down, Link Up, speed change, CLKREQ#, PERST#…)restarts (resets). The wire dropping without warning (surprise down). The side signals for power (power sideband).
Capture-tool note (marker)Marker (Buffer Wrap, Trigger, Segment, Resync, filter notes)whether the recording itself is complete. Across a gap in the recording, a missing packet proves nothing.
TimeTime Stamp (in steps of 125 ps), Time Delta (points to the next row)every timer. The time limit for an answer (completion timeout). The timer for sending a packet again (replay timer). The SSD's promised ready time (CAP.TO). The wake-up time after deep sleep (D3hot recovery). How long a command takes (command latency).

2.3 The direction column says which side is at fault

Why this part is here: Spotting an error is not enough. The reader must also know which side caused it, and this column is how the checker tells.

Link Dir = Downstream means the computer sent the packet (from its root port). Upstream means the SSD sent it. One NVMe command is always the same chain of seven packets. Each step belongs to one side. So the first step that is wrong or missing names the side at fault.

StepPacket (name in the file)Sent byWhat that side must get right
①the computer writes the new end of the command list to the doorbell (MWr SQ tail doorbell)the computer (Downstream)the computer: the value is smaller than the list size, and the list exists
②the SSD asks for the new command (MRd SQE fetch)the SSD (Upstream)the SSD: it must fetch what the doorbell announced
③the answer that carries the 64-byte command (CplD with the 64-byte SQE)the computer (Downstream)the computer or its board (platform): the fields are valid, and it arrives in time
④the data moves, to or from the addresses in the address list (MRd/MWr to PRPs)the SSD (Upstream)the SSD
⑤the 16-byte done note (MWr 16-byte CQE)the SSD (Upstream)the SSD: one done note per command, with the right command number (CID), list number (SQID) and result (status)
⑥the "work is done" signal (MWr MSI-X)the SSD (Upstream)the SSD: it uses the signal number (vector) the done list was made with
⑦the computer writes to the done list's doorbell (MWr CQ head doorbell)the computer (Downstream)the computer: it takes the done note

3. How an error is spotted from the packets

Why this part is here: This is the heart of stage 1. It shows how the checker goes from single packets to one named error.

Stage 1 reads the file once, one line at a time, from start to end (streaming). While it reads, it keeps notes about each side (see the table below). It writes a broken-rule note when something breaks one of the 167 checks. It can be one packet or a run of packets. It can be the bytes inside a packet, or a count far from normal. Section 3.1 says where the checks come from. Broken-rule notes that belong together are grouped into one problem. Each problem gets four things. It gets its first bad line, and a split into the start and the follow-on breaks. It also gets the side that caused it, and one entry from the error list.

Why the checker keeps notes, and what they are

Why this part is here: Older documents said the checker "keeps the protocol state of both ends". This part says what that means in plain words.

The capture tool sees both directions on the wire. The direction column says who sent each packet. One packet alone rarely proves anything. An answer is only wrong if nobody asked for it. A command is only lost if the SSD took it and never said it was done. So the checker must remember what happened before. For each side, it keeps notes of what that side has sent and what it is still waiting for. These notes are what older text called "protocol state". The list below comes from stage1/pcie_isolate/engine.py.

Notes aboutWhat the checker writes downWhat it can then catch
the wire itselfis the wire up or down, how fast, how many lanesthe wire slowing down, the wire restarting again and again
receipts, for each directionthe last packet number sent, which packets have no receipt yet, how many times a packet was sent againa packet number that jumps, a packet sent 4 times and still broken, a receipt that comes too late
credits, for each directionhow much room each side said it hasone side stops making room, traffic gets stuck
requests and answersevery open request, by request number (Tag), with its time and expected sizean answer that never came in time, an answer nobody asked for, a wrong size
the SSD's settings areathe SSD's address, its on/off switches, its power state and when that changed, its time-limit settingthe computer talking to the SSD while it is asleep or still restarting
the SSD's main settings (NVMe registers)is the SSD switched on, is it ready, how long it said it may take to get readythe SSD not getting ready in its own promised time, a fatal-error flag
command lists (queues)where each list is, how long it is, where the computer and the SSD are in ita doorbell number that points past the end of the list
each commandwhen it was sent and when the SSD took it. What it asked for and how much data moved. Its done note and result.a command that never finished, two commands with the same number, a done note for an unknown command
"work done" signalswhich signal belongs to which done list, which done notes still wait for a signala missing signal, a signal on the wrong number
dataa check number for the data last written to each blockdata read back that is not what was written

The checker learns all these notes from the recording itself. For example, it learns the SSD's address from the packet that set it. This is why a recording should start when the computer starts. If it starts in the middle, the checker says so. It does not blame anything it could not have known.

Why this part is here: It says where the 167 checks come from, and what each kind needs to read.

Where the 167 checks come from. They were written for this project. They use the error list and the PCIe and NVMe rule books. No rule book contains a list called "167 rules". They split like this:

Why there were no false alarms. Two things give the zero false alarms. First, the 98 checks that are clear breaks of a rule-book rule. Second, limits read from the recording itself, not guessed. These limits are the answer time range, CAP.TO and the largest packet sizes (MPS/MRRS). They come from Device Control 2, the CAP register and settings writes. The 47 "unusual or slow" checks never decide a defect alone. In 20.7 million lines of normal traffic, no problem was opened.

3.2 From broken-rule notes to one found error

Why this part is here: Many notes can point to one error. This part shows how they become one problem with one start, one side and one entry.

  1. Grouping. Some notes share a number. It can be a request number (Tag) or a command number (CID). It can be a range of packet numbers (PSN) or a command list. Others sit inside one time window. Such notes form one problem. Some checks are of the CONTEXT level, such as a normal restart or a normal action by the computer. These are attached as background, not as defects.
  2. The first bad line. The earliest DEFECT note is the start of the problem. Some later notes come from a check that is a known after-effect. Examples are a Nak after a bad LCRC, a resend after a Nak, and a stop after a timeout. These are marked as follow-on breaks. So the admin reads the cause, not its echo.
  3. Deciding which side caused it. Rules R1–R12 (the table in HOW_DEFECTS_ARE_DETECTED.html) choose between the computer, the SSD, the wire, the platform and the test set-up. They use Link Dir and the first step in the command's life that is wrong or missing.
  4. Error list entry. The problem's list of broken checks is compared with stored fingerprints. The comparison measures how alike two lists of numbers are (cosine). The fingerprints were learned from two calibration recordings. The result is multiplied by a weight for each error family (P01…P27 wire patterns). The best match becomes the entry. The next two form the look-alike group. On the 4 GB recording, 483 errors were found. For 387 of them the right entry came first, and for 442 it was in the first three.
  5. Proof lines. The lines from 15 before the first bad line to 15 after the last one are stored with the problem. The AI reviewer and the admin both see exactly these lines.

4. How the 485 errors come about, and which rule book says each one is wrong

Why this part is here: It shows the kinds of error and how many of each are found. It also names the rule book for each.

The error list names 485 kinds of defect in ten chapters. For each one, three things exist. The generator program can place one copy of it into a recording it makes. The detection document (08_defect_detection_spec) says which lines prove it. The checker's checks carry out that proof. The NVMe rule books are NVM Express Base 2.4, NVMe over PCIe Transport 1.4, NVM Command Set 1.3 and NVMe-MI. The PCIe ones are the rules of PCI Express Base 6/7. The computer-side time limits are those of Linux v7.2.

The two that stay unsolved. M-031 (chapter M, entry 31) is a short fatal-error flag (Controller Fatal Status). The computer never read it while it was set. P-01 (chapter P, entry 1) is speed lower than the wire allows. No packet breaks a rule. Proving it needs a known normal speed of the same system.

5. The computer's logs, the AI reviewer's check, and the saved AI answers

Why this part is here: Some errors cannot be proved from the wire alone. Every found error also gets a second opinion. This part explains both.

The computer's logs (for the ~46 entries the wire does not show)

Sometimes the wire shows only a sign of the error: a gap, a restart, or a new wire training. Then the computer's record of the same moment names the cause. These records are Linux kernel log lines (dmesg -x) and tool records. The tools are nvme-cli logs, fio verify, the board manager (BMC), the fabric and the capture tool's settings. The records are lined up in time with moments both sides see. For example, a write of CC.EN=0 on the wire matches the log line "resetting controller". They are then placed on the packet timeline and added as tier-H notes. For each error, the admin's full-record page answers three questions. Was outside evidence needed? Which source did it come from? Why does that source prove it?

The AI reviewer's check (Claude Haiku 5.5, effort low)

The AI reviewer is an AI program that reads the same packets and says agree, disagree or not sure. For each problem it gets only the proof lines (X−15…Y+15), the broken-rule notes and the three candidate entries. It must answer in a fixed form (a JSON schema). The answer holds its verdict (CONFIRMED, NOT_CONFIRMED or INCONCLUSIVE). It also holds the entry, the side that caused it, and which checks it agrees or disagrees with. It names packets, gives its ideas, and says what it would still need. The program checks that every packet it names was really shown to it. The AI can agree or disagree. It never creates an error. On the 4 GB recording it checked 88 problems. It agreed with 51 and was not sure about 36. For 1 it agreed with the start but disagreed about one follow-on detail. No disagreement was left open.

Saved AI answers (the pattern, or verdict, cache)

Each saved answer has a key. The key is a fingerprint of these details: sha256(card, first-abnormal rule, failure pattern, layer, set of rule ids, sequence of evidence-row kinds, model id, prompt version). A later problem with the same key gets the saved answer. The proof packets in it are pointed to the new problem's own lines. It is marked backend = pattern-cache. The AI is not called. Measured: a second run of the same recording needed 0 calls (3 of 3 came from saved answers). Stage 1 went from 53 s to 14.5 s. A new AI model, or a new message sent to it, changes the key. So an out-of-date answer is never reused.

6. The knowledge base: what the AI is given to read (RAG)

Why this part is here: Stage 2 learns only by adding to this knowledge base. So this part shows what it stores.

Looking up the knowledge base first, then giving what was found to the AI, is called RAG (retrieval-augmented generation). Here it means this. The AI never answers from its own memory about this SSD. It is given what the knowledge base holds about this error. That is the stored steps, approved examples from the same chapter, lessons and the check. It also gets the proof lines. The admin's decisions change what the knowledge base gives back next time. Today the knowledge base is a SQLite file. Its table design also works on PostgreSQL. Every change is added as a new event at the end of a log (event-sourced). All tables are built from that log and can be rebuilt from it. So any decision can be undone exactly.

Sets of steps are stored in two places. The steps box (scenario node) holds the plan: the steps, the timing and the power state. It also holds the success counts gathered across all causes. The REPRODUCED_BY link holds how the plan was run for one cause. That is the steps as run, plus the admin's changes from revise. It holds that cause's own counts. The look-up uses both.

7. Looking up the knowledge base for a new problem (retrieval)

Why this part is here: This is how stage 2 finds what it already knows about a new error.

The search question is built from the stage-1 problem. It uses the entry, the error family and the first broken check. It uses the layer, the side it came from and the verdict. It also uses a fingerprint of the SSD program (firmware context hash), detail words and free text (titles and details). Last, it uses the order of line kinds around the first bad line (TLP, DLLP and ordered-set types). The things searched are the fingerprints, past cases, causes, solutions (with their fingerprints) and lessons. Their search index is updated a little at a time, whenever new events are added.

The formula block below is the exact rule. In plain words, each line does this:

LineWhat it does
structDo the stored item's fields match? The same entry counts 1.0. Only the same family counts 0.5. Agreement on check, layer, side and verdict adds up to 0.25. The same SSD program adds 0.25.
bm25How many of the same words appear, with rare words counting more (Okapi BM25).
triHow alike the free text is, in groups of three letters (character trigrams).
rowsHow alike the order of packet kinds is, starting at the first bad line (longest common subsequence).
denseA comparison by meaning. It is off by default, because no such model runs offline.
fusedThe five rankings are mixed into one score (reciprocal rank fusion).
finalThe mixed score is scaled by the admin's counts (m) and the admin's ordering (pl). The square root keeps this gentle. Feedback can swap near-equal items. It cannot lift an item that does not match.
slotsPlaces 1 to 4 are the best final scores. Place 5 tries something less proven. It is a random draw among items with fused ≥ 0.4 and fewer than 5 judgements (Thompson sample).
struct(d) = 1.0·[card equal] | 0.5·[family equal] + 0.25·(rule, layer, origin, verdict agree)/4 + 0.25·[context equal] bm25(d) = Okapi BM25 (k1 = 1.2, b = 0.75) over field-prefixed tokens (card:T-42, rule:CFG.D0_EARLY, k:CplD, w:d3hot …), inverted index tri(d) = cosine over hashed character trigrams of the free text (2^18 buckets) rows(d) = position-weighted longest common subsequence over evidence-row kinds (anchor = first abnormal row) dense(d) = optional sentence-embedding cosine (off by default: no model offline) fused(d) = Σ_c w_c / (60 + rank_c(d)) normalised so rank 1 on every channel = 1.0 w = struct 1.0 · bm25 1.0 · tri 0.7 · rows 0.7 · dense 0.7 final(d) = fused(d) · sqrt(0.5 + 0.5·m(d)) · exp(0.5·tanh(pl(d))) m = Beta posterior mean a/(a+b) of the candidate's live counts (cause edge, or procedure edge + node) pl = Plackett-Luce rating from the admin's rankings sqrt = tempering: feedback re-orders near-ties, it cannot promote a dissimilar candidate slots 1–4 = top by final; slot 5 = exploration: Thompson sample among candidates with fused ≥ 0.4 and n < 5

Seen before? The answer comes from the best stored set of steps. match means the entry and the situation are the same. Also fused ≥ 0.70, and at least two of the four field checks agree. Then the stored steps apply. ambiguous means one of three things. It is the same entry in another situation or showing in another way. Or it is the same family. Or the lines are very alike. Then the stored steps are changed to fit, never replayed blindly. new means anything else. Then new steps are made from the proof lines. The admin's card shows this answer in plain words. It shows the stored steps next to the AI's proposal. The stored steps come with their approval, lowest repeat rate, admin score and tests. The card also shows the top 5, with the reason each was shown.

The AI's two jobs in stage 2. (1) A short summary for the admin. It names the packets that decide the case. It explains how the error works in two sentences. It says whether the stored steps apply. It gives the smallest order and timing of commands the proof supports. It lists differences from the stored steps, and the risks. All of this comes in a fixed form (JSON schema). The program checks that named packets exist, commands are allowed and timings are in range. (2) The starting point for the search, when nothing is stored. The AI never changes the status of an item in the solution list.

8. How the system learns from the admin: learning by counting, in plain words and exactly

Why this part is here: The project asks for learning from the admin's decisions. This part shows exactly what each decision changes, and nothing else.

In one paragraph. Nothing is trained for this. The system keeps a score card for every item it can show. An item is a possible cause of an error. Or it is a set of steps that makes the error happen again (the order and timing of commands). Each admin decision on the screen is one observation. It changes the score of exactly the item that was judged, and nothing else. When the same error appears again, the items are ranked by their scores. One place is kept for trying something less proven. The best stored steps are run first in the lab, before anything new is searched. Every decision is an event in a log that is only ever added to. Any decision can be undone, and the scores are then rebuilt from the log. This is learning by counting (online learning, the bandit family of reinforcement learning). It is not model training. It needs tens of decisions, not thousands. The manager can read every number.

8.1 The learning loop

Why this part is here: It shows the path from a found error to a changed score, and back.

8.2 Which methods are used, by name

Why this part is here: Each method has a technical name. This table says in plain words what each one does here, and in which file it runs.

MethodWhat it does hereWhere it runs
Counting successes and failures, with a random draw to give less-proven items a chance (Beta–Bernoulli bandit, Thompson sampling)Every cause and every set of steps carries a belief Beta(a, b) that "this is right". A success adds 1 to a. A failure adds 1 to b. The score is the mean a/(a+b). For the trial place, the system draws a random number from each item's Beta and shows the winner. So a newer item with few observations still gets its chance. This is the "C2 Beta-count" method that won the comparison of 15 implementations (section 12).kgdb.py (cause links), procgraph.py (steps boxes and links), retrieval_v3.py (trial place)
Only the judged item changes (localised credit assignment)Only the item the admin judged changes. "Not correct" on a set of steps does not punish its cause. The items he did not touch are never punished. This choice kept the ranking steady in the comparison. There, the method "blame everything shown" broke down.admin_actions.py → verdict / proc_credit events
Learning from the admin's order (Plackett–Luce listwise rating, stochastic gradient, η = 0.3)When the admin drags cards into an order, the system learns the order, not a success. The rating pl of each item moves a small step. The step makes this order more likely (the gradient of the Plackett–Luce likelihood). Ratings only tilt the ranking, by a factor e^{0.5·tanh(pl)}. They can never make an unproven item look proven.procgraph.py proc_rank, kgdb.py ranking
Older evidence fades, with an upper limit (discounting + cap, non-stationary bandit)On every verdict for an error, all its counts move 2 % back toward the starting values (γ = 0.02). The sum a+b is capped at 50. So newer evidence counts more. A long-approved item can still be overturned by a few new decisions.kgdb.py verdict rebuild, _credit
A change of situation (context shift)A change of SSD program (firmware) halves all evidence, because the SSD changed. Editing the text of a cause shrinks its evidence ×0.7 and keeps the mean. The claim changed, but its history did not vanish.firmware_change, node_edit events
Two kinds of truthTwo questions are counted apart. "Could it be made to happen in the lab" uses ta, tb. "Is it the right cause" uses a, b. Not reproducible raises only tb. A set of steps can be right and still hard to repeat.verdict "lab"
A second counting method in the lab (section 9)The search picks which kind of change (mutation operator) to try next. It draws from each kind's Beta counts of "it got better" (Thompson sampling). It restarts from a saved good spot (a Go-Explore archive cell). It accepts a candidate only when its lowest likely hit rate is at least 0.5. (That is the Wilson 95 % lower bound.)optimizer.py
PPO can be chosen as a search option (section 9.1). No AI language model is trained or changed. DQN is not used.For the admin's feedback, the signal is a few dozen decisions per error. So it is learned by counting. The 2 GB comparison showed that the counting methods reach the goal more reliably from an empty knowledge base. A table-based learner (tabular Q-learning) scored lower. For the search, the setting stage2.optimizer = "ppo" picks another method. It learns a small choosing rule during one search (a clipped-surrogate policy gradient). The default is the counting method, which needs no training. The AI only reads proof and makes suggestions. No AI language model is trained or changed anywhere in the project.ppo_optimizer.py (option)

8.3 What each button on the manager's screen does to the knowledge base

Why this part is here: The admin's buttons are the only way the system learns. This table shows exactly what each one changes.

Words used in the table. The cause link joins an error to one of its causes. The steps link joins a cause to one set of steps. The steps box is the set of steps itself. The letter a counts "right" and b counts "wrong". The letters ta and tb count lab successes and lab failures. The letter r is the result of one judgement: 1 for success, 0 for failure.

ButtonRecorded actionExact changeWhat the manager notices next time
Correctaccept on the stored steps (or on the cause in the AI's proposal)On the cause link: a ← a+1 and ta ← ta+1. On the steps link and steps box: r = 1 (a+1). The lab then runs the steps again (repeat check, 6 runs). If the error still happens, the steps are reused with 0 search tries and the test file is written.These steps are ranked first and run first for this error. They show "judged +1".
Needs changes → Save corrected versionadd_procedure with the edited order or timingA new steps box is made as proposed, under the same cause. The manager is recorded as its author. It is run first. If the error happens, it becomes validated-by-execution. After the second admin, it becomes admin-approved. The old version is linked by SUPERSEDES and keeps its history. The old version is not punished.His version shows first, with its own lab numbers. The stored one drops to "superseded".
Not correct (+ reason) on stored stepsreject on those stepsOn that steps link and steps box: b ← b+1. The cause is not touched. The reason is saved with the event. It shows as "earlier marked not correct by …".It ranks lower. The next admin sees the warning and the reason.
Not correct (+ reason) on the AI's new proposallesson (note "NOT CORRECT: …")Nothing stored was judged, so no count changes. A lesson is written under the cause. It goes into the next message to the AI for this error. The history shows a "no" decision with the reason.The AI is told what was wrong. Stored knowledge keeps its scores.
Not correct + "also retire from the database"deprecate (two people)Refused unless the approver is a different person from the requester. Then the status becomes deprecated, and a failure is counted on the steps box.It no longer shows as a stored solution.
Record failed trial (−1) and restart (after a search found nothing)restart_failedThis is the "no" answer (Negative Ack) in the project diagram. For a cause: b ← b+1 on the cause link, so its ranking weight goes down. Also tb ← tb+1 (lab count). For a set of steps: r = 0 on the steps link. A lesson "FAILED TRIAL" is written. The search restarts on the next random sequence (attempt counter).The next try searches in a different way. The failure is in the history.
Sweep the neighbourhoodsweepNo weights change. Changed versions near the error that make it fail are proposed and checked (made by sweep). They are filed as tests and never approved automatically.The risky areas around the error have tests.
Drag to rank / Move to toprerankOnly the Plackett–Luce ratings change. The counts a, b and n stay the same. (Checked in the live exercise: a 4.88 = 4.88, n 4 = 4.)The order changes. No item looks more proven.
UndoundoThe event is marked undone, and every table is rebuilt from the log. This reverses it exactly (checked: deprecated → undo → admin-approved).As if the decision had not happened.

The same rules, written as formulas:

prior Beta(a=1, b=1) on every new edge/node accept (chosen) a ← a + 1 on the chosen cause edge, the procedure edge and the procedure node (success on the whole chosen path) reject (x) b ← b + 1 on the rejected item ONLY. Items the admin did not touch are never punished revise content gets a new version; (a,b) ← 1 + (a−1)·0.7, 1 + (b−1)·0.7 (evidence shrunk, mean kept, no credit) not_reproducible tb ← tb + 1 (lab counts). "could not reproduce" ≠ "wrong": a, b untouched rerank / prefer Plackett-Luce: for i in order: for m ≥ i: pl_m += η·((1−p_m) if m = i else −p_m)/K, p_m = e^{pl_m}/Σ_{j≥i} e^{pl_j}, η = 0.3 rankings never count as successes decay on every verdict for a signature, all its edges: (a,b) ← 1 + (a−1)(1−γ), 1 + (b−1)(1−γ), γ = 0.02 cap if a + b > 50: scale both to 50 (evidence stops growing; a few new signals can still move it) firmware change all evidence halved: (a,b) ← 1 + (a−1)/2, 1 + (b−1)/2 (old situation, new SSD program) merge (duplicate_of) the kept item gets the union of raw counts; steps re-pointed; both histories stay in the log promote / deprecate / delete_approve need approver ≠ requester (two people); otherwise the server refuses undo the event is marked undone and every table is rebuilt from the log → exact reversal

8.4 How the scores are used: where the learning shows up

Why this part is here: Counting is useful only if it changes what the admin sees. This part names the four places where it does.

  • Ranking of stored items (look-up, section 7). Each item's text and structure match is mixed into one score (reciprocal-rank fusion). It is then scaled by its score card: final = fused × √(0.5 + 0.5·a/(a+b)) × e^{0.5·tanh(pl)}. A set of steps judged correct three times ranks above an equally alike one judged wrong. A dragged order tilts near-ties. The last place shown is a random draw (Thompson sample) from the remaining items, to try something less proven.
  • The "seen before?" answer. A repeat is a match only when entry and situation agree in structure (fused ≥ 0.70 and struct ≥ 1.375). Then the stored steps are run first (repeat check). They are reused with no search (live: 0 tries, 26 s to check). Otherwise the answer is adapt (the stored steps are the starting point for the search) or new.
  • What is shown. The AI's suggested order of the items is mixed with the knowledge base's ranking by adding up places (Borda count). The AI can tilt the order, but can never override the counts.
  • The lab search. Within one search, the search program learns which kind of change works better for this error. Kinds of change include a timing nudge, adding a command, a swap and mixing two candidates (crossover). Approved examples from the same failure family are extra starting points.
Live numbers for error T-42 (chapter T, timeouts, entry 42). Read from db/knowledge.sqlite after the exercise, through the knowledge base's interface.
cause c0 link: a = 7.23, b = 1.00, n = 12, ta = 12, tb = 4 → score 0.88. This is after the two exercise runs and the browser test.
steps 755341… admin-approved by second_admin. 800 µs between commands. Made the error happen in at least 61 % of runs. 4 tests on file.
steps 93d32f… (400 µs) and 074e18… (200 µs) superseded. The SUPERSEDES chain is kept, and their evidence stays.
steps a71680… (the manager's 1600 µs version from the browser test) failed-validation: 0 of 6 lab runs. The lab searched from it instead.
How a score moves (one cause, using the exact rules above)
start Beta(1, 1) → score 0.50
Correct → (2.00, 1.00) → 0.67
Correct → (2.98, 1.00) → 0.75 (2 % fade first, then +1)
Not correct → (2.94, 2.00) → 0.60
Not reproducible → a, b only fade (2.90, 1.98) → 0.59; tb 1 → 2
Drag to rank → a, b unchanged; the rating pl moves
Undo of the "Not correct" → the log is replayed without it → (2.94, 1.00) → 0.75

Where every number comes from. Each limit, formula and fixed number used above and in sections 9 and 10 is listed in docs/PROVENANCE_AUDIT.md. For each, it gives the kind of source and the checked references. There are eight kinds of source. A part of a rule book. A value the SSD reports about itself. A choice of the computer's software. A modelled value. A maths rule. A research paper. A rule from the user. An engineering choice. The from-scratch run of the package that can be mailed is in docs/VERIFICATION_FROM_SCRATCH.md.

8.6 What testing found, and what was fixed

Why this part is here: It lists every fault the tests found. So the reader can see what was wrong before, and how it was fixed.

  1. "Seen before" was too easy to pass. Another way of showing the same entry (another check, another layer) was treated as a match. The stored steps were reused. Fix: a match now needs agreement in structure (entry + situation + fields, struct ≥ 1.375 and fused ≥ 0.70). Otherwise the screen says "DIFFERENT MANIFESTATION", and the stored steps are only a starting point for the search. The repeat check runs only when the accepted steps belong to the same entry.
  2. The "must stay quiet" test could pass by accident. This test runs on the fixed SSD program. There, a decoy entry's second-place candidate was counted as "found". Fix: the lab check demands that the entry is the top-1 CONFIRMED result (isolated_top1). A decoy neighbour is always present in the fixed-program traffic.
  3. Connection errors with the AI were saved as answers. Fix: an error is never written to the saved answers. There is one retry. The command-line call with a fixed answer form needs --max-turns 3.
  4. Blame went to the wrong place, but in the test, not in the system. Check C7 expected that "reject on stored steps" would blame its cause. The system blamed only the steps, which is how it is meant to work. The check was corrected. The design was kept.
  5. The look-up rebuilt its search index on every question. This was slow on the 2 GB comparison. The fingerprint also lacked the check field. Fix: the index is updated a little at a time, per fingerprint. The fingerprint now has all its fields.
  6. Made pytest files did not run on their own. There were three faults. JSON words (true/null) were used inside Python. A conftest path assumed the project's folder layout. Two tests of one entry had the same file name. Fix: Python words, a path search upward to the test-machine module, and files named by test id. Now 24/24 run as plain pytest.
  7. Recordings with a single entry were not solved by the checker, so the lab check could not close. Cause: the generator wrote DATA with sizes only, no drive size and no computer logs. Fix: hex DATA + made-up computer documents + --nsze in the test run. Now 49 of 50 entries can be found.
  8. The 4 GB recording gave 189 of 485 errors. The same cause, on the user's side. There was no side file with the bytes, no drive size (nsze), and no dmesg or events. Fix: the input form explains each field. It finds the companion files next to the CSV and warns before the run.
  9. Stage 2 showed before stage 1 had finished, and the stage-2 screen showed engineering detail first. Fix: five locked phases, with a gate on the server (code 409 before "start stage 2"). Also the manager decision view below.
  10. A search could run past the first-look time limit. Fix: a clock budget (600 s) on top of the tries budget. The status triage_timeout is reported as a failure of the diagram's "> 10 min" rule.
  11. Old (superseded) steps could be recommended as "the stored one". This was found by running the live exercise a second time, on a knowledge base that already had history. The search index keeps superseded versions, because they still carry evidence. The engineer card recommended whichever version matched best. Fix: before recommending, the program follows the SUPERSEDES chain to the current approved version. (The manager view already listed only approved or validated steps.) Checks C4 and C20 went from fail to pass.
  12. "Not correct" on the AI's fresh proposal blamed the stored cause. Nothing stored had been judged. Fix: a new action, lesson (one of the 26 actions), that changes no weights. It records the reason as a lesson that the next AI message sees. The counts stay as they were (checked by the browser test). The proposal then stays folded as "marked not correct earlier", with "Show it again". It no longer comes back on the next visit.
  13. A manager's corrected version that failed in the lab stayed "proposed" for ever, and the manager was not told. Fix: it is recorded as failed-validation with a lesson. The Result says "your version did not reproduce the defect (k of 6 lab runs); the lab searched from it and found the version below".
  14. After a server restart, the first action on an error ran the whole presentation again before acting. That included a 38 s AI call. The browser test found it (its wait ran out). Fix: the presentation details are saved with the error's state, so a restart costs nothing.
  15. Admin actions were logged without the problem they were taken on. So an earlier verdict could not be shown next to the same proposal. Fix: every admin_action event carries the problem and the run.
  16. Steps replaced because a sibling was approved have no SUPERSEDES link. So the first fix for item 11 (walking the links) did not cover them. The third exercise run on the growing knowledge base caught it. Fix: the best match may be superseded, deprecated or failed. Then the card shows the current steps under the same cause (approved, else validated). It finds them by asking the graph, not by walking the links.
  17. The package that can be mailed could not find errors. This was found by unpacking it into an empty folder and running the 4 GB recording. The packer left out every folder named runs. That also dropped the checker's stored fingerprints under stage1/runs. Fix: the left-out folders are now counted from the application's top folder. The from-scratch run then gave the same 544 problems as the reference.
  18. A made test did not run as plain pytest from the package. There were two causes, both found by the from-scratch runs. First, stage 2 looked for the checker and the recording generator in the development folders. It did so unless the app had set environment variables. Second, the test's conftest.py looked for the stage-2 package only in folders above it. That is true in the development folders. It is not true in the package, where stage2/ sits next to suite/. Fix: the package layout (stage1/, data/, a stage2/ in a folder above) is found by default. So python3 -m pytest suite/<test> works from an unpacked package with no environment variable.
  19. On an empty knowledge base, the first search depended on the AI's proposal alone. In one of four from-scratch runs, the first search for T-42 used up its 300-try budget. (The two others made the error happen in 242 and 183 tries.) The starting point changed with the AI's answer. Fix: the entry family's known trigger shape (error list XII.4) is always an extra starting point. When the first search finds nothing, it is tried once more from that template. It uses another random sequence, inside the same time budget. The screen records this as "first search found nothing; retried from the family template".
  20. The "Generate test case" button did nothing on the real page. The browser test found it. The control code looked up the entry's target before the compose branch, and read an empty (null) card. Fix: the compose branch runs first. The browser test now waits for the written variants.
  21. Proposing again steps that had already failed checking was silently ignored. The solution list keeps one row per content fingerprint. So the manager's version was not run first, and the search started from nothing. Fix: failed steps that are proposed again go back to proposed and are checked again. The run path finds the admin's version, whatever its status in the solution list.

8.7 The manager's screen for one error (stage 2)

Why this part is here: This is the screen where the admin makes the decisions that the earlier parts count.

It was designed from the research note research_notes_v3/manager_decision_view.md. The note asks for six things. The answer comes first. There are two levels of detail. Verdicts are named by their outcome. Ranking works without dragging too. Undo replaces "are you sure?" boxes. Words for likelihood stand next to their numbers. What is on the screen, top to bottom:

  1. Bottom line: three lines. What the packets showed (one sentence). What is proposed (how many, from where, how often the top one made the error happen). The running count of his decisions.
  2. What the packets showed: a flow picture between the computer and the SSD. It shows the 12 key packets around the first bad one. Time runs top to bottom. Each line shows Δt, the time since the line before. Arrows point the way each packet went. The bad line is shaded. Gaps of 1 ms or more are drawn as bands. Receipts are greyed. "Show the full exchange (N packets)" is the only way to open more.
  3. Proposed ways to make it happen again: ranked cards, best first. Each has a plain title ("Flush, then write — 400 µs apart, idle 1.87 s"). It shows the command chips with the spacing between them, and the timing chips that can be changed. One line says where it came from. Two examples of that line follow. "Saved in the database · approved by … · reproduced in at least 61 % of lab runs (likely) · judged +1 / −0 · 1 test on file", or "Proposed now by the AI reviewer · fresh model call". Buttons: Correct (1) · Needs changes (2) · Not correct (3). There is a drag handle and a "…" menu. The menu has Move to top / up / down / bottom, "Why is this proposed?" and "All details".
  4. Needs changes opens the card in place. Stored (read-only) is above Your version. Your version has chips and timing fields that can be edited, changed items highlighted, and a change counter. "Save corrected version" runs it in the lab first. It is stored under the manager's name only if it makes the error happen.
  5. Not correct folds the card to a grey stub, with Undo and reason chips. The reasons are: wrong timing · wrong command order · does not match the packets · own words. For approved steps, it also offers "also retire it from the database (second admin)".
  6. Generate test case from the stored knowledge: this button is there when steps are stored for the error. It asks the AI to write up to three test variants from them. Each is run in the lab. It is kept only if it makes the error happen. It is filed with its sources (section 10.1).
  7. Result: the final order and timing after the search, lab runs, likelihood, the lab-check counts and the test-file links. Save decisions records removals and the ranking together. Correct and Save corrected version act at once, because they start the lab run. Everything for engineers (AI summary, all 26 actions, the raw lines, history) is behind "All details".

9. Making the error happen again (the search)

Why this part is here: stage 2 proves an error is real by making it happen again in the lab. This part explains how the program searches for the right steps.

The project statement asks for a program that learns by trying (the "RL agent"). It starts from the steps the AI reviewer suggests. Then it changes the commands and their timing, again and again. Each try gets a score: how close it came to making the same error happen (reward).

The default way to choose the next change needs no training. It looks at which kinds of change worked before and favours them (bandit with Thompson sampling). Why this is the default: a test compared 15 versions on 2 GB of hard cases. It showed that this simple learner reaches the goal reliably. A second way can be chosen instead. It learns a small choosing rule during the search (PPO). The setting is stage2.optimizer = "ppo" (section 9.1). Both ways use the same kinds of change. Neither way trains or changes the AI program. The list below names each part of the search.

What is tried (scenario): commands in a fixed order. They come from: read, write, flush, trim, write_zeroes, reset, power_cycle, aspm_idle, identify, get_log, set_feature, abort. Plus five timing values {inter_cmd_us, burst_len, idle_gap_ms, qd, bs_kb} and a power state. The five values are: time between commands, commands per burst, idle pause, commands waiting at once (queue depth), block size. Score of one try (reward): R = stage + closeness. The stage is a whole number from 0 to 4. 0 = nothing seen. 1 = an error of the right kind (family). 2 = the target error marked SUSPECT. 3 = the target error CONFIRMED. 4 = CONFIRMED with matching details (parameters). Closeness is a part-mark between 0 and 1 inside that stage. Example: how near a delay came to its limit. Starting points (seeds): the AI reviewer's suggestion · a saved procedure · 2 approved examples of that kind of error. Also the command order in the AI's short summary (digest). Each round (loop): make one small change to the best version so far (hill-climb). A change can add, remove, swap, replace or repeat a command. It can nudge a timing value or step it to a standard point. It can also mix two versions (crossover). Each kind of change keeps a count of how often it improved the score (Beta counts). The kind of change is picked from these counts (Thompson sampling). A new version is kept if it scores the same or better. After 25 tries with no improvement, the search restarts from a saved stepping stone. The program saves the best version for each (stage, motif) pair. It picks one with the same counting method (Go-Explore archive). The AI reviewer is asked only once: for the starting steps and the allowed range of each value. Confirm: a version that makes the error happen is run 8 more times. It is accepted when a careful lowest guess of its success rate is at least 0.5. This careful lowest guess stays low when only a few runs were made (Wilson 95 % lower bound). Make it smaller (minimise): remove commands that are not needed, a group at a time (ddmin). Then halve the change on each timing value, step by step (bisection). After every step, re-check that the error still happens in k of n runs. Limits (budgets): 300 tries per search. If the first search finds nothing, one more search runs. It starts from the standard steps for that kind of error (family template). So there are up to 600 tries. Everything must fit in 600 seconds, the time allowed for a first look at a failure (first-level triage). Over that time, the result is "triage_timeout" (the diagram's "> 10 min = fail"). Only the search stops. The lab check still finishes. "Best found" mark (optimal): 3 lab runs in a row each score above 0.9. This is the diagram's "score > 0.9 three times". The score is the three yes/no checks of section 9.1. The search itself stops at the Wilson check above. Saved steps first (guard): if a saved procedure exists for the same error type, it runs FIRST, 6 times. If it still makes the error happen, it is used again and no search is needed. If it stopped working, a lesson is written and the search starts from it (adapt). A procedure that an admin edited is checked the same way. Safety: some commands are never sent (deny-list). These are format, sanitize, firmware download/commit and namespace delete. They wipe the drive, load a new SSD program or delete a storage area. There is also a limit on how much is written (write budget). And a check on the fixed firmware too (canary).

9.1 The diagram's two rules as fixed numbers, and the PPO choice

Why this part is here: the project's system diagram sets two rules for the search. This part shows where they live in the code and what the "score" really counts.

The file stage2/loop_rules.py holds three fixed numbers: SCORE_THRESHOLD = 0.9, OPTIMAL_CONSECUTIVE = 3, FIRST_LEVEL_TRIAGE_S = 600. The checker program is run on the recording of one lab run. Its "test score" comes from three yes/no checks. (1) Did it find the same error type? (2) Did the same check break first, as in the recording from the field? (3) Is the result Confirmed? All three passed gives 1.0. Two of three gives 0.667. So "score above 0.9" means exactly this: the same error, by the same check, confirmed. "Optimal" means this happened in three lab runs in a row. There are no weights to tune. The 10-minute limit comes from the system diagram. It is the time allowed for a first look at a failure (first-level triage). A search that has not made the error happen again by then is reported as failed.

9.2 The most stressful conditions: pushing the timing harder after a confirmed repeat (added 2026-10-27)

Why this part is here: the project statement asks for the hardest conditions that still cause the error. This part explains how they are found and saved as a second test.

The project statement says the search program finds the most stressful conditions that still cause the error. These must become test files that a computer can run. Until 2026-10-27 this happened only when the manager pressed Try nearby variations. Now every confirmed repeat ends with a push to harder timing (stress ascent). The code is Optimizer.stress_ascent in stage2/optimizer.py, called from Stage2V3._stress.

It starts from the confirmed procedure, after it was made smaller. Each timing value is pushed one step in its harder direction. Commands come twice as close together. Twice as many commands wait at once (queue depth). The burst is twice as long. Blocks are twice as big. The idle pause is twice as long. A step is kept only when the error still appears in 2 of 3 lab runs. This repeats until no value can be pushed further, or the limit is used up. The limit is the setting stage2.stress_trials: 30 lab runs by default, inside the 10-minute limit.

The result is the hardest procedure that still causes the error. It shows how far each value was pushed (ratio). It goes through the same lab check on known-bad and fixed firmware. If it passes, it is saved as a second repeat test (regression test). Its label is "most stressful conditions that still trigger the defect". It is marked stress in manifest.json and optimizer:stress in the knowledge base. Those marks record where it came from.

Why a second test: the procedure's own test guards the exact point where the error happens. This test guards the space around that point. So a firmware fix must hold under the hardest timing at which the drive was seen to fail.

The push runs in three cases. After a search (the modes "searched from the evidence" and "searched from the saved procedure"). After a saved procedure that was used again. After a procedure the manager wrote that worked as given. The screen shows it under "Most stressful conditions", with the values pushed. "How the search went" lists the tries, the stepping stones kept, and which kinds of change improved the score.

The manager's editor and the search use the same building blocks. These are twelve commands, the ones the lab test machine can send. They are NVMe read, write, flush, trim, write zeroes, Identify, Get Log Page, Set Features and Abort. Then controller reset, power cycle and ASPM idle (letting the wire rest). Both also use the same five timing values and the same power state. Nothing else is fixed. Any order of up to twelve steps is allowed. The manager's version is run as given first. If it does not show the error reliably, the search starts from it. The search's kinds of change are: add, remove, swap, replace or repeat a command. Halve, double, nudge or step each timing value to a standard point. Change the power state. Combine two procedures.

10. Test files that repeat the error

Why this part is here: an error that happens again in the lab must become a test for later. This part shows what that test does and how it decides pass or fail.

A made test does not just "run the steps and hope". The same checker as in stage 1 decides whether it passes (the test's oracle).

prepare   firmware, power state and a spare storage area (scratch namespace), as written in the manifest
act       run the approved procedure (steps with timing)
record    the capture tool's table file of that run (113-column CSV)
check     python3 -m pcie_isolate.cli run --backend dry-run --nsze … [--dmesg … --events …]      ← the same checker as stage 1
pass if   known-bad firmware: the error type is found as CONFIRMED or SUSPECT in at least 1 of n repeats
          (or the group of look-alike error types the checker cannot tell apart, as measured)
          n comes from the measured repeat rate; the Wilson lower bound is reported
          fixed firmware, with traffic of a neighbouring error type added as a decoy:
          the error type is NOT the main result in any of m repeats

Files for each test:

  • manifest.json: the agreement for this test. It names the problem, the error type and the expected error types. It lists the steps to send, the recording window, the check command, the pass rules and the safety limits.
  • test_<id>.py: a test file a computer can run (pytest file). It holds two tests. On known-bad firmware the error happens and is found. On fixed firmware it stays silent.
  • conftest.py: the set-up for the lab test machine. Here it is the practice one made of software (GeneratorBench). For your hardware it goes through app/bench_hook.py.

On test data, the "SSD" is a hidden software model that makes the error when the right steps are sent. The generator then writes the recording the capture tool would have seen. That includes the bytes in hex and made-up computer logs, as in the 4 GB test. The real checker then searches that recording. 24 of 24 made tests passed as ordinary pytest files. 49 of 50 sampled error types can be found and pinned down on such recordings.

10.1 "Generate test case": the AI writes new tests from saved knowledge, and running them decides

Why this part is here: it explains the Generate test case button. It also shows why the AI cannot invent an unchecked test.

The knowledge base may hold one or more correct or improved command lists (sequences) for an error. A list counts if an admin approved it, or if it worked in the lab and waits for approval. Then the manager's screen shows the button Generate test case. This is one of five places where the AI program is asked something. The other four are the stage-1 confirmation, the stage-1 recording check, the stage-2 summary (digest) and the stage-2 suggestion (proposal). Here the program first looks up the knowledge base, then gives what it found to the AI. So the AI never invents a test from nothing. It builds on what the admins already judged. Design and sources: research_notes_v3/llm_test_composition.md.

StepWhat happensWho decides
1 · Look upThe saved command lists for this error come first: admin-approved ones, then ones that worked in the lab. Up to two approved examples of the same kind of failure are added. Each comes with its status and approver. It also shows its repeat rate (lower bound) and how often admins called it right or wrong.the knowledge base (compose.sources_for)
2 · WriteOne message goes to the AI, with a fixed answer form (JSON schema). It holds the evidence packets, the check's text, the lessons and what the packets showed. It also holds the saved command lists, named S1…Sn. The AI returns up to three versions (variants). The first is a strong copy: the trigger plus the set-up the evidence shows. The second is the same trigger at the edge of its timing. The third is a different command path to the same SSD state. Each version has a name and a reason that names packets and sources. It also lists the packet kinds the capture tool must show, the sources used and the risks.the AI program (Haiku, low effort, fixed answer form)
3 · Check by codeOnly the 12 allowed commands may be used. Timing is pulled back inside the allowed ranges. The power state must come from the list. A version that copies a saved list or another version is dropped. Copies are spotted by a content fingerprint (hash). Every repair is shown on the screen as "repaired by code".code (compose.clean_variants)
4 · RunEvery version runs six times on the lab test machine. It counts as repeated when the Wilson 95 % lower bound of its success rate is at least 0.5. If no version works, the search of section 9 changes the best one in the time left. It uses whichever search method was chosen. The changed version is reported as changed.the SSD and the lab test machine
5 · Lab checkEach version that works goes through the same lab check as any procedure. On known-bad firmware the stage-1 checker must find the error. On fixed firmware it must stay silent, with a decoy present. Then it is saved as a test. manifest.json gets a composition block. It holds the version name, reason, expected packets and risks, and which AI model wrote it. It also lists the sources with their version fingerprint (vhash), status, approver and lower bound. The pytest file's description says the same in words.the checker; files can only be downloaded
6 · RecordEach saved version moves from proposed to validated-by-execution (it worked in the lab). It is marked as made by llm:composed. It is never approved automatically. So it cannot push out the admin's approved procedure. Under the error it shows as "validated, awaiting approval". Approving it still needs two people. No weight changes anywhere.admins (two different people, "four-eyes")

What the manager sees: the section says how many saved command lists exist, and how many of the same kind. The button runs the whole chain as one job. The result lists each version with its lab numbers. For example: made the error in 5 of 6 lab runs, at least 54 %, likely. The checker found it 6 of 6 times, and 0 of 3 times on fixed firmware. Each version also shows its reason, the expected packets, its sources and the links to its test files. If nothing is saved yet, the button is switched off and the text says what to do first.

10.2 "Sweep the neighbourhood": trying nearby conditions to find other weak spots

Why this part is here: the project statement asks for the failure-prone areas around a known error. This part explains how the sweep tries nearby conditions and saves tests for the weak ones.

The project statement asks for "surrounding failure-prone areas". The explained statement asks for a sweep "including link-level stress via a jammer where a bench has one". A jammer is a tool on the wire that breaks or delays packets on purpose. Once a procedure makes the error happen, the manager's screen shows Sweep the neighbourhood (stage2/sweep.py, action sweep).

It tries up to 15 versions. Each timing value is tried at half and at double (inside the lab ranges). Every other power state is tried (L1, L1.2, D3hot, APST). The burst is doubled. A long idle pause is added when the original has none. Some lab machines have the optional inject(spec) part in app/bench_hook.py. There it also tries three jammer faults. These are broken request packets (TLP corruption 10⁻⁴), late answers (delayed completions) and a forced wire re-start (forced Recovery).

Each version runs three times. A version that makes the error in at least two runs marks a weak spot (failure-prone area). The three most stressful ones go through the lab check. "Most stressful" means the most repeats first, then how far the value was pushed. For a jammer version, the fault is switched on for the known-bad runs. It is cleared afterwards with clear_faults(). These versions are saved as repeat tests next to the procedure's own test. manifest.json marks them as coming from the sweep. Jammer versions are saved like the others. Nothing is approved automatically. The practice lab machine made of software has no inject(). So there, the jammer versions are reported as "hardware bench only".

11. One error followed from packets to test

Why this part is here: it shows every step of the project on one real case. The case is error type T-42 (chapter T, timeouts and time limits, entry 42). All numbers come from the live application.

  1. Packets. The computer writes to the SSD's power setting (a settings write, CfgWr0, to PMCSR). It puts the SSD to sleep (D3hot, packet #59769), then wakes it (D0, packet #59773). 2.000 ms later the computer sends a read request (MRd, packet #59777). It reads the SSD's status setting (CSTS, at BAR0+0x1C). The answer (completion, packet #59780) says UR: the request was not supported. 21 ms later the same read works.
  2. Checks. Check CFG.D0_EARLY breaks (tier B: it needs the checker's memory of earlier packets). It means: an access less than 10 ms after the wake-up from D3hot to D0. The 10 ms wait comes from the PCI Power Management rule book (recovery time). Check TLP.CPL_STATUS also breaks (tier A: one packet is enough). The answer says UR. With the Linux kernel log (dmesg) added, H.KERNEL_ERROR also breaks. Its message "Config reads return garbage or all-ones" lines up with packet #59775.
  3. Problem. The first packet that went wrong is #59777 (the start of the problem). Packet #59780 is a follow-on break. The read was sent by the computer (Downstream), so the computer accessed the SSD too early. Rule R4 decides the side: the computer (host). The checker compares the problem with the stored fingerprints of each error. Match scores: T-42 (0.65), L-31 (0.33), L-20 (0.25). Status: found and pinned down. The AI reviewer agrees (CONFIRMED). It names packets #59773, #59777 and #59780, and says the computer is responsible.
  4. Stage 2, first time. Knowledge base lookup: new, nothing like it was saved. The Haiku AI wrote a short summary (digest). It said: "Host accessed the card 2.001 ms after the D3hot→D0 PMCSR write, before the 10 ms recovery". Admin: accept. The search starts from the AI's command list. It is confirmed in 37 tries (lower bound 0.68). Lab check: the checker found T-42 in 6 of 6 known-bad runs, and 0 of 3 on fixed firmware. The test is accepted. A second admin approves it in the record. Files: T-T-42-…/test_T_T_42_….py.
  5. Stage 2, the error comes back (next recording). Lookup: match. It is the same error type and the same firmware context, with a combined match score of 0.99. The saved procedure is shown next to a new summary. Accept. The saved steps run first (the guard): 5 of 6. So they are used again, with no search. Lab check 6 of 6 and 0 of 3. The test is accepted again. The cause's "right" count rose (a 2.98 → 3.94).
  6. A "no" decision. The admin rejects with the reason "timing wrong for this firmware". The "wrong" count b of that procedure goes up by 1, and nothing else changes. The history shows the "no" entry with the note. The admin then changes the timing in the editor. The changed procedure is proposed and run first. Only when it works in the lab (validated by execution) is it saved and approved.

Why this part is here: these are the numbers the project measured on its own data. Each row names the file where the number comes from, so it can be checked.

Limits, said plainly. The practice lab machine is made of software. It measures the program's steps, not the physics of a real SSD. Two error types cannot be proven on this recording. The meaning-based lookup (dense-embedding channel) is built in but switched off, because no such model is available offline. On real hardware, two parts change. The lab machine hook and your AI service address (API endpoint) replace the made-up parts. Nothing else changes.

13. What stage 1 hands to stage 2, and what each admin button changed

Why this part is here: it names the files that link the two stages. It also shows what each admin action really changed.

Stage 1 writes three files: incidents.json (the problems), incident_rows.jsonl (their packets) and llm_reviews.jsonl (the AI reviewer's answers). Stage 2 reads them and builds the question for the knowledge base lookup. From then on, every admin action is saved as an event. The table shows the real counts before and after each action. They come from the test run on error type T-42. The events are in db/knowledge.sqlite, and the knowledge base page shows them.

How to read the counts (section 8 explains them in full). Every saved cause and procedure keeps some counts. Count a grows when it is judged right. Count b grows when it is judged wrong. Both start at 1, written Beta(1,1). Count tb grows when the lab cannot make the error happen with it. Count n is the number of decisions on it.

recording B, the error comes backaccept the saved procedurematch combined score 0.99: the saved procedure next to a new summarysaved steps run first: 5 of 6 → reused, 0 search tries. Cause link a 3.94 → 4.88. Procedure link and record a +1.test accepted again

How the lookup works after stage 1, step by step. The program looks up the knowledge base first, then gives what it found to the AI (RAG). This was the question for the T-42 repeat: {card T-42, family P19, rule CFG.D0_EARLY, layer config, origin host, verdict CONFIRMED, context FW-A, tokens, row kinds [CfgWr0, CfgWr0, MRd, Cpl …]}. In words: error type T-42, error family P19, first check CFG.D0_EARLY, settings level. Then: caused by the computer, confirmed, firmware FW-A. Last come its key words and its packet kinds. Four ways of matching ran (channels), each with its own score:

  • matching fields (structured) 1.5: the error type, the context and 4 of 4 fields agree;
  • shared key words, where rare words count more (BM25) 33;
  • shared 3-letter pieces of text, so small spelling differences do not matter (trigram) 0.95;
  • the same order of packet kinds (row-LCS) 1.0.

These were combined into one score (fused) of 0.99, which means "match". The record found was procedure 074e18b2 with its fingerprint. The message sent to the AI held the evidence packets and the check's text. It also held that saved procedure with its status, repeat lower bound and maker. Two approved examples of family P19 and the lessons were added. The summary came back in the right form and named packets #59773, #59777 and #59780. No AI model learned anything in this flow. The knowledge base and its counts decided what was shown.

What the rule book says should happen

What should happen: the PCIe rule book (PCIe Base Specification) defines the answer status CA (Completer Abort Status).

How this error shows instead: bit [15] (CmpltAbrt) is set in the error log. The side that refused records it ("Completer ID"). The packet's header is saved. By default this counts as not fatal (Non-fatal). Suppose the SSD refuses a read from the computer's processor (an MMIO read). Then the processor usually sees data of all ones. Suppose the computer side refuses a read from the SSD (a DMA read). Then the SSD's command fails.

How to fix it and prove the fix: CAUTION: do this on a system you can afford to break. From a test tool, send reads of unusual size to reserved places. These are in the SSD's memory window (MMIO reads to BAR offsets). Decode the saved header: it gives the address and who asked (requester). If the address is inside the SSD's memory window (BAR0), look at the read size and its position (offset).

The answering side (the completer) understood the request but refused it because of its own rule. The reason can be a forbidden access, or a read size that a setting does not support. Or the SSD is in a state where it cannot serve the request. It sends back an answer with status CA and sets bit 15 in its error log. The side that asked sees an "unsuccessful completion".

Partly seen in the packets: error type X-14, glitches when the wire rests or wakes up (problem INC-0066)

Why this part is here: here the packets show a sign of the error, but full proof needs more. Error type X-14 is in chapter X (wire-level errors only the capture tool sees), entry 14. It covers glitches when the wire rests (Electrical Idle). It also covers failures to enter or leave the power-saving states L0s and L1.

What the packets in the table file show

PHY.EIDLE_NO_EIOS CONFIRMED The wire went quiet without the signal that must come first: Electrical Idle (no EIOS).
the first packet that went wrong

Packet=2153229 | Link Dir=Upstream | Link Event=Electrical Idle (no EIOS) | Time Stamp=0134.138166337000s | Line=2153231

PHY.EIDLE_NO_EIOS CONFIRMED The same again: Electrical Idle (no EIOS).
a separate break, not caused by the first

Packet=2153315 | Link Dir=Upstream | Link Event=Electrical Idle (no EIOS) | Time Stamp=0134.138186997000s | Line=2153317

What the rule book says should happen

What should happen: the PCIe rule book (PCIe Base Specification) has rules for the wire's resting state (Electrical Idle). It covers the signals before and after it (EIOS/EIEOS) and the power-saving states L0s (N_FTS) and L1. It also covers how to enter and leave them, and the wire's automatic power saving (ASPM).

How this error shows instead: delays jump up after the wire was quiet. Bursts of receive errors (RxErr) appear when it wakes up. Sometimes the wire drops. Switching off the automatic power saving (ASPM) makes the problem go away.

How to fix it and prove the fix: CAUTION: switch on ASPM L0s/L1, and the deeper L1 sub-states where supported. Run work that comes in short bursts with long rests. Then the wire goes quiet and wakes up thousands of times. Measure each wake-up: the time from the first wake-up signal (EIEOS/FTS) to the first good request packet (TLP). Count errors in that time. Compare with ASPM switched off. Use the ASPM field of LnkCtl in lspci -vvv, or the kernel setting pcie_aspm=off. Errors may appear only in the capture tool and not in either side's error counters. Then suspect that the capture tool itself lost the signal (analyzer re-lock).

Evidence needed to decide

Partly seen in the packets
Partly: seen as a timing or order shape; proof needs evidence from outside the recording		PHY.EIDLE_NO_EIOS, PHY.EIDLE_NO_EIOSnone neededagrees (CONFIRMED)X-14 · side: the SSD (device). Rule R6: the computer did nothing before the wire was lost. · status: found and pinned down (ISOLATED)

In the L0s and L1 states the sender stops driving the lane (one wire pair). On wake-up, the receiver must lock onto the signal again within a set time. For L0s it gets a number of short training signals (N_FTS fast training sequences). For L1 the wire goes through a re-start step (Recovery). What can go wrong: the wire goes quiet without EIOS first. A lane drifts into quiet on its own (inferred idle). There are too few FTS for the receiver to lock. Or a wake-up fails and falls into Recovery, or into Detect (the very first start-up step).

Why this part is here: this error happens on a different wire, so the main recording cannot show it. Only logs from outside the recording prove it. Error type N-02 is in chapter N (failures outside the recorded wire), entry 2. Its old title: out-of-band management (NVMe-MI over SMBus/I²C, BMC power and reset control) changes device state.
