Packet=1380300 | Slave Address=0x6A | Write=1 | Byte Count=8 | PEC=0x55 | Time Stamp=0128.672119897000s | Line=1380302

What the rule book says should happen

What should happen: the NVMe management rule book (NVMe Management Interface specification) covers this. It describes messages over SMBus/I²C and over PCIe (MCTP over SMBus/I²C and over PCIe VDM). It describes the basic management command over SMBus (NVMe-MI Basic Management Command). It lists the Admin commands that may be sent by this side path (out-of-band). Check which edition (revision) applies.

How this error shows instead: the computer's driver restarts the SSD for no clear reason (nvme reset_controller). This comes after CSTS.CFS or CSTS.RDY changes. The firmware version read at start-up (nvme id-ctrl) differs from the one read later. Product data (VPD) or temperature limits differ from what the operating system set. The wire goes down and the SSD is found again (re-enumeration) while the computer did nothing.

How to fix it and prove the fix: CAUTION: use the board management chip (BMC). From it, send an NVMe-MI health check (Controller Health Status Poll). Also send a Get Log Page passed through that path (tunnelled), while recording. Nothing appears on the main PCIe wire. EXPERT: start a firmware switch-over (firmware activation) from the BMC while reads and writes run. Evidence to collect: the BMC logs (Redfish event log, IPMI SEL). Also a capture tool for I²C/SMBus on the connector's SMBus pins. The SSD's Persistent Event Log (LID 0Dh) records Firmware Commit, Set Features and Power-on/Reset events. It records them whatever path caused them (check which fields your drive fills in). The nvme mi commands of nvme-cli, or libnvme-mi, can ask the management side from the computer. They go through an SMBus adapter.

A board management chip (baseboard management controller, BMC), or a drive-bay expander, talks to the SSD's management side. It uses the SMBus pins of the connector. NVMe-MI lets it read the SSD's health and set the management settings (Management Endpoint configuration). It can also write product data (VPD) and pass on a limited set of Admin commands. Vendor tools also use it to update firmware on running systems. Software on the main path sees the SSD's state change for no visible reason.

How to read an error type id such as T-42 or M-020

The error list holds 485 known error types. The app screens call it the catalogue. It is split into ten chapters. The letter is the chapter. The number is only the place inside that chapter and means nothing else. Every screen writes the id out in words. Example:
"error type T-42 (chapter T = timeouts and time limits, entry 42): D3hot→D0 transition: access before the 10 ms recovery time".
In plain words, the computer used the SSD less than 10 ms after waking it from sleep.

LetterChapter
Serrors reported with a status code
Ttimeouts and time limits
Dsilent failures (said "success" but the work was not done)
LPCIe wire and request errors
CNVMe controller and computer-driver failures
Xwire-level errors only the capture tool sees
Vrule breaks visible in the recording
Pspeed problems
Mtiming, missing-evidence and cross-step failures
Nfailures outside the recorded wire

The screens number problems "Defect 1, Defect 2 …", in the order the checker met them in the recording. The internal record id (such as INC-0001) is never shown on the screens. This document still uses it, so an engineer can search for it.

15. All 485 errors

Why this part is here: this is the full error list. Each entry puts the real packets for one error next to what the rule book says.

There is one entry for each of the 485 errors in the error list. Click an entry to open it. Here is how to read one entry.

  • Left side: the real packets. They come from the main test recording (pcie_trace_485_errors.csv). Our generator made this recording and placed each error at known packets. Each packet line has a plain caption above it that says what it shows. A line below names the error family: one of the 27 ways an error shows on the wire. It also says whether the packets alone are enough.
  • Right side: the rule book. It says what the rule book says should happen and what goes wrong. It says how you can tell, and how to fix it and prove the fix. It also says what else to collect when the packets are not enough. That can be the packets alone, the bytes inside the packets, or the computer's own logs.
  • One of three labels. Each entry carries one label, so you know at once how much the packets can prove.
    • Seen in the packets: the recording itself shows the error. A marked value or a wrong order of packets proves it.
    • Partly seen in the packets: the packets show a sign, such as an odd timing or order. Full proof needs evidence from outside the recording, such as the computer's own logs.
    • Not seen in the packets: this error cannot be seen on the recorded wire. The packets give only the surroundings. The proof is outside the recording.

Chapter X: wire-level errors only the capture tool sees (30 entries)

Why this part is here: these 30 entries are errors in the signals on the wire itself (the physical layer).

X-01 A broken 10-bit code on a slow-speed lane (Invalid 10b symbol) Seen in the packets Wire signal and capture-tool errors

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 268515: a broken 10-bit code (Invalid 10b Symbol) on lane 2, at speed 2.5 GT/s.

Packet=268515 | Link Dir=Upstream | Link Event=Invalid 10b Symbol (Lane 2) | Time Stamp=0130.047553073000s | Time Delta=64.000 ns

Error family: P09, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. P09 means broken wire signals and capture-tool mistakes. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. The checker sees it from the order and timing of the packets. Examples are a missing answer, a long gap, or packets in the wrong order.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book (PCIe Base Specification) sets these rules. At the slow speeds, each 8 bits of data travel as a 10-bit code (8b/10b). The rule book says how to turn each code back into data. A broken code must be reported as a receiving error (Receiver Error). The report goes to the error-report feature, as a fixable error (AER Correctable Error Status).

What goes wrong: One or more bits flip on a lane. A lane is one of the wire's side-by-side paths. The 10-bit code then matches no valid 8-bit value. The receiver reports a receiving error (Receiver Error). It throws away the packet that held the broken code. The sender then sends that packet again.

How you can tell: The receiving side records a receiving error in its error-report feature (AER). Its names are PCI_ERR_COR_RCVR and "RxErr". A "fixable error" message (ERR_COR) is sent. Often a broken-packet error (Bad TLP) is recorded too. Nothing shows at the NVMe level (the SSD's command rules).

How to fix it and prove the fix: Safe: run the same work through different slots or extension cables, and compare the error counts. Risky, test machine only: add a part that weakens the signal on the wire. Or force speed Gen2 on a wire built for Gen1. Count the marked codes for each lane and direction, over a fixed amount of work. If the errors are real, two other things happen. The receiver sends a "send again" receipt (Nak) back the other way. The SSD's receiving-error counter (AER RxErr) also goes up. Read it in /sys/bus/pci/devices/<BDF>/aer_dev_correctable. Errors on one lane only point to that lane's path. Some capture tools can show the raw 10-bit codes. A code one bit away from a valid code suggests noise. A fully scrambled code suggests a lost timing lock or alignment.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Yes (Reported). The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Suspect the wire path of that lane first. Suspect the sender if the errors follow the SSD to other slots. Suspect the capture tool if the other side does not react. · Test that confirms it: Compare slots and extension cables.

X-02 Ones and zeros out of balance on a slow-speed lane (Running-disparity error) Seen in the packets Wire signal and capture-tool errors

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 269946: the balance of ones and zeros broke (Running Disparity Error) on lane 2, at speed 2.5 GT/s.

Packet=269946 | Link Dir=Upstream | Link Event=Running Disparity Error (Lane 2) | Time Stamp=0130.109458962000s | Time Delta=64.000 ns

Error family: P09, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. P09 means broken wire signals and capture-tool mistakes. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. The checker sees it from the order and timing of the packets. Examples are a missing answer, a long gap, or packets in the wrong order.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book (PCIe Base Specification) has rules for the 8-bit-to-10-bit codes (8b/10b). These rules come from the IBM 8b/10b code. A broken code must be reported as a receiving error (Receiver Error).

What goes wrong: The 10-bit codes keep the number of ones and zeros balanced. Each code has a plus form and a minus form. The balance so far (running disparity) picks which form comes next. A flipped bit can make a valid code in the wrong form. The receiver can only see this as a balance error (disparity violation).

How you can tell: The receiving side records a receiving error in its error-report feature (AER), as in error type X-01. The packet is thrown away and sent again.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Same as error type X-01. Normal hardware cannot create balance errors from software. Risky, test machine only: use a test sender (exerciser) that can send a wrong balance on purpose. The exact spot of the error is not certain. So look at the packet the receiver refused with a "send again" receipt (Nak), not only the marked code. Sometimes many balance errors appear on every lane at once. This happens just after the wire wakes from its quiet state (electrical idle). It is usually the capture tool getting its timing lock back (error type X-28). It is not a wire problem.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Yes (Reported). The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Suspect the wire path when single bits flip. Suspect the capture tool when errors bunch up on all lanes after waking, and nothing reacts. · Test that confirms it: Error counts for each lane.

X-03 A broken block start mark at the faster speeds (Invalid sync header) Seen in the packets Wire signal and capture-tool errors

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 271481: a data block starts with a broken start mark (invalid 128b/130b sync header).

Packet=271481 | Link Dir=Upstream | Link Event=Invalid Sync Header (Lane 3) | Time Stamp=0130.119369991000s | Time Delta=0.000 ns

Error family: P09, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. P09 means broken wire signals and capture-tool mistakes. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. This table file marks a wrong detail or a wrong order. The packet's check number shows it arrived broken (lcrc_flagged_bad). The same packet was sent again with the same packet number (tlp_replayed_same_psn).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book (PCIe Base Specification) sets rules for the faster speeds. There, each 128 bits travel in a 130-bit block (128b/130b). Each block starts with a 2-bit start mark (sync header). The rule book also sets how the data stream is framed. A chip maker's register guide (Efinix) lists "00 and 11 are Invalid Sync Headers".

What goes wrong: Each 130-bit block starts with a start mark. It says either "data block" or "wire-training signal block" (ordered-set block). Only two of the four values are valid. A flipped bit in the start mark leaves the receiver unsure how to read the next 128 bits. So the data stream on that lane is lost.

How you can tell: The receiving side records a receiving error (RxErr). The receiver usually treats it as a framing error. It then sends the wire into a short re-tune step (Recovery). This last point is not yet checked against the rule book. Linux sees a burst of receiving errors. It may also see a notice that the wire speed or width changed.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Safe: run the work with the SSD in different slots, with and without an extension cable. Careful: on Gen4 and faster platforms, use lane margining. Lane margining moves the receiver's timing or voltage, step by step, toward the edge of a good signal. Risky, test machine only: add a long wire or a part that weakens the signal. Read the error counters at both ends with cat /sys/bus/pci/devices/<BDF>/aer_dev_correctable. lspci -vvv shows CESta: RxErr+ and DevSta: CorrErr+. For detail on each lane, read the Lane Error Status setting. It sits in the Secondary PCIe Extended Capability. Use setpci only to read it. Or use the platform's lane-margining tool (Gen4+ Lane Margining at the Receiver).

Does the SSD or computer report it? Yes (Reported). The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Suspect the wire path first. At Gen3 and above, that means signal margin, tuning (equalization) or a signal booster chip (retimer). Suspect the platform's power saving (ASPM) when it comes back after power saving. Suspect the capture tool when nothing reacts. · Test that confirms it: Lane margining (move timing or voltage to find the signal edge).

X-04 A badly formed wire-training signal (malformed ordered set) Seen in the packets Wire start-up and speed changes

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 164941: a training signal (TS1) uses a data-rate code that is reserved (not allowed).

Packet=164941 | Link Dir=Upstream | Ord.Set Type=TS1 | Time Stamp=0127.994953258120s | Time Delta=0.880 ns

Packet 164942: a badly formed wire-training signal (malformed ordered set).

Packet=164942 | Link Event=Invalid Ordered Set (Lane 1) | Time Stamp=0127.994953259000s | Time Delta=7.250 ns

Error family: P08, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. P08 means wire start-up, re-tuning, and speed or width changes. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. The checker sees it from the order and timing of the packets. Examples are a missing answer, a long gap, or packets in the wrong order.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book (PCIe Base Specification) defines each wire-training signal (ordered set). The training signals TS1 and TS2 have fields. These are Link Number, Lane Number, N_FTS, the data-rate code, training control and tuning fields. Gen3 and above add data-stream rules. For example, an end-of-data mark (EDS) must come before a training signal.

What goes wrong: Wire-training signals start the wire and keep it working. A well-built receiver ignores a badly formed one. If it ignores them too often, start-up takes longer. Or the wire falls back to a lower speed or fewer lanes. Or start-up runs out of time.

How you can tell: Often nothing directly. There are indirect signs. The wire takes longer to come up. It enters the re-tune step (Recovery) more often. The present speed or width (LnkSta) is lower than what both sides can do (LnkCap). At Gen3 and above, a receiving error (RxErr) appears when the signal breaks framing rules.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Risky, test machine only: use a test sender (exerciser) to send TS1/TS2 with bad fields. Check that the device under test (DUT) ignores them correctly. Compare the same training signal across lanes. All lanes of one wire must agree on the link number and the training fields. Lane numbers must follow one after another. The same bad signal again and again points to a design bug. Random bad signals point to flipped bits. Use the capture tool's start-up view (LTSSM view) to see which start-up step each one belongs to.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No (Degraded). No error is reported. Things still work, but slower or on a weaker wire. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Look at which way the bad signal travels. If the SSD sent it (Upstream), suspect the SSD's wire circuit or firmware. If the computer side sent it (Downstream), suspect the computer's port (root port) or signal booster (retimer). If it is random on many lanes, suspect the wire. · Test that confirms it: Insert errors with an in-line fault tool or test sender (jammer or exerciser, confirmation test T16).

X-05 The receiver loses where packets start and end (framing error) Seen in the packets Wire signal and capture-tool errors

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 273338: a broken start or end mark between packets (framing token error).

Packet=273338 | Link Dir=Upstream | Link Event=Framing Error: STP expected | Time Stamp=0130.119689473000s | Time Delta=0.000 ns

Error family: P09, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. P09 means broken wire signals and capture-tool mistakes. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. The checker sees it from the order and timing of the packets. Examples are a missing answer, a long gap, or packets in the wrong order.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book (PCIe Base Specification) sets framing rules for both code types (8b/10b and 128b/130b). Framing marks (tokens) show where packets start and end. Their names are STP, SDP, END, EDB, EDS and IDL. Gen3 and above have extra framing-error rules.

What goes wrong: The receiver loses track of where packets start and end. With 8b/10b codes, framing uses special symbols (K symbols). STP…END marks a request or data packet (TLP). SDP…END marks a small receipt packet (DLLP). With 128b/130b codes, the STP mark carries the packet length. A small check number and a parity bit protect that length. Any mismatch means the rest of the data stream on that wire cannot be trusted.

How you can tell: The receiving side records a receiving error. With 128b/130b codes, the receiver must also enter the re-tune step (Recovery) to restart the data stream. This is not yet checked against the rule book. Packets that were on the way are sent again after the re-tune.

How to fix it and prove the fix: First, tell random errors from repeating ones. A framing error that repeats with the same packet type and length is a sender bug. Prove it with the exact bytes. Compare the length in the STP mark with the real number of 4-byte words (Dwords) up to the next mark. A random framing error, with a signal error on the same lane just before it, is a wire path problem.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Yes (Reported). The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: It depends on the pattern. For random events with earlier signal errors, suspect the wire path. For a repeating same-format pattern, suspect the sender. That is the SSD if Upstream, or the computer's port if Downstream. · Test that confirms it: Look at the raw symbols on the wire (raw symbol view).

X-06 A cancelled packet appears where none is expected (Nullified TLP) Seen in the packets Wire signal and capture-tool errors

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 273761: a cancelled packet (nullified TLP, EDB end mark, flipped check number) sent by an end device (endpoint).

Packet=273761 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=1448 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000003:922DA000 | Length=64 | DATA=256 B | Time Stamp=0130.119763269370s | Time Delta=0.000 ns | LCRC=0x1C6D90CD (Nullified)

Error family: P09, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. P09 means broken wire signals and capture-tool mistakes. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. This table file marks a wrong detail or a wrong order. A packet was cancelled on purpose by its sender (nullified_tlp).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book (PCIe Base Specification) sets rules for cancelled packets (nullified TLPs). They belong to the receipt-and-resend layer (Data Link Layer). The rules also cover the cancel end mark (EDB).

What goes wrong: Some middle chips start passing on a packet before all of it has arrived (cut-through). Such a chip is a switch or a signal booster (retimer). It may find an error at the end of the packet. It then ends the packet with the cancel mark (EDB). It also flips every bit of the check number (inverted LCRC). The receiver quietly drops the packet. No Nak is sent and no error is recorded. The packet number is not used up.

How you can tell: Normally nothing, by design. Sometimes the check number is not exactly flipped. Then the receiver treats it as a broken packet (Receiver Error or Bad TLP in AER).

How to fix it and prove the fix: Risky, test machine only: put errors on a switch's upstream wire with cut-through turned on. Record the wire below the switch. Count cancelled packets for each sender. Sometimes the computer's port connects straight to the SSD, with no switch. Then cancelled packets from the SSD point to a problem inside the SSD's sending path. Cancelled packets from a switch point to errors on the switch's other wire. Record that wire next.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No (Silent). Nothing reports this error. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: It depends on the sender. Suspect the SSD when the cancelled packets go Upstream from it on a direct wire. Suspect the switch or its other wire when they come from a switch port. Suspect the receiver when it sends a Nak for them, or accepts them. · Test that confirms it: Record the other wire.

X-07 Lanes arrive too far apart in time (lane-to-lane skew) Seen in the packets Wire start-up and speed changes

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 167222: the receiver could not line up lane 3 with the others (deskew failure).

Packet=167222 | Link Event=Lane-to-Lane Skew Exceeded (Lane 3) | Time Stamp=0128.077191717000s | Time Delta=0.000 ns

Packet 167333: the wire started with 2 lanes (x2), although both ends can use 4 (x4).

Packet=167333 | Link Event=Width Change: x2 | Time Stamp=0128.081394408000s | Time Delta=0.000 ns

Error family: P08, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. P08 means wire start-up, re-tuning, and speed or width changes. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. The checker sees it from the order and timing of the packets. Examples are a missing answer, a long gap, or packets in the wrong order.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book (PCIe Base Specification) limits the time difference between lanes (lane-to-lane skew). It sets limits for the sender and the receiver, at each speed. One patent summary says a receiver must handle 20 ns at Gen1 and 8 ns at Gen2. These two numbers are not sure. Limits for Gen3 and later are tighter. Check the rule book's table for your speed.

What goes wrong: The lanes of one wire pass through slightly different lengths of board track, cable and signal booster. The receiver lines them up with a shared mark. At 8b/10b speeds this is the COM symbol in SKP or TS signals. At 128b/130b speeds it is the edge of a SKP, SDS or EIEOS block. The receiver has a buffer to line them up (deskew buffer). If the time difference is bigger than this buffer, bytes from different lanes join in the wrong order.

How you can tell: Receiving errors and packets sent again. Or the wire starts with fewer lanes and leaves out the worst lanes (error type L-25).

How to fix it and prove the fix: Risky, test machine only: on a cable wire (MCIO, OCuLink), fit cable pairs of unequal length. Record the width and the errors. Read the capture tool's time-difference report for each lane, in the same recording, at each speed. A difference that grows with speed changes or heat points to the wire path. Sometimes the capture tool reports a steady difference, but the device has no receiving errors (no RxErr). Then the difference is within what the device can handle. The capture tool's own limit may be tighter (error type X-29).

Does the SSD or computer report it? Yes (Reported). The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Check what the other side shows. Suspect the wire path when the other side also has errors. That means the cable, the board tracks, or how a signal booster handles SKP. Suspect the capture tool's own limit when the error-report feature (AER) shows no errors. · Test that confirms it: The capture tool's time-difference report for each lane (skew report).

X-08 Swapped lane order or swapped wire pair not handled (lane reversal, polarity) Seen in the packets Wire start-up and speed changes

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 172551: the lane numbers are in reverse order, and nothing handles it.

Packet=172551 | Link Event=Lane Reversal Detected | Time Stamp=0128.264486011000s | Time Delta=0.000 ns

Packet 172662: the wire started with 2 lanes (x2), although both ends can use 4 (x4).

Packet=172662 | Link Event=Width Change: x2 | Time Stamp=0128.268688710000s | Time Delta=0.000 ns

Error family: P08, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. P08 means wire start-up, re-tuning, and speed or width changes. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. The checker sees it from the order and timing of the packets. Examples are a missing answer, a long gap, or packets in the wrong order.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book (PCIe Base Specification) covers this in two start-up steps. In the Polling step, the receiver finds a swapped wire pair from the TS1/TS2 signals (polarity inversion). In the Configuration step, the two sides agree on lane numbers and on reversed lane order (lane reversal).

What goes wrong: PCIe lets board designers reverse the order of the lanes. It also lets them swap the two halves of a lane's wire pair (D+ and D−). Every receiver must find and undo a swapped pair on each lane during Polling. Support for reversed lane order is optional on each side. So it works only if at least one side handles it. If neither side handles it, or a device bug stops it, the wire starts with fewer lanes. Or it does not start at all.

How you can tell: The present width (LnkSta) is lower than the possible width (LnkCap). lspci -vvv shows "LnkSta: … Width x1 (downgraded)". Speed is lower. The wire may not come up at all.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Risky, test machine only: use an adapter or an in-between board (interposer) that reverses the lanes. Check both the start-up and how the capture tool reads it. Record the start-up from power-on, with the capture tool set to the real lane layout. Compare the lane numbers in TS1/TS2 from both ends. The capture tool must also be told about any reversal on the in-between board. Otherwise it reports false errors (error type X-29).

Does the SSD or computer report it? No (Degraded). No error is reported. Things still work, but slower or on a weaker wire. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Look at both sides. Suspect the wire or the board layout when neither side corrects it. Suspect the device whose datasheet claims reversal or swap support, but which fails. · Test that confirms it: Check the datasheet and the list of known chip bugs (errata).

X-09 The wire changes speed or width while working (unexpected renegotiation) Seen in the packets Wire start-up and speed changes

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 178371: the wire speed changed while packets were flowing.

Packet=178371 | Link Event=Speed Change: 8.0 GT/s (autonomous) | Time Stamp=0128.393831700000s | Time Delta=304.000 ns

Error family: P08, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. P08 means wire start-up, re-tuning, and speed or width changes. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. The checker sees it from the order and timing of the packets. Examples are a missing answer, a long gap, or packets in the wrong order.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book (PCIe Base Specification) covers the re-tune step (Recovery) and the Configuration step of wire start-up (LTSSM). It also covers the Link Status setting, with its two change flags (LBMS and LABS). And it covers the Target Link Speed in the Link Control 2 setting.

What goes wrong: A port can change speed or width by itself. For example, after many errors, or to save power. Or software can ask for the change. A drop from Gen4 to Gen1, or from x4 to x1, keeps the SSD working. But it works at a small part of its speed.

How you can tell: The port on the computer side (downstream port) sets a Link Status flag. One flag is Link Bandwidth Management Status (LBMS). The other is Link Autonomous Bandwidth Status (LABS). In Linux v7.2, the bandwidth controller handles that signal. It updates the saved wire speed. There is no NVMe error, only lower speed.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Careful: on a test machine, change the Target Link Speed. Then re-tune through the kernel's bandwidth-control interface. Or damage one lane on purpose. Record the change. In the recording, find the first TS1 signal after normal work (L0). Look back for the signal errors or the go-quiet signal (EIOS) that caused it. Note who started the re-tune: the direction where TS1 appears first. On the computer, read lspci -vvv LnkSta over time. Also read the sysfs files current_link_speed and current_link_width over time.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No (Degraded). No error is reported. Things still work, but slower or on a weaker wire. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Look at what came just before the change. Suspect the wire when bursts of errors come first. Suspect the computer or platform when software first wrote a Target Link Speed and asked for Retrain Link. · Test that confirms it: Compare what the wire can do with what it is doing now (E02, a copy of the SSD's settings area).

X-10 Clock-matching signals missing, too frequent or badly formed (SKP errors) Seen in the packets Wire signal and capture-tool errors

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 286307: the time between clock-matching signals (SKP) broke the rule (SKP interval violated).

Packet=286307 | Link Dir=Upstream | Ord.Set Type=SKP | Time Stamp=0130.120223287120s | Time Delta=0.880 ns

Error family: P09, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. P09 means broken wire signals and capture-tool mistakes. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. The checker sees it from the order and timing of the packets. Examples are a missing answer, a long gap, or packets in the wrong order.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book (PCIe Base Specification) has rules for clock differences. Clock-matching signals (SKP ordered sets) must be sent at set intervals. The interval differs between clock set-ups: shared clock, SRNS and SRIS. The rule book also sets the SKP format for 8b/10b and 128b/130b. The exact intervals depend on the set-up and speed. This is not yet checked against the rule book.

What goes wrong: The two ends have slightly different clock speeds. SKP signals let receivers make up for this. Receivers and signal boosters (retimers) add or remove SKP symbols. At Gen1/2 a SKP signal is a COM symbol followed by SKP symbols. At Gen3+ it is a block of SKP bytes, an end mark and LFSR/parity bytes. At Gen4+ it can also carry margining commands. If too few SKP signals arrive over time, the receiver's stretch buffer (elastic buffer) runs over or runs empty.

How you can tell: Receiving errors, when the stretch buffer runs over or runs empty. Sometimes each end has its own clock (SRIS) and the SKP interval is set wrong. Then error bursts come at regular times.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Risky, test machine only: run a wire with separate spread-spectrum clocks and SRIS turned off, under heavy traffic. Export the SKP times for each direction. Work out how the intervals spread. Compare them with the rule book's maximum for that clock set-up. Check the platform's clock set-up. Does the SSD use the slot's clock, or its own?

Does the SSD or computer report it? Yes (Reported). The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Look at the sender and the clocks. Suspect the sender (a bug in when it sends SKP). Or suspect a signal booster that sends badly formed SKP. Suspect the platform clock settings when SRIS is set wrong. · Test that confirms it: Record with no filter (unfiltered capture).

X-11 The wire keeps leaving normal work to re-tune (Recovery storm) Seen in the packets Wire start-up and speed changes

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 197169: re-tune step (Recovery) number 1, with no speed change and no errors.

Packet=197169 | Link Event=Electrical Idle Exit | Time Stamp=0128.397118317000s | Time Delta=0.000 ns

Packet 197274: re-tune step (Recovery) number 2, with no speed change and no errors.

Packet=197274 | Link Event=Electrical Idle Exit | Time Stamp=0128.422143298000s | Time Delta=0.000 ns

Packet 197557: re-tune step (Recovery) number 3, with no speed change and no errors.

Packet=197557 | Link Event=Electrical Idle Exit | Time Stamp=0128.447218079000s | Time Delta=0.000 ns

Error family: P08, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. P08 means wire start-up, re-tuning, and speed or width changes. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. The checker sees it from the order and timing of the packets. Examples are a missing answer, a long gap, or packets in the wrong order.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book (PCIe Base Specification) describes the re-tune step (Recovery), which is part of wire start-up (LTSSM). It sets the inner steps of Recovery and when the wire may enter it.

What goes wrong: The re-tune step gets back the bit, symbol or block lock. It is how a wire handles errors and speed changes. A healthy wire enters it rarely. A wire that enters it all the time still works. But it has big delays and less speed.

How you can tell: Fixable errors in the error-report feature (AER) on one or both ends. These are receiving errors (RxErr), resend timer timeouts (Replay Timer Timeout) and resend counter roll-overs (REPLAY_NUM Rollover). Linux limits how often it prints them in the kernel log (dmesg). NVMe reads and writes get sudden delays. Sometimes the computer's time limits run out.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Careful: turn on the power-saving mode ASPM L1 on a wire with weak timing. Or use receiver margining to reduce the signal margin. Then record. Count re-tunes per second from the start-up view (LTSSM view). Plot them against the work and time. Sort each re-tune by its cause: error, roll-over, speed-change request or waking from quiet. Check the error counters (AER) of both ends over the same period.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No (Degraded). No error is reported. Things still work, but slower or on a weaker wire. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Look at what comes just before each re-tune. Suspect the wire when receiving or check-number errors come first. Suspect the platform's power saving (ASPM) when wake-ups from L1 come first. Suspect one side when it always starts the re-tune on a clean wire. · Test that confirms it: Compare the error counters before and after (AER counter snapshot, confirmation test T1).

X-12 Wire start-up gets stuck or keeps looping (LTSSM stuck in training) Seen in the packets Wire start-up and speed changes

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 207173: wire start-up is stuck in a test mode (Polling.Compliance).

Packet=207173 | Link Dir=Upstream | Ord.Set Type=Compliance Pattern | Time Stamp=0128.939399493000s | Time Delta=1.000 ms

Error family: P08, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. P08 means wire start-up, re-tuning, and speed or width changes. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. The checker sees it from the order and timing of the packets. Examples are a missing answer, a long gap, or packets in the wrong order.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book (PCIe Base Specification) sets the wire start-up steps (LTSSM). These include Detect, Polling (Active, Compliance, Configuration) and Configuration. It also sets their time limits.

What goes wrong: Polling.Compliance is a test mode. A port enters it when it finds a receiver on a lane but gets no TS1 signals there. It may also be told to, by the Enter Compliance bit or a test signal. In normal work, it means one side sees a partner that is not starting up. Other loops come from link numbers that do not match. Or from lanes that never get a lock. Or from time limits running out in Configuration.

How you can tell: The SSD never shows in lspci, or shows only after a long delay. On the computer's port (Root Port), the "wire is active" flag never turns on (Data Link Layer Link Active). Linux waits and then gives up. Or it uses its fix-up that re-tunes at 2.5 GT/s.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Risky, test machine only: tape off or cut a lane's receive pair on an adapter. Or hold the SSD in reset. Record the start-up from power-on. Start recording when the reset pin is released (PERST# deassertion). Use a capture tool that brings out the PERST# pin. Measure the time from PERST# to the first TS1 from each side. Find which side stops moving forward. Note which lanes show the test pattern.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No (Timer only). No error message is sent. Only a time limit running out shows it. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: It depends on which lanes and which side. Suspect the wire or board when one lane shows the test mode with a receiver found. Suspect the SSD when it is silent on all lanes after PERST#. Suspect the platform for PERST# timing. · Test that confirms it: Record the power lines and side pins with a scope or logic analyser (E07).

X-13 Signal tuning fails, so speed drops or errors rise (equalization failure) Seen in the packets Wire start-up and speed changes

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 211371: signal tuning step 3 ran out of time at 16 GT/s. The wire falls back to 8 GT/s.

Packet=211371 | Link Dir=Upstream | Ord.Set Type=SDS | Time Stamp=0129.058629527250s | Time Delta=16.250 ns

Error family: P08, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. P08 means wire start-up, re-tuning, and speed or width changes. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. The checker sees it from the order and timing of the packets. Examples are a missing answer, a long gap, or packets in the wrong order.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book (PCIe Base Specification) sets the signal tuning steps (Link Equalization Procedure). It also defines the Lane Equalization Control settings. In Linux these are PCI_SECPCI_LE_CTRL, PCI_PL_16GT_LE_CTRL, PCI_PL_32GT_LE_CTRL and PCI_PL_64GT_LE_CTRL. The Link Status 2 setting holds the tuning result bits.

What goes wrong: At 8 GT/s and above, the two ends tune each other's sender (equalization). They do this in steps 0 to 3. In step 2, the upstream port asks the downstream port to adjust its sender. In step 3, it is the other way round. A bad result leaves a wire that works with little margin. Or the port gives up the higher speed.

How you can tell: The tuning result bits in Link Status 2 are clear for the failing speed. These bits are Equalization Complete and Phase 1/2/3 Successful. The wire runs at a lower speed. Or it runs at full speed with a steady count of receiving errors (RxErr).

How to fix it and prove the fix: Risky, test machine only: force one tuning setting (preset). Use the platform's firmware settings or the device's debug interface. Then record the next tuning and its error rate. Start recording on the first TS1 with the tuning bit set after a speed change. Or start it on a speed change. Record the whole procedure. List each lane's asked-for and final preset. Match them against the errors on each lane after tuning. For the electrical view, Teledyne LeCroy describes CrossSync PHY. It lines up an oscilloscope recording in time with the packet recording.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No (Degraded). No error is reported. Things still work, but slower or on a weaker wire. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: It depends on how tuning failed. Suspect the wire path when steps run out of time, or lanes end on different presets because of signal loss. Suspect the wire circuit (PHY) that does not answer requests in time. Suspect device firmware for illegal or odd presets. · Test that confirms it: Compare what the wire can do with what it is doing now (E02, a copy of the SSD's settings area).

X-14 Quiet-state glitches, or failures entering or leaving power saving (L0s/L1) Partly seen in the packets Wire start-up and speed changes

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 216273: the wire briefly went quiet (electrical idle glitch) during normal work (L0).

Packet=216273 | Link Dir=Upstream | Link Event=Electrical Idle (no EIOS) | Time Stamp=0129.171815980000s | Time Delta=2.000 us

Error family: P08 and P20, two of the 27 ways an error shows on the wire. Proof from outside the recording also counts here. E02 is a copy of the SSD's settings area (lspci). E07 is measurements of power and side pins (oscilloscope). P08 means wire start-up, re-tuning, and speed or width changes. P20 means power-saving handshakes. · Can the packets alone prove it? Partly. The order and timing of the packets show its shape. The proof needs evidence from outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book (PCIe Base Specification) has rules for the quiet state (Electrical Idle). They cover the go-quiet and wake signals (EIOS and EIEOS). They cover entering and leaving the power-saving states L0s (with N_FTS) and L1. They also cover the power-saving set-up (ASPM).

What goes wrong: In L0s and L1, the sender stops driving the lane. On leaving, the receiver must get its lock back within a set time. For L0s it uses N_FTS fast training signals. For L1 it uses the re-tune step (Recovery). Four things can go wrong. The wire goes quiet without the go-quiet signal (EIOS). A lane drifts into quiet on its own (inferred idle). There are too few fast training signals for the receiver to lock. Or a wake-up fails and falls into Recovery or Detect.

How you can tell: Sudden delays after quiet periods and bursts of receiving errors at wake-up. Sometimes the wire drops. Turning off power saving (ASPM) makes it go away.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Careful: turn on ASPM L0s/L1, and L1 substates where supported. Use bursty, light work so the wire goes quiet and wakes thousands of times. Measure each wake-up: the time from the first EIEOS/FTS to the first good packet. Count the errors in that window. Compare with ASPM turned off. See the ASPM field in lspci -vvv LnkCtl, or the kernel setting pcie_aspm=off. Sometimes errors appear only in the capture tool, not in either device's counters. Then suspect the capture tool getting its lock back.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No (Degraded). No error is reported. Things still work, but slower or on a weaker wire. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: It depends on which side fails. Suspect the SSD when it cannot lock with the N_FTS number it announced. Suspect the platform when the reference clock or CLKREQ# pin is not restored (check with a logic probe). Suspect the capture tool when only it has to lock again. · Test that confirms it: Turn off ASPM and L1 substates (confirmation test T13).

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 321262: a request or data packet (TLP) arrived with a broken check number (bad LCRC).

Packet=321262 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=1581 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000003:73C63300 | Length=64 | DATA=256 B | Time Stamp=0130.949813506620s | Time Delta=0.000 ns | LCRC=0xCC4DF62A (Bad)

Packet 321272: the refused packet is sent again with the same packet number (PSN).

Packet=321272 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=1581 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000003:73C63300 | Length=64 | DATA=256 B | Time Stamp=0130.949814049120s | Time Delta=0.000 ns | LCRC=0xCCBDF92A

Error family: P06, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. P06 means packets that arrive broken and are sent again. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. This table file marks a wrong detail or a wrong order. The packet's check number shows it arrived broken (lcrc_flagged_bad). The same packet was sent again with the same packet number (tlp_replayed_same_psn).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book (PCIe Base Specification) covers the receipt-and-resend layer (Data Link Layer). This includes the check number (LCRC), the receive rules and when to send a Nak. The error-report feature (AER) records it as a broken packet (Bad TLP).

What goes wrong: A bit flips inside a packet, and the signal layer does not catch it. For example, it flips in a scrambled data byte, which has no code-level check. This breaks the check number (LCRC). The receiver throws the packet away. It reports a broken packet (Bad TLP). It sends an "arrived broken, send again" receipt (Nak).

How you can tell: The receiving side records a fixable broken-packet error in AER. Its names are PCI_ERR_COR_BAD_TLP and "BadTLP". A receiving error (RxErr) may appear too. Nothing shows at the NVMe level.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Risky, test machine only: use a test sender (exerciser) or an error-making signal booster. It breaks the check number on chosen packets. Or, careful: margin the receiver. For each marked packet, check how the receiver reacts. A Nak, or a resend of the same packet number, proves the other side saw it too. Sometimes the next Ack covers the marked packet with no resend. Then the receiver accepted it, and the mark is a capture-tool reading error (error type X-27). Work out the rate: check-number errors per 10^9 packets, for each direction.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Yes (Reported). The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: It depends on the pattern. Random errors point to the wire path. Errors that repeat on the same format point to the sender in that direction. Packets the receiver accepted point to the capture tool. · Test that confirms it: Compare the error counters before and after (AER counter snapshot, confirmation test T1).

X-16 A small receipt packet arrives broken (DLLP CRC error) Seen in the packets Broken packets sent again

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 322066: an "arrived fine" receipt (Ack DLLP) has a broken check number (bad CRC 16). The receiver ignores it.

Packet=322066 | Link Dir=Downstream | DLLP Type=ACK | Time Stamp=0131.080186581370s | Time Delta=85.750 ns | AckNak Seq Num=1939

Error family: P06, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. P06 means packets that arrive broken and are sent again. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. This table file marks a wrong detail or a wrong order. A receipt packet's check number shows it arrived broken (dllp_crc_flagged_bad).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book (PCIe Base Specification) covers the check number on receipt packets (DLLP CRC). It also covers the receive rules of the receipt-and-resend layer (Data Link Layer). The error-report feature (AER) records it as a broken receipt (Bad DLLP).

What goes wrong: The receiver quietly throws away a receipt packet with a bad check number. It reports Bad DLLP. Each Ack and each room-left message (UpdateFC) also covers all earlier ones. So losing one does no harm. Losing many causes resends, and stalls while waiting for room (credit stalls).

How you can tell: A fixable Bad DLLP error in AER (PCI_ERR_COR_BAD_DLLP). Sometimes the other side's resend timer runs out (Replay Timer Timeout).

How to fix it and prove the fix: Risky, test machine only: use a test sender (exerciser) that breaks receipt check numbers. Watch how the device under test (DUT) resends and handles room. Count bad receipts for each direction. Check what follows each one. A resend after the timer runs out means the Ack really was lost. A later receipt that covers it means no harm was done.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Yes (Reported). The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: It depends on the direction. Suspect the wire path in that direction, and match it with symbol errors there. Suspect the sending port if one receipt type keeps breaking on an otherwise clean wire. · Test that confirms it: Compare the error counters before and after (AER counter snapshot, confirmation test T1).

Error family: P06, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. P06 means packets that arrive broken and are sent again. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. This table file marks a wrong detail or a wrong order. The packet's check number shows it arrived broken (lcrc_flagged_bad). A packet number is out of order (psn_out_of_sequence). The same packet was sent again with the same packet number (tlp_replayed_same_psn).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book (PCIe Base Specification) sets the numbering rules of the receipt-and-resend layer (Data Link Layer). The receiver tracks the next number it expects (NEXT_RCV_SEQ). The sender tracks the next number to send (NEXT_TRANSMIT_SEQ). It also tracks the last acknowledged number (ACKD_SEQ). Breaking these rules is a receipt-rule error (Data Link Protocol Error).

What goes wrong: The receiver accepts only the next number it expects. A lower number is a repeat. It is thrown away, and an Ack is planned. This is allowed after resends. A higher number means packets were lost. So the receiver throws it away and sends a Nak (Bad TLP). Sometimes an Ack or Nak names a number the sender is not waiting on. That is a receipt-rule error (Data Link Protocol Error).

How you can tell: Case 2 (an allowed repeat): nothing. Case 1: a broken-packet error (Bad TLP) at the receiver, plus a Nak. Case 3: a receipt-rule error that cannot be fixed (PCI_ERR_UNC_DLP, "DLP"). It is often set as Fatal. It leads to a wire reset, or the port shuts the wire off (DPC).

How to fix it and prove the fix: Risky, test machine only: use a test sender (exerciser). It sends packets with skipped numbers, or Acks for numbers never sent. Check that the device under test (DUT) sends a Nak or reports DLP. Write a script. For each direction, keep the next expected number. Mark resends: same number and same contents as an earlier packet. Mark new packets with unexpected numbers. For case 3, keep the set of numbers not yet acknowledged. Check each Ack or Nak against it. A DLP error in AER right after the event confirms it.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Yes (Reported). The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Look at the direction. A skipped or reused number going Upstream points to the SSD's sender. Going Downstream, it points to the computer's port (root port). A bad Ack or Nak points to the side that sent it. If only packet edges look wrong, suspect how the capture tool reads them. · Test that confirms it: Compare the error counters before and after (AER counter snapshot, confirmation test T1).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book (PCIe Base Specification) sets the Ack/Nak receipt rules. It sets no "maximum Nak rate". So this is a quality problem. It is judged against the expected bit error rate.

What goes wrong: Each Nak makes the sender resend every unacknowledged packet after the broken one. With large packets and a deep resend buffer, this can waste much of the speed. The data still arrives correct.

How you can tell: The fixable error counters Bad TLP and RxErr rise steadily on the receiving side. Linux prints fixable-error lines, but limits how often. Speed is lower than expected. The slowest responses get slower (higher latency percentiles). There is no NVMe error.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Careful: run full-speed reading or writing in address order (for example fio with large blocks). Use a weak extension cable, and record. Work out the resend cost: resent bytes ÷ all packet bytes, for each direction, each second. Plot it against the work. Errors that grow with traffic on nearby lanes or wires suggest signal leaking between wires (crosstalk). They may also suggest power-supply noise. Errors bunched on one packet type suggest a design bug.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No (Degraded). No error is reported. Things still work, but slower or on a weaker wire. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Look at which packets were refused. Suspect the wire path when they share no format and follow the load or lane errors. Sometimes the same packet size or type is always refused on a clean wire. Then suspect a bug in the receiver that sends the Naks. · Test that confirms it: Compare the error counters before and after (AER counter snapshot, confirmation test T1).

Error family: P06, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. P06 means packets that arrive broken and are sent again. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. This table file marks a wrong detail or a wrong order. The same packet was sent again with the same packet number (tlp_replayed_same_psn).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book (PCIe Base Specification) sets the resend rules of the receipt-and-resend layer (Data Link Layer). The error-report feature (AER) has a REPLAY_NUM Rollover error for this.

What goes wrong: The sender keeps a 2-bit resend counter (REPLAY_NUM). Each resend without progress adds 1 to it. When it rolls over, the sender decides the wire is in trouble. It re-tunes the wire. Any Ack that moves forward sets the counter back to the start.

How you can tell: The sender records a fixable REPLAY_NUM Rollover error in AER (PCI_ERR_COR_REP_ROLL, "Rollover"). The wire enters the re-tune step. There is a delay as long as the re-tune plus all the resend time.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Look at the other direction during the resends. No receipt packets at all means the receiver is not sending Acks. That is a receiver bug or hang. Naks mean it gets the packet but refuses it every time. Broken receipts mean the return path is bad.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Yes (Reported). The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: It depends on what comes back. No receipts, or Acks that never move forward, point to the receiver's Ack logic (a hang or bug). Naks point to an error tied to the packet contents. That is the sender or the wire in that direction. Broken receipts point to the wire in the other direction. · Test that confirms it: Compare the error counters before and after (AER counter snapshot, confirmation test T1).

Error family: P06, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. P06 means packets that arrive broken and are sent again. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. This table file marks a wrong detail or a wrong order. The same packet was sent again with the same packet number (tlp_replayed_same_psn).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book (PCIe Base Specification) has tables for Ack/Nak delay limits and resend timer limits. They depend on the wire width, speed, Max_Payload_Size and an internal-delay term. The exact formula is not yet checked against the rule book.

What goes wrong: The receiver must send an Ack within a time limit. The rule book gives this limit as a table. It depends on wire width, speed and the largest data size per packet. The sender's resend timer is set to a larger multiple of the same amount. Sometimes the receiver delays its Acks. For example, it sends its own packets or room-left messages (UpdateFC) first. Then the sender's timer runs out. It resends packets that had already arrived fine.

How you can tell: The sender records a fixable resend timer error in AER (PCI_ERR_COR_REP_TIMER, "Timeout"). It shows on the sender, although the fault is in the receiver. The receiver gets repeat packets and quietly throws them away. Speed is wasted.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Careful: stress the signal. Lower the sender's signal strength, or weaken the signal on a riser card. Or use a test sender (exerciser) that drops Ack receipts. To prove it: lspci -vvv shows CESta "Timeout+". The sysfs aer_dev_correctable counters include counts for each error bit. In the capture tool, a packet is resent with the same number, with no Nak in between.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No (Timer only). No error message is sent. Only a time limit running out shows it. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Find the side that sends the Acks. That is the receiver of the resent packets. Late Acks from the SSD (for packets going Downstream) point to the SSD. Late Acks from the computer's port (for packets going Upstream) point to the platform. · Test that confirms it: Run work that measures speed and delay (throughput and latency).

Packet=361431 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=1235 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000004:799D7700 | Length=64 | DATA=256 B | Time Stamp=0161.913046639250s | Time Delta=0.000 ns | LCRC=0x764BB9EE

Error family: P07, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. P07 means room-left messages (credits) that stop or go wrong. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. The checker sees it from the order and timing of the packets. Examples are a missing answer, a long gap, or packets in the wrong order.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book (PCIe Base Specification) sets the room rules (Flow Control). The receiver tells the sender how much room it has, in units called credits. The rules cover the credit types and the start and update messages (InitFC/UpdateFC). They cover how to work out the credit limit. They cover endless credits: end devices must announce endless room for answers (infinite completion credits). They also cover two errors, Receiver Overflow and Flow Control Protocol Error. A chip maker's controller guide (Efinix) gives the most unused credits allowed without scaling. These are 2,047 data credits and 127 header credits. It reports breaks as FCPE.

What goes wrong: Credits stop the receiver's buffer from running over. A sender that ignores them overfills the receiver's buffer, and packets are lost. A receiver that announces nonsense credits breaks the sender's check before sending.

How you can tell: A buffer overflow error (Receiver Overflow, PCI_ERR_UNC_RX_OVER, "RxOF"). Or a room-rule error (Flow Control Protocol Error, PCI_ERR_UNC_FCP, "FCP"). Both are errors the wire cannot fix (uncorrectable). Often a wire reset or a port shut-off (DPC) follows.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Risky, test machine only: use a test sender (exerciser). It sends packets past the announced credits, or announces out-of-range credits. Then it checks how the device under test (DUT) reports errors. Credit sums wrap round at a fixed size (modular). Compare (credit limit − credits used) mod 2^(field size) with the amount needed, as the rule book describes. A capture tool that tracks credits can do this. So can a script over a table file with receipt packets and packet lengths. A recording that starts after the start message (InitFC) can only check changes, not the real limits.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Yes (Reported). The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Find who broke the rule. If a packet went out without room, blame its sender. Upstream means the SSD, Downstream means the platform. If the announced room was wrong, blame the side that announced it. · Test that confirms it: Compare the error counters before and after (AER counter snapshot, confirmation test T1).

Error family: P07, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. P07 means room-left messages (credits) that stop or go wrong. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. The checker sees it from the order and timing of the packets. Examples are a missing answer, a long gap, or packets in the wrong order.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book (PCIe Base Specification) sets the rules for room updates (Flow Control update). It recommends how often to send room-left messages (UpdateFC). It also defines an optional room-update timer (Flow Control Update timer).

What goes wrong: The receiver gives room back only through room-left messages (UpdateFC). If it stops, the sender must wait. It may stop because its buffers are full, or because of a bug. Requests that need an answer, such as reads, can then pile up behind. The whole device stalls. The rule book defines an optional watchdog. It re-tunes the wire when no UpdateFC arrives for a while. One patent summary gives 200 µs for PCIe 2.0, but this is not sure. It also notes that the watchdog cannot catch UpdateFCs that arrive with an unchanged value.

How you can tell: NVMe commands stall and run out of time, with no AER error. The exception is when the optional watchdog is built in. Then it shows as a fixable or unfixable error and a re-tune, depending on the design. Linux shows read and write timeouts and an NVMe controller reset.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Risky, test machine only: use a test sender (exerciser) that holds back UpdateFC for one credit type. Watch whether the device under test (DUT) stalls, recovers or reports an error. Plot the UpdateFC values for each type over time, with the packet counts of that type. Look for a flat UpdateFC with no packets of that type, while other types still flow. This shows the starved type and which side holds the credits. Note the time of the last UpdateFC. Compare it with the NVMe command time limit on the computer.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No (Timer only). No error message is sent. Only a time limit running out shows it. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Find the side that stopped giving room. If the computer's port stops returning write credits, blame the computer or platform. That means a memory or IOMMU stall. If the SSD stops, blame the SSD's firmware. · Test that confirms it: Read the error lines in the kernel log (Kernel AER log decode, confirmation test T2).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book (PCIe Base Specification), version 6.0 and later, has a block mode (Flit mode). In it, data travels in fixed-size blocks (Flits). The rules cover the repair code (FEC), the check number (CRC) and resending Flits (Flit replay).

What goes wrong: Sometimes more errors hit a Flit than the repair code (FEC) can fix. Then the check number fails, and the receiver throws the Flit away. Its packets and receipt content come back by resending. A rising count of repaired Flits is the early warning. A rising count of check-number failures costs speed and adds delay.

How you can tell: Fixable errors in AER on the receiving side. The exact AER bits, and any Flit-only counters, depend on the rule book version and the design. This is not sure. Linux v7.2 can log packet headers saved in Flit format (PCI_ERR_CAP_TLP_LOG_FLIT). Nothing shows at the NVMe level, unless resends get worse.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Risky, test machine only: use Gen6 receiver margining or a lossy wire path. Or insert errors with a Gen6 test sender (exerciser). Track repaired and check-failed Flits for each lane, each second. Work out the resend cost. Compare repaired-Flit rates between slots or cables, as a measure of margin. Confirm check-number failures by the other side's Nak.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No (Degraded). No error is reported. Things still work, but slower or on a weaker wire. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: It depends on the spread. For random failures, suspect the wire path margin: the PAM4 signal eye, tuning or signal boosters. Suspect one sender if failures follow one direction only, after a settings change. · Test that confirms it: A raw copy of the settings area (Raw config snapshot, E02).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book (PCIe Base Specification), version 6.0 and later, covers block mode. This includes Flit sequence numbers, Ack/Nak in Flit mode, and resend rules.

What goes wrong: Block mode keeps Ack/Nak resending, but for whole Flits. Public papers mention speed-ups. One is not resending Flits that carry only empty content (NOP). Another is resending only the failed Flit. This is not sure. Bugs in this new set of rules show as needless resends. At worst, packets are lost.

How you can tell: Mostly lost speed and added delay. Errors that break the rules should be reported as Data Link Protocol errors, or similar unfixable errors. This is not yet checked against the rule book.

How to fix it and prove the fix: For each direction, list the new Flit sequence numbers and the resends. Pair each Nak with the check-failed Flit it refers to. Sometimes a Nak comes, but the capture tool saw no check failure. This is either a receiver bug or something the capture tool missed. Check the lane errors at that moment.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No (Degraded). No error is reported. Things still work, but slower or on a weaker wire. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Look at the direction of the odd receipt or Flit. If it comes from the SSD, blame the SSD's receipt or Flit logic. If it comes from the computer's port or a signal booster, blame the platform or the wire. · Test that confirms it: Compare the error counters before and after (AER counter snapshot, confirmation test T1).

Error family: P08, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. P08 means wire start-up, re-tuning, and speed or width changes. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. The checker sees it from the order and timing of the packets. Examples are a missing answer, a long gap, or packets in the wrong order.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book (PCIe Base Specification), version 6.0 and later, covers block mode (Flit mode). It defines the Flit fields in the training signals. It defines the Flit Mode Supported bit in the PCI Express Capabilities setting. It also defines the Flit Mode Status bit in the Link Status 2 setting.

What goes wrong: Both ends must support Flit mode before it is used. The 64 GT/s speed needs it. A missing support bit, a firmware setting or failed tuning can leave a Gen6 SSD running at Gen5 or lower.

How you can tell: In lspci -vvv, the present speed (LnkSta) is below the possible speed (LnkCap). Linux v7.2 prints the available bandwidth, and whether the wire is in Flit mode. The bits are PCI_EXP_FLAGS_FLIT (Flit Mode Supported) and PCI_EXP_LNKSTA2_FLIT (Flit Mode Status).

How to fix it and prove the fix: Safe: compare with and without a signal booster or riser card. Record the start-up each time. Record start-up from reset, and read what both sides announce. Compare this with the support bits that software reads from the settings area.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No (Degraded). No error is reported. Things still work, but slower or on a weaker wire. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Find the side that did not announce the speed or Flit mode. If it is the SSD, blame the SSD. If it is the computer's port or BIOS, blame the platform. If both announce it but tuning fails, blame the wire. · Test that confirms it: Compare what the wire can do with what it is doing now (E02, a copy of the SSD's settings area).
