The checker sees it from the order and timing of the packets. Examples are a missing answer, a long gap, or packets in the wrong order.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book (PCIe Base Specification) lets devices report errors with messages. The Device Control setting has switches that turn error reporting on. The error-report feature (AER) records the details.

What goes wrong: An end device finds an error, and its reporting is on. It sends an error message to the computer's port (Root Port). A wire with constant fixable errors makes a steady stream of ERR_COR messages. Each one causes an AER interrupt on the computer.

How you can tell: On the computer: AER interrupts, kernel log (dmesg) lines limited in rate, and counters in sysfs. Sometimes a message flood uses a measurable amount of processor time.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Safe: run work on a wire with known fixable errors. Match the message counts in the recording with the sysfs counters. Count the error messages per second in the recording. For each one, look back for its cause in the other direction. That means errors in packets the SSD received. Sometimes no cause is visible. Then the error is inside the SSD, or on its receive side below what the capture tool could read.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Yes (Reported). The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Count the causes. Blame the wire when the causes are Nak, RxErr or BadDLLP. Blame the SSD when there is no cause and CorrIntErr is set. The count of causes decides. · Test that confirms it: Compare the counters with the recording.

X-27 The capture tool's probe causes or hides errors (probe effects) Partly seen in the packets Wire signal and capture-tool errors

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 290225: the capture tool shows a broken check number (bad LCRC). But the other side accepts it with an Ack, not a Nak. So it is a recording mistake (capture artefact).

Packet=290225 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=3621 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000003:CE6B5000 | Length=64 | DATA=256 B | Time Stamp=0130.120670144500s | Time Delta=0.000 ns | LCRC=0xC3FA1EE0 (Bad)

Error family: P09 and P27, two of the 27 ways an error shows on the wire. Proof from outside the recording also counts here. E08 is a second capture tool, switch counters or other logs. P09 means broken wire signals and capture-tool mistakes. P27 means signs of a recording problem that must stop a false alarm. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. This table file marks a wrong detail or a wrong order. The packet's check number shows it arrived broken (lcrc_flagged_bad).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: No rule applies directly. The rule book describes how the two sides behave, not probes. Use the receipt rules as the test: a bad check number (LCRC) must get a Nak.

What goes wrong: There are two cases. (a) The in-between board (interposer) weakens or reflects the signal. So the real wire gets worse, but only while the probe is fitted. There are more errors, lower speed and extra re-tunes. (b) The capture tool's own receiver reads worse than the two sides do. The recording shows errors the wire does not have.

How you can tell: Case (a): real AER counts and speed changes that go away without the in-between board. Case (b): nothing on the system.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Safe: record a lightly loaded wire with ASPM L1 turned on, then turned off. Compare the error marks. Check the packet numbers across each wake-up. The other side's Ack may cover numbers the recording never shows. Then the capture tool lost packets. Some errors fall only in the first few hundred nanoseconds after every wake-up. They are on all lanes, with no Nak. These come from the capture tool getting its lock back. Turn off ASPM and record again to confirm.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No (Silent). Nothing reports this error. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Blame the capture tool or the test set-up. That means the in-between board, the probe cables, or the capture tool's tuning settings. · Test that confirms it: A control run with the probe taken out.

X-28 The capture tool loses the first packets after a quiet period (re-lock) Partly seen in the packets Wire signal and capture-tool errors

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 292599: the capture tool locks onto the signal again after the wire wakes from quiet.

Packet=292599 | Link Dir=Upstream | Link Event=Analyzer: Loss of Lock / Resync | Marker=Resync | Time Stamp=0130.122856048000s | Time Delta=0.000 ns

Packet 292600: the capture tool shows a broken check number (bad LCRC). But the other side accepts it with an Ack, not a Nak. So it is a recording mistake (capture artefact).

Packet=292600 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(32) | PSN=619 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=57B90000 | Length=64 | DATA=256 B | Time Stamp=0130.122856048000s | Time Delta=0.000 ns | LCRC=0x6F6B504B (Bad)

Error family: P09 and P27, two of the 27 ways an error shows on the wire. Proof from outside the recording also counts here. E08 is a second capture tool, switch counters or other logs. P09 means broken wire signals and capture-tool mistakes. P27 means signs of a recording problem that must stop a false alarm. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. This table file marks a wrong detail or a wrong order. The packet's check number shows it arrived broken (lcrc_flagged_bad).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: No rule applies to the capture tool. The two sides follow the rules for L0s, L1 and the re-tune step (Recovery).

What goes wrong: After a quiet period, every receiver must get its bit, symbol or block lock back. The two sides get training signals for this. The capture tool only listens, so it may need longer. This is worse after a speed change. Then it must also follow the new speed and tuning. While it locks again, it either drops data or reads rubbish.

How you can tell: Nothing on the system.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Check the packet numbers across each wake-up. The other side's Ack may cover numbers the recording never shows. Then the capture tool lost packets. Some errors fall only in the first few hundred nanoseconds after every wake-up. They are on all lanes, with no Nak. These come from the capture tool getting its lock back. Turn off ASPM and record again to confirm.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No (Silent). Nothing reports this error. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Blame the capture tool (the test set-up). Strong power saving (ASPM) makes it happen more often, but it is not the fault. · Test that confirms it: Record again with ASPM turned off.

X-29 The capture tool is set up wrongly (analyzer setup errors) Partly seen in the packets Wire signal and capture-tool errors

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 293262: the capture tool shows a broken check number (bad LCRC). But the other side accepts it with an Ack, not a Nak. So it is a recording mistake (capture artefact).

Packet=293262 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=829 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000001:9EA33000 | Length=64 | DATA=256 B | Time Stamp=0130.123062571000s | Time Delta=0.000 ns | LCRC=0x54504839 (Bad)

Error family: P09 and P27, two of the 27 ways an error shows on the wire. Proof from outside the recording also counts here. E08 is a second capture tool, switch counters or other logs. P09 means broken wire signals and capture-tool mistakes. P27 means signs of a recording problem that must stop a false alarm. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. This table file marks a wrong detail or a wrong order. The packet's check number shows it arrived broken (lcrc_flagged_bad).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: No rule applies to the capture tool. Rules for reversed lanes, swapped pairs and scrambling are in the PCIe rule book. They are in its signal layer (PCIe Base Specification, Physical Layer).

What goes wrong: The capture tool must be told, or must learn, several facts about the wire. These are its width, lane order, swapped pairs, speed and clock set-up (common clock, SRNS, SRIS). At Gen3 and above, it also needs the scrambler and tuning state. If the recording starts after start-up, some of this cannot be learned from the wire. Its lane-matching limits may also be tighter than the device's.

How you can tell: Nothing on the system.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Safe: on a wire known to be good, set a wrong lane order in the capture tool on purpose. Learn what the false errors look like. Record again from start-up (reset or hot-plug). Turn on automatic wire set-up detection if the capture tool has it. If the errors go away, they came from the set-up. A real wire with that many errors would not run without AER reports and re-tunes.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No (Silent). Nothing reports this error. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Blame the capture tool's set-up. Check its lane map, swapped pairs, speed, clock, and descrambler or tuning state. · Test that confirms it: Record again from start-up.

X-30 Recording gaps or filters make a packet look missing (capture gaps) Partly seen in the packets Wire signal and capture-tool errors

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 295471: the first row after the recording buffer wrapped round (buffer wrap). 412 ms of traffic is missing.

Packet=295471 | Link Dir=Downstream | TLP Type=MWr(32) | Marker=Buffer Wrap: 412 ms not recorded | PSN=411 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=000:00:0 | Address=FCE01018 | Length=1 | DATA=4 B | Time Stamp=0130.535324073620s | Time Delta=142.130 ns | LCRC=0x89A3C961

Error family: P09 and P27, two of the 27 ways an error shows on the wire. Proof from outside the recording also counts here. E08 is a second capture tool, switch counters or other logs. P09 means broken wire signals and capture-tool mistakes. P27 means signs of a recording problem that must stop a false alarm. · Can the packets alone prove it? Partly. The order and timing of the packets show its shape. The proof needs evidence from outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: No rule applies to the capture tool. Some errors are claimed from something missing. An example is an answer that never came in time (Completion Timeout, error type L-14). Before such a claim, prove the recording has no gaps in that window.

What goes wrong: Hardware filters drop items before they are saved. Ring buffers write over the oldest data until the trigger. Some capture tools pause saving while the buffer is uploaded. Some pause when their inside speed limit is passed. This depends on the capture tool. The recording then shows something missing that did not happen on the wire.

How you can tell: Nothing on the system. The risk is a false report, such as "completion timeout", "missing interrupt" or "credit starvation".

How to fix it and prove the fix: Safe: record the same work with and without receipt-packet (DLLP) filtering. Compare what the checks report. Use packet numbers to check that nothing is missing. In each direction, new packet numbers must follow on without gaps (error type X-17). Ack numbers in the other direction must refer to packets in the recording. A jump with no Nak and no error means the recording lost data, not the wire. Write the filter settings into every report.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No (Silent). Nothing reports this error. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Blame the capture tool. Check its filters, its ring buffer wrapping round, and pauses in saving. · Test that confirms it: Compare a filtered and an unfiltered recording.

Chapter L: PCIe wire and request errors (40 entries)

Why this part is here: these 40 entries are errors in how packets, receipts and requests travel across the wire.

L-01 The receiver sees broken signals on the wire (Receiver Error, RxErr) Partly seen in the packets Wire signal and capture-tool errors

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 266382: a data block starts with a broken start mark (invalid 128b/130b sync header).

Packet=266382 | Link Dir=Upstream | Link Event=Invalid Sync Header (Lane 3) | Time Stamp=0129.995257138000s | Time Delta=0.000 ns

Packet 266406: the SSD reports a receiving error (Receiver Error) with a fixable-error message (ERR_COR).

Packet=266406 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=Msg | PSN=3770 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Length=0 | Time Stamp=0129.995257889370s | Time Delta=16.380 ns | LCRC=0xE1C5E8C0

Error family: P09, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. Proof from outside the recording also counts here. E01 is the Linux kernel log (dmesg). E02 is a copy of the SSD's settings area (lspci). P09 means broken wire signals and capture-tool mistakes. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. This table file marks a wrong detail or a wrong order. The packet's check number shows it arrived broken (lcrc_flagged_bad). The same packet was sent again with the same packet number (tlp_replayed_same_psn).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book (PCIe Base Specification) defines the fixable-error status setting (AER Correctable Error Status register). It has a Receiver Error Status bit. The signal layer (Physical Layer) has the receiving-error rules.

What goes wrong: The receiver sees a broken symbol, a balance error or a block-code error. Or it sees a framing error, or lanes that cannot be lined up (deskew). The packet or receipt that held it is dropped. Normally it is sent again.

How you can tell: Fixable-status bit 0 (PCI_ERR_COR_RCVR), and an ERR_COR message to the computer's port (Root Port). Linux v7.2 prints "PCIe Bus Error: severity=Correctable, type=Physical Layer, (Receiver ID)" and "[ 0] RxErr". It prints them at warning level (KERN_WARNING), limited in rate. The RxErr counter in aer_dev_correctable goes up. The NVMe layer reports nothing.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Read the counters at both ends (cat /sys/bus/pci/devices/<BDF>/aer_dev_correctable). lspci -vvv shows CESta: RxErr+ and DevSta: CorrErr+. For detail on each lane, read the Lane Error Status setting. It sits in the Secondary PCIe Extended Capability. Use setpci only to read it. Or use the platform's lane-margining tool (Gen4+ Lane Margining at the Receiver).

Does the SSD or computer report it? Yes (Reported). The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Blame the wire path by default. Blame the SSD or the platform when errors occur only at one end's receiver. That is on a clean wire, with normal margining. Blame the capture tool when the other side does not react. The Link Dir column tells which receiver saw it. · Test that confirms it: Compare the error counters at both ends.

L-02 A broken or wrongly numbered packet is sent again (Bad TLP) Seen in the packets Broken packets sent again

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 317656: a request or data packet (TLP) arrived with a broken check number (bad LCRC).

Packet=317656 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=556 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000003:F7B93300 | Length=64 | DATA=256 B | Time Stamp=0130.949051674500s | Time Delta=0.000 ns | LCRC=0x23EB4E6D (Bad)

Packet 317665: the refused packet is sent again with the same packet number (PSN).

Packet=317665 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=556 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000003:F7B93300 | Length=64 | DATA=256 B | Time Stamp=0130.949052217000s | Time Delta=0.000 ns | LCRC=0x231B416D

Error family: P06, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. Proof from outside the recording also counts here. E01 is the Linux kernel log (dmesg). E02 is a copy of the SSD's settings area (lspci). P06 means packets that arrive broken and are sent again. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. This table file marks a wrong detail or a wrong order. The packet's check number shows it arrived broken (lcrc_flagged_bad). The same packet was sent again with the same packet number (tlp_replayed_same_psn).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book (PCIe Base Specification) covers the receipt-and-resend layer (Data Link Layer). This includes the check number (LCRC), the packet number (Sequence Number) and the Ack/Nak rules. AER has a Bad TLP status bit for it.

What goes wrong: A packet arrives with a bad check number or an unexpected packet number. The receiver sends a Nak, and the sender sends it again. The NVMe command is delayed by about one resend round trip.

How you can tell: Fixable bit 6 (PCI_ERR_COR_BAD_TLP), shown as "[ 6] BadTLP". Linux reports it as Data Link Layer / Receiver ID. The BadTLP counter goes up.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Same as error type L-01. Risky, test machine only: an error-making in-between board or fault tool (jammer) can break the check number of chosen packets. It needs lab equipment. Read the counters at both ends. Sometimes BadTLP rises only during large data moves (DMA). Writes to the SSD stress the computer-to-SSD direction (RC→EP). Reads stress the SSD-to-computer direction (EP→RC). Then the problem depends on direction. Look at the sender on the far side.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Yes (Reported). The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: It depends on the pattern. Blame the wire path when bad check numbers are spread over many packet types. Blame the sender in that direction when one packet format fails the same way each time. The side that reports it is the receiver (Receiver ID). Marked packets going Upstream point to the SSD's sender, or the wire toward the root port. · Test that confirms it: Compare the error counters before and after (AER counter snapshot, confirmation test T1).

L-03 A small receipt packet arrives broken (Bad DLLP) Seen in the packets Broken packets sent again

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 318308: an "arrived fine" receipt (Ack DLLP) has a broken check number (bad CRC 16). The receiver ignores it.

Packet=318308 | Link Dir=Downstream | DLLP Type=ACK | Time Stamp=0130.949210135870s | Time Delta=42.620 ns | AckNak Seq Num=728

Error family: P06, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. Proof from outside the recording also counts here. E01 is the Linux kernel log (dmesg). E02 is a copy of the SSD's settings area (lspci). P06 means packets that arrive broken and are sent again. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. This table file marks a wrong detail or a wrong order. A receipt packet's check number shows it arrived broken (dllp_crc_flagged_bad).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book (PCIe Base Specification) covers the check number on receipt packets (DLLP CRC). AER has a Bad DLLP status bit for it.

What goes wrong: A receipt packet fails its 16-bit check number and is thrown away. It may be an Ack, a Nak, a room-left message (UpdateFC) or a power message (PM). A lost Ack does no harm, because later Acks also cover earlier packets. But if the next Ack is also late, error type L-05 follows. A lost UpdateFC can leave the sender short of room for a moment.

How you can tell: Fixable bit 7 (PCI_ERR_COR_BAD_DLLP), shown as "[ 7] BadDLLP", Data Link Layer.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Same as error types L-01 and L-02. Read the counters. Look for speed dips at the same time as bursts of BadDLLP. These show the sender running out of room (credit starvation).

Does the SSD or computer report it? Yes (Reported). The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: It depends on the marks. Blame the wire quality in that direction for random or bursty marks. Blame the sending port when one receipt type keeps breaking on a clean wire. The side that reports it in AER is the receiver of the receipt packet. · Test that confirms it: Compare the error counters before and after (AER counter snapshot, confirmation test T1).

Packet=319202 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=Msg | PSN=1038 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Length=0 | Time Stamp=0130.949467777000s | Time Delta=171.120 ns | LCRC=0x03366AEF

Error family: P06, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. Proof from outside the recording also counts here. E01 is the Linux kernel log (dmesg). E02 is a copy of the SSD's settings area (lspci). P06 means packets that arrive broken and are sent again. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. This table file marks a wrong detail or a wrong order. The same packet was sent again with the same packet number (tlp_replayed_same_psn).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book (PCIe Base Specification) covers the resend counter (REPLAY_NUM) and entering the re-tune step (Recovery). AER has a REPLAY_NUM Rollover status bit.

What goes wrong: The same packet was resent until the 2-bit resend counter (REPLAY_NUM) rolled over. The sender starts the re-tune step of wire start-up (LTSSM Recovery). No new packets move while the wire re-tunes. This usually takes microseconds, but sometimes much longer. If re-tuning picks a lower speed, the wire stays slower (error type L-25).

How you can tell: Fixable bit 8 (PCI_ERR_COR_REP_ROLL), shown as "[ 8] Rollover", Data Link / Transmitter ID. The sender logs it. So the device that logs it is the one whose packets were not getting through. If the port supports bandwidth notices, the Link Status flag LBMS may also be set. Linux bwctrl tracks this.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Risky, test machine only: use an in-between board that refuses or breaks every copy of one packet. Or margin the wire until roll-overs appear. Read the Rollover counter. Check the LnkSta speed and width before and after. In the capture tool, look for TS1/TS2 training signals in the middle of traffic (Recovery). Repeated roll-overs are the "recovery storm" of error type L-26.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Yes (Reported). The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: It depends on what goes with the resends. Blame the wire when Naks or bad receipts come with them. That means a very poor signal, clock recovery (CDR) losing lock, or a dead lane. Blame the receiver when it never sends an Ack for a clean packet. The side that reports it in AER is the sender. Its packets were not getting through. · Test that confirms it: Compare the error counters before and after (AER counter snapshot, confirmation test T1).

L-05 No receipt in time, so packets are resent (Replay Timer Timeout) Seen in the packets Broken packets sent again

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 319513: a resend after the resend timer ran out, with no Ack or Nak in between.

Packet=319513 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=1180 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000001:217E8000 | Length=64 | DATA=256 B | Time Stamp=0130.949642673120s | Time Delta=159.630 ns | LCRC=0x09BA4A3A

Packet 319515: the fixable error Replay Timer Timeout is recorded.

Packet=319515 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=Msg | PSN=1181 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Length=0 | Time Stamp=0130.949643673120s | Time Delta=141.130 ns | LCRC=0xFD7163FE

Error family: P06, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. Proof from outside the recording also counts here. E01 is the Linux kernel log (dmesg). E02 is a copy of the SSD's settings area (lspci). P06 means packets that arrive broken and are sent again. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. This table file marks a wrong detail or a wrong order. The same packet was sent again with the same packet number (tlp_replayed_same_psn).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book (PCIe Base Specification) covers the resend timer (REPLAY_TIMER) and its limit formula. The limit depends on the wire width, the largest data size, and the L0s wake-up delay. AER has a Replay Timer Timeout status bit.

What goes wrong: The sender's resend timer runs out before any Ack or Nak arrives for its waiting packets. So it resends them all. At wire level this is "timer only", but AER does report it.

How you can tell: Fixable bit 12 (PCI_ERR_COR_REP_TIMER), shown as "[12] Timeout", Data Link / Transmitter ID. Do not mix it up with the time limit for answers (Completion Timeout, unfixable bit 14, error type L-14).

How to fix it and prove the fix: Careful: turn on strong power saving. Set /sys/module/pcie_aspm/parameters/policy to powersupersave. Use bursty reads and writes with few commands waiting (low queue depth). Compare the counts with ASPM off. Read the Timeout counter. It may follow ASPM being on, and go away after a test boot with pcie_aspm=off. Then suspect the wake-up delay from power saving (error type L-37).

Does the SSD or computer report it? Yes (Reported). The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: It depends on the cause. Blame the wire when an Ack was lost. Blame the receiver that sends Acks when its Acks are late. Blame the platform's power-saving policy, or that receiver's wire circuit, when it was in low power. Blame a stall inside the other side when it is silent. The side that reports it in AER is the sender. · Test that confirms it: Compare the error counters before and after (AER counter snapshot, confirmation test T1).

L-06 An unfixable error reported as a fixable one (Advisory Non-Fatal Error) Partly seen in the packets Error report messages

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 373312: an answer that says "request not supported" (UR completion).

Packet=373312 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=Cpl | PSN=971 | Tag=29 | RequesterID=000:00:0 | CompleterID=002:00:0 | Cpl Status=UR | Byte Cnt=4 | Time Stamp=0194.541182630370s | Time Delta=161.630 ns | LCRC=0x80DB39F6

Packet 373314: the UR is reported as advisory, with a fixable-error message (Advisory Non-Fatal, ERR_COR).

Packet=373314 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=Msg | PSN=972 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Length=0 | Time Stamp=0194.541182830370s | Time Delta=142.130 ns | LCRC=0xD1EE5E50

Error family: P10, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. Proof from outside the recording also counts here. E01 is the Linux kernel log (dmesg). E02 is a copy of the SSD's settings area (lspci). P10 means error report messages and what is missing around them. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. This table file marks a wrong detail or a wrong order. An answer says the request is not supported (UR) (completion_status_UR).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book (PCIe Base Specification) lists when an Advisory Non-Fatal Error applies. AER has a status bit and a mask bit for it. A set mask bit hides the error.

What goes wrong: The PCIe rules let some unfixable, non-fatal errors be sent as "advisory". This applies when the side that found the error is not the side that must act. A common case is a side that answers a request with UR and also logs the error. It sends ERR_COR instead of ERR_NONFATAL. This is because the side that asked will handle the failed answer. The unfixable status bit (for example UR) is still set as well.

How you can tell: Fixable bit 13 (PCI_ERR_COR_ADV_NFAT), shown as "[13] NonFatalErr". The real unfixable bit is also set in the same device's unfixable status. Linux does not print that bit on this path. The rule book hides (masks) it by default, so many systems never show it.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Safe, if not hidden: use lspci to scan functions that do not exist. Careful: un-hiding the bit with setpci changes the platform settings. In lspci -vvv, look for CESta: AdvNonFatalErr+ together with UESta: UnsupReq+ on the same device. Read both settings with setpci, only reading.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Yes (Reported). The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Look at what the request asked for. Blame the computer's software when it asks for a missing function or a setting that is not built. That shows as RequesterID 000:00:0. Blame the SSD when it answers UR/CA for a setting that its address map (bar_map) or NVMe says is built. · Test that confirms it: Read the AER status.

L-07 The SSD fixed an error inside itself (Corrected Internal Error) Not seen in the packets Error report messages

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 374259: a fixable-error message (ERR_COR) with no cause visible on the wire.

Packet=374259 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=Msg | PSN=1213 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Length=0 | Time Stamp=0194.541392036120s | Time Delta=152.130 ns | LCRC=0xD3D25104

Error family: P10, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. Proof from outside the recording also counts here. E01 is the Linux kernel log (dmesg). E02 is a copy of the SSD's settings area (lspci). P10 means error report messages and what is missing around them. · Can the packets alone prove it? No. It cannot be seen on this wire. The rows shown only give what happened around it. The proof is outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book (PCIe Base Specification) has an optional Corrected Internal Error status bit and mask bit.

What goes wrong: The device found and fixed an error inside itself. An example is a one-bit memory error fixed by its repair code (ECC). This could be in a buffer memory of the PCIe or NVMe front end. The device decides what counts as an internal error.

How you can tell: Fixable bit 14 (PCI_ERR_COR_INTERNAL), shown as "[14] CorrIntErr". It is hidden (masked) by default. Linux v7.2 un-hides internal errors only for CXL devices. The function is pci_aer_unmask_internal_errors(), shared only with cxl_core. Its comment says internal errors are "too device-specific to enable generally".

How to fix it and prove the fix: Only the maker's own error insertion can create it. Careful: un-hide it on a lab machine with setpci, then watch the counter. Match it with the NVMe health log (SMART) field "Media and Data Integrity Errors". Also match it with the maker's own records (telemetry).

Does the SSD or computer report it? Yes (Reported). The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Blame the SSD: it fixed a fault inside itself. Blame the wire instead if the status read shows RxErr or BadTLP, not CorrIntErr. · Test that confirms it: Read the AER status.

Error family: P10, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. Proof from outside the recording also counts here. E01 is the Linux kernel log (dmesg). E02 is a copy of the SSD's settings area (lspci). P10 means error report messages and what is missing around them. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. This table file marks a wrong detail or a wrong order. The packet's "bad data" mark (EP bit) is on (header_bit_EP_set).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book (PCIe Base Specification) covers saving several packet headers (Multiple Header Recording). It also has a Header Log Overflow status bit.

What goes wrong: Saving several headers is turned on, and the device's header log is full. So the packet header of the next error is lost. Information is lost just when errors arrive fastest.

How you can tell: Fixable bit 15 (PCI_ERR_COR_LOG_OVER), shown as "[15] HeaderOF". It is hidden (masked) by default.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Take it as a sign that the logged header may not be typical. Look at the first error, not the last.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Yes (Reported). The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Find where the burst comes from. Blame the SSD when the burst comes from its data mover (DMA engine). The bad packets then carry the SSD's RequesterID. Blame the computer when software is slow to clear the log. That shows as a long gap between the message and the settings write (CfgWr) to AER+0x04. · Test that confirms it: Read the AER settings (AER capability read).

L-09 An unused error bit is set (old "Training Error" bit) Not seen in the packets Error report messages

Packet 379107: bit 0 of the unfixable-error status is set. This bit is unused today (Undefined). It was once the "Training Error" bit.

Packet=379107 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=CplD | PSN=2840 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=000:00:0 | CompleterID=002:00:0 | Cpl Status=SC | Length=1 | Byte Cnt=4 | DATA=4 B | Time Stamp=0194.543957254870s | Time Delta=7.000 ns | LCRC=0x0BD35727

Error family: P10, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. Proof from outside the recording also counts here. E01 is the Linux kernel log (dmesg). E02 is a copy of the SSD's settings area (lspci). P10 means error report messages and what is missing around them. · Can the packets alone prove it? No. It cannot be seen on this wire. The rows shown only give what happened around it. The proof is outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book (PCIe Base Specification) says bit 0 of the unfixable-error status is unused (Undefined) in current versions.

What goes wrong: In early PCIe versions, bit 0 of the unfixable status was "Training Error". It is now unused. A device that sets it is either very old or has a bug.

How you can tell: "[ 0] Undefined" in the AER log (PCI_ERR_UNC_UND).

How to fix it and prove the fix: Read UESta with lspci -vvv. Report it to the maker as a failure to follow the rule book (compliance issue).

Does the SSD or computer report it? Yes (Reported). The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Blame the SSD. An old reused circuit design (legacy IP) or its firmware writes the wrong bit. · Test that confirms it: Read the status.

L-10 Receipt rules broken (Data Link Protocol Error, DLP) Seen in the packets Error report messages

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 381035: an Ack for a packet number (PSN) that was never sent. This is a Data Link Protocol Error.

Packet=381035 | Link Dir=Downstream | DLLP Type=ACK | Time Stamp=0194.544112014500s | Time Delta=127.880 ns | AckNak Seq Num=3444

Packet 381038: a fatal-error message (ERR_FATAL).

Packet=381038 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=Msg | PSN=3344 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Length=0 | Time Stamp=0194.544112514500s | Time Delta=138.120 ns | LCRC=0xAD4013E9

Error family: P10, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. Proof from outside the recording also counts here. E01 is the Linux kernel log (dmesg). E02 is a copy of the SSD's settings area (lspci). P10 means error report messages and what is missing around them. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. This table file marks a wrong detail or a wrong order. A receipt names a packet number that was never sent (ack_for_unsent_psn).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book (PCIe Base Specification) defines the Data Link Protocol Error. It also defines checks on the receipt number (AckNak_Seq_Num).

What goes wrong: The receipt-and-resend layer (Data Link Layer) got an Ack or Nak with a wrong packet number. The number matches no packet still waiting for a receipt. Or the layer saw another break of its rules. The resend records can no longer be trusted. By default the error is Fatal.

How you can tell: "[ 4] DLP", severity=Uncorrectable (Fatal), type=Data Link Layer. Linux v7.2 calls pcie_do_recovery(..., pci_channel_io_frozen, aer_root_reset). This takes the wire down and up again. The NVMe driver logs "frozen state error detected, reset controller", then "restart after slot reset". Reads and writes that were on the way are retried or failed.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Risky, test machine only: use a test sender or in-between board that inserts bad AckNak_Seq_Num values. Software insertion with aer-inject (CONFIG_PCIEAER_INJECT) only tests the recovery steps, not the hardware. Read the AER log and the DLP count in the aer_dev_fatal counter. Record with the capture tool, triggered on "Ack/Nak sequence out of range".

Does the SSD or computer report it? Yes (Reported). The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Find who sent the bad receipt. Downstream means the root port's receipt layer (platform). Upstream means the SSD. Blame a signal booster (retimer) when both ends' packet streams look sane. The damage is then seen at one probe point only. Two probes are needed. · Test that confirms it: The AER log and counter.

L-11 The wire drops without warning (Surprise Down Error, SDES) Partly seen in the packets Wire goes down, power, restart

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 1351322: the wire goes quiet with no go-quiet signal (EIOS), no power message and no Hot Reset. Nobody asked the wire to go down.

Packet=1351322 | Link Event=Electrical Idle | Time Stamp=1319.021667436000s | Time Delta=0.000 ns

Error family: P12, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. Proof from outside the recording also counts here. E01 is the Linux kernel log (dmesg). E02 is a copy of the SSD's settings area (lspci). P12 means the wire going down while packets are on the way. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. This table file marks a wrong detail or a wrong order. A request was lost when the wire went down (request_lost_across_link_down).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book (PCIe Base Specification) covers the Surprise Down Error. It covers reporting whether the wire is active (Data Link Layer Link Active reporting). It also covers sudden removal from hot-plug slots (Hot-Plug surprise).

What goes wrong: A port on the computer side (Downstream Port) supports Surprise Down reporting. It may be a Root Port or a switch port (DSP). It sees its wire go from active (DL_Active) to inactive (DL_Inactive) without being told to. To the computer, the SSD has vanished. Every read of an SSD setting (MMIO read) returns all ones. Writes are dropped. Data moves (DMA) on the way are lost.

How you can tell: Unfixable bit 5 is set on the Downstream Port, not on the SSD. By default it is Fatal. Linux prints "[ 5] SDES" as "Transaction Layer". Sometimes the port shut-off feature (DPC) is on, and the port is a hot-plug bridge. Then dpc_is_surprise_removal() treats it as an expected removal. It quietly cleans up (dpc_handle_surprise_removal()). Otherwise DPC or AER recovery runs. The NVMe driver then sees CSTS == ~0 on its next setting read, or in nvme_timeout(). It logs "controller is down; will reset: CSTS=0xffffffff, PCI_STATUS=0xffff" or "PCI_STATUS read failed". The hint lines about power saving follow (error type C-01).

How to fix it and prove the fix: Careful: pull a hot-plug U.2 or E3.S drive out of a hot-plug bay while reads and writes run. Risky, test machine only: cut slot power with a controllable riser or power in-between board. Never do this on an M.2 slot that is not hot-plug. On the port, lspci -vvv -s <port> shows UESta: SDES+ and LnkSta DLActive-. On the SSD, settings reads return ff. Afterwards, check the "unsafe shutdowns" counter in nvme smart-log. If it went up by one, the drive lost power or reset without a shutdown notice.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Yes (Reported). The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Look at who went silent first. Blame the SSD if it drops the wire (Upstream silent first) while slot power is steady. Blame the platform or the wire if slot power fails, the connector is loose, or both directions stop together. · Test that confirms it: Read the port's AER.

Packet=401087 | Link Dir=Downstream | TLP Type=CplD | PSN=1458 | Tag=96 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | CompleterID=000:02:4 | Cpl Status=SC | Length=64 | Byte Cnt=512 | DATA=256 B | Time Stamp=0195.066578203250s | Time Delta=0.000 ns | LCRC=0xA0F4A4CA

Error family: P11, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. Proof from outside the recording also counts here. E01 is the Linux kernel log (dmesg). E02 is a copy of the SSD's settings area (lspci). P11 means packets that are marked bad, broken or too big. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. This table file marks a wrong detail or a wrong order. The packet's "bad data" mark (EP bit) is on (header_bit_EP_set).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book (PCIe Base Specification) covers marking data as bad (Data Poisoning). It defines the EP bit and the Poisoned TLP Received status. The NVMe rule book (NVMe Base Specification) lists general result numbers a controller can return. Examples are Data Transfer Error and Internal Error. Check which one your device uses.

What goes wrong: A packet arrives with its bad-data mark on (EP, Error Poisoned bit). Its data is known to be bad. Most often, the computer's memory controller found an unfixable memory error (ECC). This happened while it served the SSD's read of write data (DMA read). It then sent the answer (CplD) marked as bad. The opposite case is the SSD sending bad-marked read data. That happens because of an unfixable error inside the SSD.

How you can tell: Unfixable bit 12 is set at the receiver. By default it is Non-fatal, and the packet header is logged. Linux prints "[12] TLP" and a "TLP Header:" line. Recovery runs with pci_channel_io_normal. nvme_error_detected() returns CAN_RECOVER, so there is no reset. The controller decides what happens to the NVMe command. A well-behaved SSD fails the write with a data-transfer or internal-error result. It does not save the bad data. This depends on the design. A poor SSD may write it. Sometimes the computer receives bad-marked read data. Then the platform's error policy (RAS policy) decides the result. It may be a machine check, dropped data, or the bad mark spreading in memory. This also depends on the design.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Risky, test machine only: insert errors while saving several headers (multiple-header recording) is on. Take it as a sign that the logged header may not be typical. Look at the first error, not the last.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Yes (Reported). The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Look at the direction. A Downstream answer (CplD) with EP = 1 points to the platform. That means host memory or the root complex (CompleterID 000:02:4). An Upstream write or answer with EP = 1 points to the SSD. It had an unfixable error inside, or it passed bad data on. Blame a switch if the bad mark appears only on its way out (two probes). · Test that confirms it: Match the header in the AER log (AER header match).

L-13 Room rules broken (Flow Control Protocol Error, FCP) Seen in the packets Room-left messages (credits)

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 355710: write packets that need no answer (posted TLPs) were sent past the room the receiver announced.

Packet=355710 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=925 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000004:576AB700 | Length=64 | DATA=256 B | Time Stamp=0161.616827900750s | Time Delta=0.000 ns | LCRC=0xDD0BBE4C

Packet 355712: a room-left message (UpdateFC) announces more than 2^(n-1) credits.

Packet=355712 | Link Dir=Upstream | DLLP Type=UpdateFC-P | Time Stamp=0161.616827936370s | Time Delta=0.000 ns

Error family: P07, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. Proof from outside the recording also counts here. E01 is the Linux kernel log (dmesg). E02 is a copy of the SSD's settings area (lspci). P07 means room-left messages (credits) that stop or go wrong. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. The checker sees it from the order and timing of the packets. Examples are a missing answer, a long gap, or packets in the wrong order.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book (PCIe Base Specification) covers the room rules (Flow Control) and the Flow Control Protocol Error.

What goes wrong: The room-credit rules were broken. For example, the start message (InitFC) announced illegal values. Or the credits overflow the counter field. The credit records are now broken. By default this is Fatal, and the wire is reset.

How you can tell: "[13] FCP", Fatal. Recovery runs with a frozen channel, and the NVMe controller is reset. The messages are as in error type L-10.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Record the start and update messages (InitFC and UpdateFC receipt packets) with the capture tool. Record around wire start-up or around the event.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Yes (Reported). The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Find the side that announced the room. Illegal values from the SSD (Upstream receipt packets) point to the SSD. From the root port (Downstream), they point to the platform. Bugs in a port's built-in circuit design are more likely on FPGA prototypes. · Test that confirms it: Compare the error counters before and after (AER counter snapshot, confirmation test T1).

L-14 A read request never gets an answer (Completion Timeout) Partly seen in the packets Answer never arrives in time

Packet 1299064: a read request (MRd) fetching write data. The wire confirmed it arrived, but no answer ever came.

Packet=1299066 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=Msg | PSN=2451 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Length=0 | Time Stamp=1265.685842702250s | Time Delta=148.120 ns | LCRC=0x4FFE5483
