Packet=1299068 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=2452 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000004:83430020 | Length=4 | DATA=16 B | Time Stamp=1265.685882702250s | Time Delta=0.000 ns | LCRC=0x7458C9C1

Error family: P03, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. Proof from outside the recording also counts here. E01 is the Linux kernel log (dmesg). E02 is a copy of the SSD's settings area (lspci). P03 means a read request that never gets an answer. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. This table file marks a wrong detail or a wrong order. An answer did not arrive within the time limit (completion_timeout).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book (PCIe Base Specification) covers the answer time limit (Completion Timeout). The Device Control 2 setting holds the "Completion Timeout Value" and "Completion Timeout Disable". The Device Capabilities 2 setting lists the "Completion Timeout Ranges Supported". The time limit can be set. A default range of 50 µs to 50 ms is often quoted. This is not yet checked against the rule book.

What goes wrong: A side sent a request that needs an answer (MRd, CfgRd, and so on). No answer arrived within its time limit. In NVMe there are two cases. (a) The computer never answers the SSD's read. The SSD was reading a command (SQE), a memory address list (PRP or SGL), or write data. Causes are an IOMMU quietly dropping it, a deadlock in the root complex, or a switch problem. The SSD logs CmpltTO. It usually ends the command with an error result, or hangs. (b) The computer's processor reads an SSD setting (MMIO read), but gets no answer. The controller's PCIe front end is hung. The root port logs CmpltTO. The processor receives all ones, or on some platforms a machine check. This depends on the design.

How you can tell: Unfixable bit 14 is set on the side that asked. By default it is Non-fatal, and the reporting agent is "Requester ID". A header is logged only if the device announces PCI_ERR_CAP_COMP_TIME_LOG. Effects on NVMe: case (a) gives a done-note error or an NVMe read/write timeout. The log line is "I/O tag N (cid) opcode 0x.. (...) QID n timeout, aborting ...". Case (b) gives "CSTS=0xffffffff → controller is down; will reset".

How to fix it and prove the fix: Risky, test machine only: use a test sender (exerciser) acting as host memory. It holds back the answers (CplD) for chosen request numbers. Careful: on a test machine, shorten the SSD's Completion Timeout Value. Do it in Device Control 2 with setpci. This makes borderline delays visible. See which device logged it: the SSD (case a) or the Root Port (case b). In lspci -vvv, DevCtl2 shows "Completion Timeout: 50us to 50ms" or similar. It also shows whether it is turned off. Match it with IOMMU fault logs and the NVMe timeout messages.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No (Timer only). No error message is sent. Only a time limit running out shows it. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Find who got no answer. Blame the SSD if the computer's setting read gets no answer (the SSD front end hung). Blame the platform if the SSD's read gets no answer from the root complex. Causes are an IOMMU drop, a root complex deadlock, or a switch. · Test that confirms it: Read the AER completion-timeout log.

L-15 The answering side refuses a request (Completer Abort, CA) Seen in the packets Answer says the request failed

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 78046: the root complex answers the SSD's data read with CA (refused).

Packet=78046 | Link Dir=Downstream | TLP Type=Cpl | PSN=2563 | Tag=239 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | CompleterID=000:02:4 | Cpl Status=CA | Byte Cnt=512 | Time Stamp=0063.979653964620s | Time Delta=0.000 ns | LCRC=0x31331975

Packet 78071: the done note (CQE) says Data Transfer Error.

Packet=78071 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=856 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000004:80790020 | Length=4 | DATA=16 B | Time Stamp=0063.979664423870s | Time Delta=26.870 ns | LCRC=0x3B493D76

Error family: P04, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. Proof from outside the recording also counts here. E01 is the Linux kernel log (dmesg). E02 is a copy of the SSD's settings area (lspci). P04 means an answer that says the request failed. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. This table file marks a wrong detail or a wrong order. An answer says the receiving side refused the request (CA) (completion_status_CA).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book (PCIe Base Specification) covers the answer result CA (Completion Status CA). It also covers the Completer Abort status bit.

What goes wrong: The answering side understood the request, but refused it because of its own rule. Reasons are an access that is not allowed, or an access size a setting does not support. Or the device is in a state where it cannot serve it. It returns an answer with result CA and logs bit 15. The side that asked sees an "unsuccessful completion".

How you can tell: "[15] CmpltAbrt", reporting agent "Completer ID", header logged, Non-fatal by default. If the SSD refuses a setting read from the computer (MMIO read), the processor usually sees all ones. If the root complex refuses an SSD data read (DMA read), the SSD's command fails.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Careful, on a throw-away machine only: use a test tool to make odd-size setting reads. Aim them at reserved places in the SSD's memory window (BAR). Read the logged header: address and requester. If the address is inside the SSD's first memory window (BAR0), look at the access size and offset.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Yes (Reported). The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Look at the request. Blame the computer when its setting access is wrong for that setting: size, boundary or reserved. Blame the SSD when a legal access gets CA. Blame the platform when the root complex answers the SSD's data move with CA. · Test that confirms it: Read the header in the AER log (AER header log decode).

L-16 An answer arrives that nobody asked for (Unexpected Completion) Seen in the packets Wrong request number or sender

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 105258: an answer with data (CplD) for request number 63, but no open request has that number.

Packet=105258 | Link Dir=Downstream | TLP Type=CplD | PSN=2468 | Tag=63 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | CompleterID=000:02:4 | Cpl Status=SC | Length=16 | Byte Cnt=64 | DATA=64 B | Time Stamp=0125.571032426870s | Time Delta=12.630 ns | LCRC=0xD0CCF295

Packet 105261: Unexpected Completion is reported as advisory, with a fixable-error message (ERR_COR).

Packet=105261 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=Msg | PSN=641 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Length=0 | Time Stamp=0125.571032926870s | Time Delta=172.130 ns | LCRC=0x71442E57

Error family: P05, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. Proof from outside the recording also counts here. E01 is the Linux kernel log (dmesg). E02 is a copy of the SSD's settings area (lspci). P05 means an unexpected answer, or a wrong request number or sender. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. This table file marks a wrong detail or a wrong order. An answer arrived that nobody asked for (unexpected_completion).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book (PCIe Base Specification) covers the Unexpected Completion status and the rules for matching answers to requests.

What goes wrong: An answer arrives whose Requester ID and request number (Tag) match no open request. Usually the answer arrives after the side that asked already gave up (Completion Timeout). Another case is an answer sent to the wrong function. The receiver drops it.

How you can tell: "[16] UnxCmplt", header logged, Non-fatal by default. It is often seen right after error type L-14 on the same device. It can be handled as advisory (error type L-06).

How to fix it and prove the fix: Risky, test machine only: use a test sender (exerciser) that delays an answer past the SSD's answer time limit. Read the header's request number (Tag) and Requester ID. Check whether 10-Bit Tag Requester Enable is set. See lspci -vvv DevCtl2 "10BitTagReq". Also check that every hop supports it.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Yes (Reported). The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Look at when the answer came. A late answer may come from slow memory or a switch, after the time limit ran out. Then blame the platform or computer. The same holds if the time limit was set too short. Blame the SSD when it returns a wrong Requester ID or Tag. Or when it sends answers after a function reset (FLR). · Test that confirms it: Read the header in the AER log (AER header log decode).

L-17 The receiver's buffer overflows (Receiver Overflow, RxOF) Seen in the packets Room-left messages (credits)

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 357909: write packets that need no answer (posted TLPs) were sent past the room the receiver announced.

Packet=357909 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=906 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000004:15EA5700 | Length=64 | DATA=256 B | Time Stamp=0161.743966533000s | Time Delta=0.000 ns | LCRC=0xB9605F89

Error family: P07, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. Proof from outside the recording also counts here. E01 is the Linux kernel log (dmesg). E02 is a copy of the SSD's settings area (lspci). P07 means room-left messages (credits) that stop or go wrong. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. The checker sees it from the order and timing of the packets. Examples are a missing answer, a long gap, or packets in the wrong order.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book (PCIe Base Specification) covers the Receiver Overflow error and the room rules. Checking for it is optional.

What goes wrong: The receiver got more packets or data than the credits it announced. So its buffer overflowed. Data is lost and the credit records are broken. By default it is Fatal.

How you can tell: "[17] RxOF", Fatal. The wire is reset, and the NVMe controller is reset.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Risky, test machine only: use a test sender (exerciser) that ignores credits. In the capture tool, compare the announced credits with the packets sent.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Yes (Reported). The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Find the sender that overran. Upstream packets point to the SSD. Downstream packets point to the platform. It often happens after a re-tune or a power change, when credits were not set up again. · Test that confirms it: Compare the error counters before and after (AER counter snapshot, confirmation test T1).

L-18 A packet breaks the format rules (Malformed TLP) Seen in the packets Badly built or bad-data packets

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 401811: a write packet (MWr) carries 260 bytes of data, but its Length field says 64. It breaks the size and length rules (MPS). This is a Malformed TLP.

Packet=401811 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(32) | PSN=2755 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=3830A000 | Length=64 | DATA=260 B | Time Stamp=0195.066771864750s | Time Delta=164.620 ns | LCRC=0x86E1C4AB

Error family: P11, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. Proof from outside the recording also counts here. E01 is the Linux kernel log (dmesg). E02 is a copy of the SSD's settings area (lspci). P11 means packets that are marked bad, broken or too big. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. This table file marks a wrong detail or a wrong order. The data size does not match the length the packet states (data_size_ne_length).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book (PCIe Base Specification) sets how packets must be built (TLP formation rules). It defines the Malformed TLP error and the Max_Payload_Size rules.

What goes wrong: A packet breaks the format rules. One example is data longer than the receiver's largest allowed size (Max_Payload_Size). Others are a Length field that does not match the real data, or a request crossing a 4 KB boundary. Others are illegal byte enables, an undefined Type, or breaks of the traffic-class mapping (TC/VC). By default it is Fatal.

How you can tell: "[18] MalfTLP", with the header logged. It is Fatal, recovery runs with a frozen channel, and NVMe resets. If it repeats on every large transfer, Linux keeps resetting. This is a reset loop (error type C-06).

How to fix it and prove the fix: Careful or risky, test machine only: set the Root Port's MPS lower than the SSD's with setpci. Then run large reads. This makes a fatal error on purpose. So use a throw-away machine with no valuable data. Read the logged header. Compare its Length with the MPS of the receiving device (lspci -vvv DevCtl "MaxPayload"). Check that the whole path uses the same MPS.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Yes (Reported). The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Look at the direction. A malformed packet going Upstream points to the SSD's sender. The exception is an MPS break where the SSD's own MPS was set above the root port's. That points to the computer or platform (error type L-32). A malformed packet going Downstream points to the computer or platform. · Test that confirms it: Read the header in the AER log (AER header decode).

L-19 The end-to-end check number does not match (ECRC Error) Seen in the packets Badly built or bad-data packets

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 404060: the extra check number is attached (TD=1), but it does not match (ECRC mismatch).

Packet=404060 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=862 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000003:49A05100 | Length=64 | DATA=256 B | Time Stamp=0195.182972079370s | Time Delta=18.000 ns | LCRC=0x5505FB5D

Error family: P11, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. Proof from outside the recording also counts here. E01 is the Linux kernel log (dmesg). E02 is a copy of the SSD's settings area (lspci). P11 means packets that are marked bad, broken or too big. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. This table file marks a wrong detail or a wrong order. The packet's "extra check number attached" mark (TD bit) is on (header_bit_TD_set).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book (PCIe Base Specification) covers the end-to-end check number (ECRC). It is carried at the end of the packet (TLP Digest, TD bit). AER has ECRC settings: Generation/Check Capable and Enable.

What goes wrong: ECRC making and checking are turned on. The receiver found the 32-bit end-to-end check number wrong. The normal check number (LCRC) protects each hop. But a packet can get damaged inside a switch or signal booster buffer, between hops. ECRC catches that.

How you can tell: "[19] ECRC" with the header, Non-fatal by default. Without ECRC, the same damage is silent. The switch makes a new valid LCRC around the damaged data.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Safe: turn it on (pci=ecrc=on) on a test machine. Risky, test machine only: insert check-number errors with a test sender (exerciser). Check whether ECRC is on at all. lspci -vvv AERCap shows "GenCap+ CGenEn- ChkCap+ ChkEn-". Linux v7.2 has an ecrc= boot policy: "bios" (default), "off" or "on". See ecrc_policy_str and pcie_set_ecrc_checking. Pass it as pci=ecrc=on.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Yes (Reported). The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Find where the damage first appears. An Upstream packet from the SSD may already be bad on its own wire, with a good LCRC. Then blame the SSD's ECRC maker. Good at the start but bad after a switch means the switch (platform). Bad going Downstream on the root-port wire means the computer's root complex, or a switch above. · Test that confirms it: Check the ECRC switches (ECRC enables).

L-20 The receiver does not support the request at all (Unsupported Request, UR) Seen in the packets Answer says the request failed

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 80660: an answer with result UR, for a setting read (MMIO read) past the SSD's memory window (BAR).

Packet=80660 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=Cpl | PSN=2031 | Tag=7 | RequesterID=000:00:0 | CompleterID=002:00:0 | Cpl Status=UR | Byte Cnt=4 | Time Stamp=0063.979851934250s | Time Delta=152.620 ns | LCRC=0x48FDB673

Packet 80662: advisory non-fatal: the UR is reported with a fixable-error message (ERR_COR).

Packet=80662 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=Msg | PSN=2032 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Length=0 | Time Stamp=0063.979852234250s | Time Delta=0.000 ns | LCRC=0x76AC4A80

Packet 80668: a write (posted MWr) to an address nobody claims. A non-fatal error message (ERR_NONFATAL) follows.

Packet=80668 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=Msg | PSN=2033 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Length=0 | Time Stamp=0063.979852634250s | Time Delta=129.120 ns | LCRC=0xF10A81C3

Error family: P04, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. Proof from outside the recording also counts here. E01 is the Linux kernel log (dmesg). E02 is a copy of the SSD's settings area (lspci). P04 means an answer that says the request failed. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. This table file marks a wrong detail or a wrong order. An answer says the request is not supported (UR) (completion_status_UR).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book (PCIe Base Specification) covers the Unsupported Request error, the answer result UR, and address decoding.

What goes wrong: The answering side does not support the request at all. One reason is an address that no memory window (BAR) claims. Another is that Memory Space Enable is turned off. Others are a message type it does not know, or a settings request to a missing function. Requests that need an answer get one with result UR. Writes that need no answer are dropped. These include data writes (DMA writes) and doorbells.

How you can tell: "[20] UnsupReq", reporting agent "Requester ID", header logged, Non-fatal by default. The kernel documentation example is exactly this line: "severity=Uncorrectable (Fatal), type=Transaction Layer, (Requester ID) ... [20] UnsupReq (First)". That was on a platform where severity was set to fatal. Effects on NVMe: the SSD may write read data or a done note to an unmapped computer address. That write is dropped. From the SSD's view, the command "completes". But the computer never sees the done note, so it times out. A doorbell write while Memory Space is turned off is dropped silently.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Fairly safe: a setpci read of a function that does not exist (normally masked). Risky, test machine only: use a user-space NVMe test driver (SPDK or vfio), with the IOMMU on. Give it a wrong memory address list (PRP) on purpose. The IOMMU should block it. That proves the protection works. Read the header address. Look for a matching IOMMU fault (error type L-36). Check that lspci -vvv shows Control: "Mem+ BusMaster+" on the SSD.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Yes (Reported). The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Find who supplied the address. Blame the computer when it gave the refused address. Examples are a setting read past the memory window, or a PRP pointing at unmapped memory. Blame the SSD when the computer never gave that address (stray DMA). Or when the SSD does not decode a legal setting. · Test that confirms it: Read the header in the AER log (AER header log decode).

L-21 A port blocks a packet its access rules forbid (ACS Violation) Partly seen in the packets Settings area and readiness

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 43707: the SSD writes straight into another device's memory window (peer-to-peer MWr to BAR 0xFB000000).

Packet=43707 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(32) | PSN=265 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=FB000000 | Length=64 | DATA=256 B | Time Stamp=0001.363897474870s | Time Delta=205.130 ns | LCRC=0xFBFA55AA

Error family: P19, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. Proof from outside the recording also counts here. E01 is the Linux kernel log (dmesg). E02 is a copy of the SSD's settings area (lspci). P19 means reading and writing the SSD's settings area, and restarts. · Can the packets alone prove it? Partly. The order and timing of the packets show its shape. The proof needs evidence from outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book (PCIe Base Specification) covers the access control feature (Access Control Services, ACS). It has an ACS Violation status bit.

What goes wrong: A switch port or root port with access control (ACS) turned on blocked a packet that broke its policy. Usually this is device-to-device traffic (peer-to-peer, P2P). An example is the SSD writing to a graphics card's or network card's memory window. ACS Source Validation, P2P Request Redirect or Egress Control may forbid it. Or the packet carries a faked Requester ID. See also error type L-33, about the settings side.

How you can tell: "[21] ACSViol" with the header, logged at the port, Non-fatal by default. The device-to-device data move (P2P DMA) fails. An NVMe command that uses a P2P buffer times out or returns an error.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Careful: try a device-to-device data move (P2PDMA) between two devices under one switch, with ACS P2P redirect on. Read lspci -vvv ACSCtl on each port. Linux logs "Configured ACS to %#06x" (the pci_std_enable_acs path). The pci=config_acs= setting changes it.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Yes (Reported). The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Look at the packet. Blame the platform's switch or root ACS policy when the packet is a real, intended P2P transfer. Blame the computer's software if the address came from a wrong PRP (a driver bug). Blame the SSD only if the Requester ID in the packet is wrong. Or if the SSD moves data outside its PRPs. · Test that confirms it: Read the ACS status and control settings.

L-22 An inside error the device cannot fix (Uncorrectable Internal Error) Not seen in the packets Error report messages

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 385572: a fatal-error message (ERR_FATAL) with no cause on the wire.

Packet=385572 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=Msg | PSN=1542 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Length=0 | Time Stamp=0194.855466569250s | Time Delta=148.120 ns | LCRC=0xE0F24EF2

Packet 385576: unfixable-status bit 22 is set, Uncorrectable Internal Error (UESta).

Packet=385576 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=CplD | PSN=1543 | Tag=18 | RequesterID=000:00:0 | CompleterID=002:00:0 | Cpl Status=SC | Length=1 | Byte Cnt=4 | DATA=4 B | Time Stamp=0194.856467154250s | Time Delta=0.000 ns | LCRC=0x42354BD1

Error family: P10, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. Proof from outside the recording also counts here. E01 is the Linux kernel log (dmesg). E02 is a copy of the SSD's settings area (lspci). P10 means error report messages and what is missing around them. · Can the packets alone prove it? No. It cannot be seen on this wire. The rows shown only give what happened around it. The proof is outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book (PCIe Base Specification) has an optional Uncorrectable Internal Error status, mask and severity setting.

What goes wrong: The device found an error inside itself that it could not fix. Examples are a parity or memory (ECC) error in its inside memory (SRAM). Or a fault on an inside bus of the PCIe or NVMe front end. By default it is Fatal, but also hidden (masked). So most systems never see it as AER. The NVMe controller may set the fatal flag CSTS.CFS instead (error type C-01). Or it may send a Persistent Internal Error event (error type C-11).

How you can tell: If not hidden: "[22] UncorrIntErr", and Fatal recovery. If hidden: nothing in AER. Look at the NVMe-level signs.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Only the maker's own error insertion can create it. Check UEMsk in lspci -vvv. Careful: on a lab machine, un-hide it and watch. Match it with NVMe telemetry and the error log.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Yes (Reported). The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Blame the SSD: an inside memory, ECC or bus fault. Blame the computer only if a bad packet from its side comes before the message. · Test that confirms it: Read the AER status.

L-23 A port refuses to pass a packet on (egress-blocked errors) Partly seen in the packets Badly built or bad-data packets

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 405041: a write from the SSD marked as bad data (poisoned MWr). The root port blocks it on its way out (egress).

Packet=405041 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=1110 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000001:8FDF0000 | Length=64 | DATA=256 B | Time Stamp=0195.183120926500s | Time Delta=187.620 ns | LCRC=0x2DE1D120

Error family: P11, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. Proof from outside the recording also counts here. E01 is the Linux kernel log (dmesg). E02 is a copy of the SSD's settings area (lspci). P11 means packets that are marked bad, broken or too big. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. This table file marks a wrong detail or a wrong order. The packet's "bad data" mark (EP bit) is on (header_bit_EP_set).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book (PCIe Base Specification) covers several blocking rules. These are AtomicOp routing and blocking, End-End TLP Prefix rules, Poisoned TLP Egress Blocking and Deferrable Memory Write. The default severity and mask for bits 26, 27 and 31 are not sure. They are not yet checked against the rule book.

What goes wrong: A port refused to pass a packet out of its exit port (egress). Either the next hop cannot take that packet type, or a policy says to block it. Bit 23 is a blocked multicast packet. Bit 24 is an AtomicOp toward a port without AtomicOp routing or support. Bit 25 is an End-End TLP Prefix toward a port that does not support prefixes. PASID in some forms is such a prefix. Bit 26 is a bad-data packet blocked by policy. Bit 27 is a blocked Deferrable Memory Write. Bit 31 is blocking linked to address translation.

How you can tell: Bits 23–27 and 31 are all in AER_LOG_TLP_MASKS, so the header is logged. Linux names: "BlockedTLP", "AtomicOpBlocked", "TLPBlockedErr", "PoisonTLPBlocked", "DMWrReqBlocked", "TLPXlatBlocked". The sender's request fails. From its view this is usually a Completion Timeout or a UR.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Risky, test machine only: use a test sender (exerciser) to send AtomicOps or prefixed packets through a port without support. Read the logged header. Is a prefix present? Is Fmt/Type an AtomicOp? Check DevCap2 AtomicOpsCap and AtomicOp routing on each port. Also check End-End TLP Prefix support.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Yes (Reported). The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Blame the platform when the port lacks routing or support, or blocks by policy. Blame the SSD when it sends a packet type it was not allowed to send, or bad-marked data. · Test that confirms it: Read the port's AER status.

L-24 Wire encryption checks fail (IDE Check Failed, Misrouted IDE TLP) Partly seen in the packets Happens away from this wire

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 1989025: IDE Check Failed is reported as unfixable (uncorrectable).

Packet=1989025 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=Msg | PSN=592 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Length=0 | Time Stamp=1832.732999277750s | Time Delta=134.000 ns | LCRC=0x0679D275

Error family: none of the 27 ways an error shows on the wire. Proof from outside the recording also counts here. E01 is the Linux kernel log (dmesg). E02 is a copy of the SSD's settings area (lspci). · Can the packets alone prove it? Partly. The order and timing of the packets show its shape. The proof needs evidence from outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book (PCIe Base Specification) covers wire encryption (IDE). It was added by 6.0-era change notices (ECNs). The default severities are not yet checked against the rule book.

What goes wrong: PCIe Integrity and Data Encryption (IDE) is on. It is used for confidential computing and TDISP-style device assignment. A received packet failed one of three checks. It failed its integrity check (MAC, bit 28). Or it arrived on the wrong IDE stream or port (bit 29). Or it failed the optional plain-text check number (PCRC, bit 30). IDE treats an integrity failure as a security event. The rule book defines how the IDE stream is affected. For example, the stream is torn down and must get new keys. This example is not sure and not yet checked against the rule book.

How you can tell: "IDECheck", "MisIDETLP", "PCRC_CHECK", with the header logged. The NVMe device's data moves (DMA) stop working until the stream is set up again.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Risky, test machine only: program keys that do not match on a test set-up. Read the AER log and the platform security or TSM logs. Capture tools that understand IDE need the keys to read the traffic.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Yes (Reported). The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Check the keys and stream ID. Blame the computer or platform if the programmed key or stream ID does not match the packet's stream. Blame the SSD if the keys match and its packets still fail the MAC check. · Test that confirms it: Read the AER errors in the kernel log (AER decode, E01).

L-25 The wire starts slower or narrower than both sides can do Seen in the packets Wire start-up and speed changes

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 140836: the wire started with 2 lanes (x2), although both ends can use 4 (x4).

Packet=140836 | Link Event=Width Change: x2 | Time Stamp=0127.048198408000s | Time Delta=0.000 ns

Error family: P08, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. Proof from outside the recording also counts here. E01 is the Linux kernel log (dmesg). E02 is a copy of the SSD's settings area (lspci). P08 means wire start-up, re-tuning, and speed or width changes. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. The checker sees it from the order and timing of the packets. Examples are a missing answer, a long gap, or packets in the wrong order.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book (PCIe Base Specification) covers these parts. What the wire can do: Link Capabilities (Max Link Speed, Maximum Link Width). What the wire is doing: Link Status (Current Link Speed, Negotiated Link Width). The Target Link Speed in Link Control 2. The start-up steps Configuration and Recovery (speed change, tuning).

What goes wrong: Wire start-up (LTSSM) settled on a lower speed, such as 8 GT/s instead of 16 GT/s. Or it settled on fewer lanes, such as x2 instead of x4. Everything works, and no error is logged. But the speed of large in-order transfers is capped. A Gen4 x4 wire carries about 7–7.5 GB/s of data. Gen3 x2 manages under 2 GB/s.

How you can tell: No AER bit and no NVMe result. Linux v7.2 prints one information line when it first looks for the devices (enumeration). It comes from pcie_report_downtraining() → __pcie_print_link_status(dev, false). It prints only when the available speed is less than possible. The line is: "%u.%03u Gb/s available PCIe bandwidth, limited by %s x%d link at %s (capable of %u.%03u Gb/s with %s x%d link)". The "at %s" part names the limiting device. That may be a switch port or Root Port above, not the SSD. A drop after boot (re-tuning while running) does not print this line. The bwctrl part of Linux updates the saved speed in sysfs when the port supports Link Bandwidth Notification.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Safe: limit the speed in BIOS. Then check that the log line appears and the fio speed drops. Careful: write the LnkCtl2 Target Link Speed with setpci on the Root Port, and set Retrain Link. This changes the live wire and may drop it. Compare LnkCap with LnkSta at each hop under load. Run dmesg | grep 'limited by'. Prove the speed loss with fio in-order reads at a high queue depth. The speed should be close to the lower wire's limit. Re-seat the drive or swap slots. Check the LnkCtl2 Target Link Speed. Check the BIOS settings.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No (Degraded). No error is reported. Things still work, but slower or on a weaker wire. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Look at what each side announced. Blame the wire when both sides announced full speed and width, but start-up fell back. Signs are PAD lanes or a failed Recovery.Speed step. Blame the platform when a settings write (CfgWr) lowered the Target Link Speed. Or when the BIOS limited it, or the slot is wired narrower. · Test that confirms it: Linux messages about lower wire speed and bandwidth (E01).

P08 means wire start-up, re-tuning, and speed or width changes. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. The checker sees it from the order and timing of the packets. Examples are a missing answer, a long gap, or packets in the wrong order.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book (PCIe Base Specification) covers the re-tune step (Recovery). It covers two Link Status flags: Link Bandwidth Management Status and Link Autonomous Bandwidth Status. It also covers the Link Bandwidth Management Interrupt Enable.

What goes wrong: The wire keeps entering the re-tune step (LTSSM Recovery). This happens after a resend counter roll-over, after receiving errors, or after a quiet-state glitch. Each re-tune stalls all traffic for microseconds to milliseconds. Data is never lost, so no unfixable error appears. The only signs are fixable error counts (RxErr, BadTLP, BadDLLP, Rollover, Timeout). There are also regular delay spikes. Sometimes the speed or width changes over time.

How you can tell: Fixable-error lines (severity=Correctable), limited in rate. By default the limit is 10 per 5 s per device, so the log hides the true rate. The aer_dev_correctable counters show it. Hardware may change speed or width "to correct unreliable link operation". Then it sets the LnkSta flag LBMS (Link Bandwidth Management Status). Linux bwctrl records it (PCI_LINK_LBMS_SEEN). The NVMe layer shows no errors. It shows only p99.9 delay spikes and lower speed.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Careful: heat and cool the riser or SSD under load. Risky, test machine only: use lane margining at an offset that causes occasional errors. Read aer_dev_correctable on both ends every second, and plot the changes. Read LnkSta. Run fio delay tests with --percentile_list=99:99.9:99.99. A storm shows as all queues stalling together. A capture tool triggered on TS1 training signals during normal work (L0) shows each re-tune.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No (Degraded). No error is reported. Things still work, but slower or on a weaker wire. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Look at what comes before each re-tune. Blame the wire when receiving errors or LCRC Naks come first in both directions, and heat changes it. Blame power saving (ASPM, on the platform or device) when re-tunes follow L1 wake-ups only. · Test that confirms it: Compare the error counters before and after (AER counter snapshot, confirmation test T1).

L-27 The wire drops silently (no Surprise Down reporting) Partly seen in the packets Wire goes down, power, restart

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 1352886: the wire goes quiet with no go-quiet signal (EIOS), no power message and no Hot Reset. Nobody asked the wire to go down.

Packet=1352886 | Link Event=Electrical Idle | Time Stamp=1321.031495012000s | Time Delta=0.000 ns

Error family: P12, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. Proof from outside the recording also counts here. E01 is the Linux kernel log (dmesg). E02 is a copy of the SSD's settings area (lspci). E07 is measurements of power and side pins (oscilloscope). P12 means the wire going down while packets are on the way. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. This table file marks a wrong detail or a wrong order. A request was lost when the wire went down (request_lost_across_link_down).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book (PCIe Base Specification) has two optional features. One reports whether the wire is active (Data Link Layer Link Active Reporting Capable). The other reports a sudden drop (Surprise Down Error Reporting Capable). A read to a device that does not answer ends in a Completion Timeout at the side that asked.

What goes wrong: The wire drops (DL_Active goes to 0). But the Downstream Port does not support Surprise Down reporting. Or the error is hidden (masked). Or there is no hot-plug or DPC service on that port. Nothing is reported. The computer finds out the next time it touches the device. Setting reads (MMIO reads) return all ones. That comes after a Completion Timeout at the Root Port, if it is logged. Doorbell writes vanish. Every waiting NVMe command waits for its timer.

How you can tell: The sign comes up to io_timeout (30 s default in Linux v7.2) or admin_timeout (60 s) later. The function nvme_timeout() reads CSTS = 0xffffffff. The function nvme_should_reset() decides it must reset, because the CFS bit looks set in all ones. The driver logs "controller is down; will reset: CSTS=0xffffffff, PCI_STATUS=0xffff". It adds "Does your device have a faulty power saving mode enabled?". It also adds "Try "nvme_core.default_ps_max_latency_us=0 pcie_aspm=off pcie_port_pm=off" and report a bug". The reset then fails (nvme_pci_enable sees CSTS == -1). "Disabling device after reset failure: -19" follows (error type C-17).

How to fix it and prove the fix: Read the port's LnkSta (DLActive-) and LnkCap. LnkCap has the "Surprise-" and "DLActive-" capability flags. Compare the time of the first NVMe timeout with the kernel times of earlier traffic. A capture tool left waiting for the quiet state catches the moment.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No (Timer only). No error message is sent. Only a time limit running out shows it. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Look at who went quiet first. Blame the wire path by default (a sudden quiet). Blame the SSD if its sender goes quiet first while the root port still sends (firmware hang). Blame the platform if both stop together (power or connector). · Test that confirms it: Read the port's capability flags.

L-28 The port cuts the wire on purpose after an error (DPC containment) Partly seen in the packets Wire goes down, power, restart

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 1354788: a fatal-error message (ERR_FATAL).

Packet=1354788 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=Msg | PSN=800 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Length=0 | Time Stamp=1323.043029340370s | Time Delta=148.130 ns | LCRC=0x8D9FAAE7

Packet 1354792: the root port sends a training signal (TS1) with Disable Link. This is the port shut-off (DPC containment).

Packet=1354792 | Link Dir=Downstream | Ord.Set Type=TS1 | Time Stamp=1323.043031356620s | Time Delta=0.380 ns

Error family: P12, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. Proof from outside the recording also counts here. E01 is the Linux kernel log (dmesg). E02 is a copy of the SSD's settings area (lspci). P12 means the wire going down while packets are on the way. · Can the packets alone prove it? Partly. The order and timing of the packets show its shape. The proof needs evidence from outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book (PCIe Base Specification) covers the port shut-off feature (Downstream Port Containment, DPC). It covers the DPC Status Trigger Reason and the Root Port extensions for setting reads (RP PIO).

What goes wrong: A Downstream Port with DPC turned on saw an unfixable error. Linux v7.2 sets DPC to trigger only on ERR_FATAL, as the dpc_handler comment says. The port turns off its wire at once. So no possibly damaged packets travel further up. It also signals the operating system. Every request to the SSD fails until software clears the trigger and the wire re-tunes.

How you can tell: The function dpc_process_error() logs one of these lines. "containment event, status:%#06x: unmasked uncorrectable error detected" is the port's own error, followed by AER details. "containment event, status:%#06x, ERR_FATAL received from DDDD:BB:DD.F" is an error message from the SSD. The third is "containment event, status:%#06x: RP PIO error detected / software trigger detected". With Root Port extensions, RP PIO details follow. An example is "[18] Memory Request Completion Timeout". Then pcie_do_recovery(pdev, pci_channel_io_frozen, dpc_reset_link) runs. The NVMe driver logs "frozen state error detected, reset controller", then "restart after slot reset". If the wire does not come back, the logs say one of these. "Data Link Layer Link Active not cleared in 1000 msec", "root port still busy", or "device recovery failed".

How to fix it and prove the fix: Careful: trigger it by software through DPC Control (setpci) on a test port. Risky, test machine only: insert a fatal error with a test sender (exerciser). The effect is a full SSD reset, and data on the way is lost. Run dmesg | grep -E 'DPC|containment'. lspci -vvv -s <port> shows the DPC capability and DpcSta. When the driver starts (probe), Linux prints "enabled with IRQ". It also prints an "error containment capabilities: Int Msg #%d, RPExt%c PoisonedTLP%c SwTrigger%c RP PIO Log %d, DL_ActiveErr%c" line. That line tells you what is turned on.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Yes (Reported). The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Look at the trigger. Blame the SSD if the trigger came from the SSD's RequesterID before the wire went down. The trigger is then an ERR_FATAL or a malformed packet. Blame the platform if the trigger is an RP PIO completion timeout, or an EDR or software trigger. · Test that confirms it: Read the DPC log.

L-29 The SSD is pulled out while reads and writes run (hot-plug removal) Partly seen in the packets Wire goes down, power, restart

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 1372739: the wire goes quiet with no go-quiet signal (EIOS), no power message and no Hot Reset. Nobody asked the wire to go down.

Packet=1372739 | Link Event=Electrical Idle | Time Stamp=1323.554998457000s | Time Delta=0.000 ns

Error family: P12, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. Proof from outside the recording also counts here. E01 is the Linux kernel log (dmesg). E02 is a copy of the SSD's settings area (lspci). P12 means the wire going down while packets are on the way. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. This table file marks a wrong detail or a wrong order. A request was lost when the wire went down (request_lost_across_link_down).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book (PCIe Base Specification) covers hot-plug: Presence Detect, Data Link Layer State Changed and Attention Button. How NVMe handles it is up to the computer.

What goes wrong: The SSD is removed or powered off in a hot-plug slot. In an orderly removal, the operating system unbinds the driver first. This uses the attention button or echo 0 > /sys/bus/pci/slots/N/power. In a surprise removal, the device is already gone when the driver is told. The PCI core marks it disconnected. Waiting reads and writes must fail rather than hang.

How you can tell: The hot-plug driver (pciehp) logs slot link-down and presence-change events. It is not in the local source tree used here, so the exact wording is not sure. In Linux v7.2 NVMe, nvme_remove() sets the state to DELETING. If !pci_device_is_present(), it sets DEAD and calls nvme_dev_disable(dev, true) at once. So waiting requests are cancelled, and namespaces are marked dead (nvme_mark_namespaces_dead → blk_mark_disk_dead). File systems see read and write errors. In nvme_timeout(), if pci_dev_is_disconnected() is true, the controller goes straight to DELETING and is turned off. The source comment says this frees a deadlock between error recovery and removal.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Careful: do an orderly hot-remove through sysfs slot power, with fio running on a scratch namespace. Then check for hung tasks. Risky, test machine only: physically pull the drive out of a certified hot-plug bay. Check dmesg around the removal. lspci no longer lists the BDF. /sys/block/nvme* disappears. Check that no task is left in D state (ps -eo stat,pid,cmd | grep '^D'). That would mean a hang in the read/write path.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Yes (Reported). The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Blame the computer, platform or person that removed it. Blame the SSD only if SMART or the SSD's logs (E03) show a drive failure that caused the presence change. · Test that confirms it: The kernel log.

L-30 The SSD answers "try again" forever (Configuration RRS / CRS loop) Seen in the packets Answer says the request failed

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 82725: "not ready, try again" answers (CRS) for 60 s. Then the Linux wait (pci_dev_wait) gives up.

Packet=82725 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=Cpl | PSN=2931 | Tag=2 | RequesterID=000:00:0 | CompleterID=002:00:0 | Cpl Status=CRS | Byte Cnt=4 | Time Stamp=0120.175180291870s | Time Delta=166.630 ns | LCRC=0xBC128CDB

Error family: P04 and P19, two of the 27 ways an error shows on the wire. Proof from outside the recording also counts here. E02 is a copy of the SSD's settings area (lspci). P04 means an answer that says the request failed. P19 means reading and writing the SSD's settings area, and restarts. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. This table file marks a wrong detail or a wrong order. An answer says the SSD is not ready yet, try again (CRS) (completion_status_CRS).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book (PCIe Base Specification) covers the "try again" answer (Configuration Request Retry Status). It also covers its Software Visibility option. It has a rule that a device must be ready for settings requests within a set time after reset. Readiness Notifications are an optional speed-up.

What goes wrong: After reset or power-up, a function may answer settings requests with "try again" while it starts. This answer is called RRS (formerly CRS). If its firmware never finishes starting, it keeps answering RRS. Looking for the devices (enumeration), or restoring after a reset, waits and then gives up. The device is missing from lspci, or present but unusable.

How you can tell: The Root Port may have Configuration RRS Software Visibility turned on. Linux turns it on if supported: PCI_EXP_RTCAP_RRS_SV → PCI_EXP_RTCTL_RRS_SVE. Then a Vendor ID read returns a special value. Linux spots it with pci_bus_rrs_vendor_id(). While looking for devices, pci_bus_wait_rrs() doubles its delay each time. Past 1000 ms, it logs "pci DDDD:BB:DD.F: not ready after %dms; waiting" once. Then it logs "ready after %dms" or "not ready after %dms; giving up". After resets, pci_dev_wait() logs "not ready %dms after %s; waiting / giving up". The time limit for reset waits is PCIE_RESET_READY_POLL_MS = 60000 ms. Past PCI_RESET_WAIT (1000 ms), it tries one wire re-tune through pcie_failed_link_retrain(). Without RRS visibility, the hardware retries silently. In the end it returns all ones.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Risky, test machine only: use a test sender (exerciser) as the end device that answers RRS for N seconds. Or use a maker's command that holds the SSD in its boot loader. Run dmesg | grep -E 'not ready|ready after'. A long "ready after" (several seconds) on every boot is a hidden problem, even when it works. Time the SSD's start-up after power-on with the capture tool. Count the RRS answers.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No (Timer only). No error message is sent. Only a time limit running out shows it. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Check the reset pin and the power. Blame the SSD (firmware stuck in boot ROM, or a failed update) when PERST# is released and power is steady. Blame the platform if the PERST# or power order is wrong. · Test that confirms it: The readiness messages in the kernel log.

L-31 The SSD's memory window gets no address (BAR not assigned) Partly seen in the packets Answer says the request failed

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 84414: the first memory window (BAR0) reads 0, and memory access is off (Command.MEM=0). No addresses were given.

Packet=84414 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=CplD | PSN=525 | Tag=21 | RequesterID=000:00:0 | CompleterID=002:00:0 | Cpl Status=SC | Length=1 | Byte Cnt=4 | DATA=4 B | Time Stamp=0124.386706698620s | Time Delta=0.000 ns | LCRC=0x23D605A3

Packet 84418: the driver's setting read (MMIO read) is answered with UR (not supported).

Packet=84418 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=Cpl | PSN=526 | Tag=22 | RequesterID=000:00:0 | CompleterID=002:00:0 | Cpl Status=UR | Byte Cnt=4 | Time Stamp=0124.386707205620s | Time Delta=166.630 ns | LCRC=0x77DB2FEC

Error family: P04 and P19, two of the 27 ways an error shows on the wire. Proof from outside the recording also counts here. E02 is a copy of the SSD's settings area (lspci). P04 means an answer that says the request failed. P19 means reading and writing the SSD's settings area, and restarts. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. This table file marks a wrong detail or a wrong order. An answer says the request is not supported (UR) (completion_status_UR).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCI/PCIe settings area (configuration space) has memory windows (BARs) and bridge memory windows. In NVMe, BAR0 and BAR1 hold the controller's settings. They are the 64-bit MLBAR/MUBAR pair.

What goes wrong: The SSD's first memory window (BAR0) holds its settings and doorbells. It got no address. Or its address clashes with another device, or lies outside the bridge window above it. The NVMe driver fails at start (probe). Or setting reads and writes (MMIO) go to the wrong place.

How you can tell: Messages from probe.c while looking for devices (enumeration). One example is "%s: can't handle BAR larger than 4GB". Others are "%s: can't handle BAR above 4GB" and "initial BAR value %#010llx invalid". Others are "device has non-compliant BARs; disabling IO/MEM decoding". Or "devices behind bridge are unusable because %pR cannot be assigned for them". Messages about failed address giving come from setup-res.c. That file is not in the local tree, so their wording is not sure. NVMe start then fails in nvme_dev_map() / pci_request_mem_regions, or reads all ones. The function nvme_pci_enable logs "reading CSTS register failed" at debug level only. Start ends with "probe failed" (dev_err_probe).

How to fix it and prove the fix: Safe: boot with many devices and the BIOS option "above 4G decoding" off, then look. Careful: hot-plug into a slot whose bridge window is too small. Check lspci -vv -s <BDF>. It shows "Region 0: Memory at <unassigned>" or "[disabled]". Also check cat /proc/iomem and dmesg | grep -i 'BAR\|bridge window'. Try pci=realloc as a test boot option.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Yes (Reported). The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Look at the size the SSD reported. Sometimes the SSD reported a valid size, but got no address, or one outside the bridge window. Then blame the computer platform. Blame the SSD when its size answer is invalid. · Test that confirms it: Look at the address list (resource view).

L-32 Size limits differ along the path (MPS / MRRS mismatch) Seen in the packets Badly built or bad-data packets

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 406670: the largest packet size in Device Control (MPS) is set to 128 bytes.

Packet=406670 | Link Dir=Downstream | TLP Type=CfgWr0 | PSN=1148 | Tag=26 | RequesterID=000:00:0 | Length=1 | DATA=4 B | Time Stamp=0195.183236102250s | Time Delta=106.120 ns | LCRC=0x797651F7

Packet 406673: a write packet (MWr) carries 512 bytes (Length 128). It breaks the size and length rules (MPS). This is a Malformed TLP.

Packet=406673 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=1462 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000001:7109D000 | Length=128 | DATA=512 B | Time Stamp=0195.183236598870s | Time Delta=164.000 ns | LCRC=0x84BD67E1

Error family: P11 and P19, two of the 27 ways an error shows on the wire. Proof from outside the recording also counts here. E02 is a copy of the SSD's settings area (lspci). P11 means packets that are marked bad, broken or too big. P19 means reading and writing the SSD's settings area, and restarts. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. This table file marks a wrong detail or a wrong order. A packet carries more than 256 bytes of data, the set limit (payload_exceeds_mps_256).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book (PCIe Base Specification) covers the largest packet size a device supports (Device Capabilities Max_Payload_Size Supported). It covers the sizes set in Device Control: Max_Payload_Size and Max_Read_Request_Size. Its rule is that a packet's data must not be bigger than the receiver's MPS.

What goes wrong: The largest packet size (MPS) must not be bigger than what each receiver on the path accepts. Sometimes the SSD's MPS is larger than the Root Port's or a switch's. Then its large writes (read data to the computer) are malformed at the receiver (error type L-18). That is fatal by default. A mismatch of the largest read request size (MRRS) is allowed. But too small hurts speed, and too large hurts fairness. Some devices handle some MRRS values badly. The comment in pcie_write_mrrs() says: "issues with setting MRRS to 0 on a number of devices".

How you can tell: A fatal MalfTLP during the first large read, then a reset loop. Or, with the same but small MPS/MRRS everywhere, a quiet speed loss (Degraded). Linux v7.2 messages include these. "Max Payload Size set to %d (was %d, max %d)". "Upstream bridge's Max Payload Size set to %d ...". "Max Payload Size %d, but upstream %s set to %d; if necessary, use "pci=pcie_bus_safe" and report a bug". That line comes with pci=pcie_bus_tune_off. "can't set Max Payload Size to %d ...". "Failed attempting to set the MPS". "Failed attempting to set the MRRS". "MRRS was unable to be configured with a safe value. If problems are experienced, try running with pci=pcie_bus_safe". In non-default modes: "Max Payload Size set to %4d/%4d (was %4d), Max Read Rq %4d".

How to fix it and prove the fix: Careful or risky, test machine only: set mismatched MPS with setpci and run a large read. Expect MalfTLP and a fatal reset. Run lspci -vvv | grep -E 'MaxPayload|MaxReadReq' on every device on the path. Each DevCtl line lists "MaxPayload N bytes, MaxReadReq M bytes". Each must be ≤ its partner's capability. The payload size must be the same across the path. Boot-option tests: pci=pcie_bus_safe, pcie_bus_perf, pcie_bus_tune_off, pcie_bus_peer2peer.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Yes (Reported). The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Blame the platform or computer. The BIOS or operating system set the SSD's MPS above the root port's. Blame the SSD only if it ignores the MPS it was given (error type V-26). · Test that confirms it: Check MPS and MRRS along the whole path.

L-33 Device-to-device access rules are set wrong (ACS misconfiguration) Partly seen in the packets Settings area and readiness

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 45754: the SSD writes straight into another device's memory window (peer-to-peer MWr to BAR 0xFB000000).

Packet=45754 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(32) | PSN=847 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=FB000000 | Length=64 | DATA=256 B | Time Stamp=0001.364126780500s | Time Delta=185.120 ns | LCRC=0xEF3EAADB

Error family: P19, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. Proof from outside the recording also counts here. E02 is a copy of the SSD's settings area (lspci). P19 means reading and writing the SSD's settings area, and restarts. · Can the packets alone prove it? Partly. The order and timing of the packets show its shape. The proof needs evidence from outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book (PCIe Base Specification) covers the access control parts of ACS. These are Source Validation, Translation Blocking, P2P Request Redirect and P2P Completion Redirect. Also Upstream Forwarding, P2P Egress Control and Direct Translated P2P.

What goes wrong: Access control (ACS) can fail in two directions. Too strict: device-to-device traffic (SSD ↔ graphics or network card) is sent up to the root complex. There it may be refused (UR or ACS Violation), or run slowly through the IOMMU. Too loose: a switch without ACS lets an SSD write straight into another device's memory window. This skips the IOMMU. Keeping devices apart (isolation) is broken, with no error anywhere. A wrong memory address list (PRP) that points at another device's window then damages that device silently.

How you can tell: Too strict: error type L-21 (ACSViol), or device-to-device speed far below what is expected. Too loose: nothing. The only sign is IOMMU groups that contain several devices (/sys/kernel/iommu_groups/*/devices).

How to fix it and prove the fix: Safe: list the ACS abilities and the IOMMU groups. Careful: run P2PDMA tests with ACS on and off. Check lspci -vvv ACSCap and ACSCtl on every downstream port. Linux logs "Configured ACS to %#06x" when it applies an override. Check which devices share each IOMMU group.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No (Silent). Nothing reports this error. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Blame the platform in both directions. That means the firmware or operating system ACS settings, or a switch without ACS. Blame the computer's software if the P2P address came from a wrong PRP. The SSD is not involved unless its Requester ID is wrong (error type L-21). · Test that confirms it: List the ACS settings on every port (ACS inventory).

L-34 Address translation or page requests fail (ATS / PRI errors) Seen in the packets Settings area and readiness

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 47773: a translation request (AT=01) while address translation (ATS) is turned off.

Packet=47773 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MRd(64) | PSN=1327 | Tag=16 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000002:00000000 | Length=2 | Time Stamp=0001.364256397120s | Time Delta=160.130 ns | LCRC=0x9E747CEA

Packet 47775: the answer is UR (not supported).

Packet=47775 | Link Dir=Downstream | TLP Type=Cpl | PSN=2805 | Tag=16 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | CompleterID=000:02:4 | Cpl Status=UR | Byte Cnt=8 | Time Stamp=0001.364257197120s | Time Delta=127.630 ns | LCRC=0x6F8C34F7

Error family: P19, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. Proof from outside the recording also counts here. E02 is a copy of the SSD's settings area (lspci). P19 means reading and writing the SSD's settings area, and restarts. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. This table file marks a wrong detail or a wrong order. The address-type field (AT) is not zero (address_type_nonzero). An answer says the request is not supported (UR) (completion_status_UR).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book (PCIe Base Specification) covers address translation (ATS): Translation Request and Completion, Invalidate Request and Completion. It covers page requests (PRI): Page Request Message and PRG Response. It also covers PASID.

What goes wrong: With Address Translation Services (ATS), the device keeps copies of address translations in its own cache (ATC). These turn device addresses (IOVA) into real memory addresses. It then sends "translated" requests that the IOMMU does not check again. Things can go wrong in three ways. First, a stale cache entry. The computer removed and cancelled a translation, but the device missed the cancel or confirmed it too late. So data goes to freed memory (silent damage). Second, a cancel confirmation (Invalidate Completion) never arrives, so the IOMMU's cancel times out. Third, with page requests (PRI), a page request is never answered or fails. Then the data move waits forever.

How you can tell: The IOMMU driver reports cancel timeouts and page-request failures, not AER. The drivers are Intel VT-d, AMD-Vi and Arm SMMU. The exact message wording is not sure here, because those drivers are not in the local source tree. Data moves through a stale cache entry are silent. Most NVMe SSDs do not build in ATS or PRI. So this matters mainly for SVA/PASID-capable or computational storage devices. This depends on the design.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Risky, test machine only: use a test sender (exerciser) that delays Invalidate Completions. Or stress the IOMMU with frequent unmaps during data moves. Check lspci -vvv: ATSCap/ATSCtl "Enable+", the PRI capability and the PASID capability. Read the IOMMU fault logs. For stale-translation damage, run a read-back check (fio verify=crc32c). Run it during heavy map and unmap churn, for example with the IOMMU in strict mode (iommu.strict=1).

Does the SSD or computer report it? Yes (Reported). The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Look at who broke the handshake. Blame the SSD if it uses ATS or PRI without being allowed to. Or if it misses or delays Invalidate Completions, or uses a translation after it was cancelled. Blame the platform or IOMMU if it refuses translations for an allowed device. Or if it never sends Invalidate or PRG responses (error type M-063). · Test that confirms it: Read the capability state.

L-35 "Work done" signals get lost or go to the wrong place (MSI/MSI-X) Seen in the packets Wrong order or missing signal

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 578966: the "work done" signal (MSI-X) was written to 0xFEE0F000, not to the address set for it.

Packet=578966 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(32) | PSN=3094 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=FEE0F000 | Length=1 | DATA=4 B | Time Stamp=0401.094840538250s | Time Delta=109.120 ns | LCRC=0x73118471

Error family: P16, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. Proof from outside the recording also counts here. E02 is a copy of the SSD's settings area (lspci). E05 is a record of the computer's storage steps (blktrace). P16 means data, done note and signal in the wrong order, or a lost signal. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. The checker sees it from the order and timing of the packets. Examples are a missing answer, a long gap, or packets in the wrong order.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCI/PCIe rules define the MSI and MSI-X settings. These include the MSI-X Table and Pending Bit Array, the Function Mask, and a mask for each signal. In NVMe, the INTMS/INTMC settings mask only pin-based and single-message MSI, not MSI-X. The "IV" field of the Create I/O CQ command picks the signal number.

What goes wrong: The SSD writes a done note (CQE). Then it sends its "work done" signal as a write (MWr) to the MSI or MSI-X address. Sometimes the signal is masked, or has the wrong address or data. Or interrupt remapping blocks it. Or it is never sent, because of a device bug. Then the processor never runs the done handler. The done note sits in computer memory, already written.

How you can tell: After io_timeout, the Linux v7.2 function nvme_timeout() first checks the done list itself. The source says "Did we miss an interrupt?". If the request was in fact done, it logs "I/O tag %d (%04x) QID %d timeout, completion polled". It then finishes the request with no reset. One such line means a lost signal. Many mean the signals fail all the time. There are other signs. The /proc/interrupts counts for the nvme0qN signals stay flat while reads and writes are sent. The MSI core may log "arch assigned 64-bit MSI address %#llx above device MSI address mask %#llx".

How to fix it and prove the fix: Careful: mask one MSI-X signal through the table (with a debug tool) while reads and writes run. Expect "completion polled" after the timeout. Safe: lower nvme.io_timeout on a test machine to make the test shorter. Search dmesg for "completion polled". Compare the /proc/interrupts changes with the read and write counts. Check lspci -vvv "MSI-X: Enable+ Count=N Masked-". Boot with nvme.use_threaded_interrupts=1, or use poll queues (nvme.poll_queues=N, with io_uring hipri). See whether the problem goes away when signals are skipped.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No (Timer only). No error message is sent. Only a time limit running out shows it. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Compare the wire with the settings. Blame the SSD if the MSI-X on the wire differs from the set entry. Or if it is missing while unmasked and turned on. Blame the computer if the table, IV or enable settings are wrong (seen as computer MWr or CfgWr). Blame the platform if the MSI-X on the wire is correct but not delivered (interrupt remapping). · Test that confirms it: A copy of the settings area (config snapshot).

L-36 SSD data move to an address it was not given (IOMMU fault) Partly seen in the packets Answer says the request failed

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 87603: the root complex answers the SSD's data read with UR (not supported).

Packet=87603 | Link Dir=Downstream | TLP Type=Cpl | PSN=1003 | Tag=114 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | CompleterID=000:02:4 | Cpl Status=UR | Byte Cnt=512 | Time Stamp=0125.386986105000s | Time Delta=0.000 ns | LCRC=0xCA07CF8C

Packet 87632: the done note (CQE) says Data Transfer Error.

Packet=87632 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=1583 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000004:80830030 | Length=4 | DATA=16 B | Time Stamp=0125.386999564250s | Time Delta=32.880 ns | LCRC=0x72741053

Error family: P04 and P17, two of the 27 ways an error shows on the wire. Proof from outside the recording also counts here. E02 is a copy of the SSD's settings area (lspci). P04 means an answer that says the request failed. P17 means data moved to the wrong place in memory. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. This table file marks a wrong detail or a wrong order. An answer says the request is not supported (UR) (completion_status_UR).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The platform's memory guard (IOMMU) has its own rule books (VT-d, AMD IOMMU, SMMU). In NVMe, the CSTS.CFS flag is how the controller says it can no longer work. In PCIe, the answer results UR and CA apply.

What goes wrong: The SSD starts a data move (DMA) to a device address (IOVA) that has no valid mapping or no permission. It may be a command fetch, a PRP-list fetch, a data read or write, or a done-note write. Or it may be the MSI address, when that is not remapped. The memory guard (IOMMU) blocks it. Blocked reads end with an error (UR or CA, or a timeout at the device). Blocked writes are dropped. The NVMe command fails. More often its done note is lost, and the computer times out.

How you can tell: An IOMMU fault message names the device's Requester ID and the faulting address. On Intel it often looks like "DMAR: [DMA Read/Write] Request device [bb:dd.f] ... fault addr 0x... [fault reason 0xNN] ...". On AMD it looks like "AMD-Vi: Event logged [IO_PAGE_FAULT device=... address=...]". These IOMMU driver lines were not checked against the local tree, so they are not sure. The QEMU NVMe model shows what a careful device does when its own command-list or done-list data move fails. The functions nvme_process_sq() and nvme_post_cqes() trace pci_nvme_err_addr_read / _write and pci_nvme_err_cfs. Then they set CSTS to NVME_CSTS_FAILED. Real SSDs may instead set CFS, log an error, or carry on. This depends on the design.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Risky, test machine only: use a user-space NVMe driver (vfio-based). Send a command with a PRP that points outside its mapped buffer. The IOMMU must fault. The SSD's response (CFS, an error result, or a hang) is the test result. Run dmesg | grep -iE 'DMAR|AMD-Vi|iommu|smmu'. Match the fault address to an NVMe structure. Use the nvme_setup_cmd tracepoint (/sys/kernel/tracing/events/nvme/) and look for the same IOVA in PRP1/PRP2. A test reboot with iommu=pt or the IOMMU off can show whether faults turn into silent damage. So check the data.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Yes (Reported). The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Look at the faulting address. Blame the computer when it is inside PRPs or queues the computer supplied. Examples are use after unmap, or a wrong mapping. Blame the SSD when it is outside every supplied range, or cut short (for example a 48-bit DMA limit). · Test that confirms it: Read the IOMMU fault log.

L-37 Power saving makes the wire drop or stall (ASPM) Partly seen in the packets Wire start-up and speed changes

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 161810: waking from power saving (L1) fails. The device never answers, and the wire drops.

Packet=161810 | Link Dir=Downstream | Link Event=Link Down | Time Stamp=0127.887229454000s | Time Delta=96.000 ms

Error family: P08 and P20, two of the 27 ways an error shows on the wire. Proof from outside the recording also counts here. E02 is a copy of the SSD's settings area (lspci). P08 means wire start-up, re-tuning, and speed or width changes. P20 means power-saving handshakes. · Can the packets alone prove it? Partly. The order and timing of the packets show its shape. The proof needs evidence from outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book (PCIe Base Specification) covers the power-saving states ASPM L0s/L1 and L1 PM Substates (L1.1, L1.2). It covers LTR, and the wake-up delays in Link Capabilities and Device Capabilities (acceptable latencies). It also covers the Common Clock Configuration.

What goes wrong: When idle, the wire goes into L0s, L1 or L1.1/L1.2. On the next request it must wake up. Sometimes the wake-up delay is longer than the end device can accept. Or the wake-up fails: the CLKREQ# handshake, the reference clock not restored, or a wire circuit (PHY) bug. Then the wire either stalls (resend timeouts, re-tune) or goes down entirely. Often this happens only after minutes or hours of idle. That makes it look random.

How you can tell: Mild cases: fixable Replay Timer Timeout and Receiver Errors after idle periods. Bad cases: the SSD drops off. The first read or write after idle times out with CSTS=0xffffffff. The driver hint is: Try "nvme_core.default_ps_max_latency_us=0 pcie_aspm=off pcie_port_pm=off" and report a bug. NVMe APST (the controller's own power states) often mixes with ASPM. The quirk table in the error list (chapter VI.3) has many "drops off the PCIe bus" entries for APST. Linux ASPM messages include these. "ASPM: current common clock configuration is inconsistent, reconfiguring". "ASPM: Could not configure common clock". "ASPM: Link Capabilities L0s/L1 treated as unsupported to avoid device defect" (from pcie_aspm_remove_cap() via quirks). "can't disable ASPM; OS doesn't have ASPM control".

How to fix it and prove the fix: Safe: run an idle-then-burst loop with ASPM policy powersupersave versus performance. Count the timeouts. Careful: run for hours. A drop may need a power cycle to recover. Test boots: pcie_aspm=off, or set /sys/module/pcie_aspm/parameters/policy to performance. Control for each wire is under /sys/bus/pci/devices/<BDF>/link/, for example l1_2_aspm. What is there depends on the kernel version. Check lspci -vvv: LnkCtl "ASPM L1 Enabled", and L1SubCtl1. An idle-then-burst test loop: sleep N seconds, read 4 KiB, measure the delay, raise N.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No (Timer only). No error message is sent. Only a time limit running out shows it. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Look at the clock and the wake-up. Blame the platform when L1.2 is on without proper CLKREQ# wiring, or with wrong T_POWER_ON/LTR. Blame the SSD's wire circuit (PHY) when the reference clock is present and the SSD fails to wake. · Test that confirms it: Turn off ASPM and L1 substates (confirmation test T13).

L-38 The SSD saves data that was marked as bad (poison committed) Seen in the packets Badly built or bad-data packets

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 408960: the done note (CQE) says 0 (success) after a bad-marked answer (poisoned CplD). The bad data was saved.

Packet=408960 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=547 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000004:81B90030 | Length=4 | DATA=16 B | Time Stamp=0195.681322367370s | Time Delta=57.870 ns | LCRC=0xB23F71BA

Packet 408931: an answer with data (CplD) has its bad-data mark on (EP=1).

Packet=408931 | Link Dir=Downstream | TLP Type=CplD | PSN=629 | Tag=205 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | CompleterID=000:02:4 | Cpl Status=SC | Length=64 | Byte Cnt=512 | DATA=256 B | Time Stamp=0195.681308840500s | Time Delta=0.000 ns | LCRC=0x93AEADD6

Error family: P11, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. Proof from outside the recording also counts here. E02 is a copy of the SSD's settings area (lspci). P11 means packets that are marked bad, broken or too big. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. This table file marks a wrong detail or a wrong order. The packet's "bad data" mark (EP bit) is on (header_bit_EP_set).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rules cover bad-marked packets (Data Poisoning rules). A receiver of such a packet must not use the data as if it were good. How an NVMe controller then fails the command is up to the design.

What goes wrong: The SSD receives a bad-marked answer (poisoned CplD) carrying write data (error type L-12). AER logs it at the SSD. But the controller's data path ignores the mark. It writes the bad data to flash (NAND) and reports the Write as successful. Later reads return the damaged data with a good result.

How you can tell: One AER Poisoned TLP line (non-fatal, no reset, perhaps limited in rate). The NVMe done note says Success. Nothing else.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Risky, test machine only: insert the bad-data mark (EP) on the answer path with a test sender or capture tool. This destroys the data at the target blocks (LBAs). Insert a bad-marked answer for a known write (exerciser). Then read back that block. Check that either the write failed or the data is intact. Match AER poison events in the field with later application checksum errors.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No (Silent). Nothing reports this error. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Blame the SSD: it saved bad-marked data. The bad mark itself comes from the computer platform (error type L-12). · Test that confirms it: Read the data back.
