Packet 158236: the wire drops before it becomes active (DL_Active), try 3.

Packet=158236 | Link Dir=Downstream | Link Event=Link Down | Time Stamp=0127.782786524000s | Time Delta=20.000 ms

Packet 158246: the wire drops before it becomes active (DL_Active), try 4.

Packet=158246 | Link Dir=Downstream | Link Event=Link Down | Time Stamp=0127.802786716000s | Time Delta=20.000 ms

Packet 158256: the wire drops before it becomes active (DL_Active), try 5.

Packet=158256 | Link Dir=Downstream | Link Event=Link Down | Time Stamp=0127.822786908000s | Time Delta=50.000 ms

Error family: P08, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. Proof from outside the recording also counts here. E02 is a copy of the SSD's settings area (lspci). P08 means wire start-up, re-tuning, and speed or width changes. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. The checker sees it from the order and timing of the packets. Examples are a missing answer, a long gap, or packets in the wrong order.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book (PCIe Base Specification) covers wire start-up (LTSSM). It covers the "wire is active" flag (Data Link Layer Link Active). It also covers the Link Bandwidth Management Status flag and the Target Link Speed.

What goes wrong: Start-up never finishes. The start-up steps cycle between Detect, Polling, Configuration and Recovery. Or they keep switching speed. The comment on pcie_failed_link_retrain() in quirks.c describes a real case (ASMedia ASM2824 switches). There the wire "continues switching between the two speeds indefinitely and the data link layer never reaches the active state, with link training reported repeatedly active ~84% of the time". The SSD never appears.

How you can tell: The SSD is not found (not enumerated). Linux v7.2 may log "broken device, retraining non-functional downstream link at 2.5GT/s". Then it logs "removing 2.5GT/s downstream link speed restriction" on success, or "retraining failed" on failure. It may also log "Data Link Layer Link Active not set in %d msec". That comes from pci_bridge_wait_for_secondary_bus() in pci.c, after pcie_wait_for_link_delay() fails.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Risky, test machine only: use a test sender (exerciser) that refuses speed changes. Or use a weakened wire path at the target speed. The port's LnkSta shows Link Training set or switching on and off, DLActive-, and LBMS+. The quirk uses exactly this: DLLLA clear plus LBMS seen. Try forcing a 2.5 GT/s Target Link Speed to see whether the wire comes up.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No (Timer only). No error message is sent. Only a time limit running out shows it. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Look at what both sides announced. Blame the wire or tuning when both sides announce matching speeds and lane numbers. Otherwise blame the side that sends badly formed training signals, or has a known chip bug (erratum). · Test that confirms it: Compare what the wire can do with what it is doing now (E02, a copy of the SSD's settings area).

L-40 Request-number or ordering features mismatch (10-bit tags, Relaxed Ordering) Seen in the packets Wrong request number or sender

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 109435: 10-bit request number (tag) 260 is used, although 10-Bit Tag Requester Enable=0.

Packet=109435 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MRd(64) | PSN=2114 | Tag=260 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000003:1D75D000 | Length=64 | Time Stamp=0125.571267235620s | Time Delta=0.000 ns | LCRC=0x25F748A3

Packet 109436: 10-bit tag 261 is used, although 10-Bit Tag Requester Enable=0.

Packet=109436 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MRd(64) | PSN=2115 | Tag=261 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000002:F2CE1000 | Length=64 | Time Stamp=0125.571267238750s | Time Delta=141.000 ns | LCRC=0xFC1E56BF

Packet 109439: the answer comes back with tag 4. The number wrapped round at 8 bits.

Packet=109439 | Link Dir=Downstream | TLP Type=CplD | PSN=3269 | Tag=4 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | CompleterID=000:02:4 | Cpl Status=SC | Length=64 | Byte Cnt=256 | DATA=256 B | Time Stamp=0125.571268038750s | Time Delta=149.120 ns | LCRC=0xFA31AC21

Packet 109441: the answer comes back with tag 5. The number wrapped round at 8 bits.

Packet=109441 | Link Dir=Downstream | TLP Type=CplD | PSN=3270 | Tag=5 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | CompleterID=000:02:4 | Cpl Status=SC | Length=64 | Byte Cnt=256 | DATA=256 B | Time Stamp=0125.571268238750s | Time Delta=151.120 ns | LCRC=0x51321FF0

Error family: P05 and P19, two of the 27 ways an error shows on the wire. Proof from outside the recording also counts here. E02 is a copy of the SSD's settings area (lspci). P05 means an unexpected answer, or a wrong request number or sender. P19 means reading and writing the SSD's settings area, and restarts. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. This table file marks a wrong detail or a wrong order. A request was lost when the wire went down (request_lost_across_link_down). An answer arrived that nobody asked for (unexpected_completion).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book (PCIe Base Specification) covers the Extended Tag Field Enable and the 10-Bit Tag Requester/Completer bits. It covers the Relaxed Ordering mark, and Enable Relaxed Ordering in Device Control.

What goes wrong: There are two linked failures. (1) Request numbers (tags). A side may use 8-bit (Extended) or 10-bit tags toward a side or root that handles them badly. That gives answers with wrong tags (Unexpected Completion, Completion Timeout). Turning them off limits how many reads can be open. So the SSD's read speed drops at a high queue depth. (2) Relaxed Ordering. Some root complexes have known bugs (errata) with Relaxed Ordering (RO) packets. Linux turns off RO for listed root ports. It prints "Disable Relaxed Ordering Attributes to avoid PCIe Completion erratum". The quirks.c comment cites a Flow Control credit issue on Broadwell/Haswell Xeon root complexes, causing "performance problems".

How you can tell: Messages from probe.c: "enabling Extended Tags" or "disabling Extended Tags". Also "Relaxed Ordering disabled because the Root Port didn't support it". Otherwise only lower speed.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Risky, test machine only: use a test sender (exerciser) that delays an answer past the SSD's answer time limit. Read the header's request number (Tag) and Requester ID. Check whether 10-Bit Tag Requester Enable is set. See lspci -vvv DevCtl2 "10BitTagReq". Also check that every hop supports it.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No (Degraded). No error is reported. Things still work, but slower or on a weaker wire. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Look at the enable bits. Blame the computer platform when the root complex or switch handles turned-on tags or RO badly (errata). Or when the enable bits are set toward a path that does not support them. Blame the SSD when it uses 10-bit tags or RO without the enable bit. · Test that confirms it: Check the tag and RO settings.

Chapter V: rule breaks visible in the recording (37 entries)

Why this part is here: these 37 entries are packets that clearly break a PCIe or NVMe rule.

V-01 Command-list doorbell number is past the list size (SQ tail doorbell) Seen in the packets Wrong doorbell number

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 486307: the doorbell of command list 1 (SQ1 tail doorbell) is 1024, on a list with 1024 places.

Packet=486307 | Link Dir=Downstream | TLP Type=MWr(32) | PSN=1195 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=000:00:0 | Address=FCE01008 | Length=1 | DATA=4 B | Time Stamp=0370.683805590750s | Time Delta=148.120 ns | LCRC=0xFE8C5379

Packet 486310: a warning event (AEN): Error, Invalid Doorbell Write Value (01h), log page LID 01h.

Packet=486310 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=2146 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000004:82C400E0 | Length=4 | DATA=16 B | Time Stamp=0370.683835590750s | Time Delta=54.880 ns | LCRC=0x3C793FDB

Error family: P14, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. P14 means wrong doorbell numbers. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. The checker sees it from the order and timing of the packets. Examples are a missing answer, a long gap, or packets in the wrong order.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book (NVMe Base) sets what the command-list doorbell (SQ Tail Doorbell) means. It also defines a warning event, "Invalid Doorbell Write Value" (Error event type). QEMU quotes the rule from NVMe 1.3d in nvme_process_db. The rule: "If host software writes an invalid value to the Submission Queue Tail Doorbell or Completion Queue Head Doorbell register and an Asynchronous Event Request command is outstanding, then an asynchronous event is posted…".

What goes wrong: The computer writes a command-list doorbell (SQ y Tail Doorbell). The value is ≥ the number of places in that list. For example, tail = 70 on a 64-place list. Such a value cannot be a place number.

How you can tell: The controller ignores the write. An event request (Asynchronous Event Request) may be waiting. Then it may send an Error-type warning event, "Invalid Doorbell Write Value". It may also log an entry in the Error Information log. If no event request is waiting, nothing is reported. Commands put in the command list are simply never fetched. Later they time out.

How to fix it and prove the fix: On QEMU (safe): a user-space driver or nvme-cli is not enough. Write the doorbell through a raw mapping of the emulated device's memory window (BAR). Watch the QEMU trace event pci_nvme_ub_db_wr_invalid_sqtail. On real hardware this is risky, test machine only. You need an unbound device, a vfio-based test harness, and an event request sent beforehand. Checker rule: for each doorbell write, work out the list number from the address offset. Compare the value against QSIZE+1 from the Create I/O SQ command. For the setup command list (admin queue), use AQA.ASQS+1. On Linux, look for nvme_async_event trace events and NVMe error-log entries. Linux v7.2 records the result in ctrl->aen_result.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Yes (Reported). The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Blame the computer's software (list position maths). The SSD is not involved, except for the optional warning event. · Test that confirms it: The error log, or a kernel notice (uevent).

V-02 Done-list doorbell number is past the list size (CQ head doorbell) Seen in the packets Wrong doorbell number

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 488178: the doorbell of done list 2 (CQ2 head doorbell) is past the list size.

Packet=488178 | Link Dir=Downstream | TLP Type=MWr(32) | PSN=1391 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=000:00:0 | Address=FCE01014 | Length=1 | DATA=4 B | Time Stamp=0370.694032816370s | Time Delta=144.130 ns | LCRC=0x17D2E6FA

Packet 488180: a warning event (AEN): Invalid Doorbell Write Value.

Packet=488180 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=2914 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000004:82CE00C0 | Length=4 | DATA=16 B | Time Stamp=0370.694062816370s | Time Delta=54.870 ns | LCRC=0x406CE272

Error family: P14, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. P14 means wrong doorbell numbers. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. The checker sees it from the order and timing of the packets. Examples are a missing answer, a long gap, or packets in the wrong order.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book (NVMe Base) sets what the done-list doorbell (CQ Head Doorbell) means. The same warning event as in error type V-01 applies.

What goes wrong: The computer writes a done-list doorbell (CQ y Head Doorbell) with a value ≥ the list size. The controller cannot tell how many places were freed.

How you can tell: The write is ignored. An optional Error warning event, "Invalid Doorbell Write Value", may follow. The head does not move forward. So in time the controller sees the done list as full, and stops writing done notes. All reads and writes stall, on every command list that shares that done list. Then they time out.

How to fix it and prove the fix: QEMU (safe): on an idle done list, write a raw doorbell of size+2. Watch for pci_nvme_ub_db_wr_invalid_cqhead. With an event request waiting, a warning event appears on the setup done list. Use the same checker rule as error type V-01. Compare against the done-list size from Create I/O CQ (QSIZE+1) or AQA.ACQS+1. Match it up: after the bad doorbell, the done-note writes on that list stop at exactly size−1 unfreed entries.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Yes (Reported). The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Blame the computer's software. · Test that confirms it: The warning event or a kernel notice (AEN/uevent).

V-03 A doorbell is written for a list that does not exist Seen in the packets Wrong doorbell number

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 489510: doorbell of command list 7 (SQ7 tail doorbell), but list 7 was never made.

Packet=489510 | Link Dir=Downstream | TLP Type=MWr(32) | PSN=1545 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=000:00:0 | Address=FCE01038 | Length=1 | DATA=4 B | Time Stamp=0370.705293632750s | Time Delta=112.120 ns | LCRC=0x0FD6EE9B

Packet 489512: a warning event (AEN): Invalid Doorbell Register (00h).

Packet=489512 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=3440 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000004:82D800C0 | Length=4 | DATA=16 B | Time Stamp=0370.705323632750s | Time Delta=54.880 ns | LCRC=0x3CDEF7FD

Error family: P14, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. P14 means wrong doorbell numbers. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. The checker sees it from the order and timing of the packets. Examples are a missing answer, a long gap, or packets in the wrong order.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book (NVMe Base) sets where each doorbell sits: 1000h + (2y)·(4<<CAP.DSTRD). It also defines a warning event, "Invalid Doorbell Register".

What goes wrong: The computer writes a doorbell address that belongs to a list number that was never made. Or the list was already deleted. Or the number is above the lists granted by Set Features Number of Queues.

How you can tell: The controller ignores it. An optional Error warning event, "Invalid Doorbell Register", may follow. A QEMU comment notes that the rule book defines this code. But "nowhere does it specify when to use it". QEMU uses it for lists that do not exist. So other controllers may report it differently, or not at all. This depends on the design.

How to fix it and prove the fix: QEMU (safe): write the command-list doorbell of list number conf_ioqpairs+1. Look for the QEMU trace pci_nvme_ub_db_wr_invalid_sq. An example made by a program, not real hardware, appears as check DB-NOQ (error list, section 7.6). A checker keeps the set of live list numbers. It learns them from Create/Delete I/O SQ/CQ commands and their successful done notes. Any doorbell outside the set is marked. A wrong spacing (stride) shows as doorbells whose offsets are not multiples of 4<<DSTRD apart.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Yes (Reported). The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Blame the computer's software: wrong spacing (stride), a race while tearing down, or virtual function (VF) numbering. · Test that confirms it: A QEMU control run.

V-04 A doorbell is written with the wrong size or position Seen in the packets Wrong doorbell number

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 492481: a doorbell write (MWr) with first byte enables 0011b. It writes only 16 bits.

Packet=492481 | Link Dir=Downstream | TLP Type=MWr(32) | PSN=2139 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=000:00:0 | Address=FCE01008 | Length=1 | DATA=4 B | Time Stamp=0370.705762893120s | Time Delta=101.130 ns | LCRC=0xEAAE8412

Error family: P14, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. P14 means wrong doorbell numbers. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. This table file marks a wrong detail or a wrong order. A write covers only part of a 4-byte block (partial_dword_write).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book (NVMe Base) says controller settings are read and written at their natural width. Doorbells are 32-bit settings. Other access sizes are outside the defined behaviour.

What goes wrong: A doorbell is written with a 1-byte or 2-byte access. Or at an address that is not on a 4-byte (dword) boundary. Or a 64-bit write covers two doorbells at once: the command-list tail and the done-list head of the same pair.

How you can tell: Nothing is reported. QEMU logs a guest-error trace (pci_nvme_ub_db_wr_misaligned) and ignores the write. Real controllers may ignore it, keep only some bytes, or update both doorbells. This depends on the design.

How to fix it and prove the fix: QEMU (safe): write 16 bits to a doorbell, and check the QEMU trace output. Checker: mark a doorbell write whose length is not 4 bytes. Or whose first or last byte enables are not 1111b. Or whose address is not on a 4-byte boundary.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No (Silent). Nothing reports this error. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Blame the computer's software: wrong access width, or writes merged together (store merging). · Test that confirms it: A QEMU control run.

V-05 The command-list end moves back, or overwrites waiting commands Seen in the packets Wrong doorbell number

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 495580: the end of command list 1 (SQ1 tail) moves backwards, without wrapping round.

Packet=495580 | Link Dir=Downstream | TLP Type=MWr(32) | PSN=2778 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=000:00:0 | Address=FCE01008 | Length=1 | DATA=4 B | Time Stamp=0370.706029569250s | Time Delta=105.120 ns | LCRC=0x26D1B3C0

Error family: P14, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. P14 means wrong doorbell numbers. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. The checker sees it from the order and timing of the packets. Examples are a missing answer, a long gap, or packets in the wrong order.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book (NVMe Base) list model says this. The computer must not add to a full command list. Full means tail+1 == head. Entries between head and tail belong to the controller, and the computer must not change them. The computer learns the head from SQHD in the done notes.

What goes wrong: The new tail value means one of two things. It may mean a negative number of new entries. The tail moved "backwards", so the computer took entries back. Or it may mean so many new entries that the list would hold ≥ N items. Then the computer has overwritten commands the controller had not yet fetched.

How you can tell: Nothing is reported. The value is in range, so error type V-01 does not trigger. Wrap-round sums hide the problem: a backwards move looks like "N−k new commands". The results range from repeated commands to lost commands. With repeats, the controller runs old commands from an earlier pass again. For example, an old Write writes old data again. Lost commands time out.

How to fix it and prove the fix: QEMU (safe): QEMU does not check this (error list, section 7.1.3). Write tail values out of order and watch commands run again. This is a good negative test for your checker. Checker: keep the computer's tail T and the controller's head H. H comes from the latest SQHD and from seen fetches. For a new tail T', new = (T'−T) mod N. Mark it if new > (N−1) − ((T−H) mod N). Also mark it if a re-fetched place holds the same data as a command already done (an old repeat).

Does the SSD or computer report it? No (Silent). Nothing reports this error. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Blame the computer's software: list position maths, or locking. · Test that confirms it: A QEMU negative test.

V-06 The computer frees done-list places the SSD has not filled Seen in the packets Wrong doorbell number

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 498911: the head of done list 1 (CQ1 head) is moved past the controller's last written place.

Packet=498911 | Link Dir=Downstream | TLP Type=MWr(32) | PSN=3576 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=000:00:0 | Address=FCE0100C | Length=1 | DATA=4 B | Time Stamp=0370.706347712870s | Time Delta=112.130 ns | LCRC=0xB5E8F2D3

Error family: P14, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. P14 means wrong doorbell numbers. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. The checker sees it from the order and timing of the packets. Examples are a missing answer, a long gap, or packets in the wrong order.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book (NVMe Base) list model says the computer frees only entries it has used. Those are entries with the current phase.

What goes wrong: The computer writes a done-list head that frees more entries than the controller has written. The controller now thinks there is free space. But that space holds its own future places. Its full/empty sums are broken.

How you can tell: No result number. Later the controller may overwrite done notes the computer has not used yet, because it thinks they were freed. This gives lost done notes (timeouts). Or, together with phase reuse, old done notes are handled twice.

How to fix it and prove the fix: QEMU (safe) with a test harness: send one command, then write CQ head = 3. QEMU will not complain, but your checker should. A checker counts done-note writes per done list (the device tail). It compares every done-list doorbell: freed = (H'−H) mod N must be ≤ (Tail−H) mod N. This is check CQDB-PAST-TAIL (error list, section 7.6).

Does the SSD or computer report it? No (Silent). Nothing reports this error. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Blame the computer's software: it uses entries by index, has a size mismatch, or missed a wrap-round. · Test that confirms it: A QEMU test harness.

V-07 The done list overflows or stops moving (CQ overflow) Seen in the packets Wrong doorbell number

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 502492: the doorbell for done list 4 (CQ4 head) comes only after 6 done notes piled up. The computer stopped reading the list.

Packet=502492 | Link Dir=Downstream | TLP Type=MWr(32) | PSN=284 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=000:00:0 | Address=FCE01024 | Length=1 | DATA=4 B | Time Stamp=0370.708626347620s | Time Delta=154.130 ns | LCRC=0x52077499

Error family: P14, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. P14 means wrong doorbell numbers. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. The checker sees it from the order and timing of the packets. Examples are a missing answer, a long gap, or packets in the wrong order.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book (NVMe Base) defines a full done list: head == tail+1. The controller does not write to a full done list. The computer must size done lists so that all commands that can be open on its command lists fit. QEMU's nvme_post_cqes leaves its loop when nvme_cq_full.

What goes wrong: There are two kinds. (a) The computer stops moving the done-list head. Causes are a lost signal, a stuck processor, or a driver bug. The done list fills to N−1 entries, and the controller must stop writing. Reads and writes stall. (b) The controller writes while the done list is full. It overwrites an entry the computer has not used.

How you can tell: (a) Only the computer's read/write timeout. Linux often logs "completion polled", if the done note was really there (error type V-15). (b) Nothing. The overwritten done note is lost, and its command times out. The overwriting entry may carry the "wrong" phase, from the computer's view.

How to fix it and prove the fix: QEMU (safe): send N commands while never writing the done-list head. Check that QEMU stops at N−1 done notes. On real hardware, kind (b) needs a capture tool to prove. Checker: keep the done-list tail (count of done-note writes) and head (doorbells). Mark a done-note write when (tail+1) mod N == head. For (a), mark "CQ head unchanged for X ms while CQ non-empty".

Does the SSD or computer report it? No (Timer only). No error message is sent. Only a time limit running out shows it. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: It depends on the kind. For (a), blame the computer: the reader stopped (lost signal, stuck processor, driver bug). For (b), blame the SSD: it wrote into a full done list. · Test that confirms it: A QEMU stop test.

V-08 A command number is used again while still open (CID reuse) Seen in the packets Wrong details in done note

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 554368: the computer sends a second command (SQE) with a command number (CID) that is still open.

Packet=554368 | Link Dir=Downstream | TLP Type=CplD | PSN=981 | Tag=192 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | CompleterID=000:02:4 | Cpl Status=SC | Length=16 | Byte Cnt=64 | DATA=64 B | Time Stamp=0371.079333739120s | Time Delta=166.750 ns | LCRC=0x9E96240F

Error family: P15, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. P15 means wrong details in done notes. · Can the packets alone prove it? Only if the bytes inside the packets are kept. The result number or content is inside those bytes (DATA column). The table file version that keeps the bytes marks it. A command number was used again while still open (nvme_cid_reused_while_open). A done note names an unknown or already finished command number (nvme_cqe_unknown_or_completed_cid).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book (NVMe Base) says two numbers together name one open command. They are the command number (CID) and the list number (SQ Identifier). The general result "Command ID Conflict" exists for this.

What goes wrong: The computer sends a command whose number equals that of a command still open on the same list. Done notes become unclear. The computer cannot tell which of the two finished. The Abort command, which names SQID+CID, becomes unclear too.

How you can tell: Usually nothing. A controller may catch it and end the new command with general result 03h, "Command ID Conflict" (Linux NVME_SC_CMDID_CONFLICT). Many controllers do not check. QEMU does not check. Its nvme_abort would match the first request with that CID. This depends on the design.

How to fix it and prove the fix: A checker keeps the set of open commands for each list. It adds (SQID,CID) when a command is fetched, and removes it on its done note. It marks repeats (check CID-REUSE, error list, section 7.6). Linux puts a 4-bit generation counter in the top bits of the CID. So a reused tag normally gets a different CID. A repeat in a Linux recording is strong evidence of a real bug.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No (Silent). Nothing reports this error. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Blame the computer's software. It reused a tag before the done note came, or a user-space driver uses fixed command numbers. · Test that confirms it: Check the controller.

V-09 A done note names an unknown or already finished command Seen in the packets Wrong details in done note

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 558416: a done note (CQE) for command number 0x0003, which finished long ago.

Packet=558416 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=3951 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000004:82D902C0 | Length=4 | DATA=16 B | Time Stamp=0371.080054748620s | Time Delta=25.870 ns | LCRC=0x35BBD34E

Error family: P15, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. P15 means wrong details in done notes. · Can the packets alone prove it? Only if the bytes inside the packets are kept. The result number or content is inside those bytes (DATA column). The table file version that keeps the bytes marks it. A done note names an unknown or already finished command number (nvme_cqe_unknown_or_completed_cid).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book (NVMe Base) says each command is finished exactly once. One done note names it by SQID+CID.

What goes wrong: The controller writes a done note whose command number matches no open command on that list. It may be a repeated done note or a damaged command number. Or a done note for a command the computer already gave up on (aborted or timed out).

How you can tell: Linux v7.2 logs "invalid id %d completed on queue %d", or "request %#x genctr mismatch (got … expected …)". It drops the entry. Other drivers may finish the wrong request. This is a silent data danger, because the wrong buffer is declared ready.

How to fix it and prove the fix: This is check CQE-UNKNOWN. In Linux, search dmesg for "invalid id" and "genctr mismatch". A recording tells a "repeat" (number seen in an earlier done note) from "never sent" (number never fetched).

Does the SSD or computer report it? Yes (Reported). The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Look at the history of that number. Blame the SSD for a repeat or a never-fetched number. Blame the computer for done notes of commands it already aborted or timed out. In that case the done note itself is allowed: it comes from a late controller. · Test that confirms it: The kernel log (dmesg).

V-10 Wrong list number or stuck head in a done note (SQID, SQHD) Seen in the packets Wrong details in done note

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 561318: a done note on done list 1 names command list 2 (SQID 2).

Packet=561318 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=1241 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000004:82D90300 | Length=4 | DATA=16 B | Time Stamp=0371.080366213750s | Time Delta=29.880 ns | LCRC=0x974C933C

Error family: P15, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. P15 means wrong details in done notes. · Can the packets alone prove it? Only if the bytes inside the packets are kept. The result number or content is inside those bytes (DATA column). The table file version that keeps the bytes marks it. A done note names an unknown or already finished command number (nvme_cqe_unknown_or_completed_cid).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book (NVMe Base) defines the SQID and SQHD fields in word 2 (DW2) of the done note. SQHD gives the current head of the command list named by SQID.

What goes wrong: The done note's list number (SQ Identifier, DW2 bits 31:16) names the wrong list. It is not the list the command came from. Or its head value (SQ Head Pointer, DW2 bits 15:0) moves backwards or past the tail. Or it never moves, although commands are being taken.

How you can tell: With a shared done list, a wrong SQID makes the computer look up the command number in the wrong list. The wrong request is finished, or "invalid id" appears. A frozen SQHD can fool a computer that uses SQHD to pace itself (flow control). It thinks the command list is full. Speed falls to zero, with no error. Linux does not use SQHD this way, so it is not affected. So the same SSD "works on Linux, hangs on another OS".

How to fix it and prove the fix: Checker: SQID must equal the list the command was fetched from. SQHD must meet (SQHD − previous SQHD) mod N ≤ the number of fetches since. It must never pass the computer's tail.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No (Silent). Nothing reports this error. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Blame the SSD: it builds the done note wrongly. · Test that confirms it: Test with a computer driver that obeys SQHD.

V-11 Phase bit not flipped when the done list wraps round (Phase Tag) Seen in the packets Wrong details in done note

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 563584: done list 5 (CQ5) wrapped back to place 0, but its phase bit (phase tag) was not flipped.

Packet=563584 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=1908 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000004:82E10000 | Length=4 | DATA=16 B | Time Stamp=0371.080969838620s | Time Delta=26.870 ns | LCRC=0x26119088

Error family: P15, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. P15 means wrong details in done notes. · Can the packets alone prove it? Only if the bytes inside the packets are kept. The result number or content is inside those bytes (DATA column). The table file version that keeps the bytes marks it. A done note's phase bit has the wrong value (nvme_cqe_phase_wrong).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book (NVMe Base) defines the Phase Tag. It "identifies whether a completion queue entry is new". It is flipped on each pass through the done list. The computer fills the done-list memory with zeros at the start. So the first pass uses P=1.

What goes wrong: After the controller wraps from the last done-list place to place 0, it must flip the Phase Tag. That is P, bit 0 of the status half of DW3. Sometimes it keeps the old value. The computer expects the new phase, so it sees the new entry as "old" and does not use it. If the controller flips too early, the computer uses old entries.

How you can tell: Missing flip: the done notes are invisible to the computer, so reads and writes time out. Linux may report "completion polled" only if the phase matches. Here it does not, so a plain timeout and an abort or reset follow. Early flip: old done notes are handled twice. This gives "invalid id" messages or double completion.

How to fix it and prove the fix: A checker keeps the tail and the expected phase for each done list. It starts at 1 and flips at each wrap. It compares every done note (check PHASE, error list, section 7.6). A phase error is often the sign of an earlier overflow (error type V-07, kind b). Always report the first packet that went wrong.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No (Timer only). No error message is sent. Only a time limit running out shows it. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Blame the SSD: its wrap logic. Blame the computer if the done-list size in Create I/O CQ differs from what the driver assumes. · Test that confirms it: A stress test with a small done list that wraps often.

V-12 Shadow doorbell copy and real doorbell disagree (shadow doorbell out of sync) Partly seen in the packets Wrong doorbell number

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 504331: the controller reads the shadow doorbell copy in memory, and gets an old value.

Packet=504331 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MRd(32) | PSN=4078 | Tag=199 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=41E66000 | Length=1 | Time Stamp=0370.711855814620s | Time Delta=108.630 ns | LCRC=0xA1AC6BBB

Error family: P14, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. Proof from outside the recording also counts here. E01 is the Linux kernel log (dmesg). E03 is the SSD's own logs and settings (nvme-cli). E05 is a record of the computer's storage steps (blktrace). P14 means wrong doorbell numbers. · Can the packets alone prove it? Partly. The order and timing of the packets show its shape. The proof needs evidence from outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book (NVMe Base) has the Doorbell Buffer Config command. It sets up a Shadow Doorbell buffer and an EventIdx buffer. QEMU quotes this rule: "the host shall also update the controller's corresponding doorbell property to match the value of that entry in the Shadow Doorbell buffer".

What goes wrong: The Doorbell Buffer Config setup command is used mainly by emulated or virtual controllers. With it, the computer writes doorbell values into a shadow copy in its own memory. It rings the real doorbell (MMIO) only when the controller's EventIdx says so. The computer may update one but not the other, or ignore EventIdx. Then the controller works from an old tail or head.

How you can tell: Stalls that clear when any later doorbell is rung. Delay spikes. No error. QEMU's nvme_process_db has a comment about this. It says "various drivers including ones that run on Linux, are not updating Admin Queues" in the shadow copy. So QEMU writes the setup-list values back itself. This depends on the design.

How to fix it and prove the fix: QEMU (safe): turn on shadow doorbells. They are used automatically when the controller supports the command. Stress small-queue work while tracing pci_nvme_mmio_doorbell_sq. In a virtual machine, the "recording" is QEMU's own tracing (pci_nvme_* events), or a vhost/vfio capture. Compare the shadow value reads (data reads of the shadow copy) with the real doorbells.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No (Silent). Nothing reports this error. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Blame the computer's software. It missed a shadow update, or a barrier before reading EventIdx, or it left out the setup list. · Test that confirms it: A QEMU trace.

V-13 The done note arrives before all the data (ordering error) Seen in the packets Wrong order or missing signal

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 605855: the done note (CQE) is written before the last data writes.

Packet=605855 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=804 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000004:82E503D0 | Length=4 | DATA=16 B | Time Stamp=0491.199022985370s | Time Delta=51.380 ns | LCRC=0xAF3E4E2E

Packet 605858: a data write (MWr) after the done note.

Packet=605858 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=805 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000003:37E79E00 | Length=64 | DATA=256 B | Time Stamp=0491.199023214370s | Time Delta=178.630 ns | LCRC=0xE84DB147

Error family: P16, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. P16 means data, done note and signal in the wrong order, or a lost signal. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. The checker sees it from the order and timing of the packets. Examples are a missing answer, a long gap, or packets in the wrong order.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCI Express rule book (PCI Express Base) has ordering rules for writes that need no answer (posted requests). One such write must not pass another, unless the Relaxed Ordering (RO) mark is set. The NVMe rule book (NVMe Base) says a done note means the command's data move is complete.

What goes wrong: For a Read, the controller writes the done note before all data writes for that command are sent. Or it sets RO on data or done-note packets in a way that lets the done note overtake. The computer sees "success" and hands the buffer to the program. The program reads old bytes. The real data arrives microseconds later, after the program has already used the buffer.

How you can tell: Nothing in any log. The signs are data damage that comes and goes. It disappears when tracing is on, because the timing changes. Programs see checksum failures, usually on the last packet(s) of a transfer.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Only the capture tool can show it. Run fio verify with RO on and off on a test machine, and compare. Use two probes (above and below a switch), and compare the packet order. On a single wire, check that no done note or MSI-X packet has RO=1. Also check that the SSD-to-computer writes follow the NVMe order: data → done note → MSI-X.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No (Silent). Nothing reports this error. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Blame the SSD: its data movers and done-note writer are not kept in order, or the done note has RO. Blame the switch fabric only with a second probe. It must show the right order at the device and the wrong order above. RO must also have allowed it. · Test that confirms it: Check the data (data verify).

V-14 The "work done" signal comes before its done note Seen in the packets Wrong order or missing signal

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 609468: the "work done" signal (MSI-X write) is sent before its done note.

Packet=609468 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(32) | PSN=2058 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=FEE01000 | Length=1 | DATA=4 B | Time Stamp=0491.199367172500s | Time Delta=123.120 ns | LCRC=0xECB4B9D9

Error family: P16, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. P16 means data, done note and signal in the wrong order, or a lost signal. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. The checker sees it from the order and timing of the packets. Examples are a missing answer, a long gap, or packets in the wrong order.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book (NVMe Base) says signals are made for new done-list entries. The PCI Express write-order rules make sure the MSI-X write cannot pass the earlier done-note write. That holds if the device sends them in order, without RO.

What goes wrong: The signal write reaches the computer before the done-note write. Or there is no new done note at all. The signal handler checks the done list, finds nothing with the expected phase, and returns.

How you can tell: Unneeded signals (spurious interrupts). Linux nvme_irq returns IRQ_NONE. If this happens very often, the kernel's spurious-signal detector can turn off the signal line ("nobody cared"). After that, done notes are found only by the timeout handler. Then error type V-07 (kind a) and "completion polled" messages follow. Before that point, there is extra delay, because the real done note waits for the next signal.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Check MSIX-NO-CQE: each MSI-X for signal number v must have at least one new done note before it. That note must be on a done list linked to v, since the previous MSI-X. On Linux, compare the counts for each signal in /proc/interrupts with the done notes. Spurious counts show in /proc/irq/<n>/spurious.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No (Degraded). No error is reported. Things still work, but slower or on a weaker wire. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Blame the SSD. Its signal maker is not kept in order after the done-note write. Or the MSI-X write has RO. · Test that confirms it: Read the spurious-signal counter.

V-15 A done note is written, but no "work done" signal follows Seen in the packets Wrong order or missing signal

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 611246: a done note (CQE) with no MSI-X signal.

Packet=611246 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=2691 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000004:82E70440 | Length=4 | DATA=16 B | Time Stamp=0491.199760603500s | Time Delta=128.120 ns | LCRC=0x17DFE735

Packet 618297: the done-list doorbell, after the timeout handler checked the list itself (completion polled).

Packet=618297 | Link Dir=Downstream | TLP Type=MWr(32) | PSN=3574 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=000:00:0 | Address=FCE01014 | Length=1 | DATA=4 B | Time Stamp=0521.199760603500s | Time Delta=159.120 ns | LCRC=0x50F56E5F

Error family: P16, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. P16 means data, done note and signal in the wrong order, or a lost signal. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. The checker sees it from the order and timing of the packets. Examples are a missing answer, a long gap, or packets in the wrong order.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book (NVMe Base) defines two fields of Create I/O Completion Queue. They are Interrupt Vector (IV) and Interrupts Enabled (IEN). The PCI rules define the MSI-X table and Pending Bit Array. A masked signal sets its pending bit instead of being sent.

What goes wrong: The controller writes a done note but never sends the signal. The signal may be masked in the MSI-X table. Or the wrong signal number was set in Create I/O CQ. Or the function-mask bit is set, or there is a firmware bug.

How you can tell: Linux v7.2: the request times out. Then nvme_timeout checks the done list itself and finds the done note. It prints "I/O tag … QID … timeout, completion polled". This line is the sign of a lost signal. The delay equals the time limit (30 s by default for reads and writes).

How to fix it and prove the fix: Checker: a done note is written, but no MSI-X for its signal comes within a window (for example 1 ms). IEN=1 for that done list. On the computer, look for "completion polled" in dmesg. Read the MSI-X PBA through the memory window (BAR), only reading, to see the pending bits.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No (Timer only). No error message is sent. Only a time limit running out shows it. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Look at the settings. Blame the SSD if everything on the computer side is set and unmasked. Blame the computer if it set a mask bit, set IV out of range, or left MSI-X turned off. · Test that confirms it: The kernel log (dmesg).

V-16 The SSD touches a command's buffer after its done note Seen in the packets Wrong order or missing signal

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 623335: a data move (DMA) into the command's buffer after its done note.

Packet=623335 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=3168 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000001:D129D000 | Length=64 | DATA=256 B | Time Stamp=0521.200175027750s | Time Delta=126.620 ns | LCRC=0xEDA608ED

Error family: P16, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. P16 means data, done note and signal in the wrong order, or a lost signal. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. The checker sees it from the order and timing of the packets. Examples are a missing answer, a long gap, or packets in the wrong order.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book (NVMe Base) says writing the done note hands the data buffers back to the computer. The memory address lists (PRP/SGL) are valid only while the command is open.

What goes wrong: The controller writes to, or reads from, a command's memory after it wrote that command's done note. An example is the end of the data for a read. Another is a retried data read for a write. By then the computer may have freed or reused the buffer.

How you can tell: Random memory damage elsewhere in the system, because the page has been given to something else. Or IOMMU faults if the mapping was removed. These are DMAR/AMD-Vi fault messages in dmesg that name the device. Or nothing at all.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Boot a test machine with iommu.strict=1 (or the platform's version of it). Run mixed reads and writes with many commands waiting (high queue depth). Any IOMMU fault naming the SSD is a broken-rule note. Match it with a recording. Check DMA-NOCMD: a data write or read whose address belongs to a command that already finished. No newer command may own that address. With an IOMMU in strict mode, a late data move causes a translation fault. That is strong evidence on the computer side.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No (Silent). Nothing reports this error. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Blame the SSD. Blame the computer only if it aborted or freed the command first, while the SSD could still finish. Then report it as SUSPECT. · Test that confirms it: Run with the IOMMU in strict mode.

Error family: P18, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. P18 means wrongly filled commands. · Can the packets alone prove it? Only if the bytes inside the packets are kept. The result number or content is inside those bytes (DATA column). The table file version that keeps the bytes marks it. A done note has a result number that is not 0 (nvme_status_nonzero).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book (NVMe Base) sets the format of a memory address entry (PRP Entry). It has an offset field and must be on a 4-byte (dword) boundary. It also sets the PRP List rules. The general result "PRP Offset Invalid" exists for this.

What goes wrong: PRP1 has bits 1:0 set. Or an entry inside a PRP list has a page offset that is not zero. The list pointer is the allowed exception.

How you can tell: A checking controller ends the command with general result 13h, "PRP Offset Invalid" (Linux NVME_SC_PRP_INVALID_OFFSET). Usually DNR is set. A non-checking controller moves data to the wrong address. This silently damages unrelated memory.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Checker: decode DPTR. Fetch the PRP list through the read request (MRd) and answer (CplD) that follow. Test each entry against the rules in the table above (in the error list). On the computer, the nvme error-log shows result 13h with the CID and SQID.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Yes (Reported). The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Blame the computer: the driver or tool builds the PRPs. Blame the SSD only if it moves data to addresses that valid PRPs do not describe. Or if it refuses a valid PRP1 with 13h. · Test that confirms it: The error log.

Packet=694373 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=3965 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000004:82E50A90 | Length=4 | DATA=16 B | Time Stamp=0522.106980563370s | Time Delta=44.870 ns | LCRC=0xACEB2434

Error family: P18, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. P18 means wrongly filled commands. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. The checker sees it from the order and timing of the packets. Examples are a missing answer, a long gap, or packets in the wrong order.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book (NVMe Base) sets what PRP Entry 2 means. It is either a data pointer or a PRP List pointer. PRP entries other than PRP1 and the list pointer must have a zero offset.

What goes wrong: The transfer needs exactly two pages. What is left after PRP1's page fits in one page. So PRP2 is a data pointer. It must point at the start of a page, but it holds an offset.

How you can tell: Result 13h, PRP Offset Invalid, with DNR (from QEMU and checking controllers). A lenient controller writes the second part of the data to PRP2, offset included. It then runs across the next page boundary, damaging the neighbouring page.

How to fix it and prove the fix: QEMU (safe): a passthrough read of 8 KiB with PRP2 offset 10h. Expect pci_nvme_err_invalid_prp2_align and result 13h. Check PRP2-OFFSET (error list, section 7.6): work out first = page − (PRP1 mod page). If first < len ≤ first + page, then PRP2 mod page must be 0.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Yes (Reported). The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Blame the computer: it worked out PRP2 wrongly. Blame the SSD only if it refuses a page-aligned PRP2, or reads a data pointer as a list. · Test that confirms it: Compare with strict QEMU (QEMU strict reference).

Packet=695428 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=221 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000004:82E50AB0 | Length=4 | DATA=16 B | Time Stamp=0522.107145383250s | Time Delta=35.880 ns | LCRC=0x71AA7B16

Error family: P18, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. P18 means wrongly filled commands. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. The checker sees it from the order and timing of the packets. Examples are a missing answer, a long gap, or packets in the wrong order.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book (NVMe Base) sets the PRP List rules. A list fills one memory page. When more entries are needed, the last entry in the page points to the next PRP list.

What goes wrong: The PRP list is laid out wrongly, in one of three ways. Entries run past the end of the list's memory page. The last entry is not used as a pointer to the next page. Or the last entry is used as a data pointer when more entries follow. Or the list has fewer entries than the transfer needs.

How you can tell: The controller reads a data page address as a list pointer, or the other way round. Data moves to or from the wrong memory. A Data Transfer Error (04h) comes if the access fails. Result 13h comes when the misread entry happens to have an offset. Often it is silent.

How to fix it and prove the fix: QEMU (safe), user-space harness: make a 1 MiB transfer with no chaining. Its PRP list starts at offset FF0h of its page. Watch for misbehaviour, and whether result 13h comes back. A checker walks the list exactly as nvme_map_prp does. It compares the data bytes described with the command length. That length is NLB+1 × LBA size, plus metadata if interleaved.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Yes (Reported). The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Blame the computer if its list breaks the one-page or chain rules, or is too short. Blame the SSD if the list is valid but the SSD moves data elsewhere, or ignores the chain pointer. · Test that confirms it: A QEMU test harness.

Packet=698713 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=1722 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000004:82E50B20 | Length=4 | DATA=16 B | Time Stamp=0522.107480327250s | Time Delta=51.880 ns | LCRC=0xF5E9AA0A

Error family: P18, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. P18 means wrongly filled commands. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. This table file marks a wrong detail or a wrong order. A read request asks for more than 512 bytes, the set limit (read_exceeds_mrrs_512).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book (NVMe Base) has the MDTS field in Identify Controller. It applies to a command's data move. The NVM Command Set says how it applies to commands like Write Zeroes, which move no data. Those have separate limits, such as WZSL in the NVM Command Set Identify Controller structure.

What goes wrong: A command moves more data than Maximum Data Transfer Size allows. MDTS (in Identify Controller) is a power of two, in units of the smallest memory page size (CAP.MPSMIN). 0 means no limit. MDTS = 5 with 4 KiB MPSMIN gives 128 KiB.

How you can tell: QEMU and most controllers: general result 02h, "Invalid Field in Command", with DNR. Some controllers move the data anyway, and may cut it short silently.

How to fix it and prove the fix: QEMU (safe): start with -device nvme,mdts=5. Then send a 256 KiB read with nvme io-passthru. Expect result 02h and the trace pci_nvme_err_mdts. Check MDTS (error list, section 7.6): (NLB+1)·LBA size (+ metadata if extended LBA) > 2^MDTS·MPSMIN. On the computer, run nvme id-ctrl /dev/nvme0 | grep mdts and cat /sys/block/nvme0n1/queue/max_hw_sectors_kb.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Yes (Reported). The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Compare the length with MDTS. Blame the computer if the length is above MDTS (a passthrough tool or user-space driver). Blame the SSD if it refuses a command within MDTS, or silently runs an oversize one. The last case is the SSD's silent half. · Test that confirms it: Read MDTS.

Packet 700205: the done note (CQE) has result SCT0/SC0x00 (success).

Packet=700205 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=2167 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000004:82E50B40 | Length=4 | DATA=16 B | Time Stamp=0522.107776481750s | Time Delta=63.880 ns | LCRC=0xE04CD647

Error family: P18, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. P18 means wrongly filled commands. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. The checker sees it from the order and timing of the packets. Examples are a missing answer, a long gap, or packets in the wrong order.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book (NVMe Base) has a general rule: the writer must clear reserved fields to 0. Receivers are generally not required to check. Check the exact wording for your version in the rule book.

What goes wrong: The computer sets bits that are reserved in the command (SQE). Examples are CDW0 bits 13:10, CDW2–3 in commands that do not define them, and reserved CDW10–15 bits. Or it sets them in a data structure it passes, such as feature data or PRP list padding.

How you can tell: Today usually nothing, because most controllers ignore reserved bits. Later, a newer rule book version may give those bits a meaning. Then the same computer software suddenly turns on a feature it never meant to. An example is a bit that later became a "storage tag" or "directive" field. Some controllers return Invalid Field in Command. This depends on the design.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Safe, on a scratch namespace: send a read with nvme io-passthru and one reserved CDW bit set. Record whether the controller ignores it or returns 02h. This is a good data point for rule-book compliance. Use a checker with a mask of defined bits for each opcode. Build it from the rule book version the device claims in VS. Mark any 1 outside the mask. Run the check again against the masks of the next rule book version. This spots "future meaning" dangers.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No (Silent). Nothing reports this error. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Blame the computer: command memory not cleared, or a newer-version structure sent to an older device. Blame the SSD only if it refuses commands whose reserved bits are zero. Or if it silently misbehaves when reserved bits are set. · Test that confirms it: A passthrough compliance probe.

Error family: P18, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. P18 means wrongly filled commands. · Can the packets alone prove it? Only if the bytes inside the packets are kept. The result number or content is inside those bytes (DATA column). The table file version that keeps the bytes marks it. A done note has a result number that is not 0 (nvme_status_nonzero).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book (NVMe Base) covers joined commands (Fused Operations). Identify Controller has a FUSES field (Fused Operation Support). The NVM Command Set defines Compare and Write as the joined pair.

What goes wrong: FUSE is in CDW0 bits 9:8. 01b means the first command of a joined pair, 10b the second, and 11b is reserved. The rule breaks are these. A first without a second. A second without a first. The two not in neighbouring list places. An opcode that cannot be joined (only Compare + Write is defined for the NVM Command Set). Joined commands sent to a controller that does not report support in FUSES. Or the reserved value 11b.

How you can tell: Defined results: general 09h "Command Aborted due to Failed Fused Command", and 0Ah "Command Aborted due to Missing Fused Command". In Linux these are NVME_SC_FUSED_FAIL and NVME_SC_FUSED_MISSING. Or 02h Invalid Field. QEMU returns Invalid Field (without DNR) for any FUSE value, because it does not support joined commands.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Careful, on a scratch device: this needs a user-space driver (SPDK-style). Send a lone FUSE=01b Compare. Expect 0Ah or 02h. Checker: for FUSE=01b at list place k, require FUSE=10b at place (k+1) mod N in the same doorbell batch. Require FUSES bit 0 set. Require opcodes 05h then 01h.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Yes (Reported). The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Blame the computer for missing, split, non-neighbouring or non-joinable pairs, and for joined use without FUSES. Blame the SSD when it fails a valid neighbouring Compare+Write pair in one doorbell batch with 09h or 0Ah. · Test that confirms it: Reproduce it with a user-space driver.

P18 means wrongly filled commands. · Can the packets alone prove it? Only if the bytes inside the packets are kept. The result number or content is inside those bytes (DATA column). The table file version that keeps the bytes marks it. A setup (admin) command was put on a normal data command list (nvme_admin_opcode_on_io_queue). A done note has a result number that is not 0 (nvme_status_nonzero).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book (NVMe Base) separates the setup (Admin) command set from the data (I/O) command sets. Each command set has its own opcode table. The Commands Supported and Effects log page lists them.

What goes wrong: Opcodes are read by list type. Command list 0 carries setup opcodes. Data command lists carry data opcodes. A setup opcode on a data list is not a setup command. It is whatever data command shares that opcode value. Setup 01h Create I/O SQ becomes NVM Write. 02h Get Log Page becomes Read. 00h Delete I/O SQ becomes Flush. 09h Set Features becomes Dataset Management (possibly a deallocate!). 06h Identify, 0Ah Get Features and 10h Firmware Commit match opcodes that are reserved or optional in the NVM set. They normally return Invalid Command Opcode.

How you can tell: When the opcode matches a built-in data command, nothing is reported. The controller runs a real read or write, with values taken from setup fields. For example, CDW10 (PRP or feature data) becomes SLBA/NLB…. Otherwise general result 01h, "Invalid Command Opcode", with DNR.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Careful, scratch namespace only: nvme io-passthru /dev/nvme0n1 --opcode=0x06 … should return Invalid Command Opcode. Never try opcodes 01h or 09h on a namespace with data. Checker: sort each command by its list number. For lists other than 0, check the opcode against the namespace's command set. Use the Commands Supported and Effects log for that CSI. Mark setup-only opcodes on data lists when the command layout looks like a setup command. An example is NSID = 0 or FFFFFFFFh with opcode 09h. Then read back the affected blocks (LBAs).

Does the SSD or computer report it? No (Silent). Nothing reports this error. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Blame the computer: a passthrough tool or user-space driver chose the wrong list. The SSD runs what the opcode means on that list. Blame the SSD only if it treats a data-list command as a setup command. · Test that confirms it: Read back the affected blocks (LBAs).

Error family: P18, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. P18 means wrongly filled commands. · Can the packets alone prove it? Only if the bytes inside the packets are kept. The result number or content is inside those bytes (DATA column). The table file version that keeps the bytes marks it. A done note has a result number that is not 0 (nvme_status_nonzero).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book (NVMe Base) defines the scatter-gather list (SGL). An SGL describes data with pieces called descriptors. The types are Data Block, Bit Bucket, Segment, Last Segment, Keyed Data Block and Transport. It also defines the SGLS and PSDT fields. For NVMe over PCIe, setup (Admin) commands use PRPs.

What goes wrong: Typical rule breaks are these. PSDT picks SGL on a setup command, which NVMe over PCIe does not allow. SGL is used although Identify Controller SGLS reports no support. A Segment or Last Segment descriptor has length zero, or not a multiple of 16. A Last Segment's final descriptor is not a Data Block. A Segment descriptor sits inside a segment, but not in the last place. The total data block length is smaller than the transfer. Or it is larger without "excess length" support. A reserved descriptor type is used. An SGL Data Block's address plus length overflows 64 bits.

How you can tell: QEMU results, all with DNR: NVME_INVALID_SGL_SEG_DESCR (0Dh), NVME_INVALID_NUM_SGL_DESCRS (0Eh), NVME_DATA_SGL_LEN_INVALID (0Fh), NVME_SGL_DESCR_TYPE_INVALID (11h). Metadata SGL length problems map to NVME_MD_SGL_LEN_INVALID. SGL on a setup command gives Invalid Field. Linux names for the same general codes follow. NVME_SC_SGL_INVALID_LAST 0Dh, _COUNT 0Eh, _DATA 0Fh, _METADATA 10h, _TYPE 11h, _OFFSET 16h, _GRANULARITY 1Eh.

How to fix it and prove the fix: QEMU (safe): QEMU supports SGLs. A user-space harness can send a Last Segment that ends with a Segment descriptor. Watch for 0Dh. A checker walks the SGL segments as QEMU's nvme_map_sgl does. This includes the "no forward progress" rule QEMU adds to stop endless loops. It compares the described length with the command length.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Yes (Reported). The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Blame the computer for SGL on a setup command, unsupported SGL use, badly formed segments, or a wrong total length. Blame the SSD when it refuses a valid SGL, or moves data outside the described blocks. · Test that confirms it: A QEMU test harness.

V-25 A command or done list is created with illegal values Seen in the packets Wrongly filled command

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 716309: a command (SQE). The fields this rule checks are in its 64-byte data.

Packet=716309 | Link Dir=Downstream | TLP Type=CplD | PSN=3774 | Tag=75 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | CompleterID=000:02:4 | Cpl Status=SC | Length=16 | Byte Cnt=64 | DATA=64 B | Time Stamp=0522.151232453500s | Time Delta=154.750 ns | LCRC=0x9932DFE6

Packet 716311: the done note (CQE) has result SCT1/SC0x02, with DNR (do not retry).

Packet=716311 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=3757 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000004:82E40100 | Length=4 | DATA=16 B | Time Stamp=0522.151241453500s | Time Delta=24.880 ns | LCRC=0x0E3A8846

Error family: P18, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. P18 means wrongly filled commands. · Can the packets alone prove it? Only if the bytes inside the packets are kept. The result number or content is inside those bytes (DATA column). The table file version that keeps the bytes marks it. A done note has a result number that is not 0 (nvme_status_nonzero).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book (NVMe Base) defines the Create I/O Submission Queue and Create I/O Completion Queue commands. It also defines CAP.MQES (counted from 0) and CAP.CQR.

What goes wrong: Create I/O SQ/CQ is sent with a bad value. The list number (QID) is 0, above the granted number of lists, or already in use. A command list points to a done list that does not exist. QSIZE is 0 or bigger than CAP.MQES. A non-contiguous list (PC=0) is asked for on a controller with CAP.CQR=1. The list base is not on a page boundary. Or the signal number is past the end of the MSI-X table.

How you can tell: Command-specific results: Completion Queue Invalid (00h), Invalid Queue Identifier (01h), Invalid Queue Size (02h), Invalid Interrupt Vector (08h). Or general PRP Offset Invalid / Invalid Field. QEMU's nvme_create_sq returns NVME_INVALID_CQID, NVME_INVALID_QID, NVME_MAX_QSIZE_EXCEEDED, NVME_INVALID_PRP_OFFSET or NVME_INVALID_FIELD (PC=0). All come with DNR.

How to fix it and prove the fix: QEMU (safe): use nvme admin-passthru to send Create I/O SQ with QSIZE beyond MQES, on an unused QID. Expect result 0102h (SCT 1, SC 02h) in QEMU's encoding. A checker checks Create commands against CAP. CAP is read during start-up, so record from controller enable. It also checks the number of lists granted in the Set Features Number of Queues done note (DW0).

Does the SSD or computer report it? Yes (Reported). The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Blame the computer. It counted QSIZE from 1 instead of 0, ignored MQES or CQR, or set a signal number past the table. Blame the SSD only when it refuses legal values or accepts illegal ones. · Test that confirms it: Compare with QEMU (QEMU reference).

V-26 A packet carries more data than the size limit (MPS) Seen in the packets Badly built or bad-data packets

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 409796: a write packet (MWr) carries 512 bytes (Length 128). It breaks the size and length rules (MPS). This is a Malformed TLP.

Packet=409796 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(32) | PSN=814 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=62498000 | Length=128 | DATA=512 B | Time Stamp=0195.681526985750s | Time Delta=182.620 ns | LCRC=0x313C723F

Error family: P11, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. P11 means packets that are marked bad, broken or too big. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. This table file marks a wrong detail or a wrong order. A packet carries more than 256 bytes of data, the set limit (payload_exceeds_mps_256).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book (PCI Express Base) sets the largest packet size (Max_Payload_Size). Senders must not send packets with more data than MPS. Receivers treat such packets as Malformed. All functions on a path must use an MPS no larger than every part supports.

What goes wrong: Error types L-18 (Malformed TLP) and L-32 (MPS/MRRS mismatch) in the error list cover how the receiver reports this. This entry is the rule a checker tests on the recording. A sender sends a packet whose data is bigger than the MPS set in its own Device Control setting. For the SSD, that is data writes for reads, or answers (CplD) to a computer read of the CMB. A receiver with a smaller MPS cannot accept it.

How you can tell: The receiver treats it as a Malformed TLP: unfixable AER bit 18, "MalfTLP". It is fatal by default. On Linux this starts AER recovery (a reset of the wire or device). With DPC, the port below is shut off instead. The NVMe controller vanishes for a short time, and reads and writes are retried or failed.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Risky, test machine only: lower the root port's MPS below the device's with setpci. This crashes reads and writes to the device, so do it only with no mounted file systems. In the capture tool, compare each packet's Length field with the sender's set MPS. Record the settings writes at start-up, or read lspci -vvv of every device on the path. This is check TLP-MPS (error list, section 7.6). On the computer: dmesg AER lines naming MalfTLP, and /sys/bus/pci/devices/<bdf>/aer_dev_fatal.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Yes (Reported). The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Look at the set MPS. Blame the SSD when it goes over its own set MPS. Blame the platform when settings writes show that the BIOS or operating system changed the MPS after start-up. Compare the settings from each period. · Test that confirms it: Check the set MPS (Programmed MPS).

V-27 A read request asks for more than the set limit (MRRS) Seen in the packets Badly built or bad-data packets

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 411367: a read request (MRd) for 1024 bytes, more than the limit (MRRS) of 512 bytes.

Packet=411367 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MRd(64) | PSN=406 | Tag=205 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000002:75D60000 | Length=256 | Time Stamp=0195.880264703620s | Time Delta=133.130 ns | LCRC=0x63BBC52C

Error family: P11, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. P11 means packets that are marked bad, broken or too big. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. This table file marks a wrong detail or a wrong order. A read request asks for more than 512 bytes, the set limit (read_exceeds_mrrs_512).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book (PCI Express Base) sets the largest read request size (Max_Read_Request_Size) in Device Control. The side that asks must not make read requests larger than this.

What goes wrong: Error type L-32 in the error list covers how the receiver reports this. This entry is the rule a checker tests on the recording. The SSD, as the side that asks, sends a memory read with a length above its set MRRS. It reads to fetch write data, commands or PRP lists.

How you can tell: MRRS is a limit for the side that asks. Whether the answering side marks an oversize read depends on the design. Check the receiver rules in the PCIe rule book. Usually the computer's bridge just serves it, so the break is silent. But it breaks the fairness and buffer plans the operating system made when it chose MRRS. Examples are time-critical (isochronous) or peer devices.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Safe, just watching: record a large in-order write. Check the read request sizes against lspci -vvv MaxReadReq. In the capture tool, mark it when MRd Length × 4 > the requester's MRRS.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No (Silent). Nothing reports this error. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Blame the SSD, as the side that asks. Blame the platform or computer if MRRS was rewritten after wire start-up without setting the device up again. · Test that confirms it: Check the set MRRS (Programmed MRRS).

V-28 A request crosses a 4 KiB address boundary Seen in the packets Badly built or bad-data packets

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 412364: a 256-byte write (MWr) starting at ...F80 crosses a 4 KiB boundary.

Packet=412364 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=694 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000002:3F3CAF80 | Length=64 | DATA=256 B | Time Stamp=0195.880406187750s | Time Delta=81.000 ns | LCRC=0x95D2B4BB

Error family: P11, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. P11 means packets that are marked bad, broken or too big. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. This table file marks a wrong detail or a wrong order. A request crosses a 4 KB address boundary (crosses_4k_boundary).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book (PCI Express Base) sets a limit on requests. Their address and length must not make a memory access cross a 4 KB boundary.

What goes wrong: A memory read or write request whose address + length spans a 4 KiB-aligned boundary. An example is an MWr of 256 bytes starting at …0F80h.

How you can tell: Receivers may check this rule, but do not have to. If they do, the packet is Malformed (AER MalfTLP). Many root complexes do not check, so the request is served. The second part may land in a page with a different IOMMU mapping. That causes an IOMMU fault for "half" a packet, or silent access to the wrong page. This depends on the design.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Safe: send reads with PRP1 offsets such as 0F80h through passthrough. Look at how the device splits its writes. Rule for the capture tool: mark any MRd/MWr where (addr mod 4096) + len > 4096. It is cheap and needs no memory of earlier packets. Always turn it on.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No (Silent). Nothing reports this error. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Look at the direction. Upstream points to the SSD's data mover (DMA engine). Downstream points to the root complex or platform. · Test that confirms it: Probe with PRP offsets (safe).

V-29 Answers are split at the wrong places (Read Completion Boundary) Seen in the packets Badly built or bad-data packets

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 413529: the first answer with data (CplD) ends at byte 100. That is not on a 64-byte split boundary (RCB).

Packet=413529 | Link Dir=Downstream | TLP Type=CplD | PSN=861 | Tag=192 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | CompleterID=000:02:4 | Cpl Status=SC | Length=25 | Byte Cnt=512 | DATA=100 B | Time Stamp=0195.880618880750s | Time Delta=0.000 ns | LCRC=0x5F632AA7

Error family: P11, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. P11 means packets that are marked bad, broken or too big. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. This table file marks a wrong detail or a wrong order. A packet carries more than 256 bytes of data, the set limit (payload_exceeds_mps_256).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book (PCI Express Base) defines the Read Completion Boundary (RCB, in Link Control). Root ports use 64 or 128 bytes. It also sets the rules for splitting answers to memory read requests.

What goes wrong: A side may answer one read request with several answers (CplD packets). It must split only at RCB-aligned addresses (64 or 128 bytes). Each part except the last must end on an RCB boundary. For one request, the data must come back in increasing address order. A side that splits at any point (for example 100 bytes) breaks this rule.

How you can tell: Some requesters depend on RCB-aligned splits to size their answer buffers. They may put the data together wrongly. A strict requester marks a Malformed TLP. Often it is silent. This depends on the design.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Safe, just watching, on devices with a controller memory buffer (CMB). Read the CMB area with large reads while recording. Use a test harness, or dd on a resource file, only reading. In the capture tool, check each request that got several answers. Each non-final answer's end address is Lower Address + data length. It must be a multiple of RCB.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No (Silent). Nothing reports this error. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Look at who answered. Downstream answers (from the root port) point to the platform. Upstream answers (the SSD answering a CMB or BAR read) point to the SSD. In the made-up recording from the generator program, the root port does the splitting. · Test that confirms it: Check the RCB setting.

V-30 Wrong byte count or start address in answers (Byte Count, Lower Address) Seen in the packets Badly built or bad-data packets

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 421049: the second answer (CplD) repeats Byte Cnt 512 and Lwr Addr 0x000.

Packet=421049 | Link Dir=Downstream | TLP Type=CplD | PSN=1757 | Tag=120 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | CompleterID=000:02:4 | Cpl Status=SC | Length=64 | Byte Cnt=512 | DATA=256 B | Time Stamp=0195.880952199250s | Time Delta=56.880 ns | LCRC=0x6E67A4B5

Error family: P11, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. P11 means packets that are marked bad, broken or too big. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. This table file marks a wrong detail or a wrong order. The answer's count of bytes still to come does not add up (byte_count_inconsistent).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book (PCI Express Base) defines the answer header fields Byte Count and Lower Address. It sets their rules for split answers.

What goes wrong: In an answer, Byte Count must equal the bytes still needed to finish the request, counting this answer's bytes. Lower Address must be the low address bits of the first byte in this answer. A side that reports wrong values breaks how the requester puts the data back together. Examples are Byte Count = data length on every part, or Lower Address not moving forward.
