How you can tell: The requester may treat the answer as malformed or unexpected. Or it may decide the request is finished too early, and later get "unexpected" answers. That shows as AER "UnxCmplt" (bit 16) or "MalfTLP". Or the read silently returns only part of the data. This depends on the design.

How to fix it and prove the fix: This is a bug on the answering device's side. Risky, test machine only: check with a test sender (exerciser) that inserts a wrong Byte Count. It needs lab equipment. In the capture tool, track the bytes still needed for each request number (tag). Every answer must have Byte Count == bytes still needed. Lower Address must == (next expected address mod 128).

Does the SSD or computer report it? Yes (Reported). The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Look at who answered. Downstream answers (the root complex answering the SSD's read) point to the platform. Upstream answers (the SSD answering a CMB or BAR read) point to the SSD. · Test that confirms it: The receiver's report.

V-31 An answer arrives for an unknown request number (Unexpected Completion) Seen in the packets Wrong request number or sender

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 112860: an answer with data (CplD) for request number 63, but no open request has that number.

Packet=112860 | Link Dir=Downstream | TLP Type=CplD | PSN=4007 | Tag=63 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | CompleterID=000:02:4 | Cpl Status=SC | Length=16 | Byte Cnt=64 | DATA=64 B | Time Stamp=0125.571534251620s | Time Delta=127.750 ns | LCRC=0x29D56BE7

Packet 112862: Unexpected Completion is reported as advisory, with a fixable-error message (ERR_COR).

Packet=112862 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=Msg | PSN=3252 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Length=0 | Time Stamp=0125.571534751620s | Time Delta=104.130 ns | LCRC=0xA5357BD5

Error family: P05, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. P05 means an unexpected answer, or a wrong request number or sender. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. This table file marks a wrong detail or a wrong order. An answer arrived that nobody asked for (unexpected_completion).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book (PCI Express Base) covers matching answers by Transaction ID. It defines the Unexpected Completion error. It also defines the answer time limit (Completion Timeout), with its range in Device Control 2.

What goes wrong: Error type L-16 in the error list covers how the receiver reports this. This entry is the rule a checker tests on the recording. An answer arrives whose Transaction ID (Requester ID + Tag) matches no open request of the receiver. The request may already be done, or timed out, or never sent. Or the answering side copied the wrong tag or requester ID.

How you can tell: The receiver logs Unexpected Completion: AER unfixable bit 16, "UnxCmplt". It is non-fatal by default. It is often handled as an advisory non-fatal error and reported as fixable ("NonFatalErr"). It is often the second half of an answer timeout ("CmpltTO", bit 14). The late answer for a request that already timed out arrives, and is unexpected.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Risky, test machine only: shorten the answer time limit range in Device Control 2 with setpci on the requester. Do it while the answering side is slow (for example in a deep power state). In the capture tool, keep the open (Requester ID, Tag) pairs for each requester. Mark CplD/Cpl that match none. Measure the time from request to answer, to see if a timeout explains it.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Yes (Reported). The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Look at when the answer came. Blame the computer or platform when the answer is late, after the requester's time limit (CTO). The time limit was too short for the path. Blame the SSD when it returns a wrong Tag or Requester ID, or answers after a function reset (FLR). · Test that confirms it: Read the header in the AER log (AER header log decode).

V-32 A request number is used again while still open (tag reuse) Seen in the packets Wrong request number or sender

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 115141: a second read request (MRd) with the same request number (tag), while the first is still open.

Packet=115141 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MRd(32) | PSN=3841 | Tag=215 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=2DCCD000 | Length=64 | Time Stamp=0125.571831562500s | Time Delta=134.620 ns | LCRC=0x0AA12170

Error family: P05, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. P05 means an unexpected answer, or a wrong request number or sender. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. This table file marks a wrong detail or a wrong order. A request number was used again while still open (tag_reused_while_outstanding). An answer arrived that nobody asked for (unexpected_completion).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book (PCI Express Base) sets a rule for open requests that need an answer. Each must have a unique Transaction ID for its requester. The Transaction ID is Requester ID + Tag. Tags can be 8-bit, 10-bit (optional, Gen4+) or 14-bit (Flit mode).

What goes wrong: Error type L-40 in the error list (tag feature mismatch) covers how the receiver reports this. This entry is the rule a checker tests on the recording. A requester sends a new request with a Tag that an open request still uses, with the same Requester ID. The answering side cannot tell them apart. Answers may be matched to the wrong request.

How you can tell: Silent data mix-up. The SSD gets data meant for a different read. For example, PRP list bytes arrive as write data, or one write's data lands in another write. Later an Unexpected Completion may follow, when the "second" answer for the tag arrives.

How to fix it and prove the fix: This is a bug on the device side. Watch with a capture tool during deep-queue in-order writes, with many reads open at once. That is where bugs from running out of tags appear. In the capture tool, for each requester, mark a request whose tag is in the open set. This is the PCIe twin of error type V-08.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No (Silent). Nothing reports this error. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Look at the tags on each side. Blame the SSD (its tag allocator) for a second Upstream request with the same Tag. Blame the platform if a switch cut 10-bit tags short. The tags then differ on each side of the switch. · Test that confirms it: Turn off 10-bit tags.

V-33 Writes pass each other in a forbidden order (ordering violation) Partly seen in the packets Badly built or bad-data packets

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 423122: a data write (MWr) comes after the done note, with no RO. This breaks the ordering rules.

Packet=423122 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(32) | PSN=548 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=71B26F00 | Length=64 | DATA=256 B | Time Stamp=0196.115201651620s | Time Delta=0.000 ns | LCRC=0x6734EEC8

Error family: P11, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. Proof from outside the recording also counts here. E01 is the Linux kernel log (dmesg). E03 is the SSD's own logs and settings (nvme-cli). E05 is a record of the computer's storage steps (blktrace). P11 means packets that are marked bad, broken or too big. · Can the packets alone prove it? Partly. The order and timing of the packets show its shape. The proof needs evidence from outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book (PCI Express Base) sets the packet ordering rules. There is an ordering table for writes that need no answer (Posted), requests (Non-Posted) and answers (Completion). It also defines the Relaxed Ordering and ID-Based Ordering marks.

What goes wrong: Error type L-40 in the error list (Relaxed Ordering bugs) covers how the receiver reports this. This entry is the rule a checker tests on the recording. A part reorders packets in a way the ordering table forbids. A posted write passes an earlier posted write without RO. Or an answer passes a posted write in the same direction. That would let a read return before an earlier write is visible. Or a read passes a posted write. In NVMe terms, a computer doorbell write cannot overtake the computer's earlier command write on PCIe. That is because the command stays in computer memory and is not sent to the device. But the device can reorder data, done notes and MSI-X (error types V-13 and V-14). Switches can reorder too.

How you can tell: Old reads, old data, unneeded signals. Never a result number.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Use two probes (above and below a switch) and compare the packet order. On a single wire, check that no done note or MSI-X packet has RO=1. Also check that the SSD-to-computer writes follow the NVMe order: data → done note → MSI-X.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No (Silent). Nothing reports this error. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Blame the SSD for the order it sends in, and for RO on packets where order matters. Blame a switch or root complex only with evidence from two probes. · Test that confirms it: Compare with RO on and off (A/B test).

V-34 The end-to-end check number does not match (ECRC mismatch) Seen in the packets Badly built or bad-data packets

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 425664: the extra check number is attached (TD=1), but it does not match (ECRC mismatch).

Packet=425664 | Link Dir=Downstream | TLP Type=MWr(32) | PSN=3104 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=000:00:0 | Address=FCE0201C | Length=1 | DATA=4 B | Time Stamp=0196.115522965370s | Time Delta=42.630 ns | LCRC=0xF3BB5356

Packet 425670: the SSD reports an ECRC Error.

Packet=425670 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=Msg | PSN=1346 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Length=0 | Time Stamp=0196.115523565370s | Time Delta=2.000 ns | LCRC=0x243AD1AB

Error family: P11, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. P11 means packets that are marked bad, broken or too big. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. This table file marks a wrong detail or a wrong order. The packet's "extra check number attached" mark (TD bit) is on (header_bit_TD_set).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book (PCI Express Base) defines the end-to-end check number (ECRC) and the TLP Digest. AER has ECRC Generation/Check Capable/Enable bits.

What goes wrong: Error type L-19 in the error list covers how the receiver reports this. This entry is the rule a checker tests on the recording. When ECRC is on, the sender adds a 32-bit TLP Digest (TD bit = 1). A receiver with ECRC checking on works it out again. A mismatch means the packet was damaged inside a part. An example is a switch's inside memory (SRAM). The damage came after the wire's LCRC was already checked and removed.

How you can tell: AER unfixable bit 19, "ECRC". Linux logs the packet header from the AER Header Log. Without ECRC on (the common default), the same inside damage is silent.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Safe: boot a lab machine with pci=ecrc=on, and record. Risky, test machine only: a test sender (exerciser) can insert ECRC errors. The capture tool works out ECRC again on every packet with TD=1, at both ends of a switch. On the computer, lspci -vvv shows "ECRCGenCap/ECRCChkCap" and the enable bits. Look for dmesg AER messages with "ECRC".

Does the SSD or computer report it? Yes (Reported). The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Find where the damage first appears. Bad going Upstream on the SSD's own wire points to the SSD's ECRC maker. Bad going Downstream on the root-port wire points to the platform. That is the root complex, a switch or the computer's ECRC maker. · Test that confirms it: Record both sides of a switch.

V-35 Resend pattern: Nak, resend, missing Ack, counter roll-over (replay pattern) Seen in the packets Broken packets sent again

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 341766: a request or data packet (TLP) arrived with a broken check number (bad LCRC).

Packet=341766 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=819 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000003:68420300 | Length=64 | DATA=256 B | Time Stamp=0131.082740958500s | Time Delta=0.000 ns | LCRC=0xEEB91918 (Bad)

Packet 341775: the refused packet is sent again with the same packet number (PSN).

Packet=341775 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=819 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000003:68420300 | Length=64 | DATA=256 B | Time Stamp=0131.082741501000s | Time Delta=0.000 ns | LCRC=0xEE491618

Error family: P06, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. P06 means packets that arrive broken and are sent again. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. This table file marks a wrong detail or a wrong order. The packet's check number shows it arrived broken (lcrc_flagged_bad). The same packet was sent again with the same packet number (tlp_replayed_same_psn).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book (PCI Express Base) covers the receipt-and-resend layer (Data Link Layer). This includes packet numbers, the check number (LCRC), the Ack/Nak rules, the resend buffer, the resend timer and REPLAY_NUM.

What goes wrong: The single wire-level errors are covered as AER errors in the error list. They are Bad TLP, Bad DLLP, Replay Timer Timeout and REPLAY_NUM Rollover (error types L-02, L-03, L-04, L-05). This entry is the checker's view. The receiver throws away a packet with a bad LCRC or an out-of-order number, and sends a Nak. The sender resends from its resend buffer. If no Ack or Nak arrives before the resend timer runs out, it resends anyway. After four resends of the same packet, the wire re-tunes.

How you can tell: Fixable AER bits "BadTLP", "BadDLLP", "Timeout", "Rollover" (Linux names), if software reads them. Otherwise only lower speed and bursts of delay.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Checker rules. (1) Resend count = packets whose number was already sent. (2) Ack delay = time from a packet to the first Ack whose AckNak_Seq_Num covers it. Compare it with the rule book's limit for that speed and width. Check that table in the rule book. (3) Four sends of one packet number → expect a re-tune (Recovery). Report resends per million packets, for each direction.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No (Degraded). No error is reported. Things still work, but slower or on a weaker wire. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: It depends on the break. Blame the sender in that direction for breaking the resend-from-the-broken-packet rules (Go-Back-N). Blame the wire for the underlying LCRC errors. Blame the receiver in that direction for missing Acks (see error types T-37 and X-20). · Test that confirms it: Insert errors from the controller side of the wire (confirmation test T15).

V-36 Block-mode errors at 64 GT/s: repair, check number, resend (Flit errors) Partly seen in the packets Broken packets sent again

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 346821: a request or data packet (TLP) arrived with a broken check number (bad LCRC).

Packet=346821 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=2541 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000003:FD9CD300 | Length=64 | DATA=256 B | Time Stamp=0131.083027285500s | Time Delta=0.000 ns | LCRC=0xC3626438 (Bad)

Packet 346830: the refused packet is sent again with the same packet number (PSN).

Packet=346830 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=2541 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000003:FD9CD300 | Length=64 | DATA=256 B | Time Stamp=0131.083027828000s | Time Delta=0.000 ns | LCRC=0xC3926B38

Error family: P06, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. Proof from outside the recording also counts here. E02 is a copy of the SSD's settings area (lspci). P06 means packets that arrive broken and are sent again. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. This table file marks a wrong detail or a wrong order. The packet's check number shows it arrived broken (lcrc_flagged_bad). The same packet was sent again with the same packet number (tlp_replayed_same_psn).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book (PCI Express Base), version 6.0 and later, covers block mode (Flit mode). This includes the repair code (FEC), the Flit check number (CRC), Flit sequence numbers and NAK/retry. The names of the exact counters and settings are not yet checked against the rule book.

What goes wrong: At 64 GT/s with PAM4 signalling, Flit mode carries traffic in fixed 256-byte blocks (FLITs). Maker overviews give 236 bytes of TLP, 6 of DLP, 8 of CRC and 6 of ECC. A light repair code (FEC) fixes small symbol errors on the fly. A FLIT whose CRC still fails after FEC is resent as a whole FLIT. This uses Flit sequence numbers and standard or selective NAK. The per-packet LCRC and the old per-packet number and Ack scheme are replaced by this Flit-level method. This depends on the rule book version.

How you can tell: A rising repaired count costs nothing yet. It is an early warning. CRC-failed FLITs cause resends (lost speed and added delay). Failures that keep coming cause a re-tune or the wire going down. How these reach software depends on the design and the rule book version. That may be AER bits, maker counters or new settings. Check the PCIe 6.x rule book and the device's documents. This is not sure.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Lab only (risky, test machine only): use margining tools, lane margining at the receiver, or cable or wire stress. Compare FEC/CRC counters at different temperatures. Use a Gen6 capture tool that reads Flits. Count FEC repairs per lane, Flit CRC failures and NAKs. Match them with temperature and wire speed. On the computer, lspci -vvv shows speed 64GT/s and the Flit mode state, if your lspci version supports it.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No (Degraded). No error is reported. Things still work, but slower or on a weaker wire. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Look at the directions. Blame the wire path (PAM4 margin) when both directions are hit. Blame the wire circuit (PHY) of one end when resends follow one sender after a settings change. · Test that confirms it: Compare what the wire can do with what it is doing now (E02, a copy of the SSD's settings area).

V-37 Data marked as bad is accepted as good (poisoned TLP) Seen in the packets Badly built or bad-data packets

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 427646: the done note (CQE) says 0 (success) after a bad-marked answer (poisoned CplD). The bad data was saved.

Packet=427646 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=2178 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000004:81C301A0 | Length=4 | DATA=16 B | Time Stamp=0196.115705863620s | Time Delta=53.870 ns | LCRC=0xC815F55C

Packet 427619: an answer with data (CplD) has its bad-data mark on (EP=1).

Packet=427619 | Link Dir=Downstream | TLP Type=CplD | PSN=3290 | Tag=114 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | CompleterID=000:02:4 | Cpl Status=SC | Length=64 | Byte Cnt=512 | DATA=256 B | Time Stamp=0196.115693336750s | Time Delta=0.000 ns | LCRC=0xE82D333B

Error family: P11, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. P11 means packets that are marked bad, broken or too big. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. This table file marks a wrong detail or a wrong order. The packet's "bad data" mark (EP bit) is on (header_bit_EP_set).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book (PCI Express Base) covers marking data as bad (Data Poisoning, EP bit). It also defines the Poisoned TLP Received error. The NVMe rule book (NVMe Base) has the general result Data Transfer Error.

What goes wrong: Error types L-12 and L-38 in the error list cover how the receiver reports this. This entry is the rule a checker tests on the recording. A packet carries the bad-data mark (EP, Error Poisoned bit). Its data is known to be bad. For example, a computer memory read hit an unfixable memory error (ECC). The receiving NVMe controller must not treat the data as valid. For example, it must not write bad-marked write data to storage as if it were good.

How you can tell: Correct behaviour: AER "Poisoned TLP" received (unfixable bit 12, shown by Linux as "TLP"). The NVMe command fails, usually with Data Transfer Error 04h. Wrong behaviour: success, and the damaged bytes are now kept on storage. This is silent damage.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Risky, test machine only: insert errors (EINJ, on servers that support it). Or use a PCIe test sender (exerciser) that sets EP on answers. In the capture tool, check every CplD or MWr with EP=1. A failing done note for its command must follow. Or by the device's documented handling of bad-marked data. A success done note after a bad-marked answer is a broken-rule note.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No (Silent). Nothing reports this error. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Blame the SSD: it ignores EP, or it sends EP data with a success result. Where the bad mark came from is covered in error type L-12. · Test that confirms it: Insert errors (risky, test machine only).

Chapter C: NVMe controller and computer-driver failures (28 entries)

Why this part is here: these 28 entries are errors in the SSD's controller state, or in the computer's driver.

C-01 The SSD says it has failed and cannot go on (Controller Fatal Status, CSTS.CFS) Seen in the packets SSD main settings and status

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 449792: the SSD's status setting (CSTS) reads 0x3. That means "ready" (RDY=1) and "failed" (CFS=1, Controller Fatal Status).

Packet=449792 | Link Dir=Downstream | TLP Type=MRd(32) | PSN=351 | Tag=25 | RequesterID=000:00:0 | Address=FCE0001C | Length=1 | Time Stamp=0230.163867018750s | Time Delta=112.620 ns | LCRC=0xA2EF8FC4

Error family: P13, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. · Proof from outside the recording: The SSD's own logs and settings read with nvme-cli (E03). · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. A check on order and timing proves it. For example: a missing answer, a long gap, or packets in the wrong order.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book describes the SSD's status setting (CSTS) and its fatal-error flag (CFS, "Controller Fatal Status"). It also describes how to restart the SSD's controller (controller reset). When the flag is set, the computer should restart the controller.

What goes wrong: The SSD's controller hit an error it cannot fix by itself. So it set the fatal-error flag (CFS). Commands still waiting will never finish. The computer must restart it. It does this by turning the "switch on" setting off (CC.EN from 1 to 0), or with a stronger reset.

How you can tell: Linux v7.2 reads the status setting (CSTS) in its timeout code (nvme_timeout()). The function nvme_should_reset() says "yes, restart" when the fatal flag (CFS) is set. It also says yes when the subsystem-restart flag (NSSRO) is set on an SSD that supports that restart. It does this only if the controller is not already restarting (RESETTING) or reconnecting (CONNECTING). Then nvme_warn_reset() writes this line to the log: controller is down; will reset: CSTS=0x%x, PCI_STATUS=0x%hx. If CSTS reads all ones (~0), the SSD is gone, not failed with CFS. Then two more lines follow. The first is Does your device have a faulty power saving mode enabled? The second is Try "nvme_core.default_ps_max_latency_us=0 pcie_aspm=off pcie_port_pm=off" and report a bug. The driver (the computer's program that talks to the SSD) then switches the controller off and plans a restart. The fatal flag is noticed only when a command runs out of time. Linux v7.2 does not check CSTS at regular times for SSDs on PCIe.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Take care: use QEMU (a program that pretends to be a computer with an SSD). Switch the controller on with a badly lined-up admin list address (misaligned ASQ). Use a test driver that runs as a normal program (user-space). The pretend SSD then sets CFS. Risky, test machine only: use the maker's own fault commands on real SSDs. Run dmesg | grep 'controller is down'. The CSTS value is in the message: 0x3 means ready plus failed (RDY+CFS), and 0xffffffff means gone. Run nvme show-regs /dev/nvme0 to print the SSD's settings without changing them. After recovery, save the error log (nvme error-log) and the persistent event log. Also save the maker's own data (nvme telemetry-log). Do this before another restart writes over them.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Reported. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD is at fault when the fatal flag (CFS) appears after a valid switch-on setting. The computer is at fault when its switch-on write just before (CC) had bad values. Bad values can be in the page size (MPS), the command set (CSS) or the list entry sizes (IOSQES/IOCQES). It is also the computer's fault if the admin list addresses (ASQ/ACQ) were badly lined up. They must line up as the SSD's abilities setting (CAP) needs (error list, section XII.8). · Test that confirms it: Kernel log.

C-02 The SSD is switched on but never says "ready" (CSTS.RDY never sets after CC.EN=1) Seen in the packets SSD main settings and status

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 452326: the computer switches the SSD on (CC.EN=1). Then it reads the "ready" flag (CSTS.RDY) about every 100 ms, and it stays 0.

Packet=452326 | Link Dir=Downstream | TLP Type=MRd(32) | PSN=487 | Tag=3 | RequesterID=000:00:0 | Address=FCE00000 | Length=2 | Time Stamp=0230.177709547250s | Time Delta=120.620 ns | LCRC=0xD03ED5E6

Packet 452764: the computer gives up and switches the SSD off again (CC.EN=0).

Packet=452764 | Link Dir=Downstream | TLP Type=MWr(32) | PSN=595 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=000:00:0 | Address=FCE00014 | Length=1 | DATA=4 B | Time Stamp=0230.356826719250s | Time Delta=120.000 ns | LCRC=0xCF349DBE

Error family: P13, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. A check on order and timing proves it. For example: a missing answer, a long gap, or packets in the wrong order.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book sets a time limit in the SSD's abilities setting (CAP.TO). It is the "worst-case time that host software should wait for CSTS.RDY to transition". The book also describes a second ready-time setting (CRTO). It describes a "ready without media" switch (CC.CRIME, Controller Ready Independent of Media Enable). It also lists the steps for starting the controller.

What goes wrong: The computer switched the controller on. But the controller never says "ready" within the time it promised. So the admin command list (admin queue) cannot be used.

How you can tell: The start-up code nvme_enable_ctrl() calls nvme_wait_ready(ctrl, NVME_CSTS_RDY, NVME_CSTS_RDY, (timeout + 1) / 2, "initialisation"). That logs Device not ready; aborting initialisation, CSTS=0x%x and returns -ENODEV. Watch the units: the wait is in seconds, but CAP.TO counts in steps of 500 ms. If CAP.CRMS says the SSD supports CRTO, the driver reads CRTO. It then uses the larger of CRTO.CRWMT and CAP.TO. When CRTO is smaller, it logs bad crto:%x cap:%llx once (error type C-13 in the error list). The restart then fails with Disabling device after reset failure: -19.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Take care: cut the power during heavy writing (an unsafe shutdown). Then time the next switch-on. Repeat 100 or more times. Plot the time to "ready" against CAP.TO. The dmesg line gives the last CSTS value. Compare the time taken with CAP.TO. You can read CAP.TO with nvme show-regs: the "cap" field, TO bits 31:24. Repeat cold-start and warm-restart tests, and most of all after an unsafe power loss.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Not reported. Nothing reports it. A timer runs out because something expected never arrived in time (timer only). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD is at fault when "ready" never sets within CAP.TO and the switch-on setting (CC) was valid. The computer is at fault when the CC values were bad. It is also the computer's fault if it gave up before CAP.TO or CRTO ran out (error list, section XII.8). · Test that confirms it: Kernel log.

C-03 The SSD never stops saying "ready" after switch-off, so restart hangs (CSTS.RDY never clears) Seen in the packets SSD main settings and status

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 453549: the computer switches the controller off (CC.EN=0).

Packet=453549 | Link Dir=Downstream | TLP Type=MWr(32) | PSN=787 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=000:00:0 | Address=FCE00014 | Length=1 | DATA=4 B | Time Stamp=0230.863494361250s | Time Delta=130.120 ns | LCRC=0x7D204EAB

Packet 453597: the "ready" flag (CSTS.RDY) is still 1, longer than the time limit (CAP.TO) after switch-off.

Packet=453597 | Link Dir=Downstream | TLP Type=MRd(32) | PSN=799 | Tag=28 | RequesterID=000:00:0 | Address=FCE0001C | Length=1 | Time Stamp=0242.863500462250s | Time Delta=155.620 ns | LCRC=0xAEC14B71

Packet 453600: the computer uses a stronger restart of the whole PCIe function (Function Level Reset, Device Control bit 15).

Packet=453600 | Link Dir=Downstream | TLP Type=CfgWr0 | PSN=800 | Tag=29 | RequesterID=000:00:0 | Length=1 | DATA=4 B | Time Stamp=0242.863501129250s | Time Delta=134.120 ns | LCRC=0xDCC1266C

Error family: P13, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. The checker flags an answer that says "not ready yet, try again" in this table file (completion_status_CRS).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book says the computer restarts the controller by turning off the switch-on setting (CC.EN). The time limit is in CAP.TO. The PCIe rule book adds a stronger restart of the whole function (Function Level Reset).

What goes wrong: The computer asked the controller to restart. The controller never confirmed it by clearing the "ready" flag (RDY). Its inside state is stuck.

How you can tell: The code nvme_disable_ctrl(ctrl, false) calls nvme_wait_ready(..., NVME_CSTS_RDY, 0, (CAP.TO + 1)/2, "reset"). That logs Device not ready; aborting reset, CSTS=0x%x. Linux v7.2 then steps up in nvme_pci_configure_admin_queue(). The comment in its code says "The NVMe Controller Reset method did not get an expected CSTS.RDY transition... Use the lower level and bigger hammer PCIe Function Level Reset". It calls pcie_reset_flr() and puts the saved settings back. It tries the switch-off again. If that works, it logs controller reset completed after pcie flr.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Take care, test drive only: start a long admin command, for example a sanitize or a self-test, where allowed. Right away, restart the controller (nvme reset /dev/nvme0). Measure how long "ready" takes to clear. In dmesg, "aborting reset" followed by "controller reset completed after pcie flr" has a meaning. It means the normal restart (CC) is broken and the function restart (FLR) works around it. Report it to the SSD maker even though the system recovered.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Not reported. Nothing reports it. A timer runs out because something expected never arrived in time (timer only). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD is at fault when this computer switched the controller on and the CC write was valid. Report it as the maker's bug even if the function restart (FLR) fixes it. · Test that confirms it: Kernel log.

C-04 The SSD never finishes its shutdown (SHST never reaches 10b) Seen in the packets SSD main settings and status

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 454210: the computer asks for a normal shutdown (CC.SHN=01b).

Packet=454210 | Link Dir=Downstream | TLP Type=MWr(32) | PSN=952 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=000:00:0 | Address=FCE00014 | Length=1 | DATA=4 B | Time Stamp=0243.027690967250s | Time Delta=152.120 ns | LCRC=0x94A34906

Packet 454243: the shutdown flag (CSTS.SHST) still says 01b, "in progress", when the power is cut.

Packet=454243 | Link Dir=Downstream | TLP Type=MRd(32) | PSN=960 | Tag=16 | RequesterID=000:00:0 | Address=FCE0001C | Length=1 | Time Stamp=0251.027694992250s | Time Delta=98.620 ns | LCRC=0x57934C59

Error family: P13, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. A check on order and timing proves it. For example: a missing answer, a long gap, or packets in the wrong order.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book describes the shutdown request (CC.SHN) and the shutdown status (CSTS.SHST). It also describes the promised shutdown time (RTD3E). And it describes the "Unsafe Shutdowns" count in the SMART / Health Information log (the SSD's health log).

What goes wrong: The computer told the controller to shut down. The controller did not say "done" in time. The computer cuts the power anyway. Data in the SSD's fast temporary memory (volatile write cache) may not be saved. The SSD's map of where data lives (FTL metadata) may not be saved either. That can lose data or make the next start very slow.

How you can tell: The code nvme_disable_ctrl(ctrl, true) calls nvme_wait_ready(ctrl, NVME_CSTS_SHST_MASK, NVME_CSTS_SHST_CMPLT, ctrl->shutdown_timeout, "shutdown"). That logs Device not ready; aborting shutdown, CSTS=0x%x. The wait time is a setting in Linux (module parameter nvme_core.shutdown_timeout). In Linux v7.2 it is 5 s by default. The SSD may state its shutdown time (RTD3E, in Identify Controller). Then Linux uses that time, kept between shutdown_timeout and 60 s. When that differs from the setting, it logs D3 entry latency set to %u seconds. An SSD that states too short a time gets only the default 5 s. At the next start, the SMART "Unsafe Shutdowns" count goes up by one.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Safe: do 500 restarts of the computer while writing. Check unsafe_shutdowns each time. Take care: on a test system, lower nvme_core.shutdown_timeout to 1 to show slow shutdowns. Compare nvme smart-log unsafe_shutdowns before and after a clean restart. It must not go up. Check nvme id-ctrl rtd3e against the wait time the computer really uses. A data test: write a known pattern, Flush, restart cleanly, read it back.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Not reported. Nothing reports it. A timer runs out because something expected never arrived in time (timer only). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD is at fault when SHST never reaches 10b, though the computer waited at least RTD3E. If RTD3E is not stated, the wait is 5 s. The computer is at fault when it waited less than RTD3E (error list, section XII.8). · Test that confirms it: Unsafe shutdowns count.

C-05 A whole-SSD restart drops the wire and loses work in progress (NVM Subsystem Reset, NSSR) Seen in the packets Wire down, power or restart

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 1374702: the computer writes the word 'NVMe' into the whole-SSD restart setting (NSSR) at BAR0+0x20.

Packet=1374702 | Link Dir=Downstream | TLP Type=MWr(32) | PSN=387 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=000:00:0 | Address=FCE00020 | Length=1 | DATA=4 B | Time Stamp=1325.566013501120s | Time Delta=0.880 ns | LCRC=0x2E940E9F

Packet 1374864: after the restart, the "subsystem restart happened" flag (CSTS.NSSRO) is 1.

Packet=1374864 | Link Dir=Downstream | TLP Type=MRd(32) | PSN=12 | Tag=1 | RequesterID=000:00:0 | Address=FCE0001C | Length=1 | Time Stamp=1325.621231488870s | Time Delta=116.000 ns | LCRC=0x6425B5FB

Error family: P12, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. A check on order and timing proves it. For example: a missing answer, a long gap, or packets in the wrong order.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book describes the whole-SSD restart setting (NSSR, at offset 20h). It describes the "supports it" bit (CAP.NSSRS) and the "it happened" flag (CSTS.NSSRO). It also says what this restart covers (NVM Subsystem Reset scope).

What goes wrong: Writing "NVMe" into the NSSR setting restarts the whole SSD. That includes the PCIe wire of every controller in it. Every command still in progress on every controller is lost. That means both ports of a two-port drive. The computer sees what looks like a sudden wire loss (error type L-11 or L-27 in the error list). After recovery, CSTS.NSSRO=1 tells the computer what happened.

How you can tell: In Linux v7.2, nvme_pci_subsystem_reset() marks the controller as restarting (RESETTING). It writes NVME_SUBSYS_RESET to NVME_REG_NSSR. It moves the controller through CONNECTING to LIVE. Then it reads CSTS on purpose "to flush the previous write and trigger a pcie read error". Recovery comes from the PCIe error report (AER), the port lock-down (DPC) or the timeout path. The function nvme_should_reset() treats NSSRO as "loss of adapter communication". At start-up, nvme_pci_configure_admin_queue() clears an old NSSRO flag (write 1 to clear). Expect a "Surprise Down" error report (AER) or a port lock-down (DPC). Also expect "controller is down; will reset".

How to fix it and prove the fix: Risky, test machine only, and it destroys work in progress: run nvme subsystem-reset /dev/nvme0 on a test system under load. Record the wire and the AER/DPC logs at the same time. After the event, nvme show-regs shows NSSRO=1, if not yet cleared. The QEMU pretend SSD does not support it. Writing the magic value only writes the trace line pci_nvme_ub_mmiowr_ssreset_unsupported. Clearing NSSRO writes ..._ssreset_w1c_unsupported. Do not test NSSR handling on QEMU.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Reported. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The computer's software is at fault when the NSSR write is on this wire before the wire is lost. Otherwise, the other computer of a two-port SSD is at fault, or the SSD itself (error list, section XII.8). · Test that confirms it: Kernel log and PCIe error report (AER).

C-06 The SSD keeps being restarted again and again (controller reset loop) Seen in the packets SSD main settings and status

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 457789: the status setting reads CSTS = 0x3. That means "ready" (RDY=1) and "failed" (CFS=1, Controller Fatal Status).

Packet=457789 | Link Dir=Downstream | TLP Type=MRd(32) | PSN=634 | Tag=2 | RequesterID=000:00:0 | Address=FCE0001C | Length=1 | Time Stamp=0254.138118224750s | Time Delta=139.620 ns | LCRC=0x19CEA0A1

Packet 458092: the same again, CSTS = 0x3: RDY=1 CFS=1 (Controller Fatal Status).

Packet=458092 | Link Dir=Downstream | TLP Type=MRd(32) | PSN=691 | Tag=10 | RequesterID=000:00:0 | Address=FCE0001C | Length=1 | Time Stamp=0254.149609017620s | Time Delta=113.000 ns | LCRC=0x6FEF9C98

Packet 458393: the same a third time, CSTS = 0x3: RDY=1 CFS=1 (Controller Fatal Status).

Packet=458393 | Link Dir=Downstream | TLP Type=MRd(32) | PSN=748 | Tag=18 | RequesterID=000:00:0 | Address=FCE0001C | Length=1 | Time Stamp=0254.159887730000s | Time Delta=173.000 ns | LCRC=0xAE90FE2A

Error family: P13, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. A check on order and timing proves it. For example: a missing answer, a long gap, or packets in the wrong order.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: This is how the computer behaves. The NVMe rule book does not define it.

What goes wrong: Each restart works. But the same cause hits again soon after. It can be a command that always runs out of time. It can be a fatal PCIe error report on the first large transfer, because of a packet size mismatch (MPS). Or it can be an automatic power-saving step (APST) that drops the SSD. The system spends its time restarting. Reads and writes that keep failing after retries reach the programs as errors.

How you can tell: The log shows repeated I/O tag ... timeout, reset controller or controller is down; will reset lines. The controller's restart counter keeps going up. It is called nr_reset and goes up in nvme_change_ctrl_state() each time the state becomes RESETTING. Linux has no general "stop after N restarts" for PCIe SSDs. Retries for each request are limited by nvme_core.max_retries. The loop ends only when a restart itself fails (error type C-17 in the error list).

How to fix it and prove the fix: Take care: send the suspected command again and again in a loop with nvme io-passthru. Use a spare storage area (scratch namespace). Count restarts per hour from dmesg. The NVMe trace points (nvme:nvme_setup_cmd, nvme:nvme_complete_rq) show the last command before each timeout. Check whether the same command type (opcode) and block address (LBA) show up every time.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Reported. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The computer is at fault if the repeated cause is a bad command, or a settings mismatch on its side. An example is the packet size (MPS). The SSD is at fault if a valid command causes the fatal flag or a timeout each time. See the error list, section XII.8. · Test that confirms it: Restart count.

C-07 The SSD gets stuck asleep or drops off after power saving (APST or D3) Partly seen in the packets Wire down, power or restart

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 1375526: no answer from the SSD when it should wake up. It is stuck in a low-power state.

Packet=1375526 | Link Dir=Downstream | Link Event=Link Down | Time Stamp=1326.002183524000s | Time Delta=300.000 ms

Error family: P12, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. · Proof from outside the recording: The Linux kernel log (E01). Measuring the power and signal pins (E07). · Can the packets alone prove it? Partly. The packets show an odd order or timing. The proof needs evidence from outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book describes the power states the SSD lists (Power State Descriptors: ENLAT, EXLAT, NOPS). It describes automatic power saving (Autonomous Power State Transition feature, FID 0Ch). It describes the power setting (Power Management feature, FID 02h). It also describes power states where the SSD does no work (Non-Operational Power States).

What goes wrong: The controller goes into a power state where it does no work. This happens by itself (APST) or because the computer asked. Or the PCIe function goes to sleep (D3). Then it does not come back correctly. Either it answers nothing (wire down, CSTS all ones), or it wakes up having lost its state. Linux keeps a list of known SSD faults (quirk table, error list chapter VI.3). It shows this is the most common bug in shipped SSDs. It is listed as NVME_QUIRK_NO_DEEPEST_PS (10 PCI IDs, plus Samsung cases matched by the computer's maker data, DMI). It is also listed as NVME_QUIRK_NO_APST. That covers a Toshiba and a Kioxia model, plus cases matched by DMI. A comment says they "seem to drop off the PCIe bus randomly when APST is on and uses the deepest sleep state". The Kioxia CD6 entry says it "times out and aborts I/O during any load, but more easily reproducible with discards".

How you can tell: A read or write runs out of time after a quiet period. Then the log shows controller is down; will reset: CSTS=0xffffffff and the power-saving hint lines. Setting messages can also show. One is NPSS is invalid; not using APST. Another is failed to set APST feature (%d). A third is forcibly allowing APST due to nvme_core.force_apst -- use at your own risk.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Safe: leave the SSD idle for hours with normal APST, then do one read. Repeat with APST off. Take care: put the computer to sleep and wake it (s2idle) 500 times. Start the computer for testing with nvme_core.default_ps_max_latency_us=0, which turns APST off. The command nvme get-feature -f 0x0c -H /dev/nvme0 shows the APST table. The command nvme id-ctrl -H shows the power states the SSD lists. Run idle-then-busy loops with longer and longer idle times.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Not reported. Nothing reports it. A timer runs out because something expected never arrived in time (timer only). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD is at fault if the computer's port starts the wake-up and the SSD does not answer. It is also at fault if it answers later than its promised wake-up time (EXLAT). The computer's hardware is at fault if the clock request pin or the clock (CLKREQ#/REFCLK) is not brought back. A logic probe shows this. It is also at fault if the port never starts the wake-up (error list, section XII.8). · Test that confirms it: Test with APST turned off.

C-08 An admin command never finishes, so the admin list hangs (admin queue hang) Seen in the packets Command never finishes (timing)

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 1194095: the SSD fetched an admin command (admin SQE) but never sent its done note.

Packet=1194095 | Link Dir=Downstream | TLP Type=CplD | PSN=1179 | Tag=203 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | CompleterID=000:02:4 | Cpl Status=SC | Length=16 | Byte Cnt=64 | DATA=64 B | Time Stamp=0922.898451033750s | Time Delta=152.750 ns | LCRC=0x47E7A5F6

Error family: P02, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. A check on order and timing proves it. For example: a missing answer, a long gap, or packets in the wrong order.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book describes the admin command list (admin queue). Some admin commands may take a long time, set by each SSD maker. Examples are Format NVM, Sanitize (it runs in the background and has its own log) and Device Self-test.

What goes wrong: An admin command never finishes. It can be Identify, Get Log Page, Format, Sanitize, Firmware Commit or Set Features. Linux does not cancel admin commands. A timeout on list 0 (QID 0, the admin list) goes straight to a controller restart.

How you can tell: The admin time limit is 60 s by default (nvme_core.admin_timeout). After it, the log shows I/O tag %d (%04x) opcode %#x (%s) QID 0 timeout, reset controller. The code path in nvme_timeout() is if (!nvmeq->qid || (iod->flags & IOD_ABORTED)). The tool that sent the command (nvme-cli) gets an error such as EINTR or ENODEV after the restart cancels it.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Read the command type (opcode) from the dmesg line. The %s part is nvme_opcode_str(). Send that command again, alone, with a long time limit. This tells "slow" apart from "hung".

Does the SSD or computer report it? Not reported. Nothing reports it. A timer runs out because something expected never arrived in time (timer only). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD is at fault if it fetched the admin command and never answered. If it never fetched it, the front part of the SSD is hung. The computer is at fault if the command is a known long one. Then its time limit was shorter than the command takes. · Test that confirms it: The dmesg timeout steps (timeout, then restart).

C-09 The computer wrote a bad doorbell, and the SSD warns about it (Invalid Doorbell) Seen in the packets Wrong doorbell number

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 483256: the computer writes the tail doorbell of command list 7 (SQ7). But list 7 was never created.

Packet=483256 | Link Dir=Downstream | TLP Type=MWr(32) | PSN=517 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=000:00:0 | Address=FCE01038 | Length=1 | DATA=4 B | Time Stamp=0370.683331704000s | Time Delta=128.120 ns | LCRC=0x916651CC

Packet 483258: the SSD sends a warning (AEN): Invalid Doorbell Register (00h).

Packet=483258 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=1148 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000004:82C400C0 | Length=4 | DATA=16 B | Time Stamp=0370.683361704000s | Time Delta=54.880 ns | LCRC=0xCC262026

Error family: P14, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. · Can the packets alone prove it? Only if the table file keeps the bytes. The result sits inside the DATA column as bytes. One version of the file keeps them (hex version). There the checker flags a done note for a command number that is unknown or already finished (nvme_cqe_unknown_or_completed_cid).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book describes the SSD's error warnings (Asynchronous Event Information for Error Status). Two of them are Invalid Doorbell Register and Invalid Doorbell Write Value. It also gives the doorbell rules. The QEMU source code quotes NVMe 1.3d section 4.1 on this behaviour.

What goes wrong: The computer writes a doorbell for a list that does not exist, or a number bigger than the list size. The cause is a driver bug, or a driver that runs as a normal program (user-space). The controller ignores the write. If a "tell me about events" command (AER) is waiting, it sends an Error-type warning (asynchronous event). Some controllers then also need a restart.

How you can tell: The warning itself (AEN). In Linux v7.2, nvme_complete_async_event() stores the result in ctrl->aen_result for Error-type warnings and waits for the next one. It sends a device event (uevent, through nvme_aen_uevent, carrying NVME_AEN=%#08x). It does not write a kernel log line. So check udevadm monitor --kernel. The QEMU pretend SSD sends NVME_AER_INFO_ERR_INVALID_DB_REGISTER / _VALUE, with the Error Information log page. Its trace lines are pci_nvme_ub_db_wr_invalid_cq, ..._invalid_cqhead, ..._invalid_sq and ..._invalid_sqtail.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Run nvme error-log to see the error entries, if the SSD keeps them. Watch the device events (udev). The recording (above) is the final proof.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Reported. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The computer's software wrote the doorbell. The SSD is at fault only if it warns about a bad doorbell that was valid by the list map. That is a false warning. · Test that confirms it: Device event (udev).

C-10 The "still alive" timer runs out (Keep Alive lost, fabrics or KATO set) Partly seen in the packets Not seen on this wire

Packets seen in the test recording

Proof from outside the recording: Logs from the network that carries NVMe (fabrics) (E10). · Can the packets alone prove it? Partly. The packets show an odd order or timing. The proof needs evidence from outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book describes the "still alive" timer (Keep Alive Timer feature, FID 0Fh). It describes the "still alive" command (Keep Alive). It also describes a mode where normal traffic counts as "still alive" (Traffic Based Keep Alive, CTRATT.TBKAS).

What goes wrong: The controller's "still alive" timer runs out. The computer did not send a Keep Alive in time. Or, in traffic-based mode, no traffic was seen. The controller then treats the computer as gone. Over a network (fabrics), that means it closes the connection. On the computer's side, a Keep Alive that fails or runs out of time leads to a restart.

How you can tell: Linux v7.2 logs long keepalive RTT (%u ms) when a Keep Alive took longer than its period. It logs failed nvme_keep_alive_end_io error=%d. It logs keep-alive failed: %ld when memory could not be reserved, followed by nvme_reset_ctrl(). It logs keep alive interval updated from %u ms to %u ms. Over a network, the time limit (KATO) must be set (keep-alive support is mandatory for fabrics). PCIe SSDs usually run with KATO=0, so Keep Alive is not started. (nvme_start_keep_alive returns early when kato == 0.)

How to fix it and prove the fix: Run nvme get-feature -f 0x0f /dev/nvmeX. Look for the dmesg lines above. Over a network, record the network traffic.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Not reported. Nothing reports it. A timer runs out because something expected never arrived in time (timer only). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The computer is at fault when its Keep Alive commands are further apart than KATO. The SSD is at fault when they are within KATO and its timer still runs out. · Test that confirms it: The KATO setting.

C-11 The SSD warns of an inside error that will not go away (Persistent Internal Error) Seen in the packets Not seen on this wire

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 1992316: the SSD sends a warning (AEN): Persistent Internal Error.

Packet=1992316 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=1504 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000004:848200D0 | Length=4 | DATA=16 B | Time Stamp=1835.733517333370s | Time Delta=54.870 ns | LCRC=0x69B0E691

Proof from outside the recording: The SSD's own logs and settings read with nvme-cli (E03). · Can the packets alone prove it? Only if the table file keeps the bytes. The result sits inside the DATA column as bytes. One version of the file keeps them (hex version). There the checker flags a done note for a command number that is unknown or already finished (nvme_cqe_unknown_or_completed_cid).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book describes an error warning (Asynchronous Event Type Error Status) called Persistent Internal Error (03h). QEMU uses the same value (NVME_AER_INFO_ERR_PERS_INTERNAL_ERR = 3).

What goes wrong: The controller reports an inside error that will not go away. It stays until someone steps in.

How you can tell: Linux v7.2 handles this kind of warning in a special way in nvme_complete_async_event(). For NVME_AER_ERROR_PERSIST_INT_ERR it calls nvme_handle_aer_persistent_error(). That logs resetting controller due to persistent internal error and calls nvme_reset_ctrl(). It does not ask for the next warning again (re-arm the AER). The restart does that.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Only the SSD maker's own fault commands can cause it. On QEMU, the pretend SSD would have to be changed. Check dmesg and nvme error-log. Check the SMART critical warnings. Save the maker's own data (telemetry) right away.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Reported. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD is at fault. The cause is an inside memory error, a firmware fault, or a failed storage-chip controller. · Test that confirms it: Kernel log (E01).

C-12 Loading new SSD firmware never finishes, so the SSD stays paused (CSTS.PP stays set) Seen in the packets SSD main settings and status

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 459072: the firmware switch command (Firmware Commit, action CA=3) finishes.

Packet=459072 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=1609 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000004:825400E0 | Length=4 | DATA=16 B | Time Stamp=0254.200754718000s | Time Delta=49.880 ns | LCRC=0xED4D1276

Packet 459178: the "paused" flag (CSTS.PP) is 1 for longer than the promised time (MTFA, 2 s stated).

Packet=459178 | Link Dir=Downstream | TLP Type=MRd(32) | PSN=914 | Tag=18 | RequesterID=000:00:0 | Address=FCE0001C | Length=1 | Time Stamp=0266.700771121000s | Time Delta=106.620 ns | LCRC=0x738D6F68

Error families: P13 and P25, two of the 27 ways an error shows on the wire. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. A check on order and timing proves it. For example: a missing answer, a long gap, or packets in the wrong order.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book describes the firmware switch actions (Firmware Commit). It describes the "paused" flag (CSTS.PP) and the longest switch time (MTFA, in Identify Controller). It also describes the firmware switch warnings (Firmware Activation Notices).

What goes wrong: When new firmware (the program inside the SSD) starts without a restart, the controller pauses command work (CSTS.PP=1). It stays paused while it switches firmware. It promises a longest time for this (Maximum Time for Firmware Activation, MTFA). If it never goes back to work within that time, the computer must restart it.

How you can tell: In Linux v7.2, nvme_handle_aen_notice() gets NVME_AER_NOTICE_FW_ACT_STARTING. It then marks the controller as RESETTING. The code comment says "(ab)using the RESETTING state to prevent subsequent recovery actions from interfering". It runs nvme_fw_act_work(). That stops reads and writes and checks nvme_ctrl_pp_status() again and again. If time runs out, it logs Fw activation timeout, reset controller. Related lines are Firmware is activated after next Controller Level Reset and Get FW SLOT INFO log error. They come from reading the firmware slot log.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Take care, risky, test machine only: load firmware on a test drive. Switch it with the action "activate immediately". Do it while reads and writes run, and record the wire. A wrong firmware file can break the drive for good. Compare the measured PP=1 time with nvme id-ctrl mtfa. Check that reads and writes go on without a restart.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Not reported. Nothing reports it. A timer runs out because something expected never arrived in time (timer only). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD is at fault when PP stays set longer than MTFA. The computer is at fault only if it checked for less than MTFA (error list, section XII.8). · Test that confirms it: Kernel log.

C-13 The SSD states two ready-time limits that do not agree (CRTO smaller than CAP.TO) Seen in the packets Result number in the done note

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 1091669: the ready-time setting CRTO = 0x000A000A (5 s), but the other limit CAP.TO = 40 (20 s). They do not agree.

Packet=1091669 | Link Dir=Downstream | TLP Type=MRd(32) | PSN=2739 | Tag=2 | RequesterID=000:00:0 | Address=FCE00068 | Length=1 | Time Stamp=0562.528180761120s | Time Delta=129.630 ns | LCRC=0xE78DB5E6

Error families: P01 and P13, two of the 27 ways an error shows on the wire. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. A check on order and timing proves it. For example: a missing answer, a long gap, or packets in the wrong order.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book describes the "supports CRTO" bit (CAP.CRMS). It describes the ready-time setting (CRTO) with its two parts (CRWMT/CRIMT).

What goes wrong: The controller states a ready-time limit (CRTO, Controller Ready With Media Timeout) smaller than its other limit (CAP.TO). A computer that trusts CRTO alone may give up too early.

How you can tell: Linux v7.2 logs bad crto:%x cap:%llx once and uses the larger value. The code comment says: "CRTO should always be greater or equal to CAP.TO, but some devices are known to get this wrong."

How to fix it and prove the fix: Only by looking. Run nvme show-regs. Check dmesg.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Reported. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD is at fault. The program inside the SSD (firmware) fills in CRTO wrongly. · Test that confirms it: Print the SSD's settings (register dump).

C-14 A read or write command runs out of time and is cancelled (I/O timeout, Abort) Seen in the packets Command never finishes (timing)

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 1211207: the SSD fetches the command (SQE).

Packet=1211207 | Link Dir=Downstream | TLP Type=CplD | PSN=3852 | Tag=210 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | CompleterID=000:02:4 | Cpl Status=SC | Length=16 | Byte Cnt=64 | DATA=64 B | Time Stamp=0983.043857245370s | Time Delta=153.750 ns | LCRC=0x87C98B02

Packet 1218400: the cancelled command's done note has result 0x007, "Command Abort Requested".

Packet=1218400 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=1161 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000004:83330180 | Length=4 | DATA=16 B | Time Stamp=1013.044025449370s | Time Delta=0.000 ns | LCRC=0x90FCC721

Packet 1218398: the cancel command (Abort, opcode 08h) on the admin command list (SQ0), sent after a 30 s timeout.

Packet=1218398 | Link Dir=Downstream | TLP Type=CplD | PSN=694 | Tag=153 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | CompleterID=000:02:4 | Cpl Status=SC | Length=16 | Byte Cnt=64 | DATA=64 B | Time Stamp=1013.043906982370s | Time Delta=152.750 ns | LCRC=0x9DA13280

Error family: P02, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. · Proof from outside the recording: The Linux kernel log (E01). · Can the packets alone prove it? Only if the table file keeps the bytes. The result sits inside the DATA column as bytes. One version of the file keeps them (hex version). There the checker flags a done note whose result number is not 0 (nvme_status_nonzero).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book describes the cancel command (Abort). It also says how many cancels may wait at once (Abort Command Limit, ACL). It also describes the result "Command Abort Requested".

What goes wrong: A read or write command does not finish within the time limit (io_timeout). The driver asks the controller to cancel it. The SSD only tries its best to cancel, and it may say no.

How you can tell: The log shows the "aborting req_op" line, then Abort status: 0x0 (or an error). The original command may finish with "Command Abort Requested". Then the computer's block layer (blk-mq) retries it, up to nvme_core.max_retries (5 by default). It does not retry if the "do not retry" bit (DNR) is set. If the command does not finish within another time limit, the second-timeout path restarts the controller.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Safe: on a test computer, lower nvme_core.io_timeout. Run a workload that makes the SSD do long inside work. The NVMe fault tool in Linux (CONFIG_FAULT_INJECTION_DEBUG_FS, drivers/nvme/host/fault_inject.c) makes result errors, not timeouts. Check dmesg. The recording (above) tells three cases apart. The command was never fetched. Or it was fetched but not finished. Or it finished but the done note was lost or sent to the wrong place.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Not reported. Nothing reports it. A timer runs out because something expected never arrived in time (timer only). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD is at fault when it fetched the command and did not finish it for about 30 s. The computer is at fault when the doorbell was written but nothing was fetched. Then check the doorbell value and address, or look for a lost doorbell. · Test that confirms it: The dmesg timeout steps (timeout, cancel, restart).

C-15 The "work is done" signal is lost, so the result is found late (completion polled) Seen in the packets Order and work-done signals

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 586584: a done note (CQE) with no "work is done" signal (MSI-X) after it.

Packet=586584 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=1645 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000004:82E701E0 | Length=4 | DATA=16 B | Time Stamp=0431.095300402750s | Time Delta=104.120 ns | LCRC=0x71385668

Packet 593403: the computer moves the done list's read point (CQ head doorbell). This is after its timeout code looked at the list itself ("completion polled").

Packet=593403 | Link Dir=Downstream | TLP Type=MWr(32) | PSN=3676 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=000:00:0 | Address=FCE01014 | Length=1 | DATA=4 B | Time Stamp=0461.095300402750s | Time Delta=120.120 ns | LCRC=0xB8C07AB0

Error family: P16, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. · Proof from outside the recording: The Linux kernel log (E01). · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. A check on order and timing proves it. For example: a missing answer, a long gap, or packets in the wrong order.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book says each done list has its own "work is done" signal. This is set when the list is created (Create I/O CQ, fields IEN/IV). The PCIe rule book describes that signal (MSI-X).

What goes wrong: The SSD finished the command. But the computer never read the done note until its timeout code looked at the done list itself.

How you can tell: The log shows I/O tag %d (%04x) QID %d timeout, completion polled. That read or write took 30 seconds. There is no restart.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Count how often "completion polled" shows. Check /proc/interrupts. Narrow it down by testing with lists that the computer checks itself (poll queues).

Does the SSD or computer report it? Not reported. Nothing reports it. A timer runs out because something expected never arrived in time (timer only). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD or the signal path is at fault if no MSI-X is on the wire. The computer or its hardware is at fault if the MSI-X is there. The computer is at fault if it blocked that signal number (error type M-011 in the error list). · Test that confirms it: Count of the message in dmesg.

C-16 The SSD is gone: its status reads as all ones (CSTS = 0xFFFFFFFF) Partly seen in the packets Request refused or not ready

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 91838: the read of the status setting (CSTS) gets the answer "request not supported" (UR). So the computer sees 0xFFFFFFFF.

Packet=91838 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=Cpl | PSN=2762 | Tag=25 | RequesterID=000:00:0 | CompleterID=002:00:0 | Cpl Status=UR | Byte Cnt=4 | Time Stamp=0125.387318604500s | Time Delta=128.620 ns | LCRC=0x688A5D25

Error families: P04 and P12, two of the 27 ways an error shows on the wire. · Proof from outside the recording: The Linux kernel log (E01). · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. The checker flags an answer that says "request not supported" in this table file (completion_status_UR).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book says a failed read returns all ones on most computers (this depends on the computer's hardware).

What goes wrong: The driver reads 0xFFFFFFFF from the status setting (CSTS). The PCIe read failed, so the SSD is not answering at all.

How you can tell: In nvme_timeout, the log shows controller is down; will reset: CSTS=0xffffffff, PCI_STATUS=0xffff and the two power-saving hint lines. In nvme_wait_ready(), all ones returns -ENODEV at once with no message. In nvme_pci_enable() a debug-level line shows reading CSTS register failed and -ENODEV. So the restart fails (error type C-17 in the error list).

How to fix it and prove the fix: See error types L-11 and L-27 in the error list. lspci -s <BDF> -vv shows "!!! Unknown header type 7f" or all ff. Check the port above the SSD: its wire status (LnkSta) should show the wire is active (DLActive).

Does the SSD or computer report it? Reported. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD is at fault if its sender went quiet first, without a restart (Hot Reset) or a power-saving step. It is also at fault if the wire is up and it answers a read of its settings with UR. The computer's hardware is at fault if port lock-down (DPC), slot power or the computer's side dropped the wire. · Test that confirms it: The driver's "controller is down" message.

C-17 Restart fails, so the SSD is marked dead and all its work fails Partly seen in the packets SSD main settings and status

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 460606: starting again, "ready" (RDY) never becomes 1. So the driver marks the controller DEAD.

Packet=460606 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=CplD | PSN=2164 | Tag=2 | RequesterID=000:00:0 | CompleterID=002:00:0 | Cpl Status=SC | Length=1 | Byte Cnt=4 | DATA=4 B | Time Stamp=0266.889900121250s | Time Delta=0.000 ns | LCRC=0xBBE10242

Error family: P13, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. · Proof from outside the recording: The Linux kernel log (E01). · Can the packets alone prove it? Partly. The packets show an odd order or timing. The proof needs evidence from outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: This is how the computer behaves.

What goes wrong: The restart code (nvme_reset_work()) fails at one of its steps. The first steps are: switch on PCI, set up the admin list, switch on the SSD, and Identify. Later steps are: set up memory lent to the SSD (HMB), create the read/write lists, or change state. Then the controller is marked DELETING and switched off with a shutdown. Its storage areas are marked dead (blk_mark_disk_dead). Its state becomes DEAD. Programs get read and write errors. The drives stay listed but cannot be used until the SSD is removed and found again (rescan).

How you can tell: The log shows Disabling device after reset failure: %d. The number is usually -19 (ENODEV) for a missing SSD. Often another line comes first. It can be Device not ready; aborting initialisation or Identify Controller failed (%d). It can also be Could not set queue count (%d) or IO queues lost.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Take care: cut power to the slot (sysfs slot power) without removing the driver. Then start a read or write. cat /sys/class/nvme/nvme0/state shows dead (or deleting). Check dmesg. To try to recover, run echo 1 > /sys/bus/pci/devices/<BDF>/remove, then echo 1 > /sys/bus/pci/rescan. Take care: this removes the SSD.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Reported. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD is at fault, because it cannot finish starting again. The computer marking it DEAD is only the result. The computer is at fault only if the failed step was its own badly formed command (error list, section XII.8). · Test that confirms it: The controller state.

C-18 The computer's PCIe error recovery runs for the SSD (error_detected, slot_reset, resume) Partly seen in the packets Wire down, power or restart

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 1377568: a "non-fatal error" message (ERR_NONFATAL) starts the PCIe error recovery (AER).

Packet=1377568 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=Msg | PSN=733 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Length=0 | Time Stamp=1327.132502704500s | Time Delta=148.120 ns | LCRC=0xAE4BBA8F

Error families: P12 and P19, two of the 27 ways an error shows on the wire. · Proof from outside the recording: The Linux kernel log (E01). · Can the packets alone prove it? Partly. The packets show an odd order or timing. The proof needs evidence from outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: Linux has a set of steps for PCI error recovery (Documentation/PCI/pci-error-recovery.rst). PCIe has a restart of the wire below a port (secondary bus reset) and a port lock-down (DPC).

What goes wrong: The PCIe error report (AER) or the port lock-down (DPC) decides the path is frozen. The NVMe driver shuts the controller down. The wire is restarted, and the driver starts the SSD again. Commands in progress are cancelled and retried.

How you can tell: The log shows these steps in order. First comes frozen state error detected, reset controller. Then the port logs Root Port link has been reset (0) or DPC messages. Then comes restart after slot reset, and last device recovery successful. If it fails: failure state error detected, request disconnect and device recovery failed. For non-fatal errors, nvme_error_detected returns CAN_RECOVER. There is no NVMe log line and nothing is restarted. There are also nvme_reset_prepare and nvme_reset_done. They run for restarts a user starts through /sys/bus/pci/devices/<BDF>/reset.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Check the order of lines in dmesg. Check the pci_uevent_ers device events. Check the PCIe error counters (AER counters).

Does the SSD or computer report it? Reported. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD is at fault if the cause is an error message (ERR_*) from the SSD. It is also at fault for a badly formed packet with the SSD's sender number (RequesterID). The computer or its hardware is at fault if the badly formed packet is sent by the computer's port. It is also the computer's side if the error is on the port's side (error list, section XII.8). · Test that confirms it: Kernel log.

C-19 A done note comes for an unknown or old command number (CID) Seen in the packets Wrong details in the done note

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 550367: a done note (CQE) for command number 0x0003 (CID), which finished long ago.

Packet=550367 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=527 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000004:82D90250 | Length=4 | DATA=16 B | Time Stamp=0370.813935561620s | Time Delta=32.870 ns | LCRC=0x77E80380

Error family: P15, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. · Can the packets alone prove it? Only if the table file keeps the bytes. The result sits inside the DATA column as bytes. One version of the file keeps them (hex version). There the checker flags a done note for a command number that is unknown or already finished (nvme_cqe_unknown_or_completed_cid).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book says each command still open on a command list must have its own command number (CID). It also sets the done note layout: list number (SQ ID), command number (CID) and phase bit.

What goes wrong: The controller sends a done note whose command number the computer cannot match. Linux v7.2 puts a 4-bit "generation" counter in the top bits of the command number. It skips this only if NVME_QUIRK_SKIP_CID_GEN is set. So late or doubled done notes for a reused number are caught. They do not finish the wrong request.

How you can tell: The log shows request %#x genctr mismatch (got %#x expected %#x) or could not locate request for tag %#x. Then it shows invalid id %d completed on queue %d. The done note is thrown away. The real request, if any, later runs out of time.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Risky, test machine only: change the QEMU pretend SSD so it sends a done note twice. Check dmesg and the recording.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Reported. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD is at fault: the controller wrote a command number that does not match or is old. The computer is at fault only if it reused the number before the first command finished. This is error type V-08 in the error list. · Test that confirms it: Check dmesg for the expected message.

C-20 After restart, the SSD gives no read and write lists (no I/O queues) Seen in the packets SSD main settings and status

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 461506: the "number of lists" setting (Set Features, Number of Queues) answers that 0 lists were given.

Packet=461506 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=2421 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000004:82740010 | Length=4 | DATA=16 B | Time Stamp=0271.901910753500s | Time Delta=29.880 ns | LCRC=0xA38657B1

Error family: P13, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. A check on order and timing proves it. For example: a missing answer, a long gap, or packets in the wrong order.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book describes the "number of lists" setting (Number of Queues feature). It describes the commands that create read and write lists (Create I/O Submission/Completion Queue).

What goes wrong: After a restart, the controller takes admin commands but gives no read and write lists. Or creating the lists fails. Linux keeps the controller so people can look at it. The code says "If only admin queue live, keep it". But it removes the storage areas (namespaces).

How you can tell: The log shows IO queues lost (after a restart) or IO queues not created (at first start). It also shows Could not set queue count (%d). nvme list shows the controller but no storage areas. Admin commands sent straight through (admin passthrough) still work.

How to fix it and prove the fix: This depends on the SSD maker (for example, forcing a safe mode). Run nvme get-feature -f 7 /dev/nvme0. Check the critical warning in nvme smart-log. Check the maker's own logs.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Reported. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD is at fault when it refuses valid requests. The computer is at fault when the list size (QSIZE) is bigger than the SSD's limit (CAP.MQES). It is also at fault when other fields break Identify limits (error list, section XII.8). · Test that confirms it: Read the setting (Get Features).

C-21 Too many commands time out, and the cancel limit is used up (Abort Command Limit) Partly seen in the packets Not seen on this wire

Packets seen in the test recording

Proof from outside the recording: Tracing the computer's own read and write path (E05). · Can the packets alone prove it? Partly. The packets show an odd order or timing. The proof needs evidence from outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book describes how many cancel commands may wait at once (Abort Command Limit, ACL). It is in Identify Controller and counts from 0 (0 means 1). It also describes the result "Abort Command Limit Exceeded".

What goes wrong: Many commands run out of time at once. This usually happens when the controller has stopped working. Linux v7.2 can send only ACL+1 cancels. When none are left, nvme_timeout just starts the timer again (RESET_TIMER). So recovery for the other commands waits whole timeout periods. It waits until a cancel finishes or a restart happens.

How you can tell: The log shows a few "aborting" lines, then nothing. There are long stalls of several minutes before the final "reset controller".

How to fix it and prove the fix: Take care: make a QEMU pretend SSD stop working under a load of 128 commands at once (QD128). For example, pause its read and write thread with a debugger. Run nvme id-ctrl /dev/nvme0 | grep acl. Compare the times of the timeouts with the times of the restarts.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Not reported. Nothing reports it. A timer runs out because something expected never arrived in time (timer only). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD is at fault for the stall of the whole controller (many commands fetched with no done notes).
