The computer's own policy causes the waiting. It is the computer's bug when the SSD returns "Abort Command Limit Exceeded". · Test that confirms it: The ACL value.

C-22 The SSD drops off the wire in its deepest power-saving state (APST, deepest power state) Partly seen in the packets Wire down, power or restart

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 1379143: no answer from the SSD when it should wake up. It is stuck in a low-power state.

Packet=1379143 | Link Dir=Downstream | Link Event=Link Down | Time Stamp=1327.356493914000s | Time Delta=300.000 ms

Error family: P12, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. · Proof from outside the recording: The Linux kernel log (E01). Measuring the power and signal pins (E07). · Can the packets alone prove it? Partly. The packets show an odd order or timing. The proof needs evidence from outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book describes automatic power saving (APST). It describes the power states the SSD lists, including states where it does no work. Each state has entry and exit times (ENLAT/EXLAT).

What goes wrong: Comments in the Linux code describe it. One is about Samsung SM951/PM951/950 PRO on two Dell laptops. They "drop off the PCIe bus randomly when APST is on and uses the deepest sleep state". Samsung 960 EVO "drops off the PCIe bus after system suspend" on two ASUS boards. The Toshiba THNSF5256GPUK "seems to die using any APST states". And "NVMe SSD drops off the PCIe bus after system idle for 10 hours on a Lenovo N60z board".

How you can tell: After a quiet time, a read or write runs out of time. Then the log shows controller is down; will reset: CSTS=0xffffffff ... and the power-saving hint. The restart fails. The SSD stays gone until the power is switched off and on.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Safe: leave the SSD idle for 1, 4 and 12 hours, then read or write. Take care: put the computer to sleep and wake it (s2idle) 500 times. Make it happen again with a long idle time. Confirm the fix in one of two ways. Set nvme_core.default_ps_max_latency_us just below the deepest state's exit time. (Linux picks APST target states using this limit.) Or use nvme.quirks=VID:DID:no_deepest_ps.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Not reported. Nothing reports it. A timer runs out because something expected never arrived in time (timer only). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD's firmware or wire hardware (PHY) is at fault in the deepest state. The computer's hardware is at fault when the failure happens only on certain boards. Then the cause is the clock or power supply, matched by board maker data (DMI quirks) (error list, section XII.8). · Test that confirms it: Turn off the deepest power state and test again.

C-23 "Write zeroes" says success, but the data is not zeroed (Write Zeroes or Deallocate) Partly seen in the packets Wrong data inside the packets

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 1464509: the write of the test pattern finishes.

Packet=1464509 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=3661 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000004:841505F0 | Length=4 | DATA=16 B | Time Stamp=1353.644950868500s | Time Delta=45.880 ns | LCRC=0x5CA35226

Packet 1464521: the "write zeroes" command (Write Zeroes) finishes with success.

Packet=1464521 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=3664 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000004:84150600 | Length=4 | DATA=16 B | Time Stamp=1353.644984419620s | Time Delta=64.870 ns | LCRC=0xAC317386

Packet 1464565: the read that checks it finishes with success.

Packet=1464565 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=3683 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000004:84150610 | Length=4 | DATA=16 B | Time Stamp=1353.645057439120s | Time Delta=40.870 ns | LCRC=0x254D3E82

Error family: P23, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. · Proof from outside the recording: Reading the data back and checking it (E04). · Can the packets alone prove it? Partly. The packets show an odd order or timing. The proof needs evidence from outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe NVM command rules describe "write zeroes" (Write Zeroes, with its DEAC bit). They describe "free these blocks" (Dataset Management Deallocate). They also describe what a read of freed blocks returns (DLFEAT in Identify Namespace).

What goes wrong: Linux keeps a list of SSD models with known faults (quirk table). 19 entries in it have NVME_QUIRK_DISABLE_WRITE_ZEROES ("Broken Write Zeroes"). Linux stops sending Write Zeroes to them. Two older Intel models have NVME_QUIRK_DEALLOCATE_ZEROES. That says the SSD "deterministically returns 0's on reads to logical blocks that deallocate was called on". For those, Linux v7.2 does "write zeroes" with a Deallocate instead. (nvme_setup_write_zeroes calls nvme_setup_discard.) It also says write-zeroes may be any size (unlimited). Such an SSD might stop returning zeros after a free. A firmware change or a range that covers part of a block can cause this. Then write-zeroes would be silently wrong. This is the "trim finishes but nothing happens" case, and the Linux kernel depends on it.

How you can tell: Nothing shows. Both commands return success. On a drive in the quirk list, /sys/block/nvme0n1/queue/write_zeroes_max_bytes is 0 (DISABLE) or very large (DEALLOCATE_ZEROES).

How to fix it and prove the fix: Write a pattern. Send Write Zeroes (nvme write-zeroes) or blkdiscard -z. Read it back and compare. Change the start position and the length. Include ranges smaller than the SSD's smallest unit (sub-granularity). Also do it across a power off and on.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Not reported. Everything says success, but the SSD did not do what was asked, or gave back wrong data (silent). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD is at fault. The Linux quirk path makes the computer trust the SSD's "freed blocks read as zero" behaviour. · Test that confirms it: Read back after zeroing.

C-24 SSDs report fake or repeated storage-area names (EUI-64, NGUID, UUID) Seen in the packets Wrong data inside the packets

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 1466233: the write of the test pattern finishes.

Packet=1466233 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=389 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000004:84150630 | Length=4 | DATA=16 B | Time Stamp=1353.645302195500s | Time Delta=49.880 ns | LCRC=0x9FED01C0

Packet 1466322: the read that checks it finishes with success.

Packet=1466322 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=427 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000004:84140000 | Length=4 | DATA=16 B | Time Stamp=1354.145408070870s | Time Delta=24.870 ns | LCRC=0xC3065F8E

Error family: P23, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. A check on order and timing proves it. For example: a missing answer, a long gap, or packets in the wrong order.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book says the names of a storage area (namespace) must be unique in the whole world. These names are EUI-64, NGUID and UUID. It also describes the name list (Namespace Identification Descriptors) and the SSD's subsystem name (SUBNQN).

What goes wrong: This is the bug with the most entries in the Linux quirk list (30 models). Drives report names that are all zero, always the same, or copied. Two drives of the same model then look like the same storage area. This breaks /dev/disk/by-id, multipath and RAID membership.

How you can tell: With the quirk set, the log shows Ignoring bogus Namespace Identifiers. Without it, Linux v7.2 finds the copies in the subsystem itself. For PCIe storage areas that are not shared, it logs clearing duplicate IDs for nsid %d. It also logs use of /dev/disk/by-id/ may cause data corruption. Then it sets NVME_QUIRK_BOGUS_NID by itself. For network (fabrics) or shared storage areas, it refuses the area: ignoring nsid %d because of duplicate IDs. Also: missing or invalid SUBNQN field. (the IGNORE_DEV_SUBNQN cases).

How to fix it and prove the fix: Run nvme id-ns /dev/nvme0n1 | grep -E 'nguid|eui64' on two drives. Run nvme ns-descs. Run ls -l /dev/disk/by-id/.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Reported. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD is at fault. The maker's sample firmware, or the company that sells the drive (OEM), did not set unique values. · Test that confirms it: Compare two drives.

C-25 The older "work is done" signal never arrives (MSI, not MSI-X) Seen in the packets Order and work-done signals

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 594296: the older signal kind (MSI) is switched on, and the newer kind (MSI-X) is switched off.

Packet=594296 | Link Dir=Downstream | TLP Type=CfgWr0 | PSN=3731 | Tag=15 | RequesterID=000:00:0 | Length=1 | DATA=4 B | Time Stamp=0461.095532690500s | Time Delta=148.120 ns | LCRC=0x86794491

Packet 594339: a done note (CQE).

Packet=594339 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=517 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000004:82E503C0 | Length=4 | DATA=16 B | Time Stamp=0461.095547657870s | Time Delta=130.130 ns | LCRC=0x5EC2BFBE

Error family: P16, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. A check on order and timing proves it. For example: a missing answer, a long gap, or packets in the wrong order.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCI rule book says the older signal kind (MSI) is optional when the newer kind (MSI-X) exists. But if the SSD says it has MSI, it must work.

What goes wrong: The Linux quirk NVME_QUIRK_BROKEN_MSI says "MSI (but not MSI-X) interrupts are broken and never fire". It is set for SanDisk SN530 and SN550. If the computer falls back to MSI, every done note waits for the timeout code to find it. This happens, for example, when signal numbers run short, or MSI-X is switched off.

How you can tell: Without the quirk, every command shows "completion polled", and start-up takes minutes. With it, Linux clears PCI_IRQ_MSI. Then only MSI-X or the oldest signal kind (INTx) is used.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Take care: this needs a changed test kernel. Force MSI. (pci=nomsi forces INTx instead. To test MSI itself, switch off MSI-X on a test kernel. Or use the nvme.quirks setting on another drive.) Watch /proc/interrupts.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Not reported. Nothing reports it. A timer runs out because something expected never arrived in time (timer only). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD is at fault (the MSI path never fires) when the computer set up MSI fully. The computer must also not have blocked it. The computer is at fault if it set the block bits (INTMS/mask bits). · Test that confirms it: Check the quirk.

C-26 The SSD cuts off memory addresses above 48 bits (DMA above 48 bits) Seen in the packets Wrong memory address or sender

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 660104: the memory address in the list (PRP) is 0x1_0000_1234_0000, above 2^48. It is cut short, so the write packet (MWr) lands at 0x12340000.

Packet=660104 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(32) | PSN=2234 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=12340000 | Length=64 | DATA=256 B | Time Stamp=0521.884037896870s | Time Delta=24.380 ns | LCRC=0x3B823CB9

Error family: P17, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. A check on order and timing proves it. For example: a missing answer, a long gap, or packets in the wrong order.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: NVMe memory address entries (PRP/SGL) are 64-bit addresses. PCIe supports 64-bit addresses.

What goes wrong: The Linux quirk NVME_QUIRK_DMA_ADDRESS_BITS_48 says the SSD "does not properly handle DMA addresses over 48 bits". It is set for six Amazon models. Without the quirk, memory above 2^48 could be read or written at a cut-short address. That silently damages other memory. If the computer has a memory guard (IOMMU), it reports a fault instead.

How you can tell: With the quirk, Linux limits the SSD to 48-bit addresses (dma_set_mask_and_coherent(..., DMA_BIT_MASK(48))). Then nothing shows. Without it, damage or memory guard faults show only on systems with very large address spaces (IOVA or physical).

How to fix it and prove the fix: Force memory addresses above 2^48. Use a memory guard with a large address width, or a test memory allocator. Then check the data.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Not reported. Everything says success, but the SSD did not do what was asked, or gave back wrong data (silent). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD is at fault: its memory address settings cut the address short. · Test that confirms it: A run with high memory addresses (high-IOVA run).

C-27 The SSD needs a pause before its "ready" flag can be checked (CSTS.RDY) Seen in the packets SSD main settings and status

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 462731: a read of the status setting (CSTS) right after switch-on (CC.EN=1) returns 0xFFFFFFFF. The SSD is not ready to be read.

Packet=462731 | Link Dir=Downstream | TLP Type=MRd(32) | PSN=1566 | Tag=26 | RequesterID=000:00:0 | Address=FCE0001C | Length=1 | Time Stamp=0274.916548392000s | Time Delta=119.620 ns | LCRC=0x21AD1F84

Error family: P13, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. A check on order and timing proves it. For example: a missing answer, a long gap, or packets in the wrong order.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book says the status setting (CSTS) must show state changes within the time limit (CAP.TO). Reads of the SSD's settings should always give valid values.

What goes wrong: The Linux quirk NVME_QUIRK_DELAY_BEFORE_CHK_RDY says the SSD "needs a delay before starts checking the device readiness". It is set for Seagate Nytro, HGST and WDC SN200 cards, Memblaze Pblaze4 and Samsung PM1725/PM1725a. It is also set for the Samsung Portable SSD X5, matched by its name. Linux waits NVME_QUIRK_DELAY_AMOUNT = 2300 ms after clearing CC.EN, before it starts checking. The core quirk comment adds that the X5 "fails initialization without a delay ... and has a whole set of other problems". The X5 shares a PCI ID with the internal 970 Evo Plus, which does not need the quirk. That is why the X5 is matched by its model name.

How you can tell: Without the quirk, the log shows Device not ready; aborting reset. Or start-up fails when the SSD is first found.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Safe: do 1000 controller restarts on a test drive. Repeat restarts (nvme reset) while watching dmesg. Test with the quirk turned off through nvme.quirks=VID:DID:^delay_before_chk_rdy.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Not reported. Nothing reports it. A timer runs out because something expected never arrived in time (timer only). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD is at fault. The controller resets its settings block in the background after CC.EN changes. · Test that confirms it: Quirk off (take care).

C-28 The SSD cannot be used after a function restart (Function Level Reset) Seen in the packets SSD main settings and status

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 466338: a restart of the whole PCIe function (Function Level Reset).

Packet=466338 | Link Dir=Downstream | TLP Type=CfgWr0 | PSN=2411 | Tag=2 | RequesterID=000:00:0 | Length=1 | DATA=4 B | Time Stamp=0276.927358252120s | Time Delta=136.130 ns | LCRC=0xF02D4868

Packet 466361: a read of the SSD's abilities setting (CAP) after the restart gets the answer "request not supported" (UR). The function cannot be used.

Packet=466361 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=Cpl | PSN=3957 | Tag=7 | RequesterID=000:00:0 | CompleterID=002:00:0 | Cpl Status=UR | Byte Cnt=8 | Time Stamp=0277.027361139120s | Time Delta=121.630 ns | LCRC=0x55964DAE

Error family: P13, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. The checker flags an answer that says "request not supported" in this table file (completion_status_UR).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book describes the function restart (FLR). After it, the function must be ready for settings-area requests within the restart time. Or it must answer "not ready yet, try again" (RRS). The NVMe rule book says the controller state after FLR is the same as after a controller restart.

What goes wrong: There are two fixes for this in the Linux PCI code (drivers/pci/quirks.c). (1) The code comment says this. "The Samsung SM961/PM961 controller can sometimes enter a fatal state after FLR where config space reads from the device return -1. We seem to be able to avoid this condition if we disable the NVMe controller prior to FLR." This is nvme_disable_and_flr(), set for Samsung 0xa804. It logs Timeout waiting for NVMe ready status to clear after disable if RDY does not clear. (2) The other code comment says: "Some NVMe controllers such as Intel DC P3700 and Solidigm P44 Pro will timeout waiting for ready status to change after NVMe enable if the driver starts interacting with the device too soon after FLR". The fix is delay_250ms_after_flr(). It is set for Intel 0x0953 and 0x0a54, and Solidigm 0xf1ac.

How you can tell: Without the fixes, two things can happen. One: giving the SSD to a virtual machine (VFIO passthrough) or using /sys/bus/pci/devices/<BDF>/reset leaves it dead. Settings reads then give all ones. Two: the next switch-on fails with Device not ready; aborting initialisation.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Take care: do 1000 function restarts with the SSD unhooked from the nvme driver (or under VFIO). Check Identify after each one. Loop echo 1 > /sys/bus/pci/devices/<BDF>/reset (take care: this stops traffic), then nvme id-ctrl. Watch for "not ready ... after FLR" messages from pci_dev_wait.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Not reported. Nothing reports it. A timer runs out because something expected never arrived in time (timer only). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD is at fault when the computer waited at least 100 ms. The computer must also have put back the memory window and command settings (BAR/Command) correctly. The computer is at fault when it read too early. It is also at fault if it did not put back the memory switch and windows (MSE/BARs). See the error list, section XII.8. · Test that confirms it: Function restart loop (take care).

Chapter S: errors reported with a status code (93 entries)

Why this part is here: these 93 entries are errors the SSD reports itself. It can use a result number in a done note, or a log. It can also send an event message on its own (AEN).

S-01 The SSD says the command type is not known (Invalid Command Opcode, status 0x01) Seen in the packets Result number in the done note

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 759852: the SSD fetches the command. The answer with data (CplD) carries the 64-byte command (SQE).

Packet=759852 | Link Dir=Downstream | TLP Type=CplD | PSN=3788 | Tag=25 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | CompleterID=000:02:4 | Cpl Status=SC | Length=16 | Byte Cnt=64 | DATA=64 B | Time Stamp=0528.594019380000s | Time Delta=120.750 ns | LCRC=0xC9D41E6D

Packet 759854: the done note (CQE) is written with a write packet (MWr). Its result is not 0: SCT 0, status 0x01, with the "do not retry" bit (DNR).

Packet=759854 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=2843 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000004:82E50ED0 | Length=4 | DATA=16 B | Time Stamp=0528.594030380000s | Time Delta=65.880 ns | LCRC=0x01255184

Error family: P01, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. · Can the packets alone prove it? Only if the table file keeps the bytes. The result sits inside the DATA column as bytes. One version of the file keeps them (hex version). There the checker flags a done note whose result number is not 0 (nvme_status_nonzero).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book has a general result "Invalid Command Opcode". The command type is the opcode. The SSD's list of supported commands (Commands Supported and Effects log, LID 05h) has a CSUPP bit. It says which command types the controller claims to support.

What goes wrong: The controller does not support this command type on this kind of list (admin or read/write). Or the command type is reserved. Nothing is done.

How you can tell: A done note with SCT 0 / status 0x01. Usually DNR=1. In Linux: NVME_SC_INVALID_OPCODE 0x001 becomes BLK_STS_NOTSUPP, then -EOPNOTSUPP. dmesg shows "Invalid Command Opcode". Status code: the result number in the done note. 0 means success. SCT: which list of result numbers it comes from.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Safe: run nvme io-passthru /dev/nvme0n1 --opcode=0x7f --namespace-id=1 (a reserved read/write command type). Or run nvme admin-passthru /dev/nvme0 --opcode=0x7f. Check that DNR=1. Compare with nvme id-ctrl (OACS, ONCS) and nvme effects-log /dev/nvme0. The effects log may say CSUPP=1 while the command returns 0x01. Then the controller contradicts itself (a bug against the rule book).

Does the SSD or computer report it? Reported. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The computer is at fault when the command type is reserved or sent on the wrong kind of list. It is also at fault when the type is not listed as supported (C3). The SSD is at fault when Identify or the effects log lists it, or the same command worked before (C4). Byte 0 of the command and the list number (SQI) decide it. · Test that confirms it: Cross-check with Identify and the effects log.

S-02 The SSD says a field in the command has a bad value (Invalid Field in Command, status 0x02) Seen in the packets Result number in the done note

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 763947: the SSD fetches the command. The answer with data (CplD) carries the 64-byte command (SQE).

Packet=763947 | Link Dir=Downstream | TLP Type=CplD | PSN=371 | Tag=106 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | CompleterID=000:02:4 | Cpl Status=SC | Length=16 | Byte Cnt=64 | DATA=64 B | Time Stamp=0528.594293381870s | Time Delta=113.750 ns | LCRC=0x6160DB16

Packet 763949: the done note (CQE) is written with a write packet (MWr). Its result is not 0: SCT 0, status 0x02, with the "do not retry" bit (DNR).

Packet=763949 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=274 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000004:82E50F20 | Length=4 | DATA=16 B | Time Stamp=0528.594293707870s | Time Delta=67.870 ns | LCRC=0xCFA8D277

Error family: P01, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. · Can the packets alone prove it? Only if the table file keeps the bytes. The result sits inside the DATA column as bytes. One version of the file keeps them (hex version). There the checker flags a done note whose result number is not 0 (nvme_status_nonzero).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book has a general result "Invalid Field in Command". The SSD's error log (Error Information log) has a field that says where the bad value was. It is Parameter Error Location (parm_error_location in libnvme).

What goes wrong: A field in the command holds a reserved or unsupported value. The field can be a command word (CDW10–15), the flags, or the address list kind (PSDT). It can also be a field that depends on the storage area number (NSID), or the data length. This is the catch-all "bad value" error.

How you can tell: The done note has SCT 0 / status 0x02. Usually DNR=1. If the controller supports it, the error log entry's Parameter Error Location names the wrong byte and bit. In Linux, 0x002 becomes BLK_STS_NOTSUPP, then -EOPNOTSUPP. Status code: the result number in the done note. 0 means success. SCT: which list of result numbers it comes from.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Safe: send a Read with more blocks (NLB) than the largest transfer (MDTS) through nvme io-passthru. Or run nvme get-feature -f 0x7e with a setting number that is not supported. Or run nvme get-log -i 0x02 -l 4096 -o 0x10000 (a start point past the end of the log). Run nvme error-log /dev/nvme0 -e 16. Match the list number and command number (SQID/CID), then read parm_error_location. Check the command again against the Identify limits (MDTS, ONCS, SGLS, DMRL/DMRSL).

Does the SSD or computer report it? Reported. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The computer is at fault when a field is outside the Identify limits, or Parameter Error Location points at it. The SSD is at fault when every field is inside the limits it listed (error list, section XII.8). The command words (CDW10-15/PSDT) compared with admin_data decide it. · Test that confirms it: Parameter Error Location.

S-03 The command number is already in use (Command ID Conflict, status 0x03) Seen in the packets Result number in the done note

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 765895: the SSD fetches the command. The answer with data (CplD) carries the 64-byte command (SQE).

Packet=765895 | Link Dir=Downstream | TLP Type=CplD | PSN=561 | Tag=199 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | CompleterID=000:02:4 | Cpl Status=SC | Length=16 | Byte Cnt=64 | DATA=64 B | Time Stamp=0528.880616717500s | Time Delta=145.750 ns | LCRC=0x7E3485E3

Packet 765897: the done note (CQE) is written with a write packet (MWr). Its result is not 0: SCT 0, status 0x03, with the "do not retry" bit (DNR).

Packet=765897 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=1089 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000004:82E50F50 | Length=4 | DATA=16 B | Time Stamp=0528.880617127500s | Time Delta=73.880 ns | LCRC=0xCF27254D

Error family: P01, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. · Can the packets alone prove it? Only if the table file keeps the bytes. The result sits inside the DATA column as bytes. One version of the file keeps them (hex version). There the checker flags a command number used again while a command with that number is still open (nvme_cid_reused_while_open). It also flags a done note for a command number that is unknown or already finished (nvme_cqe_unknown_or_completed_cid). It also flags a done note whose result number is not 0 (nvme_status_nonzero).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book has a general result "Command ID Conflict". Each command still open on one command list must have its own command number (CID).

What goes wrong: The computer sent a command whose number is already in use by an open command on the same list. The controller may refuse the new command.

How you can tell: The done note has status 0x03. Many controllers do not check this. Instead they finish two commands with the same number, and the computer then mixes them up. Linux does not treat this result in a special way. It becomes -EIO. Status code: the result number in the done note. 0 means success. SCT: which list of result numbers it comes from.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Risky, test machine only: only a special sender can do this. It is a driver that runs as a normal program (user-space), or a test tool that can send doubled numbers. In a capture tool recording, list the open command numbers for each list. Flag a second command with the same number before the first one's done note. Linux v7.2 adds a 4-bit "generation" counter to bits 15:12 of the command number (nvme_cid_install_genctr()). It warns when a done note does not match. This catches the computer-side version.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Reported. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The computer is at fault when the recording shows the same number fetched twice while still open. The SSD is at fault when it returns 0x03 for a number that was not open. It is also at fault when it sends two done notes for one fetch (error list, section XII.8). The order of fetches and done notes on the same command list decides it. · Test that confirms it: Check how the computer hands out command numbers.

Packet 766909: the done note (CQE) is written with a write packet (MWr). Its result is not 0: SCT 0, status 0x04.

Packet=766909 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=1441 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000004:82E50F80 | Length=4 | DATA=16 B | Time Stamp=0528.881493199250s | Time Delta=71.880 ns | LCRC=0x5C94890F

Error families: P01 and P03, two of the 27 ways an error shows on the wire. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. The checker flags an answer that says "the SSD refused this request" in this table file (completion_status_CA).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book has a general result "Data Transfer Error". The PCIe rule book has answer results for the SSD's memory reads. They include "request not supported" (UR) and "refused" (CA, Completer Abort).

What goes wrong: Moving data or extra data (metadata) between the computer's memory and the controller failed. A memory read by the SSD got an error answer. Or a write could not be sent. Or the connection failed in the middle of a transfer.

How you can tell: The done note has status 0x04. The "do not retry" bit (DNR) varies (QEMU uses both). There is often a matching PCIe error too. The SSD's read request (MRd) gets an "Unsupported Request" or "Completer Abort" answer. Or the computer's memory guard (IOMMU) reports a fault. In Linux it becomes -EIO. Status code: the result number in the done note. 0 means success. SCT: which list of result numbers it comes from.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Risky, test machine only: use a QEMU virtual machine with a pretend memory guard (vIOMMU). Remove a buffer while a passed-through command is still open. Or use a test tool to answer the SSD's data read with UR. Look in dmesg for memory guard faults (IOMMU/DMAR) with the SSD's address (BDF) at the same time. Check the PCIe error logs (AER). In the recording, the SSD's read (MRd) to the PRP address gets a UR or CA answer. Check lspci -vvv DevSta for "UnsupReq+" / "AuxPwr".

Does the SSD or computer report it? Reported. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The computer or its hardware is at fault when the failing addresses are the command's own memory addresses (PRP/SGL). Causes are the memory guard, or a buffer that was removed or marked bad. The SSD is at fault when it read an address that is not in the command or its address list. The wire is at fault when data packets arrive broken (LCRC) or get an "arrived broken" receipt (Nak). The kind of bad read address and the receipt notes (dll_tracker) decide it. · Test that confirms it: Match against memory guard faults (IOMMU / DMAR).

Packet=768494 | Link Dir=Downstream | TLP Type=CplD | PSN=1045 | Tag=171 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | CompleterID=000:02:4 | Cpl Status=SC | Length=16 | Byte Cnt=64 | DATA=64 B | Time Stamp=0528.881945861250s | Time Delta=154.750 ns | LCRC=0xDB5DCCA7

Packet 768496: the done note (CQE) is written with a write packet (MWr). Its result is not 0: SCT 0, status 0x05.

Packet=768496 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=1991 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000004:82E51020 | Length=4 | DATA=16 B | Time Stamp=0528.881953861250s | Time Delta=44.880 ns | LCRC=0x4496B604

Error family: P01, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. · Can the packets alone prove it? Only if the table file keeps the bytes. The result sits inside the DATA column as bytes. One version of the file keeps them (hex version). There the checker flags a done note whose result number is not 0 (nvme_status_nonzero).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book has a general result "Commands Aborted due to Power Loss Notification". It also describes shutdown through the shutdown request (CC.SHN) and shutdown status (CSTS.SHST).

What goes wrong: The controller got a warning that power will be lost. For example, a shutdown request (CC.SHN), or a power-fail signal from the computer's hardware. It cancelled the open commands instead of finishing them.

How you can tell: The open commands get status 0x05. They can be tried again after power comes back. In Linux, the request becomes -EIO if it ends there. Usually the controller is being shut down anyway. Status code: the result number in the done note. 0 means success. SCT: which list of result numbers it comes from.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Take care: write CC.SHN from a driver that runs as a normal program, while reads and writes are waiting. Do not do it with the kernel driver attached. Risky, test machine only: a power-fail test rig. Match it against three things. The SMART "Unsafe Shutdowns" count goes up. The Persistent Event log shows a "Power-on or Reset" event. The recording shows CC.SHN writes. Data from writes cancelled this way is not safe. Read it back to check it.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Reported. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The computer is at fault when a CC.SHN write comes before the burst while those commands were open. The computer's hardware is at fault when there is no shutdown write and the wire drops (power fail). The SSD is at fault if 0x05 shows with neither. The history of the switch-on setting (register_shadow CC) and the wire state (link_state) decide it. · Test that confirms it: Unsafe shutdowns count and Persistent Event log (PEL).

Packet 771385: the done note (CQE) is written with a write packet (MWr). Its result is not 0: SCT 0, status 0x06.

Packet=771385 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=2784 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000004:82E51050 | Length=4 | DATA=16 B | Time Stamp=0529.160278365370s | Time Delta=38.870 ns | LCRC=0x029D80CF

Error family: P01, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. · Proof from outside the recording: The SSD's own logs and settings read with nvme-cli (E03). · Can the packets alone prove it? Only if the table file keeps the bytes. The result sits inside the DATA column as bytes. One version of the file keeps them (hex version). There the checker flags a done note whose result number is not 0 (nvme_status_nonzero).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book has a general result "Internal Error". It also has error warning values 03h and 04h (Asynchronous Event Information, Error Status). See error type S-79 in the error list.

What goes wrong: The command failed because of something inside the controller. It is not a storage-chip error, and not the computer's fault. Examples: a firmware crash, or running out of inside resources. Another example is an error in an inside bus or memory (SRAM).

How you can tell: The done note has status 0x06. The "do not retry" bit is 0 for short-lived problems. It is 1 if the firmware knows the error will happen again. It often comes with an error warning (Transient Internal Error 04h or Persistent Internal Error 03h). The Persistent Event log may show an "NVM Subsystem Hardware Error" event. In Linux it becomes -EIO after retries. Status code: the result number in the done note. 0 means success. SCT: which list of result numbers it comes from.

How to fix it and prove the fix: The computer cannot cause it reliably. Use the maker's own fault commands. Or use QEMU with a storage back end whose block-status call fails. The "error on freed blocks" setting (DULBE) must be on. Right after the event, read nvme error-log, nvme persistent-event-log and the maker's own data (nvme telemetry-log --output-file=...). Send the same command again. If it fails every time, record it as a firmware defect, with the exact command.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Reported. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD is at fault (inside the controller). A well-formed command plus status 0x06 decides it. To find the cause inside the SSD, you need the maker's data or the Persistent Event log. The computer only plays a part if the command was badly formed. · Test that confirms it: SSD logs read right after the event.

Packet=774150 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=3528 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000004:82E51080 | Length=4 | DATA=16 B | Time Stamp=0529.161026435370s | Time Delta=44.870 ns | LCRC=0x10F72823

Error family: P01, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. · Can the packets alone prove it? Only if the table file keeps the bytes. The result sits inside the DATA column as bytes. One version of the file keeps them (hex version). There the checker flags a done note whose result number is not 0 (nvme_status_nonzero).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book describes the admin cancel command (Abort). It describes how many cancels may wait at once (ACL, Abort Command Limit, in Identify Controller, counting from 0). It has a general result "Command Abort Requested".

What goes wrong: The command was cancelled because the computer sent a cancel command (admin opcode 08h). The cancel named the command's list number (SQID) and command number (CID).

How you can tell: The cancelled command finishes with status 0x07. The cancel command itself finishes too. Its Dword 0 bit 0 is 0 if the command was cancelled, and 1 if not. Linux prints "Abort status: 0x%x" from pci.c:abort_endio(). Status code: the result number in the done note. 0 means success. SCT: which list of result numbers it comes from.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Take care: in QEMU, make a storage read or write stall. For example, use a blkdebug rule with a delay. Lower io_timeout (a setting that can be changed while running) to see the cancel sooner. QEMU's nvme_abort() cancels the storage request, which finishes it with 0x07. dmesg shows "I/O tag N (cid) opcode ... QID q timeout, aborting", then "Abort status". If the command is not cancelled and times out again, Linux restarts the controller ("timeout, reset controller").

Does the SSD or computer report it? Reported. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Either side can be at fault. The SSD is at fault when it fetched the command and never finished it (a). The computer is at fault when the doorbell was never written (c). It is also at fault when the done note was sent and missed (d). The wire or SSD is at fault for a lost doorbell (b). The state of the cancelled command at the time of the Abort decides it. · Test that confirms it: The computer's timeout trail.

Error family: P01, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. · Can the packets alone prove it? Only if the table file keeps the bytes. The result sits inside the DATA column as bytes. One version of the file keeps them (hex version). There the checker flags a done note whose result number is not 0 (nvme_status_nonzero).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book describes the "delete read/write command list" command (Delete I/O Submission Queue). It has a general result "Command Aborted due to SQ Deletion".

What goes wrong: The computer deleted a read/write command list (admin opcode 00h) while commands were still open on it. The controller cancels them.

How you can tell: Each open command gets status 0x08. These done notes go to the matching done list before the delete finishes. If the done list was already cleaned up, these done notes can be lost. Status code: the result number in the done note. 0 means success. SCT: which list of result numbers it comes from.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Risky, test machine only: a driver that runs as a normal program deletes a busy command list. In the capture tool recording: the delete command, followed by done notes with status 0x08. Linux normally cancels requests itself (0x371) before deleting lists. So many 0x08 results under Linux point to something going around the driver, or a computer not running Linux.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Reported. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The computer is at fault when the delete command comes before the 0x08 done notes. The SSD is at fault when 0x08 shows without a delete, or out of order. The history of admin commands kept by the checker's command notes (nvme_cmd_tracker) decides it. · Test that confirms it: Log of the computer's actions.

Error family: P01, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. · Can the packets alone prove it? Only if the table file keeps the bytes. The result sits inside the DATA column as bytes. One version of the file keeps them (hex version). There the checker flags a done note whose result number is not 0 (nvme_status_nonzero).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book describes joined commands (Fused Operation). The FUSE field in command word 0 (CDW0) marks the first and second command. Identify lists support for this (FUSES). The general results are 0x09 and 0x0A.

What goes wrong: A joined pair did not run as a pair. An example pair is Compare + Write, which compares and writes in one step that cannot be split. 0x09 means the other half failed, so this half was cancelled. 0x0A means the next command was not the expected partner.

How you can tell: One half gets the real error, for example Compare Failure 0x285. The other half gets 0x09. A badly built pair gets 0x0A. Status code: the result number in the done note. 0 means success. SCT: which list of result numbers it comes from.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Risky, test machine only: use a driver that runs as a normal program (SPDK-style). Do compare-and-write with wrong compare data on purpose. You get 0x285 + 0x09. In the recording, both commands must be in back-to-back places in the same list. One tail doorbell write must cover both.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Reported. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The computer is at fault when the halves are not back to back, split across doorbells, or wrongly paired. Usually there is no defect for 0x09 after a real compare mismatch. The SSD is at fault when a valid pair is refused. It is also at fault when 0x09 is returned while the partner command worked. · Test that confirms it: Check the compare data.

Error family: P01, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. · Can the packets alone prove it? Only if the table file keeps the bytes. The result sits inside the DATA column as bytes. One version of the file keeps them (hex version). There the checker flags a done note whose result number is not 0 (nvme_status_nonzero).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book has a general result "Invalid Namespace or Format". Identify gives the number of storage areas (NN, namespaces). There is a list of active storage area numbers (Active Namespace ID list, CNS 02h).

What goes wrong: The storage area number (NSID) is not valid for this command. It may not be created, or not attached. It may be 0 where 0 is not allowed. It may be FFFFFFFFh where "all areas" is not allowed. Or the storage area's current format does not support the command.

How you can tell: The done note has status 0x0B. Usually DNR=1. In Linux, 0x00B becomes BLK_STS_NOTSUPP, then -EOPNOTSUPP. When Linux checks the storage areas again, it treats an Identify Namespace failure with DNR as "storage area gone". It removes the drive from the system. Status code: the result number in the done note. 0 means success. SCT: which list of result numbers it comes from.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Safe: run nvme id-ns /dev/nvme0 -n 0xfffe (an unused number). Take care: detach a storage area (nvme detach-ns) while reads and writes run. Watch the drive disappear. Compare nvme list-ns /dev/nvme0 --all with nvme list-ns /dev/nvme0 (created versus attached). Look for a "Namespace Attribute Changed" warning and the Changed Namespace List log (LID 04h).

Does the SSD or computer report it? Reported. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The computer is at fault when the number is not valid or not active at that time. For example, it is old after a detach or format, or a tool got the wrong number. The SSD is at fault when it refuses an active, working number. The command's NSID against the active list in admin_data decides it. The history of SSD warnings (AEN history) helps too. · Test that confirms it: The storage area lists.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book has a general result "Command Sequence Error". Its examples are the order of firmware download steps, and security command series. Another is setting the number of lists after lists exist.

What goes wrong: The command is fine on its own. But it is not allowed at this point in a series of commands, or in the controller's current state.

How you can tell: The done note has status 0x0C. Usually DNR=1. Status code: the result number in the done note. 0 means success. SCT: which list of result numbers it comes from.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Safe on QEMU, take care on real hardware. Run nvme set-feature /dev/nvme0 -f 7 -v 0x00030003 while the driver has lists. Rebuild the order of admin commands from a recording, or from the nvme_setup_cmd / nvme_complete_rq trace points. Check which earlier command changed the state.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Reported. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The computer is at fault when the history shows the wrong order. Examples: setting 07h after lists were created, or Commit without a full download. The SSD is at fault when the history is valid. The admin history in the checker's command notes (nvme_cmd_tracker) decides it. · Test that confirms it: Rebuild the order of admin commands.

Error families: P01 and P18, two of the 27 ways an error shows on the wire. · Can the packets alone prove it? Only if the table file keeps the bytes. The result sits inside the DATA column as bytes. One version of the file keeps them (hex version). There the checker flags a done note whose result number is not 0 (nvme_status_nonzero).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book has rules for the simple memory address list (PRP). The first entry (PRP1) may have an offset. List entries must start at a page edge, and offsets must line up to 4 bytes (Dword). It also lists the kinds of the other address list (SGL descriptor types). The Identify Controller SGLS field says which SGL kinds are supported.

What goes wrong: The controller refuses the memory address list. The causes are a bad SGL segment entry (0x0D) or a wrong number of entries (0x0E). A data SGL length can be too short or too long (0x0F). An extra-data (metadata) SGL length can be bad (0x10). An SGL entry kind can be unsupported (0x11). An SGL offset can be bad (0x16, mainly for data inside network messages). An SGL block size can be bad (0x1E). Or a PRP entry offset can be bad (0x13).

How you can tell: One of these results. QEMU sets DNR=1. In Linux it becomes -EIO. These almost always point to a bug in the computer's driver or memory guard (IOMMU), not in the drive. Status code: the result number in the done note. 0 means success. SCT: which list of result numbers it comes from.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Risky, test machine only: use a driver that runs as a normal program. Give it a badly lined-up second address (PRP2) on purpose. QEMU gives the same result every time. In the recording, decode the command's address list kind (PSDT) and pointer (DPTR). Walk the PRP list or SGL by hand. Check that the page size setting (CC.MPS) matches the page size the driver uses.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Reported. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The computer is at fault when the address list breaks the rules. Causes are the driver code that builds the list, the memory guard, or a page size mismatch (CC.MPS). The SSD is at fault when it refuses a valid list. Decoding the PRP/SGL list against CC.MPS and SGLS decides it. · Test that confirms it: Walk the address list by hand.

Error family: P01, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. · Can the packets alone prove it? Only if the table file keeps the bytes. The result sits inside the DATA column as bytes. One version of the file keeps them (hex version). There the checker flags a done note whose result number is not 0 (nvme_status_nonzero).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book describes the memory area inside the SSD that the computer can use (Controller Memory Buffer, CMB). Its settings CMBLOC (38h) and CMBSZ (3Ch) say where it is and what it can hold. The bits are SQS, CQS, WDS and RDS. Newer rule books add CMBMSC.

What goes wrong: 0x12: the memory address list mixes SSD memory (CMB, or PMR) and computer memory. The controller does not support that mix. Or it uses the CMB for something not switched on in CMBSZ. 0x1F: the command is not allowed when its command list or done list lives in the CMB.

How you can tell: The done note has status 0x12 or 0x1F. QEMU sets DNR=1. Status code: the result number in the done note. 0 means success. SCT: which list of result numbers it comes from.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Risky, test machine only: run QEMU with -device nvme,cmb_size_mb=64. Add a driver that runs as a normal program and mixes CMB and computer buffers. Compare every address in the list (PRP/SGL) with the CMB memory window range from lspci -vvv and the CMBLOC offset.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Reported. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The computer is at fault when the address list mixes CMB and computer memory. It is also at fault if it uses a CMB feature the SSD did not list. The SSD is at fault when it refuses a correct use it did list. Sorting each address against CMBLOC/CMBSZ decides it. · Test that confirms it: Check the CMB address range.

Error family: P01, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. · Can the packets alone prove it? Only if the table file keeps the bytes. The result sits inside the DATA column as bytes. One version of the file keeps them (hex version). There the checker flags a done note whose result number is not 0 (nvme_status_nonzero).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book describes the "all or nothing" write sizes (atomic write unit). They are in Identify Controller (AWUN/AWUPF) and Identify Namespace (NAWUN/NAWUPF/NABSN). There is also a setting for this (Write Atomicity Normal feature, FID 0Ah). QEMU has it in nvme_set_feature_write_atomicity().

What goes wrong: The write is longer than the "all or nothing" size. The controller is set to refuse such writes, instead of doing them without the "all or nothing" promise.

How you can tell: The done note has status 0x14. In Linux it becomes -EIO. Linux's newer "all or nothing" write support (RWF_ATOMIC) checks sizes before sending. So if a drive returns this to the kernel, its Identify limits and its behaviour do not match. Status code: the result number in the done note. 0 means success. SCT: which list of result numbers it comes from.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Safe (it only destroys data in the target block range): switch on the Write Atomicity Normal setting on QEMU. Send a too-long write with nvme write. Compare the write's start block and length (SLBA/NLB) with NAWUPF/NABSN from nvme id-ns -H. QEMU's nvme_atomic_write_check() shows how a controller decides whether a write is "all or nothing".

Does the SSD or computer report it? Reported. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The computer is at fault when the write is bigger than AWUPF/NAWUPF or crosses a NABSN/NABO edge. The SSD is at fault when the write is within the limits it listed. The command's slba/nlb against the "all or nothing" fields in admin_data decides it. · Test that confirms it: The "all or nothing" limits.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book has a general result "Operation Denied". It describes the security commands (Security Send/Receive). A related general result is 0x23, "Command Prohibited by Command and Feature Lockdown" (NVME_SC_PROHIBITED_BY_CMD_AND_FEAT in libnvme).

What goes wrong: The command was refused because it lacks access rights. The rights come from a security rule book (for example TCG Storage), or from a lock or lockdown rule.

How you can tell: The done note has status 0x15. A read of a locked TCG range usually returns this, or Access Denied 0x286. Which one depends on the SSD (this depends on the maker). Status code: the result number in the done note. 0 means success. SCT: which list of result numbers it comes from.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Take care: lock a TCG Opal range on a test drive, then read it. Use sedutil-cli --query or nvme security-recv to check the lock state. Repeat after unlocking.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Reported. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The computer is at fault when no unlock or permission happened since the last start (or a lockdown applies). The SSD is at fault when a correct unlock came before the refusal. The history of security commands plus the TCG state from outside decides it. · Test that confirms it: The lock state.

S-16 Computer name format mixed up, or the "still alive" timer ran out (0x18, 0x19, 0x1A) Not seen in the packets Result number in the done note

Packets seen in the test recording

Error family: P01, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. · Proof from outside the recording: Logs from the network that carries NVMe (fabrics) (E10). · Can the packets alone prove it? No. It cannot be seen on this wire. The packets shown only set the scene. The proof is outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book describes the computer's name setting (Host Identifier feature, FID 81h). It describes the "still alive" timer (Keep Alive Timer feature, FID 0Fh) and its step size (KAS in Identify Controller).

What goes wrong: 0x18: the SSD saw both 64-bit and 128-bit computer names used across its controllers. 0x19: the "still alive" timer ran out, and the controller closes the connection. Open commands may finish with this result. 0x1A: the computer set the "still alive" time (FID 0Fh) to a value the SSD does not accept.

How you can tell: Over a network (fabrics), 0x19 comes together with the controller disappearing. The computer sees the connection restart and tries to reconnect. On PCIe, "still alive" is optional and rarely switched on. Status code: the result number in the done note. 0 means success. SCT: which list of result numbers it comes from.

How to fix it and prove the fix: On the computer, look for "still alive" messages in dmesg from core.c:nvme_keep_alive_end_io(). On the target (the far side that holds the storage), read its log. On the network, look for a gap between Keep Alive messages that is longer than KATO.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Reported. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The computer is at fault when KATO is out of range. It is also at fault when Keep Alives stop (the processor locked up, or the network split). The SSD or target is at fault when it runs out on Keep Alives that came on time. 0x18 means the computer used mixed tools. A network recording decides it. On PCIe, how often Keep Alive commands are fetched decides it. · Test that confirms it: A network recording.

Error family: P01, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. · Can the packets alone prove it? Only if the table file keeps the bytes. The result sits inside the DATA column as bytes. One version of the file keeps them (hex version). There the checker flags a done note whose result number is not 0 (nvme_status_nonzero).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book describes reservations, which let one computer claim a storage area (Register/Acquire/Release/Report). It also describes the Reservation Notification log.

What goes wrong: Another computer ran Reservation Acquire with the action "Preempt and Abort". Commands from the computer that lost its claim, still running on that storage area, are cancelled.

How you can tell: Commands still in progress from the computer that lost its claim get status 0x1B. Later commands from that computer get Reservation Conflict (0x83). A Reservation Notification log page (LID 80h) may follow. A warning for the command set (Reservation Log Page Available) may also follow. Status code: the result number in the done note. 0 means success. SCT: which list of result numbers it comes from.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Take care: use two computers (or two controllers) on a shared storage area. Register both keys and claim the area on A. Then do preempt-and-abort from B while A runs fio. Run nvme resv-report /dev/nvme0n1 before and after. Check the cluster logs. Run nvme get-log -i 0x80.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Reported. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: A computer is the cause when the preempt or what follows it is seen. That is another computer's Preempt and Abort, or cluster fencing. The SSD is at fault if no computer preempted. The reservation commands across all paths decide it. · Test that confirms it: The reservation state.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book describes the secure erase command (Sanitize, 84h) and its status log (Sanitize Status log). It also describes the sanitize action "Exit Failure Mode".

What goes wrong: The last secure erase failed, and no recovery has finished yet. Until then, the controller refuses commands that could show data that may not be erased.

How you can tell: Commands that touch the stored data finish with status 0x1C. The Sanitize Status log (LID 81h) has SSTAT status = 3h, "completed with failure" (NVME_SANITIZE_SSTAT_STATUS_COMPLETED_FAILED in libnvme). See error type S-89 in the error list. Status code: the result number in the done note. 0 means success. SCT: which list of result numbers it comes from.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Risky, test machine only, and it destroys data. Switch the power off and on during a sanitize, on a drive you can lose. To recover, run nvme sanitize -a 1 (Exit Failure Mode), or sanitize again. Run nvme sanitize-log /dev/nvme0 and read SSTAT and SPROG. Check the Persistent Event log for Sanitize Start and Completion events (types 09h/0Ah).

Does the SSD or computer report it? Reported. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: By default the SSD is at fault when SSTAT=3h (erase failed on chips, or the key store failed). The computer's hardware is at fault when power was lost during the sanitize. Log 81h and the power and wire events decide it. · Test that confirms it: The sanitize log.

Error families: P01 and P25, two of the 27 ways an error shows on the wire. · Can the packets alone prove it? Only if the table file keeps the bytes. The result sits inside the DATA column as bytes. One version of the file keeps them (hex version). There the checker flags a done note whose result number is not 0 (nvme_status_nonzero).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book describes the secure erase (Sanitize). Its status log shows progress (SPROG, out of 65536) and SSTAT = 2h, "in progress". A sanitize keeps going across restarts and power off and on.

What goes wrong: A sanitize is running. Commands not allowed during it are refused. These are reads and writes, and most admin commands that touch the stored data.

How you can tell: The done note has status 0x1D. Usually DNR=0, because it will work once the sanitize is done. Linux retries up to max_retries. That is far shorter than a sanitize, so the read or write ends with -EIO. Partition checks at start-up fail, and the disk may look empty. Status code: the result number in the done note. 0 means success. SCT: which list of result numbers it comes from.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Destroys data, risky, test machine only: run nvme sanitize /dev/nvme0 -a 2 (block erase) on a spare drive. Then read from it with dd. nvme sanitize-log /dev/nvme0 shows SSTAT=2 and SPROG going up. Get Log Page for LID 81h is allowed during a sanitize.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Reported. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: A computer started it (this one, another one, or an earlier start) when a sanitize is running. The SSD is at fault when it reports 0x1D with no sanitize running. The Sanitize command and the state in log 81h decide it. · Test that confirms it: The sanitize progress.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book describes the write-protect setting for a storage area (Namespace Write Protection Config feature, FID 84h). It also describes the storage area flags (NSATTR in Identify Namespace).

What goes wrong: The storage area is write-protected. The setting has three protect values: Write Protect, Write Protect Until Power Cycle, and Permanent Write Protect. So writes and other commands that change data are refused.

How you can tell: Writes get status 0x20. In Linux that write becomes -EIO. Linux also reads the write-protect state when it scans the storage areas. If the write-protected bit in Identify NS NSATTR is set, it marks the disk read-only. Status code: the result number in the done note. 0 means success. SCT: which list of result numbers it comes from.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Take care: run nvme set-feature /dev/nvme0 -n 1 -f 0x84 -v 1 (Write Protect, can be undone). Write, then set it back to 0. Never use the permanent value on a drive you want to keep. Check nvme get-feature /dev/nvme0 -n 1 -f 0x84, nvme id-ns -H NSATTR, and blockdev --getro.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Reported. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The computer is at fault when a protection set with Set Features FID 84h is active. The SSD is at fault when the storage area is not protected. It is also at fault when the area became protected for good without a computer command (end of life). The FID 84h and NSATTR state decide it. · Test that confirms it: The protection state.

Error family: P01, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. · Can the packets alone prove it? Only if the table file keeps the bytes. The result sits inside the DATA column as bytes. One version of the file keeps them (hex version). There the checker flags a done note whose result number is not 0 (nvme_status_nonzero).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book has a general result "Command Interrupted". libnvme says "the host should retry the command". The done note's wait field (CRD) points to wait times (CRDT1–3). The computer switches this on with ACRE.

What goes wrong: The controller stopped work on the command. The cause is an inside event, a path state change (ANA), or moving resources around. It asks the computer to try again, often after a wait (Command Retry Delay).

How you can tell: The done note has status 0x21. The "do not retry" bit (DNR) is 0 by definition. If the retries run out, Linux turns it into BLK_STS_TARGET, then -EREMOTEIO ("critical target error"). Status code: the result number in the done note. 0 means success. SCT: which list of result numbers it comes from.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Safe: make the result 0x21 appear on purpose with dont_retry=0 (error list, section II.1.5). See how retries and the error number behave. Trace with nvme:nvme_complete_rq (status 0x21 with retries above 0) and command_retries_count. Check the CRD values against nvme id-ctrl crdt1..3.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Reported. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD is the source (controller busy, background work, or a two-port event). The computer is at fault only if it ignores the wait (retries too early) or treats 0x21 as fatal. The result, DNR and the timing of the retry chain decide it. · Test that confirms it: Trace the retries.

S-22 A short network problem made the command fail (Transient Transport Error, status 0x22) Not seen in the packets Result number in the done note

Packets seen in the test recording

Error family: P01, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. · Proof from outside the recording: Logs from the network that carries NVMe (fabrics) (E10). · Can the packets alone prove it? No. It cannot be seen on this wire. The packets shown only set the scene. The proof is outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book has a general result "Transient Transport Error". It also has rules for each network kind (TCP, RDMA, FC).

What goes wrong: A short-lived problem on the connection made the command fail. Trying again on the same controller should work. libnvme quotes the rule book. After four or more failures with this result, treat it as a lasting connection error.

How you can tell: The done note has status 0x22, with DNR=0. Linux retries (up to 5), then gives -EIO. It is not in result list 3 (SCT 3). So Linux multipath does not switch paths on it directly. Status code: the result number in the done note. 0 means success. SCT: which list of result numbers it comes from.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Check the network counters (ethtool -S, RDMA counters). Look for NVMe/TCP check-number errors (digest errors) in dmesg. Match them with retries in the trace point.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Reported. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The wire or network is at fault (for network-connected SSDs), and a network recording decides it. The SSD or target is at fault if the network is clean and errors show only in the target logs. · Test that confirms it: A network recording.

One version of the file keeps them (hex version). There the checker flags a done note whose result number is not 0 (nvme_status_nonzero).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book describes CAP.CRMS (CRWMS/CRIMS) and the "ready without media" switch (CC.CRIME). It also describes the ready-time setting (CRTO, Controller Ready Timeouts).

What goes wrong: The admin command needs the storage chips (media), but they are not ready yet. This can happen when the controller said "ready" early (CSTS.RDY). It does that when the computer set CC.CRIME (Controller Ready Independent of Media Enable).

How you can tell: Admin commands get status 0x24. Examples are Identify Namespace, Get Log Page for logs kept on the storage, and Format. Status code: the result number in the done note. 0 means success. SCT: which list of result numbers it comes from.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Risky, test machine only: use a drive that supports CAP.CRMS. A driver that runs as a normal program switches it on with CRIME=1. It sends Identify NS at once. Check CC.CRIME in a settings dump or recording. Compare the time since CC.EN with CRTO.CRIMT.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Reported. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The computer is at fault when CRIME=1 and the command came before the storage was ready. The SSD is at fault when CRIME=0, or the command came after CRWMT. The checker's copy of the settings (register_shadow CC/CRTO) and the timing decide it. · Test that confirms it: Print the SSD's settings (register dump).

Error family: P01, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. · Can the packets alone prove it? Only if the table file keeps the bytes. The result sits inside the DATA column as bytes. One version of the file keeps them (hex version). There the checker flags a done note whose result number is not 0 (nvme_status_nonzero).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book describes the command set setting (I/O Command Set Profile feature, FID 19h). It describes the Identify I/O Command Set data (CNS 1Ch) and the command set switch (CC.CSS).

What goes wrong: A command names a command set (Command Set Identifier, CSI) that the controller does not support. Or it is not switched on. Or it cannot be used together with the others.

How you can tell: Linux defines NVME_SC_INVALID_IO_CMD_SET = 0x2C in the general range. QEMU (NVME_INVALID_IOCS = 0x012c) puts it in SCT 1. So does libnvme (NVME_SC_INVALID_IOCS = 0x2c, under "Command Set Specific – Namespace Types"). That list also has 0x29 I/O Command Set Not Supported, 0x2A Not Enabled, and 0x2B Combination Rejected. Not certain: check the SCT in the rule book. A Linux name lookup for a real SCT 1 / 0x2C result prints "Unknown", because 0x12C has no entry. Status code: the result number in the done note. 0 means success. SCT: which list of result numbers it comes from.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Safe: run nvme admin-passthru /dev/nvme0 --opcode=0x06 --cdw10=0x05 --cdw11=0x05000000 -r -l 4096 --namespace-id=1. That is Identify CNS 05h with an unsupported CSI value. Run nvme id-iocs /dev/nvme0 and nvme get-feature -f 0x19.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Reported. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The computer is at fault when the CSI is not supported or not switched on. The SSD is at fault when it refuses a supported, switched-on CSI. The command's CSI against CAP.CSS, CC.CSS and CNS 1Ch decides it. · Test that confirms it: Check command set support.

One version of the file keeps them (hex version). There the checker flags a done note whose result number is not 0 (nvme_status_nonzero).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book (I/O command set) has a general result "LBA Out of Range". Identify Namespace gives the storage area size (NSZE).

What goes wrong: The start block (SLBA) plus the block count (NLB) goes past the storage area size (NSZE). Or the sum is too big for the number field. Nothing is moved.

How you can tell: The done note has status 0x80. QEMU sets DNR=1. Linux turns it into BLK_STS_TARGET, then -EREMOTEIO ("critical target error"), not EIO. This surprises people who search the logs. Status code: the result number in the done note. 0 means success. SCT: which list of result numbers it comes from.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Safe: run nvme read /dev/nvme0n1 -s <NSZE> -c 0 -z 4096 (read the block just past the end). The dmesg error line shows "@ LBA x, n blocks". Compare with nvme id-ns NSZE and blockdev --getsize64. A mismatch means the size the computer remembers is old.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Reported. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The computer is at fault when the range goes past NSZE. Causes are an old size after reformat or resize, or a partition table from a larger drive. Another cause is a bug when changing block sizes. The SSD is at fault when the range is inside NSZE. The command's SLBA/NLB against the size in Identify Namespace (NSZE) decides it. · Test that confirms it: Cross-check the size.

One version of the file keeps them (hex version). There the checker flags a done note whose result number is not 0 (nvme_status_nonzero).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: Identify Namespace gives the storage area size (NSZE), the room it may use (NCAP) and the room in use (NUSE). It also describes storage areas that get room only when used (thin provisioning, NSFEAT bit 0).

What goes wrong: Running the command would make the storage area use more than its room (NCAP). This only matters for storage areas that get room only when used, where NCAP < NSZE.

How you can tell: The done note has status 0x81. Linux turns it into BLK_STS_NOSPC, then -ENOSPC. The file system gets "no space" even though df shows free space. Status code: the result number in the done note. 0 means success. SCT: which list of result numbers it comes from.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Take care: fill a thin storage area (in QEMU or a storage array) past NCAP with fio. Watch NUSE against NCAP with nvme id-ns over time. Compare with how full the file system is. If NUSE stays high after fstrim, freeing blocks is not working.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Reported. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The computer is at fault when a thin storage area is given out too much, or never trimmed. The SSD is at fault when it accepts "free these blocks" but does not do it. It is also at fault when a fully sized storage area refuses. NCAP, NUSE, NSFEAT and the checker's record of "free these blocks" commands (DSM ledger) decide it. · Test that confirms it: Watch the room used.

Error family: P01, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. · Can the packets alone prove it? Only if the table file keeps the bytes. The result sits inside the DATA column as bytes. One version of the file keeps them (hex version). There the checker flags a done note whose result number is not 0 (nvme_status_nonzero).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book has a general result "Namespace Not Ready". Newer rule books also have "Namespace Ready" signs in Identify Namespace. They are also in the I/O Command Set Independent namespace data (check this in the rule book).

What goes wrong: The storage area cannot be used right now, for a reason other than a path state (ANA). This is how libnvme words it. Examples: it is still starting after a restart, a background job is running, or the area is being created.

How you can tell: The done note has status 0x82. DNR=0 means "try again later". DNR=1 means "will not become ready". Once retries are used up, Linux turns it into BLK_STS_TARGET, then -EREMOTEIO. Status code: the result number in the done note. 0 means success. SCT: which list of result numbers it comes from.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Safe, by making the error on purpose (status 0x082). Measure the time since CSTS.RDY. Check whether it clears by itself: read with nvme read each second. A lasting 0x82 with DNR=1 means a dead storage area.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Reported. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Either side. The computer was early (harmless) when it sent the command right after switch-on or attach, and a retry worked. The SSD is at fault when DNR=1, when it lasts longer than CAP.TO, or when every command gets it. The time since "ready", DNR and the result of the retry decide it. · Test that confirms it: Check whether it lasts.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book describes the kinds of claim on a storage area (reservation types). They are Write Exclusive, Exclusive Access, Registrants Only and All Registrants. It also describes the claim report (Reservation Report).

What goes wrong: Another computer holds a claim on the storage area that does not allow this computer in. For example, another computer holds Write Exclusive, and this computer writes.

How you can tell: The done note has status 0x83. Usually DNR=1. Linux turns it into BLK_STS_RESV_CONFLICT, then -EBADE. The claim interface (persistent-reservation API) returns PR_STS_RESERVATION_CONFLICT. Status code: the result number in the done note. 0 means success. SCT: which list of result numbers it comes from.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Take care: run nvme resv-register and resv-acquire -t 1 (Write Exclusive) from controller A. Write from controller B. nvme resv-report /dev/nvme0n1 -c 1 shows who holds it, the kind, and who is registered. Compare with this computer's name (Host ID, nvme get-feature -f 0x81).

Does the SSD or computer report it? Reported. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The computer or cluster is at fault when the claim state blocks the access. Causes are a node that was shut out (fenced), an old claim, or a missing new registration. The SSD is at fault when no claim blocks it. The Reservation Report against the computer's name and the command type (opcode) decides it. · Test that confirms it: The claim report (Reservation Report).
