What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book describes the format command (Format NVM, 80h). Identify Controller has format details (FNA, Format NVM Attributes), for example whether a format applies to all storage areas. Some drives report progress in a maker's own log.

What goes wrong: A format is running on the storage area. Reads and writes to it are refused until it finishes.

How you can tell: Reads and writes get status 0x84. DNR is usually 0. Linux retries a few times, then gives -EIO. Status code: the result number in the done note. 0 means success. SCT: which list of result numbers it comes from.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Destroys data, take care: use a spare storage area in QEMU. Run nvme format /dev/nvme0n1 -s 1 (erases user data, slower). Read from another shell. Look for an earlier Format command (opcode 80h) in the recording, or in the admin nvme_setup_cmd trace point. Check the Persistent Event log for Format NVM Start and Completion events (07h/08h).

Does the SSD or computer report it? Reported. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: A computer is the cause when a format is running. A tool or another computer started it on a live or shared storage area. The SSD is at fault when it refuses reads and writes after the format finished, or with no format sent. The timeline of the Format command and its done note, and the Persistent Event log, decide it. · Test that confirms it: The format history.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book describes "create a read/write command list" (Create I/O Submission Queue, 01h). Its command word CDW11 names the done list it uses (CQID). It also describes "delete a done list" (Delete I/O Completion Queue, 04h).

What goes wrong: Create I/O SQ named a done list number (CQID) that does not exist, or is 0. Or Delete I/O CQ named a done list that is not valid.

How you can tell: Linux shows 0x100 "Completion Queue Invalid" on the admin command (SCT 1, status 0x00). Setting up the lists goes on with fewer lists. The source also says "see callout above", which points to a note box in the error list. Status code: the result number in the done note. 0 means success. SCT: which list of result numbers it comes from.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Risky, test machine only: a driver that runs as a normal program creates command list 1. It ties it to done list 7, which was never created. Check the admin command order in the recording. Create CQ (05h) must finish well before Create SQ (01h) uses its number.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Reported. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The computer is at fault when the done list does not exist at the time of Create SQ. The SSD is at fault when it does exist. The history of list creation and deletion in the checker's list map (nvme_queue_map) decides it. · Test that confirms it: The admin command order.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book describes the "number of lists" setting (Number of Queues feature, FID 07h). Its answer gives how many lists were granted (NSQA/NCQA, counting from 0). It also describes the commands that create and delete lists.

What goes wrong: Create I/O SQ or CQ used a bad list number (QID). It is 0, already in use, or above the number of lists granted. Delete I/O SQ also uses this result for a bad list number.

How you can tell: Linux shows 0x101 (SCT 1, status 0x01). Creating lists stops at that list. Status code: the result number in the done note. 0 means success. SCT: which list of result numbers it comes from.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Safe in QEMU: start with -device nvme,max_ioqpairs=4 and create list 5 from a driver that runs as a normal program. In the recording, decode Dword 0 of the "number of lists" done note. Compare it with the highest list number created.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Reported. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The computer is at fault when the list number is outside the granted range or used twice. The SSD is at fault when it refuses a valid number. Dword 0 of the FID 07h done note and the list history decide it. · Test that confirms it: The number of lists granted.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book describes the largest list size (CAP.MQES, counting from 0). It describes the "lists must be in one piece" bit (CAP.CQR). It describes the entry size settings (CC.IOSQES/IOCQES).

What goes wrong: The list size in Create I/O SQ or CQ is 0, or bigger than CAP.MQES+1. Or (in QEMU) the entry sizes in CC.IOSQES/IOCQES are not 64 and 16 bytes.

How you can tell: Linux shows 0x102 "Invalid Queue Size" (SCT 1, status 0x02). Status code: the result number in the done note. 0 means success. SCT: which list of result numbers it comes from.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Risky, test machine only: a driver that runs as a normal program creates a list of MQES+2 entries. Read CAP (nvme show-regs /dev/nvme0 -H). Read the size field QSIZE (CDW10 bits 31:16) of the Create command.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Reported. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The computer is at fault when QSIZE is bigger than CAP.MQES or is 0, or the entry sizes are wrong. The SSD is at fault when it refuses a valid size, or reports MQES wrongly. The Create command's CDW10 against CAP and CC decides it. · Test that confirms it: Check the SSD's settings.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book describes the cancel command (Abort, 08h) and its limit (ACL in Identify Controller). The rule book advises at least 4, which means ACL ≥ 3.

What goes wrong: The computer has more cancel commands open than ACL+1 (ACL counts from 0). The extra cancel is refused. libnvme lists 0x04 as "Abort command is missing". Linux names it NVME_SC_ABORT_MISSING but prints "Reserved". This is not certain in current rule books.

How you can tell: The cancel itself finishes with 0x103 (SCT 1, status 0x03). Linux logs "Abort status: 0x103" from pci.c:abort_endio(). Status code: the result number in the done note. 0 means success. SCT: which list of result numbers it comes from.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Risky, test machine only: make commands stick on a slow QEMU storage back end. A driver that runs as a normal program sends ACL+2 cancels for them. Count the open cancel commands (opcode 08h) in the recording. Compare with ACL from nvme id-ctrl.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Reported. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The computer is at fault when more than ACL+1 cancels were open. The SSD is at fault when fewer were open (it reported ACL wrongly). Counting cancel fetches and done notes against the Identify ACL decides it. · Test that confirms it: The ACL value.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book describes the "tell me about events" command (Asynchronous Event Request, AER) and its limit (AERL). The rule book advises support for at least 4.

What goes wrong: More AER commands are open than the controller supports (Identify Controller AERL, counting from 0). The extra one finishes at once with this result.

How you can tell: An AER (opcode 0Ch) gets 0x105 (SCT 1, status 0x05). Linux's nvme_complete_async_event() stops early for any AER result that is not success. The code is if (le16_to_cpu(status) >> 1 != NVME_SC_SUCCESS) return;. It does not send it again. So the error is not logged. Status code: the result number in the done note. 0 means success. SCT: which list of result numbers it comes from.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Safe in QEMU: use -device nvme,aerl=0, plus a second AER sent with nvme admin-passthru --opcode=0x0c. (If accepted, it waits until an event comes.) Count the open opcode 0Ch commands in the recording. Compare with AERL.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Reported. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The computer is at fault when it sends more AERs than AERL+1. The SSD is at fault when the limit was not reached. Counting AER fetches and done notes against AERL decides it. · Test that confirms it: The AERL value.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book describes the firmware details in Identify Controller (FRMW). Bit 0 says slot 1 is read-only. Bits 3:1 give the number of slots. Bit 4 says firmware can start without a restart. Firmware Commit has a slot field (FS) and an action field (CA) in CDW10.

What goes wrong: Firmware Commit named a slot that does not exist. Or it named a read-only slot (slot 1 when FRMW.S1RO is set) for a "replace" action.

How you can tell: Firmware Commit (opcode 10h) gets 0x106 (SCT 1, status 0x06). nvme-cli prints the result name. Status code: the result number in the done note. 0 means success. SCT: which list of result numbers it comes from.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Safe: run nvme fw-commit /dev/nvme0 -s 7 -a 2 on a drive with fewer than 7 slots. (CA 2 = start an image already there, so no image is replaced). Run nvme id-ctrl -H /dev/nvme0 | grep -A5 frmw. The command nvme fw-log /dev/nvme0 shows which slots hold firmware.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Reported. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The computer is at fault when FRMW does not allow that slot and action together. The SSD is at fault when it refuses a valid slot. The Commit command's CDW10 against FRMW and the slot log decides it. · Test that confirms it: What the slots allow.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book describes the firmware download command (Firmware Image Download, 11h). Its size (NUMD) and start point (OFST) count in 4-byte Dwords. Identify Controller gives the download piece size (FWUG, Firmware Update Granularity). It also describes Firmware Commit.

What goes wrong: 0x07: the downloaded file failed its checks when committed. Causes: bad signature, bad check number (CRC), wrong model, or not complete. 0x14: download pieces overlapped. The same range was sent twice in a way that does not fit.

How you can tell: Firmware Commit gets 0x107 (SCT 1, status 0x07). Or the download or commit gets 0x114. The running firmware stays the same. Some drives also send an error warning, "Firmware Image Load Error" (05h), at a later start of the firmware. Status code: the result number in the done note. 0 means success. SCT: which list of result numbers it comes from.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Take care: download a cut-short file or one for another model. Then commit with CA=0 (replace, do not start). The drive must refuse it without being broken. Run this as a strength test. Log every download (start point, length) and check there are no gaps. Compare nvme id-ctrl FWUG with the piece size (nvme fw-download --xfer).

Does the SSD or computer report it? Reported. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The computer is at fault when the download pieces overlap, have gaps or the wrong size. It is also at fault if the file is wrong for the model (SKU). The SSD is at fault when it refuses a correct file with no gaps. The OFST/NUMD order and a check of the file outside the recording decide it. · Test that confirms it: Check which firmware file it is.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book says Create I/O CQ names a signal number (IV) and an on/off bit (IEN) in CDW11. The PCIe rule book says how many signal numbers the SSD has (MSI-X Table Size).

What goes wrong: Create I/O CQ named a "work is done" signal number the controller cannot use. It is past the MSI-X table size, or it is not 0 while MSI-X is switched off.

How you can tell: The done note has 0x108 (SCT 1, status 0x08). Linux goes on with fewer lists. Status code: the result number in the done note. 0 means success. SCT: which list of result numbers it comes from.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Safe in QEMU: use -device nvme,msix_qsize=2 and ask for more lists. Start with pci=nomsi to see the case without MSI-X. Compare lspci -vvv MSI-X "Count=" with the number of read/write lists. Check the nvme lines in /proc/interrupts.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Reported. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The computer is at fault when the number is outside the table, or MSI-X is off. The SSD is at fault when it refuses a valid number. The checker keeps a copy of the settings area (config_shadow). The Create CQ CDW11 against the MSI-X details there decides it. · Test that confirms it: The MSI-X table size.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book describes the "read a log" command (Get Log Page, 02h) and its log number (LID). It describes the list of supported logs (Supported Log Pages log, LID 00h, NVME_LOG_SUPPORTED in Linux). It also describes the LPA field in Identify Controller.

What goes wrong: Get Log Page asked for a log number that is not supported, or is reserved.

How you can tell: The done note has 0x109 (SCT 1, status 0x09). But QEMU returns Invalid Field (0x002) from the default case of nvme_get_log(). SSDs differ on which result they use (this depends on the maker). Status code: the result number in the done note. 0 means success. SCT: which list of result numbers it comes from.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Safe: run nvme get-log /dev/nvme0 -i 0x30 -l 512. Run nvme supported-log-pages /dev/nvme0 (if LID 00h is supported). Check the LPA bits in nvme id-ctrl -H.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Reported. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The computer is at fault when the log number is not supported or not listed. The SSD is at fault when it refuses a listed or required log number. The log number against LPA and log 00h decides it. · Test that confirms it: The supported logs.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book describes the list of block formats in Identify Namespace (NLBAF and the LBAF table). The format command (Format NVM) chooses one in CDW10, with the fields LBAF, MSET, PI, PIL and SES.

What goes wrong: Format NVM asked for a block format number that does not exist. Or it asked for a mix of protection and extra data (PI/metadata) that the storage area cannot support.

How you can tell: Format NVM gets 0x10A (SCT 1, status 0x0A). The storage area stays the same. Status code: the result number in the done note. 0 means success. SCT: which list of result numbers it comes from.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Safe (it is refused before any erase): run nvme format /dev/nvme0n1 -l 15 on a storage area with fewer formats. The command nvme id-ns -H /dev/nvme0n1 lists the block formats and marks the one "in use".

Does the SSD or computer report it? Reported. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The computer is at fault when the asked LBAF and PI mix does not exist for the storage area. The SSD is at fault when it refuses a valid one. The Format CDW10 against Identify NS NLBAF, LBAF and DPC decides it. · Test that confirms it: The format list.

One version of the file keeps them (hex version). There the checker flags a done note whose result number is not 0 (nvme_status_nonzero).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book describes the Firmware Commit actions (CA). The libnvme list is: 0 replace, 1 replace and start at restart, 2 start at restart. Then 3 replace and start now, and 6/7 boot partition. The firmware slot log has an "active firmware" field (AFI). The whole-SSD restart setting (NSSR, 20h) does a subsystem restart.

What goes wrong: These are successes reported as errors. The commit worked and the file is in the slot. But it will only run after the named kind of restart. Until then the old firmware keeps running.

How you can tell: Firmware Commit gets 0x10B, 0x110 or 0x111. Look at AFI in the firmware slot log (LID 03h). The "next active" slot (bits 6:4) is not the current slot (bits 2:0). At warning time, Linux reports this as "Firmware is activated after next Controller Level Reset". Status code: the result number in the done note. 0 means success. SCT: which list of result numbers it comes from.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Take care: download a valid file with nvme fw-download. Run nvme fw-commit -s 2 -a 1 and read the result. Then run nvme reset /dev/nvme0 and check firmware_rev. Use only a file the maker supports. Read AFI with nvme fw-log /dev/nvme0 before and after. cat /sys/class/nvme/nvme0/firmware_rev stays old until the restart. After a restart, check the version again.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Reported. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The computer is at fault when the script goes back, or does not do the needed restart. The SSD is at fault when the needed restart was done and the old version still runs. The restart rows after the commit and the Identify version (FR) decide it. · Test that confirms it: Check the firmware version.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book describes the longest firmware switch time (MTFA). FRMW bit 4 says firmware can start without a restart. Firmware Commit CA=3 means "start now".

What goes wrong: 0x12: starting now (CA=3) would take longer than MTFA. MTFA is the Maximum Time for Firmware Activation, in Identify Controller, counted in steps of 100 ms. So the controller refuses. 0x13: the controller refuses this file for the maker's own reasons. Examples are "no going back to old versions" (anti-rollback), or a downgrade that is not allowed.

How you can tell: Firmware Commit gets 0x112 or 0x113. The running firmware stays the same. Status code: the result number in the done note. 0 means success. SCT: which list of result numbers it comes from.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Take care: commit with CA=3 a file that the maker says needs a restart. Try again with CA=1 or 2 and a restart. If that works, the "start now" path was the problem. For 0x13, check the maker's release notes for the lowest allowed versions.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Reported. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Usually the computer is at fault. It asked to start now with a file that needs a restart. Or it tried to go back to an older version. The SSD is at fault when it reports 0x12 for an action that is not "start now". It is also at fault if it starts the switch after refusing. Commit CA, CSTS.PP and the SSD warnings decide it. · Test that confirms it: Try the other path (restart).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book describes "delete a done list" (Delete I/O Completion Queue). Lists must be deleted in order: command lists first, then their done list.

What goes wrong: Delete I/O CQ was sent for a done list that still has command lists tied to it. Those must be deleted first. Or it was sent for the admin done list.

How you can tell: Delete I/O CQ (opcode 04h) gets 0x10C (SCT 1, status 0x0C). QEMU returns it without DNR. So trying again after deleting the command list is expected. Status code: the result number in the done note. 0 means success. SCT: which list of result numbers it comes from.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Check the order in the recording. Delete CQ (04h) was sent before Delete SQ (00h) for a command list tied to that done list.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Reported. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The computer is at fault when a tied command list still exists, or the admin done list is named. The SSD is at fault when all command lists were deleted first. The list ties and the deletion history decide it. · Test that confirms it: The order of taking lists down.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book describes Set and Get Features and the "save" bit (SV). Get Features with SEL=11b shows what a setting supports: can be saved, per storage area, can be changed. An ONCS bit says the "Save field in Set/Get Features" is supported.

What goes wrong: 0x0D: Set Features with SV=1 for a setting that cannot be saved. 0x0E: a write to a read-only setting. 0x0F: a storage area number (NSID) used with a setting that covers the whole controller.

How you can tell: The done note has 0x10D, 0x10E or 0x10F, with DNR=1 (QEMU). The current value stays the same. Status code: the result number in the done note. 0 means success. SCT: which list of result numbers it comes from.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Safe: run nvme set-feature /dev/nvme0 -f 0x08 -v 0 --save (Interrupt Coalescing, saved) on a drive that cannot save it. Run nvme get-feature /dev/nvme0 -f <fid> -s 3 (what it supports) before setting.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Reported. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The computer is at fault when the command fields explain the result. Examples: a pass-through tool used --save, a wrong NSID, or a fixed setting. The SSD is at fault when the recorded abilities (SEL=11b DW0) or ONCS say the action is allowed. Linux nvme_set_features() never sets SV. So a 0x10D on a Linux computer comes from a pass-through tool. · Test that confirms it: Read what the setting supports.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book describes creating and deleting storage areas (Namespace Management). It describes attaching and detaching them with a list of controllers (Namespace Attachment). Identify gives the limits: TNVMCAP/UNVMCAP, NN, MNAN and ANAGRPMAX.

What goes wrong: Namespace Management (0Dh) or Namespace Attachment (15h) was refused. The results are: not enough room (0x15). No free storage area numbers (0x16). Already attached (0x18). Private, already attached to another controller (0x19). Not attached, for a detach (0x1A). Thin storage not supported, when NCAP < NSZE was asked (0x1B). Controller List Invalid (0x1C). ANA Group Identifier Invalid (0x24). ANA Attach Failed (0x25).

How you can tell: The matching 0x1xx result. Nothing changes. Status code: the result number in the done note. 0 means success. SCT: which list of result numbers it comes from.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Take care (creating and deleting destroys data). Use QEMU with -device nvme-subsys and nvme-ns,detached=true. Attach the same storage area twice. You get 0x118. Run nvme id-ctrl (tnvmcap, unvmcap, nn, cntlid), nvme list-ctrl /dev/nvme0 -n <nsid> and nvme list-ns --all.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Reported. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The computer is at fault when the data sent and Identify explain the result. Causes are set-up scripts, a wrong controller number list (CNTLID), or a private storage area on a two-port drive. The SSD is at fault when the request was valid by its Identify data. Another controller is the cause when the Persistent Event log shows a change by another controller number (CNTLID, E03). · Test that confirms it: Room and controller numbers.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book describes the self-test command and its STC field: 1h short, 2h long, Fh stop. It describes the self-test log, and the long test time in minutes (EDSTT).

What goes wrong: A self-test (opcode 14h) was started while another self-test was running.

How you can tell: The done note has 0x11D (SCT 1, status 0x1D). In the self-test log (LID 06h), byte 0 shows the test now running (1h short, 2h long). Byte 1 shows the percent done. Status code: the result number in the done note. 0 means success. SCT: which list of result numbers it comes from.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Safe: run nvme device-self-test /dev/nvme0 -s 2 twice in a row. Run nvme self-test-log /dev/nvme0. Stop it with nvme device-self-test -s 0xf.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Reported. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The computer is at fault when an earlier test is proven to be running. A watch program or a second tool started a test. The SSD is at fault when no test was running, or a stop was refused. · Test that confirms it: The self-test log.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book describes start-up areas on the SSD (Boot Partitions). They have settings CAP.BPS, BPINFO, BPRSEL and BPMBL. Newer rule books add a write-protect setting for them (Boot Partition Write Protection Config feature).

What goes wrong: Something tried to change a locked start-up area. It used Firmware Image Download/Commit with the boot-partition commit actions 6 or 7.

How you can tell: The done note has 0x11E (SCT 1, status 0x1E). Status code: the result number in the done note. 0 means success. SCT: which list of result numbers it comes from.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Risky, test machine only: use a computer whose start-up area is locked. Run nvme show-regs -H and read BPINFO. Read the Boot Partition log (LID 15h).

Does the SSD or computer report it? Reported. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The computer or its hardware is the cause when the area is locked. Firmware locked it, or a tool wrote the wrong area. The SSD is at fault when the area is unlocked. It is also at fault if it returns this result for an action not about the start-up area. · Test that confirms it: The start-up area settings.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book describes virtual controllers (Virtualization Enhancements). Identify gives the main controller's abilities (CNS 14h) and the list of extra controllers (Secondary Controller List, CNS 15h).

What goes wrong: Virtualization Management (1Ch) was refused. The extra controller is unknown. Or it is in the wrong state (online or offline) for the action. Or the resources asked for (VQ/VI) are over the limit. Or the resource kind is bad.

How you can tell: The done note has 0x11F to 0x122, with DNR=1 (QEMU). Status code: the result number in the done note. 0 means success. SCT: which list of result numbers it comes from.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Safe on QEMU with sriov_max_vfs: give resources to an extra controller that is online. Run nvme primary-ctrl-caps and nvme list-secondary.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Reported. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The computer is at fault (the order of SR-IOV set-up steps) when the lists explain the result. What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book describes a memory area that keeps its data without power (Persistent Memory Region, PMR). Its settings are CAP.PMRS, PMRCAP and PMRCTL. It also describes the secure erase (Sanitize).

What goes wrong: A sanitize was asked for while the PMR is switched on (PMRCTL.EN=1).

How you can tell: The done note has 0x123 (SCT 1, status 0x23). Linux prints "Sanitize Prohibited". Status code: the result number in the done note. 0 means success. SCT: which list of result numbers it comes from.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Risky, test machine only: use a controller with PMR (QEMU pmrdev=) with PMR switched on. Run nvme show-regs -H and read PMRCTL.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Reported. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The computer is at fault when PMRCTL.EN=1 (the script that retires the drive did not switch PMR off). Otherwise the SSD is at fault. · Test that confirms it: The PMR settings.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe NVM command rules describe the option bits of Dataset Management: AD (free these blocks), IDR and IDW. They also describe the context options.

What goes wrong: Dataset Management, or another NVM command, carries option bits that contradict each other. Or the controller cannot follow them together.

How you can tell: The done note has 0x180 (SCT 1, status 0x80). Linux turns it into BLK_STS_NOTSUPP, then -EOPNOTSUPP. A "free blocks" request (discard) that fails this way looks like "discard not supported". Claims (persistent reservations) turn it into -EINVAL. Status code: the result number in the done note. 0 means success. SCT: which list of result numbers it comes from.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Safe, by making the error on purpose. On real hardware, try mixes like nvme dsm /dev/nvme0n1 -a 1 -d -w -r. This is only an example, so check the nvme-cli wording for your version. Decode the DSM's CDW11 in the recording. Repeat with only AD set.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Reported. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The computer is at fault when the command or its range list carries the contradicting bits. These are option mixes or claim options. The SSD is at fault when the request is a plain, supported form. · Test that confirms it: Repeat with AD only.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book describes end-to-end data protection (Protection Information, PI). Identify Namespace has the protection settings (DPS/DPC). Read, Write, Compare and Verify carry the protection field (PRINFO) in CDW12.

What goes wrong: The PRINFO field (PRACT and PRCHK bits) is not valid for the storage area's protection kind. Or protection was asked for on a storage area without it.

How you can tell: The done note has 0x181 (SCT 1, status 0x81). Linux turns it into BLK_STS_PROTECTION, then -EILSEQ. Status code: the result number in the done note. 0 means success. SCT: which list of result numbers it comes from.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Safe in QEMU (a protected storage area, -device nvme-ns,pi=1,ms=8): run nvme compare with PRACT set. Run nvme id-ns -H and read DPS/DPC. Decode CDW12 bits 29:26 in the recording.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Reported. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The computer is at fault when PRINFO is not valid for DPS (a protection profile mismatch, or PRINFO built wrongly). Otherwise the SSD is at fault. · Test that confirms it: The storage area's protection settings.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book describes a setting that marks block ranges (LBA Range Type feature). A range can be marked read-only or hidden. QEMU defines NVME_WRITE_TO_RO but never returns it.

What goes wrong: A write touched a block range that the computer had marked read-only earlier. It did that with the LBA Range Type setting (FID 03h).

How you can tell: The done note has 0x182 (SCT 1, status 0x82). Linux turns it into BLK_STS_MEDIUM, then -ENODATA ("critical medium error"). This is misleading. The storage chips are fine, and the cause is a setting. Status code: the result number in the done note. 0 means success. SCT: which list of result numbers it comes from.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Take care: on a test drive that supports FID 03h, set an LBA Range Type entry with the read-only mark. Run nvme get-feature /dev/nvme0 -n 1 -f 3 -H.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Reported. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The settings of the computer or its start-up program (BIOS) are at fault when a read-only range overlaps. The SSD is at fault when none does. · Test that confirms it: The LBA Range Type setting.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe NVM command rules describe the Copy command. Identify Namespace gives its limits (MSSRL, MCL, MSRC). An ONCS bit says Copy is supported.

What goes wrong: A Copy (19h), or a similar command, goes over a limit. MSSRL is the longest single source range. MCL is the longest copy. MSRC is the most source ranges. That gives 0x83. libnvme and QEMU add four more. They are 0x85 Incompatible Namespace or Format and 0x86 Fast Copy Not Possible. The others are 0x87 Overlapping I/O Range and 0x89 Insufficient Resources. These are not in Linux's nvme.h, so Linux prints them as "Unknown".

How you can tell: The done note has 0x183 (Linux text "Command Size Limits Exceeded"). QEMU's nvme_do_copy() gives 0x185 or 0x187. Status code: the result number in the done note. 0 means success. SCT: which list of result numbers it comes from.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Safe in QEMU: run nvme copy with a range longer than MSSRL. Read mssrl, mcl and msrc with nvme id-ns -H. Then check the Copy range list.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Reported. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The computer is at fault when the limits are passed (copy built from pieces larger than MSSRL, or overlapping ranges). Otherwise the SSD is at fault. 0x86 and 0x89 are states of the SSD's resources. · Test that confirms it: The copy limits.

S-53 Connecting to an SSD over a network was refused (Fabrics Connect, 0x80 to 0x84, 0x90, 0x91) Not seen in the packets Result number in the done note

Packets seen in the test recording

Error family: P01, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. · Proof from outside the recording: Logs from the network that carries NVMe (fabrics) (E10). · Can the packets alone prove it? No. It cannot be seen on this wire. The packets shown only set the scene. The proof is outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe over network rule book (NVMe over Fabrics) describes the Connect command and its answer. It describes the Discovery log, and login checks inside the connection (DH-HMAC-CHAP in-band authentication).

What goes wrong: Connect was refused. The results are Incompatible Format (0x180), Controller Busy (0x181) and Connect Invalid Parameters (0x182). Others are Connect Restart Discovery (0x183) and Connect Invalid Host (0x184). There are also Discovery Restart (0x190) and Authentication Required (0x191). libnvme also lists 0x85 Invalid Queue Type, for Disconnect.

How you can tell: Connect fails, and nvme connect reports the error. dmesg shows lines from fabrics.c:nvmf_log_connect_error(). For 0x182, it uses the IATTR/IPO fields of the Connect answer to say which value failed. 0x191 on a read or write makes Linux log in again, then retry (its action is AUTHENTICATE). Status code: the result number in the done note. 0 means success. SCT: which list of result numbers it comes from.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Look for dmesg lines "Connect Invalid Host" or "Connect command failed ...". Read the target's logs. Check the nvme discover output.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Reported. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The computer is at fault when the connect values are wrong by the target's settings. Examples: name NQN not allowed, wrong subsystem NQN or CNTLID, or missing keys. The SSD or target is at fault when it refuses correct values. · Test that confirms it: A network recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The Zoned Namespace (ZNS) command rules split storage into zones that must be written in order. They give the zone size (ZSZE). An OZCS bit (RAZB) says whether reads may cross zone edges.

What goes wrong: A command's block range covers more than one zone. For reads, this is only an error if the storage area forbids reads across zones (Read Across Zone Boundaries, OZCS.RAZB=0).

How you can tell: The done note has 0x1B8 (SCT 1, status 0xB8). In Linux it becomes -EIO. Status code: the result number in the done note. 0 means success. SCT: which list of result numbers it comes from.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Safe in QEMU with zones: read across a zone edge with nvme read. Get zsze with nvme zns id-ns. Work out slba / zsze and (slba+nlb-1) / zsze.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Reported. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The computer is at fault when the range crosses an edge. Its splitting of reads and writes ignores the zone size. Otherwise the SSD is at fault. · Test that confirms it: The zone layout.

Error family: P01, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. · Can the packets alone prove it? Only if the table file keeps the bytes. The result sits inside the DATA column as bytes. One version of the file keeps them (hex version). There the checker flags a done note whose result number is not 0 (nvme_status_nonzero).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The Zoned Namespace (ZNS) rules give each zone a state. The states are ZSE (empty), ZSIO and ZSEO (open), and ZSC (closed). The others are ZSF (full), ZSRO (read only) and ZSO (offline). Zone Management Receive reports the zones.

What goes wrong: A write went to a full zone (ZSF, 0xB9) or a read-only zone (ZSRO, 0xBA). Or any command went to an offline zone (ZSO, 0xBB). The SSD itself moves zones to Read Only and Offline, because of problems in the storage chips. So these are really storage-health events that look like state errors.

How you can tell: The done note has 0x1B9, 0x1BA or 0x1BB. In Linux it becomes -EIO. A zone report shows the zone state. The drive may also send a "Zone Descriptor Changed" warning for zones (check this in the rule book). Status code: the result number in the done note. 0 means success. SCT: which list of result numbers it comes from.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Safe in QEMU: fill a zone, then write again (0xB9). QEMU's Offline action only works from Read Only (nvme_offline_zone()). The SSD must move zones to Read Only and Offline itself. So test 0xBA and 0xBB with the maker's fault commands, or by making the error on purpose on the computer. Run nvme zns report-zones /dev/nvme0n1 -d 10 and blkzone report. Count zones in Read Only or Offline over time, as a health number.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Reported. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: For 0xB9, the computer is at fault (it lost track of the write point). For 0xBA and 0xBB, the SSD is the source (the storage chips moved the zone). It is an SSD defect when the state does not explain the result. · Test that confirms it: The zone report.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The Zoned Namespace (ZNS) rules say zones must be written in order. The "add to zone" command (Zone Append, opcode 7Dh) avoids this, because the SSD picks the block address.

What goes wrong: A Write went to a zone that must be written in order. It did not start at the zone's write point (write pointer).

How you can tell: The done note has 0x1BC (SCT 1, status 0xBC). In Linux it becomes -EIO. It is the most common zone error in real use. Status code: the result number in the done note. 0 means success. SCT: which list of result numbers it comes from.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Safe in QEMU: write to zslba + 8 on an empty zone with nvme write. Trace the start block (SLBA) order for each zone. Compare it with the reported write pointer. A write reported as failed whose data is there means an earlier try had worked.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Reported. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The computer is at fault. Causes are writes out of order, no zone write plugging, sending again, or an old write pointer copy. The SSD is at fault only if SLBA equals the write pointer. · Test that confirms it: The write pointer.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The Zoned Namespace (ZNS) Identify Namespace data gives the limits MAR and MOR. Zones can be opened by a write (implicit) or by a command (explicit).

What goes wrong: Opening or writing a zone would go over MAR (Maximum Active Resources) or MOR (Maximum Open Resources). Both count from 0.

How you can tell: 0x1BD becomes BLK_STS_ZONE_ACTIVE_RESOURCE, then -EOVERFLOW. 0x1BE becomes BLK_STS_ZONE_OPEN_RESOURCE, then -ETOOMANYREFS. These are the only zone results with their own Linux error numbers. So the file system can tell them apart and close zones. Status code: the result number in the done note. 0 means success. SCT: which list of result numbers it comes from.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Safe in QEMU: use -device nvme-ns,zoned=true,zoned.max_open=2, then write to 3 empty zones. Read /sys/block/nvme0n1/queue/max_open_zones and max_active_zones. Count the open and closed zones from a zone report.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Reported. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The computer is at fault when the counts reach the limit (it used up the resources). Otherwise the SSD is at fault. · Test that confirms it: The limits and zone states.

One version of the file keeps them (hex version). There the checker flags a done note whose result number is not 0 (nvme_status_nonzero).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The Zoned Namespace (ZNS) rules list the zone actions. They are Close, Finish, Open, Reset and Offline. Two more are Set Zone Descriptor Extension and Flush Explicit ZRWA Range.

What goes wrong: Zone Management Send asked for a state change the zone rules do not allow. For example, Open a full zone, or Finish an offline zone. That gives 0xBF. 0xB6 is a zone action that is not valid. An example is setting up a random-write area (ZRWA) on a zone that is not empty. 0xB7 means no Zone Random Write Area is free.

How you can tell: 0x1BF becomes -EIO. Linux has no name for 0xB6 and 0xB7 and prints "Unknown". Status code: the result number in the done note. 0 means success. SCT: which list of result numbers it comes from.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Safe in QEMU: run nvme zns open-zone on a full zone. Check the zone report before the command. Check the ZNS state diagram.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Reported. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The computer is at fault when the change is not allowed. Its copy of the zone states is out of date, or a tool sends Open to full zones. Otherwise the SSD is at fault. · Test that confirms it: The zone state before the command.

Error family: P01, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. · Proof from outside the recording: The SSD's own logs and settings read with nvme-cli (E03). · Can the packets alone prove it? Only if the table file keeps the bytes. The result sits inside the DATA column as bytes. One version of the file keeps them (hex version). There the checker flags a done note whose result number is not 0 (nvme_status_nonzero).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book has a storage-chip result "Write Fault" (Media and Data Integrity Errors list). The SMART health log has a "Media and Data Integrity Errors" count. The error log has a block address (LBA) field.

What goes wrong: The controller could not save the write data to the storage chips. The data came over from the computer. But writing it to the chips failed, and the firmware could not put it somewhere else.

How you can tell: SCT 2 / status 0x80. Linux turns it into BLK_STS_MEDIUM, then -ENODATA. dmesg shows "Write Fault" and "critical medium error ... op 0x1:(WRITE)". The SMART "Media and Data Integrity Errors" count goes up. An error log entry gives the block address. Repeated faults usually come with Available Spare going down. Critical warning bit 2 or 3 may also be set (error types S-74 and S-75 in the error list). Status code: the result number in the done note. 0 means success. SCT: which list of result numbers it comes from.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Safe in QEMU: attach the storage area through a blkdebug drive. Give it a write error on purpose (event write_aio, errno 5). That gives a real 0x280 done note on the pretend wire. On real hardware, only the maker's fault commands work. Run nvme smart-log (media_errors, avail_spare, critical_warning). Run nvme error-log (LBA, NSID, and status 0x280, which is libnvme's way to write SCT 2 / status 0x80). Read back the block. The old data, the new data or junk can come back. Write down which.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Reported. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD is at fault. A write to the chips failed with no spare left. Or the power-loss capacitor failed, or it is in end-of-life read-only mode. The recording only proves that the computer sent the data and the SSD reported the fault. The SMART and error logs decide whether the storage chips or the firmware caused it. · Test that confirms it: The storage-chip error counts.

Error family: P01, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. · Proof from outside the recording: The SSD's own logs and settings read with nvme-cli (E03). · Can the packets alone prove it? Only if the table file keeps the bytes. The result sits inside the DATA column as bytes. One version of the file keeps them (hex version). There the checker flags a done note whose result number is not 0 (nvme_status_nonzero).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book has the result "Unrecovered Read Error". The Error Recovery setting (FID 05h) has a time limit for error fixing (TLER, Time Limited Error Recovery). It limits how long the drive tries before it reports. The Write Uncorrectable command (04h) marks blocks so they return this error on purpose.

What goes wrong: The data could not be read back from the storage chips. This is after the controller's full error fixing. That means error-fixing codes (ECC), read retries, finer decoding, and spare copies across chips (die parity). The data in those blocks is lost, unless the computer has another copy.

How you can tell: Read, Verify, Compare or Copy get SCT 2 / status 0x81. Linux turns it into BLK_STS_MEDIUM, then -ENODATA. The SMART media_errors count goes up. The error log has the first failing block. The controller has already tried again inside, so DNR=1 is common. If DNR=0, Linux retries up to 5 times. Status code: the result number in the done note. 0 means success. SCT: which list of result numbers it comes from.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Take care (destroys data in the range): run nvme write-uncor /dev/nvme0n1 -s 0x1000 -c 7. Then nvme read ... -s 0x1000 gives 0x281. A nvme write-zeroes or a normal write clears it. In QEMU, use blkdebug read_aio errors. Read the block range with nvme read and compare with nvme error-log. Use nvme verify (if ONCS supports it) to scan without moving data. Write the block again (that usually moves it to a good place), then read again to confirm.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Reported. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD is at fault. Causes are data fading over time, damage from nearby reads, worn blocks, or a firmware bug in the block map. The computer is the cause only when it marked the block with Write Uncorrectable. · Test that confirms it: The error log plus SMART.

Error family: P01, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. · Can the packets alone prove it? Only if the table file keeps the bytes. The result sits inside the DATA column as bytes. One version of the file keeps them (hex version). There the checker flags a done note whose result number is not 0 (nvme_status_nonzero).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book describes end-to-end data protection (Protection Information, PI), Types 1, 2 and 3. It uses a 16-bit check number (guard, CRC-16 T10-DIF). Newer rule books add 32-bit and 64-bit guards. The command's PRINFO field is PRACT plus PRCHK[2:0]. The fields ELBAT, ELBATM and ILBRT give the expected tags.

What goes wrong: The storage area is formatted with protection, and a check switched on by PRCHK failed. Guard: the check number of the data does not match the guard field. So the data or extra data was damaged. App Tag: the tag is not the expected value (under the mask). Ref Tag: the block is not the one the computer expected. For example, a write or read went to the wrong place. Storage Tag (0x88, only in libnvme and QEMU; Linux nvme.h has no name for it): the storage tag check failed.

How you can tell: 0x282, 0x283 and 0x284 become BLK_STS_PROTECTION in Linux, then -EILSEQ ("protection error"). 0x288 becomes "Unknown", then -EIO. The checks can run on writes (PRACT=0: the controller checks the protection data from the computer) or on reads. Status code: the result number in the done note. 0 means success. SCT: which list of result numbers it comes from.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Safe in QEMU (-device nvme-ns,ms=8,pi=1): write with correct protection data. Then read with PRCHK=ref and a wrong ILBRT (nvme read ... -p 1 -r 0x1234). You get 0x284. Write data with a bad guard to get 0x282. Read the block with PRCHK cleared, plus its extra data (nvme read ... -y 8 -M meta.bin). Work out the CRC-16 T10-DIF of the data again and compare it with the stored guard. The stored ref tag shows which block's data you got. This is one of the few ways to prove a write went to the wrong place.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Reported. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The computer is at fault when the protection data is wrong on the wire for a write. Causes are a bad check-number table, wrong byte order, or a reused buffer. The SSD is at fault when it was right on write and wrong on read-back. Causes are bit flips in its memory, or a wrong block map. · Test that confirms it: Read the raw block and its extra data.

Error family: P01, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. · Can the packets alone prove it? Only if the table file keeps the bytes. The result sits inside the DATA column as bytes. One version of the file keeps them (hex version). There the checker flags a done note whose result number is not 0 (nvme_status_nonzero).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe NVM command rules describe the Compare command and joined commands (Fused Operation). An ONCS bit says Compare is supported.

What goes wrong: A Compare (05h) found that the stored data is not the same as the computer's buffer. This is an expected result, not a fault, when Compare is used for compare-and-write locking. As the first half of a joined pair, it also cancels the second half (0x09).

How you can tell: 0x285 (SCT 2, status 0x85) becomes BLK_STS_MEDIUM in Linux, then -ENODATA. So it looks like a storage-chip error in dmesg. Watch tools that count "critical medium error" lines count too many on systems that use Compare. An example is VMware-style ATS-like locking over NVMe-oF. Status code: the result number in the done note. 0 means success. SCT: which list of result numbers it comes from.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Safe: run nvme compare /dev/nvme0n1 -s 0 -c 0 -z 4096 -d /dev/urandom (random data will not match). Read the block and compare it with the compare buffer. Check whether the different data matches an older write. That finds lost writes.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Reported. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The computer or program is the cause when two users wanting the same block explain it. The SSD is at fault when the buffer equals the last write it confirmed. · Test that confirms it: Compare against what is stored.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book has the storage-chip result "Access Denied". TCG Storage Opal/Enterprise sets locked ranges through the security commands (Security Send/Receive).

What goes wrong: Access to the storage area or block range is refused, because access rights are missing. Usually a range of a self-encrypting drive is locked.

How you can tell: 0x286 (SCT 2, status 0x86) becomes BLK_STS_MEDIUM in Linux, then -ENODATA. At start-up this looks like a dying disk ("critical medium error" on every read of the partition table). But the drive is just locked. Status code: the result number in the done note. 0 means success. SCT: which list of result numbers it comes from.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Take care: lock a range on a test self-encrypting drive (SED) and read it. Keep the admin password safe. sedutil-cli --query /dev/nvme0 shows Locked = Y. All failing blocks fall inside one locked range.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Reported. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The computer is at fault when no successful 81h (unlock) is seen since the last start. It did not unlock after power off and on, or after waking. The SSD is at fault when an unlock worked and reads are still refused. · Test that confirms it: The lock state.

Error family: P01, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. · Can the packets alone prove it? Only if the table file keeps the bytes. The result sits inside the DATA column as bytes. One version of the file keeps them (hex version). There the checker flags a done note whose result number is not 0 (nvme_status_nonzero).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book describes the Error Recovery setting (FID 05h) and its DULBE bit. Identify Namespace has an NSFEAT DAE bit (DULBE supported). DLFEAT says what a read of freed blocks returns.

What goes wrong: A Read, Verify, Compare or Copy touched a freed or never-written block. The computer had switched on DULBE (Deallocated or Unwritten Logical Block Error) in the Error Recovery setting. Without DULBE, the drive returns the freed-block read pattern (often zeros, see DLFEAT) with success.

How you can tell: 0x287 (SCT 2, status 0x87) becomes BLK_STS_MEDIUM in Linux, then -ENODATA. It is a useful error. Apart from LBA Status, it is the only way to prove that "free these blocks" (Deallocate) really worked. After freeing a range, reads with DULBE on must fail with 0x287. Status code: the result number in the done note. 0 means success. SCT: which list of result numbers it comes from.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Take care (the DSM step destroys data). On a spare storage area, run nvme set-feature /dev/nvme0 -n 1 -f 5 -v 0x10000. DULBE is bit 16 of the Error Recovery value. Free a range, read it, then set the setting back to its old value. The command nvme get-feature /dev/nvme0 -n 1 -f 5 shows whether DULBE is on. To prove the freeing: write a pattern, free the range with nvme dsm -d, switch on DULBE, and read. Expect 0x287. If the read returns the old pattern with success, the freeing was silently ignored.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Reported. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The computer caused it (it switched on DULBE and read unwritten space), and the SSD is correct. The SSD is at fault when DULBE is off, or the block was written. · Test that confirms it: The DULBE state.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book has a path result "Internal Path Error" (Path Related Status).

What goes wrong: The command failed because of an inside error in the controller that handled it. So another controller (path) to the same storage area may work. This is how libnvme words it.

How you can tell: The done note has 0x300 (SCT 3, status 0x00). With several paths (multipath): Linux switches to the other path, multipath_failover_count goes up, and the read or write works there. With one path: it retries, then -EIO. Status code: the result number in the done note. 0 means success. SCT: which list of result numbers it comes from.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Safe: make 0x300 appear on purpose on one path's storage device (the hidden node like nvme0c0n1). Watch reads and writes go on. Check the path states with nvme list-subsys and the switch-over counts for each path. Match with the storage array's logs.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Reported. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD is at fault (one controller or port of a two-port SSD or array has an inside fault). Confirm with the failing controller's error log and the array logs. · Test that confirms it: The path state.

One version of the file keeps them (hex version). There the checker flags a done note whose result number is not 0 (nvme_status_nonzero).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book describes path states (Asymmetric Namespace Access, ANA). The ANA log lists groups and their states (Linux enum nvme_ana_state). The states are Optimized 01h, Non-Optimized 02h, Inaccessible 03h, Persistent Loss 04h, and Change 0Fh. ANATT is the change time in seconds. ANACAP and ANAGRPID give the abilities and group number.

What goes wrong: On this controller, the storage area's path group is in a state that cannot serve the command. The state is Inaccessible (0x02), Persistent Loss (0x01) or Change (0x03).

How you can tell: The done note has 0x301, 0x302 or 0x303. With Linux multipath, nvme_failover_req() sets NVME_NS_ANA_PENDING. It queues ana_work to read the ANA log (LID 0Ch) again. Then it sends the requests again on another path. Usually an "ANA Change" warning arrives too (error type S-83 in the error list). Without multipath (nvme_core.multipath=N), it is retried on the same path and ends in -EIO. Status code: the result number in the done note. 0 means success. SCT: which list of result numbers it comes from.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Safe: use a Linux nvmet target with two ports. Change a port's ANA state through configfs (ana_groups/<id>/ana_state) to "inaccessible" or "change". Run fio on the computer. Run nvme ana-log /dev/nvme0 and cat /sys/block/nvme0c0n1/ana_state. Check the switch-over counts. dmesg shows "ANATT timeout, resetting controller." if a change lasts longer than ANATT.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Reported. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD or array is the source (switch-over, firmware upgrade, or the path belongs to the other controller). It is an SSD defect when the state and the result disagree, or a Change lasts longer than ANATT. · Test that confirms it: The ANA state.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book has a path result "Controller Pathing Error". The range 60h–6Fh is for path errors the controller finds.

What goes wrong: The controller found a path error. For example, a network connection problem between itself and the computer, or inside the subsystem.

How you can tell: The done note has 0x360 (SCT 3, status 0x60). With multipath, Linux switches paths. Otherwise it gives -EIO. Status code: the result number in the done note. 0 means success. SCT: which list of result numbers it comes from.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Safe, by making 0x360 appear on purpose. Check the target logs, the switch-over counts, and the network counters on the target side.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Reported. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD or target is at fault (a back-end or connection fault the controller saw). The wire is at fault if a network recording shows the computer's network card or port restarting. · Test that confirms it: The target logs.

S-68 The computer cannot reach the SSD, and makes this result itself (Host Pathing Error) Not seen in the packets Result number in the done note

Packets seen in the test recording

Error family: P01, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. · Proof from outside the recording: Logs from the network that carries NVMe (fabrics) (E10). · Can the packets alone prove it? No. It cannot be seen on this wire. The packets shown only set the scene. The proof is outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book has a path result "Host Pathing Error". The range 70h–7Fh is for path errors the computer finds.

What goes wrong: The computer found that it cannot reach the controller. Linux sets this result itself when it cannot queue a request to a controller that is not live. An example is during a reconnect.

How you can tell: There is no done note on the wire. Linux uses result 0x370 (SCT 3, status 0x70). With multipath it switches paths (FAILOVER). Otherwise it becomes BLK_STS_TRANSPORT, then -ENOLINK ("recoverable transport error"). Status code: the result number in the done note. 0 means success. SCT: which list of result numbers it comes from.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Look in dmesg for controller state changes just before ("resetting controller", reconnect tries). Look for trace point result 0x370 with no matching done note in a capture tool recording.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Reported. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD is at fault if a read of CSTS.CFS=1 started the restart before this time. A missing done note counts too. The computer is at fault if a restart or removal started by the driver had no SSD fault before it. The computer's hardware is at fault if a wire loss or port lock-down (DPC) started it. · Test that confirms it: The computer's trace point.

Error families: P01 and P02, two of the 27 ways an error shows on the wire. · Proof from outside the recording: The Linux kernel log (E01). The SSD's own logs and settings read with nvme-cli (E03). Tracing the computer's own read and write path (E05). · Can the packets alone prove it? Only if the table file keeps the bytes. The result sits inside the DATA column as bytes. One version of the file keeps them (hex version). There the checker flags a done note whose result number is not 0 (nvme_status_nonzero).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book has a path result "Command Aborted By Host" (NVME_SC_CMD_ABORTED_BY_HOST in libnvme).

What goes wrong: The computer cancelled the command because of something it did. Linux sets it on every request in progress when it takes down a controller's lists. That happens on a restart after a timeout or CSTS.CFS, on removal, or on network error recovery.

How you can tell: dmesg shows nvme_log_error lines with "Host Aborted Command (sct 0x3 / sc 0x71)" for many requests at once. They usually come right after "I/O tag N ... timeout, reset controller" or "controller is down; will reset". Because it is SCT 3, multipath switches paths. Otherwise it is retried after the restart, or gives -EIO if the controller is removed. Status code: the result number in the done note. 0 means success. SCT: which list of result numbers it comes from.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Take care: run nvme reset /dev/nvme0 during heavy fio. Or run echo 1 > /sys/bus/pci/devices/<bdf>/remove (risky, test machine only: the SSD disappears until a rescan). Read dmesg backwards from the first 0x371 to the first timeout, CFS or AER message. In a capture tool recording, find the last good done note and what the SSD stopped doing.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Reported. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD is at fault if the cause is a missing done note (timeout) or CSTS.CFS=1. The computer's hardware is at fault if a PCIe error report (AER) or port lock-down (DPC) started it. A sudden wire loss counts too. The computer is at fault if a take-down or restart started by the driver had no SSD fault before it. · Test that confirms it: Kernel log.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book says result list 7h is for the maker's own results (Vendor Specific, NVME_SCT_VS in libnvme).

What goes wrong: The controller reports a result the maker defined (SCT 7). Lists 4–6 are reserved. Getting one of those is an SSD bug.

How you can tell: Linux prints "Unknown (sct 0x7 / sc 0x..)". It turns it into BLK_STS_IOERR, then -EIO. It is retried unless DNR is set. Status code: the result number in the done note. 0 means success. SCT: which list of result numbers it comes from.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Safe, by making result 0x7xx appear on purpose. Ask the maker for the result table. Save the maker's own data (telemetry) right after.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Reported. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD is at fault (the maker's firmware). It is expected when the computer sent a maker's own command type. · Test that confirms it: The maker's result table.

There the checker flags a done note whose result number is not 0 (nvme_status_nonzero).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book describes the error log (Error Information log). Identify Controller gives its number of entries (ELPE, Error Log Page Entries, counting from 0). The SMART log has a count of entries (num_err_log_entries).

What goes wrong: For commands that finish with an error, the controller writes a 64-byte entry. It also does so for some errors not tied to a command. The entry holds Error Count (unique, always going up), SQID, CID and Status Field. It also holds Parameter Error Location, LBA, NSID, maker info, Transport Type and command info. Newer versions add opcode, CSI and log page version (libnvme struct nvme_error_log_page).

How you can tell: Nothing is sent to the computer, unless an error warning is raised for an error not tied to a command. The SMART "Number of Error Information Log Entries" count goes up. The done note's "More" bit says an entry exists for that command.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Run nvme error-log /dev/nvme0 -e 64 right after the failure. Match SQID and CID to the done note, or to the nvme_complete_rq trace point. Use Parameter Error Location (byte in bits 7:0, bit in bits 10:8) to find the bad command field.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Reported. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The computer is at fault when Parameter Error Location points to a command byte. It is also at fault for results like Invalid Field or Invalid Opcode. The SSD is at fault when the result is a storage-chip or inside error (SCT 2h, internal error). The entry itself is reported by the SSD. · Test that confirms it: The error log (E03).

S-72 Health warning: spare blocks are running low (SMART critical warning bit 0) Partly seen in the packets SSD warnings and log pages

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 1540349: the SSD sends a warning (AEN): SMART/Health critical warning, bit 0.

Packet=1540349 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=1543 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000004:84820010 | Length=4 | DATA=16 B | Time Stamp=1801.914701681750s | Time Delta=54.880 ns | LCRC=0x363E83C8

Error family: P26, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. · Proof from outside the recording: The SSD's own logs and settings read with nvme-cli (E03). · Can the packets alone prove it? Partly. The packets show an odd order or timing. The proof needs evidence from outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book describes the SMART/Health log: Critical Warning, Available Spare, Available Spare Threshold and Percentage Used. Bit 0 of the warning setting (Asynchronous Event Configuration) switches on this warning.

What goes wrong: Available Spare (the percent of spare blocks left) fell below the Available Spare Threshold. Spare blocks are used when worn blocks are retired. When they run out, the drive usually becomes read-only (bit 3).

How you can tell: critical_warning bit 0 is set. nvme smart-log shows avail_spare < spare_thresh. Linux does not get a warning by default, because the SMART warning bits are not switched on. If they are on, the warning becomes a device event and nothing else. It looks like NVME_AEN=0x020201 (type 1, info 02h, LID 02h; an example of how it is written).

How to fix it and prove the fix: Safe in QEMU: switch on SMART warnings (FID 0Bh bit 0). Then use QMP qom-set /machine/peripheral/<nvme-id> smart_critical_warning 1. The function nvme_set_smart_warning() raises the warning only for newly set bits. Read nvme smart-log /dev/nvme0 at regular times (smartd or node exporter). Follow avail_spare together with percent_used and media_errors over time.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Reported. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD is the source (a reported condition: end of life or early block failure). The firmware reports wrongly if the fields disagree. · Test that confirms it: Compare SMART before and after (E03).

There the checker flags a done note for a command number that is unknown or already finished (nvme_cqe_unknown_or_completed_cid).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book describes the temperature limit setting (TMPTH, TMPSEL, THSEL). Identify gives the warning and critical temperatures (WCTEMP/CCTEMP). It also describes computer-controlled heat management (Host Controlled Thermal Management, FID 10h).

What goes wrong: A temperature sensor went above (or below) the limit set with the Temperature Threshold setting (FID 04h). Above WCTEMP or CCTEMP (in Identify Controller), the drive slows itself down. It also counts the Warning and Critical Composite Temperature Time.

How you can tell: critical_warning bit 1 is set. The SMART temperature (in Kelvin), warning_temp_time and critical_comp_time go up. The heat management step counters change. Linux shows the bit as hwmon temp1_alarm.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Run sensors or cat /sys/class/nvme/nvme0/hwmon*/temp1_alarm. Run nvme smart-log (temperature, warning_temp_time). Match slow-downs in response time with temperature.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Reported. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The computer's hardware is at fault when the temperature is high under normal load (airflow or heatsink). It is also the computer's side when a tool set the limit low (Set Features FID 04h on the wire). The SSD is at fault only if it reports a temperature it does not have. Compare with an outside sensor (E06/E09). · Test that confirms it: Compare SMART before and after (E03).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book describes SMART Critical Warning bit 2. The Endurance Group Information log (LID 09h) also has critical warnings.

What goes wrong: The controller decided its reliability has dropped. The cause is many storage-chip errors, or an inside error that lowers reliability.

How you can tell: critical_warning bit 2 is set. Usually media_errors is going up. The endurance group critical warning summary (byte 6) may also be set.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Run nvme smart-log and nvme endurance-log. Save the maker's own data (telemetry). Check the Persistent Event log for NVM Subsystem Hardware Error events (05h).

Does the SSD or computer report it? Reported. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD is at fault. Causes are the storage chips, or spare copies across chips used up (RAIN/parity). Others are memory error-fixing (DRAM ECC), or an inside controller fault. · Test that confirms it: Compare SMART before and after (E03).

There the checker flags a done note for a command number that is unknown or already finished (nvme_cqe_unknown_or_completed_cid).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book describes SMART Critical Warning bit 3.

What goes wrong: The drive has made all its storage chips read-only, to protect the data already there. This usually happens at end of life, or after a serious inside failure.

How you can tell: critical_warning bit 3 is set. Writes fail, and reads still work. Linux does not mark the drive read-only from this bit. Each write fails one by one, and file systems switch themselves to read-only.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Run nvme smart-log. Copy the data off at once, with tools that only read.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Reported. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD is at fault. Causes are spare blocks used up, firmware panic mode, or a power-loss protection failure on some makers' drives. · Test that confirms it: Compare SMART before and after (E03).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book describes SMART Critical Warning bit 4. It also describes the fast temporary write memory setting (Volatile Write Cache feature, FID 06h).

What goes wrong: The backup power (capacitors) that protects the fast temporary write memory has failed. So writes the SSD already confirmed may be lost when power fails.

How you can tell: critical_warning bit 4 is set. What the SSD does next depends on the maker. Some go read-only. Some switch to writing straight to the storage chips (write-through).

How to fix it and prove the fix: Run nvme smart-log. Do a power-fail test that checks the written data (fio verify after a power cut). This proves the loss of data the SSD had confirmed.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Reported. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD is at fault (the capacitors aged, or the power-loss protection self-test failed at power-on). · Test that confirms it: Compare SMART before and after (E03).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book describes SMART Critical Warning bit 5. It also describes the settings of the memory area that keeps data without power (PMR): PMRCAP, PMRCTL and PMRSTS.

What goes wrong: The lasting memory area (PMR) became read-only or not reliable.

How you can tell: critical_warning bit 5 is set. libnvme calls it NVME_SMART_CRIT_PMR_RO. It is not in Linux nvme.h. QEMU only accepts this bit when CAP.PMRS is set.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Run nvme smart-log. Run nvme show-regs -H and read PMRSTS.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Reported. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD is at fault (the memory behind the PMR, NVRAM, failed). · Test that confirms it: Compare SMART before and after (E03).

S-78 SSD warning: a doorbell number or doorbell value was bad (AEN Error 00h, 01h) Seen in the packets Result number in the done note

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 1054087: a bad doorbell value for command list 1 (SQ1).
