Packet 1054090: the warning's done note (AEN CQE) on the admin done list. It finishes the waiting "tell me about events" command (AER). Its Dword 0 is 0x00010100.

Packet=1054090 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=3091 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000004:82E40170 | Length=4 | DATA=16 B | Time Stamp=0560.846497346250s | Time Delta=54.880 ns | LCRC=0xF30E703E

Error families: P01, P14 and P26, three of the 27 ways an error shows on the wire. · Can the packets alone prove it? Only if the table file keeps the bytes. The result sits inside the DATA column as bytes. One version of the file keeps them (hex version). There the checker flags a done note for a command number that is unknown or already finished (nvme_cqe_unknown_or_completed_cid).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book describes the doorbells: the command list tail (SQyTDBL) and the done list head (CQyHDBL). Their spacing comes from CAP.DSTRD. It also describes the error warnings (Asynchronous Event Information, Error Status).

What goes wrong: The computer wrote a doorbell for a list that does not exist (00h). Or it wrote a bad value (01h). For example, a tail number equal to or larger than the list size. Or a done list head that moves past done notes not yet written.

How you can tell: An Error-type warning (AEN). The error log has an entry. The controller may ignore the write. The list can stall, and the computer then sees read and write timeouts. Status code: the result number in the done note. 0 means success. SCT: which list of result numbers it comes from.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Risky, test machine only: use a driver that runs as a normal program. It writes a tail value equal to the list size. Or, in QEMU, write to a doorbell that is not set up, through /sys/bus/pci/devices/<bdf>/resource0. Take care: only with the kernel driver unhooked. In the capture tool, filter on write packets (MWr) to BAR0+1000h and up. Work out the list number: qid = (offset−1000h)/(4<<DSTRD)/2. Even or odd says command list or done list. Compare the value with the list size from the Create command.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Reported. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The computer is at fault when a bad doorbell is on the wire. Causes are wrong doorbell sums in the driver, wrong DSTRD, or wrong use of shadow doorbells. The SSD is at fault when the warning has no bad doorbell behind it. · Test that confirms it: Decode the doorbell.

S-79 SSD warning: self-check failed, inside error, or new firmware failed to load (02h to 05h) Partly seen in the packets Result number in the done note

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 1057554: the warning's done note (AEN CQE) on the admin done list. It finishes the waiting "tell me about events" command (AER). Its Dword 0 is 0x00010300.

Packet=1057554 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=69 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000004:82F000C0 | Length=4 | DATA=16 B | Time Stamp=0560.937335830500s | Time Delta=54.880 ns | LCRC=0x338E873C

Error families: P01 and P26, two of the 27 ways an error shows on the wire. · Proof from outside the recording: The Linux kernel log (E01). The SSD's own logs and settings read with nvme-cli (E03). · Can the packets alone prove it? Partly. The packets show an odd order or timing. The proof needs evidence from outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book describes the error warnings (Asynchronous Event Information, Error Status; NVME_AER_ERROR_* in libnvme).

What goes wrong: 02h: a self-check failed (for example the power-on self-test). 03h: an inside error that stays, so the controller needs a restart (or is broken). 04h: an inside error the controller recovered from. 05h: the firmware file could not be loaded when started. The drive went back to another firmware file.

How you can tell: In Linux, 03h shows the dmesg line "resetting controller due to persistent internal error". A full controller restart follows. Reads and writes in progress finish with 0x371 and are retried. The other kinds only make a device event (uevent). For 05h, firmware_rev after the restart is not the version you committed. Status code: the result number in the done note. 0 means success. SCT: which list of result numbers it comes from.

How to fix it and prove the fix: A normal computer cannot cause it. Only the maker's fault commands can. Run nvme error-log. Run nvme persistent-event-log (NVM Subsystem Hardware Error and Firmware Commit events). Run nvme fw-log. Save nvme telemetry-log right after, before a restart clears the short-lived state.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Reported. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD is at fault (a firmware assert, a failed inside memory test, or a damaged firmware slot). The computer is at fault only if a bad action of its own comes just before it. Examples are error type S-78 in the error list, or a bad firmware commit. · Test that confirms it: The SSD's logs.

S-80 SSD notice: a storage area was added, removed or changed (Namespace Attribute Changed) Seen in the packets Result number in the done note

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 1060865: the warning's done note (AEN CQE) on the admin done list. It finishes the waiting "tell me about events" command (AER). Its Dword 0 is 0x00040002.

Packet=1060865 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=1236 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000004:82F000E0 | Length=4 | DATA=16 B | Time Stamp=0560.937770115250s | Time Delta=54.880 ns | LCRC=0x48AB4680

Error families: P01 and P26, two of the 27 ways an error shows on the wire. · Can the packets alone prove it? Only if the table file keeps the bytes. The result sits inside the DATA column as bytes. One version of the file keeps them (hex version). There the checker flags a done note for a command number that is unknown or already finished (nvme_cqe_unknown_or_completed_cid).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book describes notice 00h. It describes the Changed Namespace List log. That log holds up to 1024 storage area numbers. FFFFFFFFh in the first entry means "more than 1024 changed". OAES bit 8 says the SSD supports this notice.

What goes wrong: A storage area was attached, detached, resized, formatted, or changed in a way Identify shows. This was done by this computer, another computer, or the SSD itself.

How you can tell: Linux checks the storage areas again. Drives appear, disappear or change size. dmesg shows size-change messages. If the names changed, it shows "identifiers changed for nsid N" and the storage area is removed. Status code: the result number in the done note. 0 means success. SCT: which list of result numbers it comes from.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Take care: run nvme detach-ns / attach-ns on a test storage area (QEMU nvme-subsys). Watch the device events (udev). Compare nvme list before and after. Check the nvme_async_event trace point.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Reported. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The computer is the cause when its own storage area command comes just before. The Persistent Event log may show another controller number. Then another computer or port, or the management channel (NVMe-MI), is the cause. The SSD is at fault when nothing explains the change, or the notice was switched off. · Test that confirms it: The list of storage areas.

S-81 SSD notice: new firmware is starting, so the SSD pauses (Firmware Activation Starting, CSTS.PP) Seen in the packets Result number in the done note

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 1062762: the warning's done note (AEN CQE) on the admin done list. It finishes the waiting "tell me about events" command (AER). Its Dword 0 is 0x00030102.

Packet=1062762 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=1992 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000004:82F00110 | Length=4 | DATA=16 B | Time Stamp=0560.938063131250s | Time Delta=54.880 ns | LCRC=0x412B92D5

Error families: P01 and P26, two of the 27 ways an error shows on the wire. · Can the packets alone prove it? Only if the table file keeps the bytes. The result sits inside the DATA column as bytes. One version of the file keeps them (hex version). There the checker flags a done note for a command number that is unknown or already finished (nvme_cqe_unknown_or_completed_cid).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book describes notice 01h, the "paused" flag (CSTS.PP) and the longest switch time (MTFA in Identify). OAES bit 9 says the SSD supports this notice.

What goes wrong: The controller starts new firmware without a restart (Firmware Commit CA=3). It sets CSTS.PP (Processing Paused) and stops working on commands until the switch is done.

How you can tell: In Linux, the controller state goes to RESETTING, to block recovery actions. The read and write lists are stopped. Linux checks CSTS.PP every 100 ms until it clears, or until MTFA×100 ms (or admin_timeout if MTFA=0). If time runs out: "Fw activation timeout, reset controller". After that, it reads the firmware slot log to update firmware_rev. Status code: the result number in the done note. 0 means success. SCT: which list of result numbers it comes from.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Take care: run nvme fw-download and nvme fw-commit -a 3 with a file the maker approved, during a fio run. Measure the pause in reads and writes. Check dmesg and the fio response-time log during the update. Measure the gap in the PEX recording.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Reported. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD is at fault when PP lasts longer than MTFA (or never clears). The computer is at fault when it does not stop reads and writes, or restarts too early. · Test that confirms it: Measure the pause.

S-82 SSD notice: the SSD saved its own inside snapshot for the maker (Telemetry Log Changed) Partly seen in the packets Result number in the done note

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 1064075: the warning's done note (AEN CQE) on the admin done list. It finishes the waiting "tell me about events" command (AER). Its Dword 0 is 0x00080202.

Packet=1064075 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=2560 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000004:82F00130 | Length=4 | DATA=16 B | Time Stamp=0562.138404251620s | Time Delta=54.870 ns | LCRC=0x7B8CE365

Error families: P01 and P26, two of the 27 ways an error shows on the wire. · Proof from outside the recording: The Linux kernel log (E01). The SSD's own logs and settings read with nvme-cli (E03). · Can the packets alone prove it? Only if the table file keeps the bytes. The result sits inside the DATA column as bytes. One version of the file keeps them (hex version). There the checker flags a done note for a command number that is unknown or already finished (nvme_cqe_unknown_or_completed_cid).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book describes two maker-data logs. One is what the computer asks for (Telemetry Host-Initiated, 07h). The other is made by the SSD itself (Controller-Initiated, 08h). They have data areas 1–3 (4 with the extended form) and a reason number.

What goes wrong: The controller saved a snapshot of its inside state (Controller-Initiated Telemetry). Usually it hit an inside error worth looking into. The header byte ctrlavail = 1, and ctrldgn (the generation number) goes up (libnvme struct nvme_telemetry_log).

How you can tell: Linux logs dev_warn(ctrl->device, "async event result %08x\n", result). This is the default case of nvme_handle_aen_notice(). This is often the only sign of an inside firmware problem. Status code: the result number in the done note. 0 means success. SCT: which list of result numbers it comes from.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Only the computer-asked kind can be made: Get Log Page LID 07h with LSP Create (NVME_LOG_TELEM_HOST_LSP_CREATE in libnvme). This is safe. Save it for the maker: nvme telemetry-log /dev/nvme0 --output-file=tele.bin. (Check your nvme-cli version for the option that reads the SSD-made kind.) Compare ctrldgn over time.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Reported. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD is the source (a firmware assert it recovered from inside, or the maker's own trigger). The recording cannot say which. · Test that confirms it: Save the maker's data (telemetry).

Packet=1064913 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=2877 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000004:82F00150 | Length=4 | DATA=16 B | Time Stamp=0562.138772239370s | Time Delta=54.870 ns | LCRC=0xFE68E6A2

Error families: P01 and P26, two of the 27 ways an error shows on the wire. · Can the packets alone prove it? Only if the table file keeps the bytes. The result sits inside the DATA column as bytes. One version of the file keeps them (hex version). There the checker flags a done note for a command number that is unknown or already finished (nvme_cqe_unknown_or_completed_cid).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book describes notice 03h and the path state log (ANA log). It also describes OAES bit 11 and the change time (ANATT).

What goes wrong: The path state (ANA state) of one or more path groups changed on this controller.

How you can tell: In Linux with multipath (CONFIG_NVME_MULTIPATH), ana_work reads the ANA log again and updates ana_state for each path. The path choice rule picks paths again. Status code: the result number in the done note. 0 means success. SCT: which list of result numbers it comes from.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Safe: change the ANA state with nvmet configfs. Run nvme ana-log. Read /sys/block/nvme*c*n*/ana_state. See the made-up example recording in the error list, chapter II.4.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Reported. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD or array is the source (switch-over, switch-back, or a lost path). Maintenance asked for by the computer makes it expected. · Test that confirms it: The ANA log.

S-84 SSD notices that Linux does not act on (04h, 05h, 06h, F0h) Seen in the packets Result number in the done note

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 1066629: the warning's done note (AEN CQE) on the admin done list. It finishes the waiting "tell me about events" command (AER). Its Dword 0 is 0x000B0402.

Packet=1066629 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=3555 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000004:82F00170 | Length=4 | DATA=16 B | Time Stamp=0562.326164102750s | Time Delta=54.880 ns | LCRC=0x4AA265DA

Error families: P01 and P26, two of the 27 ways an error shows on the wire. · Can the packets alone prove it? Only if the table file keeps the bytes. The result sits inside the DATA column as bytes. One version of the file keeps them (hex version). There the checker flags a done note for a command number that is unknown or already finished (nvme_cqe_unknown_or_completed_cid).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book lists notice values (NVME_AER_NOTICE_* in libnvme). It describes the LBA Status Information log, the Predictable Latency Event Aggregate log, and the Endurance Group Event Aggregate log.

What goes wrong: 04h: a "predictable response time" event for one NVM set (the promised time window was broken). 05h: the controller found blocks that cannot be read, or may soon not be (LBA Status Information log, LID 0Eh). This is an early storage-chip warning. 06h: an endurance group crossed a limit. F0h: the network discovery log changed.

How you can tell: For 04h–06h, Linux logs the warning "async event result %08x". For F0h, it sends a device event for nvme-cli's auto-connect rules. Linux does not switch on 04h–06h in FID 0Bh. So they come only if the controller has them on by default, or a user program switches them on. Status code: the result number in the done note. 0 means success. SCT: which list of result numbers it comes from.

How to fix it and prove the fix: This depends on the maker. The computer cannot cause it on most drives. Run nvme get-log -i 0x0e for block status, then write again or move the listed blocks. Run nvme get-log -i 0x0b (Predictable Latency summary).

Does the SSD or computer report it? Reported. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD is the source. Causes are a background check of the storage chips, or an endurance limit. Another is clean-up work (GC) breaking the promised time window. · Test that confirms it: The block status (LBA status).

S-85 SSD notices about claims and secure erase (Reservation Log 00h, Sanitize Completed 01h and 02h) Seen in the packets Result number in the done note

Error families: P01 and P26, two of the 27 ways an error shows on the wire. · Can the packets alone prove it? Only if the table file keeps the bytes. The result sits inside the DATA column as bytes. One version of the file keeps them (hex version). There the checker flags a done note for a command number that is unknown or already finished (nvme_cqe_unknown_or_completed_cid).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book lists these notices (NVME_AER_CSS_NVM_* in libnvme). It describes the Reservation Notification log (80h) and the Sanitize Status log (81h).

What goes wrong: 00h: a claim notice is waiting (a registration was preempted, or a claim was released or preempted). 01h: a sanitize finished. 02h: a sanitize finished, but the storage was freed in a way the computer did not ask for. For example, "No-Deallocate After Sanitize" could not be followed. (Check the exact meaning in the rule book.)

How you can tell: In Linux this only makes a device event, NVME_AEN=.... Status code: the result number in the done note. 0 means success. SCT: which list of result numbers it comes from.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Take care: preempt a claim from a second controller. Destroys data: sanitize a spare drive. Run nvme get-log -i 0x80 and nvme sanitize-log.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Reported. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: For 00h and 01h, this computer or another computer is the cause (it started a claim action or a sanitize). For 02h, the SSD is at fault when "do not free" was asked for. · Test that confirms it: The logs.

S-86 The SSD's lasting event history shows a failure (Persistent Event log, LID 0Dh) Partly seen in the packets SSD warnings and log pages

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 1554510: the computer reads the Persistent Event log (log page LID 0x0D).

Packet=1554510 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=2945 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000004:848200B0 | Length=4 | DATA=16 B | Time Stamp=1801.916853170000s | Time Delta=34.880 ns | LCRC=0x28099F97

Error family: P26, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. · Proof from outside the recording: The SSD's own logs and settings read with nvme-cli (E03). · Can the packets alone prove it? Partly. The packets show an odd order or timing. The proof needs evidence from outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book describes the Persistent Event log. Its LSP actions are: read, set up a reading context, and release it. Identify gives the log size (PELS).

What goes wrong: The controller keeps a history with times that lasts across power off and on. Its event kinds are SMART/Health snapshot (01h), Firmware Commit (02h), Timestamp Change (03h) and Power-on or Reset (04h). More are NVM Subsystem Hardware Error (05h), Change Namespace (06h) and Format Start/Completion (07h/08h). More are Sanitize Start/Completion (09h/0Ah), Set Feature (0Bh) and Telemetry Log Create (0Ch). More are Thermal Excursion (0Dh), Sanitize Media Verification (0Eh), maker's own (DEh) and TCG (DFh) (NVME_PEL_* in libnvme).

How you can tell: Nothing is sent to the computer. You must read it. The header has the total events (TNEV), log length (TLL), time, power-on hours, power cycle count, and reporting context (RCI).

How to fix it and prove the fix: Safe: run nvme reset /dev/nvme0, then read the log and find the new Power-on or Reset event. Run nvme persistent-event-log /dev/nvme0 (set up the context, read, release; see nvme-cli help for the action option). Match the times with the computer's logs. Set the Timestamp setting (FID 0Eh) so the drive's clock matches.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Reported. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD is at fault for an NVM Subsystem Hardware Error, or an inside restart reason. The computer or its hardware is the cause when the event matches a computer restart or a power event. Another controller's action counts too. · Test that confirms it: The Persistent Event log (E03).

S-87 The maker-data logs that hold failure evidence for the SSD maker (Telemetry, LID 07h, 08h) Partly seen in the packets SSD warnings and log pages

Packet 1558720: the computer reads the SSD-made maker-data log (log page LID 0x08).

Packet=1558720 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=382 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000004:848200C0 | Length=4 | DATA=16 B | Time Stamp=1801.917157316250s | Time Delta=62.880 ns | LCRC=0x92D7A57C

Error family: P26, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. · Proof from outside the recording: The SSD's own logs and settings read with nvme-cli (E03). · Can the packets alone prove it? Partly. The packets show an odd order or timing. The proof needs evidence from outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book describes the maker-data logs (telemetry logs). An LPA bit says they are supported. The Identify transfer limit (MDTS) splits the reading into pieces.

What goes wrong: Computer-asked: the computer asks the controller to save its inside state now (LSP Create). SSD-made: the controller saved its state by itself (see error type S-82 in the error list).

How you can tell: The header fields are lpi, IEEE OUI, and the last block of data areas 1–4 (dalb1–dalb4). Then come ctrlavail, ctrldgn, and the reason number (128 bytes).

How to fix it and prove the fix: Safe: save a computer-asked snapshot with nvme-cli. Run nvme telemetry-log /dev/nvme0 --output-file=t.bin. Send it to the maker together with the recording and the time of failure.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Reported. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD (the controller's inside state). The rows only show that the evidence was saved, and whether it is complete. · Test that confirms it: Save the maker's data (safe).

S-88 The SSD's self-test log shows a failed result (Device Self-test log, LID 06h) Partly seen in the packets Result of long setup commands

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 1526885: the last admin done note, or the log read, of the long job.

Packet=1526885 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=183 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000004:84820110 | Length=4 | DATA=16 B | Time Stamp=1403.911283828250s | Time Delta=34.880 ns | LCRC=0x847197FA

Error families: P25 and P26, two of the 27 ways an error shows on the wire. · Proof from outside the recording: The SSD's own logs and settings read with nvme-cli (E03). · Can the packets alone prove it? Partly. The packets show an odd order or timing. The proof needs evidence from outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book describes the self-test command and its log. EDSTT is the long test time. DSTO says one test runs at a time, per subsystem or per controller.

What goes wrong: A short or long self-test finished with a failure. The result codes are in the low 4 bits of DSTS (NVME_ST_RESULT_* in libnvme). 0: no error. 1: stopped by a self-test command. 2: stopped by a controller restart. 3: stopped because a storage area was removed. 4: stopped by Format NVM. 5: fatal or unknown test error. 6: finished with a failed part (part unknown). 7: finished with failed parts, the first failing part in SEG. 8: stopped for an unknown reason. 9: stopped by a sanitize. F: entry not used.

How you can tell: Each entry has the fields dsts (result and test code) and seg. Next is vdi (which of NSID, FLBA, SCT and SC are valid). Then come poh, nsid, flba (the failing block), sct and sc.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Safe: start a long test and stop it (-s 0xf), which gives result 1. Run a test, then restart, which gives result 2. Run nvme device-self-test /dev/nvme0 -s 2. Wait EDSTT minutes. Run nvme self-test-log /dev/nvme0. Read the FLBA it reports with nvme read.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Reported. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD is at fault for results 5 to 7. The computer is the cause for 1, 2, 3, 4 and 9 when the stopping command or restart is seen. It is unknown for 8. · Test that confirms it: The self-test log (E03).

Packet 1528227: the last admin done note, or the log read, of the long job.

Packet=1528227 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=811 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000004:84820160 | Length=4 | DATA=16 B | Time Stamp=1411.911690704250s | Time Delta=32.880 ns | LCRC=0x1121F2F6

Error families: P25 and P26, two of the 27 ways an error shows on the wire. · Proof from outside the recording: The SSD's own logs and settings read with nvme-cli (E03). · Can the packets alone prove it? Partly. The packets show an odd order or timing. The proof needs evidence from outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book describes the Sanitize command and its status log. The log fields are sprog, sstat, scdw10, eto, etbe, etce, etond, etbend, etcend, etpvds and ssi.

What goes wrong: SSTAT bits 2:0 have these meanings (NVME_SANITIZE_SSTAT_STATUS_* in libnvme). 0 never sanitized, 1 finished well, 2 in progress, 3 finished with failure. 4 finished well with No-Deallocate (ND). Bits 7:3 give the overwrite passes done. Bit 8 is Global Data Erased. Bit 9 says the storage check was cancelled. SPROG is progress ×65536.

How you can tell: When SSTAT=3, commands fail with Sanitize Failed (0x1C, error type S-18 in the error list) until recovery.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Destroys data, risky, test machine only: sanitize a drive you can lose, and cut power halfway. Read the log after power comes back. Run nvme sanitize-log /dev/nvme0. After "success", read random blocks. Check they hold the expected pattern: zeros, the overwrite pattern, or freed data as DLFEAT says. A sanitize can report success without erasing everything. Only reading back proves it.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Reported. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The computer's hardware is at fault when a power cut (a wire loss nobody started) falls inside the sanitize time. The SSD is at fault when SSTAT failed with steady power (a chip failed during block erase). It is also at fault when read-back shows data after a "success". · Test that confirms it: The sanitize log (E03).

S-90 The SSD says it has failed and stopped working (Controller Fatal Status, CSTS.CFS = 1) Partly seen in the packets SSD main settings and status

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 438756: the SSD's status setting reads CSTS = 0x3. That means "ready" (RDY=1) and "failed" (CFS=1, Controller Fatal Status).

Packet=438756 | Link Dir=Downstream | TLP Type=MRd(32) | PSN=962 | Tag=30 | RequesterID=000:00:0 | Address=FCE0001C | Length=1 | Time Stamp=0196.117125853500s | Time Delta=130.620 ns | LCRC=0x0DC59862

Error family: P13, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. · Proof from outside the recording: The Linux kernel log (E01). The SSD's own logs and settings read with nvme-cli (E03). Tracing the computer's own read and write path (E05). · Can the packets alone prove it? Partly. The packets show an odd order or timing. The proof needs evidence from outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book describes the fatal-error flag (CSTS.CFS, bit 1) and the controller restart (CC.EN). It also gives the ready time limit (CAP.TO).

What goes wrong: The controller hit a fatal error that it cannot report in a done note. It stopped working. Only a controller restart (CC.EN 1→0→1) or a deeper restart brings it back.

How you can tell: Linux does not check CSTS at regular times. It finds CFS when a command runs out of time. nvme_timeout() reads CSTS, and nvme_should_reset() says yes for CFS. Then nvme_warn_reset() prints "controller is down; will reset: CSTS=0x%x, PCI_STATUS=0x%hx". If CSTS reads all ones, it adds "Does your device have a faulty power saving mode enabled?". It also suggests nvme_core.default_ps_max_latency_us=0 pcie_aspm=off pcie_port_pm=off. All commands in progress are cancelled (0x371) and retried after the restart.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Look for the dmesg line above (CSTS value: 0x3 = RDY|CFS). The PEX recording shows exactly when the stall started. Afterwards read nvme error-log, persistent-event-log and the maker's data (telemetry). Check the state changes in /sys/class/nvme/nvme0/state.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Reported. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: By default the SSD is at fault (the controller said it has failed). It is the computer's fault when the CC write that switched it on had bad fields compared with CAP. It is also the computer's fault when the admin list addresses (ASQ/ACQ) did not start at a page edge. Flag the computer's power policy when a power-saving command comes less than 1 s before the stall. That is an APST or Power Management Set Features command, or an ASPM L1 entry (error list, section XII.8). · Test that confirms it: Kernel log.

S-91 A whole-SSD restart happened (NVM Subsystem Reset Occurred, CSTS.NSSRO = 1) Partly seen in the packets SSD main settings and status

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 440069: at start-up the "subsystem restart happened" flag is set (CSTS.NSSRO=1). A whole-SSD restart (NVM Subsystem Reset) took place.

Packet=440069 | Link Dir=Downstream | TLP Type=MRd(32) | PSN=1328 | Tag=8 | RequesterID=000:00:0 | Address=FCE0001C | Length=1 | Time Stamp=0196.131900891500s | Time Delta=130.620 ns | LCRC=0x5A4ADE8A

Error family: P13, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. · Proof from outside the recording: The Linux kernel log (E01). The SSD's own logs and settings read with nvme-cli (E03). Tracing the computer's own read and write path (E05). · Can the packets alone prove it? Partly. The packets show an odd order or timing. The proof needs evidence from outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book describes the "supports it" bit (CAP.NSSRS) and the whole-SSD restart setting (NSSR, 20h). It also describes the "it happened" flag (CSTS.NSSRO, write 1 to clear).

What goes wrong: A whole-SSD restart happened. The computer started it through NSSR, or the SSD did it by itself. All controllers in the SSD were restarted. That may include other ports or other computers.

How you can tell: In Linux, when dev->subsystem is set, NSSRO counts as a reason to restart in nvme_should_reset(). The code says "loss of adapter communication, possibly by a NVMe Subsystem reset". The driver clears NSSRO during the restart.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Take care: run nvme subsystem-reset /dev/nvme0 on a drive with CAP.NSSRS=1. The wire drops. Some computers report it as a "surprise down" error. Check the dmesg restart messages on both computers. Check the Persistent Event log for a Power-on or Reset event.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Reported. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The computer is at fault if its NSSR write shows on this wire before the wire loss. That is an MWr to BAR0+0x20 with value 0x4E564D65. Otherwise the SSD or the other computer or port is the cause (this needs E03/E08). The setting itself is only for information. The defect is any NSSR that nobody expected. · Test that confirms it: Check the setting and the log.

S-92 The firmware slot log shows new firmware still waiting, or the old one back Partly seen in the packets Result of long setup commands

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 1528680: the last admin done note, or the log read, of the long job.

Packet=1528680 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=984 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000004:848201A0 | Length=4 | DATA=16 B | Time Stamp=1411.911841797120s | Time Delta=41.870 ns | LCRC=0xBEDB765A

Error families: P25 and P26, two of the 27 ways an error shows on the wire. · Proof from outside the recording: The SSD's own logs and settings read with nvme-cli (E03). · Can the packets alone prove it? Partly. The packets show an odd order or timing. The proof needs evidence from outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book describes the firmware slot log (Firmware Slot Information log: AFI, FRS1–FRS7). It describes the Firmware Commit actions (CA) and the firmware version in Identify (FR).

What goes wrong: After a commit, the running firmware may not be what you expect. The switch may wait until the next restart (AFI bits 6:4 ≠ bits 2:0). The file may be refused at start-up, so the old slot is used (Firmware Image Load Error warning). Or a commit that worked is reported with a "requires reset" result (error type S-40 in the error list).

How you can tell: Linux logs "Firmware is activated after next Controller Level Reset" (nvme_get_fw_slot_info()). The file /sys/class/nvme/nvme0/firmware_rev keeps the old version until a restart.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Take care: commit with CA=2 (start at next restart). Read the slot log before and after nvme reset. Run nvme fw-log /dev/nvme0 and nvme id-ctrl | grep '^fr ' after every update and after the restart. Check the Persistent Event log for Firmware Commit events (02h) with the old and new version.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Reported. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The computer's software (a tool for many machines) is at fault when it ignores the "requires reset" result. Then no restart follows. The SSD is at fault when the restart happened and the file went back (Firmware Image Load Error). It is also at fault when FR changes without a commit. · Test that confirms it: The firmware slot and version (E03).

S-93 SMART health counts keep rising with no critical warning Not seen in the packets Wrong data inside the packets

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 1403484: the write of the test pattern finishes.

Packet=1403484 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=4032 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000004:84150050 | Length=4 | DATA=16 B | Time Stamp=1341.136879658620s | Time Delta=29.870 ns | LCRC=0x8D1BADCE

Packet 1403534: the read that checks it finishes with success.

Packet=1403534 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=4047 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000004:841400E0 | Length=4 | DATA=16 B | Time Stamp=1342.137036605120s | Time Delta=37.870 ns | LCRC=0x3145DDB3

Error families: P23 and P26, two of the 27 ways an error shows on the wire. · Proof from outside the recording: The SSD's own logs and settings read with nvme-cli (E03). · Can the packets alone prove it? No. It cannot be seen on this wire. The packets shown only set the scene. The proof is outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book describes the SMART/Health log counts (128-bit fields; struct nvme_smart_log in Linux).

What goes wrong: The drive still says "healthy" (critical_warning = 0), but the counts show trouble. The count media_errors is for data errors that could not be fixed. The count num_err_log_entries is for error log entries over the drive's life. The count unsafe_shutdowns is for power losses without a shutdown request. Then data in the fast temporary memory may be gone. The count percent_used is a wear guess and may go above 100. There are also warning and critical temperature times.

How you can tell: Nothing is sent to the computer. These counts never raise a warning on their own.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Take care: cut the power of a test machine hard. Check that unsafe_shutdowns goes up by exactly one. A clean power-off must not raise it. Save nvme smart-log -o json daily and alert on changes. After a clean restart, unsafe_shutdowns must not change. If it does, the shutdown path is broken. Check that CC.SHN was written. A PEX recording of the shutdown shows this.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Not reported. It still works, but worse than it should. No error shows anywhere (degraded). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD is at fault if media_errors, percent_used or the temperature times rise. The computer or its hardware is at fault if unsafe_shutdowns rises with no CC.SHN write before power-off. The checker's copy of the settings (register_shadow) shows this. The SSD is at fault if the shutdown request (CC.SHN) and its "complete" status (CSTS.SHST) were recorded. The count still goes up. · Test that confirms it: Daily SMART trend.

Chapter T: timeouts and time limits (51 entries)

Why this part is here: these 51 entries are errors where a time limit ran out.

T-01 A command is sent but never finished (command never completed) Partly seen in the packets Command never finishes (timing)

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 1097680: the SSD fetched one command (SQE) from the computer's command list.

Packet=1097680 | Link Dir=Downstream | TLP Type=CplD | PSN=3212 | Tag=193 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | CompleterID=000:02:4 | Cpl Status=SC | Length=16 | Byte Cnt=64 | DATA=64 B | Time Stamp=0562.529101199370s | Time Delta=147.750 ns | LCRC=0xAB7B1C3D

Packet 1104971: the SSD fetched a 'stop that command' request (Abort), but never finished it.

Packet=1104971 | Link Dir=Downstream | TLP Type=CplD | PSN=251 | Tag=235 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | CompleterID=000:02:4 | Cpl Status=SC | Length=16 | Byte Cnt=64 | DATA=64 B | Time Stamp=0592.529150903370s | Time Delta=156.750 ns | LCRC=0x6D79B6EF

Error family: P02, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. Also E01, E03 and E05 (kinds of evidence from outside the recording). · Can the packets alone prove it? Partly. The timing and order of the packets show its shape. Proof needs evidence from outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book says every command the computer sends must get a done note (CQE). The only exceptions are when the SSD is restarted or the command list is deleted. The rule book sets no time limit for one command. Time limits are chosen by the computer's own software.

What goes wrong: The computer writes one command (SQE) into its command list. Then it writes the doorbell (a number that tells the SSD new commands are waiting). The SSD may fetch the command, or may not. Either way, it never writes a done note (CQE). So there is no result number (status code), because there is no done note.

How you can tell: Nothing shows until the computer's timer runs out. Linux v7.2 prints nvme nvme0: I/O tag 17 (0011) opcode 0x2 (Read) QID 3 timeout, aborting req_op:READ(0) size:4096. This comes after 30 s (the Linux computer's setting). If the stop request (Abort) also fails, Linux prints ... timeout, reset controller.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Make the error happen on purpose with the Linux NVMe fault-injection tool (drivers/nvme/host/fault_inject.c, CONFIG_FAULT_INJECTION_DEBUG_FS). Or use a QEMU NVMe model (a software copy of an SSD) changed to add a delay. On real hardware, use the SSD maker's 'hang command' test hook. Lower /sys/class/nvme/nvme0/io_timeout (in ms, a Linux computer setting). This makes the steps after a timeout (the timeout ladder) happen faster. Safe on a spare test drive. The Linux kernel log (dmesg) timeout lines show four numbers. They are the request number (tag), the command number (CID), the command type (opcode) and the command list number (QID). Compare them with a recording from the capture tool. Did the SSD fetch the command (a read request, MRd, from the SSD to the command list address)? Did the SSD write a done note (a write packet, MWr, to the done list address)? Did the SSD send the 'work is done' signal (an MSI-X write packet)? The first missing packet shows where the fault is. The SSD's error log (nvme error-log) may have an entry for that command number. This happens if the program inside the SSD (firmware) noticed.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Only by a timer. Nothing records an error. The only sign is a time limit running out. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD is at fault if the command fetch (an MRd read request) or the done-note write (MWr) is missing. The computer is at fault in this case. The done note and the 'work is done' signal (MSI-X write) are there. But no done-list doorbell from the computer follows. And dmesg says 'completion polled' (error family P16, error type D-30 in the error list). The computer's hardware is at fault if the MSI-X write goes to the set address, but /proc/interrupts stays flat (E05). The computer is also at fault if it never wrote the command-list doorbell. · Test that confirms it: the series of timeout lines in the Linux kernel log (dmesg timeout ladder).

T-02 The SSD is not ready in its promised time (CSTS.RDY, CAP.TO) Seen in the packets SSD main settings

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 442037: the computer switches the SSD on (CC.EN=1). Then it reads the SSD's 'ready' flag (CSTS.RDY) about every 100 ms. The flag stays 0 (not ready).

Packet=442037 | Link Dir=Downstream | TLP Type=MRd(32) | PSN=2035 | Tag=17 | RequesterID=000:00:0 | Address=FCE00000 | Length=2 | Time Stamp=0196.143121097870s | Time Delta=169.630 ns | LCRC=0x125CF18C

Packet 442476: the computer gives up and switches the SSD off again (CC.EN=0).

Packet=442476 | Link Dir=Downstream | TLP Type=MWr(32) | PSN=2143 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=000:00:0 | Address=FCE00014 | Length=1 | DATA=4 B | Time Stamp=0196.320082827870s | Time Delta=101.000 ns | LCRC=0x48A93060

Error family: P13, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. A check on the order and timing of packets finds it. Examples: a missing answer, a long gap, packets out of order.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book has a setting called CAP.TO (bits 31:24). It is the SSD's own promise of the longest time the computer should wait. It covers the wait for the 'ready' flag (CSTS.RDY) to change after the 'switch on' setting (CC.EN) changes. It counts in steps of 500 ms. The largest value is 0xFF, which is 127.5 s.

What goes wrong: The computer switches the SSD on (CC.EN goes from 0 to 1). Then it keeps reading the 'ready' flag (CSTS.RDY). The SSD stays 'not ready' for longer than the longest wait it promised in CAP.TO.

How you can tell: There is no result number at all. Only the computer's timer notices. Linux v7.2 prints Device not ready; aborting initialisation, CSTS=0x0. The start-up or restart then fails with -ENODEV. If the 'ready' flag reads as 0xffffffff, the waiting loop stops at once with -ENODEV. This means the SSD is gone from the wire.

How to fix it and prove the fix: In QEMU (a software copy of an SSD), CAP.TO is 0Fh (7.5 s) in hw/nvme/ctrl.c. Change the model so it sets the 'ready' flag later than that. On real hardware, cut the power suddenly during heavy writing. Take care: the data on that drive may be lost. Then time the next start-up against CAP.TO. Measure the gap with dmesg -T times: when the driver starts, and when it fails. With the capture tool, find the write packet (MWr) to the 'switch on' setting (CC, offset 14h). Find the last read (MRd) of the status setting (CSTS, offset 1Ch). Compare the gap with CAP.TO×500 ms. Read CAP with nvme show-regs /dev/nvme0 (it only reads). Then decode bits 31:24.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Only by a timer. Nothing records an error. The only sign is a time limit running out. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD is at fault when the 'ready' flag stays 0 past CAP.TO. The CC settings must be valid and the wire working (L0). The computer's hardware is at fault when the wire was not steady as the waiting started. The wire was still doing its start-up steps after the reset signal (PERST#). The computer's software is at fault when it stopped waiting before CAP.TO. · Test that confirms it: the Linux kernel log.

T-03 Two ready-time promises disagree, or storage is not ready in time (CRTO) Partly seen in the packets SSD main settings

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 444676: the computer switches the SSD on (CC.EN=1). Then it reads the 'ready' flag (CSTS.RDY) about every 100 ms. The flag stays 0.

Packet=444676 | Link Dir=Downstream | TLP Type=MRd(32) | PSN=2923 | Tag=1 | RequesterID=000:00:0 | Address=FCE00000 | Length=2 | Time Stamp=0196.830675195370s | Time Delta=146.630 ns | LCRC=0x7511329A

Packet 444715: the computer gives up and switches the SSD off again (CC.EN=0).

Packet=444715 | Link Dir=Downstream | TLP Type=MWr(32) | PSN=2935 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=000:00:0 | Address=FCE00014 | Length=1 | DATA=4 B | Time Stamp=0196.835463464370s | Time Delta=112.130 ns | LCRC=0x6A9C9066

Error family: P13, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. Also E01 and E03 (kinds of evidence from outside the recording). · Can the packets alone prove it? Partly. The timing and order of the packets show its shape. Proof needs evidence from outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book, version 2.x, adds 'ready modes'. The SSD says which it supports in CAP.CRMS (bit 59 is CRWMS, bit 60 is CRIMS). The computer picks one with CC.CRIME (bit 24). A setting called CRTO sits at offset 68h. It holds two wait times: CRWMT (bits 15:0) and CRIMT (bits 31:16). Both count in steps of 500 ms.

What goes wrong: Some SSDs support these ready modes (CAP.CRMS). They give two wait times in the CRTO setting. CRWMT is the wait until the SSD is ready with its storage. CRIMT is the wait until it is ready without its storage. Problem: CRWMT may be smaller than CAP.TO. Or the storage may not be ready within CRWMT. Then the computer either waits too little, or gives up.

How you can tell: Linux v7.2 logs once bad crto:<value> cap:<value> when CRWMT is smaller than CAP.TO. It then uses CAP.TO instead. If the SSD still misses that time, the message from error type T-02 appears. Some computers use CC.CRIME=1. Then storage commands sent too early end with an error. It is 'Admin Command Media Not Ready' (generic result 24h) or 'Namespace Not Ready' (82h).

How to fix it and prove the fix: In QEMU or another SSD simulator, set CAP.CRMS and a CRTO that does not agree. Check for the bad crto warning. Safe. Use nvme show-regs to read CAP and CRTO. Compare CRWMT with CAP.TO. In the Linux kernel log (dmesg), look for bad crto. Time the gap from 'switch on' (CC.EN) to 'ready' (RDY) with the capture tool.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Only by a timer. Nothing records an error. The only sign is a time limit running out. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The program inside the SSD (firmware) is at fault. CRTO, CAP.TO and storage readiness are values the SSD itself gives. The computer is at fault only in one case. It used CRIME=1, sent storage commands before CRWMT, and treated result 24h or 82h as fatal. · Test that confirms it: reading the SSD's settings.

T-04 The SSD stays 'ready' after being switched off, so restart hangs (CSTS.RDY) Seen in the packets SSD main settings

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 445236: the computer writes 'switch off' (CC.EN=0).

Packet=445236 | Link Dir=Downstream | TLP Type=MWr(32) | PSN=3062 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=000:00:0 | Address=FCE00014 | Length=1 | DATA=4 B | Time Stamp=0197.342366415370s | Time Delta=112.130 ns | LCRC=0x57B690CD

Packet 445285: the 'ready' flag (CSTS.RDY) is still 1, longer than the SSD's promised wait (CAP.TO) after CC.EN=0.

Packet=445285 | Link Dir=Downstream | TLP Type=MRd(32) | PSN=3074 | Tag=26 | RequesterID=000:00:0 | Address=FCE0001C | Length=1 | Time Stamp=0209.342373383370s | Time Delta=160.630 ns | LCRC=0xDD27DA3E

Packet 445288: the computer tries a stronger restart: Function Level Reset (bit 15 of the Device Control setting).

Packet=445288 | Link Dir=Downstream | TLP Type=CfgWr0 | PSN=3075 | Tag=27 | RequesterID=000:00:0 | Length=1 | DATA=4 B | Time Stamp=0209.342374007370s | Time Delta=113.130 ns | LCRC=0x5A999B3D

Error family: P13, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. The checker marks it in this table file as a wrong detail or order. The mark means: an answer that says 'not ready yet, try again' (completion_status_CRS).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book says this. After 'switch on' (CC.EN) goes from 1 to 0, the SSD must set its 'ready' flag (CSTS.RDY) to 0. It must do so within its own promised wait (CAP.TO). Some SSDs need an extra pause before the computer starts checking the flag (see NVME_QUIRK_DELAY_BEFORE_CHK_RDY).

What goes wrong: To restart the SSD, the computer clears 'switch on' (CC.EN). Then it waits for the 'ready' flag to go to 0. The SSD keeps the flag at 1 past CAP.TO. So the restart cannot go on, and the SSD cannot be switched on again.

How you can tell: Linux v7.2 prints Device not ready; aborting reset, CSTS=0x1. Linux then marks the SSD as dead and removes its storage areas (namespaces). Every command still waiting fails.

How to fix it and prove the fix: The Linux kernel log (dmesg) shows the 'aborting reset' line after a timeout or after nvme reset. With the capture tool: a write packet (MWr) to CC with EN=0. Then reads (MRd) of CSTS that return RDY=1 for longer than CAP.TO×500 ms. Check whether the SSD sent any request or data packets (TLPs) in between. If the SSD still moves data after EN=0, that is a bug by itself.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Only by a timer. Nothing records an error. The only sign is a time limit running out. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD is at fault when RDY stays 1 past CAP.TO, the wire is up and answers are valid. The wire or the computer's hardware is at fault when CSTS reads give all ones or 'unsupported request' (UR). The computer's software is at fault only if no EN=0 write reached the SSD. · Test that confirms it: the Linux kernel log.

T-05 Power is cut before the SSD finishes shutting down (CSTS.SHST) Partly seen in the packets SSD main settings

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 447338: the computer asks for a normal shutdown (CC.SHN=01b).

Packet=447338 | Link Dir=Downstream | TLP Type=MWr(32) | PSN=3282 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=000:00:0 | Address=FCE00014 | Length=1 | DATA=4 B | Time Stamp=0209.507829897120s | Time Delta=149.130 ns | LCRC=0x23156539
