Packet=447369 | Link Dir=Downstream | TLP Type=MRd(32) | PSN=3290 | Tag=14 | RequesterID=000:00:0 | Address=FCE0001C | Length=1 | Time Stamp=0217.507833874120s | Time Delta=126.630 ns | LCRC=0xB6835BB8

Error family: P13 and P24, two of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. Also E03 and E07 (kinds of evidence from outside the recording). · Can the packets alone prove it? Partly. The timing and order of the packets show its shape. Proof needs evidence from outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book has a shutdown request, CC.SHN (01b normal, 10b sudden). It has a shutdown status, CSTS.SHST (00b normal work, 01b working on it, 10b done). The SSD's information page (Identify Controller) gives RTD3E. This is the usual time, in microseconds, to go into deep sleep (Runtime D3, a shutdown). RTD3R is the expected time to wake up.

What goes wrong: At power-off, sleep, or driver unload, the computer writes CC.SHN=01b (normal shutdown). Then it waits for CSTS.SHST=10b (shutdown done). The SSD may take longer than the computer waits. Then power may be removed while the SSD is still saving its write cache and its map tables.

How you can tell: Linux v7.2 prints Device not ready; aborting shutdown, CSTS=0x.... At the next start, the drive's health log (SMART / Health) shows a higher 'Unsafe Shutdowns' count. Start-up may also be slower while the SSD rebuilds. It may even take longer than CAP.TO (see error type T-02 in the error list).

How to fix it and prove the fix: Fill the write cache: keep writing with the volatile write cache on. Then restart and compare unsafe_shutdowns. On a test machine, try nvme_core.shutdown_timeout=1. This shows how a too-short Linux time limit looks. Take care: data still in the cache on that drive may be lost. Run nvme smart-log /dev/nvme0 before and after a clean restart. unsafe_shutdowns must not go up. Run nvme id-ctrl /dev/nvme0 | grep -i rtd3 to read RTD3E. In the Linux kernel log (dmesg), look for D3 entry latency set to N seconds (Linux used RTD3E). Also look for the 'aborting shutdown' line.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Only by a timer. Nothing records an error. The only sign is a time limit running out. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD is at fault if SHST=10b never appears within RTD3E after SHN. When RTD3E is 0, the limit is the Linux computer's 5 s wait instead. The computer or its hardware is at fault if the wire or power drops before RTD3E has passed. The same is true if the checking stopped early (error list, section XII.8). · Test that confirms it: the 'unsafe shutdown' count in the SSD's health log.

T-06 The SSD wakes from deep sleep slower than it promised (RTD3R) Partly seen in the packets Power saving and wake-up

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 1330274: the computer sets the power setting (PMCSR) to 'fully on' (D0) to wake the SSD.

Packet=1330274 | Link Dir=Downstream | TLP Type=CfgWr0 | PSN=2886 | Tag=24 | RequesterID=000:00:0 | Length=1 | DATA=4 B | Time Stamp=1298.012249029620s | Time Delta=112.130 ns | LCRC=0xACA703EA

Packet 1330666: the SSD becomes ready long after the wake-up, later than its promised wake time (RTD3R).

Packet=1330666 | Link Dir=Downstream | TLP Type=CplD | PSN=2964 | Tag=121 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | CompleterID=000:02:4 | Cpl Status=SC | Length=16 | Byte Cnt=64 | DATA=64 B | Time Stamp=1300.465470607750s | Time Delta=142.750 ns | LCRC=0xAB7AF3CB

Error family: P20, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. Also E01 and E05 (kinds of evidence from outside the recording). · Can the packets alone prove it? Partly. The timing and order of the packets show its shape. Proof needs evidence from outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: In the NVMe rule book, the SSD's information page (Identify Controller) gives RTD3R. This is the expected wake-up time from deep sleep (Runtime D3), in µs. It also gives RTD3E, the time to go into deep sleep. These are for information only. The computer uses them to decide if deep sleep is worth it.

What goes wrong: After deep sleep or a whole-computer sleep, the SSD takes much longer to wake up than its own RTD3R value. Nothing fails. But the first command after waking is held up.

How you can tell: No error. Programs see a pause of several seconds after waking. The pause may be longer than CAP.TO (the SSD's own promised ready time). Then switching on fails (see error type T-02 in the error list). Times in the Linux kernel log (dmesg) show the gap: from the start of waking to the SSD being ready.

How to fix it and prove the fix: On a laptop, run rtcwake -m mem -s 10 while fio (a disk test program) logs how long each command takes. Safe. Measure with dmesg -T, or with ftrace on the wake-up steps (pci_pm_resume, nvme_resume). Compare with RTD3R from nvme id-ctrl. Run fio with time logging across one sleep and wake.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Things keep working, only slower. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD is at fault if device_ms (the time from 'switch on' CC.EN to 'ready' RDY) is longer than RTD3R. The computer's hardware is at fault if most of the extra time comes before the wire is working (t_L0). That would be a late wake of the wire, slow start-up steps, or slow power-up. Compare pre_L0_ms, and see error types T-40 and T-41 in the error list. The computer's software is at fault if the extra time is in its own gaps. The gaps run from the working wire (L0), to 'fully on' (PMCSR D0), to 'switch on' (CC.EN). See error type M-026 in the error list. · Test that confirms it: wake-up times from the Linux kernel log (dmesg) or ftrace.

T-07 The SSD's 'are you still there?' timer runs out (Keep Alive) Not seen in the packets Not on this wire

Packets seen in the test recording

Error family: E10 (a kind of evidence from outside the recording: a network capture). · Can the packets alone prove it? No. It cannot be seen on this wire. The recording only shows packets around it. The proof is outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book has a 'still here' command (Keep Alive, admin command 18h). It has a 'still here' timer feature (FID 0Fh), with the time limit KATO in milliseconds. The SSD's information page gives KAS, the timer's step size in units of 100 ms. CTRATT.TBKAS says whether any traffic can count as 'still here' (Traffic Based Keep Alive). The computer should send 'still here' often enough to allow for the trip time. A comment in Linux quotes 'at half of the Keep Alive Timeout'.

What goes wrong: The computer sets the 'still here' time limit (KATO) when it connects, or with Set Features (FID 0Fh). Suppose the SSD gets no 'still here' command within KATO. With Traffic Based Keep Alive, it gets no command of any kind. Then the SSD decides the computer is gone.

How you can tell: On the SSD side, the connection is ended. Commands still waiting may end with 'Keep Alive Timer Expired' (generic result 19h). Things the SSD held for that computer, such as reservations and command lists, are let go. On the computer side, the network connection drops. The driver goes to RESETTING, then CONNECTING, and connects again (see error type T-28 in the error list).

How to fix it and prove the fix: Connect over nvme-tcp to a Linux nvmet target (an SSD shared over the network). Add a delay on the computer with tc qdisc add dev eth0 root netem delay 3000ms. Take care: this slows all traffic on that network port. Watch the target end the connection after KATO. In the computer's kernel log (dmesg), look for reconnect messages and long keepalive RTT (N ms). Check the target's own logs (for example, Linux nvmet prints when 'still here' runs out). In a network capture, compare the gap between 'still here' messages (admin command 18h) with KATO.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Only by a timer. Nothing records an error. The only sign is a time limit running out. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The computer is at fault if its 'still here' messages are further apart than KATO. The target SSD is at fault if they arrive within KATO and the timer still runs out. The network capture (E10) or the target's log decides. · Test that confirms it: a network capture (E10).

T-08 The computer's 'still here' command is slow or fails (Keep Alive) Not seen in the packets Not on this wire

Packets seen in the test recording

Error family: E10 (a kind of evidence from outside the recording: a network capture). · Can the packets alone prove it? No. It cannot be seen on this wire. The recording only shows packets around it. The proof is outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book has the 'still here' command (Keep Alive). When the computer sends it is up to the computer's own software.

What goes wrong: The computer's 'still here' command takes most of the 'still here' time to finish, or it fails. So the computer cannot reset the SSD's timer in time.

How you can tell: Linux v7.2 warns long keepalive RTT (N ms) when the round trip takes longer than the work period. On failure it prints failed nvme_keep_alive_end_io error=N. If the command cannot even be set up, it prints keep-alive failed: N, and then the SSD is restarted.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Run dmesg | grep -i keepalive. Trace with the nvme_setup_cmd and nvme_complete_rq trace points (/sys/kernel/tracing/events/nvme). Keep only admin command 0x18.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Only by a timer. Nothing records an error. The only sign is a time limit running out. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The computer's software is at fault when 'still here' is sent late, or waits behind long admin commands. The target SSD is at fault when only its answer is slow. Measure that with the network capture round trip (E10). Or measure the time from fetch to done note on the PCIe wire. · Test that confirms it: the Linux kernel log (E01).

T-09 A 'stop that command' request does not stop it (Abort) Seen in the packets Command never finishes (timing)

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 1117668: the SSD fetched one command (SQE).

Packet=1117668 | Link Dir=Downstream | TLP Type=CplD | PSN=2478 | Tag=36 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | CompleterID=000:02:4 | Cpl Status=SC | Length=16 | Byte Cnt=64 | DATA=64 B | Time Stamp=0622.702770393620s | Time Delta=160.750 ns | LCRC=0x4D3A9777

Packet 1125746: the SSD fetched a 'stop that command' request (Abort), but never finished it.

Packet=1125746 | Link Dir=Downstream | TLP Type=CplD | PSN=4042 | Tag=33 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | CompleterID=000:02:4 | Cpl Status=SC | Length=16 | Byte Cnt=64 | DATA=64 B | Time Stamp=0652.702820056620s | Time Delta=147.750 ns | LCRC=0xE946F30E

Error family: P02, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. A check on the order and timing of packets finds it. Examples: a missing answer, a long gap, packets out of order.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book has a 'stop that command' request (Abort). The SSD's information page gives ACL, counted from 0. The rule book suggests 3, which means four stop requests at once. Too many gives result 103h. A stopped command ends with 'Command Abort Requested' (generic result 07h).

What goes wrong: A command runs out of time. The computer then sends a stop request (admin command 08h). It names the command list (SQID) and the command number (CID). A stop request is only a try. The SSD may finish it without stopping anything. Or the computer may have no stop requests left to use.

How you can tell: In the stop request's done note, bit 0 of Dword 0 = 1 means 'command not stopped'. Linux v7.2 logs only Abort status: 0x0 and does not look at Dword 0. It waits for the second timeout to restart the SSD. If more than ACL+1 stop requests are open, the SSD answers 'Abort Command Limit Exceeded' (103h). Linux avoids that. It keeps its own count and simply starts the timer again.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Use QEMU with a stuck storage backend, for example a blkdebug or slowed disk image. Set a low io_timeout (a Linux computer setting). Watch the result in the stop request's done note. Safe. With the capture tool: the stop command is fetched from the admin command list. Its done note is written with bit 0 of DW0 = 1. And there is no done note for the command it was meant to stop. In the Linux kernel log (dmesg): 'aborting', then about one io_timeout later 'reset controller' for the same request number (tag).

Does the SSD or computer report it? Only by a timer. Nothing records an error. The only sign is a time limit running out. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD is at fault when it fetches the stop request but the stuck command stays open. It answers 'not stopped', or never answers. The computer is at fault when no stop request is ever fetched for a command that ran out of time. Maybe Linux used up its count of ACL+1 stop requests. Or the computer does not run Linux. · Test that confirms it: the series of timeout lines in the Linux kernel log (dmesg timeout ladder).

T-10 New SSD program takes longer to start than promised (MTFA) Seen in the packets SSD main settings

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 448058: the 'start the new SSD program' command (Firmware Commit, action CA=3) finishes.

Packet=448058 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=179 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000004:820200E0 | Length=4 | DATA=16 B | Time Stamp=0220.647557222620s | Time Delta=27.870 ns | LCRC=0xECD98AC4

Packet 448124: the 'work paused' flag (CSTS.PP) stays 1 longer than the promised time. That promise (MTFA) was 2 s, as the SSD stated.

Packet=448124 | Link Dir=Downstream | TLP Type=MRd(32) | PSN=126 | Tag=14 | RequesterID=000:00:0 | Address=FCE0001C | Length=1 | Time Stamp=0228.147567518620s | Time Delta=129.630 ns | LCRC=0x4FDBCEE1

Error family: P13 and P25, two of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. A check on the order and timing of packets finds it. Examples: a missing answer, a long gap, packets out of order.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: In the NVMe rule book, the SSD's information page gives MTFA. It is the SSD's own promise of the longest time to start a new program, in steps of 100 ms. The flag CSTS.PP (Processing Paused, bit 5) shows work is paused. A 'Firmware Activation Notice' message tells the computer. Result 112h is the refusal.

What goes wrong: The 'start new program without restart' command (Firmware Commit) pauses all command work (CSTS.PP=1). The pause lasts while the new program inside the SSD (firmware) starts. If the pause lasts longer than MTFA, every command on the computer waits that long. The computer may then restart the SSD.

How you can tell: Linux v7.2 prints Fw activation timeout, reset controller. Programs see a pause of up to MTFA. When MTFA=0, the pause can last up to admin_timeout (a Linux computer setting). If the SSD knows the start would take longer than MTFA, it should refuse at once. The refusal is 'Firmware Activation Requires Maximum Time Violation' (command result 112h).

How to fix it and prove the fix: Start a new program with commit action 3 (start without restart) while the SSD is busy. Risky, test machine only: a program update can break a drive for good. Use only images the SSD maker approves. Run nvme id-ctrl | grep -i mtfa. Run fio with --write_lat_log during nvme fw-commit -a 3 and measure the pause. With the capture tool: reads (MRd) of CSTS that show PP=1, and how long it stays.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Only by a timer. Nothing records an error. The only sign is a time limit running out. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD is at fault. The start time is the SSD program's own behaviour, and MTFA is the SSD's own promise. · Test that confirms it: MTFA and the program slot log (firmware slot log).

T-11 Formatting the SSD takes longer than the computer waits (Format NVM) Seen in the packets Command never finishes (timing)

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 1135624: the SSD fetched a long admin command (an SSD management command).

Packet=1135624 | Link Dir=Downstream | TLP Type=CplD | PSN=1073 | Tag=50 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | CompleterID=000:02:4 | Cpl Status=SC | Length=16 | Byte Cnt=64 | DATA=64 B | Time Stamp=0682.854261844370s | Time Delta=137.750 ns | LCRC=0x6337D697

Error family: P02 and P25, two of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. A check on the order and timing of packets finds it. Examples: a missing answer, a long gap, packets out of order.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book gives no stated length for a format (Format NVM). Commands to the storage area being formatted (namespace) end with 'Format In Progress' (84h). FNA, on the SSD's information page, says how much a format or secure erase covers.

What goes wrong: The format command (80h) gives its done note (CQE) only when the format is finished. On a large drive, or with Secure Erase Settings set to 'erase user data', that can take minutes. The computer's time limit for admin commands runs out first. In Linux that limit is 60 s (the Linux computer's setting).

How you can tell: Linux v7.2 sees the admin command run out of time and goes straight to a restart: I/O tag N (....) opcode 0x80 (Format NVM) QID 0 timeout, reset controller. The restart breaks off the format. Afterwards the storage area may answer 'Format In Progress' (84h). Or it may be unusable until a new format.

How to fix it and prove the fix: On a lab drive, format a large storage area with SES=1 and --timeout=60000. Risky, test machine only: this erases all data in that storage area. Look in the Linux kernel log (dmesg) for a line with opcode 0x80 on QID 0. To fix, give a longer time limit yourself: nvme format /dev/nvme0n1 --timeout=600000 (in milliseconds). Check what your nvme-cli version uses by default.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Only by a timer. Nothing records an error. The only sign is a time limit running out. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The computer's software is at fault in this case. The format stays within the time the SSD maker expects. But the computer used the default 60 s admin time limit. The SSD is at fault when a small storage area takes too long to format. The limit is the maker's own written time. · Test that confirms it: the series of timeout lines in the Linux kernel log (dmesg timeout ladder).

T-12 A full wipe runs far past its estimate, or never ends (Sanitize) Partly seen in the packets Long SSD jobs and their results

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 1529242: the last admin done note, or log read, of the long job.

Packet=1529242 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=1156 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000004:84820070 | Length=4 | DATA=16 B | Time Stamp=1531.912533197500s | Time Delta=39.880 ns | LCRC=0x0B028528

Error family: P25, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. Also E01 and E03 (kinds of evidence from outside the recording). · Can the packets alone prove it? Partly. The timing and order of the packets show its shape. Proof needs evidence from outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book has a wipe status log (Sanitize Status log, LID 81h). Its parts are SPROG, SSTAT, SCDW10, ETO, ETBE, ETCE. It also has the 'No-Deallocate' versions ETOND, ETBEND, ETCEND. These estimates are in seconds. 0 means the wipe finishes in the background when the command finishes. FFFFFFFFh means 'not given'. A wipe keeps going across restarts and power cuts.

What goes wrong: The wipe command (Sanitize, 84h) finishes at once, and the wipe goes on in the background. The SSD gives its time estimates in the wipe status log. The wipe may take much longer than the estimate. Or the progress number (SPROG) may stop moving. Then the drive cannot be used for that time, and no timer goes off.

How you can tell: No error. Most read and write commands, and many admin commands, fail with 'Sanitize In Progress' (generic 1Dh) the whole time. The wipe status log shows SSTAT = 'in progress', and SPROG (a count out of 65536) stuck. If the wipe fails, SSTAT says 'failed'. Later commands then get 'Sanitize Failed' (1Ch).

How to fix it and prove the fix: Run nvme sanitize /dev/nvme0 -a 2 (block erase) and read the log again and again. Risky, test machine only: this erases all user data in the whole SSD. Read nvme sanitize-log /dev/nvme0 again and again, and note SPROG against time. Compare the time passed with the matching estimate. A tool should warn when 'time passed > k × estimate'. Pick k, for example 2.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Things keep working, only slower. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD is at fault: bad storage blocks, a wrong estimate from the SSD's program, or a stuck SSD program. The computer is at fault only if it sent commands that clash, or cut the power again and again. · Test that confirms it: reading the progress again and again (E03).

T-13 The SSD's self-test runs longer than its promised time (EDSTT) Partly seen in the packets Long SSD jobs and their results

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 1529724: the last admin done note, or log read, of the long job.

Packet=1529724 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=1355 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000004:84820120 | Length=4 | DATA=16 B | Time Stamp=1681.913288745750s | Time Delta=42.880 ns | LCRC=0x8A134651

Error family: P25, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. Also E01 and E03 (kinds of evidence from outside the recording). · Can the packets alone prove it? Partly. The timing and order of the packets show its shape. Proof needs evidence from outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: In the NVMe rule book, the SSD's information page gives EDSTT. It is the SSD's own promise for the long self-test, in minutes, at full power (power state 0). The short self-test has a time limit set by the rule book: two minutes. Check this in your rule book version. Results go in the self-test log (LID 06h).

What goes wrong: The self-test (admin command 14h) runs in the background. The long test should finish in about EDSTT minutes. The short test has a fixed upper limit in the rule book. A test that keeps running hides a slow or failing part inside the SSD.

How you can tell: No error while it runs. A second self-test request gets 'Device Self-test In Progress' (command result 11Dh). The self-test log shows the current test and how many percent is done. The final result entry records why it stopped, or which part failed.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Run the long test with the SSD idle. Run it again with fio (a disk test program) keeping the SSD fully busy. Compare how long each took. Safe, because a self-test never erases data. Still, avoid it on drives in real use. Start nvme device-self-test /dev/nvme0 -s 2. Read nvme self-test-log /dev/nvme0 again and again. Compare the time passed with nvme id-ctrl | grep edstt.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Things keep working, only slower. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD is at fault when the test is slow while idle at full power (PS0). The computer or its work is at fault when the extra time shows only under heavy work or low power. · Test that confirms it: a timed self-test (safe).

T-14 Waking from a power-saving state is slower than promised (EXLAT) Seen in the packets Speed (timing counts)

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 1573564: a read after an idle time finishes after 25 ms. The SSD had to leave a power-saving state first.

Packet=1573564 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=1605 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000004:84830210 | Length=4 | DATA=16 B | Time Stamp=1819.993976157000s | Time Delta=74.880 ns | LCRC=0xDD5E1018

Error family: P22, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. · Can the packets alone prove it? Partly. The timing and order of the packets show its shape. Proof needs evidence from outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: In the NVMe rule book, each power state has a description. It gives ENLAT and EXLAT: the SSD's own promise of the time to enter and leave that state, in µs. 0 means 'not given'. A NON-OP flag marks states where the SSD does no work. The automatic power-saving feature (APST, FID 0Ch) has entries. Each entry gives the idle time before moving (in ms) and the state to move to. The SSD's information page gives APSTA and NPSS.

What goes wrong: With automatic power saving (APST), the SSD drops into a no-work power state after some idle time. The first command after the idle time must wait for the SSD to leave that state. If leaving takes longer than the SSD's promised EXLAT, the computer's time plan is broken. No error is shown.

How you can tell: No error. The first command after idle is much slower, again and again. It is often tens of milliseconds. Linux does not use states whose EXLAT is larger than ps_max_latency_us (a Linux computer setting). So an SSD that gives too small an EXLAT gets past that protection.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Run fio (a disk test program) with different --thinktime values around the APST idle times. Plot how long the first command takes. Safe. Run nvme id-ctrl -H /dev/nvme0 for the power state table. Run nvme get-feature -f 0x0c -H /dev/nvme0 for the APST table Linux set. Run fio with --thinktime longer than the idle time, and record clat (time per command). Compare the slow ones with EXLAT. Turn APST off (nvme_core.default_ps_max_latency_us=0) to confirm the slow commands go away.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Things keep working, only slower. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD is at fault if dev_exit is longer than EXLAT while the wire is working (L0). The computer's hardware or the wire is at fault if most of the time is the wire waking up. That is the wire's own power saving (L1 or L1.2). The computer's software is at fault if it chose APST states that wake too slowly. Their wake time is longer than the computer's own time plan. Linux skips states whose wake time is above ps_max_latency_us. · Test that confirms it: compare with APST off and on.

T-15 The SSD never wakes from deep power saving and leaves the wire Partly seen in the packets Wire down, power or restart

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 1347780: the SSD gives no answer when woken. It is stuck in low power.

Packet=1347780 | Link Dir=Downstream | Link Event=Link Down | Time Stamp=1315.861813966000s | Time Delta=300.000 ms

Error family: P12, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. Also E01 and E07 (kinds of evidence from outside the recording). · Can the packets alone prove it? Partly. The timing and order of the packets show its shape. Proof needs evidence from outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book has automatic power saving (APST) and power states. The PCIe rule book has wire power saving (ASPM) and its deeper L1 states (L1 PM substates). Neither rule book has a timer that catches this. Only the computer's command timer does.

What goes wrong: The SSD goes into a deep no-work state, often together with the wire's own deep power saving (ASPM L1 substates). Then it fails to come back. Reads of its settings area and its main settings (config and MMIO reads) return all ones.

How you can tell: The next command runs out of time after 30 s (the Linux computer's setting). Linux v7.2 then reads CSTS = 0xffffffff. It prints controller is down; will reset: CSTS=0xffffffff, PCI_STATUS=0x.... Then it prints Does your device have a faulty power saving mode enabled? and Try "nvme_core.default_ps_max_latency_us=0 pcie_aspm=off pcie_port_pm=off" and report a bug. The restart usually fails, and the storage area disappears.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Look for the all-ones CSTS line in the Linux kernel log (dmesg). Try again with APST off (default_ps_max_latency_us=0) and with ASPM off. If the problem goes away, it is a failure to leave a power state. Run lspci -vvv after it happens. 'Unknown header type 7f', or an all-ones settings area, means the SSD is gone.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Only by a timer. Nothing records an error. The only sign is a time limit running out. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD is at fault if the computer's port starts the wake and the SSD never answers. The port's wake-up signals are TS1 or EIEOS. The computer's hardware is at fault if the port, the CLKREQ# signal or the power never starts the wake. It is also at fault if the L1 substate timings do not match (error list, section XII.8). · Test that confirms it: turn APST off.

T-16 An SSD without own memory slows when not lent any (HMB) Partly seen in the packets Speed (timing counts)

Packets seen in the test recording

Error family: P22, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. Also E01 and E03 (kinds of evidence from outside the recording). · Can the packets alone prove it? Partly. The timing and order of the packets show its shape. Proof needs evidence from outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book has a feature where the computer lends memory to the SSD (Host Memory Buffer, FID 0Dh). The SSD's information page gives HMPRE (the size it would like) and HMMIN (the smallest it needs). Both count in 4 KiB steps. It also gives HMMINDS and HMMAXD.

What goes wrong: Some SSDs have no memory chip of their own (DRAM-less). They ask the computer to lend memory (HMB) to hold their map tables. The computer may give less than asked. Or it may turn the lent memory off, for example during sleep. The drive keeps working, but reads from random places get slower.

How you can tell: No error. Linux may log min host memory (N MiB) above limit (128 MiB). and run without it. Or it may log failed to allocate host memory buffer. ('controller must work without HMB'). Random 4 KiB reads get clearly slower. How much depends on the SSD.

How to fix it and prove the fix: On an SSD without its own memory, load the nvme driver with max_host_mem_size_mb=0. Compare the time for 4 KiB reads from random places. Safe. Run dmesg | grep -i "host memory". Run nvme get-feature -f 0x0d -H /dev/nvme0 to see if the lent memory is on. Check /sys/class/nvme/nvme0/hmb (it exists when HMPRE is not 0). Compare fio random-read times with and without lent memory.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Things keep working, only slower. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The computer's software is at fault when its Set Features 0Dh data is wrong or missing. Wrong means EHM=0, or HSIZE smaller than HMMIN. The SSD is at fault if enough memory was lent and the drive stops using it, or is slow anyway. · Test that confirms it: the computer's log and the feature setting.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: In the NVMe rule book, the done note's status has a field CRD. It is bits 12:11 of the status word as Linux stores it (mask 0x1800). The SSD's information page gives CRDT1 to CRDT3, in steps of 100 ms. A feature (Host Behavior Support, FID 16h) has an ACRE bit that turns this on.

What goes wrong: The SSD can ask the computer to wait before trying a command again. It puts 1, 2 or 3 in the CRD field. The computer then waits CRDT1, CRDT2 or CRDT3 × 100 ms. These wait times are the SSD's own values. If CRDT is zero while CRD is used, the computer tries again at once and uses up its tries. If CRDT is very large, every try adds seconds of waiting.

How you can tell: Done notes with DNR=0 (trying again is allowed) and a CRD that is not 0. Examples are 'Namespace Not Ready' (82h) and 'Command Interrupted' (21h). In Linux, each try adds 1 to command_retries_count in sysfs. After max_retries (5, a Linux computer setting), the program gets the error.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Use QEMU or a test SSD with a hook that answers 82h with CRD=1. Change CRDT1 and measure the extra waiting. Safe. The trace point nvme:nvme_complete_rq shows the result and the tries. Run nvme id-ctrl | grep -i crdt. Run nvme get-feature -f 0x16 -H for ACRE.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Yes. A setting, a result number or a log in the SSD or computer records it. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD is at fault when it uses CRD without a valid CRDT or ACRE. It is also at fault when CRDT is far too long. The computer is at fault when ACRE and CRDT are valid, and it sends the command again too early. · Test that confirms it: check CRDT and ACRE.

Error family: P01, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. · Can the packets alone prove it? Only by reading the bytes. The result number is inside the DATA column. The hex version of the recording marks a done note with a result other than 0 (nvme_status_nonzero).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book has generic result 82h, 'Namespace Not Ready'. Trying again is allowed when DNR=0. It also has 24h, 'Admin Command Media Not Ready', used with CC.CRIME=1.

What goes wrong: This happens after a restart, a wake-up or a size change. The storage area (namespace) answers 'Namespace Not Ready' (82h) or 'Admin Command Media Not Ready' (24h). It keeps doing so for longer than the computer is willing to keep trying.

How you can tell: First a few commands are tried again. Then read or write errors reach the program. These look like blk_update_request: I/O error messages, with the NVMe result in the nvme_log_error() output.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Cut and restore power on a large drive after an unsafe shutdown. Start reading and writing as soon as the drive appears. Take care. Look in the Linux kernel log (dmesg) for NVMe error lines with result 0x82. Check /sys/block/nvme0n1/device/.../command_retries_count. Match these against the time since the SSD was switched on.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Yes. A setting, a result number or a log in the SSD or computer records it. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD is at fault when the 'not ready' time is longer than the time it promised. This can be storage start-up slower than 'ready' (RDY), or RDY set too early. The computer is at fault when its number of tries covers less time than the SSD promised. · Test that confirms it: evidence from the computer (host evidence).

T-19 A path change takes longer than the SSD promised (ANATT) Not seen in the packets Not on this wire

Packets seen in the test recording

Error family: E10 (a kind of evidence from outside the recording: a network capture). · Can the packets alone prove it? No. It cannot be seen on this wire. The recording only shows packets around it. The proof is outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: In the NVMe rule book, the SSD's information page gives ANATT (in seconds) and ANACAP. There is a path log page (ANA log page). There are path results: 'ANA Persistent Loss' 301h, 'ANA Inaccessible' 302h, 'ANA Transition' 303h.

What goes wrong: Some SSDs can be reached by more than one path, and each path has a state (Asymmetric Namespace Access, ANA). A group of storage areas can show a 'change' state while it moves between fast, slow and unreachable. ANATT is the SSD's own promise of the longest time in that state. If it stays longer, the computer cannot use that path.

How you can tell: When any group is in the 'change' state, Linux v7.2 starts a timer. The timer is 2 × ANATT (the Linux computer's setting). When it runs out, Linux prints ANATT timeout, resetting controller. Commands on that path end with 'ANA Transition' (path result 303h) and are moved to another path.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Run nvme ana-log /dev/nvme0 again and again. Check ana_state in sysfs for each storage-area path. Look in the Linux kernel log (dmesg) for the ANATT line. Check multipath_failover_count in sysfs.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Only by a timer. Nothing records an error. The only sign is a time limit running out. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD or network target is at fault when the group stays in the 'change' state past ANATT. The computer is at fault only for its own timer choice (2 x ANATT in Linux). · Test that confirms it: reading the path log again and again.

Packet=1561751 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=1773 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000004:848200F0 | Length=4 | DATA=16 B | Time Stamp=1805.917567079120s | Time Delta=58.870 ns | LCRC=0x037A6D45

Error family: P26, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. Also E03 (a kind of evidence from outside the recording). · Can the packets alone prove it? Partly. The timing and order of the packets show its shape. Proof needs evidence from outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book has a clock feature (Timestamp, FID 0Eh). It holds a 48-bit count of milliseconds since midnight on 1 January 1970 UTC. It also has bits that say where the time came from. A 'Synch' bit says the count may have stopped (check the exact meaning in the rule book). An ONCS bit says the SSD supports it.

What goes wrong: The computer sets the SSD's clock with the Timestamp feature. The SSD keeps counting. Over a long time switched on, the SSD's clock can drift. In some power states it may stop. Then the SSD's own logs (Persistent Event Log, telemetry) carry wrong times.

How you can tell: Nothing shows. SSD log entries cannot be lined up with the computer's logs. An SSD event appears minutes away from the computer problem it caused.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Read the SSD's clock now and then over a week of being switched on. Plot the SSD's time minus the computer's time. Safe. Run nvme get-feature -f 0x0e -H /dev/nvme0 and compare with date +%s%3N. Do it again a day later to measure the drift.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Nothing records it. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD is at fault. Its clock part is not exact enough, or the clock stops in some power states. The computer is at fault if it never sets the clock after start-up. · Test that confirms it: measuring drift over a long run (safe).

Packet 576993: the computer's done-list doorbell, sent only after the timeout code checked the done list itself ('completion polled').

Packet=576993 | Link Dir=Downstream | TLP Type=MWr(32) | PSN=677 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=000:00:0 | Address=FCE01014 | Length=1 | DATA=4 B | Time Stamp=0401.094161513870s | Time Delta=133.130 ns | LCRC=0x36A69AE9

Error family: P16, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. Also E05 (a kind of evidence from outside the recording). · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. A check on the order and timing of packets finds it. Examples: a missing answer, a long gap, packets out of order.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rules for PCIe give each done list (CQ) its own 'work is done' signal number (MSI-X vector). Signals can be grouped (interrupt coalescing, Feature 08h). The INTMS and INTMC settings turn older signal types on and off. In the PCIe rule book, an MSI-X signal is a write packet (MWr) that needs no answer. It goes to the address in the MSI-X table.

What goes wrong: The SSD wrote the done note (CQE) and maybe sent the 'work is done' signal (MSI-X). But the computer never ran its 'done' code. So the command looks 'still running'. It stays that way until the timeout code checks the done list and finds it.

How you can tell: Linux v7.2 prints I/O tag N (CID) QID Q timeout, completion polled. The command succeeds, but 30 s late (the Linux computer's setting). There is no restart.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Block the list's MSI-X signal number with a debug tool. Or use QEMU and drop the signals in the model. With a short io_timeout (a Linux computer setting), the message appears. Safe in a virtual machine. Count 'completion polled' lines in the Linux kernel log (dmesg). Check /proc/interrupts: the count for the nvme list's signal does not go up. Look for memory-guard error messages (IOMMU faults, DMAR: ... fault). With the capture tool, find the done-note write (MWr). Check for the MSI-X write that should follow, to the signal address range (APIC).

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Things keep working, only slower. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD is at fault if no MSI-X write follows the done note. It is also at fault if the write has a wrong address or wrong data. This counts only while the signal number is set, switched on and not blocked. The computer is at fault if it set a wrong or old table entry, or blocked the signal. Its write to the table area shows this on the wire. The computer's hardware is at fault if the right MSI-X is on the wire but goes unnoticed. That hardware is the signal remapping, the memory guard (IOMMU) or the processor. · Test that confirms it: lining up the Linux kernel log (dmesg) with the packets.

Error family: P02, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. Also E01, E03 and E05 (kinds of evidence from outside the recording). · Can the packets alone prove it? Only by reading the bytes. The result number is inside the DATA column. The hex version of the recording marks a done note with a result other than 0 (nvme_status_nonzero).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: This is the computer's own choice. It uses two tools from the rule book: the 'stop that command' request (Abort) and the SSD restart.

What goes wrong: A read or write command passes its time limit (io_timeout, 30 s, the Linux computer's setting). Linux then steps up. It checks whether the SSD is dead or gone. It checks the done list (CQ) itself. It sends an NVMe stop request (Abort). If the time runs out a second time, it restarts the SSD.

How you can tell: I/O tag N (CID) opcode 0x.. (Name) QID Q timeout, aborting req_op:... size:.... Then maybe ... timeout, reset controller. If PCI error recovery is running (pci_channel_offline()), the timer is just started again. If CSTS.CFS=1 (a fatal-error flag) or NSSRO is set, the driver restarts at once. It prints controller is down; will reset: CSTS=0x..., PCI_STATUS=0x....

How to fix it and prove the fix: On a test machine, run echo 2000 > /sys/class/nvme/nvme0/io_timeout. Then make long commands, for example very large Write Zeroes or Verify ranges on a slow SSD. This shows the steps quickly. Take care: restarts break off other reads and writes. Collect the Linux kernel log (dmesg) timeout lines. They show request number (tag), command number (CID), command type (opcode), list number (QID) and size. Collect nvme error-log. Collect the PCIe error report (AER status) of the SSD and the computer's port for the same time. Use the trace points nvme:nvme_setup_cmd and nvme:nvme_complete_rq to measure each command's time before the failure.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Only by a timer. Nothing records an error. The only sign is a time limit running out. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD is at fault when it fetched the command but wrote no done note before the stop request (+IO_TO). The computer is at fault when the done note and MSI-X signal came on time, but its doorbell is late. That is slow work on the computer's side (error family P16). · Test that confirms it: the series of timeout lines in the Linux kernel log (dmesg timeout ladder).

Packet=1163713 | Link Dir=Downstream | TLP Type=CplD | PSN=409 | Tag=166 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | CompleterID=000:02:4 | Cpl Status=SC | Length=16 | Byte Cnt=64 | DATA=64 B | Time Stamp=0772.866319769370s | Time Delta=131.750 ns | LCRC=0x97EADA6D

Error family: P02, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. A check on the order and timing of packets finds it. Examples: a missing answer, a long gap, packets out of order.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: This is the computer's own choice.

What goes wrong: A command on the admin command list (QID 0) may pass admin_timeout (60 s, the Linux computer's setting). Then Linux restarts the SSD straight away. Linux never sends a 'stop that command' request (Abort) for an admin command.

How you can tell: I/O tag N (CID) opcode 0x.. (Name) QID 0 timeout, reset controller. Usual command types are Format NVM (0x80), Sanitize (0x84) and Firmware Commit (0x10). Others are Get Log Page of a large telemetry log (0x02), and the SSD maker's own commands.

How to fix it and prove the fix: See error type T-11 in the error list. Risky, test machine only, when the command erases data. Look for QID 0 in the timeout message. For tools: give a time limit yourself (nvme ... --timeout=<ms>) for long jobs.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Only by a timer. Nothing records an error. The only sign is a time limit running out. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The computer is at fault when the stuck command is a known long job, run with the default time limit. The SSD is at fault when a short admin command gets no done note. Examples: Identify 06h, Get Features 0Ah, a small Get Log Page. · Test that confirms it: the series of timeout lines in the Linux kernel log (dmesg timeout ladder).

Packet=1088860 | Link Dir=Downstream | TLP Type=CplD | PSN=2187 | Tag=206 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | CompleterID=000:02:4 | Cpl Status=SC | Length=16 | Byte Cnt=64 | DATA=64 B | Time Stamp=0562.527674011870s | Time Delta=141.750 ns | LCRC=0xC9D5365D

Packet 1088862: the write packet (MWr) with the done note. Its result is not 0 (SCT0/SC0x06).

Packet=1088862 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=747 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000004:82F102D0 | Length=4 | DATA=16 B | Time Stamp=0562.527682011870s | Time Delta=48.870 ns | LCRC=0x5BC8C536

Error family: P01, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. Also E05 (a kind of evidence from outside the recording). · Can the packets alone prove it? Only by reading the bytes. The result number is inside the DATA column. The hex version of the recording marks a done note with a result other than 0 (nvme_status_nonzero).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book has the DNR bit ('do not try again') and the CRD field ('wait before trying again'). How many times to try is the computer's own choice.

What goes wrong: Errors that allow another try (DNR=0) are tried again. So are commands cancelled by a restart. After max_retries (5 tries, the Linux computer's setting), the error goes up to the program. When DNR=1, it goes up at once.

How you can tell: The program gets a read or write error. The Linux kernel log has an NVMe error line with the final result. In sysfs, command_retries_count and command_error_count go up for that storage area.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Make errors on purpose with drivers/nvme/host/fault_inject.c. It has a debugfs folder per disk, with status and dont_retry files and the usual fault controls. Clear dont_retry to watch the tries. Safe. Run cat /sys/block/nvme0n1/device/../nvme0n1/command_retries_count. The path can differ, so find it with find /sys -name command_retries_count. The trace point nvme:nvme_complete_rq prints the tries.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Yes. A setting, a result number or a log in the SSD or computer records it. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD is at fault when it keeps giving errors that allow another try (DNR=0). Examples are 'not ready' and 'internal error'. The computer or its hardware is at fault when restarts cancel the commands and send them again. · Test that confirms it: the count of tries.

T-25 A command times out while the SSD is restarting or connecting Seen in the packets Command never finishes (timing)

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 1180458: an 'information page' command (Identify), sent during a restart or connect, never finishes.

Packet=1180458 | Link Dir=Downstream | TLP Type=CplD | PSN=2680 | Tag=218 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | CompleterID=000:02:4 | Cpl Status=SC | Length=16 | Byte Cnt=64 | DATA=64 B | Time Stamp=0832.886131204120s | Time Delta=141.750 ns | LCRC=0xC81991FC

Error family: P02, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. A check on the order and timing of packets finds it. Examples: a missing answer, a long gap, packets out of order.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: This is the computer's own choice.

What goes wrong: A command runs out of time while the SSD is already in RESETTING or CONNECTING. It is often an admin command sent during start-up again. The computer cannot restart again, so it gives up on the SSD.

How you can tell: I/O tag N (CID) QID Q timeout, disable controller (in CONNECTING or DELETING). The SSD is marked for removal, and its storage areas disappear. During RESETTING, the timer is just started again.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Make the SSD fail a second time during a restart (with the SSD maker's hook or a QEMU model). Take care. In the Linux kernel log (dmesg), look for this order. First a restart, then 'timeout, disable controller'. Then the SSD disappears from nvme list.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Only by a timer. Nothing records an error. The only sign is a time limit running out. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD is at fault when it fetches the admin command after being switched on again, but never answers. The wire is at fault when wire recovery or 'wire down' (Recovery, Link Down) shows during start-up. The computer is at fault only if its start-up steps are wrong in themselves (other entries in the error list). · Test that confirms it: the 'disable' lines in the Linux kernel log (dmesg).

T-26 Moving to another path waits for the full time limit (multipath) Not seen in the packets Not on this wire

Packets seen in the test recording

Error family: E10 (a kind of evidence from outside the recording: a network capture). · Can the packets alone prove it? No. It cannot be seen on this wire. The recording only shows packets around it. The proof is outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book has path results. They are 'Host Path Error' 370h, 'Host Aborted Command' 371h, and the path-state results 301h to 303h.

What goes wrong: NVMe can use several paths itself (native multipath). Then a path result (SCT 3h) moves work to another path at once. But a path that simply stops answering gives no result. So the move waits for the command time limit. On network SSDs (fabrics) it also waits for the network's own error recovery.

How you can tell: Reading and writing stops for about io_timeout (30 s, the Linux computer's setting). On network SSDs it is KATO or the network's detection time instead. Then work goes on over the other path. multipath_failover_count in sysfs goes up. The program sees no error.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Set up a network SSD with two ports (NVMe-oF). Block one path with iptables -j DROP (not REJECT) and measure the gap. Safe in a lab. The time log shows a gap equal to the time limit when one path is pulled. The Linux kernel log (dmesg) shows a timeout on the failed path, then reads and writes that work. Compare how each path choice behaves (iopolicy: numa, round-robin, queue-depth).

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Things keep working, only slower. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: When the path hung with no result, the computer's software choice is at fault. That choice is the time limit for multiple paths. The SSD or network target is at fault for the hang itself. · Test that confirms it: a second capture tool on the other path (E08).

T-27 All paths are gone: commands wait, then fail, or wait forever Not seen in the packets Not on this wire

Packets seen in the test recording

Error family: E10 (a kind of evidence from outside the recording: a network capture). · Can the packets alone prove it? No. It cannot be seen on this wire. The recording only shows packets around it. The proof is outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: This is the computer's own choice.

What goes wrong: When no path can be used, the computer's multipath code does one of two things. It fails commands at once, or it holds them. Held commands wait until a path comes back, or until delayed_removal_secs passes, or until every SSD connection is deleted (ctrl_loss_tmo). These are Linux computer settings.

How you can tell: Programs freeze in the 'D' state (waiting for the disk). After the hold time, they get read or write errors. io_fail_no_available_path_count in sysfs goes up.

How to fix it and prove the fix: nvme list-subsys shows all paths 'connecting' or missing. The Linux kernel log (dmesg) shows hung-task warnings. Check the sysfs counts above.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Only by a timer. Nothing records an error. The only sign is a time limit running out. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The computer's software is at fault for its settings (hold-if-no-path choice, ctrl_loss_tmo, delayed_removal_secs). The network or target is at fault for the outage itself. · Test that confirms it: the Linux kernel log (E01).

T-28 Network SSD lost: reconnecting stops, or fails fast (ctrl_loss_tmo) Not seen in the packets Not on this wire

Packets seen in the test recording

Error family: E10 (a kind of evidence from outside the recording: a network capture). · Can the packets alone prove it? No. It cannot be seen on this wire. The recording only shows packets around it. The proof is outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe over network rule book (NVMe over Fabrics) has a connection (association) and a Connect command. The timer values are the computer's own choice.

What goes wrong: After a network error, the computer tries to connect again every reconnect_delay seconds. After ctrl_loss_tmo, it gives up and deletes the SSD connection. If fast_io_fail_tmo is set, waiting commands fail after that time, even while reconnecting goes on. All three are Linux computer settings.

How you can tell: Reconnecting in 10 seconds... again and again. At the end, Removing controller (N).... With fast_io_fail_tmo: failfast expired, and waiting commands fail with a computer path error.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Run dmesg | grep -E "Reconnecting|Removing controller|failfast". Check ctrl_loss_tmo, reconnect_delay and fast_io_fail_tmo in sysfs for that SSD connection.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Only by a timer. Nothing records an error. The only sign is a time limit running out. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The target is at fault when reconnect tries get no answer. The computer is at fault when Connect is refused because of the computer's setup or log-in (DNR). · Test that confirms it: a network capture (E10).

T-29 A network SSD command runs out of time and starts error recovery Not seen in the packets Not on this wire

Packets seen in the test recording

Error family: E10 (a kind of evidence from outside the recording: a network capture). · Can the packets alone prove it? No. It cannot be seen on this wire. The recording only shows packets around it. The proof is outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe over network rules (NVMe over Fabrics, NVMe/TCP). The rest is the computer's own choice.

What goes wrong: On a network SSD there is no 'stop that command' step. A command that runs out of time while connected (LIVE) starts network error recovery. This removes all command lists and connects again.

How you can tell: I/O tag N (CID) type T opcode 0x.. (Name) QID Q timeout (TCP), then reconnect messages. Every command still running is tried again or moved to another path.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Drop only the answer packets for one command list, with a narrow firewall rule. Safe in a lab. Collect the Linux kernel log (dmesg). Collect a network capture that shows a command message with no answer message.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Only by a timer. Nothing records an error. The only sign is a time limit running out. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The target is at fault if the command arrived and was never answered. The computer or network is at fault if the command never left the computer, or network messages (PDUs) were lost. · Test that confirms it: a network capture (E10).

T-30 The secure network log-in does not finish in time (TLS handshake) Not seen in the packets Not on this wire

Packets seen in the test recording

Error family: E10 (a kind of evidence from outside the recording: a network capture). · Can the packets alone prove it? No. It cannot be seen on this wire. The recording only shows packets around it. The proof is outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe/TCP network rules support a secure connection (TLS). The time limit is the computer's own choice.

What goes wrong: With a secure (TLS) NVMe/TCP connection, the Linux kernel asks a helper to do the secure log-in (handshake). It must finish within tls_handshake_timeout (a Linux computer setting). If not, the connect try fails and reconnecting goes on.

How you can tell: Connect fails with a timeout error. 'Reconnecting in N seconds' repeats.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Stop the helper program tlshd and try a secure connect. Safe. Collect the Linux kernel log (dmesg) and the tlshd logs. Check /sys/module/nvme_tcp/parameters/tls_handshake_timeout.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Only by a timer. Nothing records an error. The only sign is a time limit running out. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The computer's software is at fault when tlshd is missing or slow, or keys are missing. The target or network is at fault when the first log-in message (ClientHello) is sent but not answered. · Test that confirms it: a network capture (E10).

T-31 The SSD needs a pause before its 'ready' flag is read (quirk) Seen in the packets SSD main settings

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 448638: the computer reads the status setting (CSTS) right after 'switch on' (CC.EN=1). It gets back 0xFFFFFFFF, because the SSD is not ready to be read.

Packet=448638 | Link Dir=Downstream | TLP Type=MRd(32) | PSN=180 | Tag=17 | RequesterID=000:00:0 | Address=FCE0001C | Length=1 | Time Stamp=0228.151736403870s | Time Delta=168.630 ns | LCRC=0x9AE3AC35

Error family: P13, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. A check on the order and timing of packets finds it. Examples: a missing answer, a long gap, packets out of order.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: This is not in the rule book. It is a work-around for SSDs that do not follow the rules.

What goes wrong: Some SSDs go wrong if the computer reads the 'ready' flag (CSTS.RDY) right after clearing 'switch on' (CC.EN). Linux works around them with a fixed 2.3 s pause. A new SSD may have the same bug but be missing from Linux's list of odd SSDs (quirk list). It then fails to restart or start up.

How you can tell: Without the work-around, restart fails (Device not ready; aborting reset), or the SSD hangs. With the work-around, every restart is 2.3 s slower.

How to fix it and prove the fix: On an SSD that needs it, load nvme with quirks=VID:DID:^delay_before_chk_rdy and run nvme reset. Take care. Compare restart time with and without the work-around. Use the nvme.quirks=VID:DID:delay_before_chk_rdy setting. Put ^ before the name to turn off a built-in work-around. Linux reads this setting in pci.c.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Only by a timer. Nothing records an error. The only sign is a time limit running out. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD is at fault: its program cannot answer setting reads right after CC changes. The computer is at fault only because its work-around list does not include that SSD's id. · Test that confirms it: compare with and without the work-around (take care).

T-32 The computer froze, but it looks like an SSD timeout Partly seen in the packets Not on this wire

Packets seen in the test recording

Error family: E01 and E05 (kinds of evidence from outside the recording). · Can the packets alone prove it? Partly. The timing and order of the packets show its shape. Proof needs evidence from outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: No rule covers this. It is the computer's own behaviour.

What goes wrong: The SSD finished on time. But the computer could not handle the done note. Maybe the processor froze (soft lockup), or signals were turned off for seconds. Maybe the virtual machine was paused or moved, or memory was under pressure (NUMA). The NVMe timer runs out anyway.

How you can tell: NVMe timeout messages appear, often with 'completion polled' (see error type T-21 in the error list). Next to them are soft-lockup or RCU-stall warnings, or a virtual machine pause in the hypervisor log. The SSD's own logs show nothing.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Pause a virtual machine (virsh suspend) for longer than io_timeout during reads and writes, then wake it. Safe. Line up the timeouts with these warnings: watchdog: BUG: soft lockup, rcu: INFO: rcu_sched detected stalls, time taken by the hypervisor ('st' in top), and perf sched. The capture tool shows the done note and the 'work is done' signal (MSI-X) were sent on time.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Things keep working, only slower. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The computer's software or hardware is at fault when the done note and MSI-X are on time. Causes: a freeze, signals turned off, a virtual machine pause, or a storm of system-management interrupts (SMI). The SSD is at fault when the done note is late. · Test that confirms it: the Linux kernel log (E01).

T-33 A request that needs an answer never gets one (completion timeout) Seen in the packets Answer never arrives in time

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 1283859: a read request (MRd) that fetches data to write. The wire gave a receipt, but no answer ever came.

Packet=1283859 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MRd(64) | PSN=1556 | Tag=104 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000002:DC3C8000 | Length=128 | Time Stamp=1235.574180650370s | Time Delta=104.130 ns | LCRC=0x31A40A21

Packet 1283862: an 'answer never arrived' error is reported: ERR_NONFATAL, about 50 ms after the read request.

Packet=1283862 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=Msg | PSN=1557 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Length=0 | Time Stamp=1235.624180650370s | Time Delta=129.130 ns | LCRC=0xA4398C0B

Packet 1283865: the done note (CQE) says 'Data Transfer Error' (SCT0 SC 0x04).

Packet=1283865 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=1558 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000004:83390040 | Length=4 | DATA=16 B | Time Stamp=1235.624220650370s | Time Delta=0.000 ns | LCRC=0xF4866996

Error family: P03, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. The checker marks it in this table file as a wrong detail or order. The mark means: an answer did not arrive in time (completion_timeout).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book has a time limit for an answer to arrive (completion timeout). It is set in the Device Capabilities 2 and Device Control 2 settings. The PCIe error report (AER) has bit 14 for it, in the 'cannot fix' group. By default it counts as not fatal (check this in the rule book). The start of the late request is saved only if the part supports saving it (header logging).

What goes wrong: A sender sends a request that needs an answer. It can be a memory read, a settings read or write, or an I/O request. No answer (completion) arrives within the time limit. The request is given up.

How you can tell: Bit 14 of the 'cannot fix' error status (Completion Timeout, PCI_ERR_UNC_COMP_TIME) is set in the sender. Linux prints the error name 'CmpltTO' and names the side as Requester. The computer's port may be the sender, for example when the processor reads the SSD's status setting (CSTS). Then the processor gets all-ones data. Some computers then raise a machine-check error. With the port's extra error features (DPC PIO), the port logs 'Memory Request Completion Timeout' or 'Configuration Request Completion Timeout'.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Hold the SSD in reset while the computer reads its memory window (BAR). Use a test device (exerciser) or a switch you can control. Or use a test device that holds back answers. On Linux, aer_inject (drivers/pci/pcie/aer_inject.c) can add the error record with no real traffic. Take care: on some computers, a real missing answer can freeze a processor core. Run dmesg | grep -i -E "aer|CmpltTO". Check the counts in /sys/bus/pci/devices/BDF/aer_dev_nonfatal. In lspci -vvv, the UESta line shows 'CmpltTO+'. With the capture tool, find a read (MRd or CfgRd) with no answer (Cpl or CplD) within the set time. Match by request number (tag).

Does the SSD or computer report it? Yes. A setting, a result number or a log in the SSD or computer records it. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD is at fault if a computer read sent to the SSD (Downstream) gets no answer. The computer's hardware is at fault if the SSD reads computer memory (Upstream) and gets no answer with data. The wire is at fault if other wire trouble happens at the same time (error families P06 and P08). That means 'arrived broken' receipts (Nak), sending again, or wire recovery. · Test that confirms it: the error report (AER) log for a missing answer.

T-34 The answer time limit is off, or longer than other timers Partly seen in the packets Answer never arrives in time

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 1288608: a read request (MRd) that never gets an answer.

Packet=1288608 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MRd(64) | PSN=2994 | Tag=193 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000002:CBB91000 | Length=128 | Time Stamp=1235.624552998250s | Time Delta=109.120 ns | LCRC=0xFF28969C

Error family: P03, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. Also E02 (a kind of evidence from outside the recording). · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. The checker marks it in this table file as a wrong detail or order. The mark means: an answer did not arrive in time (completion_timeout).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book lets the answer time limit be turned off (Completion Timeout Disable, Device Control 2 bit 4). This is allowed only if Device Capabilities 2 bit 4 says the part supports it.

What goes wrong: If the answer time limit is off, a lost answer never makes an error. The request and its request number (tag) are stuck forever. If the limit is set to Range D (seconds), it runs out after the NVMe or program time limit. So the higher software restarts first, and the real cause is never logged.

How you can tell: No error report (AER) entry. Instead there is an NVMe command timeout (see error type T-22 in the error list). Or a processor is stuck on a read (watchdog soft lockup) when the computer's port has no time limit. Running out of request numbers can stop all further data moves from the SSD.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Run lspci -vvv and check DevCtl2 for the drive and every port on the way. Look for 'TimeoutDis+' or a value in seconds. A check that only reads: setpci -s BDF CAP_EXP+28.w. Compare with /sys/class/nvme/nvme0/io_timeout.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Only by a timer. Nothing records an error. The only sign is a time limit running out. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The computer's hardware is at fault when the setting comes from the computer. The BIOS or its program writes DevCtl2 during start-up. The SSD is at fault when the limit is off although DevCap2 says that is not supported. It is also at fault when it ignores the time range it was given. · Test that confirms it: check the answer time limit settings.

T-35 A packet gets no receipt in time and is resent (replay timer) Seen in the packets Packets sent again (replay)

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 312023: a packet is sent again after the resend timer ran out. No receipt (Ack or Nak) came in between.

Packet=312023 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(32) | PSN=2919 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=0018D000 | Length=64 | DATA=256 B | Time Stamp=0130.948481789870s | Time Delta=167.130 ns | LCRC=0x6E5385FB

Packet 312025: a fixable error 'Replay Timer Timeout' is reported.

Packet=312025 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=Msg | PSN=2920 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Length=0 | Time Stamp=0130.948482789870s | Time Delta=141.130 ns | LCRC=0x21982E81

Error family: P06, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. The checker marks it in this table file as a wrong detail or order. The mark means: the same packet number sent again (tlp_replayed_same_psn).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book has a resend timer (REPLAY_TIMER). Its limit comes from tables and formulas in the rule book. They depend on the largest data size, the number of lanes and the speed, plus inside delays and power-saving adjustments. The timer starts again whenever receipts show progress.

What goes wrong: Each request or data packet (TLP) that is sent stays in a resend store. It stays until the other side sends an 'arrived fine' receipt (Ack, a small receipt packet). If the resend timer runs out first, the sender sends again every packet with no receipt.

How you can tell: Bit 12 of the fixable error status is set (Replay Timer Timeout, PCI_ERR_COR_REP_TIMER). Linux names it 'Timeout', and the side is Transmitter. Computers usually hide these or limit how often they are shown. The command takes a few microseconds longer. Many of them mean the wire is weak.

How to fix it and prove the fix: In lspci -vvv, CESta shows 'Timeout+'. Check the aer_dev_correctable counts in sysfs (they count each bit). With the capture tool, look for a packet sent again with the same packet number. No 'arrived broken' receipt (Nak) comes in between.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Yes. A setting, a result number or a log in the SSD or computer records it. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The wire is at fault if broken receipts or broken packets come just before the resend. Broken receipts have a bad CRC 16 (error types L-03 and X-16 in the error list). Broken packets have a bad LCRC. The receiver in direction D is at fault if its receipts are good but late. See error types T-37 and X-20. The receiver is the side that must send receipts. It is the computer's port when D is Upstream, and the SSD when D is Downstream. The sender in direction D is at fault if it resent too early (PREMATURE, a gap shorter than the timer). It is also at fault if its timer differs from the rule-book table. · Test that confirms it: compare error report (AER) counts before and after (T1).
