Packet=315943 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=Msg | PSN=4009 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Length=0 | Time Stamp=0130.948751010500s | Time Delta=127.120 ns | LCRC=0x4A5C9CD8

Error family: P06, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. The checker marks it in this table file as a wrong detail or order. The mark means: the same packet number sent again (tlp_replayed_same_psn).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book has a resend count (REPLAY_NUM). When it rolls over, the rule is to start the wire's start-up steps again (link retraining). It is reported as a fixable error.

What goes wrong: REPLAY_NUM is a 2-bit count of resends with no progress. It rolls over at the fourth try to resend the same packet. Then the wire's receipt layer tells its signal layer to redo the start-up steps (Recovery).

How you can tell: Fixable error bit 8 is set (REPLAY_NUM Rollover, Linux name 'Rollover'). The wire goes into recovery. If recovery fails, the wire goes down and the SSD disappears. This is 'Surprise Down' (error type T-44 in the error list). Speed drops during each restart of the wire.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Same as error type T-35, with a worse signal. Take care: the wire may go down. In lspci -vvv, CESta shows 'Rollover+'. The computer port's LnkSta 'Link Training' bit is set, or speed or lane count change. Linux speed messages come from drivers/pci/pcie/bwctrl.c. With the capture tool: the same packet sent again and again, then wire-training signals (TS1 ordered sets, meaning Recovery).

Does the SSD or computer report it? Yes. A setting, a result number or a log in the SSD or computer records it. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The wire is at fault when the other direction shows bad receipts during the series. These are 'arrived broken' receipts (Nak) or broken receipts (bad CRC 16). The receiver in direction D is at fault when the other side is silent. It is also at fault when it sends good receipt packets but never 'arrived fine' (receiver hang or bug). The sender in direction D is at fault when the wire does not restart after the rollover (NO_RETRAIN). The error report (AER) names the sender, because the error list calls Rollover a sender error. · Test that confirms it: compare error report (AER) counts before and after (T1).

T-37 Receipts come too late: needless resends and lost speed (Ack latency) Seen in the packets Packets sent again (replay)

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 316959: a needless resend. The 'arrived fine' receipt (Ack) comes after the resend timer ran out.

Packet=316959 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=215 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000003:720E4000 | Length=64 | DATA=256 B | Time Stamp=0130.948888256620s | Time Delta=0.000 ns | LCRC=0xE81E52C3

Error family: P06, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. The checker marks it in this table file as a wrong detail or order. The mark means: the same packet number sent again (tlp_replayed_same_psn).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book sets a time limit for sending receipts (AckNak_LATENCY_TIMER). It is given in tables by data size, lane count and speed. It should be well below the other side's resend limit.

What goes wrong: The receiver must send an 'arrived fine' receipt (Ack) within its receipt time limit. Some receivers wait too long to send one receipt for many packets. Then the sender's resend timer runs out, even though nothing was broken.

How you can tell: The other side reports fixable 'Replay Timer Timeout' errors (see error type T-35 in the error list). Neither side reports broken packets (Bad TLP) or broken receipts (Bad DLLP). Speed is lower than expected, because the resend store fills up and the sender has to wait.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Read and write in order at the highest speed, and check the gaps between receipts in the capture tool. Safe. In the capture tool, measure the time from the end of a packet to its receipt (Ack DLLP). Compare it with the rule-book table for the lane count, speed and largest data size (MPS) in use. Test speed with fio, reading in order with many commands at once.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Things keep working, only slower. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The receiver in direction D (the side that sends receipts) is at fault. When D is Downstream, that is the SSD (its receipts travel upstream, as the error list says). When D is Upstream, that is the computer's port (computer hardware). The wire is at fault only if broken receipts (bad CRC 16) are present. · Test that confirms it: a speed and timing test.

T-38 One side stops giving room to send (credit starvation, no UpdateFC) Seen in the packets Room-to-send counts (credits)

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 353387: the last write-type packet (posted TLP) before the room for such packets runs out.

Packet=353387 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=793 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000002:58FDE700 | Length=64 | DATA=256 B | Time Stamp=0131.481605254620s | Time Delta=0.000 ns | LCRC=0xACE14C77

Packet 353389: requests that need an answer (non-posted) still get through.

Packet=353389 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MRd(32) | PSN=794 | Tag=133 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=6D4E7000 | Length=16 | Time Stamp=0131.481605290250s | Time Delta=0.000 ns | LCRC=0x972C6A94

Error family: P07, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. A check on the order and timing of packets finds it. Examples: a missing answer, a long gap, packets out of order.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book has small receipt packets that give room to send (InitFC1, InitFC2, UpdateFC credits). There are three kinds: Posted, Non-Posted and Completion, each with header and data credits. UpdateFC is sent when room is freed. It is also sent about every 30 µs while room is not unlimited (a rule-book timing). There is an optional 200 µs watchdog for updates (check this in the rule book).

What goes wrong: A sender may send a packet only when the receiver has given room for it (credits). If the receiver stops giving room back (no UpdateFC packets), traffic of that kind stops. The rule book has no error for 'room given too slowly'. Only timers in higher software notice.

How you can tell: Nothing shows on the stuck wire itself. There are two exceptions. The optional update watchdog may restart the wire. Or a wrong room update is caught as a 'Flow Control Protocol Error' (error report bit 13, PCI_ERR_UNC_FCP). Signs show in higher software. They are missing answers (error type T-33) and NVMe command timeouts (error type T-22 in the error list).

How to fix it and prove the fix: Set a test device (exerciser) to hold back room updates for write-type packets while the computer writes doorbells. Risky, test machine only. Most capture tools count the room left. In that view, the room count stays at zero while the other side has packets waiting. lspci cannot show room counts.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Only by a timer. Nothing records an error. The only sign is a time limit running out. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Look at the side that gives room (advertiser A). If room updates stopped from the SSD (Upstream receipt packets), the SSD is at fault. If they stopped from the computer's port (Downstream receipt packets), the computer's hardware is at fault. It may also be a switch's store (error list, section XII.8). · Test that confirms it: decode the Linux kernel error report (AER) log (T2).

T-39 A wire start-up step times out: it loops, falls back or slows Seen in the packets Wire start-up steps

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 131058: the signal-tuning step (equalization phase 3) runs out of time at 16 GT/s. The wire falls back to 8 GT/s.

Packet=131058 | Link Dir=Upstream | Ord.Set Type=SDS | Time Stamp=0125.886736941250s | Time Delta=16.250 ns

Error family: P08, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. A check on the order and timing of packets finds it. Examples: a missing answer, a long gap, packets out of order.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book sets a time limit for each start-up step (LTSSM state). Detect.Quiet is 12 ms (checked). Polling.Active is 24 ms, Polling.Configuration 48 ms, Configuration.Linkwidth.Start 24 ms, and other Configuration steps 2 ms. Recovery.RcvrLock is 24 ms, Recovery.RcvrCfg 48 ms, Recovery.Idle 2 ms. These need checking in the rule book. Signal-tuning (equalization) steps at 8 GT/s and above also have time limits (check these too).

What goes wrong: Each start-up step has a time limit from the rule book. If the expected wire-training signals (ordered sets) do not come in time, the wire moves on. Detect repeats every 12 ms while no receiver is found. Polling and Configuration fall back to Detect. Recovery may fall back to Detect, which means the wire goes down. Partly working again and again ends with a wire that has fewer lanes or a lower speed.

How you can tell: No error report (AER) for a slow-down that works. lspci -vvv LnkSta shows 'Speed 8GT/s (downgraded), Width x2 (downgraded)', compared with LnkCap. Check the computer port's LnkSta2 tuning bits and Link Bandwidth Management Status. At worst the wire never reaches working state (L0), and the SSD is missing.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Turn lanes off with a lane-disabling board (interposer). Or force a target speed with setpci on Link Control 2 and restart the wire. Risky, test machine only: the wire can drop. Compare LnkCap and LnkSta at both ends. In the capture tool's start-up view, check how long each step took and which one ran out of time. Check Linux bwctrl.c speed-change messages. Look for repeated wire up and down events in the Linux kernel log (dmesg, pciehp: 'Link Down', 'Link Up').

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Things keep working, only slower. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The wire is at fault when lanes fail. They may fail to find the receiver or lock on to the signal. Or they fail tuning at 16 or 32 GT/s. The SSD or the computer's hardware is at fault when a clean wire still fails in a swap test. See the error list, section XII.8. · Test that confirms it: compare what the wire can do with what it is doing now (E02).

T-40 The wire does not come up in time after reset or power-on Seen in the packets Wire start-up steps

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 136506: the receiver is found about 1 s after reset. The requirement is 100 ms.

Packet=136506 | Link Event=Receiver Detect | Time Stamp=0126.948781634000s | Time Delta=0.000 ns

Error family: P08, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. Also E07 (a kind of evidence from outside the recording). · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. A check on the order and timing of packets finds it. Examples: a missing answer, a long gap, packets out of order.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book has timing rules for reset and wire start-up. Comments in drivers/pci/pci.c quote them. Start the Detect step within 20 ms. Wait at least 100 ms before settings requests. Wait at least 1 s before calling a silent device broken. The settings DLLLARC (Link Capabilities), DLLLA and LT (Link Status) are part of this.

What goes wrong: After a reset, the SSD must start the Detect step within 20 ms (rule book). The computer's software must then wait before sending settings requests. The wire must be up, and a further 100 ms must pass (rule book). Above 5 GT/s, the 100 ms counts from when the wire's receipt layer is active. If the wire is not active within the computer's wait, the software says the SSD is missing.

How you can tell: In Linux, the SSD is not found, or the log says not ready Nms after bus reset; giving up. For ports that allow plugging in while on, there is no 'Link Up' event. Some ports cannot report that their receipt layer is active. Then Linux just sleeps 1000 ms plus a delay and hopes.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Delay the SSD's reset signal release (PERST#) with a board you can control. Or restart the bus with /sys/bus/pci/devices/BDF/reset. Take care: this resets the SSD. Run the Linux kernel log (dmesg) with PCI debug on (dyndbg="file drivers/pci/* +p"). It shows 'waiting N ms for downstream link'. With the capture tool, note the time of the PERST# release. Compare it with the first wire-training signal (TS1) and with the working state (L0).

Does the SSD or computer report it? Only by a timer. Nothing records an error. The only sign is a time limit running out. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD is at fault if PERST# was released and the clock (refclk) was there. But no TS1 came from the SSD within 20 ms. The computer's hardware is at fault if PERST# or the clock came late. It is also at fault if its first settings read (CfgRd) came before 100 ms (error list, section XII.8). · Test that confirms it: an oscilloscope or logic capture of the power lines and side signals (E07).

T-41 SSD not ready after reset: 'try again' past 1 s, or silence Seen in the packets Answer says refused or retry

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 70548: 1535 ms after a function reset (FLR), the SSD still answers 'not ready, try again'. This answer is called Configuration Request Retry Status.

Packet=70548 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=Cpl | PSN=2165 | Tag=30 | RequesterID=000:00:0 | CompleterID=002:00:0 | Cpl Status=CRS | Byte Cnt=4 | Time Stamp=0063.585583414750s | Time Delta=118.620 ns | LCRC=0x1482B43D

Error family: P04 and P19, two of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. The checker marks it in this table file as a wrong detail or order. The mark means: an answer that says 'not ready yet, try again' (completion_status_CRS).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book says a device must be ready 1 s after a normal reset. It allows 'try again' answers (RRS). A Root Control setting, 'Configuration RRS Software Visibility Enable', makes a Vendor ID read return the special value 0001h. Other related parts are the Readiness Time Reporting feature and the 'device ready' (DRS) and 'function ready' (FRS) messages. The Status setting also has a 'ready at once' bit (Immediate Readiness).

What goes wrong: This applies after a normal reset, or after waking from full power-off (D3cold to D0). The SSD must accept settings requests within 1 s (rule book). It may answer 'try again' (Request Retry Status, RRS, once called CRS) to ask for more time. An SSD that keeps answering 'try again', or answers all ones, is 'not ready'.

How you can tell: Linux prints pci BDF: not ready 1023ms after FLR; waiting, then ready Nms after .... Or, after 60 s (the Linux computer's limit), it prints not ready 65535ms after ...; giving up. During start-up, pci_bus_wait_rrs() prints not ready after Nms; giving up. The NVMe driver never starts.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Start a function reset with echo 1 > /sys/bus/pci/devices/BDF/reset. Take care: unbind the NVMe driver first, because data on the way is lost. Time the 'ready Nms' message. Check the Linux kernel log (dmesg) lines above. lspci -s BDF -vvv may return 'Unknown header type 7f' (all ones). With the capture tool: settings reads (CfgRd0) answered again and again with result RRS.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Only by a timer. Nothing records an error. The only sign is a time limit running out. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD is at fault when power and the reset signal (PERST#) are fine. Its program may start slower than 1 s, or keep restarting itself. The computer's hardware is at fault if power or PERST# come in the wrong order (check with an oscilloscope, E07). · Test that confirms it: the Linux kernel 'ready' log.

T-42 The SSD is used before its 10 ms wake-up (D3hot to D0) Seen in the packets SSD settings area and readiness

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 37686: the computer sets the power setting (PMCSR) from light sleep (D3hot) to fully on (D0).

Packet=37686 | Link Dir=Downstream | TLP Type=CfgWr0 | PSN=781 | Tag=8 | RequesterID=000:00:0 | Length=1 | DATA=4 B | Time Stamp=0000.822445348750s | Time Delta=128.120 ns | LCRC=0x74945DE0

Packet 37693: a read of the SSD's main settings (MMIO) 2 ms after D0. That is less than the 10 ms wake-up time. The answer is 'unsupported request' (UR).

Packet=37693 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=Cpl | PSN=1981 | Tag=9 | RequesterID=000:00:0 | CompleterID=002:00:0 | Cpl Status=UR | Byte Cnt=4 | Time Stamp=0000.824446199750s | Time Delta=171.620 ns | LCRC=0x1B215539

Error family: P19, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. The checker marks it in this table file as a wrong detail or order. The mark means: an answer that says 'unsupported request' (completion_status_UR).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCI power rule book (PCI Power Management) sets a wake-up time of 10 ms. That is from light sleep (D3hot) to fully on (D0). A 'No Soft Reset' bit says whether the SSD keeps its settings.

What goes wrong: The computer's software writes PowerState=D0 to wake an SSD that was in light sleep. It must then wait 10 ms before using it (rule book), unless the SSD says otherwise. Using it earlier, or using an SSD that needs longer, gives results no one can predict.

How you can tell: Settings reads return junk or all ones. Reads of the main settings run out of time (see error type T-33 in the error list). The NVMe driver sees CSTS=0xffffffff on wake-up. For SSDs known to be bad, Linux uses a longer wait (work-arounds of 20 ms or 120 ms).

How to fix it and prove the fix: Turn on automatic power control: echo auto > /sys/bus/pci/devices/BDF/power/control. Let the SSD go idle, then measure the wake-up. Safe. Use the Linux kernel log (dmesg) with power debug on. With the capture tool, look for a settings write (CfgWr) to PMCSR (D0). Then a settings read (CfgRd) sooner than 10 ms gets a bad answer.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Only by a timer. Nothing records an error. The only sign is a time limit running out. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The computer is at fault if the gap after a proven wake-up write is too short. Too short means under 10 ms, or under the SSD's stated D3hot-to-D0 time. The SSD is at fault if the gap is long enough and its settings are back, but access still fails. The settings are the memory window (BAR) and Command. The computer's hardware is at fault only if the sender is not the operating system. The request number of the sender (RequesterID) then shows a firmware or management-chip (BMC) path. · Test that confirms it: a sleep and wake cycle while the capture tool records.

T-43 A function reset does not finish within 100 ms (FLR) Seen in the packets SSD settings area and readiness

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 39516: the computer starts a function reset (FLR).

Packet=39516 | Link Dir=Downstream | TLP Type=CfgWr0 | PSN=891 | Tag=17 | RequesterID=000:00:0 | Length=1 | DATA=4 B | Time Stamp=0000.856859348870s | Time Delta=139.130 ns | LCRC=0x39602E71

Packet 39535: the SSD still answers 'not ready, try again' (CRS) about 500 ms after the function reset.

Packet=39535 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=Cpl | PSN=2802 | Tag=21 | RequesterID=000:00:0 | CompleterID=002:00:0 | Cpl Status=CRS | Byte Cnt=4 | Time Stamp=0001.256862261870s | Time Delta=111.630 ns | LCRC=0x4232A31C

Error family: P19, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. The checker marks it in this table file as a wrong detail or order. The mark means: an answer that says 'not ready yet, try again' (completion_status_CRS).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book has a function reset (FLR). Device Capabilities has an FLR bit. Device Control bit 15 starts it. The reset must finish within 100 ms (rule book). The Device Status setting has a 'Transactions Pending' bit.

What goes wrong: After 'start function reset', the SSD must finish the reset within 100 ms (rule book). During that time it may drop requests without saying so. The computer's software should also wait for open requests to finish before starting the reset.

How you can tell: Linux prints timed out waiting for pending transaction; performing function level reset anyway. This means the 'Transactions Pending' bit was still set after about 700 ms of checking. Then pci_dev_wait() prints 'ready' messages (see error type T-41 in the error list).

How to fix it and prove the fix: Start a function reset with echo 1 > /sys/bus/pci/devices/BDF/reset. Take care: unbind the NVMe driver first, because data on the way is lost. Time the 'ready Nms' message. Check the Linux kernel log (dmesg) lines above. lspci -s BDF -vvv may return 'Unknown header type 7f' (all ones). With the capture tool: settings reads (CfgRd0) answered again and again with result RRS.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Only by a timer. Nothing records an error. The only sign is a time limit running out. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD is at fault if requests 100 ms or more after a proven reset still fail. They get 'try again' (CRS), 'unsupported' (UR), or no answer. The computer is at fault if it started the reset while the SSD's requests were still open. That means 'Transactions Pending' was not respected. It is also at fault if it used the SSD too early. Then it treated an allowed 'try again' (CRS) as a failure. · Test that confirms it: a loop of function resets while the capture tool records.

T-44 The wire drops suddenly, or the SSD is pulled out, during work Partly seen in the packets Wire down, power or restart

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 1349384: the wire goes quiet (electrical idle) with no warning. There is no 'going quiet' signal (EIOS), no power-saving receipt packet and no Hot Reset. The wire went down without anyone asking.

Packet=1349384 | Link Event=Electrical Idle | Time Stamp=1317.010127500000s | Time Delta=0.000 ns

Error family: P12, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. Also E01 and E07 (kinds of evidence from outside the recording). · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. The checker marks it in this table file as a wrong detail or order. The mark means: a request was lost when the wire went down (request_lost_across_link_down).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book has a 'Surprise Down' error and a 'Data Link Layer State Changed' event. It has settings for slots that allow plugging in while on (hot-plug). It also has port containment (Downstream Port Containment, DPC).

What goes wrong: The wire drops with no warning: a cable pulled, a power fault, or a failed wire recovery. Open requests can never finish. The port may report a 'Surprise Down' error and plug events.

How you can tell: The port's 'cannot fix' error bit 5 is set (Surprise Down, PCI_ERR_UNC_SURPDN). This needs a port that can report its receipt layer is active. Slot Status shows 'Data Link Layer State Changed' or 'Presence Detect Changed'. Port containment (DPC) may shut the port. In NVMe, reads of CSTS return all ones, and the SSD is removed. Commands fail with a computer path error. With more than one path (multipath), they move to another path.

How to fix it and prove the fix: In the Linux kernel log (dmesg), look for pciehp 'Link Down' and error report 'Surprise Down'. Also look for DPC containment messages, and NVMe 'controller is down' or removal. Run lspci -vvv on the port: SltSta shows 'DLActive-'.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Yes. A setting, a result number or a log in the SSD or computer records it. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD is at fault if its own traffic (Upstream) stops first. Meanwhile the computer keeps sending, and slot power and the reset signal (PERST#) stay steady. The computer's hardware or the wire is at fault if both directions stop together. The same if slot power or PERST# drop, or the SSD was pulled out. See E07, E01 pciehp, and section XII.8. · Test that confirms it: the Linux kernel log.

T-45 Waking the wire takes longer than the SSD accepts (ASPM exit latency) Seen in the packets Wire start-up steps

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 139242: waking the wire from power saving (L1) took about 180 us. The SSD says it can accept only 64 us (its L1 acceptable latency).

Packet=139242 | Link Dir=Downstream | Ord.Set Type=SDS | Time Stamp=0126.961704870620s | Time Delta=91.870 ns

Error family: P08 and P20, two of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. A check on the order and timing of packets finds it. Examples: a missing answer, a long gap, packets out of order.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book has these settings. Link Capabilities gives the L0s and L1 wake times (Exit Latency). Device Capabilities gives the SSD's L0s and L1 acceptable wait (Acceptable Latency). Link Control turns wire power saving on (ASPM Control).

What goes wrong: Each port says how long it needs to wake the wire from L0s and L1. Each SSD says how long a wait it can accept. These are each side's own promises. The wake time may be longer than the acceptable wait. For L1, add 1 µs for each switch on the way. Then turning that power-saving state on can starve the SSD.

How you can tell: If it is turned on anyway (by the computer's start-up program or a forced choice), commands get sudden slow spikes. Sometimes there are missing answers or resend errors after waking from L1. If Linux finds the mismatch, it quietly does not turn the state on. Power use is higher, and there is no error.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Run lspci -vvv. LnkCap shows 'ASPM L0s L1, Exit Latency L0s <1us, L1 <8us'. DevCap shows 'Latency L0s <64ns, L1 <1us'. LnkCtl shows 'ASPM L1 Enabled'. Compare with /sys/module/pcie_aspm/parameters/policy. Measure fio times with wire power saving on and off (pcie_aspm=off).

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Things keep working, only slower. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD is at fault if its wake time is longer than what it stated itself. The computer's hardware is at fault if the BIOS or operating system turned wire power saving on anyway. That is wrong when the LnkCap wake time is longer than the DevCap acceptable wait (error list, section XII.8). · Test that confirms it: compare what the wire can do with what it is doing now (E02).

T-46 Wrong deep power-saving settings: slow wake or lost wire (L1 substates, LTR) Partly seen in the packets Power saving and wake-up

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 1331246: waking from deep wire power saving (L1.2) took 380 us. The SSD's stated wait it can take (LTR) was 1 us.

Packet=1331246 | Link Dir=Downstream | Ord.Set Type=SDS | Time Stamp=1300.469966220620s | Time Delta=91.870 ns

Packet 1331284: the first command after waking.

Packet=1331284 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=2696 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000004:83610010 | Length=4 | DATA=16 B | Time Stamp=1300.470044515000s | Time Delta=52.880 ns | LCRC=0xA037CDAD

Error family: P20, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. Also E02 and E07 (kinds of evidence from outside the recording). · Can the packets alone prove it? Partly. The timing and order of the packets show its shape. Proof needs evidence from outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book has a deep power-saving feature (L1 PM Substates, feature id 1Eh). It has a capabilities part and two control parts. Control 1 has on/off switches, Common_Mode_Restore_Time, and the LTR_L1.2_THRESHOLD value and scale. Control 2 has the T_POWER_ON scale and value. It also has a 'how long I can wait' feature (LTR, id 18h) with Max Snoop and No-Snoop Latency. Device Control 2 has 'LTR Mechanism Enable'.

What goes wrong: The deeper states L1.1 and L1.2 turn off more of the wire's signal circuits. Going in depends on the SSD's 'how long I can wait' value (LTR) compared with LTR_L1.2_THRESHOLD. Waking timing depends on T_POWER_ON and Common_Mode_Restore_Time. Wrong values make waking slower than the SSD can take, or make waking fail.

How you can tell: Commands are suddenly slow after idle. In bad cases, the wire fails to start up again after L1.2, and the drive disappears. See error types T-15 and T-44 in the error list. No error is reported for a slow wake.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Run lspci -vvv. Look at 'L1SubCap', 'L1SubCtl1: PCI-PM_L1.2+ ASPM_L1.2+ ... T_CommonMode=..us LTR1.2_Threshold=..ns', 'L1SubCtl2: T_PwrOn=..us', and 'LTR+' in DevCtl2. Compare both ends of the wire. Try again with L1.2 turned off.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Things keep working, only slower. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The computer or its hardware is at fault if the two ends are set up differently. This is done by Linux aspm_calc_l12_info or by the BIOS. It is also at fault if L1.2 is entered with LTR below the threshold. The SSD is at fault if the settings agree but its LTR values are fake. See error type N-48. It is also at fault if its wire circuits need longer than the T_POWER_ON it states. · Test that confirms it: compare both ends.

T-47 The slowest few commands miss the speed target (tail latency, p99) Partly seen in the packets Speed (timing counts)

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 1580200: some reads take 48 ms, among reads that usually take about 80 us.

Packet=1580200 | Link Dir=Upstream | DLLP Type=ACK | Time Stamp=1820.048514297620s | Time Delta=2.593 ms | AckNak Seq Num=3563

Error family: P22, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. Also E05 and E09 (kinds of evidence from outside the recording). · Can the packets alone prove it? Partly. The timing and order of the packets show its shape. Proof needs evidence from outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: No rule covers this. The NVMe and PCIe rule books set no time limit per command. The speed target (SLA) is your own. Some rule-book features play a part. One is choosing which list goes next (CC.AMS, Arbitration feature 01h). One is grouping 'work is done' signals (feature 08h). And one is the wake times of SSD and wire power saving (APST, ASPM).

What goes wrong: The middle command time is fine. But a small share of commands take tens or hundreds of times longer. A service with a target for its slowest commands (a percentile target) fails, even though every command worked.

How you can tell: No error anywhere. Only the spread of command times shows it: fio clat percentiles, a program's own time charts, or blk-mq counts.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Run a read-time check with one command at a time (QD1), while a second job keeps writing to random places. Compare the slowest-command numbers with and without the writer. The check is safe. The writer erases data in the area it writes. Use fio --name=t --rw=randread --bs=4k --iodepth=1 --runtime=600 --time_based --lat_percentiles=1 --percentile_list=50:99:99.9:99.99 --filename=/dev/nvme0n1 (reads only). Use bpftrace on nvme:nvme_setup_cmd and nvme:nvme_complete_rq for each command's time. Line up slow commands with the health log temperature, the power state (nvme get-feature -f 0x02) and the error report (AER) counts.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Things keep working, only slower. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD is at fault if the extra time sits between fetch and done note, with the wire working (L0). The wire is at fault if slow commands overlap wire recovery or resends. The computer is at fault if the wire time is normal but the time it sees (E05) is high. It is also at fault if its doorbells come late. This is in a job that waits for each answer before sending more. · Test that confirms it: slowest-command numbers from fio (tail percentiles).

T-48 The SSD pauses while it tidies its storage (garbage collection stall) Partly seen in the packets Speed (timing counts)

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 1602600: gaps of 9 ms between done notes while commands are open. The SSD is tidying its storage (garbage collection, maintenance).

Packet=1602600 | Link Dir=Upstream | DLLP Type=ACK | Time Stamp=1820.069550235750s | Time Delta=3.259 us | AckNak Seq Num=3738

Error family: P22, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. Also E09 (a kind of evidence from outside the recording). · Can the packets alone prove it? Partly. The timing and order of the packets show its shape. Proof needs evidence from outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The rule book does not cover this. There are related hints the computer can give, where supported. One is 'this space is free now' (Deallocate or TRIM, DSM 09h). Others are Write Zeroes, and Streams or Flexible Data Placement. Another is Predictable Latency Mode (time windows with steady speed).

What goes wrong: When free blocks run low, the SSD must copy the still-used pages out of blocks before it erases them. The computer's commands wait behind this work. This gives slow spikes again and again, from milliseconds to hundreds of milliseconds.

How you can tell: Slow spikes that come with long writing. No error. The Tiny-Tail Flash study (FAST 2017) measured this in a basic design. It reports slow-downs of 5 to 138 times from this tidying. This is for the slowest 1% to 0.01% of commands (the 99th to 99.99th percentiles).

How to fix it and prove the fix: Run a long test that keeps writing to random places, with time logging (--write_lat_log). Plot command time against clock time, and against bytes written. If supported, check the Predictable Latency Mode logs and the Endurance Group logs.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Things keep working, only slower. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD's map and storage manager (FTL) is at fault in this case. Doorbells kept moving, the wire was clean and the computer kept sending. The computer shares the blame if a long recording never shows 'this space is free' (DSM Deallocate). That is no TRIM (error type D-04 in the error list). · Test that confirms it: a time log on a drive first filled to a steady state (preconditioned).

T-49 The SSD slows down because it is too hot (thermal throttling) Partly seen in the packets Speed (timing counts)

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 1619776: the amount of work done per second falls in steps (the SSD is slowing down to cool).

Packet=1619776 | Link Dir=Upstream | DLLP Type=ACK | Time Stamp=1820.071499257500s | Time Delta=2.603 us | AckNak Seq Num=1978

Error family: P22, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. Also E09 (a kind of evidence from outside the recording). · Can the packets alone prove it? Partly. The timing and order of the packets show its shape. Proof needs evidence from outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book has a health log (SMART / Health Information, 02h) with temperature fields and heat-control counts. The SSD's information page gives WCTEMP and CCTEMP. The computer can control heat limits (Host Controlled Thermal Management, feature 10h) within MNTMT and MXTMT. There is also a temperature limit feature (04h).

What goes wrong: The SSD's overall temperature rises past its own heat-control limits. The SSD then works slower to cool down. Commands still work, only slower.

How you can tell: After minutes of work, the work done per second drops and command times rise. The health log shows the temperature fields. They are Composite Temperature, Warning Composite Temperature Time and Critical Composite Temperature Time. Also Thermal Management Temperature 1/2 Transition Count and Total Time. A message from the SSD (Asynchronous Event, health and temperature) may come when a limit is crossed. That part is reported.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Write in order with the airflow blocked. Take care: watch the temperature, and stop before the critical limit. Read nvme smart-log /dev/nvme0 every few seconds during a fio run. Line up the work done per second with the temperature and with the heat-control counts. Check the NVMe sensors in /sys/class/hwmon (Linux drivers/nvme/host/hwmon.c).

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Things keep working, only slower. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD's heat control is the cause. The computer's hardware is at fault if airflow or the heat sink is not enough. It is also at fault if the computer set the heat limits TMT1 or TMT2 low (with Set Features 10h). The wire is at fault if the slow-down is a speed or lane-count change. · Test that confirms it: the health log temperature and heat counts during the run.

T-50 Writing gets far slower once the new SSD fills up (write cliff) Partly seen in the packets Speed (timing counts)

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 1646365: write time jumps from about 15 us to about 900 us.

Packet=1646365 | Link Dir=Downstream | TLP Type=MWr(32) | PSN=48 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=000:00:0 | Address=FCE0100C | Length=1 | DATA=4 B | Time Stamp=1820.081682956250s | Time Delta=101.120 ns | LCRC=0xF2A37AD7

Error family: P22, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. Also E09 (a kind of evidence from outside the recording). · Can the packets alone prove it? Partly. The timing and order of the packets show its shape. Proof needs evidence from outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book does not cover this. A separate rule book says how to fill a drive before testing it (preconditioning). It is the SNIA Solid State Storage Performance Test Specification.

What goes wrong: A new or freshly wiped drive writes into free blocks, and often into a fast cache area (SLC cache). After about one full drive's worth of writes, or once the cache fills, the work done per second drops sharply. It falls to the steady long-run rate.

How you can tell: No error. A chart of work per second over time shows a step down, and command times rise. Speed tests run on an empty drive show better numbers than real long-run use.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Wipe or format, then write in order twice the drive's size. This erases data. Write the whole drive while logging speed once per second (--bwavg_time=1000 --write_bw_log). Find the point where speed drops. Compare with the steady-state numbers on the SSD maker's data sheet.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Things keep working, only slower. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD is the cause when the computer sends steadily and the wire is clean. It ran out of free blocks or fast cache. The test set-up is at fault if the 'slow-down' is only new-drive speed compared with long-run speed. · Test that confirms it: a speed log while filling the whole drive.

T-51 Saving the cache to storage takes far too long (Flush or FUA) Seen in the packets Speed (timing counts)

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 1647713: a 'save the cache to storage' command (Flush) takes 2.5 s.

Packet=1647713 | Link Dir=Downstream | DLLP Type=ACK | Time Stamp=1822.581762790250s | Time Delta=1.860 us | AckNak Seq Num=1503

Error family: P22 and P24, two of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. · Can the packets alone prove it? Partly. The timing and order of the packets show its shape. Proof needs evidence from outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe storage command rule book (NVM Command Set) has Flush (00h) and the FUA bit in Write. The SSD's information page has VWC. There is a write cache feature (Volatile Write Cache, 06h).

What goes wrong: The SSD may hold writes in a cache that is lost at power-off (volatile write cache). Then a Flush, or a write with 'Force Unit Access', must wait until the cached data is in lasting storage. On some drives this takes hundreds of milliseconds or more. Databases that call fsync often get held up.

How you can tell: No error. fsync times spike. If one passes io_timeout (a Linux computer setting), it becomes error type T-22 in the error list.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Run a mix of writes and fsync calls. Compare with the write cache turned off (nvme set-feature -f 0x06 -v 0). Take care: this changes how the drive behaves until a restart or power cycle. Run fio with --fsync=1 or --fdatasync=1 and slowest-command numbers. Use trace points to time command type 0x00. Check VWC with nvme id-ctrl | grep vwc and nvme get-feature -f 0x06.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Things keep working, only slower. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD is at fault when it fetches the command quickly and the wire is working (L0). The slow part is doing the flush. The computer's work is at fault when it sends Flush too often (see error type P-14 in the error list). · Test that confirms it: fsync times.

Chapter D: silent failures, said "success" but the work was not done (33 entries)

Why this part is here: these 33 entries are about the data itself being kept safe and correct (data integrity).

D-01 The SSD says 'space freed' but frees nothing (Deallocate not done) Partly seen in the packets Wrong data in the bytes carried

Packet=1405751 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=798 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000004:841500C0 | Length=4 | DATA=16 B | Time Stamp=1342.637779448500s | Time Delta=39.880 ns | LCRC=0x6DE54FFB

Packet=1405792 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=817 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000004:841500D0 | Length=4 | DATA=16 B | Time Stamp=1342.637873288000s | Time Delta=24.880 ns | LCRC=0x62510CAE

Packet=1405792 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=817 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000004:841500D0 | Length=4 | DATA=16 B | Time Stamp=1342.637873288000s | Time Delta=24.880 ns | LCRC=0x62510CAE

Error family: P23, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. Also E04 (a kind of evidence from outside the recording). · Can the packets alone prove it? Partly. The timing and order of the packets show its shape. Proof needs evidence from outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe storage command rule book (NVM Command Set) has Dataset Management with the 'Deallocate' choice. It frees blocks the computer no longer needs. The storage area's information page (Identify Namespace) has three related parts. DLFEAT (bits 2:0) says what a read of freed blocks gives. The others are NSFEAT bit 2 (DULBE) and NUSE. Feature 05h has a DULBE bit. Whether doing nothing breaks a rule depends on these promises. The Deallocate choice (AD) is often called only a hint (check this in the rule book).

What goes wrong: The computer sends the 'free this space' command (DSM with AD=1) for a range of blocks. The SSD fetches the list of ranges and finishes with result 0 (success). But it keeps every block in the range in use. The old data, the space count and the tidying work all stay as if nothing happened.

How you can tell: Nothing is reported. The done note says 0. There is no Linux kernel log line, no error log entry and no PCIe error report (AER). blkdiscard and fstrim end with 0. Over time, long writing is slower and the drive wears faster than expected. This is because the drive keeps moving data the computer no longer needs.

How to fix it and prove the fix: 1) Confirm the free command and its ranges on the wire, or with blktrace. This rules out error type D-04 in the error list. 2) If DLFEAT RB = 001b or 010b, read back some sample blocks. Old data proves it. 3) If NSFEAT.DULBE is set, turn on Feature 05h bit 16 and read. Success instead of result 287h means the block was not freed. As a control, a block never written must give 287h. 4) Compare NUSE before and after, if the drive counts it. 5) Compare speed with a run that does not free space.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Nothing records it. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD is at fault when the decoded range list is right, and old data or Success comes back. The computer is at fault if no free command was sent (error type D-04). It is also at fault if the ranges are wrong (error type D-06). · Test that confirms it: read back after freeing (error list, lab IV.1).

D-02 The SSD frees only part of the space: ranges or edges skipped Partly seen in the packets Wrong data in the bytes carried

Packet=1407194 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=1274 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000004:84150110 | Length=4 | DATA=16 B | Time Stamp=1342.638248539370s | Time Delta=64.870 ns | LCRC=0x3A4C5FC1

Error family: P23, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. Also E04 (a kind of evidence from outside the recording). · Can the packets alone prove it? Partly. The timing and order of the packets show its shape. Proof needs evidence from outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: NPDG, NPDA, NPDGL and NPDAL give the block size and starting point the SSD prefers for freeing. Freeing ranges that do not line up is allowed. How much is then freed is up to the SSD maker. The exception is when DLFEAT promises a read value for each freed block. DMRL and DMRSL are limits the computer should keep to. What the SSD must do when they are passed: check this in the rule book.

What goes wrong: Only part of the request is done. It may free only the first range of a many-range command. Or only whole lined-up pieces, keeping the start and end that do not line up. Or every range except those larger than an inside limit. The done note still says Success.

How you can tell: Nothing is reported. Reading back gives zeros in the middle of the range, and old data near the edges or in whole parts. NUSE drops by less than NLB (the number of blocks).

How to fix it and prove the fix: Read back the first and last block of every range. Also read one block on each side of each range. With DLFEAT RB = 001b, any non-zero block inside a range breaks the rule, whatever the line-up. Check the change in NUSE against the total of NLB. For many ranges, use a different pattern in each range, so you can tell which range was skipped.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Nothing records it. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD is at fault. The computer is at fault only if the decoded range descriptions themselves are short or wrong. · Test that confirms it: read back the edges.

Error family: P23, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. Also E04 (a kind of evidence from outside the recording). · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. A check on the order and timing of packets finds it. Examples: a missing answer, a long gap, packets out of order.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The storage area's information page has DLFEAT bits 2:0. With 001b or 010b, the read result is fixed. Giving back old data fails the rule book's test (a conformance failure). Linux trusts this promise. nvme_update_ns_info_block() turns DEAC on only when RB = 001b and DLFEAT bit 3 is set.

What goes wrong: The storage area says a read of freed blocks gives zeros (001b) or FFh (010b). After a free that worked, a read gives back the block's old contents. Either the SSD's map and storage manager (FTL) did not free it. Or it freed it, but a cache (read store, write cache, read-ahead) still gives the old page.

How you can tell: The read finishes with Success, but with old data. With data protection (PI) on, the old protection fields may still match the old data. So even the protection checks pass.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Take care. Write a pattern, free it, read at once, wait 10 min idle, read, cut and restore power, read. Also overlap them. Send a Write and a free command to the same blocks, one right after the other. Keep many commands running at once. Then read. The result must be either the new data or the promised value, matching the order the done notes came in. Read back right after the done note, and again after idle time. Read once more after a clean power cycle (nvme subsystem-reset or a real power cycle). Any value that was not promised, at any point, is proof. Collect the storage area's information page (DLFEAT), a recording of the free command, and a hex dump of the read.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Nothing records it. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: First prove the free command and its range on the wire. Then the SSD is at fault: its map, read cache or free-record journal. · Test that confirms it: read back in stages.

D-04 The 'free this space' request never reaches the SSD (discard dropped) Seen in the packets Wrong data in the bytes carried

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 1412097: a write of the test pattern finishes.

Packet=1412097 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=3063 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000004:84150180 | Length=4 | DATA=16 B | Time Stamp=1342.638681345870s | Time Delta=30.870 ns | LCRC=0x9CCBFC96

Packet 1412141: the read used as proof finishes with success.

Packet=1412141 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=3082 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000004:84150190 | Length=4 | DATA=16 B | Time Stamp=1342.638770302370s | Time Delta=71.870 ns | LCRC=0x05EB4D71

Error family: P23, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. Also E04 and E05 (kinds of evidence from outside the recording). · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. A check on the order and timing of packets finds it. Examples: a missing answer, a long gap, packets out of order.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: This is not an SSD problem. ONCS bit 2, on the SSD's information page, decides whether Linux turns on freeing (discard) at all.

What goes wrong: The user believes the space was freed (trimmed), but no free command (DSM) was ever sent. Common reasons: the file system was not mounted with -o discard, and no fstrim was run. Or dm-crypt was used without passing discards through. Or LVM, MD or a virtual disk did not pass discards on. Or discard_max_bytes = 0, because ONCS.DSM is clear or the limit was changed. Or the discard was smaller than discard_granularity and was rounded away.

How you can tell: Mostly nothing is reported. blkdiscard on a drive without discard support does fail (EOPNOTSUPP). But a file-system truncate and many layers just drop the request. The drive is blamed for keeping data it was never told about.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Safe on a spare file system. Mount without discard, write and delete a file, trace for 2 minutes, and see that no free command was sent. Mount again with discard and repeat. Repeat on dm-crypt with and without passing discards through. Run lsblk --discard on every layer. Each layer needs non-zero DISC-GRAN and DISC-MAX. Run blktrace -d /dev/nvme0n1 while truncating or trimming, and look for discard requests (RWBS with D). Turn on the nvme:nvme_setup_cmd trace point, and look for DSM with attributes=4. With the capture tool: no command with OPC 09h means nothing was sent.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Nothing records it. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The computer's software is at fault: file-system mount settings, dm, LVM or virtual layers, or the granularity. The layer whose blktrace or lsblk shows the drop is the one at fault. · Test that confirms it: check discard on every layer.

Error family: P23, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. Also E04 (a kind of evidence from outside the recording). · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. A check on the order and timing of packets finds it. Examples: a missing answer, a long gap, packets out of order.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: In the NVMe storage command rule book, after Write Zeroes finishes, the blocks read as zeros. Protection fields (PI) follow PRACT and PRINFO. DEAC lets the SSD free the blocks instead, but a read must still give zeros. A Linux comment in nvme_update_ns_info_block() says DEAC 'must be a no-op if reads from deallocated data do not return zeroes'.

What goes wrong: Write Zeroes (08h), with or without DEAC, gives Success. But later reads give old data, junk, or zeros for only part of the range. File systems and databases that count on zero-filling then see old structures. Examples: turning unwritten areas into written ones, or BLKZEROOUT used to clear file-system records.

How you can tell: Nothing is reported at the NVMe level. Higher software may report damage later, far away from the cause. Examples: file-system check errors, database page check-number failures.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Take care. On a spare storage area, fill 1 GiB with a pattern. Run nvme write-zeroes with sizes 1 block, WZSL−1, WZSL and WZSL+1, with and without --deac. WZSL+1 should give an error, not a silent cut. Read back and compare. Also run blkdiscard -z, and confirm with blktrace which command Linux really used. Write a non-zero pattern. Write Zeroes over the range, with both DEAC=0 and DEAC=1 (nvme write-zeroes … --deac). Read every block back and compare with zeros. Test sizes around WZSL, WZDSL and MDTS. Any non-zero byte is proof, whatever DLFEAT says.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Nothing records it. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD is at fault. · Test that confirms it: read back after 'write zeros'.

Error family: P23, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. Also E04 (a kind of evidence from outside the recording). · Can the packets alone prove it? Partly. The timing and order of the packets show its shape. Proof needs evidence from outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: Each range description gives a Length in blocks. It counts from 1. This is unlike NLB in Read and Write (CDW12), which counts from 0. Freeing blocks that are not in any range is never allowed.

What goes wrong: Blocks outside the asked-for range read back as zeros or FFh, or fail with 287h. The drive may have rounded the range out to its own inside unit. Or it read the description wrong, for example treating the length as counting from 0, which adds one block. Or the computer sent the wrong range.

How you can tell: Nothing shows until the data is read. File systems see damaged files or records long after the trim. Cases on the computer side have really happened. A 2019 dm-devel mailing-list thread is one report. There, fstrim freed too many or the wrong blocks on Linux 5.1 with dm-crypt and LVM. This led to data loss.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Use guard blocks. Write different 'guard' blocks right before and after each range. Free the range. Check the guards with a read that checks numbers (fio --verify=crc32c over the guard areas). Decode the range list in the recording to tell a computer error from an SSD error.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Nothing records it. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The computer is at fault if the decoded range descriptions already cover the lost blocks. The same if they name the wrong storage area (NSID). The SSD is at fault if the descriptions are right and guard blocks are still lost. · Test that confirms it: guard, range, guard.

Error family: P23 and P26, two of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. Also E04 (a kind of evidence from outside the recording). · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. A check on the order and timing of packets finds it. Examples: a missing answer, a long gap, packets out of order.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The storage area's information page has NUSE ('current number of logical blocks allocated', no more than NCAP). NSFEAT has THIN and DULBE bits. Feature 05h has the DULBE bit 16. A drive that does not hand out space on demand (no thin provisioning) may rightly report NUSE = NCAP. The QEMU model does this on purpose (hw/nvme/ns.c: 'no thin provisioning').

What goes wrong: The storage area says it hands out space on demand (NSFEAT bit 0) or supports DULBE (NSFEAT bit 2). But NUSE never changes after writes or frees. Or DULBE is on, and reads of never-written or freed blocks still give Success. Management software that uses NUSE to plan space, or to warn about space, gets wrong numbers.

How you can tell: No error. NUSE stays equal to NCAP, or at its factory value. Get Features 05h shows DULBE=1, while reads of unwritten blocks succeed.

How to fix it and prove the fix: After a format, NUSE should drop to about 0 on a drive that counts. Write N blocks (NUSE goes up by N). Free them (NUSE goes down by N). For DULBE: read a never-written block (expect 287h). Write it (expect Success). Free it (expect 287h). The QEMU SSD's nvme_check_dulbe() is a good example. It returns NVME_DULB when the block-status check says the range holds no data.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Nothing records it. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD is at fault. · Test that confirms it: a table of NUSE and DULBE states.

Error family: P24, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. Also E04 and E09 (kinds of evidence from outside the recording). · Can the packets alone prove it? Partly. The timing and order of the packets show its shape. Proof needs evidence from outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe storage command rule book has Flush. The SSD's information page has VWC. Set and Get Features 06h control the write cache (Volatile Write Cache, WCE bit 0). A finished Flush is a promise: every write finished before it is safe in lasting storage.

What goes wrong: One of two things. (a) Flush says Success before the cached data is in the storage chips (NAND). (b) The drive says VWC = 0 (no cache that is lost at power-off). But really it holds writes in memory (DRAM or SRAM) with no power-loss protection. In case (b), Linux never sends a Flush at all. It set up the drive as having no write cache.

How you can tell: Nothing shows until the power is lost without warning. Then data that fsync() or fdatasync() said was safe is missing or old. Journals replay states that do not fit together.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Run a power-cut test with a record kept on the computer side (see the error list, lab IV.3). Write records, then fsync or Flush. Log each confirmed record number on a different machine. Cut power at random points. Power up and check that every confirmed record is there. Any confirmed record missing after Flush is proof. Check VWC with nvme id-ctrl -H and nvme get-feature -f 6. On Linux, /sys/block/nvme0n1/queue/write_cache shows 'write back' or 'write through'. 'write through' on a drive you think has a cache is case (b).

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Nothing records it. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD is at fault when flushed data is lost. Causes: its program finishes Flush too early, the flush empties only front stores, or VWC is reported wrong. The computer is at fault only if the lost writes were never covered by Flush or FUA. · Test that confirms it: a power-cut test machine with a record of confirmed writes (E09).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: Read and Write commands have a 'write straight to storage' bit (Force Unit Access, CDW12 bit 30). The data must be safe in lasting storage when the command finishes, whatever the write cache does.

What goes wrong: A Write with FUA = 1 finishes while its data is still only in the cache. That cache is lost at power-off. File systems and databases use FUA for journal 'commit' blocks. Linux turns REQ_FUA into NVME_RW_FUA. So a lost FUA write loses the commit record of a change the program already saw as finished.

How you can tell: Only after a power loss: the last committed changes are missing, even though the commit write finished.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Run the power-cut test with a record of confirmed writes, using only FUA writes and no Flush. Use a small program that writes with O_DIRECT|O_DSYNC. Linux can then mark the write REQ_FUA when the drive says it supports FUA. Before trusting the test, confirm with the nvme_setup_cmd trace point that the control field has bit 14 set. Any confirmed FUA write missing after power-up is proof.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Nothing records it. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD is at fault. It treats FUA as only a hint, or the data is safe but the map update is not. · Test that confirms it: a power-cut test with FUA writes only (E09). Risky, test machine only.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: No single NVMe field promises power-loss protection (PLP). Keeping data safe relies on Flush, FUA and the VWC report. The health log (SMART / Health) has Unsafe Shutdowns and Media and Data Integrity Errors. It also has Critical Warning bits, including 'volatile memory backup device has failed'.

What goes wrong: A drive claims power-loss protection, or its cache is off. Still, writes that finished before the power cut are missing or old after power-up. This also covers losing data written long before the cut. That happens when a map update that was in progress damages the map of older data. Zheng and others call this metadata corruption.

How you can tell: Mostly nothing at power-up. Sometimes the health log's Unsafe Shutdowns count goes up (it should, after every power loss without warning). Sometimes Media and Data Integrity Errors rise, if the drive notices. The worst case is 'total device failure'. The drive comes back with no storage area, in read-only mode, or with a Critical Warning bit set.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Run the power-cut test with a record of confirmed writes. Check all data written before, not just the latest records, because older data can be lost too. Run nvme smart-log before and after each cycle. Unsafe Shutdowns must go up by exactly one per cut. If it does not, the drive's own power-loss detection is broken. Check the critical warning bits.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Nothing records it. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD is at fault. Causes: its hold-up capacitors, a save not finished within the hold-up time, or a damaged map save point. · Test that confirms it: a power-cut test machine with a record of confirmed writes (E09).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The SSD's information page gives AWUN and AWUPF (counted from 0, in blocks). The storage area's information page gives NAWUN, NAWUPF and NABSPF (valid when NSFEAT bit 1 is set). Take a write no bigger than NAWUPF that does not cross an NABSPF boundary. It must be all-or-nothing, even across a power failure. A single block is always expected to be all-or-nothing.

What goes wrong: A write that should be all-or-nothing is kept only in part. Some blocks are new and some old. Or even part of one block is new (a 'shorn write', as Zheng and others call it). Databases that count on all-or-nothing 4 KiB or 16 KiB page writes (to skip double-write stores) then see half-written pages.

How you can tell: After a power loss, or after an error or restart during the write, reads give a mix. The program's page check numbers fail, but the drive reports nothing.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Write records of exactly NAWUPF size, lined up to NABSPF. Put a record number and a check number in every block, so a mix can be found. After a power cut, every record must be fully old or fully new. Also test records of NAWUPF + 1 blocks, to confirm the boundary. Half-written records are allowed there.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Nothing records it. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD is at fault. Maybe a storage-chip write was cut off, or an inside map update was split. Or NAWUPF is stated larger than the SSD can promise. · Test that confirms it: a test machine that writes all-or-nothing-sized records (E09). Risky, test machine only.

Error family: P24, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. Also E04 and E09 (kinds of evidence from outside the recording). · Can the packets alone prove it? Partly. The timing and order of the packets show its shape. Proof needs evidence from outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: NVMe does not put commands that run at the same time in order. So writes running together may be saved in any order. But Flush is a fence. Everything finished before it must be safe when it finishes. Sometimes data from after a Flush is there, but data from before it is missing. That breaks the Flush promise.

What goes wrong: After a power loss, a later write is there. It was confirmed and then followed by Flush. But an earlier write, also flushed before it, is missing. The saved state fits no order in which the computer could have seen the writes finish. Zheng and others call these 'unserializable writes'.

How you can tell: Nothing is reported. Journal software and log-style software break. They assume that if the commit record is there, the data blocks before the flush are there too.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Keep a record in rounds (epochs): round N data, then Flush, then commit record N, then Flush, then round N+1. After a cut, if commit record N is there, every block of round N must check out. Note the difference: data missing from a round whose Flush had not finished is allowed.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Nothing records it. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD is at fault. Causes: a flush per inside channel, a map journal out of order, or a cache emptied out of order. The recording proves the computer kept its side of the promise. · Test that confirms it: a power-cut test machine with a record kept in rounds (E09). Risky, test machine only.

Error family: P23, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. Also E04 (a kind of evidence from outside the recording). · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. A check on the order and timing of packets finds it. Examples: a missing answer, a long gap, packets out of order.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: This is about what a Write command means. With data protection type 1 (PI Type 1), the reference tag checks only the block address, not the version. So data protection does not catch lost writes either.

What goes wrong: A Write finishes with Success. No power event or restart follows. A later Read gives back the block's earlier contents. The write was dropped. It was never stored, or it was stored but the map was not updated.

How you can tell: Nothing is reported. A check number kept with each block cannot catch it, because the old block matches its own check number. Only a check number or version kept somewhere else catches it. That can be the parent pointer (as in ZFS and Btrfs) or a program's own index. Krioukov and others studied this case for RAID.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Write a version number into each block. Keep the expected version in the computer's memory. Use fio --verify with --verify_header-style headers, or your own tool that keeps a count per block. Read back after writing over. An old version means a lost write. Stress it with many writes to the same block at once (high queue depth).

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Nothing records it. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD is at fault. The recording proves the SSD got the new data and confirmed it. · Test that confirms it: checking version counts.

Error family: P23, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. Also E04 (a kind of evidence from outside the recording). · Can the packets alone prove it? Partly. The timing and order of the packets show its shape. Proof needs evidence from outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: This is about what a Write means, plus end-to-end data protection. With data protection type 1 (PI Type 1), the Reference Tag must match the low bits of the block address. The SSD checks it when PRCHK includes the reference tag. A write to the wrong block then fails with 'Reference Tag Check Error' (result 284h) on the read. Or it fails at write time if the SSD checks again then.

What goes wrong: The data for block X lands at block Y. This damages two places. X keeps old data (a lost write). Y is written over with data that belongs elsewhere. Zheng and others describe 'flying writes' after power faults: data showing up in an unexpected place. That is the power-fault form of this error.

How you can tell: Nothing is reported by the SSD. Check numbers that include the block's own address can find it. That can be a header holding the block address, or the PI reference tag with type 1 or 2.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Take care. Write the whole drive with fio using --verify=crc32c (the headers carry the position). Then read and check the whole drive. Repeat after heavy random writing that makes the SSD tidy up. Repeat after power cuts (risky, test machine only). On a storage area formatted with data protection, send a wrong start block (SLBA) on purpose. Confirm that it is caught. Write blocks whose content includes their own address (fio check headers include the position). On read, check that the header position equals the block read. A block holding another block's header is a misdirected write. The header tells you where it should have gone.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Nothing records it. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The computer is at fault if the Write command's start block (SLBA) is already wrong. Compare with the computer's own trace (E05, nvme_setup_cmd). The SSD is at fault if the command is right and the data shows up elsewhere. · Test that confirms it: checking with position-tagged blocks.

Packet=1432129 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=2274 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000004:84150340 | Length=4 | DATA=16 B | Time Stamp=1343.640951974250s | Time Delta=52.880 ns | LCRC=0xFFA7D54C

Error family: P23, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. Also E04 (a kind of evidence from outside the recording). · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. A check on the order and timing of packets finds it. Examples: a missing answer, a long gap, packets out of order.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: A Read that starts after a Write has finished must give that Write's data, or newer. NVMe does not put commands that run at the same time in order. So a Read sent before the Write finished may rightly give either version.

What goes wrong: A Read gives an older version of a block, although a newer Write to that block has finished. There was no power event. Unlike error type D-13, the new data may really be in storage. A later Read, after the cache is emptied or a restart, gives the right new data. So the error comes and goes.

How you can tell: Nothing is reported. It comes and goes, and is very hard to make happen again. Programs see 'my write disappeared, then came back'.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Run loops of write, finish, read, with version numbers, on the same blocks. Use different command lists (different processors). For SSDs with more than one controller, also go through different controllers. Record when the write finished and when the read was sent. This shows the read started after the write finished. That order is what turns 'odd' into 'proven'.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Nothing records it. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD is at fault. Maybe a read cache or read-ahead was not cleared. Or two command lists raced, or several controllers shared a cache. · Test that confirms it: version loops across processors.

Packet=1435442 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=3040 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000004:841503A0 | Length=4 | DATA=16 B | Time Stamp=1343.641234612500s | Time Delta=33.620 ns | LCRC=0xC8D067BA

Error family: P23, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. Also E04 (a kind of evidence from outside the recording). · Can the packets alone prove it? Partly. The timing and order of the packets show its shape. Proof needs evidence from outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: This is about what a Read means. The health log's 'Media and Data Integrity Errors' counts only errors the SSD found itself. End-to-end data protection (the PI guard check number) covers the whole way from the computer's memory to storage and back. That is when the PRCHK guard is on.

What goes wrong: A Read finishes with Success, but the data is different from what was written. It may differ by a few bits or by a whole chunk. Maybe the drive's error-fixing code (ECC) 'fixed' it wrongly, into wrong but valid-looking data. Or the damage happened outside the part ECC protects. That could be SSD memory without a parity check, or a bug in how the SSD program handles its stores. It could also be the PCIe or computer side. Damage on PCIe going unnoticed is very unlikely, because of the LCRC check number. It is possible in the computer's memory.

How you can tell: Nothing is reported by the drive. There is no storage error result and no rise in the health log's Media Errors. Only a check number from end to end catches it.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Read with check numbers. Use fio --verify=crc32c or sha256, or a file system that checks numbers (a ZFS or Btrfs scrub). Or use data protection with guard checking. Keep the bad data and compare it bit by bit with the expected data. A few scattered flipped bits point to storage or ECC. A block-sized piece of other valid data points to error types D-14 or D-15 in the error list. Check the computer's memory error counts (EDAC) to rule out the computer.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Nothing records it. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD is at fault if the read data packet (MWr) on the wire already holds the wrong bytes. The PCIe check number (LCRC) protected that step. The computer is at fault if the bytes on the wire are right and the computer's memory damages them later. · Test that confirms it: checking, with a dump of the data.

D-17 Trying again hides storage that is wearing out Partly seen in the packets Speed (timing counts)

Packets seen in the test recording

Error family: P22, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. Also E04 (a kind of evidence from outside the recording). · Can the packets alone prove it? Partly. The timing and order of the packets show its shape. Proof needs evidence from outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The done note's status has the 'do not try again' bit (DNR). It also has the 'wait before trying again' field (CRD). CRDT1 to CRDT3 are on the SSD's information page. The health log has 'Media and Data Integrity Errors', 'Available Spare' and 'Percentage Used'. The SSD maker's logs, or OCP logs, may show inside try-again and error-fixing counts (this depends on the SSD maker).

What goes wrong: Data comes back right, but only after many tries inside the SSD (shifting read levels, softer decoding). Or only after the computer tried a failed command again. Every layer reports success, while the storage wears out and the slowest commands get slower. In the end it becomes an error that cannot be fixed. Schroeder and others found such errors in 20 to 63% of drives within four years. They found the raw rate of flipped bits predicts them poorly. So you cannot trust a single 'health' number.

How you can tell: The slowest reads (p99, p99.9) get slower on certain block ranges. The health log's Percentage Used and Available Spare change slowly. On the computer side, Linux tries an error without DNR again. It tries up to max_retries times (5 by default, the Linux computer's setting). A request that works in the end gives the program no error. Only command_retries_count in sysfs, per storage area, counts it.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Safe to watch: read the whole drive now and then, with time logging. Take care: use the Linux NVMe fault-injection tool (drivers/nvme/host/fault_inject.c, debugfs fault_inject) to add results that allow trying again. Confirm that only the try count shows them. Make a time map per block area (fio with --write_lat_log and --log_avg_msec, or bpftrace on finish times by sector). Read the per-path counts in the diag sysfs group: …/diag/command_retries_count and …/diag/command_error_count. These come from Linux v7.2 sysfs.c, nvme_ns_diag_attr_group. With native multipath they appear on the hidden path disk, such as nvme0c0n1, not on nvme0n1. Track the health log over time. Compare Verify command times (command type 0Ch, which reads storage without sending data) across areas.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Things keep working, only slower. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD is the cause: storage wear, damage from reading nearby, or data fading over time. The computer's try-again choice (Linux max_retries, 5 by default, and CRD) only hides it. · Test that confirms it: a scan of read times by area.
