Error family: P23, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. Also E04 (a kind of evidence from outside the recording). · Can the packets alone prove it? Partly. The timing and order of the packets show its shape. Proof needs evidence from outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe main rule book has the wipe command (Sanitize, 84h) and the wipe status log (81h). The libnvme library gives SSTAT values. 0 is never wiped, 1 finished well, 2 in progress, 3 failed, 4 finished well with No-Deallocate. There is also a 'Global Data Erased' bit (bit 8) and a count of finished passes. The SSD's information page has SANICAP (CES, BES, OWS, NDI, NODMMAS). A wipe is meant to reach all user data, including caches and unused storage. Check the exact wording in the rule book.

What goes wrong: A wipe (Block Erase, Overwrite or Crypto Erase) runs to the end. The wipe status log says the last wipe finished well. But some user data can still be read. It may be in normal blocks (a pass that did not finish). It may be outside the normal user space: spare blocks, retired blocks, or caches. Or it may be found by reading the storage chips (NAND) directly.

How you can tell: SSTAT says success (value 1, or 4 for the No-Deallocate kind), and no error is logged. Only a read-back check, or a lab study of the storage chips, finds what is left.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Take care, this erases all data. Fill with a pattern twice. Run nvme sanitize /dev/nvme0 -a 2 (block erase; check nvme sanitize --help for your version). Read nvme sanitize-log /dev/nvme0 until done. Then read and check everything with O_DIRECT. Repeat for each wipe kind (SANACT) the drive supports. Repeat once with a power cut in the middle (risky, test machine only). The drive must carry on or report failure, never report success. Fill the whole storage area with a pattern tagged with each block address. Write over the full size several times, so spare blocks also hold the pattern. Wipe, read the log until done, then read every block with O_DIRECT and search for the pattern. Proving the chips themselves are clean needs more. Only a lab chip read or a check backed by the SSD maker can do it. Wei and others did such a chip read.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Nothing records it. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD is at fault. · Test that confirms it: a wipe check.

Error family: P23, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. Also E04 (a kind of evidence from outside the recording). · Can the packets alone prove it? Partly. The timing and order of the packets show its shape. Proof needs evidence from outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The rule book has a key-change wipe (Sanitize Crypto Erase, SANICAP.CES). It also has Format NVM with Secure Erase Setting 010b (key-change erase). These are supported when the FNA field on the SSD's information page says so (check the FNA bit). NVMe defines the command, not how keys are kept. The TCG Opal and Ruby rule books cover locked-data ranges.

What goes wrong: The drive reports a key-change erase that worked. But it did not change the secret key for the stored data. Or it changed it for some ranges only. Or it kept a copy. Reads then give old readable data (key not changed), or random-looking data (key changed). The second case looks right, even if a copy of the old key is still there.

How you can tell: Nothing is reported. The user's only check is 'reads now give something other than my data'. That passes even when the erase did not really lock the data away.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Take care. Write a pattern, do a key-change erase, read and check everything with O_DIRECT, cut and restore power, and check again. Compare with the DLFEAT read behaviour. Many drives free the blocks after a key-change erase, so reads give zeros. A drive giving scrambled data is fine. A drive giving readable old data has failed. Read back right after the erase and after a power cycle. Old readable data anywhere is proof. Strong proof needs the SSD maker's papers, a test report, or a chip study. A test report can be FIPS 140 approval of the drive's key part. That study must show scrambled data that changes between two writes of the same data.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Nothing records it. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD is at fault. · Test that confirms it: a key-change erase check.

Error family: P23, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. Also E04 (a kind of evidence from outside the recording). · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. A check on the order and timing of packets finds it. Examples: a missing answer, a long gap, packets out of order.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The format command (Format NVM, CDW10) has LBAF, MSET, PI, PIL and SES. SES 000b means no erase, 001b means erase user data, 010b means key-change erase. FNA, on the SSD's information page, says whether a format covers all storage areas. It also says whether key-change erase is supported (check the bit layout).

What goes wrong: After the format finishes, reads give the data written before. There are two different cases. (a) SES = 000b (no secure erase) was used. Then the rule book does not require the data to be destroyed, only the block format to change. With DLFEAT 000b the old data may still read back. That is a misunderstanding, not a drive failure. (b) SES = 001b (erase user data) or 010b was asked for, and data is still there. That is a real failure.

How you can tell: Nothing is reported. The format may finish in milliseconds in either case.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Check which SES was really sent (in the recording, or nvme format … --ses=1 on the command line). Fill with a pattern, format, then read and check everything with O_DIRECT. With SES of 1 or more, any old pattern is proof. Check the format's finish time against the estimate on the SSD's information page, if one is given.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Nothing records it. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The computer's software is at fault if SES = 000b was sent (the tool's default). The SSD is at fault if SES = 001b or 010b and old data reads back. · Test that confirms it: a format check.

Error family: P23, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. Also E04 (a kind of evidence from outside the recording). · Can the packets alone prove it? Partly. The timing and order of the packets show its shape. Proof needs evidence from outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe storage command rule book has end-to-end data protection. The storage area's information page has DPC and DPS, and FLBAS with the block format's MS. Read and Write have PRINFO. The results are 'Guard Check Error' 282h, 'Application Tag Check Error' 283h and 'Reference Tag Check Error' 284h. Linux calls them NVME_SC_GUARD_CHECK and so on.

What goes wrong: The storage area is formatted with data protection (PI), but damaged data gets through. Reasons: checking was not asked for (PRCHK = 0). Or the computer uses PRACT = 1, so the SSD makes and removes the protection fields. Then the way from computer to SSD is not covered. Or the PI type is 0 (extra data only, never checked). Or application tag FFFFh turns checking off for that block (a way out, check this per PI type). Or the SSD ignores PRCHK.

How you can tell: No Guard, Application or Reference Tag Check Error (282h, 283h, 284h), even though the data or block address is wrong.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Take care. On a test storage area formatted with PI Type 1, try three things. Write with a wrong reference tag. Write correctly, then read with a wrong expected reference tag. Damage the guard. Each must fail. Repeat with application tag FFFFh to see the written-down way out. Write with a wrong guard or reference tag on purpose (nvme write … --prinfo with a wrong --ref-tag) and confirm the error. Success here proves the check is not done. Check /sys/block/nvme0n1/integrity/ (format, read_verify, write_generate) to see what Linux does.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Nothing records it. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The computer's software is at fault if PRCHK = 0, PRACT = 1, or there is no integrity profile. The SSD is at fault if PRCHK is set and damaged protection fields still pass. · Test that confirms it: sending bad protection fields on purpose.

Error family: P23, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. A check on the order and timing of packets finds it. Examples: a missing answer, a long gap, packets out of order.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The storage area's information page has NGUID and EUI64. There is a list of storage-area id descriptions (CNS 03h). NSFEAT bit 3 says ids are never used again.

What goes wrong: The drive reports ids that are not one of a kind. It may give the same NGUID for every drive of a model. Or it gives junk, or the same id for two storage areas. Software for several paths may then join two different storage areas into one. /dev/disk/by-id links may point to the wrong disk.

How you can tell: Nothing is reported unless Linux finds the repeat. Linux v7.2 then prints 'clearing duplicate IDs for nsid N' and 'use of /dev/disk/by-id/ may cause data corruption'. For network SSDs or storage areas shared by several controllers, it prints 'ignoring nsid N because of duplicate IDs' instead. It also sets NVME_QUIRK_BOGUS_NID while running.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Safe. Make two storage areas, or use two drives of one model. Compare all ids, and check that by-id links point to one place each. Run nvme id-ns /dev/nvme0n1 | grep -iE 'nguid|eui64' and nvme ns-descs /dev/nvme0n1 on several drives and storage areas, and compare. Run dmesg | grep -i "duplicate IDs\|bogus".

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Nothing records it. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD is at fault. Its program or its factory did not set values that are one of a kind. · Test that confirms it: comparing ids.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The information command (Identify) has a CNS value that picks which page to give. NVMe 1.1 made CNS two bits instead of one. Later versions made it a full byte. A Linux comment in nvme_id_cns_ok() explains this history.

What goes wrong: The SSD claims a rule book version that includes a CNS value, but handles it wrongly. It may cut CNS to one bit (as in NVMe 1.0), so it answers with a different page. Or it gives Success with an empty page, instead of 'Invalid Field'.

How you can tell: Wrong values, with nothing reported: missing storage areas, a wrong storage-area list, or junk descriptions. Sometimes Linux prints 'ctrl returned bogus length' for entries in the description list.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Safe (these admin commands only read). Try every CNS from 00h to 1Fh, with NSID 0, 1 and FFFFFFFFh. Log the result and the bytes. Send each CNS with nvme admin-passthru --opcode=0x06 --cdw10=<cns> --data-len=4096 -r. Compare the page with what that CNS should give. An unsupported CNS should fail with 'Invalid Field', not give Success with unrelated data.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Nothing records it. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD is at fault. Its command reader was kept from an older version. · Test that confirms it: try every CNS value.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The storage area's information page has NSZE, NCAP, NUSE, the NSFEAT THIN bit, FLBAS and the block format table LBAF[]. The SSD's information page has TNVMCAP and UNVMCAP for the totals.

What goes wrong: The stated size is larger than the real storage. This happens with fake or wrongly set-up drives. Writes past the real size wrap around and write over earlier data. Or the block data size in the format table is wrong. Or NCAP and NSZE disagree after storage areas are managed.

How you can tell: Nothing is reported at first. Later, data at low block numbers is written over by writes to high block numbers (wrap-around). Or 'LBA Out of Range' errors appear below the stated size.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Take care. Write the whole drive with blocks tagged by address, and check. Also make, resize and delete storage areas again and again, and check the information page values each time. Write the full size with address-tagged data (fio --verify=crc32c headers include the position, or f3-style tools). Then read and check everything. Wrap-around shows as blocks holding headers of other positions. Compare blockdev --getsize64 with NSZE × block size.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Nothing records it. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD is at fault: a fake or wrongly set-up program, or a bug in managing storage areas. · Test that confirms it: a full-size write and check with address tags.

Packet 1454528: the read used as proof finishes with success.

Packet=1454528 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=599 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000004:841401C0 | Length=4 | DATA=16 B | Time Stamp=1352.143733882500s | Time Delta=42.880 ns | LCRC=0x81CA2608

Error family: P23 and P26, two of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. Also E03 (a kind of evidence from outside the recording). · Can the packets alone prove it? Partly. The timing and order of the packets show its shape. Proof needs evidence from outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The health log (SMART / Health Information, 02h) has many fields. Three are Critical Warning, Composite Temperature (in Kelvin) and Available Spare. Others are Percentage Used, and Data Units Read and Written. Data Units count thousands of 512-byte units, rounded up. There are also Host Read and Write Commands, Power Cycles, Power On Hours and Unsafe Shutdowns. The last two are Media and Data Integrity Errors, and Number of Error Information Log Entries. Temperature limits are set with Feature 04h.

What goes wrong: Counts do not change (Data Units Written is stuck). Or they change at the wrong scale, wrap around, or reset at power-off. Composite Temperature stays the same, is 0, or is far from the real value. Critical Warning bits never get set, even when limits are crossed.

How you can tell: Watching software sees a healthy drive. Wear or heat trouble is missed, or false alarms go off.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Save nvme smart-log. Write exactly N × 512,000 bytes with O_DIRECT. Save it again. Data Units Written must grow by N (give or take rounding). Host Write Commands must grow by the number of commands sent. Compare the temperature with an outside heat sensor (thermocouple) and with the hwmon value (sensors, /sys/class/hwmon/*/temp1_input). Cut and restore power, and check that the counts are kept and Power Cycles goes up.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Nothing records it. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD is at fault. · Test that confirms it: a test that writes a counted amount.

D-26 A program update says success, but the old SSD program still runs Seen in the packets Wrong data in the bytes carried

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 1457813: a write of the test pattern finishes.

Packet=1457813 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=1692 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000004:84150560 | Length=4 | DATA=16 B | Time Stamp=1352.643978175000s | Time Delta=25.880 ns | LCRC=0x5FA6E3E1

Packet 1457900: the read used as proof finishes with success.

Packet=1457900 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=1730 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000004:841401E0 | Length=4 | DATA=16 B | Time Stamp=1353.144083658870s | Time Delta=48.870 ns | LCRC=0x08BB2EF9

Error family: P23 and P25, two of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. Also E03 (a kind of evidence from outside the recording). · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. A check on the order and timing of packets finds it. Examples: a missing answer, a long gap, packets out of order.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The 'commit new program' command (Firmware Commit) has four CA values. They are: replace; replace and start at next restart; start at next restart; replace and start now. Its results include 'needs normal reset' (10Bh) and 'needs SSD subsystem reset' (110h). They also include 'needs controller reset' (111h) and 'would break the maximum time' (112h). The program slot log has AFI (active slot in bits 2:0, next slot in bits 6:4) and FRS1 to FRS7. The SSD's information page has FR and FRMW.

What goes wrong: The download and commit work, and the tool says 'updated'. But the running program version is the same. Maybe the commit action only stored the image (CA = 000b). Maybe starting it was left to a restart that never happened. A tool may have treated result 10Bh, 110h or 111h as success. Or starting failed quietly, and the drive went back to the old slot.

How you can tell: Nothing is reported if the tool ignores the result or the slot log. Linux v7.2 checks whether the slot log's next slot differs from the current one. If so, it logs 'Firmware is activated after next Controller Level Reset'.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Take care (you need an image from the SSD maker). Commit with each supported CA. Check the result, the slot log and FR before and after each restart. Do a controller restart, a subsystem restart and a power cycle. Also try a damaged image. The drive must refuse it. It must never report success while quietly running the old program. Run nvme fw-log /dev/nvme0 (AFI and slot versions) and nvme id-ctrl /dev/nvme0 | grep -i '^fr ' before and after the restart that starts it. Run cat /sys/class/nvme/nvme0/firmware_rev. The running version is FR after the restart, not what the tool printed.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Nothing records it. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The computer's software is at fault if the commit result or CA needed a restart that was not done. The SSD is at fault if the right restart happened and the old program still runs. · Test that confirms it: the program version before and after.

D-27 Zoned storage: write position does not match the data (ZNS write pointer) Partly seen in the packets Wrong data in the bytes carried

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 1460001: a write of the test pattern finishes.

Packet=1460001 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=2286 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000004:84150590 | Length=4 | DATA=16 B | Time Stamp=1353.644396951500s | Time Delta=48.880 ns | LCRC=0x34CD0609

Packet 1460045: the read used as proof finishes with success.

Packet=1460045 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=2305 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000004:841505A0 | Length=4 | DATA=16 B | Time Stamp=1353.644484758000s | Time Delta=42.880 ns | LCRC=0x9353BFA2

Error family: P23, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. Also E04 (a kind of evidence from outside the recording). · Can the packets alone prove it? Partly. The timing and order of the packets show its shape. Proof needs evidence from outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The zoned storage command rule book (Zoned Namespace Command Set) splits storage into zones, written in order from the start. It has zone states and a write position (write pointer). Zone Append gives back the block it wrote. There are Zone Management Send and Receive commands. Errors include 'Zone Invalid Write' (1BCh) and 'Zone Boundary Error' (1B8h). Linux names these in include/linux/nvme.h.

What goes wrong: The stated write position is ahead of the data really saved. Reads below it give old or unwritten content. Or it is behind the data. Data was written, but the position went back. So the computer writes over it with the next append. This usually happens after a power loss or a restart in the middle of writing.

How you can tell: Nothing is reported. Zoned file systems and programs that rebuild their state from the write position lose or repeat records. For example, they use it to find the end of a log.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Risky, test machine only. Append across many open zones while cutting power. Compare the write position with the last confirmed append in each zone, and with the data. Append records with record numbers and check numbers. Cut power or restart. Then run nvme zns report-zones and read each zone up to and past the write position. All records below the position must check out. None above it may be valid new data. What values are allowed above it follows the read rules for unwritten blocks (check this in the rule book).

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Nothing records it. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD is at fault. · Test that confirms it: append, restart, then report zones.

D-28 A done note carries the wrong command number (wrong CID) Seen in the packets Wrong details in done notes

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 541927: the done note (CQE) names command number (CID) 0x7FFE.

Packet=541927 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=1754 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000004:82D901D0 | Length=4 | DATA=16 B | Time Stamp=0370.773334832370s | Time Delta=24.870 ns | LCRC=0xDB3D2FFC

Error family: P15, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. · Can the packets alone prove it? Only by reading the bytes. The details are inside the DATA column. The hex version of the recording marks a done note for an unknown or already finished command number (nvme_cqe_unknown_or_completed_cid).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The done note holds the command number (Command Identifier, DW3) and the command list number (SQ Identifier, DW2). A command number must be the only one of its kind among the open commands on that list.

What goes wrong: The SSD finishes command A, but writes the command number of command B. If B is open, the computer finishes B (with A's result) while B's data is not there yet. A runs out of time later. Memory may be used again while the SSD is still writing data into it.

How you can tell: Partly reported. Linux v7.2 puts a 4-bit round count in the top bits of the command number (unless NVME_QUIRK_SKIP_CID_GEN is set). A command number with a wrong round count gives two messages. They are 'request 0x… genctr mismatch' and 'invalid id N completed on queue M'. A wrong command number that matches another open request with the right round count is not reported. It finishes the wrong request.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Run dmesg | grep -E "genctr mismatch|invalid id". Data checking (fio verify) catches reads that finished too early. With the capture tool, write a script. Build a map of open commands (command list and command number) from the command fetches. Check every done note against it.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Nothing records it. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD is at fault, because it writes the command number into the done note. The computer is at fault only if the command itself carried that number. Then it is error type V-08 in the error list, not D-28. · Test that confirms it: the Linux command-number check.

D-29 One command gets two done notes (duplicate completion) Seen in the packets Wrong details in done notes

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 546348: a second done note for the same command number (CID), with a different packet number (PSN).

Packet=546348 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=3149 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000004:82D90230 | Length=4 | DATA=16 B | Time Stamp=0370.813693768750s | Time Delta=54.880 ns | LCRC=0x64969550

Error family: P15, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. · Can the packets alone prove it? Only by reading the bytes. The details are inside the DATA column. The hex version of the recording marks two things. One is a done note for an unknown or already finished command number (nvme_cqe_unknown_or_completed_cid). The other is a result other than 0 (nvme_status_nonzero).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: Each command gets exactly one done note.

What goes wrong: The SSD writes two done notes for the same command. This can happen after a try-again inside the SSD, or a race with a stop request (Abort). The computer may already have given that request number to a new command. Then the second done note finishes the new command too early.

How you can tell: On Linux v7.2 it is usually reported. nvme_try_complete_req() adds 1 to the request's round count at the first done note. The second done note carries the old round count in command number bits 15:12. So it fails the check in nvme_find_rq(). It is logged as 'genctr mismatch' or 'invalid id … completed on queue …', and ignored. It goes unreported with NVME_QUIRK_SKIP_CID_GEN, or if the second note comes exactly 16 uses later. Then it can finish an unrelated new command too early.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Check the Linux kernel log (dmesg) for genctr messages. Use a capture-tool script that pairs command numbers. Check how the done list's phase bit is handled when the list wraps around. If the phase bit is wrong, the second note appears exactly at the wrap point.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Yes. A setting, a result number or a log in the SSD or computer records it. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD is at fault, because it wrote the note twice. The capture tool or its reader is at fault in two cases. The 'second note' has the same packet number, so the wire sent it again. Or it comes from a decoder that does not remove repeats. · Test that confirms it: the Linux repeat check.

D-30 A lost 'work done' signal is hidden when the timeout code checks Seen in the packets Command never finishes (timing)

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 1182465: a done note (CQE) is written, and no 'work is done' signal (MSI-X) follows.

Packet=1182465 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=75 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000004:83270010 | Length=4 | DATA=16 B | Time Stamp=0892.898247663620s | Time Delta=148.130 ns | LCRC=0xB224C42F

Packet 1190087: the computer's done-list doorbell. It comes only after 30 s (the Linux computer's setting), when the timeout code checked the done list.

Packet=1190087 | Link Dir=Downstream | TLP Type=MWr(32) | PSN=128 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=000:00:0 | Address=FCE01014 | Length=1 | DATA=4 B | Time Stamp=0922.898247663620s | Time Delta=136.130 ns | LCRC=0x661DB84B

Error family: P02 and P16, two of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. A check on the order and timing of packets finds it. Examples: a missing answer, a long gap, packets out of order.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The rule book says how 'work is done' signals are made for done-list entries. Parts are: the MSI-X table, the signal number given in 'Create I/O CQ', and grouping of signals (Feature 08h).

What goes wrong: The SSD writes the done note, but the 'work is done' signal is lost. Causes: a blocked signal number, a wrong MSI-X entry, or a bug in grouping signals. After the command time limit, Linux checks the done list itself. It finds the done note and finishes the request normally. The program sees a 30-second freeze, but no error.

How you can tell: Only a warning: 'I/O tag N (CID) QID M timeout, completion polled'. No error goes back to the program. So watching software that counts read and write errors never sees it.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Run dmesg | grep "completion polled". Look at time charts with a long tail at exactly the time limit. In /proc/interrupts, the counts for the NVMe signals do not go up while commands finish.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Only by a timer. Nothing records an error. The only sign is a time limit running out. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD is at fault if no MSI-X write packet follows the done note. The same if there is no done note at all. The computer or its hardware is at fault if the MSI-X write is right but is not handled. Right means the set address and data. The counts in /proc/interrupts stay flat. · Test that confirms it: the 'completion polled' log line.

D-31 The SSD writes data outside the memory it was given Seen in the packets Wrong memory address or sender

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 643584: a write packet (MWr) outside every memory address the command's address list (PRP) gave.

Packet=643584 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=3253 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000003:1200F000 | Length=64 | DATA=256 B | Time Stamp=0521.882617831250s | Time Delta=186.620 ns | LCRC=0x0C4FB22D

Error family: P17, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. A check on the order and timing of packets finds it. Examples: a missing answer, a long gap, packets out of order.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The rules for memory address lists (PRP or SGL) apply. The size is the PRP entries and the transfer length, NLB × block size. Linux also limits addresses for SSDs marked NVME_QUIRK_DMA_ADDRESS_BITS_48.

What goes wrong: The SSD writes data past the address list's range. Or it writes to an old address from an earlier command. Or it writes after it already wrote the done note, when the computer may have freed that memory. Without a memory guard (IOMMU), this quietly damages unrelated kernel or program memory.

How you can tell: Without a memory guard: random crashes and damaged unrelated data, with nothing pointing at the SSD. A memory guard (Intel VT-d, AMD-Vi, Arm SMMU) can be in translated mode. Then a fault message names the SSD's address on the bus (BDF) and the bad address. The wording depends on the memory guard driver. Examples only: 'DMAR: [DMA Write] … fault addr …' or 'AMD-Vi: Event logged [IO_PAGE_FAULT …]'. The write is blocked.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Safe with the memory guard in strict mode. Run fio with odd memory line-ups (--iomem_align) and sizes that end exactly at address-list page edges. Add stop requests (Abort) under load. Any memory guard fault is a broken-rule note. Start the computer with the memory guard in translated mode, not pass-through (intel_iommu=on iommu.passthrough=0, or the AMD version). Watch the Linux kernel log (dmesg) for faults naming the NVMe BDF. In the capture tool, check every write packet address against the command's address list.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Nothing records it. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD is at fault, because its address-list reader makes the addresses. The computer is at fault only if the address is inside its own address list or command. Then it is not D-31. It is also at fault if it freed the memory before the done note. That is the shape of error type V-16 in the error list. · Test that confirms it: a run with the memory guard in strict mode.

D-32 The SSD reads too much of the range list (Number of Ranges) Seen in the packets Wrong memory address or sender

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 647238: a 'free this space' command (DSM) has NR=3 (64 B). But the SSD reads 4 KiB of range list.

Packet=647238 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MRd(32) | PSN=87 | Tag=98 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=0BC2C000 | Length=1024 | Time Stamp=0521.882922453500s | Time Delta=129.620 ns | LCRC=0xA4CA3352

Error family: P17, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. The checker marks it in this table file as a wrong detail or order. The mark means: a read bigger than the 512-byte limit for one read (read_exceeds_mrrs_512).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The 'free this space' command (DSM, CDW10) has Number of Ranges, counted from 0. The data length is (NR+1) × 16 bytes.

What goes wrong: The SSD reads the largest range list size, instead of (NR+1) × 16 bytes. With a small memory area on the computer, this reads past its end. With a memory guard (IOMMU), it faults and the command fails. Linux v7.2 hides it, because it always sets aside a 4096-byte area filled with zeros. So on Linux the extra read does no harm and cannot be seen. If the SSD then also works on the extra (zero) ranges, it should do no harm (NLB 0). If the memory held old ranges, the SSD would free the wrong blocks. See error type D-06 in the error list.

How you can tell: Nothing is reported on Linux today. In the past it showed as failing trims. A 2020 Ubuntu kernel update brought back the larger area. It was the SRU 'Prevent fstrim failure so unused blocks can be discarded' (Launchpad bug 1856603). An earlier change, 'nvme: rewrite discard support', had made it smaller. Discard requests then failed on an SSD that did not follow the rules, with 'FITRIM ioctl failed: Input/output error'. Search results linked to that bug also mention memory guard faults during the trim.

How to fix it and prove the fix: With the capture tool, compare the length of the range-list read (MRd) with NR. Use an operating system that sets aside exactly (NR+1)×16 bytes. Or use your own pass-through command that puts the range list at the end of a guarded page. A memory guard fault proves it.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Nothing records it. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD is at fault (it reads a fixed-size range list). The computer is at fault only if the command's NR is larger than the computer meant. Compare with the computer's trace (E05, nvme_setup_cmd). · Test that confirms it: try a range of NR values.

D-33 Verify or Compare says success without reading the storage Partly seen in the packets Wrong data in the bytes carried

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 1460567: a write of the test pattern finishes.

Packet=1460567 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=2508 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000004:841505C0 | Length=4 | DATA=16 B | Time Stamp=1353.644716312370s | Time Delta=48.870 ns | LCRC=0x20647523

Packet 1460579: a Verify of 128 KiB finishes in about 2 us: the storage was not read.

Packet=1460579 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=2511 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000004:841505D0 | Length=4 | DATA=16 B | Time Stamp=1353.644722196500s | Time Delta=74.880 ns | LCRC=0x18343AB0

Packet 1460579: the read used as proof finishes with success.

Packet=1460579 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=2511 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000004:841505D0 | Length=4 | DATA=16 B | Time Stamp=1353.644722196500s | Time Delta=74.880 ns | LCRC=0x18343AB0

Error family: P23, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. Also E04 (a kind of evidence from outside the recording). · Can the packets alone prove it? Partly. The timing and order of the packets show its shape. Proof needs evidence from outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe storage command rule book has Verify (ONCS bit 7) and Compare (ONCS bit 0). 'Compare Failure' is result 285h. Verify on bad blocks is expected to give 'Unrecovered Read Error' 281h.

What goes wrong: Verify should read and check the data (and its protection fields) without sending it. A short-cut version gives Success without reading. So checking the drive with Verify finds nothing. Compare may give Success when the data is different, or 'Compare Failure' (285h) when it matches. That breaks users of the joined compare-and-write.

How you can tell: Nothing is reported. Drive checks say the drive is clean, but later normal reads give errors that cannot be fixed.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Take care. Run nvme write-uncor on a block. Then run nvme verify and nvme read on it; both must fail. Then write the block again to clear it. Use Write Uncorrectable (04h, ONCS bit 1) on a test block, then Verify it. It must fail ('Unrecovered Read Error' or similar). For Compare: compare data that differs only in the last byte of the last block. Also time a Verify of a large range against a Read of the same range.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Nothing records it. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD is at fault. · Test that confirms it: a test with a block made unreadable on purpose.

Chapter P: speed problems (14 entries)

Why this part is here: these 14 entries are about the work going too slowly (performance).

P-01 Work per second is far below what the wire can carry (throughput) Partly seen in the packets Speed (timing counts)

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 1683707: 128 KiB reads, one command at a time (QD1). The wire is mostly idle between commands.

Packet=1683707 | Link Dir=Downstream | TLP Type=MWr(32) | PSN=1811 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=000:00:0 | Address=FCE0100C | Length=1 | DATA=4 B | Time Stamp=1822.597350203500s | Time Delta=125.120 ns | LCRC=0xF1220108

Error family: P22, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. Also E05, E03 and E09 (kinds of evidence from outside the recording). · Can the packets alone prove it? Partly. The timing and order of the packets show its shape. Proof needs evidence from outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book gives the wire speed, the lane count and the largest data size per packet (MPS). The NVMe rule book gives MDTS (the largest size for one command) and how command lists work. The top speed is worked out by sums. It is not a field in either rule book.

What goes wrong: Large reads in order (128 KiB to 1 MiB, with 8 or more commands at once) reach, say, 4.1 GB/s. The drive is Gen4 with 4 lanes (x4). Its wire's top speed at MPS 256 B is about 7.2 GB/s, and its data sheet says 7.0 GB/s.

How you can tell: Only in the speed-test number. No error and no log.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Work out the top speed (error list, section 8.1.1) from lspci LnkSta and DevCtl MaxPayload. Run fio --rw=read --bs=1m --iodepth=32 --direct=1. Check iostat -x 1: rareq-sz (the average request size really sent) and aqu-sz (the average number of commands waiting). If rareq-sz is much smaller than the block size, the Linux block layer is cutting requests up.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Things keep working, only slower. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The computer is at fault if the SSD waits for doorbells (host_idle, few commands in the list). The SSD is at fault if doorbells are ahead, but fetches or done notes are slow. The computer's hardware or the wire is at fault if the main limit is the wire. That means its lane count, speed or MPS. · Test that confirms it: try many block sizes and command counts (bs x iodepth sweep).

P-02 Commands per second fall when many are sent at once (IOPS collapse) Partly seen in the packets Speed (timing counts)

Packets seen in the test recording

Error family: P22, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. Also E05, E03 and E09 (kinds of evidence from outside the recording). · Can the packets alone prove it? Partly. The timing and order of the packets show its shape. Proof needs evidence from outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: No rule covers this. The number of commands at once (queue depth) is limited by CAP.MQES and by the computer driver's own setting.

What goes wrong: Commands per second (IOPS) rise as more commands are sent at once. They rise until the SSD's inside parts are all busy. After that, IOPS should stay flat while time per command grows in a straight line (Little's Law). A collapse is when IOPS fall as more commands are sent at once. For example, 800k at QD 64 and 450k at QD 256. It means something gets worse when parts compete.

How you can tell: A curve of IOPS against queue depth has a peak and then falls. Average time per command grows faster than QD divided by IOPS says it should.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Safe (only reads): for qd in 1 2 4 8 16 32 64 128 256; do fio --readonly … --iodepth=$qd; done. Try --iodepth from 1 to 256 with a fixed numjobs. Then repeat with jobs fixed to processors on the SSD's NUMA node. If the computer's processor is fully busy at the peak (fio sys%, perf top), the computer is the cause. If the SSD's own time rises much more than expected, the SSD is the cause. The SSD's own time is the time from command fetch to done note in the capture tool.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Things keep working, only slower. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD is at fault if the time from fetch to done note grows with queue depth. Doorbells stay steady meanwhile. The computer is at fault if that time is flat, but doorbells or done-list updates are uneven. The same if signals all land on one signal number. · Test that confirms it: a queue-depth test with processor data.

P-03 A few commands are far slower than the rest (p99.9 and p99.99) Partly seen in the packets Speed (timing counts)

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 1702225: some reads take 48 ms, among reads that usually take about 80 us.

Packet=1702225 | Link Dir=Upstream | DLLP Type=ACK | Time Stamp=1822.649801067000s | Time Delta=2.583 ms | AckNak Seq Num=3563

Error family: P22, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. Also E05, E03 and E09 (kinds of evidence from outside the recording). · Can the packets alone prove it? Partly. The timing and order of the packets show its shape. Proof needs evidence from outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: NVMe sets no time targets for normal reads and writes. Some features exist to manage it: Predictable Latency Mode, Read Recovery Level, and I/O Determinism ideas. Check the SSD's information page to see if they are supported.

What goes wrong: The middle read time is 80 µs, but one command in a thousand takes 5 to 50 ms. Averages hide it. Databases and shared storage feel it, because a request that needs many commands waits for the slowest one.

How you can tell: fio clat percentiles show it, and so do the program's slowest times. Now and then Linux timeouts happen, if slow commands take more than 30 s (the Linux computer's setting). Then it is a timing failure, not a speed one.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Safe. Run random reads only, for a long time (30 min or more), with a medium number of commands at once. Use a drive that has been written full. Compare with a new drive. Run fio --percentile_list=99:99.9:99.99 --write_lat_log to get the time of each slow command. Use bpftrace or biolatency-style charts. Line up slow-command times with health log temperature readings, power-saving changes (APST) and other activity. The capture tool gives the SSD's own time (command fetch to done note). This separates the SSD from the computer.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Things keep working, only slower. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD is at fault if the extra time sits between command fetch and done note. The computer is at fault if the done note is on time, but its doorbell or next command is late. · Test that confirms it: a long read-only run for the slowest commands.

P-04 Writing slows sharply once the fast cache fills (write cliff, SLC cache) Partly seen in the packets Speed (timing counts)

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 1729252: write time jumps from about 15 us to about 900 us.

Packet=1729252 | Link Dir=Downstream | TLP Type=MWr(32) | PSN=1766 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=000:00:0 | Address=FCE0100C | Length=1 | DATA=4 B | Time Stamp=1822.662517991870s | Time Delta=156.130 ns | LCRC=0xF56C9AE7

Error family: P22, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. Also E09 (a kind of evidence from outside the recording). · Can the packets alone prove it? Partly. The timing and order of the packets show its shape. Proof needs evidence from outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: NVMe does not cover this. It is part of how the SSD's map and storage manager (FTL) is designed. The wear and space fields in the health log do not show the cache size.

What goes wrong: Many TLC and QLC drives first write into storage chips run in a fast one-bit mode (pseudo-SLC). A long write in order fills that cache. Then the drive must write in its normal slower mode (TLC or QLC). At the same time it must move the cache contents over. So the work per second drops sharply. Reviewers report drops. On one TLC drive, speed fell from over 2.5 GB/s to about 0.8 GB/s after about 150 GB. They report about 160 MB/s after about 80 GB on a QLC SATA drive. The cache recovers during idle time.

How you can tell: A chart of speed over time shows a step down. Average numbers from short tests look perfect.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Take care, this erases data. On a spare drive, write the full size in order with --write_bw_log and 1 s averaging. Plot GB written against MB/s. Repeat at 50% and 90% full, to show the cache getting smaller.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Things keep working, only slower. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD is the cause (how its cache is designed) when the computer sends work steadily. · Test that confirms it: fill tests at several fill levels.

P-05 Tidying pauses once the drive is full (garbage collection, steady state) Partly seen in the packets Speed (timing counts)

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 1758320: gaps of 9 ms between done notes while commands are open. The SSD is tidying its storage (garbage collection, maintenance).

Packet=1758320 | Link Dir=Upstream | DLLP Type=ACK | Time Stamp=1822.681025367000s | Time Delta=1.762 us | AckNak Seq Num=835

Error family: P22, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. Also E09 (a kind of evidence from outside the recording). · Can the packets alone prove it? Partly. The timing and order of the packets show its shape. Proof needs evidence from outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: NVMe does not cover this. Related features help. They are 'this space is free now' (Deallocate or TRIM, DSM), Write Zeroes, and extra spare space (over-provisioning). Others are Endurance Groups, NVM Sets, and Flexible Data Placement. Where supported, the last one cuts down extra writing.

What goes wrong: Once the drive is fully written, no free blocks are left. Every new write then needs tidying (garbage collection) to win back space. Random write IOPS fall from the new-drive value to a much lower steady value. There are pauses again and again when tidying falls behind.

How you can tell: A chart of IOPS over time: high, then falling, then a bumpy flat line with dips. The slowest writes (p99.9) take tens of ms.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Take care. On a spare drive, fill it the SNIA way first. Compare with and without freeing the whole drive beforehand. Take care. Fill first (twice the drive size in order, then random 4k writes). Use fio --steadystate=iops_slope:0.1%. Note the health log 'Data Units Written' before and after, to work out the computer's writes. If the SSD maker's log shows storage-chip writes, work out the extra writing (write amplification).

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Things keep working, only slower. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD is at fault. The computer shares the blame if a long recording never shows 'this space is free' (DSM Deallocate, no TRIM). · Test that confirms it: a steady-state test.

P-06 The SSD slows down to cool off (thermal throttling) Partly seen in the packets Speed (timing counts)

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 1780078: the work done per second falls in steps (the SSD is slowing down to cool).

Packet=1780078 | Link Dir=Upstream | DLLP Type=ACK | Time Stamp=1822.749764819000s | Time Delta=1.319 us | AckNak Seq Num=1957

Error family: P22, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. Also E09 (a kind of evidence from outside the recording). · Can the packets alone prove it? Partly. The timing and order of the packets show its shape. Proof needs evidence from outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book has the health log fields named above. The SSD's information page has WCTEMP, CCTEMP, MNTMT and MXTMT. Set Features has a temperature limit (04h) and computer-controlled heat limits (Host Controlled Thermal Management, 10h).

What goes wrong: As the overall temperature rises, the SSD works slower to stay within limits. These are either its own inside limits, or heat levels TMT1 and TMT2 set by the computer (HCTM).

How you can tell: The work done per second goes up and down like saw teeth, in step with temperature. The proof is in the health log. It has Composite Temperature, Warning Composite Temperature Time and Critical Composite Temperature Time. It also has Temperature Sensor 1 to 8, and Thermal Management Temperature 1/2 Transition Count and Total Time. Crossing a temperature limit can also send a health message from the SSD (the critical warning temperature bit).

How to fix it and prove the fix: Take care. On a spare drive, write in order without stopping, with the airflow blocked for a short, watched time. Stop at WCTEMP. Never go past the drive's critical temperature. Read nvme smart-log /dev/nvme0 every second during the work. Watch temperature, thm_temp1_trans_count, thm_temp1_total_time and warning_temp_time. Counts rising during the dips is proof. Linux shows temperatures through hwmon (sensors).

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Things keep working, only slower. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD's heat control is the cause. The computer's hardware is at fault if there is no heat sink or airflow. The computer's software is at fault if it set HCTM TMT1 or TMT2 too low. · Test that confirms it: the health log temperature and heat counts during the run.

P-07 Waking from power saving makes the first command slow (APST, ASPM) Partly seen in the packets Power saving and wake-up

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 1332228: waking from deep wire power saving (L1.2) took 60 us. The SSD's stated wait it can take (LTR) was 1 us.

Packet=1332228 | Link Dir=Downstream | Ord.Set Type=SDS | Time Stamp=1300.474293468620s | Time Delta=91.870 ns

Packet 1332266: the first command after waking.

Packet=1332266 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=2927 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000004:83610040 | Length=4 | DATA=16 B | Time Stamp=1300.499296047000s | Time Delta=56.880 ns | LCRC=0x18A9A2D1

Error family: P20 and P22, two of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. Also E01 and E02 (kinds of evidence from outside the recording). · Can the packets alone prove it? Partly. The timing and order of the packets show its shape. Proof needs evidence from outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book has power state descriptions (ENLAT, EXLAT, and a 'no work' flag). It has the automatic power-saving feature (APST, 0Ch). The SSD's information page has APSTA and NPSS. The PCIe rule book has wire power saving (ASPM L0s and L1) and the deeper L1 states (L1 PM Substates). Wake times are in Link Capabilities.

What goes wrong: After idle time, the drive goes into a no-work power state through automatic power saving (APST). The wire may also go into L1 or a deeper L1 state through ASPM. The first command after idle must wait for the wake-up. That is the power state's EXLAT, plus the wire's L1 wake time. It ranges from tens of µs to tens of ms.

How you can tell: Slow commands that happen only after idle times (bursty work, desktop use). Speed tests with constant load never see them. Some drive and computer pairs fail to wake at all. Then it becomes a fatal SSD error or a timeout, which is why Linux has a list of work-arounds (quirks).

How to fix it and prove the fix: Safe. Run read-only fio with pauses, as above, with APST on and off. Plot the time of the first command after idle. Read the APST table: nvme get-feature /dev/nvme0 -f 0x0c -H. Read the wake times: nvme id-ctrl /dev/nvme0 -H (power states). Read the wire power-saving state: lspci -vvv 'LnkCtl: ASPM …', and cat /sys/module/pcie_aspm/parameters/policy. Test: run fio --thinktime=2s --thinktime_blocks=1 (idle between commands). Compare p99 with APST off (nvme_core.default_ps_max_latency_us=0). A clear difference is proof.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Things keep working, only slower. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: By default, the computer's own choices are the cause. They are the APST table, ASPM powersave, and default_ps_max_latency_us (100 ms, the Linux computer's setting). The SSD is at fault if device_part is longer than the EXLAT it states for the state the computer allowed. The hardware or wire is at fault if link_part is longer than the stated wake time (L1 or LTR). · Test that confirms it: compare with APST off and on.

P-08 Too many 'work done' signals, or badly grouped signals (interrupt coalescing) Seen in the packets Order and 'work done' signals

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 626533: a 'work is done' signal (MSI-X) about every 200 ns. Grouping of signals is off while many small commands run.

Packet=626533 | Link Dir=Downstream | DLLP Type=ACK | Time Stamp=0521.200479026500s | Time Delta=701.750 ns | AckNak Seq Num=317

Error family: P16, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. A check on the order and timing of packets finds it. Examples: a missing answer, a long gap, packets out of order.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book has a signal grouping feature (Interrupt Coalescing, 08h). It sets a wait time in 100 µs steps (Aggregation Time) and a count (Aggregation Threshold). Another feature (Interrupt Vector Configuration, 09h) can turn grouping off for each signal number.

What goes wrong: One signal per done note, at 1M+ commands per second (IOPS), costs a lot of processor time (a storm). The other way round, strong grouping (Feature 08h count or wait time) saves processor time. But it adds up to the wait time to every command when few commands run at once. Signals sent to the wrong place (all signal numbers on processor 0) make one processor core the bottleneck.

How you can tell: High %irq or %soft in mpstat. One processor at 100%. Or a fixed extra time (for example +100 µs) with one command at a time (QD 1).

How to fix it and prove the fix: Take care: this changes SSD settings, so put them back after. On a test machine, run nvme set-feature /dev/nvme0 -f 0x08 -v <value> and measure the time with one command at a time, before and after. Run nvme get-feature /dev/nvme0 -f 0x08 -H. Run grep nvme /proc/interrupts (counts per processor per list). Run mpstat -P ALL 1. Compare IOPS per processor with checking instead of signals (poll_queues plus --hipri).

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Things keep working, only slower. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The computer's software is at fault (its grouping or signal-placement settings). The SSD is at fault only if its MSI-X timing goes past the grouping settings it was given. · Test that confirms it: read the feature setting.

P-09 The computer's processor cannot send commands fast enough Partly seen in the packets Speed (timing counts)

Packets seen in the test recording

Error family: P22, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. Also E05 (a kind of evidence from outside the recording). · Can the packets alone prove it? Partly. The timing and order of the packets show its shape. Proof needs evidence from outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: No rule covers this. It is the computer's software.

What goes wrong: The computer cannot make commands fast enough. One fio job on one processor core tops out at a few hundred thousand commands per second with libaio. So a drive rated for 1.5M commands per second looks 'slow'.

How you can tell: fio shows cpu: usr/sys near 100% per job. The numbers do not fit Little's Law (error list, section 8.1.2). Adding jobs raises IOPS in a straight line.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Run perf top or perf record -g during the run, to see where processor time goes. Try --ioengine=io_uring --fixedbufs --registerfiles --hipri, more numjobs, and --iodepth_batch_submit. Check cpupower frequency-info.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Things keep working, only slower. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The computer's software is at fault when the SSD answers each command quickly and then waits for doorbells. The SSD is at fault if doorbells come close together and its fetches lag behind. · Test that confirms it: add jobs and see if speed grows.

P-10 Work runs on the processor far from the SSD (NUMA placement) Not seen in the packets Speed (timing counts)

Packets seen in the test recording

Error family: P22, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. Also E05 (a kind of evidence from outside the recording). · Can the packets alone prove it? No. It cannot be seen on this wire. The recording only shows packets around it. The proof is outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: No rule covers this. It is about how the computer is built.

What goes wrong: A server can have more than one processor chip (socket or die). The SSD's port belongs to one of them (one NUMA node). Programs and their memory may be on the other chip. Then every data move and every doorbell must cross the link between the chips. This adds time and uses up that link's speed.

How you can tell: Time per command is 10 to 30% higher, or IOPS lower, depending on which processors run the test. Results change from run to run as the computer moves programs around (this depends on the computer).

How to fix it and prove the fix: Safe. Run read-only fio fixed to the near processor, then the far one. Run cat /sys/bus/pci/devices/<bdf>/numa_node and local_cpulist. Run fio with --numa_cpu_nodes=N --numa_mem_policy=bind:N (or numactl --cpunodebind=N --membind=N fio …) for the near and far N, and compare. Use perf stat counts for the link between chips, where available.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Things keep working, only slower. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The computer's software or hardware is at fault (where programs, memory or signals are placed). The SSD is not affected. · Test that confirms it: check the computer's layout.

P-11 The wire starts slower or narrower than it can (speed, lane drop) Seen in the packets Wire start-up steps

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 228843: the wire started with 2 lanes (x2), although both ends have 4 lanes (x4).

Packet=228843 | Link Event=Width Change: x2 | Time Stamp=0129.258893320000s | Time Delta=0.000 ns

Error family: P08, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. Also E02 (a kind of evidence from outside the recording). · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. A check on the order and timing of packets finds it. Examples: a missing answer, a long gap, packets out of order.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book has Link Capabilities (Max Link Speed and Width). It also has Link Status (Current Link Speed, Negotiated Link Width). Speed can change during the wire's start-up steps and during recovery.

What goes wrong: A Gen4 drive with 4 lanes connects at Gen3, or with 2 lanes (or 1). Everything works, but at half or a quarter of the speed.

How you can tell: lspci -vvv shows 'LnkSta: Speed 8GT/s (downgraded), Width x2 (downgraded)', against 'LnkCap: Speed 16GT/s, Width x4'. At start-up, Linux prints '… available PCIe bandwidth, limited by … link at … (capable of …)'. Speed-change signals may log changes the wire made by itself.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Safe: move the drive between slots and note LnkSta each time. Take care: on a test machine, force the target speed through Link Control 2 with setpci and restart the wire. Run cat /sys/bus/pci/devices/<bdf>/{current_link_speed,max_link_speed,current_link_width,max_link_width}. Check the computer port's LnkCap too, because the wire runs at the lower of the two. Run dmesg | grep 'limited by'. Speed test: reading in order tops out at about the top speed of the slower wire.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Things keep working, only slower. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The wire is at fault when both ends say full speed and width, but fall back after tuning or recovery. The computer's hardware is at fault when its port offers less (error list, section XII.8). Causes are the BIOS, slot wiring, or lane splitting. · Test that confirms it: compare what the wire can do with what it is doing now (E02).

P-12 Small packet-size limits hold back speed (MPS or MRRS too small) Seen in the packets Speed (timing counts)

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 1787344: the Device Control setting has MPS = 128 B (the largest data size per packet).

Packet=1787344 | Link Dir=Downstream | TLP Type=CfgWr0 | PSN=3063 | Tag=31 | RequesterID=000:00:0 | Length=1 | DATA=4 B | Time Stamp=1822.753820011370s | Time Delta=158.130 ns | LCRC=0x6626E129

Error family: P22, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. Also E02 (a kind of evidence from outside the recording). · Can the packets alone prove it? Partly. The timing and order of the packets show its shape. Proof needs evidence from outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book has two Device Control settings. Max_Payload_Size is the largest data per packet. Max_Read_Request_Size is the largest read request.

What goes wrong: MPS = 128 B costs about 8% of a Gen4 x4 wire, compared with 256 B. It costs about 12% compared with 512 B (error list, section 8.1.1). A small MRRS (for example 128 B) makes the SSD send many more read requests to fetch data to write. Each needs a request number (tag) and an answer. With a limited number of open request numbers, this caps write speed.

How you can tell: Reading or writing in order gets stuck at about 85 to 90% of the expected top. lspci -vvv shows 'DevCtl: MaxPayload 128 bytes, MaxReadReq 128 bytes'.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Take care. On a lab machine, start with a different pci=pcie_bus_* choice and compare. Never lower MPS on one end only (that is error type V-26 in the error list). Run lspci -vvv for every part from the computer's port to the SSD (DevCap MaxPayload against DevCtl MaxPayload). Compare speeds when reading or writing in order. The capture tool shows packet data sizes directly.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Things keep working, only slower. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The computer's hardware is at fault (the BIOS or operating system choice for MPS and MRRS). The settings write (CfgWr) to Device Control at start-up decides it. The SSD is at fault only if it sends packets smaller than the MPS or MRRS it was given. · Test that confirms it: a dump of the settings.

P-13 Writes that do not line up force extra read and rewrite work Partly seen in the packets Speed (timing counts)

Packets seen in the test recording

Error family: P22, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. Also E05 (a kind of evidence from outside the recording). · Can the packets alone prove it? Partly. The timing and order of the packets show its shape. Proof needs evidence from outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe storage command rule book has block formats. They are LBAF on the storage area's information page, with a 'Relative Performance' field. It also has hints for the best writes, when given. They are NPWG (Preferred Write Granularity), NPWA (Preferred Write Alignment) and NOWS (Optimal Write Size).

What goes wrong: A storage area is formatted with 512-byte blocks. But the drive's inside map unit is 4 KiB or larger. Some writes do not start on a 4 KiB line, or are not a whole number of 4 KiB. The SSD's map and storage manager (FTL) must read the rest of the unit, merge, and write again. That means more time and more storage-chip writes.

How you can tell: Small-write IOPS are far below the data sheet. There is more extra writing (write amplification). Nothing is in the logs.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Take care (this writes). On a spare storage area, compare lined-up and not lined-up 4k random writes. Run nvme id-ns /dev/nvme0n1 -H (block formats with 'Relative Performance', npwg, npwa, nows). Run cat /sys/block/nvme0n1/queue/{physical_block_size,optimal_io_size,minimum_io_size}. On a spare drive, run fio with --bs=4k --offset=512, against lined-up writes.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Things keep working, only slower. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The computer's software is at fault (partition line-up, the program's page size, the block format chosen). The SSD is at fault only if lined-up writes are slow too. · Test that confirms it: lined-up against not lined-up writes.

P-14 Many 'save now' requests on a drive without write cache (Flush, FUA) Seen in the packets Speed (timing counts)

Packets seen in the test recording

Error family: P22 and P24, two of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. · Can the packets alone prove it? Partly. The timing and order of the packets show its shape. Proof needs evidence from outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe main and storage command rule books cover this. They have the Flush command (00h) and the 'write straight to storage' bit in Write (Force Unit Access). They have the write cache feature (Volatile Write Cache, 06h), and VWC on the SSD's information page.

What goes wrong: Programs that call fsync after every write make Flush commands (or FUA writes). Home drives often have a write cache that is lost at power-off. On them, each Flush forces cached data into the storage chips. Saved-write time jumps from tens of µs to milliseconds. Business drives with power-loss protection can confirm flushes quickly.

How you can tell: Database commit time is high. iostat shows low speed but high w_await. Nothing is in the logs.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Take care (this writes). On a spare storage area, run fio --rw=randwrite --bs=4k --fsync=1 and compare with --fsync=0. Run nvme id-ctrl /dev/nvme0 | grep vwc, nvme get-feature /dev/nvme0 -f 0x06 and cat /sys/block/nvme0n1/queue/write_cache. Run fio with --fsync=1 against none on a spare drive. Count Flush commands with the nvme_setup_cmd trace event.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Things keep working, only slower. · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The computer's software is at fault (how the work is designed, or a write cache that was turned off). The SSD is at fault only if Flush takes far too long on a drive with VWC and power-loss protection. · Test that confirms it: compare with fsync on and off.

Chapter N: failures outside the recorded wire (58 entries)

Why this part is here: these 58 entries are newer features, or failures outside the recorded wire.

N-01 Another path changes the SSD without this wire seeing it (dual-port SSD) Not seen in the packets Not seen on this wire

Packets seen in the test recording

Error family: none. This error has no family on the wire, only proof from outside the recording. Proof from outside the recording: E03, the SSD's own logs and saved settings. E08, a second capture tool, switch counters or other logs. · Can the packets alone prove it? No. It cannot be seen on this wire. The rows shown only give background. The proof is outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book allows one SSD to have several paths. This is called multi-path I/O (CMIC). The rule book says which storage areas several paths share and which are private (NMIC). It defines an ID for each computer (Host Identifier) and locks on storage areas (reservations). It also defines a log that lists changed storage areas (Changed Namespace List, log 04h). Check this in your version of the rule book.

What goes wrong: Some SSDs have two connections to computers (dual-port U.2, U.3 or E3 drives). Each connection has its own controller, the part of the SSD that follows the NVMe rules. The SSD shows this in its ID data (Identify Controller, CMIC bit 0 and bit 1). Shared storage areas (namespaces) can be reached through both. Two computers may share one drive box. Or one computer may have both ports wired. Then the second controller is a full equal and can change anything. The same is true when several controllers sit behind one port. Examples are extra virtual controllers (SR-IOV secondaries). Network storage targets with several controllers (NVMe-oF) are another example.

How you can tell: Data seems to change between two reads. But no write was seen on the recorded wire. This looks like old data (error type D-15 in the error list) or wrong data (D-16). The command nvme list-subsys shows two controllers for one SSD name (subsystem NQN). The lock report (Reservation Report) lists a lock holder with another computer's ID. An alert says a storage area changed (Namespace Attribute Changed). Its list names a storage area this computer did not touch.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Careful: use a spare drive or a test system. Connect both ports. Write a pattern through port B while recording port A. Then read the same area through port A. The recording on A shows reads that return the new pattern, with no write. Read the SSD's multi-path bits (CMIC) and its controller list. Use nvme id-ctrl and nvme list-ctrl for this. Compare controller IDs in nvme list-subsys. Ask for a lock report (Reservation Report). Look for other computers' IDs in it. For full proof, record both wires with one shared clock. Or log every command on the second computer and merge the logs by time. The SSD's lasting event log (Persistent Event Log, error type S-86) also helps. It records Format, Set Features and storage-area changes. Each entry carries the ID of the controller that sent the command.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Everything says success. Only a careful check finds it (Silent). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Check the software on the other path. That means a second computer, the board's management chip (BMC) or a maintenance computer. Suspect the SSD only in one case. It says it has no second path (CMIC=0), and no other controller exists. · Test that confirms it: look at the whole SSD's controller list (subsystem view).

N-02 A side management wire changes the SSD (NVMe-MI over SMBus, BMC) Not seen in the packets Rare messages and side signals

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 120542: management messages (NVMe-MI) from the board's management chip (BMC). They travel on the slow management wire (SMBus).

Packet=120542 | Time Stamp=0125.588331792120s | Time Delta=50.200 ms

Error family: P21, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. It means other rare messages and hints. Proof from outside the recording: E03, the SSD's own logs and saved settings. E06, records from the slow management wire (SMBus). · Can the packets alone prove it? No. It cannot be seen on this wire. The rows shown only give background. The proof is outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: A separate rule book covers SSD management (NVMe-MI). It carries management messages (MCTP) over a second, slow management wire (SMBus or I²C). It can also carry them over the main wire, inside special vendor messages (PCIe VDM). It defines a basic management command over SMBus. It lists which normal management commands may be sent this way (out-of-band). Check your version of the rule book.

What goes wrong: A management chip on the computer's board (BMC) talks to the SSD. A drive-bay helper chip (expander) can do the same. They use the SMBus pins of the connector, not the main wire. With NVMe-MI they can read the SSD's health and change its management settings. They can write the product data (VPD). They can also send a limited set of normal management commands. Vendor tools use this path to update the program inside the SSD (firmware) on running systems. The computer's own software sees the SSD change for no visible reason.

How you can tell: The driver restarts the controller (nvme reset_controller) for no clear reason. This happens after the fatal-error flag (CSTS.CFS) or the ready flag (CSTS.RDY) changes. The firmware version shown by nvme id-ctrl at start-up differs from the one shown later. Product data (VPD) or temperature limits differ from what the operating system set. The wire goes down and the SSD is found again. Yet the computer did nothing.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Careful: use a spare drive or a test system. Send a health check from the BMC while recording (NVMe-MI Controller Health Status Poll). Also send a log request through the same path (tunnelled Get Log Page). Nothing appears on the main wire. Risky, test machine only: start a firmware switch from the BMC during reads and writes. Read the BMC logs (Redfish event log, IPMI SEL). Put an SMBus capture tool (I²C/SMBus analyzer) on the connector's SMBus pins. Read the SSD's lasting event log (Persistent Event Log, log 0Dh). It records firmware commits, setting changes and power-on or reset events. It records them whichever path caused them. Check which fields your drive fills in. The commands nvme mi in nvme-cli can ask the management side from the computer. So can the library libnvme-mi. Both need an SMBus adapter.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Everything says success. Only a careful check finds it (Silent). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Check the computer's board first. The BMC or a drive-bay helper may act through NVMe-MI. It may also use the reset pin (PERST#) or slot power. Suspect the SSD only if it changes state on its own. That would be a self-restart like error type N-32, not N-02. · Test that confirms it: the BMC logs.

N-03 Packets lost on a part of the path nobody recorded Partly seen in the packets Answer never arrived in time

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 1325805: a read request (MRd) from the SSD to fetch write data. The wire said "arrived fine", but no answer ever came.

Packet=1325805 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MRd(64) | PSN=1312 | Tag=73 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000004:1B46A000 | Length=128 | Time Stamp=1295.956922184120s | Time Delta=134.130 ns | LCRC=0x997FD9DE

Packet 1325807: the time limit for an answer ran out (Completion Timeout). An error message (ERR_NONFATAL) came about 50 ms after the read request.

Packet=1325807 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=Msg | PSN=1313 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Length=0 | Time Stamp=1296.006922184120s | Time Delta=132.130 ns | LCRC=0x0445DD21

Packet 1325809: the SSD's done note says the data move failed (Data Transfer Error, SCT0 SC 0x04).

Packet=1325809 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=1314 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000004:83570010 | Length=4 | DATA=16 B | Time Stamp=1296.006962184120s | Time Delta=0.000 ns | LCRC=0xD1129A14

Error family: P03, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. It means a read request that never gets an answer. Proof from outside the recording: E02, a copy of the SSD's settings area (lspci). E08, a second capture tool, switch counters or other logs. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. The checker marks an odd field or order in this table file (completion_timeout).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book covers how a switch chip passes packets on. It covers how a packet is cancelled on the way (TLP nullification, EDB). Each wire has its own receipts (Ack/Nak) and its own room counting (flow control). So an "arrived fine" receipt on the recorded wire proves nothing about the next wire.

What goes wrong: A request or data packet (TLP) leaves the SSD and crosses the recorded wire cleanly. The switch chip's port takes it, and the Ack is seen. Then it is lost, delayed or cancelled on a part of the path with no capture tool. Some fast switches start passing a packet on before it has fully arrived (cut-through). If the incoming copy turns out broken, they cancel it on the outgoing wire. They mark it with an end-bad mark (EDB) and an inverted check number (LCRC). This cancel is visible only on the outgoing wire.

How you can tell: On the computer side, the answer time limit runs out (Completion Timeout, L-14). This shows in the error-report bits (AER) of the computer's port (root port). Or an NVMe command runs out of time (T-22). Yet the recording shows the done note was written. The switch's own error bits may show trouble on its upward wire. They may show overflow, a bad packet or a sudden wire loss (Receiver Overflow, Bad TLP, Surprise Down). The delay measured on the SSD wire is normal. But the full round trip is slow. These are the signs of M-045 with an SSD that did nothing wrong.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Read the error-report bits of every port on the path. Do not stop at the SSD. Use lspci -vvv on the switch's upward and downward parts, and on the root port. Compare two times (M-006). One is when the SSD wire shows the done note being written. The other is when the computer saw it. The clear proof is a second capture tool on the upward wire. The switch maker's internal error and dropped-packet counters are also clear proof.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Nothing reports it.
