Only a timer notices that something did not arrive in time (Timer only). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Is the recorded wire clean? Then check the computer's side. That means the switch, or the upward wire's signal quality. It also means a signal booster chip (retimer). Or the computer's chip may run out of room (root-complex credit starvation). Suspect the SSD only if the recorded wire shows the SSD not sending. · Test that confirms it: a second capture tool, or the switch's counters.

N-04 Computer memory spoils good data, and the SSD gets the blame Not seen in the packets Not seen on this wire

Packets seen in the test recording

Error family: none. This error has no family on the wire, only proof from outside the recording. Proof from outside the recording: E01, the Linux kernel log. E04, reading the data back and checking it. · Can the packets alone prove it? No. It cannot be seen on this wire. The rows shown only give background. The proof is outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: Neither the NVMe nor the PCIe rule book covers this. The SSD's job ends when its write packet (MWr) is done. Or it ends when it has the answer with data (CplD). Extra check data can travel with each block (end-to-end protection information, PI). It exists to catch exactly this kind of problem. The program computes a check value (Guard tag), and the controller checks it. That catches damage between the two (D-21, S-61).

What goes wrong: Data was correct on the wire. Then something in the computer changes it. It may be a bit error in the computer's memory chips (DRAM), not fixed or fixed wrongly. It may be the processor's cache writing back over the data while the SSD writes it. It may be a software bug that writes over a buffer after the SSD filled it. Then the check values in the program or file system fail. The storage drive is the first one blamed.

How you can tell: The file system reports check-value errors (btrfs or ZFS "checksum mismatch"). Database pages are damaged, or fio --verify fails. Yet nvme smart-log shows no media errors, and the SSD's error log is empty. Memory error messages (EDAC or MCE) appear in the Linux kernel log (dmesg) near that time. The errors follow the memory stick (DIMM), not the SSD.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Safe to try: use a memory stick known to be bad. Run fio --verify=crc32c with it, or run memtester at the same time. Compare the data in the recording with the data the program got. Careful: use a spare drive or a test system. Then inject memory errors with the EDAC/APEI EINJ tool, on computers that support it. From the recording, take the data of the write packets for the failing block address (LBA). Compare it with (a) what the program received. Compare it with (b) what a later read returns. Check the kernel log for EDAC, mce and Machine check messages. Use rasdaemon or ras-mc-ctl --errors. Move the SSD into another computer. If the damage stays with the first computer, it is not the drive. Turn on the extra check data (PI) on a test storage area. Then the controller itself spots buffer damage on the write path.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Everything says success. Only a careful check finds it (Silent). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Is the data on the wire correct? Then check the computer. Look at memory chips, software writing over buffers, or reuse of copy buffers (bounce buffers). · Test that confirms it: the memory error logs (E01).

N-05 SSD and processor see different bytes in memory (No-Snoop) Partly seen in the packets Broken or wrongly built packets

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 431896: a data write packet (MWr) had the No Snoop flag set. But it went to a buffer that needs the cache check.

Packet=431896 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=29 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000004:81C301E0 | Length=4 | DATA=16 B | Time Stamp=0196.116247020750s | Time Delta=58.880 ns | LCRC=0x2C06F493

Error family: P11, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. It means broken, poisoned or wrongly built packets. Proof from outside the recording: E02, a copy of the SSD's settings area (lspci). · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. The checker marks an odd field or order in this table file (attributes_set_NS).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book defines flags in each packet (TLP Attr field). One flag, No Snoop, tells the computer not to check the processor's cache. The SSD's settings have a switch for it (Enable No Snoop, in Device Control). It is on by default. So the SSD may use the flag unless software turns it off. NVMe does not use this flag. NVMe expects its command lists to look the same to the controller and the processor (coherent).

What goes wrong: There are two ways this fails. (1) The SSD sets No Snoop (Attr[0] = 1) when writing to memory the computer treats as coherent. On some computers the write then skips the cache check. The processor later reads an old cached copy. (2) Some computers do not keep memory and cache in step by hardware. There the driver must clean or refresh the cache around each transfer (dma_sync_*). Sometimes that step is missing or in the wrong order. Then the SSD reads an old command (SQE), the previous one in that slot. So the same command number (CID) runs twice. That is the fingerprint of V-08. Or the processor reads an old done note (CQE) or data buffer.

How you can tell: Way 1: reads sometimes return wrong data. Often only the first few bytes of a buffer are wrong. It depends on the computer. Way 2: commands run twice (signs of V-08 and D-29). Done notes are "never" seen (sign of C-15). Data looks like it came from the previous read or write.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Risky, test machine only: use a development board without cache in step. Remove one dma_sync_single_for_device() call in a test driver. Watch the command fetched by the SSD lag behind the doorbell. In the recording, pick out SSD read and write packets with No Snoop = 1. Match their addresses to the command lists or the data buffers. Turn off Enable No Snoop in the SSD's settings and test again. The command is setpci -s <BDF> CAP_EXP+8.w. On computers without cache in step, turn on CONFIG_DMA_API_DEBUG. Compare the command bytes fetched on the wire with what the driver says it wrote. The driver's tracepoint shows what it wrote.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Everything says success. Only a careful check finds it (Silent). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: There are two cases. The SSD is at fault when No Snoop is set on writes into buffers that need the cache check. The computer is at fault when No Snoop is 0 and the cache steps are missing. That applies on a computer that does not keep cache in step. · Test that confirms it: turn off No Snoop.

N-06 A power dip restarts the SSD without the computer asking Partly seen in the packets Wire goes down, power or restart

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 1391871: the wire went quiet, and nobody asked it to go down. There was no goodbye signal (EIOS), no power-saving receipt (PM DLLP) and no restart order (Hot Reset).

Packet=1391871 | Link Event=Electrical Idle | Time Stamp=1338.614094823000s | Time Delta=0.000 ns

Error family: P12, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. It means the wire going down while work is in flight. Proof from outside the recording: E03, the SSD's own logs and saved settings. E07, measuring the power lines and side pins. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. The checker marks an odd field or order in this table file (request_lost_across_link_down).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: Each connector shape has a rule book (CEM, SFF, EDSFF form factors). These set the allowed power-line ranges. They also set limits for slot power and for the power rush when a card is plugged in. The main PCIe rule book says nothing about power lines. NVMe counts sudden power losses (SMART Unsafe Shutdowns). It also logs power-on and reset events in its lasting event log (Persistent Event Log).

What goes wrong: The 3.3 V or 12 V power line drops below the SSD's low-voltage limit. The drop lasts from microseconds to milliseconds. One cause is a shared line hit by the power rush of a nearby card being plugged in. Another is a power regulator that is too small. A bad connector contact is a third. The SSD's power-on restart then fires. The SSD behaves exactly like a cold start, and the computer did not ask for it. Open commands disappear. If the drop was short, the computer may not even see the wire go down. The SSD is already back at its first start-up step (Detect).

How you can tell: Signs of a sudden wire loss appear (Surprise Down, L-11), or signs of L-27. The kernel log says nvme nvme0: controller is down; will reset. The SMART count of unsafe shutdowns goes up while the system was running. So the drive counted a power loss. The lasting event log has "Power-on or Reset" entries (event type 04h). They match no action by the computer. These often come in groups when another device in the box is plugged in or spins up.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Risky, test machine only: use a programmable power supply. Feed the SSD from it, and make a controlled 1 to 10 ms drop during reads and writes. Or plug a card known for a large power rush into a nearby slot on the same line. Put an oscilloscope or a logging meter on the power line at the connector. Start it from the reset pin (PERST#) or from the capture tool's trigger output. Compare the unsafe-shutdown count before and after. Read the lasting event log for reset events and their times. Match them with box events in the BMC log (fan, power supply, other plug-ins).

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Nothing reports it. Only a timer notices that something did not arrive in time (Timer only). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: There are two cases. The computer's power delivery is at fault when two things hold. Nothing on the wire shows the computer caused it. And the power-line measurement shows the drop. The SSD is at fault if its lasting event log shows an internal restart reason instead (error list, section XII.8). · Test that confirms it: measure the power line with a scope (risky, test machine only).

N-07 Faults on the connector's side signal pins (PERST#, CLKREQ#, WAKE#) Not seen in the packets Wire goes down, power or restart

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 1394507: a short glitch on the clock-request pin (CLKREQ#) or the reset pin (PERST#). The wire was in its normal working state (L0).

Packet=1394507 | Link Event=CLKREQ# Deasserted | Time Stamp=1339.025468220000s | Time Delta=0.000 ns

Packet 1394508: the wire went quiet, and nobody asked it to go down. There was no goodbye signal (EIOS), no power-saving receipt (PM DLLP) and no restart order (Hot Reset).

Packet=1394508 | Link Event=Electrical Idle | Time Stamp=1339.025468220000s | Time Delta=0.000 ns

Error family: P12, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. It means the wire going down while work is in flight. Proof from outside the recording: E02, a copy of the SSD's settings area (lspci). E06, records from the slow management wire (SMBus). E07, measuring the power lines and side pins. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. The checker marks an odd field or order in this table file (request_lost_across_link_down).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The card rule book (PCIe CEM) defines the side signal pins. These are reset (PERST#) and the reference clock (REFCLK). They are also clock request (CLKREQ#), wake (WAKE#), card present (PRSNT#) and power brake (PWRBRK#). The rule book sets their timing. It sets the shortest time from "power good" to the end of reset. It also sets the shortest time from "clock steady" to the end of reset. Pin layouts come from other rule books: SFF-8639 (U.2), SFF-TA-1002/1009 (EDSFF) and PCI-SIG M.2. Check the values in the rule book for your connector shape.

What goes wrong: The connector carries control signals beside the main signal pairs. The rule books for each connector shape set their timing. One example is the CEM shortest time from power good to the end of reset. Another is the shortest time from steady clock to the end of reset. A short glitch or a slow edge can cause trouble. So can a missing pull-up part or a board wiring mistake. The wire then misbehaves. It looks like a rules fault or an SSD fault.

How you can tell: Reset (PERST#) is released before the clock is steady. Start-up then fails or keeps bouncing (X-12, L-39), and works on a retry. Clock request (CLKREQ#) problems: the SSD cannot leave its deepest sleep (L1.2). So the first command after idle runs out of time (T-46, M-024, M-025). Wake (WAKE#) problems: after system sleep (S3/S4) the SSD is missing. Settings reads return all ones (C-16). Card present (PRSNT#) problems: the hot-plug driver (pciehp) logs Card not present. It removes the SSD during reads and writes (L-29), with no wire event.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Risky, test machine only: use a side-pin breakout board. Pulse reset for 1 µs during reads and writes. Hold clock request high while leaving deep sleep (L1.2). Pull the card-present pin briefly while the wire is up. Put a logic analyzer or scope on the side pins. Line it up in time with the capture tool, using its trigger output. Measure the end of reset against power good and against a steady reference clock. Check the slot status with lspci -vvv (Slot Status: PresDet, Link Status). Check the kernel log (dmesg) for card-present changes. For clock request, read the deep-sleep control settings (Link Control, L1 PM Substates). Confirm that the board actually wires the pin.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Nothing reports it. Only a timer notices that something did not arrive in time (Timer only). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Does the wire misbehave with no rules cause? Then suspect the computer's board, its start-up program or the side-pin wiring. Confirm with a scope, or with a side-pin capture through an adapter (interposer). See the error list, section XII.8. · Test that confirms it: side-pin capture (risky, test machine only).

N-08 SSD missing after full power-off sleep or system wake-up (D3cold) Not seen in the packets Power-saving handshakes and latency messages

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 1340836: the SSD is missing after power came back from full power-off sleep (D3cold).

Packet=1340836 | Link Event=Receiver Detect: no device | Time Stamp=1308.117319625000s | Time Delta=500.000 ms

Packet 1340837: the SSD is missing after power came back from full power-off sleep (D3cold).

Packet=1340837 | Link Event=Receiver Detect: no device | Time Stamp=1308.617319625000s | Time Delta=500.000 ms

Packet 1340838: the SSD is missing after power came back from full power-off sleep (D3cold).

Packet=1340838 | Link Event=Receiver Detect: no device | Time Stamp=1309.117319625000s | Time Delta=500.000 ms

Packet 1340839: the SSD is missing after power came back from full power-off sleep (D3cold).

Packet=1340839 | Link Event=Receiver Detect: no device | Time Stamp=1309.617319625000s | Time Delta=0.000 ns

Error family: P20, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. It means power-saving handshakes and latency messages. Proof from outside the recording: E07, measuring the power lines and side pins. · Can the packets alone prove it? No. It cannot be seen on this wire. The rows shown only give background. The proof is outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book covers full power-off sleep (D3cold). It covers the restart after power returns (Conventional Reset). It sets how soon the SSD must be ready after a restart. This is the 1 s rule and the ready-time report (Readiness Time Reporting), see N-43 and T-41. The power-management rule book (PCI PM) covers waking from D3cold. That needs standby power and the wake pin (WAKE#). In NVMe, the sleep and wake times (RTD3) are advice for the driver, not for the computer's board.

What goes wrong: In full power-off sleep, the computer's board removes main power from the slot. It does this through power tables (ACPI _PS3 / _PR3) or system sleep (S3/S4). On wake-up the board must give power back. It must release reset (PERST#) after the clock is steady. The SSD must then start the wire and accept settings within its ready time. If any step fails, the SSD stays missing. Settings reads return all ones, and the driver's wake-up steps fail.

How you can tell: After wake-up the kernel log shows nvme nvme0: Device not ready; aborting reset. Or it shows Removing after probe failure. It may also show pci 0000:xx:00.0: not ready after N ms; giving up. The SSD is missing from lspci. On laptops, a drive "disappears" after sleep. It comes back after a full power-off start.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Careful: use a spare drive or a test system. Run rtcwake -m mem -s 20 in a loop. Keep reads and writes running before each sleep. Force D3cold with /sys/bus/pci/devices/<BDF>/d3cold_allowed and runtime power control. Read the kernel log around wake-up with pm_debug_messages and initcall_debug. Read /sys/bus/pci/devices/<BDF>/power_state before sleep. Watch the slot's power light, or put a scope on the slot power line. Use acpidump to read the power resources (_PR3) of the computer's port. Sometimes the SSD starts the wire in the recording, but the driver still fails. Then the problem moved to the ready step or the NVMe steps (T-41, C-02).

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Nothing reports it. Only a timer notices that something did not arrive in time (Timer only). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: There are two cases. The computer's board is at fault if something is not restored correctly. That is slot power, reset, reference clock or wake (E07, ACPI). The SSD is at fault if power and clock are correct but it never shows up on the wire. The same holds if it never starts the wire. Then also check the unsafe-shutdown counts. Being ready after start-up is covered by T-41 and N-43. · Test that confirms it: scope the power lines and side pins.

N-09 Encrypted wire hides the packet contents (IDE / TDISP) Not seen in the packets Not seen on this wire

Packets seen in the test recording

Error family: none. This error has no family on the wire, only proof from outside the recording. Proof from outside the recording: E09, a lab test whose result is the proof. · Can the packets alone prove it? No. It cannot be seen on this wire. The rows shown only give background. The proof is outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book defines encryption on the wire (IDE). IDE means Integrity and Data Encryption. The rule book covers its settings block (IDE Extended Capability). It covers two kinds of protected stream (Link IDE and Selective IDE). It covers how keys are handed out (IDE_KM over DOE/SPDM). It also covers how a device is safely given to a protected virtual computer (TDISP). Check your version of the rule book.

What goes wrong: IDE sets up encrypted, tamper-checked streams (AES-GCM). They run between the computer's port (or a switch) and the SSD. TDISP uses this to give the SSD to a protected virtual computer (confidential VM). Once the stream is secure, only the key holder can know what a packet carried.

How you can tell: The capture tool's NVMe view is empty or full of nonsense. Its packet view still shows normal counts of reads, writes and answers (MWr, MRd, CplD). The data bytes look completely random. The IDE settings block shows streams in the Secure state. Problems inside the virtual computer cannot be matched to commands. Such problems include timeouts and wrong data.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Safe to try: use a computer that supports IDE. Record the same work with and without IDE. Compare the NVMe decoder's output. Check the IDE settings state with lspci -vvv on the SSD and the computer's port. To find faults, make the error happen again on a test system with IDE turned off. Or use logs from the computer and the SSD. These are the protected-computer firmware logs (TSM, TDX, SEV-SNP) and the SSD's own reports (telemetry). Some capture tools say they can decrypt when given the keys (not certain). Check the maker's documents and your security rules. Entries based on timing (Part X of the error list) still work on encrypted data.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Everything says success. Only a careful check finds it (Silent). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: This is the test set-up. IDE is working as designed. It is not a computer or SSD fault. · Test that confirms it: the IDE state (E02).

N-10 Side effects of giving the SSD to a virtual computer (passthrough) Partly seen in the packets Wrong memory address or sender name

Packets seen in the test recording

Error family: P17, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. It means memory access to the wrong place, or with a wrong sender name. Proof from outside the recording: E08, a second capture tool, switch counters or other logs. · Can the packets alone prove it? Partly. The packets show a shape in timing or order. The proof needs evidence from outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: This is not in the NVMe or PCIe rule books. It is in the rule books for the computer's memory guard. The memory guard is called the IOMMU (Intel VT-d, AMD-Vi, ARM SMMU). It also involves remapping of "work done" signals (interrupt remapping). PCIe address translation (ATS/PRI) is used for shared memory. NVMe itself does not know about virtual computers. The exception is extra virtual functions (SR-IOV).

What goes wrong: The SSD is given to a virtual computer (guest) using VFIO. The guest's driver runs the controller. But the SSD's memory accesses and "work done" signals pass through the real computer's hardware. That is the memory guard and the signal remapping hardware. These add behaviour that neither the guest driver nor the SSD caused. The causes are address-table updates and the delay in clearing old addresses. Others are catching and faking the signal table (MSI-X), and the real computer's processor scheduling. Error type M-064 covers the delay of extra virtual functions (SR-IOV VF). This entry covers giving the whole SSD to a guest. It also covers the address mix-ups this causes when reading a recording.

How you can tell: The guest reports command timeouts that the real computer never sees. The recording shows the done note and the "work done" signal written on time (the M-006 shape). The real computer logs memory-guard faults (DMAR) for addresses the guest thinks are fine (L-36). Delay spikes line up with the guest's processor being paused (vCPU preemption). Sometimes there are two levels of address tables (nested paging). Then the list addresses in the recording do not match /proc/iomem. They also do not match what the guest expects.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Careful: use a spare drive or a test system. Run a delay test in the guest. Pin, then unpin, the guest's processors while it runs. Switch the virtual memory guard's caching mode. Compare the recordings. Note the guest's list addresses. They are in the guest kernel log with nvme debug. They are also in the admin list address writes (ASQ/ACQ) in the recording. Note the real computer's memory-guard mapping (/sys/kernel/iommu_groups, iommu tracepoints). Match three things with the recording times. These are the real computer's guard faults (DMAR/AMD-Vi), vfio messages and kvm tracepoints. Compare the same work on the bare computer and in the guest.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. It still works, only slower or worse than it should (Degraded). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Check the computer's software first. That is the program that runs virtual computers (hypervisor). It is also the virtual memory guard and signal remapping. Suspect the SSD only if the bare computer shows the same behaviour. · Test that confirms it: the real computer's logs.

N-11 Error reports switched off or kept by the start-up program (AER masked) Partly seen in the packets Error messages on the wire (AER)

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 398207: the mask for small errors (AER Correctable Error Mask) is set. It hides bad request packets (Bad TLP) and bad receipt packets (Bad DLLP).

Packet=398207 | Link Dir=Downstream | TLP Type=CfgWr0 | PSN=820 | Tag=6 | RequesterID=000:00:0 | Length=1 | DATA=4 B | Time Stamp=0195.062372150870s | Time Delta=121.130 ns | LCRC=0x4454AC0F

Packet 398211: a bad request or data packet (bad TLP).

Packet=398211 | Link Dir=Downstream | TLP Type=MWr(32) | PSN=821 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=000:00:0 | Address=FCE0200C | Length=1 | DATA=4 B | Time Stamp=0195.064372545870s | Time Delta=79.130 ns | LCRC=0x0558F5AF (Bad)

Error family: P10 and P19, two of the 27 ways an error shows on the wire. P10 means error messages, and what is missing around them. P19 means the settings area: start-up, features, restarts and being ready. Proof from outside the recording: E01, the Linux kernel log. E02, a copy of the SSD's settings area (lspci). · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. The checker marks an odd field or order in this table file (lcrc_flagged_bad, tlp_replayed_same_psn).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book defines error-report bits (AER). They include masks that hide small errors (Correctable Error Mask). They include masks that hide serious errors (Uncorrectable Error Mask). A setting says how serious each error is (Severity). Switches in the SSD's settings turn reporting on or off for each error level (Device Control). The computer's port has its own setting (Root Error Command). The power tables (ACPI) decide who owns error handling (_OSC). They also define firmware error records (APEI, HEST, GHES).

What goes wrong: Errors are left hidden (masked) by one of three things. It can be the computer's start-up program, an earlier driver or a kernel setting. Or the start-up program keeps ownership of error handling (through _OSC). Linux then has no own error handler for that port. It relies on firmware error records (APEI). These may be slowed down or delayed. They may be limited to "fatal only", or be missing.

How you can tell: The wire bounces up and down, with resends and delays. Yet the kernel error log stays completely empty. The command lspci -vvv shows error status bits set that were never logged (UESta, CESta). Early in start-up, the kernel log says something about that port. It says the operating system does not control its error reports. Lines with aer_mask: in firmware-reported errors (GHES) show which bits were hidden.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Careful: use a spare drive or a test system. Set the mask for bad request packets (Bad TLP) with setpci. Cause resends with a lane-margin offset or a weak cable. Confirm the recording shows "arrived broken" receipts (Nak). Confirm the kernel logs nothing. Read the mask and status settings directly with lspci -vvv. Look at UEMsk, CEMsk, UESta, CESta and the DevCtl reporting bits. Check dmesg | grep -i _OSC and the result of pcie_aer_is_native. The counters /sys/bus/pci/devices/<BDF>/aer_dev_* exist only for ports the kernel owns. Count the Nak and resend events in the recording. Compare that with the kernel's small-error count. A large difference means masking. Or it means the start-up program handles errors first (firmware-first).

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Everything says success. Only a careful check finds it (Silent). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Check the computer's board first. Look at start-up program defaults (BIOS) and a firmware-first rule. Look for a kernel setting such as pci=noaer. Suspect the SSD only in one variant. That is when the error message itself is missing (MISSING_MESSAGE). · Test that confirms it: read the mask and enable settings.

N-12 Each operating system has its own time limits and recovery steps Partly seen in the packets Not seen on this wire

Packets seen in the test recording

Error family: none. This error has no family on the wire, only proof from outside the recording. Proof from outside the recording: E08, a second capture tool, switch counters or other logs. · Can the packets alone prove it? Partly. The packets show a shape in timing or order. The proof needs evidence from outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: NVMe leaves time limits, retries and restart rules to the computer on purpose. The rule book only sets the SSD's own timers. These are the ready time (CAP.TO) and the ready time with media (CRTO). They are also the keep-alive time (KATO) and the firmware switch time (MTFA). The last are the sleep and wake times (RTD3).

What goes wrong: Each computer's storage software makes its own choices. These are the command time limit, the retry count, the use of Abort, and when to restart. They also cover list sizes and grouping of "work done" signals. They cover the power-saving rule (APST) and the shutdown steps. They cover the SSD's use of computer memory (HMB). NVMe requires none of these. The same SSD recording is normal for one computer. It only looks like a rule break if you judge it by the wrong computer's habits.

How you can tell: The controller is restarted without an Abort first. (Linux always tries Abort first for read and write commands.) The gap before recovery is much shorter or longer. There is one command list per processor, or a small fixed number. Done notes are checked by polling instead of signals (SPDK, io_uring polling). No power-saving setting (APST) is sent, because Windows uses its own power rules. Keep Alive is sent on PCIe by some software. Linux sends none.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Safe to try: use two operating systems on one SSD. Record its start-up and a timeout under each. Compare the recovery steps. Work out which computer software it is from the recording itself. Look at the Identify and Set Features steps. Look at the number and size of command lists. Look at how signal numbers (MSI-X) are handed out. See whether Doorbell Buffer Config or HMB is used. Read the computer's ID (Host Identifier, Host NQN) if set. Then get that software's documented or set time limits. One source is the Windows registry TimeOutValue and the StorNVMe settings. Others are ESXi esxcli nvme device settings and FreeBSD hw.nvme.* sysctls. For SPDK it is nvme_ctrlr_opts. The exact defaults are not certain. Check them for each version.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Nothing reports it. Only a timer notices that something did not arrive in time (Timer only). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: This is the test set-up. The wrong computer's rules were used. Judge the real event again with the right operating system's rules. · Test that confirms it: evidence of which computer software it is (E08).

N-13 Stored data fades over time, heat or many reads Not seen in the packets Not seen on this wire

Packets seen in the test recording

Error family: none. This error has no family on the wire, only proof from outside the recording. Proof from outside the recording: E03, the SSD's own logs and saved settings. E04, reading the data back and checking it. E09, a lab test whose result is the proof. · Can the packets alone prove it? No. It cannot be seen on this wire. The rows shown only give background. The proof is outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: This is not in the NVMe rule book. It is in the JEDEC rule books. JESD218 sets how long an SSD must keep data, and how much writing it must survive. Data must last a set time at a stated temperature after the rated wear. Home and business drives have different classes. JESD219 sets the test workloads. NVMe only shows the results, through the health log (SMART) and the error log.

What goes wrong: Charge slowly leaks out of the memory cells (NAND) over time. It leaks faster when hot and in worn blocks (retention loss). Reading nearby pages many times shifts the cell voltages (read disturb). Data written at one temperature and read at a very different one shifts the read levels (cross-temperature). Controllers fight this with background checking and rewriting (scrubbing and refresh). That work is hidden too. It shows as regular background activity (M-098).

How you can tell: A drive that was fine sits a month without power in a hot store room. Then it shows read errors or slow reads on old data. Reads right after power-on are slow. They get faster after the controller rewrites the data. The media error count in SMART climbs with no new writes. Archived data fails its check values more often as it gets older.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Risky, test machine only: wear out a drive on purpose. Bring it near its rated total writes (TBW). Write a pattern, then bake it without power as JESD218 says. Read it back and time the reads. Ageing test: write a known pattern and note the SMART values. Store the drive hot for a set time, using the JESD218 speed-up rules. Then read everything back. Compare the data and the spread of read times. In daily use, run planned full-drive reads. Use nvme device-self-test extended. Or run a check pass with nvme verify where supported (see D-33 for its limits). Track SMART trends. Maker reports (telemetry) often have read-retry counters.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Everything says success. Only a careful check finds it (Silent). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Is the wire clean? Then suspect the SSD. The cause is the physics of its memory cells (retention, read disturb, cross-temperature). · Test that confirms it: compare SMART values before and after (E03).

N-14 Computer software sends data to the wrong place, the SSD obeys Partly seen in the packets Not seen on this wire

Packets seen in the test recording

Error family: none. This error has no family on the wire, only proof from outside the recording. Proof from outside the recording: E04, reading the data back and checking it. E05, a trace of the computer's storage steps. · Can the packets alone prove it? Partly. The packets show a shape in timing or order. The proof needs evidence from outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: No rule covers this. NVMe trusts the command (SQE). Only one thing can catch it. That is extra check data with a block-number check (end-to-end PI with Reference Tag checking, S-61, D-21). It catches a computer that writes the data meant for block n into block m. The block number the computer put in the check data will not match. The controller sees a different block. Linux sets this number from the request's sector for PI Type 1 storage areas.

What goes wrong: A bug sends a correct-looking command to the wrong place. The bug can be in the file system. It can be in the block layer (a bad merge or split). It can be in the partition start or a remapping layer (dm, md, LVM). It can be in a user-space driver, or in the program itself. The SSD carries out the command. Later the program finds data missing or written over. The SSD is blamed for a misplaced write (D-14) or a lost write (D-13).

How you can tell: File system damage happens again on different drives from different makers. The damage lines up with a partition or stripe edge. Failing systems share a device-mapper layer or a kernel version. The tool blktrace shows the request was sent to the wrong sector.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Careful: use a spare drive or a test system. On a scratch drive, make a dm-linear layer with a wrong offset on purpose. Run fio --verify. The recording shows writes to the offset blocks, exactly as dm asked. Run blktrace / blkparse on the computer while recording. The block:block_rq_issue tracepoint also works. Match each command in the recording to a block request. Check the command's block address. Does it equal the request's sector plus the partition start? Then the computer meant it. Then work upward: file system journal, program logs. Format a test storage area with PI Type 1. Then the controller rejects misplaced writes with a block-number check error (Reference Tag Check Error). It no longer accepts them.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Everything says success. Only a careful check finds it (Silent). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: There are two cases. The computer's software is at fault when the command matches the driver but not what was meant. That includes the file system and the block layer. It includes dm or md, partitions, a user-space driver or the hypervisor. The SSD is at fault if data lands somewhere other than where the command says. · Test that confirms it: NVMe tracepoints or blktrace (E05).

N-15 Copying through extra buffers makes reads and writes slow (SWIOTLB) Partly seen in the packets Wrong memory address or sender name

Packets seen in the test recording

Error family: P17, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. It means memory access to the wrong place, or with a wrong sender name. Proof from outside the recording: E01, the Linux kernel log. · Can the packets alone prove it? Partly. The packets show a shape in timing or order. The proof needs evidence from outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: No NVMe or PCIe rule covers this. It is an operating-system feature. NVMe uses 64-bit addresses by default. The driver sets a 64-bit address limit (DMA mask). So copying through extra buffers (bounce buffering) comes from the computer or its settings. It is not an SSD feature.

What goes wrong: Sometimes the SSD cannot reach all of the computer's memory. Its address limit may be below the installed memory (C-26 covers the 48-bit case). The memory guard (IOMMU) may be off, with memory beyond the SSD's reach. Or a virtual computer's memory may be encrypted (AMD SEV, Intel TDX). And the SSD was not given to it by TDISP. Then the kernel passes every transfer through an extra buffer (bounce buffer). The processor copies the data. The copy costs processor time and adds delay. The buffer pool can run out.

How you can tell: At start-up the kernel log shows software IO TLB: mapped [mem ...]. Under load it shows swiotlb buffer is full with read or write errors. These are -ENOMEM in the driver's address mapping step. The processor spends a lot of time copying memory (memcpy) during storage work. Speed falls sharply for large block sizes. Protected virtual computers show slow storage. It is much slower than the same virtual computer without memory encryption.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Compare the memory addresses in the recording with /proc/iomem. Also compare them with the extra-buffer range printed at start-up. Run cat /sys/kernel/debug/swiotlb/io_tlb_used (debugfs) under load. Check the SSD's address limit in /sys/bus/pci/devices/<BDF>/dma_mask_bits. Turn on the memory guard, or give the SSD to the virtual computer with TDISP. Then compare.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. It still works, only slower or worse than it should (Degraded). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Check the computer's software or settings. Look at the address limit and whether the memory guard is off. Look for an encrypted virtual computer. It is not the SSD. · Test that confirms it: the start-up log.

N-16 Failure before the operating system starts (UEFI driver, start-up loader) Partly seen in the packets Not seen on this wire

Packets seen in the test recording

Error family: none. This error has no family on the wire, only proof from outside the recording. Proof from outside the recording: E08, a second capture tool, switch counters or other logs. · Can the packets alone prove it? Partly. The packets show a shape in timing or order. The proof needs evidence from outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: NVMe has the same controller start-up rules for every computer. Some computers use a start-up area on the SSD (Boot Partition, S-46). PCIe defines the extra start-up program address (Expansion ROM BAR) and its image format. The UEFI rule book defines how start-up programs send NVMe commands (NVM Express Pass Thru). Start-up program time limits are up to each maker (not certain).

What goes wrong: The computer's start-up program (UEFI) starts the controller to read the start-up loader. It uses EDK2's NvmExpressDxe or a maker's driver. It uses its own command lists, time limits and shutdown steps. Some SSDs fail here. One kind is slow to get ready. Another needs a wait that Linux adds just for it (NVME_QUIRK_DELAY_BEFORE_CHK_RDY). A third handles a second start badly without a restart. The system never reaches the operating system. So there is no kernel log (dmesg).

How you can tell: The screen says "No bootable device". The start-up settings screen does not list the drive. Yet an operating system started from elsewhere sees it fine. Start-up time changes by tens of seconds. The operating system's driver finds the controller already on, with someone else's command lists. It restarts it. SSDs with an extra start-up program (Option ROM) stall during discovery while it is read.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Careful: use a spare drive or a test system. Use a test computer where the start-up time limit can be changed. Set it below the SSD's measured ready time. Record from the end of reset (PERST#), with a trigger on the first settings write. Measure the start-up program's time from switch-on (CC.EN=1) to ready (CSTS.RDY=1). Compare it with the promised ready time (CAP.TO). Also compare it with the same time measured under the operating system. Did the start-up program send a shutdown (CC.SHN) or a restart? Check whether it came before the driver's switch-off (CC.EN=0). The start-up program's serial console or UEFI debug logs are the only computer-side evidence.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Nothing reports it. Only a timer notices that something did not arrive in time (Timer only). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: There are two cases. The computer's UEFI driver is at fault if it gives up before CAP.TO x 500 ms. It is also at fault if it skips the restart when handing over. The SSD is at fault if the ready flag (CSTS.RDY) stays 0 too long. That means beyond CAP.TO after switch-on (CC.EN=1). · Test that confirms it: the start-up program's log (E08).

The rows shown only give background. The proof is outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book defines a save flag for settings (Set Features CDW10.SV). The get-setting command can pick current, default, saved or what is supported (Get Features CDW10.SEL). Settings that cannot be saved get an error (Feature Identifier Not Saveable, S-43). A saved value must last through power cycles and restarts. Check the wording in your version of the rule book.

What goes wrong: Set Features with the save flag asks the controller to keep the value. It must last through power states and restarts. Some controllers say settings can be saved (ONCS "Save/Select" bit, Get Features SEL=011b). But they answer Success without saving. Or they save some fields and not others. On the next power-up they quietly go back to defaults. This hits temperature limits and the computer-set heat limits (Host Controlled Thermal Management). It hits write cache on/off and the power-saving table (APST). It also hits signal grouping and the power state. It hits the clock time setting, and write protection of a storage area (N-19).

How you can tell: A fleet tool sets --save once at set-up. After the first restart the setting is gone on some drives. Heat alerts go back to defaults. Write cache comes back on, on a drive set on purpose to write-through. A power-saving table was tuned to avoid a deep sleep state. It comes back with that state allowed. So C-22 comes back "randomly".

How to fix it and prove the fix: Careful: use a spare drive or a test system. Set the temperature limit (Temperature Threshold, FID 04h) with --save. Cut power at once, then read the saved and current values. Do this for each setting the site sets with SV=1. Use nvme get-feature -f <FID> -s 3 (what is supported) to confirm it is saveable. Set it, then read it back with -s 2 (saved). Then turn power fully off and on. A controller restart alone is not enough. Read -s 0 and -s 2 again. Repeat with a power cut within one second of Set Features. That catches saves that are put off.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Everything says success. Only a careful check finds it (Silent). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Usually the SSD is at fault. The value may be kept only in short-term memory (RAM). The supported-settings list may be wrong. A firmware update may have reset the tables. The computer is at fault if its tool never used the save flag. It is also at fault if it set the value again later. · Test that confirms it: a table of save and read-back tests (E03).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book defines locks on storage areas (reservations). One command signs a computer up (Reservation Register, with the CPTPL field). Others take a lock (Acquire, including Preempt and Preempt and Abort). Others drop it (Release) and list them (Report). A setting keeps locks through power loss (Reservation Persistence, FID 83h, PTPL). Another setting holds the computer's ID (Host Identifier, FID 81h). There is a lock log (Reservation Notification, log 80h) and an alert for it (S-85). The storage area's ID data shows lock support (Identify Namespace RESCAP).

What goes wrong: Cluster software uses locks to shut out a failed computer (fencing). Examples are Pacemaker fence_scsi/fence_mpath, Windows failover clustering and VMware. It can fail in four ways. (1) The controller drops sign-ups or the lock, even though PTPL was asked for. This happens on a controller restart, firmware switch or power loss. (2) A shared storage area on a dual-port drive (N-01) shows a different lock state through each controller. (3) Preempt and Abort answers Success. But commands from the shut-out computer keep finishing. (4) The lock report's computer IDs or key list is wrong.

How you can tell: One computer "shut out" the other, but both still write. Data is damaged (split-brain). fence_scsi succeeds, but the shut-out computer's writes still land. After a power cut, the cluster finds no sign-ups. The lock report (nvme resv-report) lists a key that was released. Or it misses one that was signed up.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Careful: use a spare drive or a test system. Run the test table below on a scratch storage area. Include a controller restart and a firmware switch between sign-up and check. The test table goes like this. Sign up from two computers. Take a Write Exclusive lock from A. Write from B, which must get 0x83. Preempt and Abort from B. Write from A, which must fail. Power-cycle the drive. If PTPL was on, the lock report must still list the sign-ups. Run the same report through the second port. In the recording, look for writes that finished with Success. Pick those from the command list or computer that should have been shut out.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Everything says success. Only a careful check finds it (Silent). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Usually the SSD is at fault. Lock state may be kept only in short-term memory. PTPL may be ignored. Two controllers may be out of step. The computer is at fault if it never set its ID (Host Identifier) or PTPL. · Test that confirms it: the lock report (E03).

Proof from outside the recording: E03, the SSD's own logs and saved settings. E09, a lab test whose result is the proof. · Can the packets alone prove it? Partly. The packets show a shape in timing or order. The proof needs evidence from outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book defines write protection for each storage area. The setting is Namespace Write Protection Config (FID 84h). The storage area's ID data shows the state (Identify Namespace NSATTR). The controller's ID data shows which states are supported (NWPC). Writes to a protected area get a fixed result (Namespace is Write Protected, SCT 0 / SC 0x20). The rule book lists the commands that are not allowed while protected. Check this in your version.

What goes wrong: The write-protection setting has four states. They are no protection, write protect, write protect until power-off, and permanent write protect. While protected, the controller must refuse every command that changes user data. That includes the extra data stored with it (metadata). It must show the state in NSATTR. It must change states only as the rules allow. Some firmware checks only the Write command. It lets Write Zeroes, Deallocate or Copy through. Some forgets the state across a controller restart. Some allows a change out of "permanent". Each breaks the promise without any error.

How you can tell: A master copy or an audit storage area gets changed. NSATTR bit 0 disagrees with Get Features FID 84h. Linux marks the disk read-only at discovery (from NSATTR). Yet a direct write from a user program succeeds.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Careful: use a spare drive or a test system. Run the test table below. For the permanent state, use a storage area you are willing to lose. Set each supported state on a scratch storage area. Try every data-changing command with nvme io-passthru / admin-passthru. These are Write, Write Zeroes, Write Uncorrectable, Dataset Management (deallocate) and Copy. They also include fused Compare-and-Write, Format NVM and Sanitize. Add Zone Management Send if the drive is zoned (ZNS). Each must return 0x20, or the rule book's alternative. Restart the controller, then power-cycle. Check the state and NSATTR again.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Everything says success. Only a careful check finds it (Silent). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD is at fault here. The command check may be incomplete. The state may be kept only in short-term memory. A Format path may skip the check. A restart may reload defaults. · Test that confirms it: a table of commands (careful, use a spare drive).

N-20 SSD alerts stop arriving (AEN masked, RAE misuse, wrong alert settings) Partly seen in the packets Rules for what a command holds

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 717586: a health alert from the SSD (SMART AEN).

Packet=717586 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=199 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000004:82E40110 | Length=4 | DATA=16 B | Time Stamp=0522.426626970620s | Time Delta=54.870 ns | LCRC=0x1C71353B

Error family: P18 and P26, two of the 27 ways an error shows on the wire. P18 means rules about what goes inside a command. P26 means alerts from the SSD, and log pages. Proof from outside the recording: E01, the Linux kernel log. E03, the SSD's own logs and saved settings. · Can the packets alone prove it? Partly. The packets show a shape in timing or order. The proof needs evidence from outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book defines the alert-request command (Asynchronous Event Request). It defines a rule that hides further alerts of one type. It defines the keep-alert bit (RAE) in the log-read command (Get Log Page CDW10). It defines the alert setting (Asynchronous Event Configuration, FID 0Bh). It defines the alert-request limit (AERL in Identify Controller). Going past it gives an error (S-34). Check this in your version of the rule book.

What goes wrong: The controller sends an alert (AEN) of one type. Then it must not send another of that type yet. It waits until the computer reads the matching log page with the keep-alert bit (RAE) clear. It can fail in three ways. (1) Computer bug: the log is read with RAE=1, or not at all. That alert type stays hidden forever. Every later change is quietly missed. (2) Controller bug: it sends the same alert again and again without the reset step. That is a flood of alerts. Or it never sends the alert, because it ignored the alert setting (FID 0Bh). (3) The computer has no alert request waiting. All were used and none sent again. Then alerts pile up in the controller or are dropped.

How you can tell: A storage area is made or resized through another path (N-01). The computer never notices. A firmware switch finishes, but the computer does not read the firmware log again. A health warning passes its limit with no alert. A path-state change (ANA) is missed by the multi-path software until the next read or write error. Or the opposite happens: thousands of identical alert done notes each second.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Careful: use a spare drive or a test system. After an alert, use a user-space tool to read the changed-areas log with RAE=1. That log is the Changed Namespace List. Change a storage area again. Confirm no second alert arrives. In the recording, look at every alert done note. Find the next log read with the same log number (LID). Check that bit 15 of CDW10 (RAE) is 0. Count the alert requests waiting over time. The count must stay at the number the computer intended. Cause a change twice: attach a storage area, detach it, attach again. Confirm two alerts. Use nvme get-feature -f 0xb to confirm which alert types are on.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Everything says success. Only a careful check finds it (Silent). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: There are two cases. The computer is at fault if it reads with RAE=1 or never reads. It is also at fault if it stops sending alert requests. The SSD is at fault if it repeats alerts without the reset step. It is also at fault if it never sends an alert that is turned on and visible. · Test that confirms it: cause the change twice.

N-21 SSD ignores the turn order set for its command lists (arbitration) Seen in the packets Rules for what a command holds

Packets seen in the test recording

Error family: P18, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. It means rules about what goes inside a command. Proof from outside the recording: E09, a lab test whose result is the proof. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes, by a rule about order or timing. For example: a missing answer, a long gap, or rows in the wrong order.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book defines how the SSD picks the next command list. This is called arbitration. It can be taking turns (round-robin) or weighted turns with an urgent class (WRR with urgent). It can also be the maker's own way. The settings are CAP.AMS, CC.AMS and the Arbitration feature (AB, LPW, MPW, HPW). Each command list gets a priority when it is made (Create I/O Submission Queue QPRIO). Arbitration decides the order of fetching commands. It does not decide the order of finishing them.

What goes wrong: CC.AMS picks the turn method. The choices are taking turns, weighted turns with an urgent class, or the maker's own way. The Arbitration feature (FID 01h) sets the burst size and the three weights. Making a command list (Create I/O SQ CDW11.QPRIO) gives each list a class. Some firmware says it supports weighted turns (in CAP.AMS) but just takes simple turns. Some lets one long list starve the others beyond the burst size. Some serves "urgent" after "low". All give correct results, but with the wrong spread of delays.

How you can tell: A list that needs fast answers (urgent or high) is as slow as the bulk list. One list's commands are fetched hundreds at a time while others wait. Quality-of-service features are offered but have no effect you can measure. Head-of-line blocking (M-057) shows up. That happens even though the work was split onto priority lists.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Take the command fetches from the recording, with times and list numbers. For each list, count how many fetches came in a row. Count only while other lists had commands waiting. A list has commands waiting when its doorbell value is past its last fetched slot. Compare these runs with 2 to the power AB (the burst size). Compare their ratios with the weights. Other computer software can make lists with different priorities (SPDK, user-space drivers). Linux cannot.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. It still works, only slower or worse than it should (Degraded). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: First check the computer's settings. Then the SSD is at fault. Its firmware scheduler ignores the burst, the weights or urgent. The computer is at fault only if it set values it did not mean. One example is AB = 7, which means no limit. · Test that confirms it: a test of the turn-order rules.

N-22 SSD ignores hints on where to place data (Streams, FDP, NPWG) Not seen in the packets Not seen on this wire

Packets seen in the test recording

Error family: none. This error has no family on the wire, only proof from outside the recording. Proof from outside the recording: E09, a lab test whose result is the proof. · Can the packets alone prove it? No. It cannot be seen on this wire. The rows shown only give background. The proof is outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule books cover hints about data placement. These are Directives (Identify, Streams, Data Placement) and the Directive Send and Receive commands. They cover Flexible Data Placement (FDP). FDP has Reclaim Unit Handles and Placement Identifiers. It has four logs: Configurations (20h), Reclaim Unit Handle Usage (21h), Statistics (22h) and Events (23h). It has two results: FDP Disabled and Invalid Placement Handle List. The rule books also cover Dataset Management hints. Storage area ID data gives best write sizes and edges (NPWG, NPWA, NPDG, NPDA, NOWS). Check this in your version.

What goes wrong: The computer can group data that will be deleted at about the same time. It uses Streams (Directive Type 01h) or Flexible Data Placement (Directive Type 02h). Then the controller can wipe whole blocks without copying. Access hints and best-size fields help the computer too. They let it size and line up writes to the controller's inner page size. Some controllers accept the hints and ignore them. Some report best-size values (NPWG/NOWS) that do not match their real inner page. They use up the drive's life faster. They are slower in steady use. No error shows anywhere.

How you can tell: Look at write amplification: bytes written to the memory chips divided by bytes the computer wrote. It is no better with FDP on than off. The SMART wear figure (percentage_used) climbs faster than the rated total writes (TBW) predict. The FDP Statistics log shows far more chip writes than computer writes. Steady write speed is the same with and without stream separation.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Careful: use a spare drive or a test system. Run two fio workloads that overwrite at very different rates. Run them once with separate placement handles and once without. Compare the FDP Statistics and the changes in percentage_used. Measure write amplification directly before and after a fixed workload. Do this with and without hints. Use the FDP Statistics log (computer bytes written with hints versus chip bytes written). Or use maker SMART extras (NAND bytes written). Compare the FDP Events log for Reclaim Unit changes. For the best-size values, compare lined-up and not lined-up write patterns (P-13). Compare speed and write amplification (WAF).

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. It still works, only slower or worse than it should (Degraded). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Usually the SSD is at fault. It accepts hints but does not use them. It may map all handles to one pool. It may report a wrong best size (NPWG). The computer is at fault if the hints are missing from its commands. · Test that confirms it: compare write amplification with and without hints (E09).

N-23 Zone Append returns the wrong block address, or zone report disagrees Partly seen in the packets Wrong data inside the packets

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 1469235: the write of the reference pattern finishes.

Packet=1469235 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=1352 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000004:84150640 | Length=4 | DATA=16 B | Time Stamp=1354.730652698870s | Time Delta=29.870 ns | LCRC=0xDD94711F

Packet 1469287: the read or command used as evidence finishes with success.

Packet=1469287 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=1363 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000004:84150650 | Length=4 | DATA=16 B | Time Stamp=1354.730670298750s | Time Delta=74.880 ns | LCRC=0x1F5AFB38

Error family: P23, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. It means comparing written data with data read back later. Proof from outside the recording: E04, reading the data back and checking it. · Can the packets alone prove it? Partly. The packets show a shape in timing or order. The proof needs evidence from outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book for zoned storage (ZNS) covers Zone Append. The SSD returns the block it chose (ALBA, in DW0/DW1). The size limit is ZASL. It covers the zone report (Zone Management Receive, Report Zones). Each zone report gives the state (ZS), type (ZT), capacity (ZCAP), start (ZSLBA) and write pointer (WP). It covers the zone states, write-pointer rules and zone extra data. Check this in your version.

What goes wrong: With Zone Append, the controller picks the block address. The computer notes that address (ALBA) in its own records, such as a file system or log. Later it reads from there. A wrong ALBA quietly damages everything that depends on it. It may be one block off or point at the previous append. It may go past the zone capacity (ZCAP). Two appends at the same time may get the same address. A zone report may give an old write pointer or state. Then the computer sends writes that fail with Zone Invalid Write (S-56). Worse, they may succeed in the wrong place.

How you can tell: File systems on zoned drives report check-value errors at the noted block. Examples are btrfs zoned, f2fs and ZenFS. Two appends at the same time return the same ALBA. After a restart, the zone report shows a write pointer that moved backwards. Mixing up zone capacity and zone size gives an ALBA past ZCAP.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Careful: use a spare drive or a test system. Run fio --zonemode=zbd --rw=write with --ioengine=io_uring at high depth on one zone. Then check the ALBA order and read back. Write a script over the table file. For each zone, list appends in finishing order with ALBA and block count (NLB). Check that they only go up and stay in bounds. Then compare with the next zone report's write pointer. Read back at each ALBA. Compare the data with the append's data packets. Repeat across a controller restart and a power cycle.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Everything says success. Only a careful check finds it (Silent). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD is at fault here. The cause is its append address picker. Or it is its cached write pointer after a restart or power loss. · Test that confirms it: an append consistency check.

Error family: P24, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. It means flush and power cuts: the recording before and after the cut. Proof from outside the recording: E03, the SSD's own logs and saved settings. E04, reading the data back and checking it. E09, a lab test whose result is the proof. · Can the packets alone prove it? No. It cannot be seen on this wire. The rows shown only give background. The proof is outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book defines a memory buffer inside the SSD (CMB). CMB means Controller Memory Buffer. Its settings are CMBLOC, CMBSZ, CMBMSC, CMBSTS, CMBEBS and CMBSWTP. Rules say which lists and data may be placed there. It also defines a lasting memory region (Persistent Memory Region, PMR). Its settings are PMRCAP, PMRCTL, PMRSTS, PMREBS, PMRSWTP and PMRMSCL/U. PMRCAP includes the write-barrier methods (PMRWBM) and the time limit (PMRTO). PMRSTS includes ERR, NRDY, HSTS and CBAI. Sanitize is not allowed while PMR is on (S-48). SMART warning bit 5 covers it (S-77).

What goes wrong: PMR promises lasting storage that can be written byte by byte. Writes confirmed after the write barrier must survive power loss. CMB offers SSD memory for command lists, address lists and data. That saves trips to computer memory. Things can go wrong in several ways. PMR writes are lost or reordered at power loss. The PMR health state is not raised when it should be (read-only, unreliable, restore error). CMB addresses are mapped wrongly. Then the controller reads command slot n from the computer's slot n−1. Or the CMB size reported (CMBSZ) is bigger than the real memory. Then high addresses land on low ones.

How you can tell: Program data in PMR is missing or old after a power cycle, with no error. PMRSTS.HSTS says "normal" for a region that lost data. With command lists in CMB, commands run twice or are skipped (V-08, D-29 shapes). Or data traffic does not match the command the computer wrote. Linux nvme_map_cmb() succeeds. But reads and writes act strangely only when use_cmb_sqes is on.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Risky, test machine only: test PMR with power cuts. Also sweep CMB with a pattern while recording. For PMR, write a pattern with sequence numbers inside it. Use the barrier as PMRWBM says. Cut power, read back and compare. Repeat hundreds of times (the D-10 method). For CMB, put command lists in CMB. In the recording, compare each computer write into the list area with the data traffic and done note that follow. Check opcode, block address and length agree. Sweep the whole CMBSZ range with a pattern. Read it back through memory-mapped access (MMIO).

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Everything says success. Only a careful check finds it (Silent). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD is at fault here. It may lack enough stored energy to finish writes. Its barrier may do nothing. Its CMB address decoding may be wrong. Its inner view of commands may be old. · Test that confirms it: a PMR power-cut record (E09, risky, test machine only).

N-25 Drive lock and encryption state wrong (TCG Opal range not locked) Partly seen in the packets Not seen on this wire

Packets seen in the test recording

Error family: none. This error has no family on the wire, only proof from outside the recording. Proof from outside the recording: E04, reading the data back and checking it. · Can the packets alone prove it? Partly. The packets show a shape in timing or order. The proof needs evidence from outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book defines Security Send and Security Receive (SECP, SPSP0/1, NSSF). The controller ID data shows support (Identify Controller OACS security bit). The TCG rule books define the drive locking itself. These are Storage Architecture Core, Opal SSC and Enterprise SSC. A locked area gets Access Denied (SCT 2 / SC 0x86). TCG defines what a locked read does. NVMe only carries the TCG messages.

What goes wrong: Self-encrypting drives use TCG Opal or Enterprise over Security Send and Receive. Things can go wrong in several ways. An area reported locked still returns readable data. An area the computer unlocked locks again by itself. Or the reverse happens after waking from sleep (S3). The stand-in start-up area (shadow MBR) is not shown when it should be. A factory reset (Revert or PSID revert) finishes but leaves data readable (overlaps D-19). Security Receive never returns (T-01 shape), because the session state (ComID) is wrong. Some answers are errors, but sit inside the TCG data. A capture tool cannot mark them as errors.

How you can tell: Data can be read from an area that sedutil-cli --query says is locked. After waking, reads fail (0x286) until someone unlocks by hand. That happens even though opal_unlock_from_suspend ran. A drive refuses all reads and writes after a firmware update. Its lock state was reset. Audit tools disagree with the drive's own status.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Careful: use a spare drive or a test system. Lock an area on a scratch drive. Sleep, wake, and read before unlocking, while recording. Set up a locked area, lock it, and read through it with nvme read. Expect 0x286, or zeros if the maker documents that. Never expect readable data. Wake from S3/S4 and repeat before any unlock. Compare sedutil-cli --query with real read results. To find faults in the TCG messages, take the Security Send and Receive data from the recording. Decode it with a TCG-aware tool or script. Look at the ComPacket, Packet and Subpacket headers, method IDs and status codes.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Everything says success. Only a careful check finds it (Silent). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: There are two cases. The SSD is at fault when a locked area returns readable data. It is also at fault when lock state changes with no Security Send. The computer is at fault when its unlock-after-sleep step is missing. · Test that confirms it: the lock state (E04).

N-26 Extra per-block data (metadata) moved wrongly, missing or wrong size Seen in the packets Rules for what a command holds

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 721289: the command (SQE), with the fields this rule checks in its 64 bytes.

Packet 721333: the done note says success (SCT0/SC0x00).

Packet=721333 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=1731 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000004:82E50CE0 | Length=4 | DATA=16 B | Time Stamp=0524.580303001750s | Time Delta=73.880 ns | LCRC=0x9A3AC25A

Error family: P18, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. It means rules about what goes inside a command. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes, by a rule about order or timing. For example: a missing answer, a long gap, or rows in the wrong order.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe command rule book covers extra data stored with each block (metadata). It can sit at the end of each block (extended LBA) or in a separate buffer. Storage area ID data describes it (FLBAS, LBAF MS, MC, DPS, DPC). The separate buffer has its own address (MPTR). It must be one piece for PRP. It may be an SGL segment when MSDBD allows. The PRINFO bits PRACT and PRCHK say what to add, strip or check. PRACT works differently when MS = 8 and when MS > 8. The check data (PI) sits in the first or last 8 bytes. Check this in your version.

What goes wrong: Firmware can go wrong in three ways. It ignores MPTR. Then metadata is never written to the computer on read, or never fetched on write. It moves MS bytes when PRACT says it should not. It treats an extended-LBA area as a separate-buffer one. The result is Success with missing or old metadata. Or the SSD reads or writes an address the computer did not expect (M-061). Or the length is wrong, and the computer does not check because the data part is fine. D-21 (PI not checked) and S-61 (PI errors) assume the metadata arrived. This entry is about whether it arrived, and how much.

How you can tell: Program tags or storage tags read back as zeros. Or they read back as the previous command's values. Integrity errors happen only on some block sizes. The memory guard faults on MPTR addresses (L-36). That happens on a storage area that "does not use metadata". Linux integrity checks fail, but the controller reports no PI error.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Careful: use a spare drive or a test system. Format a scratch area with MS = 16 and PI Type 1. Write with PRACT=1 and with PRACT=0. Compare the bytes moved in the recording. Do this for each format the area supports (the LBAF list in nvme id-ns). Format a scratch area for each. Run reads and writes with and without PRACT, using nvme read/write --prinfo. Write a script over the table file to count bytes. Count data bytes, MPTR bytes, and the bytes each rule expects. Read back metadata with nvme read --metadata-size. Compare it with what was written.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Everything says success. Only a careful check finds it (Silent). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: There are two cases. The SSD is at fault if the command is correct and the metadata move goes wrong. It may be missing, the wrong size or unexpected. It may use the wrong format. The computer is at fault in two cases. It leaves out MPTR for a separate-buffer format without PRACT. Or it assumes the wrong format (LBAF). · Test that confirms it: a table of formats.

Error family: P23, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. It means comparing written data with data read back later. Proof from outside the recording: E04, reading the data back and checking it. · Can the packets alone prove it? No. It cannot be seen on this wire. The rows shown only give background. The proof is outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe command rule book defines Copy. Copy has source range formats, a target start (SDLBA), a count of ranges and check-data (PI) handling. Support shows in the ONCS Copy bit. Limits show in storage area ID data (MSSRL, MCL, MSRC). The rule book also defines Write Uncorrectable (an ONCS bit) and Compare. Check this in your version.

What goes wrong: Copy (19h) copies a list of source ranges to a target block. It uses range format 0h or 1h. The controller must copy the data. It must copy the metadata too, by the rules in the command. It must keep within the MSSRL, MCL and MSRC limits (S-52 covers limit errors). Write Uncorrectable (04h) marks blocks so reads fail until they are written again. It is used to fake media errors and to make data unreadable on purpose. Firmware bugs happen. Copy may write old source data, read from a cache before an earlier write landed. It may copy the wrong length or copy metadata wrongly. Write Uncorrectable may mark only the first block of the range. Or the mark may not survive a power cycle.

How you can tell: File systems that copy inside the drive find different data at the target. So do nvme copy tests. nvme write-uncor is followed by a read that succeeds. Error-injection test plans "pass", because the drive stops returning errors after a power cycle.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Careful: use a spare drive or a test system. Run the two steps below on a scratch storage area. For Copy, write different patterns into several source ranges. Send Copy with several source ranges. Read the target and compare every byte, including metadata. Repeat with a write to a source range just before the Copy. For Write Uncorrectable, mark a range. Read every block in it. All must fail with 0x281. Power-cycle and read again. Then write over it and read. That read must succeed.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Everything says success. Only a careful check finds it (Silent). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD is at fault. · Test that confirms it: a copy of several ranges.
