The rows shown only give background. The proof is outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book defines computer-set heat limits. The feature is Host Controlled Thermal Management (FID 10h: TMT1, TMT2). Controller ID data gives HCTMA, MNTMT, MXTMT, WCTEMP and CCTEMP. A temperature limit feature exists too (FID 04h: TMPTH, TMPSEL, THSEL). The health log (SMART) has temperature fields. These are Composite Temperature and Temperature Sensors 1-8. It has counts and total times for heat steps 1 and 2. It has times spent at warning and critical temperature.

What goes wrong: The computer can set two temperatures. At TMT1 the controller should start slowing down a little. At TMT2 it should slow down a lot. Both must be within the MNTMT to MXTMT range. The temperature limit feature sets high and low limits for each sensor. Passing one must raise SMART warning bit 1 (S-73) and its alert. Some firmware accepts the values but keeps its own fixed slow-down curve. Some never counts the steps. Some slows down far below TMT1, losing speed for nothing. Some does not raise the alert. Each breaks a promise the computer needs for speed and safety.

How you can tell: Speed rises and falls in a saw-tooth at a temperature unrelated to TMT1/TMT2. The SMART step count (thm_temp1_trans_count) stays at zero. Yet the temperature passed TMT1. No alert comes when the temperature crosses the set limit. Or the drive goes past its critical temperature without slowing down. Then it shuts down (SMART critical warning, S-73), because the computer's limits were ignored.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Careful: use a spare drive or a test system. Block the airflow on a scratch drive during long writes. Log SMART and compare with the heat limits you set. Use a heat chamber or controlled airflow. Sweep the temperature while logging nvme smart-log every second. Log temperature, step counts, total times and speed. Set TMT1/TMT2 inside the sweep. Check that slow-down start, step counts and alerts move with them. Set a temperature limit just above the current temperature. Confirm the alert and critical warning within seconds.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. It still works, only slower or worse than it should (Degraded). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Usually the SSD is at fault. It may have a fixed slow-down curve. It may only report the heat limits and not act on them. It may use the wrong sensor or not raise the alert. The computer is at fault when the alert type is hidden or alerts are not on (AEC). · Test that confirms it: a temperature sweep (E09).

N-29 One virtual function's fault spreads to others (SR-IOV separation broken) Partly seen in the packets Wrong memory address or sender name

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 688100: a done note for a list owned by a virtual function (VF). It was written with the main function's sender name (PF Requester ID).

Packet=688100 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=1655 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000004:82E50A40 | Length=4 | DATA=16 B | Time Stamp=0522.106334740000s | Time Delta=28.880 ns | LCRC=0x07D26F57

Error family: P17, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. It means memory access to the wrong place, or with a wrong sender name. Proof from outside the recording: E09, a lab test whose result is the proof. · Can the packets alone prove it? Partly. The packets show a shape in timing or order. The proof needs evidence from outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book has virtualization features. There are main and extra controllers and shared resources. There is a Virtualization Management command, and ID data (Identify CNS 14h/15h). The PCIe rule book defines extra virtual functions (SR-IOV Extended Capability). This covers VF Offset, VF Stride and VF BARs. A restart of one virtual function must affect only that one (FLR scope). The rule book also covers ARI, sender-name rules (Requester ID) and ACS Source Validation.

What goes wrong: NVMe SR-IOV shows extra controllers as virtual functions (VFs). Each has its own command lists and "work done" signals (VQ and VI resources). To the computer and the memory guard, each also has its own sender name. Separation can fail in several ways. A restart of one VF (Function Level Reset) resets shared firmware state. This disturbs the main function (PF) or other VFs. A VF's fatal error (CSTS.CFS) takes the PF down. A VF reads or writes memory with a wrong sender name (RID). Then the memory guard thinks another function did it, or faults (L-36). One function's CMB or PMR can be reached from another. Resources are moved by Virtualization Management while a VF is in use (S-47 results). M-064 covers delay inside one VF. This entry covers effects across functions.

How you can tell: One user's virtual computer restarts. Commands time out in another user's. Memory-guard faults (DMAR) name a function that was idle. The main driver restarts when a guest restarts. Sender names in the recording do not match the function that owns the list address. The extra controller list (CNS 15h) changes state with no Virtualization Management command.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Careful: use a spare drive or a test system. Run two fio workloads that overwrite at very different rates. Run them once with separate placement handles and once without. Compare the FDP Statistics and the changes in percentage_used. Measure write amplification directly before and after a fixed workload. Do this with and without hints. Use the FDP Statistics log (computer bytes written with hints versus chip bytes written). Or use maker SMART extras (NAND bytes written). Compare the FDP Events log for Reclaim Unit changes. For the best-size values (NPWG/NOWS), compare lined-up and not lined-up write patterns (P-13). Compare speed and write amplification (WAF).

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Everything says success. Only a careful check finds it (Silent). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD is at fault. Look at how it makes sender names (RID). Look at firmware state shared across functions. Look at what a function restart (FLR) touches. · Test that confirms it: check sender names against the memory guard.

Packet=1093201 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=2418 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000004:82F10350 | Length=4 | DATA=16 B | Time Stamp=0562.528389004750s | Time Delta=51.880 ns | LCRC=0xBA1FA598

Error family: P01, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. It means a result number that is not 0 in a done note. · Can the packets alone prove it? Only by reading the bytes inside the packets. The code is in the DATA column. The hex version of the file marks it (nvme_status_nonzero).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book (version 2.x) covers several newer features. One is the Lockdown command and its log (Command and Feature Lockdown, LID 14h). Others are a key for each read or write (Key Per I/O) and spread-out storage areas (Dispersed Namespaces). There is moving a running controller (Live Migration: Track Memory Changes, Migration Send/Receive). There is a separate Key Value rule book, and FDP. There is a central list of network storage (Discovery Information Management, NVMe-oF).

What goes wrong: These result numbers had no entry before. SCT 0 / 0x23 means a command was blocked by Lockdown. The Lockdown command (24h) blocked this command or feature on this path. The path may be the main wire or the management wire. The SSD reports it when the computer tries anyway. 0x25 (Invalid Key Tag) and 0x28 (Incorrect Key) are about Key Per I/O keys. 0x26 (Host Dispersed Namespace Not Enabled) and 0x27 (Host Identifier Not Initialized) mean a needed step was skipped. 0x29 (FDP Disabled) and 0x2A (Invalid Placement Handle List) mean FDP misuse (N-22). SCT 0 / 0x85-0x89 are Key Value results. They are Invalid Value Size, Invalid Key Size, KV Key Does Not Exist, Unrecovered Error and Key Exists. SCT 1 / 0x26 is Insufficient Capacity. 0x27 is Namespace Attachment Limit Exceeded. 0x28 is Prohibition of Command Execution Not Supported. 0x2D is Identifier Unavailable. SCT 1 / 0x2F-0x34 are about central discovery (zoning and sign-up). SCT 1 / 0x37-0x3B are about Live Migration. They cover a bad data list, too few resources, paused or not paused, and a full data list. Exact names and values come from libnvme nvme_status_field. Check them against your version of the rule book.

How you can tell: Lockdown: a set-up tool suddenly gets 0x23 for Format, Firmware Commit or Security Send. That happens after the platform owner locked the path. Key Value: a KV library reports program-level errors. FDP: 0x29 when placement handles are used with FDP off. 0x2A when the Placement Handle List in Namespace Management is wrong. Live Migration: errors only on the migration controller's path.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Careful: use a spare drive or a test system. Use nvme lockdown on a scratch drive to block Format. Then run nvme format and expect 0x23. On a drive with FDP, turn FDP off and write with a placement handle. Expect 0x29. Decode SCT and SC from DW3 of the done note. Read the Lockdown log (LID 14h) to confirm what is blocked. Use nvme fdp configs / nvme fdp status for the FDP state. For KV, read the KV storage area's ID data limits (CSI 1).

Does the SSD or computer report it? Yes. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself (Reported). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Most often the computer is at fault. It did not read the settings it is breaking. The SSD is at fault when its settings logs say the command is allowed. Examples are a wrong Lockdown scope, or FDP state that does not agree after Set Features. · Test that confirms it: check what Lockdown blocks.

Error family: P01, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. It means a result number that is not 0 in a done note. · Can the packets alone prove it? Only by reading the bytes inside the packets. The code is in the DATA column. The hex version of the file marks it (nvme_status_nonzero).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book defines the result field in the done note (DW3). It has DNR, M, CRD, SCT and SC. The controller ID data gives retry wait times (Command Retry Delay Times). The Host Behavior Support feature has a switch for them (ACRE). Each result comes with advice on whether to retry. Check this in your version.

What goes wrong: The do-not-retry bit (DNR) tells the computer something. It says whether sending the same command again could work. CRD picks one of three retry wait times (CRDT1-3 in controller ID data, in 100 ms units). The computer must wait that long before retrying. But only if it turned on ACRE in Host Behavior Support (FID 16h). Wrong bits waste the computer's retries and time (T-24). With five retries, each waiting up to 25.5 s, one read can take minutes to fail. Or wrong bits fail a read that would have recovered. One example is Namespace Not Ready during a short inner event, marked DNR=1. Or the computer must wait on a CRD it never agreed to. T-17 covers the computer ignoring CRD, or CRD being too long. This entry covers the SSD choosing the bits wrongly.

How you can tell: A read of a block that cannot be fixed takes minutes to report -EIO. The same start block (SLBA) shows N+1 times in the recording with the same result. A read fails at once while a Format runs on another storage area. The command nvme error-log repeats entries with the same block address. Done notes carry CRD values. Yet the computer never sent Set Features FID 16h, or set ACRE=0.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Careful: use a spare drive or a test system. Mark a range with Write Uncorrectable and read it. Look at DNR and the number of retries in the recording. In QEMU, set a blkdebug error on a sector. Compare how the fake SSD sets DNR. Write a script over the table file. Group failed commands by opcode, NSID, SLBA and NLB. Count retries and DNR values. Flag CRD≠0 when no Set Features FID 16h with ACRE=1 came first in the recording. If the recording started late, read the feature with nvme get-feature -f 0x16. Inject a lasting error (Write Uncorrectable, N-27). Confirm the read fails with DNR=1 on the first try.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Yes. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself (Reported). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD is at fault. Its firmware DNR table ignores the cause. Or it sets CRD every time. Or it loses track of ACRE across restarts. · Test that confirms it: a lasting-error probe.

N-32 SSD restarts itself while the wire stays up (watchdog reboot) Partly seen in the packets SSD's main on/off and status settings

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 481751: the ready flag dropped to 0 (CSTS.RDY=0). The computer never turned the SSD off (CC.EN). So the controller restarted itself, and the wire stayed up.

Packet=481751 | Link Dir=Downstream | TLP Type=MRd(32) | PSN=150 | Tag=18 | RequesterID=000:00:0 | Address=FCE0001C | Length=1 | Time Stamp=0370.668012042250s | Time Delta=155.620 ns | LCRC=0xCF552025

Error family: P13, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. It means the timing of the SSD's main on/off and status settings. Proof from outside the recording: E03, the SSD's own logs and saved settings. E06, records from the slow management wire (SMBus). · Can the packets alone prove it? Partly. The packets show a shape in timing or order. The proof needs evidence from outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book defines the fatal-error flag (CSTS.CFS). It defines event types in the lasting event log. Examples are Power-on or Reset, NVM Subsystem Hardware Error and Telemetry Log Created. It defines reports the controller starts itself (controller-initiated telemetry). It defines an alert for lasting inner errors (Persistent Internal Error AEN). The rule book does not define a "self-restart". It defines what the controller must report when it fails.

What goes wrong: The firmware hits a failed check (assertion), or an inner watchdog timer runs out. Or an inner error that cannot be fixed forces the controller core to restart. Well-behaved firmware sets the fatal-error flag (CSTS.CFS, C-01) first. It may send a fatal error message (ERR_FATAL) or a lasting inner-error alert (C-11, S-79). Less well-behaved firmware simply restarts. It comes back with CSTS.RDY=0 and empty command lists. The computer must find out by timeout. C-06 covers restart loops driven by the computer. This entry is the SSD restarting itself.

How you can tell: The kernel log shows nvme nvme0: I/O tag N (…) QID M timeout, reset controller. No wire event comes before it. It shows controller is down; will reset after a status read (CSTS). The lasting event log has "Power-on or Reset" (04h) or "NVM Subsystem Hardware Error" (05h) events with a reason. A Telemetry Log Changed alert (S-82) comes just before or after. The firmware version is the same, but uptime counters in maker logs go back to zero.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Risky, test machine only: use maker debug firmware. It must let you trigger a failed check. Or run a long stress test and collect reports after each unexplained restart. In the recording, mark the last good done note and the first doorbell with no answer. Read the lasting event log (nvme persistent-event-log). Look for a restart or hardware-error event between those times. Use the controller's clock, and mind the M-053 limits. Get the reports the controller made itself (nvme telemetry-log --ctrl) for the maker. Then check the recording for a computer write to CC, a TS1 Hot Reset, Link Disable or reset (PERST#). If none of these is there, that proves the computer did not cause it.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Nothing reports it. Only a timer notices that something did not arrive in time (Timer only). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD is at fault: the controller restarted itself. The recording has no computer write to CC, NSSR, FLR, Hot Reset, Link Disable or PERST#. That absence proves the computer did not cause it. · Test that confirms it: the SSD's logs.

Error family: P18 and P26, two of the 27 ways an error shows on the wire. P18 means rules about what goes inside a command. P26 means alerts from the SSD, and log pages. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes, by a rule about order or timing. For example: a missing answer, a long gap, or rows in the wrong order.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book defines the log-read command (Get Log Page). Its fields are NUMDL/NUMDU, LPOL/LPOU, RAE, LSP, LSI, UUID index and Offset Type. The controller must return exactly the number of 4-byte words (dwords) asked for. The rule book sets the size of the ID data (Identify). Controller ID data shows whether reading from an offset is supported (LPA). Check this in your version.

What goes wrong: Computers read large logs in pieces, using an offset (LPO). Examples are Telemetry, Persistent Event, FDP Events and Changed Namespace List. Some firmware supports only offset zero. Some quietly caps the length at 4 KiB. Some rebuilds the log between pieces. The buffer then looks fine but is wrong. Most logs have no check value. So the computer trusts the bytes.

How you can tell: nvme telemetry-log makes a file with repeated or zero blocks. The lasting event log fails to decode at piece edges. The tool nvme-cli shows old SMART data after a known event. The nvme id-ctrl fields hold leftover data from an earlier ID read. Buffer reuse hides this error until a fresh, zeroed buffer is used.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Safe to try: a marker-buffer test on any drive. Use nvme get-log at several offsets and lengths. Fill the computer's buffer with a marker pattern before each log read. Use a user-space tool. Ask for a long log in one read, and again in 4 KiB pieces. Compare them. No marker may remain. The pieces joined must equal the single read. In the recording, add up the write bytes for each log read. Compare with (NUMD+1)×4. Check the LPA bit in controller ID data for offset support. Do this before blaming the SSD for offset misuse.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Everything says success. Only a careful check finds it (Silent). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Usually the SSD is at fault. It may have a fixed 4 KiB buffer, ignore the offset, or take a new copy for each piece. The computer is at fault only in two cases. It asks for offsets without LPA support. Or it encodes NUMD wrongly (it counts dwords, starting at zero). · Test that confirms it: a marker buffer.

N-34 Promised-delay window broken or left quietly (Predictable Latency Mode) Partly seen in the packets SSD alerts and log pages

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 1571031: the log page with number 0x0A is read.

Packet=1571031 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=381 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000004:84820160 | Length=4 | DATA=16 B | Time Stamp=1819.918696486870s | Time Delta=66.870 ns | LCRC=0x7D1B6B75

Error family: P26, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. It means alerts from the SSD, and log pages. Proof from outside the recording: E09, a lab test whose result is the proof. · Can the packets alone prove it? Partly. The packets show a shape in timing or order. The proof needs evidence from outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book defines Predictable Latency Mode (PLM). It uses groups of storage called NVM Sets. Two features set it up (Config, FID 13h, and Window, FID 14h). A log per set (LID 0Ah) gives window details, status and event type. A summary log (LID 0Bh) and an alert go with it. Check this in your version.

What goes wrong: PLM splits time into two kinds of window. In a promised window, delay is promised if the computer stays within the stated budget. This is the promised window (deterministic window, DTWIN). In the other window, the SSD does background work (NDWIN). If the computer goes over the budget or time limit, the controller may switch to NDWIN by itself. It can fail in two ways. On the computer side, it goes over the budget and then blames the SSD for delay. On the SSD side, the controller leaves DTWIN early. Or it does not keep the delay promise inside it. Or it does not send the event. Then the computer keeps sending urgent work into a window that is no longer promised.

How you can tell: Slow-answer spikes (P-03) happen in what should be a promised window. The per-set log shows DTWIN exits with the reason "Reads/Writes exceeded" or "Time exceeded". Yet the computer's counts say otherwise. The alert is never seen, because the computer did not turn it on in FID 0Bh.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Careful: use a spare drive or a test system. Turn on PLM on a drive that supports it. Run work at 90 % of the DTWIN read budget, then at 110 %. Compare the per-set log's exit reasons with your counts. From the recording, count reads and writes for each set and window, in the log's units. Note each window's length. Compare with the window details read by nvme predictable-lat-log. Read the per-set log after each window. See the controller's status and exit reason. Match slow answers with the window state.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. It still works, only slower or worse than it should (Degraded). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: There are two cases. The computer is at fault if its reads and writes go over the stated budget. The SSD is at fault if delay rises while within budget. It is also at fault if the window ends without the alert. · Test that confirms it: the PLM logs.

N-35 SSD settings area built wrongly (broken feature chain, wrong class, changing IDs) Seen in the packets Settings area and being ready

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 60085: the power feature block's next-pointer is 0x00. So the PCIe and MSI-X feature blocks cannot be reached.

Packet=60085 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=CplD | PSN=1524 | Tag=14 | RequesterID=000:00:0 | CompleterID=002:00:0 | Cpl Status=SC | Length=1 | Byte Cnt=4 | DATA=4 B | Time Stamp=0062.155571533500s | Time Delta=160.120 ns | LCRC=0x4C288D5B

Error family: P19, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. It means the settings area: start-up, features, restarts and being ready. Proof from outside the recording: E02, a copy of the SSD's settings area (lspci). · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes, by a rule about order or timing. For example: a missing answer, a long gap, or rows in the wrong order.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCI and PCIe rule books define the SSD's settings area. Its start is the Type 0 configuration header. Feature blocks form a chain. The first-pointer and next-pointer rules say they are 4-byte aligned and within the first 256 bytes. The extended chain is 4-byte aligned, from 0x100 to 0xFFF, and ends with Next = 0. Device type numbers come from a list (PCI Code and ID Assignment Specification). Each setting has a type: read-only, read-write, write-1-to-clear or set by hardware (RO, RW, RW1C, HwInit). The rules cover BAR size probing. For NVMe over PCIe, the device type (Class Code) is 010802h.

What goes wrong: The firmware builds the settings area. Errors there confuse discovery before any driver runs. The computer walks the feature chain with a loop guard. It quietly gives up on a loop or a bad pointer. So feature blocks after the bad link are simply not found. These are often PCIe, MSI-X, AER or SR-IOV. A wrong device type (Class Code) means the NVMe driver never takes the SSD. IDs that change after a firmware update break driver matching. They also break special-case tables (section VI.3 of the error list) and equipment lists. Some read-only settings accept writes. Then software can damage settings the rule book says are fixed. BAR size probing writes all ones. If the BAR does not mask its low bits, the computer works out a wrong size.

How you can tell: lspci -vvv is missing features the SSD is known to have. The kernel log says pci 0000:xx: ... capability chain is corrupt. Or the driver does not take the SSD (it is present, but no nvme node). A BAR is sized as 0 or as the whole address space. Special cases tied to the Device ID stop working after a firmware update. The Subsystem ID changes between start-ups.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Careful: use a spare drive or a test system. In QEMU, change the fake SSD's feature list to make a loop. Watch the kernel's discovery. On real hardware this can only be done by firmware. Take the settings-read answers (CfgRd) from discovery and rebuild the chain. Or use lspci -xxxx and setpci. Write all ones to each BAR and read back. Linux does this at start-up. On a live system, do it only on a test device. Compare lspci -nn output before and after a firmware switch. For read-only settings, write a different value with setpci and read back. Do this on test systems only.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Yes. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself (Reported). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Usually the SSD is at fault. Its firmware builds the settings area, so every structure fault is its own. The computer is at fault only if it reads a valid chain wrongly. Compare with lspci on the same SSD. · Test that confirms it: a raw dump of the settings area.

N-36 Old-style interrupt messages out of balance (Assert_INTx without Deassert_INTx) Seen in the packets Order and work-done signals

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 639676: an old-style "work done" signal turned on (Assert_INTA). No matching turn-off (Deassert_INTA) follows.

Packet=639676 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=Msg | PSN=1531 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Length=0 | Time Stamp=0521.566050045250s | Time Delta=0.000 ns | LCRC=0xC6F23519

Error family: P16, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. It means the order of data, done note and "work done" signal. Proof from outside the recording: E01, the Linux kernel log. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes, by a rule about order or timing. For example: a missing answer, a long gap, or rows in the wrong order.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book defines old-style "work done" signals. They are sent as messages (INTx emulation). There is a turn-on message (Assert_INTx) and a turn-off message (Deassert_INTx). Switches route and merge them. A device must not send INTx messages while MSI or MSI-X is on. It must not send them while Interrupt Disable is set. The Status setting has an Interrupt Status bit. The power-management rule book (PCI PM) says INTx must be turned off before D3.

What goes wrong: Computers normally use MSI-X for NVMe. But INTx is used in some cases. One is early discovery on some software. Another is a fallback when MSI-X set-up fails (C-25 shape). Some start-up program drivers use it, and so does pci=nomsi. A stuck turn-on makes the shared signal line fire again and again. The kernel's false-signal detector then turns off that line for every device sharing it. A device that sends INTx messages while MSI-X is on breaks the rules. The message may be ignored. Or it may start an unrelated handler.

How you can tell: The kernel log shows irq N: nobody cared (try booting with the "irqpoll" option). Then it shows Disabling IRQ #N. Signal counts for the line climb with no SSD activity. A device works with MSI-X but hangs or floods with pci=nomsi. The tool lspci shows Interrupt: pin A with the Status bit INTx+ stuck.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Careful: use a spare drive or a test system. Start with pci=nomsi and run reads and writes. Then, with MSI-X on, restart the function (FLR) while an old-style signal is waiting. This needs a device that uses INTx during discovery. In the recording, pick out messages with the INTx codes. Pair each turn-on with a turn-off for each line. Lay over them the settings writes to the MSI/MSI-X Enable bits and the Command setting. On the computer, use /proc/interrupts and grep -r . /sys/kernel/irq/*/. Watch for the irqpoll sign. Force the old path with pci=nomsi on a test system.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Nothing reports it. Only a timer notices that something did not arrive in time (Timer only). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD is at fault. It loses track of the INTx line state across the MSI-X switch or a restart. · Test that confirms it: the computer's signal-line symptom.

N-37 Byte-enable and address-format rules broken in request packets Seen in the packets Broken or wrongly built packets

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 435904: a write packet (MWr) of length 2. Its first byte-enable field is 0101b, which has gaps (non-contiguous).

Packet=435904 | Link Dir=Downstream | TLP Type=MWr(32) | PSN=262 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=000:00:0 | Address=FCE01008 | Length=2 | DATA=8 B | Time Stamp=0196.116787344370s | Time Delta=145.630 ns | LCRC=0x558D2975

Error family: P11, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. It means broken, poisoned or wrongly built packets. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. The checker marks an odd field or order in this table file (noncontiguous_or_partial_first_be).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book defines the request packet layer (Transaction Layer Protocol). It sets byte-enable rules for memory, I/O and settings requests. Byte enables say which bytes in a 4-byte word are used. It covers zero-length requests. It sets address format rules: a 3-word header versus a 4-word header. Addresses must be 4-byte aligned. A request must not cross a 4 KiB edge (V-28). It must not exceed the largest data size (Max_Payload_Size, V-26). Check the exact wording in your version.

What goes wrong: Some senders build packets with a general copy circuit (DMA engine). These can produce byte-enable patterns or header formats the rules forbid. Receivers act differently. Some mark the packet as wrongly built (Malformed TLP, L-18). Some treat it as not supported (UR, L-20). Some accept it and write or read the wrong bytes. Writes with illegal byte enables can damage nearby bytes of a done note or a command. A 64-bit header for an address below 4 GiB is accepted by most receivers. But it breaks the rules and may fail on a strict switch.

How you can tell: Wrongly built packet or not-supported errors come and go on one computer, and never on another. Done note or command fields have a few stray bytes changed. A device passes on a desktop computer and fails behind a business-grade switch. The capture tool's rule checker flags "BE rules" on some writes. One example is a 16-byte done note written in two packets with a wrong last byte-enable.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Careful: use a spare drive or a test system. Use QEMU, or a programmable chip (FPGA) that can build any packet. On real SSDs you can only watch. Run checks over the table file. For each read, write and settings write, apply the byte-enable rules and the format and address rule. List the senders that break them by sender name (Requester ID). Match these with error reports for wrongly built and not-supported packets. Check how the receiver acted: did it accept? The capture tools' own rule checkers usually include these as "TLP header rule" checks. That depends on the tool.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Yes. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself (Reported). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Look at the packet's direction. Sent by the SSD (Upstream, its memory access): the SSD is at fault. Sent by the computer (Downstream, its settings access): the computer is at fault. · Test that confirms it: how the receiver reacted.

N-38 Answer packets carry wrong sender or receiver names Seen in the packets Answers marked not supported or failed

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 95344: the answer's sender name (CompleterID) says bus 003. But the function was found on bus 002 at start-up.

Packet=95344 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=CplD | PSN=1138 | Tag=12 | RequesterID=000:00:0 | CompleterID=003:00:0 | Cpl Status=SC | Length=1 | Byte Cnt=4 | DATA=4 B | Time Stamp=0125.569716950500s | Time Delta=112.120 ns | LCRC=0xA6599B96

Error family: P04 and P05 and P19, three of the 27 ways an error shows on the wire. P04 means an answer marked "not supported", "failed" or "not ready, try again" (UR, CA or CRS). P05 means an answer nobody asked for, or a wrong request number or sender name. P19 means the settings area: start-up, features, restarts and being ready. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. The checker marks an odd field or order in this table file (completer_id_wrong_bus).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book defines the answer header. It holds the answerer's name (Completer ID) and the asker's name (Requester ID). It holds the request number (Tag), the result (Completion Status) and BCM. A device learns its bus number from settings writes sent to it (Type 0). The "not ready, try again" result (CRS) is only for settings requests. The rule book also covers answers nobody asked for (Unexpected Completion).

What goes wrong: The SSD's answering logic fills the name fields from inner settings. The path delivers answers exactly as written. So an answer with a wrong asker's name goes to the wrong function. Or it goes to the computer's port as an answer nobody asked for (L-16). A wrong answerer's name is accepted by most computer ports. But it confuses the capture tool's pairing, ACS Source Validation and the memory guard's blame. CRS on a memory read breaks the rules. The computer treats it as a failed read (all ones) or as an answer nobody asked for.

How you can tell: The computer's port reports answers nobody asked for (L-16). Yet the SSD's own view is "I answered". Settings reads sometimes return all ones. This happens right after bus numbers change or a hot-plug. The capture tool shows answers from a function that sent no request. After SR-IOV is turned on, answers from VFs carry the main function's name (see N-29).

How to fix it and prove the fix: Careful: use a spare drive or a test system. Change bus numbers on a test system and watch the answerer names. Remove a bridge, then run echo 1 > /sys/bus/pci/rescan. Turn on SR-IOV and check VF answers. Checker rule: for each answer, find the request by asker name and request number, and compare. Check the answerer's bus number against the last settings write (Type 0 CfgWr) seen on the wire. Flag CRS on any request that is not a settings request. On the computer, run lspci -vvv and look for Unexpected Completion in UESta. The computer port's error header log shows the bad answer's header.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Yes. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself (Reported). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD is at fault here. Its answer name fields are wrong. That covers Completer ID, the Requester ID it copies back, CRS on memory reads, and BCM. · Test that confirms it: decode the error header log.

N-39 Power-saving handshakes broken (no PM_Request_Ack, no PME_TO_Ack, PME lost) Seen in the packets Power-saving handshakes and latency messages

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 1343808: the computer asked to turn power off (PME_Turn_Off). The SSD sent no reply (PME_TO_Ack).

Packet=1343808 | Link Dir=Downstream | TLP Type=Msg | PSN=653 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=000:00:0 | Length=0 | Time Stamp=1309.845912356620s | Time Delta=118.130 ns | LCRC=0xE45C4606

Packet 1343813: the SSD asked to enter light sleep (PM_Enter_L1). Then it went quiet without the reply (PM_Request_Ack).

Packet=1343813 | Link Dir=Upstream | Link Event=Electrical Idle | Time Stamp=1309.855912358000s | Time Delta=100.000 us

Error family: P20, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. It means power-saving handshakes and latency messages. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes, by a rule about order or timing. For example: a missing answer, a long gap, or rows in the wrong order.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book covers power management. It covers how the wire moves between power states (PCI-PM link states). It covers the sleep request and reply receipts (PM_Enter_L1/L23 and PM_Request_Ack). It covers the power-off request and reply (PME_Turn_Off/PME_TO_Ack). It covers the wake message (PM_PME) and its flags (PME_Status/PME_En). It sets a time limit for handling a wake message, and when to send it again. Check the exact time values in your version.

What goes wrong: The computer writes a power state change (D0 to D3hot) to the PMCSR setting. That makes the SSD ask for light sleep (L1) with PM_Enter_L1. System sleep makes the computer send PME_Turn_Off. Waking from low power is announced with PM_PME. Rules break in several ways. An SSD goes quiet without waiting for PM_Request_Ack, while the other end may still be sending. An SSD never sends PME_TO_Ack. Then the computer waits, and then forces power off with the SSD mid-write. An SSD sends PM_PME once and never again. The wake is lost if the first was missed. Or an SSD keeps sending PM_PME after PME_Status was cleared. That floods the computer port's wake handler.

How you can tell: System sleep takes the full time limit, or fails with pci_pm_suspend_noirq messages. The kernel log shows pcieport ... PME: Spurious native interrupt!. Wake-on-device never works. PMCSR says the drive is in D3hot, but its wire never entered L1. So it uses power, and the heat budget is wrong. Data is lost on sleep because the SSD had not finished flushing (D-10 shape).

How to fix it and prove the fix: Careful: use a spare drive or a test system. Loop rtcwake -m mem -s 15 while recording. Pair every PME_Turn_Off with its PME_TO_Ack. With the driver detached, write D3hot using setpci. Watch for PM_Enter_L1. In the receipt and message views, pair the handshakes and time them. Lay over them the settings writes to PMCSR: power state writes and PME_Status clears. On the computer, use /sys/bus/pci/devices/<BDF>/power/wakeup*, pm_debug_messages and the kernel log's PME messages. Put a scope on the slot's power lines during sleep. See whether L2/L3 Ready was reached before power was removed.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Nothing reports it. Only a timer notices that something did not arrive in time (Timer only). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Usually the SSD is at fault. It may skip PME_TO_Ack or go quiet without PM_Request_Ack. It may flood PME or never send it again. The computer's board is at fault in two cases. Its port never sends PM_Request_Ack. Or it never clears PME_Status. · Test that confirms it: a sleep loop.

N-40 Slot power limit ignored or sent wrongly (Set_Slot_Power_Limit) Partly seen in the packets Rare messages and side signals

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 124123: the slot power limit message (Set_Slot_Power_Limit) has the value 0 W.

Packet=124123 | Link Dir=Downstream | TLP Type=MsgD | PSN=1188 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=000:00:0 | Length=1 | DATA=4 B | Time Stamp=0125.774697151620s | Time Delta=145.630 ns | LCRC=0x2C1EDB6E

Error family: P21, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. It means other rare messages and hints. Proof from outside the recording: E02, a copy of the SSD's settings area (lspci). E07, measuring the power lines and side pins. · Can the packets alone prove it? Partly. The packets show a shape in timing or order. The proof needs evidence from outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book defines the slot power limit message (Set_Slot_Power_Limit). The slot's settings hold the limit (Slot Power Limit Value/Scale). The device's settings hold the limit it caught (Captured Slot Power Limit Value/Scale). There is a power budget block (Power Budgeting Extended Capability). There is an emergency power cut (Emergency Power Reduction, in Device Capabilities 2 and Device Control 2). Connector rule books (CEM, EDSFF) set power classes. NVMe has power state descriptions (MP, MXPS), a power feature (FID 02h) and a power state count (NOPS).

What goes wrong: A slot tells a card how much power it may draw. The card must not go over it. It should scale its speed, and its NVMe power states, to match. Things can go wrong in several ways. A computer port sends a wrong or zero limit. Then the SSD slows down for no reason (P-01). An SSD ignores the limit and draws more than the slot can give. That causes a power-line drop (N-06), or a power fault that cuts the slot. An SSD reports NVMe power states that do not fit the slot limit (Identify Controller power descriptions, MP field). An SSD says it supports emergency power cut, but does nothing when asked.

How you can tell: A Gen5 SSD runs like a Gen3 one in one slot. EDSFF drives slow down in bays that offer 25 W when the drive needs more. Or drives draw more than 25 W and trip the bay's power controller. Power-fault hot-plug events appear (Slot Status Power Fault Detected). Heat shutdowns follow the slot, not the drive.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Risky, test machine only: lower a test port's slot power limit. Use setpci, where the setting can be written. Watch the message and the SSD's behaviour. Measure current. Read the limit message from the recording. Compare it with lspci -vvv on the computer's port (SltCap) and the SSD (DevCap: SlotPowerLimit). Measure current on the slot power line with an inline meter at full load. Ask for the emergency power cut (EPR) through Device Control 2, and measure. Check the SSD's NVMe power states against the limit.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. It still works, only slower or worse than it should (Degraded). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: There are three cases. The computer's board is at fault if the message is missing, zero or wrong. The SSD is at fault if it does not catch the limit, or runs above it. The computer's power rules are at fault if they pick an NVMe power state above the slot limit. · Test that confirms it: compare both ends.

N-41 Wire signal has little safety margin: an early warning (Lane Margining) Partly seen in the packets Wire start-up steps (link training)

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 263666: the lane margin status reports no margin.

Packet=263666 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=CplD | PSN=2478 | Tag=18 | RequesterID=000:00:0 | CompleterID=002:00:0 | Cpl Status=SC | Length=1 | Byte Cnt=4 | DATA=4 B | Time Stamp=0129.994990018370s | Time Delta=20.000 ns | LCRC=0xB1AADD73

Error family: P08, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. It means wire start-up steps, restarts, or changes of speed or width. Proof from outside the recording: E02, a copy of the SSD's settings area (lspci). E09, a lab test whose result is the proof. · Can the packets alone prove it? Partly. The packets show a shape in timing or order. The proof needs evidence from outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book defines a way to measure each lane's safety margin. It is called Lane Margining at the Receiver. It has a settings block (Margining Extended Capability). It has control and status settings for each lane. Margin commands are coded inside a special timing signal (Control SKP ordered set). The rule book sets the margin each speed needs. PCI-SIG also has a margin test method. Check the required minimums in your version.

What goes wrong: Lane Margining is required for ports at 16 GT/s and faster. Software moves each lane's sampling point step by step and counts errors. This gives a margin for each lane in time units (UI). It can also give a margin in millivolts (mV). Some computers or SSDs report no margin on one lane. Some fail to run the margin test. Some report margins that do not match reality. Each hides a wire that is about to fail. L-25 and P-11 cover a wire that already slowed down. This entry is the wire that has not slowed down yet.

How you can tell: A system passes all tests in the lab. Then it starts logging small errors in use. Margin results differ between lanes by a large factor, with one lane near zero. The margin feature block is missing on a Gen4 or newer port. Margin commands time out or return a "NAK" status.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Careful: use a spare drive or a test system. Measure the margin of a known-weak wire (a long riser) and a short one. Compare them. Use the margin offset to cause controlled errors for other entries' tests. Several entries in section V-B of the error list suggest this. Run the computer maker's margin tool. Or drive the margin test with setpci on the computer's port. Drive it with Control SKP on the SSD's port. Do each lane, at working temperature and with traffic. Note the time and voltage margins. Compare them with the rule book minimums and with the other lanes. Repeat after a long burn-in run. Pair this with the capture tool over long recordings. A lane with low margin should match any symbol errors seen (X-01/X-03).

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. It still works, only slower or worse than it should (Degraded). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: There are two cases. The wire itself is at fault when the same lane is low at both ends, with no logic errors. The port's firmware is at fault when margin commands fail or report values that do not agree. See the error list, section XII.8. · Test that confirms it: lane margining (T11).

N-42 Clock-sharing requests get no answer, so SSD time drifts (PTM) Seen in the packets Rare messages and side signals

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 127127: a clock-sharing request (PTM Request) gets no answer (no PTM Response or ResponseD).

Packet=127127 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=Msg | PSN=1462 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Length=0 | Time Stamp=0125.774941189870s | Time Delta=171.130 ns | LCRC=0x890AF3FF

Error family: P21, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. It means other rare messages and hints. Proof from outside the recording: E02, a copy of the SSD's settings area (lspci). · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes, by a rule about order or timing. For example: a missing answer, a long gap, or rows in the wrong order.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book defines clock sharing across the wire (PTM). PTM means Precision Time Measurement. It has a settings block with Capability and Control settings. It has three messages: PTM Request, Response and ResponseD. It defines three roles: root, requester and responder. It defines how fine the clock is. In the NVMe rule book, the clock time setting (Timestamp, FID 0Eh) is separate from PTM. Makers may link them.

What goes wrong: PTM keeps an SSD's clock in step with the computer's clock. It uses a request and an answer, and measures the travel time. The computer's chip or a switch may not act as PTM root or responder. Then the SSD's clock runs free. Its time stamps drift away from the computer's time (T-20, M-052, M-053 shapes). These are in its reports, its lasting event log and possibly its Timestamp setting. The last only applies if the firmware takes it from PTM. A switch that does not pass PTM on breaks every device below it.

How you can tell: The SSD's time stamps move away from the computer's time by growing amounts. The tool lspci -vvv shows PTM "Root+ Responder+" on the computer's port. But the SSD's PTM Control shows "Enabled-" after the kernel tried to turn it on. The recording shows PTM Requests with no Response.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Safe to try: turn PTM off on the computer's port. Use setpci on PTM Control. Watch the SSD's PTM Requests go unanswered. Turn it on again and confirm answers come back. In the recording, pair PTM Requests with Responses on each wire. Work out the exchange time. Work out how the ResponseD time stamps drift from the capture tool's clock. On the computer, read the PTM parts of lspci -vvv on every port of the path. Run dmesg | grep -i ptm. On the SSD, compare its Timestamp setting (nvme get-feature -f 0xe) with the computer's time over hours.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. It still works, only slower or worse than it should (Degraded). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: There are two cases. The computer's board is at fault if requests go unanswered. Its responder may be off, or a switch may lack PTM. The SSD is at fault in two cases. It says it can ask and is turned on, but never asks. Or it misuses the answers. · Test that confirms it: a list of PTM support on every part of the path.

N-43 Ready messages missing or too early (FRS/DRS, Readiness Time Reporting) Seen in the packets Settings area and being ready

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 62238: a function ready message (FRS).

Packet=62238 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=Msg | PSN=2374 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Length=0 | Time Stamp=0062.155789260370s | Time Delta=108.130 ns | LCRC=0x4BCB8F6E

Packet 62243: the SSD said it was ready, but it still answers "not ready, try again" (CRS).

Packet=62243 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=Cpl | PSN=2375 | Tag=15 | RequesterID=000:00:0 | CompleterID=002:00:0 | Cpl Status=CRS | Byte Cnt=4 | Time Stamp=0062.155889723370s | Time Delta=131.630 ns | LCRC=0x2622DC11

Error family: P19 and P21, two of the 27 ways an error shows on the wire. P19 means the settings area: start-up, features, restarts and being ready. P21 means other rare messages and hints. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. The checker marks an odd field or order in this table file (completion_status_CRS).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book defines ready messages (Readiness Notifications). There are two: DRS and FRS. The computer's port can queue them (FRS Queueing Extended Capability). Support bits are in Device Capabilities 2. Switches are in Device Control 2. A settings block reports ready times (Readiness Time Reporting Extended Capability). The rule book also sets ready rules after a restart and after a function restart (Conventional Reset, FLR). Check this in your version.

What goes wrong: Ready messages let the computer stop asking again and again. Without them, it waits the worst case. That is 1 s, or 100 ms after a function restart (FLR). With them, it waits for DRS or FRS, or for the ready time the SSD reported. Some SSDs report a ready time that is too short. Some send FRS before their command lists and settings work (M-039 shape). A computer that trusts the ready message then fails its first access. It gets CRS or all ones. Or the NVMe controller has CSTS.RDY=0 and then does not respond to CC writes.

How you can tell: Some computers use ready messages: their start-up program, some hypervisors and newer kernels (depends on version). There, "device not ready" errors appear right after FLR or wake-up. Yet the SSD "announced" it was ready. On computers that keep asking, there is no symptom. That hides the bug until the computer changes.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Careful: use a spare drive or a test system. Loop function restarts (FLR) with the NVMe driver detached. In the recording, measure from FLR to FRS. Measure from FLR to the first good settings read. Compare with the reported FLR Time. Checker: for each DRS or FRS, find the next settings access to that function. Check that it did not return CRS. Measure three times: restart to DRS, FLR to FRS, and D3hot to D0 to FRS. Compare them with the ready-time report. Read it with a settings read of that block, or with lspci -vvv. Repeat at different temperatures and after a firmware switch. Ready times can change.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Nothing reports it. Only a timer notices that something did not arrive in time (Timer only). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Usually the SSD is at fault. It may send FRS or DRS from the wrong point in its restart steps. It may report times that are too short, or a wrong function number. The computer is at fault only in one case. It trusts a ready message the SSD did not send for that function. · Test that confirms it: a function-restart loop.

N-44 Cache-steering hints misused in packets (TLP Processing Hints, TPH) Seen in the packets Settings area and being ready

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 63539: the hint bit is set (TH=1), but the hint switch (TPH Requester Enable) is off.

Packet=63539 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=2966 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000002:00010000 | Length=64 | DATA=256 B | Time Stamp=0062.206062842620s | Time Delta=105.000 ns | LCRC=0xB8699B42

Error family: P19 and P21, two of the 27 ways an error shows on the wire. P19 means the settings area: start-up, features, restarts and being ready. P21 means other rare messages and hints. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. The checker marks an odd field or order in this table file (header_bit_TH_set).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book defines hints inside packets (TLP Processing Hints, TPH). These are the TH bit and the PH code. A steering tag (ST field) has a set place in memory writes and reads. A settings block for senders gives the place and size of the tag table (TPH Requester Extended Capability). Receiver support is in Device Capabilities 2 (TPH Completer). The rule book says when TH is allowed. Check this in your version.

What goes wrong: TPH lets a device tell the computer's chip where a write or read should go. It names a cache or processing part, so the data lands in the right cache. For NVMe, that means the done note and read data near the processor that will use them. Wrong tags send data to the wrong cache. That costs delay and bandwidth, with no error. Some paths do not support hints. Strict computers then mark the packet as wrongly built or not supported. Lenient ones quietly ignore it. So the failure depends on the computer.

How you can tell: Answers are slower with TPH on than off. Traffic between processor sockets (NUMA, P-10 shape) is higher than expected. That is because data goes to the wrong socket's cache. Wrongly built or not-supported packets show up on a computer where the same drive worked elsewhere. A device sets TH on every write, whatever the settings say.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Careful: use a spare drive or a test system. Use a device that uses TPH. Fill its tag table with wrong tags on purpose. Measure delay and traffic between sockets. Turn off TPH Completer on the computer's port, where it can be written. Watch for wrongly built or not-supported packets. Checker: pick out requests with TH=1 and list their tag values. Compare them with the tag table caught in the recording. The table comes from settings writes to the TPH block or MSI-X table entries. Match with writes to TPH Requester Control. On the computer, read the TPH parts of lspci -vvv on the SSD and the computer's port. Measure answer delay with TPH off (setpci TPH Requester Control = 0) and on.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. It still works, only slower or worse than it should (Degraded). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: There are three cases. The SSD is at fault if TH appears while off, or with tags never set. The computer is at fault if it turns on TPH without writing tag entries. The computer's board is at fault if its chip lacks TPH Completer support. Strict computers then mark the packets as not supported or wrongly built. · Test that confirms it: the settings state.

N-45 Vendor and management messages on the main wire go wrong (VDM, MCTP) Seen in the packets Answers marked not supported or failed

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 96410: a management message (MCTP VDM Type 0) goes to an SSD function. That function has no MCTP over PCIe.

Packet=96410 | Link Dir=Downstream | TLP Type=MsgD | PSN=813 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=000:00:0 | Length=2 | DATA=8 B | Time Stamp=0125.570017257120s | Time Delta=100.130 ns | LCRC=0x6E47A13C

Packet 96412: "not supported" (UR) for a message is reported with an error message (ERR_NONFATAL). A message never gets an answer.

Packet=96412 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=Msg | PSN=1578 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Length=0 | Time Stamp=0125.570017857120s | Time Delta=157.130 ns | LCRC=0x5B491459

Error family: P04 and P21, two of the 27 ways an error shows on the wire. P04 means an answer marked "not supported", "failed" or "not ready, try again" (UR, CA or CRS). P21 means other rare messages and hints. Proof from outside the recording: E06, records from the slow management wire (SMBus). · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes, by a rule about order or timing. For example: a missing answer, a long gap, or rows in the wrong order.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book defines vendor messages (Vendor-Defined Messages). There are Type 0 and Type 1. It covers their routing and their Vendor ID field. It says when to answer "not supported" (UR) and when to drop quietly. DMTF rule books cover management messages over PCIe (DSP0238, MCTP PCIe VDM Transport Binding). They also cover the MCTP basics (DSP0236) and firmware update (DSP0267, PLDM). NVMe-MI has its own MCTP binding.

What goes wrong: Management messages over PCIe vendor messages (MCTP over PCIe VDM) carry NVMe-MI (N-02). They also carry PLDM firmware updates and other management messages on the main wire. Things can go wrong in several ways. A BMC or management program sends vendor messages to a function without MCTP. That causes floods of not-supported errors (UR storms, L-20). Management address set-up (MCTP endpoint ID) fails. Then management traffic goes to the wrong function. Vendor message traffic uses up room for posted requests. That delays NVMe doorbells or done notes (M-020 shape). An SSD sends maker-specific messages that a strict computer chip rejects. Management commands change the SSD with no cause NVMe can see, such as a firmware update over PLDM.

How you can tell: Not-supported errors show in the SSD's or computer port's error bits (AER). Their header logs show message packets. The command nvme fw-log shows a new firmware image after a management update on the main wire. Slow answers line up with bursts of message packets. MCTP tools on the computer or BMC report that discovery failed.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Careful: use a spare drive or a test system. Use a BMC with MCTP over PCIe. Run discovery against the SSD while recording. Compare which functions answer and which return UR. Pick out message packets by type and Vendor ID. Decode the MCTP headers with a script. Match them with the error header logs for UR. Match them with management events in the BMC log. Count vendor message bytes per second against the room for posted requests (the X-21/X-22 method).

Does the SSD or computer report it? Yes. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself (Reported). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: There are two cases. The computer's board is at fault when Type 0 vendor messages reach a function without MCTP. The BMC or its management software sends them. The SSD is at fault when it sends floods of vendor messages upward. It is also at fault when it errors on Type 1 vendor messages. · Test that confirms it: decode the error header log.

N-46 SSD's own packets carry a wrong sender name (Requester ID) Seen in the packets Wrong request number or sender name

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 117847: a write packet (MWr) from the SSD with sender name 002:00:1. Function 1 does not exist.

Packet=117847 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=561 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:1 | Address=00000001:ACC31000 | Length=64 | DATA=256 B | Time Stamp=0125.572280431000s | Time Delta=193.620 ns | LCRC=0x41038548

Error family: P05 and P17, two of the 27 ways an error shows on the wire. P05 means an answer nobody asked for, or a wrong request number or sender name. P17 means memory access to the wrong place, or with a wrong sender name. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. The checker marks an odd field or order in this table file (unexpected_ssd_function_rid).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book defines how the sender name is built (Requester ID). A device learns its bus number from settings writes sent to it (Type 0). The rule book also covers ARI and extra function numbers (Phantom Functions). Their support and switch are in the device settings. It sets how SR-IOV virtual functions get their names (First VF Offset, VF Stride). It covers ACS Source Validation.

What goes wrong: The sender name (RID) says who sent a packet. The path, ACS, the memory guard and answer routing all use it. A wrong RID causes several problems. Answers to the SSD's reads go elsewhere. The SSD sees a timeout (Completion Timeout, L-14/T-33). Meanwhile the recording shows an answer going to a name nobody owns (L-16 on another function). The memory guard uses the wrong device's address tables. That gives a memory fault (L-36). Worse, it may succeed into another device's buffers. ACS Source Validation flags a rule break (L-21). L-21 and L-36 describe the error bits that catch it. This entry is the cause inside the SSD.

How you can tell: Memory-guard faults (DMAR/AMD-Vi) name a function that was idle or does not exist. ACS errors show on the computer's port. Timeouts appear in the SSD right after bus numbers change. The SSD reports them as Data Transfer Error (S-04). VFs work up to some number N and fail after that (a stride error). The capture tool's decoder puts one function's command lists under another.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Careful: use a spare drive or a test system. Turn on SR-IOV with the most VFs while recording. Check every sender name. Change bus numbers with a rescan and repeat. Checker: build the list of allowed names from the discovery part of the recording. Or build it from lspci -vvv SR-IOV and ARI fields plus the bus number. Flag every SSD packet with a name outside the list. Run it again after any bus number change or VF turn-on in the recording. On the computer, memory-guard fault logs include the bad sender name. lspci -vvv shows ACS status on the computer's port.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Yes. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself (Reported). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: There are two cases. The SSD is at fault when its sender name differs from the caught bus, function or VF route. The computer is at fault only if it set the SR-IOV offset or stride wrongly. The same holds if it set the extra-function switches wrongly. · Test that confirms it: the memory-guard fault log.

N-47 Power-window messages misused (OBFF sent while off, or ignored) Seen in the packets Power-saving handshakes and latency messages

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 1345008: a power-window message (OBFF) is sent while the OBFF switch is off (OBFF Enable = 0).

Packet=1345008 | Link Dir=Downstream | TLP Type=Msg | PSN=1087 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=000:00:0 | Length=0 | Time Stamp=1309.856425426870s | Time Delta=143.130 ns | LCRC=0xBD620A2B

Error family: P20, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. It means power-saving handshakes and latency messages. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes, by a rule about order or timing. For example: a missing answer, a long gap, or rows in the wrong order.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book defines power-window messages (Optimized Buffer Flush/Fill, OBFF). It defines the OBFF message and its codes. Support is in Device Capabilities 2 (OBFF Supported). The switch is in Device Control 2 (OBFF Enable). It can be signalled with the wake pin (WAKE#) or by message. Check this in your version.

What goes wrong: OBFF lets the computer tell devices when its processor and memory are in a low-power window. Then devices can group their traffic. It is mostly used in home and office computers. Breaking the rules costs power, because the device wakes the computer for no need. Or it costs delay, because the device holds back work it should not. It never makes data wrong. T-45 and T-46 cover ASPM and LTR delay. OBFF is the third computer power feature, and it had no entry.

How you can tell: The computer spends less time in low power than expected with the SSD in. Slow answers line up with OBFF Idle messages. OBFF messages come to a device that says it supports only wake-pin signalling. That support is shown in Device Capabilities 2 (OBFF Supported).

How to fix it and prove the fix: Safe to try: use a test computer that supports message signalling. Turn on OBFF with setpci. Watch whether the SSD changes how it uses memory. Pick out OBFF messages. Lay over them the Device Control 2 write. Compare the SSD's memory activity inside Idle windows. Read the OBFF fields with lspci -vvv (DevCap2/DevCtl2) on both ends.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. It still works, only slower or worse than it should (Degraded). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: There are two cases. The computer's board is at fault if it sends messages to a device whose OBFF switch is off. The same holds if the switch is set for the wake pin. The SSD is at fault if OBFF is on but its traffic ignores it. · Test that confirms it: the settings state.

N-48 Delay-tolerance messages carry wrong values (LTR) Seen in the packets Power-saving handshakes and latency messages

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 1346563: a delay-tolerance message (LTR) says 1 us with Requirement=1 while the SSD is idle.

Packet=1346563 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=Msg | PSN=1804 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Length=0 | Time Stamp=1309.856656876750s | Time Delta=169.120 ns | LCRC=0x3D8C274A

Error family: P20, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. It means power-saving handshakes and latency messages. Proof from outside the recording: E02, a copy of the SSD's settings area (lspci). · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes, by a rule about order or timing. For example: a missing answer, a long gap, or rows in the wrong order.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book defines delay-tolerance messages (Latency Tolerance Reporting, LTR). It defines the LTR message format. Support is in Device Capabilities 2 (LTR Mechanism Supported). The switch is in Device Control 2 (LTR Mechanism Enable). The port's LTR block holds the largest allowed delays (Max Snoop/No-Snoop Latency). It also covers deep sleep steps (L1 PM Substates) and the LTR_L1.2_THRESHOLD link. Check this in your version.

What goes wrong: LTR tells the computer's chip how long the SSD can wait before its requests are served. The computer uses it to pick deep sleep steps for the wire and processor (L1 substates, package C-states). A wrong value either keeps the computer awake, costing power. Or it lets the computer sleep too deeply, adding delay (M-025). The computer also uses the SSD's LTR to decide whether L1.2 may be on at all.

How you can tell: The processor almost never reaches deep sleep with the SSD in. The kernel log shows L1 substates not turned on for the SSD. The first read or write after idle is far slower than the SSD's own LTR value. The recording shows LTR messages with Requirement = 0 (no requirement). Yet the same SSD then complains about delay.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Decode LTR messages over time. Work out value × scale, and read the Requirement bit. Lay over them the Device Control 2 writes and the L1.2 entries. Compare with lspci -vvv L1SubCtl1 LTR_L1.2_THRESHOLD. Also compare with the port's LTR largest values.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. It still works, only slower or worse than it should (Degraded). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Usually the SSD is at fault. Its LTR values may be fixed or wrong. It may send LTR while LTR is off. The computer's board is at fault only for the L1.2 limit it works out from LTR (T-46). · Test that confirms it: an idle and busy cycle.

N-49 Old or ignored messages sent, or answered with "not supported" Seen in the packets Answers marked not supported or failed

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 98752: an old indicator-light message. It must be quietly ignored.

Packet=98752 | Link Dir=Downstream | TLP Type=Msg | PSN=1532 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=000:00:0 | Length=0 | Time Stamp=0125.570248421750s | Time Delta=123.120 ns | LCRC=0xE6604952

Packet 98754: the SSD marks it as not supported (UR) instead of ignoring it.

Packet=98754 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=Msg | PSN=2193 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Length=0 | Time Stamp=0125.570249021750s | Time Delta=131.000 ns | LCRC=0x749072A5

Error family: P04 and P21, two of the 27 ways an error shows on the wire. P04 means an answer marked "not supported", "failed" or "not ready, try again" (UR, CA or CRS). P21 means other rare messages and hints. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes, by a rule about order or timing. For example: a missing answer, a long gap, or rows in the wrong order.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book defines kinds of message. These include hot-plug signal messages, Unlock and Lightweight Notification (LN). It says which messages receivers must ignore. From version 4.0 on, it marks some as no longer used. Check this in your version.

What goes wrong: These messages were made for cards with lights and buttons on them. They were also made for old locked requests. Modern computers never use them. Devices built on general PCIe chip designs sometimes still send them or handle them badly. They are harmless when ignored, and noisy when not. One "not supported" error (UR) per message floods the error logs (X-26). That hides real errors.

How you can tell: The SSD's or computer port's error bits (AER) show repeated UR entries. The header log shows a message packet. LN messages come from a device that does not say it supports LN. A device sends Attention_Button_Pressed. That makes a hot-plug controller start removing it.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Careful: use a spare drive or a test system. These can only be watched on real devices. QEMU computer ports can be changed to send indicator messages, to test receivers. Pick out message packets by code. List who sent them. Pair each with any ERR_ message or UR answer that follows. The tool lspci -vvv shows UESta UnsupReq with a message in the header log.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Yes. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself (Reported). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: There are two cases. The SSD is at fault when it sends downward-only messages upward. It is also at fault when it answers ignored messages with UR. Its PCIe chip design may have old options left on. The computer's board is at fault when an old computer port sends indicator, LN or Unlock messages down to it. · Test that confirms it: decode the error header log.

N-50 Atomic memory requests sent wrongly, or to a part that cannot answer Seen in the packets Answers marked not supported or failed

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 101319: an atomic compare-and-swap request (AtomicOp CAS) from the SSD.

Packet=101319 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=CAS | PSN=2903 | Tag=39 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000002:D6BBB000 | Length=4 | DATA=16 B | Time Stamp=0125.570475414500s | Time Delta=141.120 ns | LCRC=0x60D7664A

Packet 101321: the computer's chip cannot answer atomic requests, so it answers "not supported" (UR).

Packet=101321 | Link Dir=Downstream | TLP Type=Cpl | PSN=2282 | Tag=39 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | CompleterID=000:02:4 | Cpl Status=UR | Byte Cnt=4 | Time Stamp=0125.570476214500s | Time Delta=37.380 ns | LCRC=0x04EAB4A0

Error family: P04 and P21, two of the 27 ways an error shows on the wire. P04 means an answer marked "not supported", "failed" or "not ready, try again" (UR, CA or CRS). P21 means other rare messages and hints. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. The checker marks an odd field or order in this table file (completion_status_UR).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book defines atomic requests (AtomicOps). An atomic request reads and changes memory in one step. There are three kinds: FetchAdd, Swap and CAS. The rule book sets their data sizes, alignment and answer rules. Support for routing and answering is in Device Capabilities 2. The sender switch and a blocking switch are in Device Control 2 (AtomicOp Requester Enable, Egress Blocking). It also covers how ACS and switches route them.

What goes wrong: NVMe controllers do not use PCIe atomic requests. An SSD that sends one is running firmware or a chip design meant for another product. Or it misuses them as a kind of doorbell signal. Receivers answer UR or CA. Or the outgoing port blocks the request and raises AtomicOp Egress Blocked. The SSD then sees an answer error or a timeout. It may report Data Transfer Error (S-04).

How you can tell: Atomic requests get UR or CA answers. A switch port's error bits show AtomicOp Egress Blocked. A device reports S-04 with no NVMe cause. Atomic request traffic comes from an SSD at all.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Careful: use a spare drive or a test system. These can only be watched on real devices. Programmable chips (FPGA) or QEMU can make wrongly built atomic requests to test receivers. Pick out packets with Type = AtomicOp. Check their length, alignment and the history of the switch bit. Pair each with the answer's result. Read DevCap2/DevCtl2 with lspci -vvv on the SSD, the switch and the computer's chip.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Yes. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself (Reported). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: There are two cases. The SSD is at fault when an NVMe SSD sends atomic requests at all. It is also at fault when they have a bad size or alignment. The computer's board is at fault when it reported answer support wrongly. · Test that confirms it: the atomic request support bits.

N-51 Packet prefixes and address-type bits misused (PASID, ATS, AT) Seen in the packets Settings area and being ready

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 65749: a request marked as already translated (AT=10), while address translation (ATS) is off.

Packet=65749 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MRd(64) | PSN=3977 | Tag=58 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000002:00020000 | Length=64 | Time Stamp=0062.206358561250s | Time Delta=126.120 ns | LCRC=0x39C094E8

Error family: P19 and P21, two of the 27 ways an error shows on the wire. P19 means the settings area: start-up, features, restarts and being ready. P21 means other rare messages and hints. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. The checker marks an odd field or order in this table file (address_type_nonzero, completion_status_UR).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book defines packet prefixes (TLP Prefixes, Local and End-End). It defines a process ID block (PASID Extended Capability). That covers Max PASID Width, Execute/Privileged Mode Supported and PASID Enable. It defines an address translation block (ATS Extended Capability: ATS Enable, STU). It defines what the address type field means (AT field). It covers blocking of translated requests (ACS Translation Blocking).

What goes wrong: Devices that share memory addresses with programs use PASID and ATS. NVMe SSDs normally use neither. A device may send translated requests while ATS is off. The computer treats that as an attack on the memory guard. The computer's chip drops the request (ACS Translation Blocking). Or the memory guard faults (L-36). Wrongly built prefixes give a wrongly-built-packet error (Malformed TLP, L-18).

How you can tell: Memory-guard faults give the reason "translated request". The error bits show ACS Violation or TLP Translation Egress Blocked. A wrongly-built-packet error has a prefix in its header log. A device's memory access works with the memory guard in passthrough mode. It fails in translated mode.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Careful: use a spare drive or a test system. Put the memory guard in translated mode. Watch whether the SSD ever sends AT ≠ 00b. Any faults name the sender name (RID) and the reason. Pick out requests with a prefix or with AT ≠ 00b. Compare them with the history of settings writes to the PASID and ATS control settings. Pair them with memory-guard fault logs. The fault reason codes name translated-request breaks.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Yes. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself (Reported). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The SSD is at fault. Shared chip design defaults may be left on. Its firmware may turn ATS or PASID on inside. Its descriptor templates may hold old AT bits. The computer's board matters only in how it reacts (drop, UR or memory-guard fault). · Test that confirms it: the settings state.

N-52 Reserved codes or bits used on the wire Seen in the packets Broken or wrongly built packets

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 436792: an answer with a result code that is reserved, so not allowed (reserved Completion Status).

Packet=436792 | Link Dir=Downstream | TLP Type=Cpl | PSN=348 | Tag=162 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | CompleterID=000:02:4 | Cpl Status=Reserved (0x3) | Byte Cnt=64 | Time Stamp=0196.117006644500s | Time Delta=114.620 ns | LCRC=0xE337D96E

Error family: P11, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. It means broken, poisoned or wrongly built packets. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. The checker marks an odd field or order in this table file (reserved_completion_status).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book has a table of packet header codes (Fmt/Type). It has rules for wrongly built packets (Malformed TLP). It defines the answer result codes. It defines receipt packet types (DLLP types). Reserved receipt types must be thrown away. A general rule covers reserved bits: the sender sends zero, and the receiver ignores them.
