What goes wrong: Reserved codes come from three places. One is firmware bugs. Another is a chip design set up for a newer version than its partner. A code from a later version looks reserved to an older receiver. The third is bit errors that got past the check number (LCRC). That is possible in principle only in Flit mode before error correction (FEC). It is also possible when a broken header gets a correctly recomputed LCRC. That is a cancel or resend bug. Receivers act differently. Some report a wrongly built packet (L-18). Some quietly throw it away. Some accept it, and what happens next is not defined.

How you can tell: Wrongly-built-packet errors (AER) appear. Their header log has an Fmt/Type that the capture tool labels reserved. An answer has result 011b or 1x1b. The capture tool cannot name some receipt packets. A new device and an old switch fail to work together.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Run a checker rule over all headers and receipt packets. Flag any code not in the table. Use the table for the older of the two partners' versions. Flag reserved bits that the sender set. Match with wrongly-built-packet error reports.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Yes. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself (Reported). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Look at who sent it. Sent by the computer (Downstream): the computer's chip is at fault. Sent by the SSD (Upstream): the SSD is at fault. Damage that only appears past a signal booster or switch means the wire is at fault. · Test that confirms it: the receiver's report.

N-53 Room-counting start-up never finishes, so the wire is up but useless Seen in the packets Room on the wire (credits)

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 370102: the first start-up receipt for room counting (InitFC1) keeps repeating. The second one (InitFC2) is never sent. So the start-up step (DL_Init) does not finish.

Packet=370102 | Link Dir=Upstream | DLLP Type=InitFC1-Cpl | Time Stamp=0194.445917340000s | Time Delta=2.000 ms

Error family: P07, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. It means setting up and using room on the wire (flow-control credits). · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes, by a rule about order or timing. For example: a missing answer, a long gap, or rows in the wrong order.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book defines how room counting starts (Flow Control initialisation). It has two steps (FC_INIT1 and FC_INIT2). It defines what InitFC1 and InitFC2 receipts contain. It sets the smallest starting room for each kind of packet, and the resend timing. It defines the wire's control steps (DLCMSM: DL_Inactive, DL_Init, DL_Active). It defines reporting that the wire is active (Data Link Layer Link Active). Check the room minimums and timing in your version.

What goes wrong: The wire's control steps move from DL_Init to DL_Active at one point only. That is when room counting for channel 0 (VC0) is set up. Some devices do not start InitFC after the wire reaches L0. Some report illegal room values. Some reset their room count on every small recovery. Each keeps the wire up electrically, but dead for data. The computer sees settings reads time out or return all ones (C-16). After retries, it gives up.

How you can tell: The kernel log shows pci 0000:xx:00.0: not ready after N ms. Link Status shows the wire up at full speed and width. But the Data Link Layer Link Active bit is clear, where the port reports it (DLLLA). The capture tool shows TS1/TS2. Then InitFC1 receipts repeat with no InitFC2. There are no request or data packets at all on the wire.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Risky, test machine only: use a programmable chip (FPGA). Make it hold back InitFC. On real devices it shows as a rare hang after a speed change or hot reset. In the receipt view, pair InitFC1 and InitFC2 for each type and direction. Check room values against the minimums. Measure from L0 entry to the first request or data packet. On the computer, check the Link Status DLLLA bit and the "not ready" messages. A scope confirms the lanes are alive.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Nothing reports it. Only a timer notices that something did not arrive in time (Timer only). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Look at which side never sends InitFC2 or InitFC. If the SSD's receipts are missing (Upstream), the SSD's link firmware or chip design is at fault. If the computer's port is silent, the computer's board is at fault. See the error list, section XII.8. · Test that confirms it: a snapshot of wire support versus wire status (E02).

N-54 Request types an NVMe wire must never carry Seen in the packets Answers marked not supported or failed

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 102886: an old-style I/O-space read to an SSD that has no I/O address range (no I/O BAR).

Packet=102886 | Link Dir=Downstream | TLP Type=IORd | PSN=2354 | Tag=13 | RequesterID=000:00:0 | Address=0000E000 | Length=1 | Time Stamp=0125.570689876370s | Time Delta=111.630 ns | LCRC=0x833823DC

Packet 102889: the answer says "not supported" (Cpl UR).

Packet=102889 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=Cpl | PSN=3639 | Tag=13 | RequesterID=000:00:0 | CompleterID=002:00:0 | Cpl Status=UR | Byte Cnt=4 | Time Stamp=0125.570690476370s | Time Delta=148.630 ns | LCRC=0xB4D3AB5E

Error family: P04, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. It means an answer marked "not supported", "failed" or "not ready, try again" (UR, CA or CRS). · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. The checker marks an odd field or order in this table file (completion_status_UR).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book lists which requests each kind of part may send. It covers how settings requests are routed. Bridges turn Type 1 into Type 0 at the last step. It covers old-style I/O requests, and that I/O space is no longer used. It covers that Memory Read Lock is no longer used.

What goes wrong: On the computer side, a driver or start-up program may try old I/O ports. It tries them on an NVMe SSD. Or a switch may fail to turn Type 1 into Type 0 at the last step. On the SSD side, a chip design with a computer-port mode may leak settings or I/O requests upward. Receivers answer UR, and the error logs fill. Real traffic is not affected. But the UR noise hides real errors (X-26 shape).

How you can tell: A UR shows with an I/O or Type 1 settings header in the error header log. UR entries are put on the computer's port for requests the SSD sent. An SSD works, but logs small or medium errors on every start-up during an old-style check.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Safe to try: record a full start-up. Look for any I/O or Type 1 request to the SSD. Careful: use a spare drive or a test system. Run inb on a port inside the SSD's bridge window from a user program (test systems only). Pick out by type: any IORd/IOWr, and any CfgRd1/CfgWr1 sent to the SSD. Also pick any settings or I/O request carrying the SSD's sender name. Pair each with UR answers.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Yes. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself (Reported). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: There are two cases. The SSD is at fault if settings or I/O requests travel upward from it. The computer or its board is at fault if I/O or Type 1 settings requests go down to the SSD. · Test that confirms it: decode the error header log.

N-55 Storage-area number rules broken (NSID 0, broadcast, too high) Seen in the packets Rules for what a command holds

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 730370: the command (SQE), with the fields this rule checks in its 64 bytes.

Packet=730370 | Link Dir=Downstream | TLP Type=CplD | PSN=2607 | Tag=224 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | CompleterID=000:02:4 | Cpl Status=SC | Length=16 | Byte Cnt=64 | DATA=64 B | Time Stamp=0524.580871943120s | Time Delta=138.750 ns | LCRC=0xB8F45582

Packet 730372: the done note result is SCT0/SC0x0B with do-not-retry (DNR).

Packet=730372 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=286 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000004:82E50D60 | Length=4 | DATA=16 B | Time Stamp=0524.580872479120s | Time Delta=29.870 ns | LCRC=0x0A8D3A03

Error family: P18, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. It means rules about what goes inside a command. · Can the packets alone prove it? Only by reading the bytes inside the packets. The code is in the DATA column. The hex version of the file marks it (nvme_status_nonzero).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book defines the storage area number field (NSID). It defines the "all areas" value (broadcast). It lists, for each command, whether that value is allowed. Controller ID data gives the highest number (NN). It also gives write-cache bits (VWC), which say if a broadcast Flush works. There are lists of active and allocated storage area numbers. A wrong number gets Invalid Namespace or Format. Check the per-command rules in your version.

What goes wrong: Computers build storage area numbers from their own table. Direct-command tools let users type any value. Controllers that do not check the number can go wrong in three ways. They may work on area 1 when given NSID 0. They may run a broadcast Write on every area, destroying data everywhere. They may read past the end of an inner table (C-01 Controller Fatal Status shape).

How you can tell: Result 0x0B comes back on commands the computer thought were controller-wide. A Flush with FFFFFFFFh is rejected. The drive's VWC field says broadcast is not supported. Data in a storage area is changed by a command sent to NSID 0. A controller fatal error follows a number that is too high.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Careful: use a spare drive or a test system. Try random storage area numbers as below, on a drive you can lose. Checker: for each opcode, list which kinds of number are allowed. Flag rule breaks and the controller's answer to each. Try numbers with nvme io-passthru / admin-passthru on a scratch drive. Use 0, NN+1, FFFFFFFFh and inactive IDs. Expect the right result every time.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Yes. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself (Reported). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The computer is at fault for wrong numbers. Tool defaults or a stale saved NN can cause them. The SSD is also at fault when it finishes such commands with Success. · Test that confirms it: random numbers on a scratch drive.

N-56 Size limits for some commands ignored (WZSL, DMRL, DMRSL, VSL) Seen in the packets Rules for what a command holds

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 735382: the command (SQE), with the fields this rule checks in its 64 bytes.

Packet=735382 | Link Dir=Downstream | TLP Type=CplD | PSN=3149 | Tag=238 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | CompleterID=000:02:4 | Cpl Status=SC | Length=16 | Byte Cnt=64 | DATA=64 B | Time Stamp=0524.581125767370s | Time Delta=180.750 ns | LCRC=0x55140C25

Packet 735384: the done note says success (SCT0/SC0x00).

Packet=735384 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=2380 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000004:82E50D80 | Length=4 | DATA=16 B | Time Stamp=0524.590125767370s | Time Delta=26.870 ns | LCRC=0x5D125AFC

Error family: P18, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. It means rules about what goes inside a command. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes, by a rule about order or timing. For example: a missing answer, a long gap, or rows in the wrong order.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe command rule book gives extra controller ID data per command set. It holds size limits: WZSL, DMRL, DMRSL and VSL. It defines Write Zeroes, Dataset Management with its range count and length rules, and Verify. Check the field names and units in your version.

What goes wrong: Since NVMe 2.0, a controller can state separate limits for some commands. These are commands whose cost does not grow with the bytes moved. A computer that ignores them gets Invalid Field (S-02). Some controllers do not enforce the limits. Then the command takes far longer than expected (T-01 shape). Or it is only partly done.

How you can tell: Large blkdiscard or fallocate --zero-range jobs get 0x02 on one drive and not another. Discards take seconds. Write Zeroes finishes in microseconds for a range the drive could not have zeroed. Then reads show old data.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Careful: use a spare drive or a test system. Run nvme write-zeroes with a block count above WZSL on a scratch storage area. Run nvme dsm with more ranges than DMRL. Read the ID data CNS 06h, with nvme id-ctrl --nvm style output or raw. Compare it with the block counts and range lists in the recording for each command. Send a Write Zeroes just above WZSL and expect 0x02. Send one just below, and check the zeros by reading back.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Yes. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself (Reported). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: There are two cases. The computer is at fault for going over the stated limits. The SSD is at fault if it rejects commands within the limits. It is also at fault if it accepts commands over the limits and only does part of them. · Test that confirms it: a test at the limit edge.

N-57 Messages sent with wrong routing or in the wrong direction Seen in the packets Rare messages and side signals

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 129521: the SSD sends a message to everyone that only the computer may send downward.

Packet=129521 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=Msg | PSN=2646 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Length=0 | Time Stamp=0125.778125642750s | Time Delta=92.000 ns | LCRC=0xB61CCB71

Error family: P21, one of 27 ways an error shows on the wire. It means other rare messages and hints. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes, by a rule about order or timing. For example: a missing answer, a long gap, or rows in the wrong order.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The PCIe rule book defines how messages are routed. Its message code table says, for each code, the allowed routing and direction. It also says whether the message carries data. Messages that break these rules are wrongly built packets (Malformed TLP).

What goes wrong: Switches route messages by a routing field. A wrong field sends a message nowhere, or everywhere. A downward-only message from an SSD is a wrongly built packet. The switch or computer port logs it (L-18), and may raise a fatal error (ERR_FATAL). A wake message (PM_PME) with wrong routing never reaches the computer's wake handler. The wake-up is lost (N-39). An old-style signal message (INTx) routed by ID is quietly dropped. The "work done" signal is lost (N-36).

How you can tell: A switch port's error bits (AER) show a wrongly built packet with a message header. Wake or signal features work when the SSD sits right on a computer port. They fail behind a switch. Messages show on the recorded wire but never have their effect at the computer.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Careful: use a spare drive or a test system. On real devices you can only watch. Use QEMU or a programmable chip (FPGA) to make such messages. Checker: for each message, look up its code. Check the routing field, the direction (by sender name), the format (Msg versus MsgD) and the length. Pair with wrongly-built-packet errors on other ports. Use lspci -vvv on the switch and the computer's chip.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Yes. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself (Reported). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Blame the sender, shown by the direction column. The SSD is at fault for upward breaks. Its chip design may use a computer-port message table, or build messages by hand. The computer's port or a switch port is at fault for downward breaks. · Test that confirms it: the receiver's logs.

N-58 Risky management command sent while reads and writes are still running Seen in the packets Rules for what a command holds

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 755923: a Format NVM command is fetched while read and write commands are still open.

Packet=755923 | Link Dir=Downstream | TLP Type=CplD | PSN=3630 | Tag=203 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | CompleterID=000:02:4 | Cpl Status=SC | Length=16 | Byte Cnt=64 | DATA=64 B | Time Stamp=0524.593784427370s | Time Delta=143.750 ns | LCRC=0x3120724A

Packet 755923: the command (SQE), with the fields this rule checks in its 64 bytes.

Packet=755923 | Link Dir=Downstream | TLP Type=CplD | PSN=3630 | Tag=203 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | CompleterID=000:02:4 | Cpl Status=SC | Length=16 | Byte Cnt=64 | DATA=64 B | Time Stamp=0524.593784427370s | Time Delta=143.750 ns | LCRC=0x3120724A

Packet 755925: the done note says success (SCT0/SC0x00).

Packet=755925 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=989 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000004:82E40140 | Length=4 | DATA=16 B | Time Stamp=0528.593784427370s | Time Delta=59.870 ns | LCRC=0x1684C9D5

Error family: P18 and P25, two of the 27 ways an error shows on the wire. P18 means rules about what goes inside a command. P25 means long management jobs, such as Format or firmware update. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes, by a rule about order or timing. For example: a missing answer, a long gap, or rows in the wrong order.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The NVMe rule book defines a log of supported commands and their effects. It is the Commands Supported and Effects log (LID 05h). Each entry has effect bits: CSUPP, LBCC, NCC, NIC, CCC, CSE and UUID selection. The rule book sets what the computer must do for commands with those effects. Check this in your version.

What goes wrong: The rule book says the computer must follow the effects log. Some commands have the effect "Namespace Inventory Change" or "Controller Capability Change". Some have a CSE limit. For these, the computer should pause reads and writes first. For some, it must read the ID data again afterwards. Several things break this rule. A user tool runs nvme format on a mounted drive. A fleet program commits firmware with activation during live work. A hypervisor manages storage areas under a running guest. The SSD's behaviour is then up to its maker. It may stop the commands, stall or, worst of all, mix them.

How you can tell: File system errors or damaged data show right after a management command. Reads and writes time out during a Format or Sanitize. A controller restarts in the middle of a firmware commit. Linux prints a message about a command with effects (nvme nvme0: ... effects debugging). That happens when a direct command starts a rescan.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Careful: use a spare drive or a test system. Use SPDK or nvme-cli on an unmounted scratch storage area. Run fio on another storage area of the same controller. Send Format NVM. In the recording, watch what happens to reads and writes on the other lists. Checker: look at each admin command whose opcode has NIC, NCC, CCC or CSE set in the caught effects log. Count the read and write commands open at that moment. Flag any count above zero. Read the log with nvme effects-log. On the computer, check which path the tool used. The kernel's direct-command path pauses work. A user-space driver may not.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Everything says success. Only a careful check finds it (Silent). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: The computer is at fault. Its tool or driver ignores the effects log. When the rule is broken, the SSD may stop the commands, stall or mix them. That is up to its maker. It only counts as an SSD defect if it returns old or mixed data (chapter D entries). · Test that confirms it: the effects log.

Chapter M: timing, missing-evidence and cross-step failures (101 entries)

Why this part is here: these 101 entries cross several levels of the rules. Some come from the test method or the recording itself.

M-001 SSD is slow to fetch a new command after the doorbell (SQ doorbell-to-SQE-fetch gap) Seen in the packets Command never finishes in time

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 1221047: the computer writes the doorbell for a command list (SQ tail doorbell).

Packet=1221047 | Link Dir=Downstream | TLP Type=MWr(32) | PSN=1417 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=000:00:0 | Address=FCE01008 | Length=1 | DATA=4 B | Time Stamp=1013.045318615120s | Time Delta=4.750 ns | LCRC=0x632A782E

Packet 1221051: the SSD fetches the command (SQE fetch) 4 ms after the doorbell.

Packet=1221051 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MRd(64) | PSN=1925 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000004:833000C0 | Length=16 | Time Stamp=1013.049318615120s | Time Delta=126.130 ns | LCRC=0x9703AB94

Error family: P02, one of the 27 ways an error shows on the wire. P02 means: a command was sent but never finished, so the computer gave up and recovered. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. A check on order and timing finds it. Examples: a missing answer, a long gap, or packets in the wrong order.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The rule book has no rule for this entry. Why it happens: The SSD's task planner is overloaded. Or the list or address mapping is wrong. Or the end marker (tail) was never really published. Or the SSD lost the list state, or its firmware stalled. Any of these can delay the fetch.

What goes wrong: The computer moves the end marker of a command list (SQ tail) forward. This says a new command (SQE) is waiting. But the SSD does not fetch the new command quickly.

How you can tell: The doorbell write (MMIO doorbell) arrives. Then there is an unusually long gap before the SSD reads the command from memory (DMA read). Match the list number (QID), the list start address (SQ base) and the end marker (tail).

How to fix it and prove the fix: Keep the capture tool's own file and its details. Make the error happen again in a controlled test. Change only one thing at a time. Compare with a run that is known to be good. Then compare the result with other proof. Use the driver's doorbell notes (tracepoints), the command list set-up and the SSD's own reports (controller telemetry). Also use a run with only one command open at a time. Write down the first thing that went wrong. Also write down the later signs of recovery. Do not name the cause only because two things happened close in time. First, collect the full setting. Note where the capture tool sat. Check that both directions were recorded. Note which command list (queue) and which part of the SSD (function) is involved. Note the time units. Note any mark that says the capture tool lost packets. Note the time window of the event. Then look for this error's own fingerprint. The doorbell write (MMIO doorbell) arrives. Then there is an unusually long gap before the SSD reads the command from memory (DMA read). Match the list number (QID), the list start address (SQ base) and the end marker (tail). Match packets by command list and command number (CID). Or match them by sender id and request number (Requester ID and Tag). Use whichever fits. Split the measured time into its steps. Compare each step with a written limit, or with a normal run of the same work. If the start event, the expected answer or the deadline cannot be found, say UNKNOWN (cannot tell), not FAIL.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Nothing reports it. A timer runs out because something expected never came (timer only). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Evidence that shows which side is at fault. The SSD is at fault if the doorbell number and its place are correct. The wire and its room to send (credits) must also allow a read request (MRd). The computer is at fault if the doorbell number or place is wrong, or it was never written. · Test that confirms it: a run with only one command open at a time (single-outstanding reproduction).

M-002 SSD's read of a command gets no answer (SQE read, no completion) Seen in the packets Answer never arrives (completion timeout)

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 1302206: the SSD asks to read a command from memory (SQE fetch, MRd). No answer with data (CplD) comes back.

Packet=1302206 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MRd(64) | PSN=3664 | Tag=128 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000004:83460380 | Length=16 | Time Stamp=1265.686408250000s | Time Delta=120.120 ns | LCRC=0x80BD6724

Packet 1302208: the time limit for the answer runs out. An error message is sent (Completion Timeout, ERR_NONFATAL).

Packet=1302208 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=Msg | PSN=3665 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Length=0 | Time Stamp=1265.736408250000s | Time Delta=121.120 ns | LCRC=0x9D26603C

Error family: P03, one of the 27 ways an error shows on the wire. P03 means: a read request got no answer in time. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. The checker marks an odd value or odd order in this table file. Here it is an answer that did not arrive in time (completion_timeout).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The rule book has no rule for this entry. Why it happens: The answering side or the root complex may have a fault. Or there is a routing error or a memory guard (IOMMU) problem. Or a wire recovery, or a lost or badly built packet. Any of these can break the memory transfer (DMA).

What goes wrong: The SSD sends a read request to fetch command data. This kind of request must get an answer (non-posted Memory Read). No full, matching answer (completion) comes back.

How you can tell: Match the sender id, the request number (Tag), the address and the byte count. Include answers that come in several pieces (split completions). Record both directions.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Keep the capture tool's own file and its details. Make the error happen again in a controlled test. Change only one thing at a time. Compare with a run that is known to be good. Then compare the result with other proof. Use the error logs of the computer's port where the wire starts (root-port AER, completion timeout). Also use faults from the memory guard (IOMMU faults) and the platform's error reports (RAS). Make a full new recording with no filter. Write down the first thing that went wrong. Also write down the later signs of recovery. Do not name the cause only because two things happened close in time. First, collect the full setting. Note where the capture tool sat. Check that both directions were recorded. Note which command list (queue) and which part of the SSD (function) is involved. Note the time units. Note any mark that says the capture tool lost packets. Note the time window of the event. Then look for this error's own fingerprint. Match the sender id, the request number (Tag), the address and the byte count. Include answers that come in several pieces (split completions). Record both directions. Match packets by command list and command number (CID). Or match them by sender id and request number (Requester ID and Tag). Use whichever fits. Split the measured time into its steps. Compare each step with a written limit, or with a normal run of the same work. If the start event, the expected answer or the deadline cannot be found, say UNKNOWN (cannot tell), not FAIL.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Yes. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself (reported). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Evidence that shows which side is at fault. The computer's side (the root complex or the memory guard, IOMMU) can be at fault. That is when the command read reached it and got no answer (CplD), and the wire is clean. The wire is at fault when packets were sent again or the wire restarted (Recovery) at the same time. The capture set-up is at fault when only one direction was recorded. · Test that confirms it: the error log entry for the answer time limit (AER completion-timeout log).

M-003 SSD fetches a command but never works on it Partly seen in the packets Command never finishes in time

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 1223866: the SSD fetches the command (SQE fetched).

Packet=1223866 | Link Dir=Downstream | TLP Type=CplD | PSN=1873 | Tag=225 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | CompleterID=000:02:4 | Cpl Status=SC | Length=16 | Byte Cnt=64 | DATA=64 B | Time Stamp=1013.419825075120s | Time Delta=132.750 ns | LCRC=0xAC13D992

Packet 1230857: the done note for the stuck command has result 0x007. This means the command was stopped on request (Command Abort Requested).

Packet=1230857 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=MWr(64) | PSN=1581 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Address=00000004:833302E0 | Length=4 | DATA=16 B | Time Stamp=1043.419993280120s | Time Delta=0.000 ns | LCRC=0x783FD54B

Packet 1230855: after a 30 s wait, the computer sends a stop command (Abort, opcode 08h). It goes on the management command list (admin SQ0).

Packet=1230855 | Link Dir=Downstream | TLP Type=CplD | PSN=2824 | Tag=173 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | CompleterID=000:02:4 | Cpl Status=SC | Length=16 | Byte Cnt=64 | DATA=64 B | Time Stamp=1043.419875061120s | Time Delta=137.750 ns | LCRC=0xDE192E64

Error family: P02, one of the 27 ways an error shows on the wire. P02 means: a command was sent but never finished, so the computer gave up and recovered. Proof from outside the recording: E01 means the Linux kernel log (dmesg). E03 means the SSD's own logs and settings (nvme-cli). · Can the packets alone prove it? Only if the bytes inside the packets are read. The result number sits in the DATA column. The checker reads the file version that keeps those bytes. It marks a result number that is not 0 (nvme_status_nonzero).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The rule book has no rule for this entry. Why it happens: The SSD's firmware may be stuck waiting on itself (deadlock), or out of resources. Or its command reader stalled, or its list state is wrong. Then the command stays fetched but is never served.

What goes wrong: The SSD fetches a command (SQE). Then it does not move on. The next step for that kind of command never happens, and no done note (CQE) comes.

How you can tell: The timeline for each command number (CID) shows the fetch. After it there is no data, no management answer and no done note. The cause inside the SSD is not visible on the wire.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Keep the capture tool's own file and its details. Make the error happen again in a controlled test. Change only one thing at a time. Compare with a run that is known to be good. Then compare the result with other proof. Use the SSD's debug reports (telemetry) and repeated reads of its fatal-error flag (CSTS.CFS). Also use the NVMe logs and a good run of the same command type for comparison. Write down the first thing that went wrong. Also write down the later signs of recovery. Do not name the cause only because two things happened close in time. First, collect the full setting. Note where the capture tool sat. Check that both directions were recorded. Note which command list (queue) and which part of the SSD (function) is involved. Note the time units. Note any mark that says the capture tool lost packets. Note the time window of the event. Then look for this error's own fingerprint. The timeline for each command number (CID) shows the fetch. After it there is no data, no management answer and no done note. The cause inside the SSD is not visible on the wire. Match packets by command list and command number (CID). Or match them by sender id and request number (Requester ID and Tag). Use whichever fits. Split the measured time into its steps. Compare each step with a written limit, or with a normal run of the same work. If the start event, the expected answer or the deadline cannot be found, say UNKNOWN (cannot tell), not FAIL.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Nothing reports it. A timer runs out because something expected never came (timer only). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Evidence that shows which side is at fault. The program inside the SSD (firmware) is at fault when the command is valid. The computer is at fault when the command is wrong. But then the SSD should have refused it with an error result. In that case the SSD's own fault is the missing error result. · Test that confirms it: the SSD's own reports (controller telemetry) or its error-recovery log (OCP error-recovery log).

M-004 Done note arrives after the computer's deadline Partly seen in the packets Command never finishes in time

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 1233508: the SSD fetches the command (SQE fetched).

Packet=1233508 | Link Dir=Downstream | TLP Type=CplD | PSN=3465 | Tag=223 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | CompleterID=000:02:4 | Cpl Status=SC | Length=16 | Byte Cnt=64 | DATA=64 B | Time Stamp=1043.421610063250s | Time Delta=147.750 ns | LCRC=0x14686382

Packet 1240592: the done note (CQE) arrives after the computer's 30 s deadline. The computer has already sent a stop command (Abort).

Error family: P02, one of the 27 ways an error shows on the wire. P02 means: a command was sent but never finished, so the computer gave up and recovered. Proof from outside the recording: E01 means the Linux kernel log (dmesg). E03 means the SSD's own logs and settings (nvme-cli). · Can the packets alone prove it? Partly. The packets show the timing or the order. Proof needs evidence from outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The rule book has no rule for this entry. Why it happens: Several things may start recovery before software sees the success. These are the computer's deadline rules, a long service time in the SSD, task scheduling or a late signal (interrupt).

What goes wrong: The done note packet (CQE) does arrive. But it comes after the computer's timer ran out, or after the computer started recovery.

How you can tell: Line up the done-note time in the recording with the computer's timeout and restart times. The recording alone does not show when the computer's timer fired.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Keep the capture tool's own file and its details. Make the error happen again in a controlled test. Change only one thing at a time. Compare with a run that is known to be good. Then compare the result with other proof. Use the Linux kernel's block and NVMe notes (tracepoints) and clocks lined up so they never go backwards (monotonic clock). Also use the restart count and the SSD's logs. Write down the first thing that went wrong. Also write down the later signs of recovery. Do not name the cause only because two things happened close in time. First, collect the full setting. Note where the capture tool sat. Check that both directions were recorded. Note which command list (queue) and which part of the SSD (function) is involved. Note the time units. Note any mark that says the capture tool lost packets. Note the time window of the event. Then look for this error's own fingerprint. Line up the done-note time in the recording with the computer's timeout and restart times. The recording alone does not show when the computer's timer fired. Match packets by command list and command number (CID). Or match them by sender id and request number (Requester ID and Tag). Use whichever fits. Split the measured time into its steps. Compare each step with a written limit, or with a normal run of the same work. If the start event, the expected answer or the deadline cannot be found, say UNKNOWN (cannot tell), not FAIL.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Nothing reports it. A timer runs out because something expected never came (timer only). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Evidence that shows which side is at fault. The SSD is at fault if fetch to done note takes much longer than usual for that command type. The computer is at fault if the done note time is normal but its deadline is too short. · Test that confirms it: the kernel log's list of timeout steps (dmesg timeout ladder).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The rule book has no rule for this entry. Why it happens: The firmware may group done notes before sending them. Inside locks, order fences or a crowded done-note path can also delay the done note.

What goes wrong: The data seems to have finished moving. But the SSD writes the done note (CQE) only after a long gap.

How you can tell: Measure the time from the last data packet to the done-note write (CQE Memory Write). Measure it apart from the time from doorbell to done note.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Keep the capture tool's own file and its details. Make the error happen again in a controlled test. Change only one thing at a time. Compare with a run that is known to be good. Then compare the result with other proof. Use charts of command times (latency histograms), the SSD firmware's reports and the driver's done times. Write down the first thing that went wrong. Also write down the later signs of recovery. Do not name the cause only because two things happened close in time. First, collect the full setting. Note where the capture tool sat. Check that both directions were recorded. Note which command list (queue) and which part of the SSD (function) is involved. Note the time units. Note any mark that says the capture tool lost packets. Note the time window of the event. Then look for this error's own fingerprint. Measure the time from the last data packet to the done-note write (CQE Memory Write). Measure it apart from the time from doorbell to done note. Match packets by command list and command number (CID). Or match them by sender id and request number (Requester ID and Tag). Use whichever fits. Split the measured time into its steps. Compare each step with a written limit, or with a normal run of the same work. If the start event, the expected answer or the deadline cannot be found, say UNKNOWN (cannot tell), not FAIL.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Nothing reports it. Things still work, but slower or weaker than they should (degraded). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Evidence that shows which side is at fault. The SSD is at fault when the done list (CQ) has room. That means the computer's head doorbells are up to date. A head doorbell is the number the computer writes to say how far it has read the done list. The computer is at fault when the done list is full because its head doorbell is old. · Test that confirms it: the SSD's slow-command monitor (OCP latency monitor).

When the computer actually runs its signal handler is not visible in the recording. Match packets by command list and command number (CID). Compare each step with a written limit, or with a normal run of the same work. If the start event, the expected answer or the deadline cannot be found, say UNKNOWN (cannot tell), not FAIL.

It is also at fault if it still groups signals that are marked "do not group" (Coalescing Disable). · Test that confirms it: read the setting back (feature read).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The rule book has no rule for this entry. Why it happens: Possible causes: a wrong table entry or an old mapping. Or a race while the signal settings change, or a defect in signal re-routing (interrupt remapping).

What goes wrong: Commands keep finishing. But the signal for one number (vector) is blocked (masked), left waiting (pending) or sent to the wrong place.

How you can tell: The recording may show a done note without the expected signal (MSI-X). Or it may show the signal packet. The blocking flags, the waiting-signal table (PBA) and delivery inside the computer need setting reads or system evidence.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Keep the capture tool's own file and its details. Make the error happen again in a controlled test. Change only one thing at a time. Compare with a run that is known to be good. Then compare the result with other proof. Use the signal table and the waiting-signal table (MSI-X table, PBA) and the kernel's signal counters (IRQ counters). Also use signal re-routing logs and the driver's signal set-up. Write down the first thing that went wrong. Also write down the later signs of recovery. Do not name the cause only because two things happened close in time.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Yes. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself (reported). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Evidence that shows which side is at fault. The SSD is at fault if it sends the signal while it is blocked. It is also at fault if it loses a waiting signal when unblocked. The computer is at fault if it leaves the signal blocked, or blocks the wrong entry. The platform is at fault when signal re-routing (remapping) fails and the wire is clean. · Test that confirms it: look at the table of waiting signals (PBA inspection).

Compare each step with a written limit, or with a normal run of the same work. If the start event, the expected answer or the deadline cannot be found, say UNKNOWN (cannot tell), not FAIL.

Things still work, but slower or weaker than they should (degraded). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Evidence that shows which side is at fault. The test set-up or the test method. This is not a defect in the SSD or the computer. · Test that confirms it: the computer's queuing times (host enqueue times).

M-014 Doorbell is late, or not seen where the capture tool sits Partly seen in the packets Doorbell written wrong or late

Packets seen in the test recording

Error family: P14, one of the 27 ways an error shows on the wire. P14 means: doorbell mistakes. Proof from outside the recording: E08 means a second capture tool, switch counters, or logs from other parts. · Can the packets alone prove it? Partly. The packets show the timing or the order. Proof needs evidence from outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The rule book has no rule for this entry. Why it happens: Several things can explain why it is missing. Examples: queuing in the computer, a bridge holding back writes, or a wrong address area or offset (BAR). Others are a crowded bridge, or where the capture tool sits.

What goes wrong: The expected doorbell write (MMIO doorbell) is late or goes to the wrong place. Or it is not visible where the capture tool sits.

How you can tell: Only the doorbell's arrival on the wire is visible. Writes that need no answer (posted Memory Writes) get no normal answer packet.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Keep the capture tool's own file and its details. Make the error happen again in a controlled test. Change only one thing at a time. Compare with a run that is known to be good. Then compare the result with other proof. Use the software doorbell notes (tracepoint) and the map of the address area and settings (BAR/register map). Also use root-port counters and where the capture tool sat (probe topology). Write down the first thing that went wrong. Also write down the later signs of recovery. Do not name the cause only because two things happened close in time.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Nothing reports it. A timer runs out because something expected never came (timer only). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Evidence that shows which side is at fault. The platform is at fault (a bridge holding back writes) in one case. The doorbell is seen on time nearer the computer, but late nearer the SSD. The computer's driver is at fault if the address is wrong. The computer is at fault if the doorbell is missing everywhere. · Test that confirms it: the computer's doorbell trace (host doorbell trace).

Error family: P02, one of the 27 ways an error shows on the wire. P02 means: a command was sent but never finished, so the computer gave up and recovered. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. A check on order and timing finds it. Examples: a missing answer, a long gap, or packets in the wrong order.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The rule book has no rule for this entry. Why it happens: After the fetch, something inside the SSD takes the time. Examples: repeat reads of flash (NAND retry), clean-up work (garbage collection) and error correction (ECC). Others are a firmware lock, heat or power state, or resource scheduling.

What goes wrong: The SSD fetches the command on time. But moving the data, or finishing the work, starts much later.

How you can tell: The time from doorbell to fetch is short. But the time from fetch to the first data, or from data to the done note, is long.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Keep the capture tool's own file and its details. Make the error happen again in a controlled test. Change only one thing at a time. Compare with a run that is known to be good. Then compare the result with other proof. Use the health log and reports (SMART, telemetry) and temperature and power readings. Also use a mark for each work phase and a profile of the same command type. Write down the first thing that went wrong. Also write down the later signs of recovery. Do not name the cause only because two things happened close in time.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Nothing reports it. Things still work, but slower or weaker than they should (degraded). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Evidence that shows which side is at fault. Something inside the SSD is at fault when the fetch is quick and the computer and the wire are idle. Examples given are repeat reads of the flash memory (NAND retry), clean-up work (GC) and heat. The platform is at fault when room to send (credits) or the wire state blocks the data step. · Test that confirms it: a snapshot of the SSD's health log and temperature (SMART).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The rule book has no rule for this entry. Why it happens: Several things can stop the pieces being put back together. The answering side is crowded, the wire is recovering, or a piece is lost. Or there is a bug in counting bytes or request numbers.

What goes wrong: A read request gets one or more answer pieces (completions). But the full set of requested bytes never arrives in time.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Keep the capture tool's own file and its details. Make the error happen again in a controlled test. Change only one thing at a time. Do not name the cause only because two things happened close in time. First, collect the full setting. Note where the capture tool sat. Check that both directions were recorded. Note which command list (queue) and which part of the SSD (function) is involved. Note the time units. Note any mark that says the capture tool lost packets. Note the time window of the event. Compare each step with a written limit, or with a normal run of the same work. If the start event, the expected answer or the deadline cannot be found, say UNKNOWN (cannot tell), not FAIL.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Nothing reports it. A timer runs out because something expected never came (timer only). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Evidence that shows which side is at fault. The platform is at fault if the stuck answer pieces are sent by the computer's root complex (Downstream). The SSD is at fault if they are sent by the SSD as the answering side (Upstream). The wire is at fault if a wire restart (Recovery) or a send-again happens at the same time. · Test that confirms it: the error log entry for the answer time limit (AER completion-timeout log).

What the rule book says should happen: The rule book has no rule for this entry. Why it happens: Some things make the gap longer. Examples: buffering in a bridge, crowding in a traffic class, or order and fence rules.

Note where the capture tool sat. Check that both directions were recorded. Note which command list (queue) and which part of the SSD (function) is involved. Note the time units. Note any mark that says the capture tool lost packets. Note the time window of the event. Then look for this error's own fingerprint. A burst of writes comes before a later request that needs an answer (non-posted). Arrival on the wire does not prove the data is stored inside. Match packets by command list and command number (CID). Or match them by sender id and request number (Requester ID and Tag). Use whichever fits. Split the measured time into its steps. Compare each step with a written limit, or with a normal run of the same work. If the start event, the expected answer or the deadline cannot be found, say UNKNOWN (cannot tell), not FAIL.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Nothing reports it. Things still work, but slower or weaker than they should (degraded). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Evidence that shows which side is at fault. The computer's platform is at fault when packets are valid and in order. Its fault is buffering in the root complex or a bridge. The SSD must also have sent its read quickly. The SSD is at fault if it is slow to send its own read. · Test that confirms it: a test with the "relaxed order" flag on and then off (A/B with RO).

Then look for this error's own fingerprint. Long times from request to answer line up with something else. That is other traffic, low room to send (credit pressure), or one traffic class. What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The rule book has no rule for this entry. Why it happens: Several things limit the data speed. Examples: heavy use, late room updates, how buffers are given out, or how the receiver is built.

What goes wrong: The sender keeps waiting for a room update (UpdateFC). This is because it has used up all its room to send (credits).

How you can tell: The room count shows no usable room. Then a late room update comes, and the packets start again.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Keep the capture tool's own file and its details. Make the error happen again in a controlled test. Change only one thing at a time. Compare with a run that is known to be good. Then compare the result with other proof. Use the capture tool's decoding of room counts (credit decode) and the SSD and switch counters. Also run tests with a controlled amount of traffic. Write down the first thing that went wrong. Also write down the later signs of recovery. Do not name the cause only because two things happened close in time. First, collect the full setting. Note where the capture tool sat. Check that both directions were recorded. Note which command list (queue) and which part of the SSD (function) is involved. Note the time units. Note any mark that says the capture tool lost packets. Note the time window of the event. Then look for this error's own fingerprint. The room count shows no usable room. Then a late room update comes, and the packets start again. Match packets by command list and command number (CID). Or match them by sender id and request number (Requester ID and Tag). Use whichever fits. Split the measured time into its steps. Compare each step with a written limit, or with a normal run of the same work. If the start event, the expected answer or the deadline cannot be found, say UNKNOWN (cannot tell), not FAIL.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Nothing reports it. Things still work, but slower or weaker than they should (degraded). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Evidence that shows which side is at fault. The side whose room updates are late is at fault. Say the late update is sent by the computer (Downstream). Then the receiver in the root port or platform is at fault. If it is sent by the SSD (Upstream), the SSD's receiver is at fault. · Test that confirms it: a speed and wait-time workload (throughput / latency workload).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The rule book has no rule for this entry. Why it happens: Several things can cause retries. Examples: signal loss in the channel, a tuning setting (preset) that does not match, or signal-booster settings. Others are a lane problem or the training firmware. What goes wrong: The wire repeats its training or signal-tuning steps (equalization) before it reaches its normal state (L0). Or it settles at a lower speed or width.

How you can tell: Look for this sign. Repeated training signals (TS) and tuning activity, recovery loops, or a wire status (LnkSta) below what the parts can do.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Keep the capture tool's own file and its details. Make the error happen again in a controlled test. Change only one thing at a time. Note which command list (queue) and which part of the SSD (function) is involved. Note the time units. Note any mark that says the capture tool lost packets. Note the time window of the event. Then look for this error's own fingerprint. Repeated training signals (TS) and tuning activity, recovery loops, or a wire status (LnkSta) below what the parts can do. Match packets by command list and command number (CID). Or match them by sender id and request number (Requester ID and Tag). Use whichever fits. Split the measured time into its steps. Compare each step with a written limit, or with a normal run of the same work. If the start event, the expected answer or the deadline cannot be found, say UNKNOWN (cannot tell), not FAIL.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Nothing reports it. A timer runs out because something expected never came (timer only). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Evidence that shows which side is at fault. The channel or signal booster is at fault when both ends offer the same abilities and the retries go on. Otherwise the fault is with one end. It rejects valid tuning settings (presets), or sends training signals whose fields do not agree. · Test that confirms it: compare with the same set-up of parts when it works (same-topology baseline).

M-024 Clock signal comes back late and slows wake-up (CLKREQ / reference clock) Partly seen in the packets Wire goes down, power, restart

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 1380037: the SSD starts to wake 400 us after it asks for the clock (CLKREQ#). The clock signal (refclk) was late.

Packet=1380037 | Link Dir=Upstream | Link Event=Electrical Idle Exit | Time Stamp=1328.467420810000s | Time Delta=0.000 ns

Error family: P12 and P20, two of the 27 ways an error shows on the wire. P12 means: the wire went down while packets were still on their way. P20 means: power-saving steps and wake-up time messages (LTR). Proof from outside the recording: E07 means measurements of the power lines and side signal lines (oscilloscope). · Can the packets alone prove it? Partly. The packets show the timing or the order. Proof needs evidence from outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The rule book has no rule for this entry. Why it happens: Clock switching off (clock gating) or clock-request wiring or polarity (CLKREQ) may delay the wire's wake-up. So may the platform's power-up order or a firmware race.

What goes wrong: The SSD does not answer quickly after leaving a power-saving state. This is because the clock, the clock request or the power steps start again late.

How you can tell: The recording may show the wire leaving idle, then traffic that comes late. It cannot prove the clock's quality or the order of signals on the pins.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Compare the slowest answer times at two power-saving settings (pcie_aspm.policy). Use "performance" and then "powersupersave". Safe to run. Run lspci -vvv and read these lines. LnkCap: "ASPM L0s L1, Exit Latency L0s <1us, L1 <8us". DevCap: "Latency L0s <64ns, L1 <1us". LnkCtl: "ASPM L1 Enabled". Compare them with /sys/module/pcie_aspm/parameters/policy. Measure the answer times with the fio tool. Do it with the wire's power saving (ASPM) on, and then off (pcie_aspm=off).

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Nothing reports it. A timer runs out because something expected never came (timer only). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Evidence that shows which side is at fault. The platform is at fault if the SSD asks for the clock (CLKREQ#) but gets it back late (REFCLK). The SSD is at fault if it is slow to ask for the clock. It is also at fault if it is slow to wake while the clock is good. Telling these apart needs an oscilloscope. · Test that confirms it: Risky, test machine only: line up oscilloscope readings with the recording (scope correlation).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The rule book has no rule for this entry. Why it happens: Several things may make the wake take too long. Examples: the wait-time or power-saving settings (LTR/ASPM), or bringing the clock back. Others are a platform power delay or the SSD's firmware.

What goes wrong: The SSD leaves a deep power-saving state (L1.1 or L1.2). The first packet after that arrives later than the platform allows.

How you can tell: A gap in the packets around the wake may be visible. The software's scheduling after the wire is back (L0) can add to the total.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Keep the capture tool's own file and its details. Make the error happen again in a controlled test. Change only one thing at a time. Compare with a run that is known to be good. Then compare the result with other proof. Use a dump of the power settings and the wait-time settings (LTR). Also use electrical measurements and a trace of the computer's task scheduling. Write down the first thing that went wrong. Also write down the later signs of recovery. Do not name the cause only because two things happened close in time. First, collect the full setting. Note where the capture tool sat. Check that both directions were recorded. Note which command list (queue) and which part of the SSD (function) is involved. Note the time units. Note any mark that says the capture tool lost packets. Note the time window of the event. Then look for this error's own fingerprint. A gap in the packets around the wake may be visible. The software's scheduling after the wire is back (L0) can add to the total. Match packets by command list and command number (CID). Or match them by sender id and request number (Requester ID and Tag). Use whichever fits. Split the measured time into its steps. Compare each step with a written limit, or with a normal run of the same work. If the start event, the expected answer or the deadline cannot be found, say UNKNOWN (cannot tell), not FAIL.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Nothing reports it. Things still work, but slower or weaker than they should (degraded). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Evidence that shows which side is at fault. The SSD is at fault if its signal part (PHY) is slower than its own promised wake time. Then its training signal (Upstream TS1) is late. It is also at fault if its wait-time message (LTR) asks for less time than its wake really needs. The platform is at fault if bringing the clock back (CLKREQ# to clock) or the computer-side port is slow. It is also at fault if the power-saving or wait-time rules (ASPM/LTR policy) are too aggressive. · Test that confirms it: turn off the deepest power-saving state (disable L1.2).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The rule book has no rule for this entry. Why it happens: The power handler (runtime-PM callback), restarting the SSD and making the lists again add delay. So do scanning storage areas and the device manager.

What goes wrong: The SSD can be reached on the wire again. But programs see it as ready only later. They wait for the driver, the command lists and the storage areas (namespaces) to be set up.

How you can tell: The recording shows the wire traffic starting again. It does not show the power handler's start and end, or the storage area being registered.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Keep the capture tool's own file and its details. Make the error happen again in a controlled test. Change only one thing at a time. Compare with a run that is known to be good. Then compare the result with other proof. Use the power notes (runtime-PM tracepoints), kernel logs, driver times and a timeline of each wake step. Write down the first thing that went wrong. Also write down the later signs of recovery. Do not name the cause only because two things happened close in time. First, collect the full setting. Note where the capture tool sat. Check that both directions were recorded. Note which command list (queue) and which part of the SSD (function) is involved. Note the time units. Note any mark that says the capture tool lost packets. Note the time window of the event. Then look for this error's own fingerprint. The recording shows the wire traffic starting again. It does not show the power handler's start and end, or the storage area being registered. Match packets by command list and command number (CID). Or match them by sender id and request number (Requester ID and Tag). Use whichever fits. Split the measured time into its steps. Compare each step with a written limit, or with a normal run of the same work. If the start event, the expected answer or the deadline cannot be found, say UNKNOWN (cannot tell), not FAIL.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Nothing reports it. Things still work, but slower or weaker than they should (degraded). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Evidence that shows which side is at fault. The computer's software is at fault when its own steps take most of the time. Examples: the order of power handlers, or the driver setting up again. The SSD is at fault if its own steps take most of the time. These are switch-on to ready (D1: CC.EN to RDY) and its management command times. See error types T-06 and T-02 in the error list. · Test that confirms it: time the power handlers (PM callback timing).

What the rule book says should happen: The rule book has no rule for this entry. Why it happens: An overloaded work queue, a processor with no free time or tasks waiting on locks delay recovery. So do many signals (IRQ pressure) or a stall of the whole computer. This has nothing to do with the SSD.

What goes wrong: The computer finds a fault. But it starts the restart or recovery work late, because of task scheduling on its processor (CPU, workqueue).

How you can tell: The recording alone cannot prove it or rule it out. The recording shows silence until recovery traffic starts. It cannot show when the work was queued or scheduled.

Also use a trace of the task scheduler and work queue, and numbers on how busy the processor was. Write down the first thing that went wrong. Also write down the later signs of recovery. Note which command list (queue) and which part of the SSD (function) is involved. Note the time units. Note any mark that says the capture tool lost packets. Note the time window of the event. Then look for this error's own fingerprint. The recording shows silence until recovery traffic starts. It cannot show when the work was queued or scheduled. Match packets by command list and command number (CID). Or match them by sender id and request number (Requester ID and Tag). Use whichever fits. Split the measured time into its steps. Compare each step with a written limit, or with a normal run of the same work. If the start event, the expected answer or the deadline cannot be found, say UNKNOWN (cannot tell), not FAIL.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Nothing reports it. A timer runs out because something expected never came (timer only). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Evidence that shows which side is at fault. The computer's software is at fault when the SSD is idle during the silence. What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The rule book has no rule for this entry. Why it happens: Many layers have their own timers. They are the program, the block layer, the NVMe command, the PCIe answer (Completion Timeout) and multi-path. These timers cover different things and have different default values.

What goes wrong: One layer gives up on the work before another layer's recovery or answer deadline has run out.

How you can tell: A done note (CQE) can arrive after the computer has restarted. The recording does not give every deadline that was set.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Keep the capture tool's own file and its details. Make the error happen again in a controlled test. Change only one thing at a time. Compare with a run that is known to be good. Then compare the result with other proof. Use the driver settings with their version, the SSD's time-limit settings (CAP, CRTO) and the platform's time-limit settings. Add a timeline of all deadlines. Write down the first thing that went wrong. Also write down the later signs of recovery. Do not name the cause only because two things happened close in time. First, collect the full setting. Note where the capture tool sat. Check that both directions were recorded. Note which command list (queue) and which part of the SSD (function) is involved. Note the time units. Note any mark that says the capture tool lost packets. Note the time window of the event. Then look for this error's own fingerprint. A done note (CQE) can arrive after the computer has restarted. The recording does not give every deadline that was set. Match packets by command list and command number (CID). Or match them by sender id and request number (Requester ID and Tag). Use whichever fits. Split the measured time into its steps. Compare each step with a written limit, or with a normal run of the same work. If the start event, the expected answer or the deadline cannot be found, say UNKNOWN (cannot tell), not FAIL.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Nothing reports it. A timer runs out because something expected never came (timer only). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Evidence that shows which side is at fault. The computer's software (how its time limits fit together) is at fault in one case. The SSD answers in its normal time, but after the computer gave up. · Test that confirms it: check the timer settings (timer configuration).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The rule book has no rule for this entry. Why it happens: A fault in the wire or SSD does not go away. Together with eager retry and recovery rules, it creates follow-on signs.

What goes wrong: Retries, restarts and rebuilding of command lists repeat many times. They hide what started it, and they add load.

How you can tell: The recording shows repeated SSD set-up, wire training (LTSSM) or command-list rebuild cycles. The operating system error that started it is outside the recording.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Keep the capture tool's own file and its details. Make the error happen again in a controlled test. Change only one thing at a time. Compare with a run that is known to be good. Then compare the result with other proof. Use the kernel recovery logs, restart counts and the error and containment state (AER/DPC). Also keep the recording from before the restart. Write down the first thing that went wrong. Also write down the later signs of recovery. Do not name the cause only because two things happened close in time. First, collect the full setting. Note where the capture tool sat. Check that both directions were recorded. Note which command list (queue) and which part of the SSD (function) is involved. Note the time units. Note any mark that says the capture tool lost packets. Note the time window of the event. Then look for this error's own fingerprint. The recording shows repeated SSD set-up, wire training (LTSSM) or command-list rebuild cycles. The operating system error that started it is outside the recording. Match packets by command list and command number (CID). Or match them by sender id and request number (Requester ID and Tag). Use whichever fits. Split the measured time into its steps. Compare each step with a written limit, or with a normal run of the same work. If the start event, the expected answer or the deadline cannot be found, say UNKNOWN (cannot tell), not FAIL.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Nothing reports it. Everything looks like success (silent). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Evidence that shows which side is at fault. The SSD is at fault if the first odd event is an SSD error. That is an error done note, the fatal flag (CFS) or an ERR_* message from the SSD. The wire is at fault if the first event is a wire problem. That is a broken check number, a "send again" receipt or a wire recovery (LCRC, Nak, Recovery). The computer's retry rules are at fault if none of these come before the first restart. · Test that confirms it: the kernel log (outside proof E01).

What the rule book says should happen: The rule book has no rule for this entry. Why it happens: Other reads and writes running at the same time are affected. Causes: shared storage resources, firmware that does one thing at a time, or the scheduler's design.

What goes wrong: A self-check operation is running. Other, unrelated requests become very slow or run out of time.

How you can tell: Bursts of slow answers line up with the self-test. How the SSD shares its inside resources is hidden.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Keep the capture tool's own file and its details. Make the error happen again in a controlled test. Change only one thing at a time. Compare with a run that is known to be good. Then compare the result with other proof. Compare the work before, during and after the test. Use the self-test log, firmware reports and exactly what the operation is meant to do. Write down the first thing that went wrong. Also write down the later signs of recovery. Do not name the cause only because two things happened close in time. First, collect the full setting. Note where the capture tool sat. Check that both directions were recorded. Note which command list (queue) and which part of the SSD (function) is involved. Note the time units. Note any mark that says the capture tool lost packets. Note the time window of the event. Then look for this error's own fingerprint. Bursts of slow answers line up with the self-test. How the SSD shares its inside resources is hidden. Match packets by command list and command number (CID). Or match them by sender id and request number (Requester ID and Tag). Use whichever fits. Split the measured time into its steps. Compare each step with a written limit, or with a normal run of the same work. If the start event, the expected answer or the deadline cannot be found, say UNKNOWN (cannot tell), not FAIL.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Nothing reports it. Things still work, but slower or weaker than they should (degraded). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Evidence that shows which side is at fault. The SSD is at fault (how it shares its resources during the self-check). The computer is at fault only for starting a self-test under real working load. · Test that confirms it: a test with and without the self-test (self-test A/B).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The rule book has no rule for this entry. Why it happens: Several things delay sending. Examples: a processor with no free time, paused work queues or timer rules. Others are sleep and wake, or a crowded management list.

What goes wrong: The computer sends its regular "I am still here" command (Keep Alive) later than planned. It comes close to, or past, the SSD's set time limit for it (KATO).

How you can tell: The recording gives the times between packets on the wire. It does not show when the computer's timer was meant to fire.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Keep the capture tool's own file and its details. Make the error happen again in a controlled test. Change only one thing at a time. Compare with a run that is known to be good. Then compare the result with other proof. Use the KATO setting and a trace of the timer and work queue. Also use the computer's sleep state and the delay on the management list. Write down the first thing that went wrong. Also write down the later signs of recovery. Do not name the cause only because two things happened close in time. First, collect the full setting. Note where the capture tool sat. Check that both directions were recorded. Note which command list (queue) and which part of the SSD (function) is involved. Note the time units. Note any mark that says the capture tool lost packets. Note the time window of the event. Then look for this error's own fingerprint. The recording gives the times between packets on the wire. It does not show when the computer's timer was meant to fire. Match packets by command list and command number (CID). Or match them by sender id and request number (Requester ID and Tag). Use whichever fits. Split the measured time into its steps. Compare each step with a written limit, or with a normal run of the same work. If the start event, the expected answer or the deadline cannot be found, say UNKNOWN (cannot tell), not FAIL.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Nothing reports it. A timer runs out because something expected never came (timer only). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Evidence that shows which side is at fault. The computer's software is at fault when the list is idle and the doorbell is late. Causes: the processor is too busy, the work queue is paused, sleep and wake, or the timer rules. The SSD is at fault if it runs out of time even though the gaps are inside KATO. That case is error type C-10 in the error list. · Test that confirms it: a trace of the timer and work queue (outside proof E05).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The rule book has no rule for this entry. Why it happens: Packets may break now and then. Causes: signal margin, temperature, the state of connectors or signal boosters, signal tuning or power quality.

What goes wrong: Fixable errors and send-agains rise sharply. The traffic still succeeds, but the slowest answers get slower.

How you can tell: Some events group together with very slow answers. They are errors of the kind the error reports count (AER-like), send-agains, "send again" receipts (replay, NAK) and signal events.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Keep the capture tool's own file and its details. Make the error happen again in a controlled test. Change only one thing at a time. Compare with a run that is known to be good. Then compare the result with other proof. Use changes in the counters, signal margin tests, and heat and voltage logs. Also do controlled swaps of slot, cable or signal booster (retimer). Write down the first thing that went wrong. Also write down the later signs of recovery. Do not name the cause only because two things happened close in time. First, collect the full setting. Note where the capture tool sat. Check that both directions were recorded. Note which command list (queue) and which part of the SSD (function) is involved. Note the time units. Note any mark that says the capture tool lost packets. Note the time window of the event. Then look for this error's own fingerprint. Some events group together with very slow answers. They are errors of the kind the error reports count (AER-like), send-agains, "send again" receipts (replay, NAK) and signal events. Match packets by command list and command number (CID). Or match them by sender id and request number (Requester ID and Tag). Use whichever fits. Split the measured time into its steps. Compare each step with a written limit, or with a normal run of the same work. If the start event, the expected answer or the deadline cannot be found, say UNKNOWN (cannot tell), not FAIL.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Nothing reports it. Things still work, but slower or weaker than they should (degraded). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Evidence that shows which side is at fault. The channel is at fault when the bursts appear in both directions and follow temperature or the connector. One end is at fault when they appear on one side only, after a settings change. · Test that confirms it: compare error counter snapshots taken before and after (AER counter snapshot diff, test T1).
