What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The rule book has no rule for this entry. Why it happens: The evidence can be wiped. Causes: settings that clear when 1 is written to them, automatic recovery, repeated events, or set-up at start-up.

What goes wrong: Software or a restart clears the status bits and header logs. This happens before anyone saves them for study.

How you can tell: The recording may keep an error message packet (ERR). It does not keep the setting values after recovery.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Keep the capture tool's own file and its details. Make the error happen again in a controlled test. Change only one thing at a time. Compare with a run that is known to be good. Then compare the result with other proof. Use a snapshot taken by the event before clearing, and the kernel error logs. Also use the error-report service (RAS daemon) and the restart count. Write down the first thing that went wrong. Also write down the later signs of recovery. Do not name the cause only because two things happened close in time. First, collect the full setting. Note where the capture tool sat. Check that both directions were recorded. Note which command list (queue) and which part of the SSD (function) is involved. Note the time units. Note any mark that says the capture tool lost packets. Note the time window of the event. Then look for this error's own fingerprint. The recording may keep an error message packet (ERR). It does not keep the setting values after recovery. Match packets by command list and command number (CID). Or match them by sender id and request number (Requester ID and Tag). Use whichever fits. Split the measured time into its steps. Compare each step with a written limit, or with a normal run of the same work. If the start event, the expected answer or the deadline cannot be found, say UNKNOWN (cannot tell), not FAIL.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Nothing reports it. Everything looks like success (silent). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Evidence that shows which side is at fault. The test set-up or the handling of evidence. The computer's system or firmware cleared the status before the snapshot. · Test that confirms it: record the values before they are cleared (pre-clear recording).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The rule book has no rule for this entry. Why it happens: How the answering side schedules work, request numbers and switch buffers make packets wait in line. So do room to send (credits) and competing traffic.

What goes wrong: With few open requests, the time to a full answer is fine. With many at once, a long tail of very slow answers appears.

How you can tell: For each read, measure from the request to the last answer piece. The time grows with the number of open requests.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Keep the capture tool's own file and its details. Make the error happen again in a controlled test. Change only one thing at a time. Compare with a run that is known to be good. Then compare the result with other proof. Use a test that steps up the number of open requests (depth sweep). Group by size and traffic class. Use switch counters and SSD reports. Write down the first thing that went wrong. Also write down the later signs of recovery. Do not name the cause only because two things happened close in time. First, collect the full setting. Note where the capture tool sat. Check that both directions were recorded. Note which command list (queue) and which part of the SSD (function) is involved. Note the time units. Note any mark that says the capture tool lost packets. Note the time window of the event. Then look for this error's own fingerprint. For each read, measure from the request to the last answer piece. The time grows with the number of open requests. Match packets by command list and command number (CID). Or match them by sender id and request number (Requester ID and Tag). Use whichever fits. Split the measured time into its steps. Compare each step with a written limit, or with a normal run of the same work. If the start event, the expected answer or the deadline cannot be found, say UNKNOWN (cannot tell), not FAIL.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Nothing reports it. Things still work, but slower or weaker than they should (degraded). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Evidence that shows which side is at fault. The SSD is at fault when it is the slow answerer. That means answers with data sent by the SSD (Upstream CplD), or from its own memory buffer (CMB). The platform is at fault when the root complex's answers to the SSD's reads slow down as the number grows. · Test that confirms it: a test that steps up the number of open requests (depth sweep).

Note the time units. Note any mark that says the capture tool lost packets. Note the time window of the event. Then look for this error's own fingerprint. Compare each step with a written limit, or with a normal run of the same work. If the start event, the expected answer or the deadline cannot be found, say UNKNOWN (cannot tell), not FAIL.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Nothing reports it. Everything looks like success (silent). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Evidence that shows which side is at fault. The test set-up or the measuring method, not the computer or the SSD. · Test that confirms it: NVMe notes or block traces from the computer (tracepoints / blktrace, outside proof E05).

Error family: P26, one of the 27 ways an error shows on the wire. P26 means: event notes from the SSD and its log pages. Proof from outside the recording: E03 means the SSD's own logs and settings (nvme-cli). · Can the packets alone prove it? Partly. The packets show the timing or the order. Proof needs evidence from outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The rule book has no rule for this entry. Why it happens: The count may start again. Causes: the counter size, a restart, a firmware defect or a change of clock source.

What goes wrong: The time the SSD reports jumps or starts over. The recording and the computer clocks keep going.

How you can tell: Time or log values jump backwards or repeat around a restart. The outside clocks keep going forward.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Keep the capture tool's own file and its details. Make the error happen again in a controlled test. Change only one thing at a time. Compare with a run that is known to be good. Then compare the result with other proof. Use the written counter size and meaning, restart events, SSD reports and repeated sync points. Write down the first thing that went wrong. Also write down the later signs of recovery. Do not name the cause only because two things happened close in time. First, collect the full setting. Note where the capture tool sat. Check that both directions were recorded. Note which command list (queue) and which part of the SSD (function) is involved. Note the time units. Note any mark that says the capture tool lost packets. Note the time window of the event. Then look for this error's own fingerprint. Time or log values jump backwards or repeat around a restart. The outside clocks keep going forward. Match packets by command list and command number (CID). Or match them by sender id and request number (Requester ID and Tag). Use whichever fits. Split the measured time into its steps. Compare each step with a written limit, or with a normal run of the same work. If the start event, the expected answer or the deadline cannot be found, say UNKNOWN (cannot tell), not FAIL.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Nothing reports it. Everything looks like success (silent). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Evidence that shows which side is at fault. The SSD's firmware is at fault when the jump has no restart. With a restart, a new clock start is expected and is not a defect. The computer is at fault if it never sets the clock again. · Test that confirms it: read the clock again and again over time (periodic read). Safe to run.

Error family: P20, one of the 27 ways an error shows on the wire. P20 means: power-saving steps and wake-up time messages (LTR). Proof from outside the recording: E01 means the Linux kernel log (dmesg). E02 means a copy of the SSD's settings area (lspci). E07 means measurements of the power lines and side signal lines (oscilloscope). · Can the packets alone prove it? Partly. The packets show the timing or the order. Proof needs evidence from outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The rule book has no rule for this entry. Why it happens: Three things may overlap in time. They are the SSD's automatic power states (NVMe APST) and the wire's power saving (PCIe ASPM, L1 substates). The third is the computer's power management.

What goes wrong: The first read or write after idle is slow. The cause may be the SSD leaving its own power state, or the wire leaving its power-saving state (PCIe L1). Or it may be the computer's task scheduling.

How you can tell: The idle and wake gap can be visible. The SSD's inside power state (APST) or the software's wake time may not be.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Keep the capture tool's own file and its details. Make the error happen again in a controlled test. Change only one thing at a time. Compare with a run that is known to be good. Then compare the result with other proof. Use the SSD's power states and their wake times, its automatic power-state rules (APST) and the wire power settings (LTR/ASPM). Also use a platform power trace and software times. Write down the first thing that went wrong. Also write down the later signs of recovery. Do not name the cause only because two things happened close in time. First, collect the full setting. Note where the capture tool sat. Check that both directions were recorded. Note which command list (queue) and which part of the SSD (function) is involved. Note the time units. Note any mark that says the capture tool lost packets. Note the time window of the event. Then look for this error's own fingerprint. The idle and wake gap can be visible. The SSD's inside power state (APST) or the software's wake time may not be. Match packets by command list and command number (CID). Or match them by sender id and request number (Requester ID and Tag). Use whichever fits. Split the measured time into its steps. Compare each step with a written limit, or with a normal run of the same work. If the start event, the expected answer or the deadline cannot be found, say UNKNOWN (cannot tell), not FAIL.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Nothing reports it. Things still work, but slower or weaker than they should (degraded). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Evidence that shows which side is at fault. The platform and the wire power saving (ASPM) are at fault if the wire wake time (link_us) is biggest. The SSD's power states (APST) are at fault if the fetch and service steps are the biggest part. They must take longer than the wake time it promised (EXLAT). The computer is at fault if neither: the time before the doorbell, taken from outside proof E05. · Test that confirms it: turn off the SSD's automatic power states (APST off).

M-055 Heating and cooling cause regular slow-answer spikes (thermal cycling) Partly seen in the packets Speed and timing numbers

The packets show the timing or the order. Proof needs evidence from outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The rule book has no rule for this entry. Why it happens: At temperature limits the SSD changes its clocks or its storage scheduling. Air flow and load can make it slow down and recover again and again.

What goes wrong: Answer times and data speed go up and down with the SSD's temperature. The packets still follow the rules.

How you can tell: Each command's service time changes in a regular rhythm. Decoding the packets alone does not show that heat is the cause.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Keep the capture tool's own file and its details. Make the error happen again in a controlled test. Change only one thing at a time. Compare with a run that is known to be good. Then compare the result with other proof. Use frequent health-log and heat samples (SMART), slow-down counters and air flow data. Also run a test with a controlled load. Write down the first thing that went wrong. Also write down the later signs of recovery. Do not name the cause only because two things happened close in time.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Nothing reports it. Things still work, but slower or weaker than they should (degraded). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Evidence that shows which side is at fault. The SSD's heat control. The platform is at fault if the cooling causes the cycling (air flow, fan control). The same is true for a heat limit set too low (HCTM). · Test that confirms it: the SSD's health-log temperature and heat counters during the run (SMART).

M-056 SSD clean-up work causes long write pauses (garbage collection, wear levelling) Partly seen in the packets Speed and timing numbers

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 1843917: 9 ms gaps in done notes while commands are open (clean-up or upkeep work, GC / maintenance).

Packet=1843917 | Link Dir=Upstream | DLLP Type=ACK | Time Stamp=1823.200473643000s | Time Delta=47.000 ns | AckNak Seq Num=2250

Error family: P22, one of the 27 ways an error shows on the wire. P22 means: speed and slow-answer numbers worked out from the recording. Proof from outside the recording: E09 means a lab test whose result is the proof. Examples: power cut, heat chamber, signal margin. · Can the packets alone prove it? Partly. The packets show the timing or the order. Proof needs evidence from outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The rule book has no rule for this entry. Why it happens: Some inside work affects the storage service. Examples: clean-up work (GC), moving data out of the fast cache (SLC folding) and saving the map. Others are spreading wear and a shortage of free blocks.

What goes wrong: Long write pauses appear after a long, steady load. There are no PCIe errors and no failed command results.

How you can tell: Long service steps line up with writes during pre-fill or a steady load. Flash memory work (NAND) is not in the recording.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Keep the capture tool's own file and its details. Make the error happen again in a controlled test. Change only one thing at a time. Compare with a run that is known to be good. Then compare the result with other proof. Use pre-filled work loads, health-log and wear reports and firmware logs. Also run a standard steady-load test. Write down the first thing that went wrong. Also write down the later signs of recovery. Do not name the cause only because two things happened close in time.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Nothing reports it. Things still work, but slower or weaker than they should (degraded). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Evidence that shows which side is at fault. The SSD. Its clean-up work (GC) and moving data out of its fast cache (SLC folding). Also saving its map and spreading wear evenly (wear levelling). The computer is at fault only in one case. Over a long recording, it never sends a "these blocks are free" command (DSM Deallocate). · Test that confirms it: a standard steady-load test (standardised steady state).

The checker marks an odd value or odd order in this table file. Here it is a read that asks for more than the 512-byte limit (read_exceeds_mrrs_512).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The rule book has no rule for this entry. Why it happens: Unfair delay may come from several things. Examples: lists served one at a time, crowded channels, firmware locks or the SSD's own rules.

What goes wrong: Long read, write or flush work delays other requests that share a list or an inside resource.

How you can tell: Look for this sign. Timelines for each command number show slow answers tied to a shared list, or to bursts of mixed command types. The SSD's inside scheduler stays hidden.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Keep the capture tool's own file and its details. Make the error happen again in a controlled test. Change only one thing at a time. Compare with a run that is known to be good. Then compare the result with other proof. Compare one list with many lists, and different mixes of read, write and flush. Use SSD reports and charts of answer times for each command type. Write down the first thing that went wrong. Also write down the later signs of recovery. Do not name the cause only because two things happened close in time. First, collect the full setting. Note where the capture tool sat. Check that both directions were recorded. Note which command list (queue) and which part of the SSD (function) is involved. Note the time units. Note any mark that says the capture tool lost packets. Note the time window of the event. Then look for this error's own fingerprint. Timelines for each command number show slow answers tied to a shared list, or to bursts of mixed command types. The SSD's inside scheduler stays hidden. Match packets by command list and command number (CID). Or match them by sender id and request number (Requester ID and Tag). Use whichever fits. Split the measured time into its steps. Compare each step with a written limit, or with a normal run of the same work. If the start event, the expected answer or the deadline cannot be found, say UNKNOWN (cannot tell), not FAIL.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Nothing reports it. Things still work, but slower or weaker than they should (degraded). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Evidence that shows which side is at fault. The computer is at fault if the small command waits on the same command list. It waits behind a long command the computer itself sent. The SSD is at fault if the small command was on another list. It is also at fault if it fetched the command quickly but held back its done note. · Test that confirms it: a test with the work on separate lists and then on one list (queue separation A/B).

Examples: power cut, heat chamber, signal margin. · Can the packets alone prove it? Partly. The packets show the timing or the order. Proof needs evidence from outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The rule book has no rule for this entry. Why it happens: Three things decide what a done note means for safe storage. They are the write-cache rules (volatile cache), support for "write through now" (FUA) and the order of commands.

What goes wrong: A finished write is treated as safely stored. Or the timing of a "save everything now" command (Flush) is measured wrongly. It leaves out the earlier writes it is meant to make safe.

How you can tell: The recording can show the order of Write, Flush and FUA, and the done note. It cannot show real storage in flash, or power-loss protection.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Keep the capture tool's own file and its details. Make the error happen again in a controlled test. Change only one thing at a time. Compare with a run that is known to be good. Then compare the result with other proof. Use the write-cache setting and abilities (VWC) and evidence of power-loss protection (PLP). Also run a controlled test: write, Flush, cut the power, then read back. Write down the first thing that went wrong. Also write down the later signs of recovery. Do not name the cause only because two things happened close in time.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Nothing reports it. Everything looks like success (silent). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Evidence that shows which side is at fault. The test set-up or the measuring method. · Test that confirms it: a controlled test: write, Flush, cut the power, then read back (outside proof E09).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The rule book has no rule for this entry. Why it happens: Those network methods carry NVMe commands over a network. What goes wrong: Someone expects a local PCIe capture tool to decode a command timeout. But the SSD is reached over a network (NVMe/TCP or NVMe/RDMA).

How to fix it and prove the fix: Keep the capture tool's own file and its details. Make the error happen again in a controlled test. Change only one thing at a time. Compare with a run that is known to be good. Then compare the result with other proof. Confirm how the SSD is reached. Use a network recording and the network storage logs (fabrics logs). Use the PCIe recording only for the network card's memory traffic and PCIe errors. Write down the first thing that went wrong. Also write down the later signs of recovery. Do not name the cause only because two things happened close in time. First, collect the full setting. Note where the capture tool sat. Check that both directions were recorded. Note which command list (queue) and which part of the SSD (function) is involved. Note the time units. Note any mark that says the capture tool lost packets. Note the time window of the event. Then look for this error's own fingerprint. The PCIe recording may show the network card's memory traffic (NIC DMA). It does not show the request and reply times at the network side. Match packets by command list and command number (CID). Or match them by sender id and request number (Requester ID and Tag). Use whichever fits. Split the measured time into its steps. Compare each step with a written limit, or with a normal run of the same work. If the start event, the expected answer or the deadline cannot be found, say UNKNOWN (cannot tell), not FAIL.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Nothing reports it. Everything looks like success (silent). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Evidence that shows which side is at fault. The test set-up (the capture tool is in the wrong place). · Test that confirms it: a network recording (outside proof E10).

M-060 Missing settings mean a time-limit check cannot be judged Partly seen in the packets Problems with the recording itself

Packets seen in the test recording

Error family: P27, one of the 27 ways an error shows on the wire. P27 means: signs that the recording itself is incomplete, so a check must not say FAIL. Proof from outside the recording: E02 means a copy of the SSD's settings area (lspci). E03 means the SSD's own logs and settings (nvme-cli). · Can the packets alone prove it? Partly. The packets show the timing or the order. Proof needs evidence from outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The rule book has no rule for this entry. Why it happens: The rules differ by rule-book version, optional feature, wire generation and set mode. The export may also leave out the state.

What goes wrong: A check applies a time limit without knowing enough. It lacks the SSD's abilities, its active settings, the wire's speed generation, the command type or the rule-book version.

How you can tell: The time can be measured. But the time stamps alone cannot tell the legal limit, or whether it applies.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Keep the capture tool's own file and its details. Make the error happen again in a controlled test. Change only one thing at a time. Compare with a run that is known to be good. Then compare the result with other proof. Attach a timed snapshot of the settings and abilities, and the official rule with its version. Otherwise give UNKNOWN, not pass or fail. Write down the first thing that went wrong. Also write down the later signs of recovery. Do not name the cause only because two things happened close in time.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Nothing reports it. Everything looks like success (silent). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Evidence that shows which side is at fault. The test set-up (missing setting information). · Test that confirms it: a snapshot of the settings (outside proof E02 and E03).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The rule book has no rule for this entry. Why it happens: An old list start address after a restart, or a bug reading the address lists (PRP/SGL). Or a problem with how long a memory mapping lasts, or a memory guard (IOMMU) setting problem.

What goes wrong: The SSD uses a memory address that does not fit. It matches none of the lists and address lists set up (SQ, CQ, PRP, SGL). It may reach the wrong memory.

How you can tell: The SSD uses an address that differs from the known set-up. It is not the known start address or mapping. The address map is needed to judge it.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Keep the capture tool's own file and its details. Make the error happen again in a controlled test. Change only one thing at a time. Compare with a run that is known to be good. Then compare the result with other proof. Use the list-creation settings, the computer's memory-transfer logs (DMA API) and the memory guard's fault log. Do not name the cause only because two things happened close in time.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Yes. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself (reported). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Evidence that shows which side is at fault. The SSD is at fault if it uses an old address, or reads the address wrongly. The computer is at fault if it set that start address, or freed or moved the buffer first. · Test that confirms it: the memory guard's fault log (IOMMU fault log).

M-062 Memory-guard address work makes reads and writes slower (IOMMU delay) Partly seen in the packets Memory place the SSD uses

Packets seen in the test recording

Error family: P17, one of the 27 ways an error shows on the wire. P17 means: the SSD reads or writes the wrong memory place. Proof from outside the recording: E01 means the Linux kernel log (dmesg). What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The rule book has no rule for this entry. Why it happens: The SSD's memory transfers can be delayed. Causes: mapping and unmapping very often, pressure on the address cache, or competition inside the platform's memory guard.

What goes wrong: A command is slowed by the address work of the memory guard (IOMMU). This means mapping, a miss in its address cache (IOTLB), or clearing old entries. It is not slowed by the SSD's storage or by the PCIe wire.

How you can tell: The recording shows gaps between exchanges. It does not show the memory guard's inside queues and counters. Match with the computer's notes (tracepoints).

How to fix it and prove the fix: Keep the capture tool's own file and its details. Make the error happen again in a controlled test. Change only one thing at a time. Compare with a run that is known to be good. Then compare the result with other proof. Use the memory guard's counters and faults, and notes on memory mapping (DMA-map tracepoints). Also compare with fixed buffers, and use the platform's speed counters. Write down the first thing that went wrong. Also write down the later signs of recovery. Do not name the cause only because two things happened close in time. First, collect the full setting. Note where the capture tool sat. Check that both directions were recorded. Note which command list (queue) and which part of the SSD (function) is involved. Note the time units. Note any mark that says the capture tool lost packets. Note the time window of the event. Then look for this error's own fingerprint. The recording shows gaps between exchanges. It does not show the memory guard's inside queues and counters. Match with the computer's notes (tracepoints). Match packets by command list and command number (CID). Or match them by sender id and request number (Requester ID and Tag). Use whichever fits. Split the measured time into its steps. Compare each step with a written limit, or with a normal run of the same work. If the start event, the expected answer or the deadline cannot be found, say UNKNOWN (cannot tell), not FAIL.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Nothing reports it. Things still work, but slower or weaker than they should (degraded). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Evidence that shows which side is at fault. The computer's platform. The memory guard maps and unmaps too often. Or its address cache has too much load (IOTLB pressure). · Test that confirms it: a test with the memory guard bypassed and then normal (passthrough A/B).

What the rule book says should happen: The rule book has no rule for this entry. Why it happens: Parts of the SSD can be treated differently. These are limits for each virtual part, or list and signal settings. Or memory guard separation (IOMMU isolation), or firmware scheduling.

What goes wrong: One virtual part (VF) or part of the SSD (function) stalls. The others keep going on the same SSD and wire.

How you can tell: Group packets by sender id or part, and by list. Hidden SSD limits for each part need the settings or SSD reports.

Compare each step with a written limit, or with a normal run of the same work. If the start event, the expected answer or the deadline cannot be found, say UNKNOWN (cannot tell), not FAIL.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Nothing reports it. Things still work, but slower or weaker than they should (degraded). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Evidence that shows which side is at fault. The computer is at fault if that part's doorbells, list set-up or signal set-up (MSI-X) are missing. · Test that confirms it: counters for each part (per-function counters).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The rule book has no rule for this entry. Why it happens: The file reader does not know about restart periods. Or it starts without the information on when lists were made or removed.

What goes wrong: A late done note (CQE) is paired with a new command. This is because list numbers and command numbers (queue IDs, CIDs) were used again after a restart.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Keep the capture tool's own file and its details. Make the error happen again in a controlled test. Change only one thing at a time. Compare with a run that is known to be good. Then compare the result with other proof. Track the device address and part (BDF, function) and the SSD's restart period. Also track the list number (QID), the command number (CID), each list's life and the computer's recovery logs. Write down the first thing that went wrong. Also write down the later signs of recovery. Do not name the cause only because two things happened close in time.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Nothing reports it. Everything looks like success (silent). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Evidence that shows which side is at fault. The test set-up or the study (a mistake made by the file reader). The SSD is at fault only for real done notes, sent after the restart, for commands from before it. · Test that confirms it: the computer's recovery log (host recovery log).

Compare each step with a written limit, or with a normal run of the same work. If the start event, the expected answer or the deadline cannot be found, say UNKNOWN (cannot tell), not FAIL.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Nothing reports it. A timer runs out because something expected never came (timer only). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Evidence that shows which side is at fault. The SSD is at fault only if fetched commands get no done note. · Test that confirms it: the computer's list state (host queue state).

This is fine product behaviour only if it is written down. · Test that confirms it: a test alongside other work and then alone (concurrent vs isolated).

Then look for this error's own fingerprint. The header flags and ids explain why two events may legally pass each other. Match packets by command list and command number (CID). Compare each step with a written limit, or with a normal run of the same work. If the start event, the expected answer or the deadline cannot be found, say UNKNOWN (cannot tell), not FAIL.

Error family: P08 and P12, two of the 27 ways an error shows on the wire. P08 means: the wire's start-up steps ran again, or its speed or width changed. P12 means: the wire went down while packets were still on their way. Proof from outside the recording: E07 means measurements of the power lines and side signal lines (oscilloscope). · Can the packets alone prove it? Partly. The packets show the timing or the order. Proof needs evidence from outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The rule book has no rule for this entry. Why it happens: The wire may become unsteady. Causes: the clock signal, the power lines, the signal booster or clock-request state, or sensitivity to signal margin.

What goes wrong: The wire's training repeats around load changes or power-state changes.

How you can tell: The wire keeps leaving its normal state (L0) for the recovery, detect or polling steps. This lines up with load or power changes.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Keep the capture tool's own file and its details. Make the error happen again in a controlled test. Change only one thing at a time. Compare with a run that is known to be good. Then compare the result with other proof. Use oscilloscope and logic recordings taken at the same time, and power controller logs. Also use root-port counters and a control run with fixed power. Write down the first thing that went wrong. Also write down the later signs of recovery. Do not name the cause only because two things happened close in time. First, collect the full setting. Note where the capture tool sat. Check that both directions were recorded. Note which command list (queue) and which part of the SSD (function) is involved. Note the time units. Note any mark that says the capture tool lost packets. Note the time window of the event. Then look for this error's own fingerprint. The wire keeps leaving its normal state (L0) for the recovery, detect or polling steps. This lines up with load or power changes. Match packets by command list and command number (CID). Or match them by sender id and request number (Requester ID and Tag). Use whichever fits. Split the measured time into its steps. Compare each step with a written limit, or with a normal run of the same work. If the start event, the expected answer or the deadline cannot be found, say UNKNOWN (cannot tell), not FAIL.

Does the SSD or computer report it? Yes. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself (reported). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Evidence that shows which side is at fault. The computer's platform is at fault when the episodes have no errors and line up with power or clock events. Its parts are the clock signal, power lines, signal booster or clock-request state. The wire is at fault when broken check numbers in both directions come first. · Test that confirms it: an oscilloscope or logic recording of the power lines and side signals (outside proof E07).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The rule book has no rule for this entry. Why it happens: Some steps add cost at a cold start. Examples: set-up done only when first needed (lazy initialization), storage getting ready and warming up the map cache. Others are scanning storage areas and power changes.

What goes wrong: The first few commands are slow compared with later, steady work.

How you can tell: The recording shows the first visible command and its done note. It may miss earlier start-up or driver events.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Keep the capture tool's own file and its details. Make the error happen again in a controlled test. Change only one thing at a time. Compare with a run that is known to be good. Then compare the result with other proof. Record the times of power and restart, and of the wire's normal state (L0). Also record device search, driver start, ready (CSTS.RDY), list creation and the first read or write. Write down the first thing that went wrong. Also write down the later signs of recovery. Do not name the cause only because two things happened close in time. First, collect the full setting. Note where the capture tool sat. Check that both directions were recorded. Note which command list (queue) and which part of the SSD (function) is involved. Note the time units. Note any mark that says the capture tool lost packets. Note the time window of the event. Then look for this error's own fingerprint. The recording shows the first visible command and its done note. It may miss earlier start-up or driver events. Match packets by command list and command number (CID). Or match them by sender id and request number (Requester ID and Tag). Use whichever fits. Split the measured time into its steps. Compare each step with a written limit, or with a normal run of the same work. If the start event, the expected answer or the deadline cannot be found, say UNKNOWN (cannot tell), not FAIL.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Nothing reports it. Things still work, but slower or weaker than they should (degraded). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Evidence that shows which side is at fault. The SSD is at fault if the fetch is quick but the done note is late. The computer is at fault if the delay comes before the first doorbell (storage-area scan, driver set-up). · Test that confirms it: time a cold start (cold-start timing).

Note any mark that says the capture tool lost packets. Note the time window of the event. Then look for this error's own fingerprint. Settings exchanges may be visible. Software registration is not in the recording. Match packets by command list and command number (CID). Or match them by sender id and request number (Requester ID and Tag). Use whichever fits. Split the measured time into its steps. Compare each step with a written limit, or with a normal run of the same work. If the start event, the expected answer or the deadline cannot be found, say UNKNOWN (cannot tell), not FAIL.

What the rule book says should happen: The rule book has no rule for this entry. Why it happens: Some things create a long tail of very slow answers. Examples: clean-up work (GC), bursts of send-agains, heating cycles, restarts and waiting in line.

What goes wrong: The average looks healthy. But rare, extreme pauses break the promised service level (SLA).

A percentile such as p99 is the time that 99 out of 100 commands stay under. Line up the slow ones with events. Make sure there are enough samples for the extreme percentiles. Write down the first thing that went wrong. Also write down the later signs of recovery. Do not name the cause only because two things happened close in time. First, collect the full setting. Note any mark that says the capture tool lost packets. Note the time window of the event. Then look for this error's own fingerprint. A chart of each command's time has slow ones hidden by the average or the middle value (mean, median). Match packets by command list and command number (CID). Or match them by sender id and request number (Requester ID and Tag). Use whichever fits. Split the measured time into its steps. Compare each step with a written limit, or with a normal run of the same work. If the start event, the expected answer or the deadline cannot be found, say UNKNOWN (cannot tell), not FAIL.

Error family: P27, one of the 27 ways an error shows on the wire. P27 means: signs that the recording itself is incomplete, so a check must not say FAIL. Proof from outside the recording: E05 means a trace of the computer's own work steps (blktrace, NVMe tracepoints). · Can the packets alone prove it? Partly. The packets show the timing or the order. Proof needs evidence from outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The rule book has no rule for this entry. Why it happens: Some settings leave out important parts. Trigger settings, buffer size or stop rules can leave out list set-up, wire training or the recovery after the error.

What goes wrong: The recording starts in the middle of a command. Or it ends before the effects of the failure are visible.

How you can tell: The setting at the start is unknown. Command numbers or lists are not set up in the recording. Or exchanges are still open at the end of the file.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Keep the capture tool's own file and its details. Make the error happen again in a controlled test. Change only one thing at a time. Compare with a run that is known to be good. Then compare the result with other proof. Use the capture details and a longer buffer before and after the trigger. Also use why the capture tool stopped, and the computer's start and stop times. Write down the first thing that went wrong. Also write down the later signs of recovery. Do not name the cause only because two things happened close in time. First, collect the full setting. Note where the capture tool sat. Check that both directions were recorded. Note which command list (queue) and which part of the SSD (function) is involved. Note the time units. Note any mark that says the capture tool lost packets. Note the time window of the event. Then look for this error's own fingerprint. The setting at the start is unknown. Command numbers or lists are not set up in the recording. Or exchanges are still open at the end of the file. Match packets by command list and command number (CID). Or match them by sender id and request number (Requester ID and Tag). Use whichever fits. Split the measured time into its steps. Compare each step with a written limit, or with a normal run of the same work. If the start event, the expected answer or the deadline cannot be found, say UNKNOWN (cannot tell), not FAIL.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Nothing reports it. Everything looks like success (silent). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Evidence that shows which side is at fault. The capture tool and its capture settings. · Test that confirms it: record again with a wider window (re-capture with wider window).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The rule book has no rule for this entry. Why it happens: The numbers mix different end points. These are power good, firmware, wire up, device search, SSD ready and user programs.

Do not name the cause only because two things happened close in time. First, collect the full setting. Note where the capture tool sat. Check that both directions were recorded. Note which command list (queue) and which part of the SSD (function) is involved. Note the time units. Note any mark that says the capture tool lost packets. Note the time window of the event. Then look for this error's own fingerprint. The recording only fixes events on the recorded wire. Without a mark, it cannot fix power-on or the firmware start. Match packets by command list and command number (CID). Or match them by sender id and request number (Requester ID and Tag). Use whichever fits. Split the measured time into its steps. Compare each step with a written limit, or with a normal run of the same work. If the start event, the expected answer or the deadline cannot be found, say UNKNOWN (cannot tell), not FAIL.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Nothing reports it. Things still work, but slower or weaker than they should (degraded). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Evidence that shows which side is at fault. Match packets by command list and command number (CID). Or match them by sender id and request number (Requester ID and Tag). Use whichever fits. Split the measured time into its steps. Compare each step with a written limit, or with a normal run of the same work. If the start event, the expected answer or the deadline cannot be found, say UNKNOWN (cannot tell), not FAIL.

What the rule book says should happen: The rule book has no rule for this entry. Why it happens: A restart (hot reset) or wire drop can cut off open work. The expected behaviour is different from a timeout on a wire that stays up.

Count a timeout before a restart apart from an answer cut off by the restart. Write down the first thing that went wrong. Also write down the later signs of recovery. Does the SSD or computer report it? Yes. The SSD or the computer reports this error itself (reported). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Evidence that shows which side is at fault. The test set-up (the checker ignores restart periods) when the missing answer was cut off by the restart. M-094 The computer's task scheduling adds delay while the wire is idle Not seen in the packets Speed and timing numbers

The rows here only show the setting around it. The proof is outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The rule book has no rule for this entry. Why it happens: An overloaded processor, or the choice of processor for signals (IRQ affinity), delays the software. So can idle states, memory placement (NUMA) or tasks waiting on locks.

What goes wrong: The SSD has finished, or is ready. But the computer's task for sending commands or handling done notes is not run quickly.

How you can tell: The recording alone cannot prove it or rule it out. The recording shows idle gaps or on-time done notes. But the computer's own done time is late.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Keep the capture tool's own file and its details. Make the error happen again in a controlled test. Change only one thing at a time. Compare with a run that is known to be good. Then compare the result with other proof. Use scheduler traces (perf, ftrace, eBPF) and which processor gets the signals (IRQ affinity). Also use processor use, memory placement (NUMA) and program time stamps. Write down the first thing that went wrong. Also write down the later signs of recovery. Do not name the cause only because two things happened close in time.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Nothing reports it. Things still work, but slower or weaker than they should (degraded). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Evidence that shows which side is at fault. The computer's software (task scheduling, which processor gets the signals, idle states). The SSD is at fault only if the done note itself is late. · Test that confirms it: a trace of the task scheduler (scheduler trace).

M-095 Too many done signals overload the computer (interrupt storm) Partly seen in the packets Error messages on the wire (AER)

Packet=394205 | Link Dir=Downstream | DLLP Type=ACK | Time Stamp=0195.061951660250s | Time Delta=214.880 ns | AckNak Seq Num=3818

Error family: P10, one of the 27 ways an error shows on the wire. P10 means: error messages sent on the wire (ERR_COR, ERR_NONFATAL, ERR_FATAL). What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The rule book has no rule for this entry. Why it happens: All processor time can be used up. Causes: bad signal grouping, shared signal numbers, false signals or the choice of processor. So can very many tiny reads and writes.

What goes wrong: Many signals use up processor time. They delay sending commands and handling done notes.

How you can tell: Signal packets (MSI/MSI-X) and done notes are visible. How long the signal handler runs, and its effect on the processor, are not in the recording.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Keep the capture tool's own file and its details. Make the error happen again in a controlled test. Change only one thing at a time. Compare with a run that is known to be good. Then compare the result with other proof. Use counts for each signal number, signal-handler time and the signal count file (/proc/interrupts). Also use driver settings and a scheduler trace. Write down the first thing that went wrong. Also write down the later signs of recovery. Do not name the cause only because two things happened close in time.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Nothing reports it. Things still work, but slower or weaker than they should (degraded). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Evidence that shows which side is at fault. The computer is at fault when signals come with tiny batches of done notes and late head doorbells. Causes: signal grouping, which processor gets them, shared signal numbers. The SSD is at fault when it sends signals (MSI-X) with no new done notes, which are spurious. It is also at fault if it sends a storm of error messages (ERR_*). That case is error type X-26 in the error list. · Test that confirms it: count the signals (interrupt counts).

Proof from outside the recording: E05 means a trace of the computer's own work steps (blktrace, NVMe tracepoints). · Can the packets alone prove it? No. It cannot be seen on this wire. The rows here only show the setting around it. The proof is outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The rule book has no rule for this entry. Why it happens: A path to memory or signals on another processor socket adds cost on the computer side. So does keeping memory in step across sockets (coherency).

What goes wrong: Speed changes with which processor runs the work and where the list memory sits. It also changes with which processor gets the signals. The PCIe behaviour stays about the same.

How you can tell: The recording alone cannot prove it or rule it out. Wire recordings look alike even though the end-to-end times differ.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Keep the capture tool's own file and its details. Make the error happen again in a controlled test. Change only one thing at a time. Compare with a run that is known to be good. Then compare the result with other proof. Run a controlled test that fixes which processor and memory are used. Also use which processor gets the signals and the memory layout (NUMA). Measure submit to doorbell, and done note to handler. Write down the first thing that went wrong. Also write down the later signs of recovery. Do not name the cause only because two things happened close in time.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Nothing reports it. Things still work, but slower or weaker than they should (degraded). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Evidence that shows which side is at fault. The computer's software or the layout of the platform. · Test that confirms it: a test with different placements (placement A/B).

M-097 Frequent log reads change the test they measure (telemetry polling) Partly seen in the packets Speed and timing numbers

Packets seen in the test recording

Error family: P22, one of the 27 ways an error shows on the wire. P22 means: speed and slow-answer numbers worked out from the recording. Proof from outside the recording: E05 means a trace of the computer's own work steps (blktrace, NVMe tracepoints). · Can the packets alone prove it? Partly. The packets show the timing or the order. Proof needs evidence from outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The rule book has no rule for this entry. Why it happens: What is measured gets changed. Causes: the cost of the reads, firmware doing one thing at a time, large log transfers or shared resources.

What goes wrong: Frequent log, health (SMART) or report commands add management traffic. They may make the slowest answers slower.

How you can tell: Bursts of management and report traffic line up with slow-answer spikes in the recording.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Keep the capture tool's own file and its details. Make the error happen again in a controlled test. Change only one thing at a time. Compare with a run that is known to be good. Then compare the result with other proof. Compare with no reads, few reads and many reads. Use command times and how busy the SSD and the computer are. Write down the first thing that went wrong. Also write down the later signs of recovery. Do not name the cause only because two things happened close in time. First, collect the full setting. Note where the capture tool sat. Check that both directions were recorded. Note which command list (queue) and which part of the SSD (function) is involved. Note the time units. Note any mark that says the capture tool lost packets. Note the time window of the event. Then look for this error's own fingerprint. Bursts of management and report traffic line up with slow-answer spikes in the recording. Match packets by command list and command number (CID). Or match them by sender id and request number (Requester ID and Tag). Use whichever fits. Split the measured time into its steps. Compare each step with a written limit, or with a normal run of the same work. If the start event, the expected answer or the deadline cannot be found, say UNKNOWN (cannot tell), not FAIL.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Nothing reports it. Things still work, but slower or weaker than they should (degraded). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Evidence that shows which side is at fault. The test set-up or the measuring tools (the tool that keeps reading). The SSD firmware doing such work one at a time can add to it. · Test that confirms it: a test with a low and then a high read rate (poll rate A/B).

M-098 Regular SSD upkeep work makes gaps in done notes (firmware maintenance) Partly seen in the packets Speed and timing numbers

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 1911296: 9 ms gaps in done notes while commands are open (clean-up or upkeep work, GC / maintenance).

Packet=1911296 | Link Dir=Upstream | DLLP Type=ACK | Time Stamp=1823.774912620500s | Time Delta=3.456 us | AckNak Seq Num=204

Error family: P22, one of the 27 ways an error shows on the wire. P22 means: speed and slow-answer numbers worked out from the recording. Proof from outside the recording: E01 means the Linux kernel log (dmesg). E03 means the SSD's own logs and settings (nvme-cli). · Can the packets alone prove it? Partly. The packets show the timing or the order. Proof needs evidence from outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The rule book has no rule for this entry. Why it happens: Some inside work uses the SSD's resources. Examples: upkeep work, saving the map and spreading wear. Others are report counters rolling over and clean-up work (GC).

What goes wrong: Pauses repeat at a steady rhythm, even though the wire follows the rules.

How you can tell: The time series shows regular gaps in command service. It does not show the inside task itself.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Keep the capture tool's own file and its details. Make the error happen again in a controlled test. Change only one thing at a time. Compare with a run that is known to be good. Then compare the result with other proof. Use reports and maker logs, the work pattern, temperature, wear state and controlled idle and write tests. Call the cause a guess until it is confirmed. Write down the first thing that went wrong. Also write down the later signs of recovery. Do not name the cause only because two things happened close in time. First, collect the full setting. Note where the capture tool sat. Check that both directions were recorded. Note which command list (queue) and which part of the SSD (function) is involved. Note the time units. Note any mark that says the capture tool lost packets. Note the time window of the event. Then look for this error's own fingerprint. The time series shows regular gaps in command service. It does not show the inside task itself. Match packets by command list and command number (CID). Or match them by sender id and request number (Requester ID and Tag). Use whichever fits. Split the measured time into its steps. Compare each step with a written limit, or with a normal run of the same work. If the start event, the expected answer or the deadline cannot be found, say UNKNOWN (cannot tell), not FAIL.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Nothing reports it. Things still work, but slower or weaker than they should (degraded). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Evidence that shows which side is at fault. The SSD firmware's upkeep work, when the wire is clean and the computer keeps sending. · Test that confirms it: the SSD's own slow-command monitor or reports (drive-side latency monitor / telemetry).

M-099 The part that reports an error is wrongly blamed for causing it Partly seen in the packets Error messages on the wire (AER)

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 396916: the root port sends a bad packet.

Packet=396916 | Link Dir=Downstream | TLP Type=MWr(32) | PSN=741 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=000:00:0 | Address=FCE0200C | Length=1 | DATA=4 B | Time Stamp=0195.062222499500s | Time Delta=104.120 ns | LCRC=0x1A91742F (Bad)

Packet 396919: the SSD is the one that reports it, not the cause.

Packet=396919 | Link Dir=Upstream | TLP Type=Msg | PSN=907 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=002:00:0 | Length=0 | Time Stamp=0195.062222899500s | Time Delta=104.000 ns | LCRC=0xAC3A47EF

Error family: P10, one of the 27 ways an error shows on the wire. P10 means: error messages sent on the wire (ERR_COR, ERR_NONFATAL, ERR_FATAL). Proof from outside the recording: E08 means a second capture tool, switch counters, or logs from other parts. · Can the packets alone prove it? Yes. The checker marks an odd value or odd order in this table file. Here it is a check number marked broken, then the same packet number sent again (lcrc_flagged_bad, tlp_replayed_same_psn).

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The rule book has no rule for this entry. Why it happens: Error and shutdown status (AER/DPC) is kept by each reporting part. The reporter, the affected exchange and the starting side can all be different.

What goes wrong: An error is blamed on the SSD. But a switch or root port owns the status or the shutdown.

How you can tell: The recording shows an error message. But the setting log names a different device address (BDF) or port.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Keep the capture tool's own file and its details. Make the error happen again in a controlled test. Change only one thing at a time. Compare with a run that is known to be good. Then compare the result with other proof. Use the full map of connected parts and the status and header log of each port. Also use the kernel's error and shutdown records (AER/DPC), and a recording nearer the computer. Write down the first thing that went wrong. Also write down the later signs of recovery. Do not name the cause only because two things happened close in time. First, collect the full setting. Note where the capture tool sat. Check that both directions were recorded. Note which command list (queue) and which part of the SSD (function) is involved. Note the time units. Note any mark that says the capture tool lost packets. Note the time window of the event. Then look for this error's own fingerprint. The recording shows an error message. But the setting log names a different device address (BDF) or port. Match packets by command list and command number (CID). Or match them by sender id and request number (Requester ID and Tag). Use whichever fits. Split the measured time into its steps. Compare each step with a written limit, or with a normal run of the same work. If the start event, the expected answer or the deadline cannot be found, say UNKNOWN (cannot tell), not FAIL.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Nothing reports it. Everything looks like success (silent). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Evidence that shows which side is at fault. Decided by where the packet that set it off came from. The platform or channel is at fault when the computer sent it (Downstream). The SSD is at fault when the SSD sent it (Upstream), or when it came from inside the SSD. · Test that confirms it: the map of connected parts and the status of each port (topology and per-port status).

M-100 Wire is back up, but the command lists never start again (DL_Active) Partly seen in the packets SSD main settings and ready state

Packets seen in the test recording

Packet 480146: a doorbell after wire recovery. The SSD is still switched off, so no command is fetched.

Packet=480146 | Link Dir=Downstream | TLP Type=MWr(32) | PSN=12 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=000:00:0 | Address=FCE01008 | Length=1 | DATA=4 B | Time Stamp=0340.660269112870s | Time Delta=128.500 ns | LCRC=0x714E59C8

Packet 480150: a doorbell after wire recovery. The SSD is still switched off, so no command is fetched.

Packet=480150 | Link Dir=Downstream | TLP Type=MWr(32) | PSN=13 | Tag=0 | RequesterID=000:00:0 | Address=FCE01010 | Length=1 | DATA=4 B | Time Stamp=0340.661269112870s | Time Delta=100.130 ns | LCRC=0xA6784EC8

Error family: P13, one of the 27 ways an error shows on the wire. P13 means: timing of the SSD's main settings: switch on, ready, restart, shut down, fatal error. Proof from outside the recording: E01 means the Linux kernel log (dmesg). E03 means the SSD's own logs and settings (nvme-cli). · Can the packets alone prove it? Partly. The packets show the timing or the order. Proof needs evidence from outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The rule book has no rule for this entry. Why it happens: The lists were lost, the driver's recovery is incomplete, or the firmware is stuck. Or the ready step (CSTS.RDY) or the management path failed after the wire came back.

What goes wrong: The wire's lower layers are active again. But the SSD's readiness or its list service has not recovered.

How you can tell: Wire training succeeds. Then there is no NVMe list traffic, or only settings reads.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Keep the capture tool's own file and its details. Make the error happen again in a controlled test. Change only one thing at a time. Compare with a run that is known to be good. Then compare the result with other proof. Use the kernel recovery logs, reads of the SSD's state and a trace of list creation. Also mark the first successful read or write. Write down the first thing that went wrong. Also write down the later signs of recovery. Do not name the cause only because two things happened close in time. First, collect the full setting. Note where the capture tool sat. Check that both directions were recorded. Note which command list (queue) and which part of the SSD (function) is involved. Note the time units. Note any mark that says the capture tool lost packets. Note the time window of the event. Then look for this error's own fingerprint. Wire training succeeds. Then there is no NVMe list traffic, or only settings reads. Match packets by command list and command number (CID). Or match them by sender id and request number (Requester ID and Tag). Use whichever fits. Split the measured time into its steps. Compare each step with a written limit, or with a normal run of the same work. If the start event, the expected answer or the deadline cannot be found, say UNKNOWN (cannot tell), not FAIL.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Nothing reports it. A timer runs out because something expected never came (timer only). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Evidence that shows which side is at fault. The computer is at fault in one case. After the wire is active (DL_Active), only settings reads or doorbells happen. There are no set-up writes (CC.EN, AQA, ASQ, ACQ). The SSD is at fault if the computer switches it on (CC.EN=1) and ready (RDY) never reads 1. It is also at fault if the first management command gets no done note. · Test that confirms it: the kernel log.

M-101 A pass or fail is impossible because needed fields are missing Not seen in the packets Problems with the recording itself

Packets seen in the test recording

Error family: P27, one of the 27 ways an error shows on the wire. P27 means: signs that the recording itself is incomplete, so a check must not say FAIL. Proof from outside the recording: E02 means a copy of the SSD's settings area (lspci). E03 means the SSD's own logs and settings (nvme-cli). · Can the packets alone prove it? No. It cannot be seen on this wire. The rows here only show the setting around it. The proof is outside the recording.

What the rule book says, what goes wrong, and how to prove it

What the rule book says should happen: The rule book has no rule for this entry. Why it happens: Too little is left to judge the rule. Causes: a limited export, a decoder summary, missing raw packets or an unknown clock source.

What goes wrong: The exported recording lacks time stamps, request numbers, list state, mode or settings, or capture status. These are needed to judge a rule.

How you can tell: The recording alone cannot prove it or rule it out. A rough time exists. But the timer's start, what counts as finished, or whether the recording is complete cannot be proven.

How to fix it and prove the fix: Keep the capture tool's own file and its details. Make the error happen again in a controlled test. Change only one thing at a time. Compare with a run that is known to be good. Then compare the result with other proof. Use a field checklist. Attach the capture tool's own file, a snapshot of abilities and settings, and the clock details. Give UNKNOWN and list the missing fields. Write down the first thing that went wrong. Also write down the later signs of recovery. Do not name the cause only because two things happened close in time. First, collect the full setting. Note where the capture tool sat. Check that both directions were recorded. Note which command list (queue) and which part of the SSD (function) is involved. Note the time units. Note any mark that says the capture tool lost packets. Note the time window of the event. Then look for this error's own fingerprint. A rough time exists. But the timer's start, what counts as finished, or whether the recording is complete cannot be proven. Match packets by command list and command number (CID). Or match them by sender id and request number (Requester ID and Tag). Use whichever fits. Split the measured time into its steps. Compare each step with a written limit, or with a normal run of the same work. If the start event, the expected answer or the deadline cannot be found, say UNKNOWN (cannot tell), not FAIL.

Does the SSD or computer report it? No. Nothing reports it. Everything looks like success (silent). · What else to collect when the packets are not enough: Evidence that shows which side is at fault. The test set-up or the export. · Test that confirms it: a field checklist.

Details saved with every run, decision, procedure and test (metadata)

Who: the person must type their name when a recording is checked. It is filled in as "Your name" on every stage-2 decision. Both go into the knowledge base. When: every event carries a date and time. A procedure entry shows when it was proposed and when the lab last made the error happen with it. It also shows when and by whom it was approved, and who last judged it. Which device: the checker reads the model number, serial number and firmware version from the packets. They come from the SSD's answer to the Identify Controller command (NVMe Base Specification, Identify Controller data structure). It reads the maker and device numbers (Vendor ID and Device ID) from the SSD's settings area (PCIe configuration header). The person may type a device name instead. Procedures and repeat tests are saved per device model, and the test id carries the device. Why: the same error type needs its own test on each drive.
